<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of a "universal language," moving from the mechanics of sound to the philosophical and mathematical necessity of naming every individual element in the universe.</meta>

# On the Voice.

The same principle applies to the fur of all animals and the hair of men. Each individual hair requires its own specific name to be distinguished from the others; thus, if a man has 100,000 hairs on his head and another 100,000 hairs on the rest of his body, it would require 200,000 names or terms to name them all.

Now, what I have said regarding hair should be understood for all parts of the body, for all <term>individuals</term><note>In 17th-century philosophy, an "individual" refers to a single, unique existing thing (like a specific dog or a specific stone) as opposed to a general species (like "dogs" or "stones").</note>, and for their constituent parts. Because the nature of all these things is different, they can only be explained by different names. Such names are lacking in every language and among every nation in the world, which are instead forced to use general terms to signify specific, individual things.

As for the number of <term>dictions</term><note>Meaning unique words or combinations of sounds.</note> that can be formed from the 10 vowels and 30 consonants which I discussed in the 48th proposition—especially when one is allowed to create words from 30 consonants and 20 vowels—it is marvelously vast. This system encompasses a scale of 73 characters <note>The author is discussing the "length" of a number in digits. He is comparing the number of possible words to the number of grains of sand in the universe.</note>. Now, it takes only 46 characters to express the number of grains of sand that would fill the entire solidity of the firmament—that is, the entire world known to us—as I demonstrated regarding the first verse of Genesis in my 16th argument. From this, it is easy to conclude that every individual thing in nature can have a specific name in the universal language. This can be achieved according to the precepts and rules I provided in the 47th and 48th propositions and elsewhere, provided that these things do not exceed the number of grains of sand by more than a number composed of 73 characters exceeds one of 46. Since the 47th character makes this latter number ten times larger, and the 48th and 49th characters increase it a hundredfold and a thousandfold, it is evident that this language has one hundred thousand times more words than there would be grains of sand in the entire world, and even in a hundred million worlds larger than ours. Consequently, it has far more words than there are men and animals in the world, even if they had as many hairs as there would be grains of sand in all those worlds.

And if it is said that God can always produce new individuals unto infinity, whose number will surpass that of the aforementioned words, I reply likewise that one can always add new words by increasing the number of their letters.

I respond in the second place, to resolve the other part of the proposition, that one must have several names for each individual if one wishes to express all its properties. However, because we cannot know them all—for several reasons that could be offered—it is sufficient to have as many names or different terms as there are different properties we recognize within them.

Here it must be noted that those who believe that the different names by which various nations have called species signify the different properties they envisioned in those species have no foundation other than their imagination, or some imaginary relationship to the <term>primitive language</term><note>The "primitive language" usually refers to the "Adamic" language, which many Renaissance scholars believed was a perfect language spoken by Adam that directly reflected the essence of things.</note>. For if one takes the names that the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins gave to water, fire, and other things, one will not find that some had better reasons than others; rather, they simply had the same thoughts regarding the same properties, which they then sought to express in their own languages.

Nevertheless, if one takes the liberty of inventing a universal language...

# Book One

composed of all possible words, whose roots, or radical words <term>primitive words from which others are derived</term>, were in a sufficiently large number to provide different names for each property of every species, or of every individual; and assuming that Adam (whom Christians and Jews recognize as the first man) had perfect knowledge of all the sciences, and of the properties of each thing, one can imagine that he gave as many names to each species—for example, to each animal—as he recognized different properties within it. Consequently, the different words across all languages that signify the same thing would be derived from the names he invented and established from the beginning of the world, or during the span of nine hundred and thirty years <note>The lifespan of Adam according to Genesis 5:5</note> that he lived.

To this one might add that he gave at least a thousand names to each species in order to derive from them all the different names that all the nations of the earth give to the said species, in each of which Adam could have observed a thousand different properties, whether absolute or relative. For one could give as many different names to water as there are other bodies in nature to which it can be compared, whether in hardness or in weight; for example, if one compares it to gold, it would need to be given a name that explains that it is nineteen times lighter than the said gold, and other names must be composed to express how much more or less light or heavy it is than all other bodies, about which the same could be said as of water. From this it follows that as many different words would be required to signify the relative properties of each body as there are different things in nature.

But because we have no testimony of this assigning of names, and because Adam could not have pronounced even a hundredth part of these names in all the time he lived—and indeed, he would not have pronounced even a hundredth part of them yet, even if he had lived until the present day and had assigned a hundred thousand names every minute of the hour—it is evident that he did not find all the words, nor did he assign all the names that could serve to explain all the properties of species and individuals.

This can be confirmed by the fewness of words in the Hebrew language, which are so vague and so general that Holy Scripture often uses the same word to signify very different things. From this, one can conclude the simplicity of the first inhabitants of the earth, who, needing only a small number of things, invented only a small number of terms. Perhaps they judged that the best language of all possible ones is the shortest, and the one that requires the fewest words; just as mathematicians have judged that the best way to use weights is to take those that follow a triple progression <note>A mathematical sequence (1, 3, 9, 27, 81, 243, 729, 2187) used in balance scales to measure any value with the minimum number of physical weights</note> from one pound up to 2,187 pounds, even though one only has eight kinds of weights, the proof of which depends on Mechanics.

Indeed, all things are usually more excellent the more simple they are, as the theologians teach, who place only one idea, or a single act of knowledge, in God, by which He knows and names all things. They also hold that the most excellent Angels have a smaller number of ideas, or species, which serve them as names to express the nature and properties of each thing.

<meta>This page continues the author’s investigation into the nature of language and sound, moving from the mathematical potential of a limited vocabulary to the concept of a "natural language" where sounds physically represent their meanings.</meta>

### On the Voice.

One can similarly prove that the excellence of a language consists in few <term>words</term> <note>original: "dictions"</note> through the practice of <term>Arithmetic</term> and <term>Algebra</term>, which use only 10 different characters to express everything within their power and scope. 
And if one could express all the things we need with 10 words, or <term>terms</term>, or with as many vocables as there are letters in the alphabet, one could conclude that this language would be the simplest of all those that have existed until now; and because I have shown in another place that ten things can be varied a thousand million times, it follows that one can express a thousand million things with ten vocables, or even with ten letters, or characters.

## PROPOSITION 50.

*To determine if the sounds of the voice, that is to say the <term>vowels</term>, the <term>consonants</term>, the <term>syllables</term>, and the <term>words</term> can have such an analogy and such a relationship with the things signified, that one could form a natural language.*

If letters signify something naturally when they are pronounced or written, it seems that one could compose vocables from them to make a natural language, since languages are composed of <term>words</term>, and words of letters, as if from their elements. Now, many have remarked that there are letters suited for expressing sweetness and roughness, and other qualities of bodies, actions, and passions: for the two vowels *a* and *o* are suited to signify that which is great and full. Because *a* is pronounced with a wide opening of the mouth, it signifies open things, and the actions used to open and to begin some work. From this it comes that Virgil began his *Aeneid* with this word *Arma* <note>Latin: "Arms" or "Weapons"</note>, and that he judged that this vowel signifies the love that opens the hearts of lovers to pour themselves into one another, as one sees in these words, *Phyllis, [his] love above all others* <note>original: "Phillida amor ante alias"</note>, in which there are five *a*’s following one another.

As for the vowel *e*, it signifies slender and subtle things, and is suited to express mourning and pain, because the mouth narrows in pronouncing it; from this it comes that Virgil uses this letter several times in describing misery:
> *Alas, what land, what seas can now receive me in my misery, etc.* <note>original: "Heu quæ me miferum tellus, quæ me æquora poffunt, Accipere, &c."</note> 
It is also suited to represent an echo, as one sees in these words: *the hills resound with the cry* <note>original: "colles clamore refultant"</note>.

The vowel *i* signifies very thin and very small things; from this comes the word *minime* <note>Latin: "least" or "very small"</note>, which has two *i*'s and one *e*, and which consequently is more suited to signify humility than any other word. It also expresses that which is penetrating like a lightning bolt:
> *She herself cast Jove's swift fire from the clouds.* <note>original: "Ipfe Iouis rapidum iaculata è nubibus ignem."</note>
For that which is slender penetrates more easily, as does the rain:
> *They let in the hostile rain and the seams gape open.* <note>original: "Accipiunt inimicum imbrem riuique fatifcunt."</note>

The vowel *o* serves to express great passions, when its pronunciation is long, as happens in these words: *O my country! O the times! O the customs!* <note>original: "O patria! ô tempora! ô mores!"</note> and

The vowel *u* signifies obscure and hidden things, following the nature of its pronunciation. I will leave aside many other things that could be said about vowels—of which I have already spoken elsewhere—to add something about consonants. These are also suited to express the things they represent or with which they have a relationship. For example, *f* is suited to represent wind and fire; from this comes the Latin word *flo* <note>original: "flo"; meaning "I blow" or "I breathe"</note> and several other similar terms.

The letter *s*, and *x* (which is composed of *c* and *s*), are suited to signify things that have a certain kind of harshness, such as winds and tempests, particularly when *s* is added to *r*, as in the word *stridor* <note>original: "stridor"; meaning a creaking, whistling, or hissing sound</note>. The letter *l* <note>The OCR reads 'r' here, but the context of "soft and liquid" indicates the author is discussing the letter 'l'.</note> signifies humble, soft, and liquid things, whereas *r* signifies harsh, rough, hard, and rugged things, as well as vehement and impetuous actions; it is called the "canine letter" <note>The letter 'r' was called the *littera canina* because its trilled sound resembles a dog growling.</note>.

*m* signifies that which is large, such as Machines and many other similar things. From this it follows that the Romans called it *magnum* <note>original: "magnum"; meaning "great" or "large"</note>, and that the Poets do not pronounce this letter at all <note>A reference to "elision" in Latin poetry, where a final 'm' is silenced before a vowel.</note> because it is harsh, as one sees in these words: *a monster, horrendous, and huge* <note>original: "monstrum horrendum ingens"; a famous line from Virgil’s Aeneid describing the Cyclops.</note>.

*n* has a contrary significance, for it is suited to express things that are black, hidden, and obscure. I leave aside the other letters, about which anyone can easily speak from their own experience, for their pronunciation clearly shows what they are suited for.

As for syllables and words composed of vowels and consonants that follow one another in such a way that they are pronounced softly and easily, they are suited to express sweet, even, and polished things. Others, whose pronunciation is harsh and difficult, are suited to signify hard and troublesome things. Now, it is enough to have touched upon this difficulty, because Grammarians and Rhetoricians treat it at greater length, as one can see in the works of Quintilian, Scaliger in the 4th book of his *Poetics*, Lipsius, Sturmius, Keckermann, Vossius, and several others <note>These were prominent 16th and 17th-century scholars of rhetoric, linguistics, and philosophy.</note>. One can also consider the verses which Poets have used to represent vividly and naturally what they have described, such as when Virgil represents a running horse:

> *The hoof shakes the crumbling field with a four-footed sound.* <note>original: "Quadrupedante putrem sonitu quatit ungula campum"; a famous example of onomatopoeia from Virgil's Aeneid where the rhythm of the dactylic hexameter mimics the galloping of a horse.</note>

And as Homer represents a breaking sword in the 3rd book of the *Iliad*:

> *The arrow hissed as it leapt from the bowstring.* <note>original: "Τετρίγη δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ὀϊστὸς ἀπὸ νευρῆφιν ὀρούσας"; The author cites this as a breaking sword, though the Greek text describes the whizzing or screeching sound of an arrow.</note>

Scaliger recorded the most beautiful verses of Virgil and Homer in the 5th book of his *Poetics*, where he compares them both together, from which one can draw enlightenment regarding the "natural language," if such a thing is possible.

If external objects affected the eye and the other senses so much that we felt certain movements of the imagination which made us move the tongue and the other parts used for the voice—and which made us push air from the lungs in different ways to express the different impressions of everything that affects us—and if everyone experienced these same movements and affections within themselves when touched equally by objects, we would have words that signified things naturally. From these, one could compose a natural language; but no one witnesses such feelings. When one looks at the Sun and the Stars, one does not perceive that the imagination...

## On the Voice.

...[that the imagination] provides specific movements of the tongue to form perceived words. 

This is why I do not believe there is any natural language, unless one argues that words pronounced slowly and having many syllables naturally signify long and slow things; and that what I have said about letters is sufficient to serve as the foundation for a natural language, for which it would be easy to create a Grammar and a Dictionary if one wished to put it into use. For all the words composed of the two vowels *a* and *o* and the stronger-sounding consonants would be intended to express great, high, and elevated things; and those composed of the vowels *e*, *i*, and *u* would signify actions and other low and humble things. <note>The author is discussing "phonetic symbolism," the idea that specific sounds inherently carry certain meanings—a popular topic in 17th-century linguistics.</note>

### COROLLARY.

If one wishes to know the properties of vowels and consonants, one must consult the book Scaliger wrote on the causes of the Latin language <note>original: *De causis linguae Latinae* by Julius Caesar Scaliger</note>, Terentianus <note>likely Terentianus Maurus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note>, the Dictionary of Martinius <note>Matthias Martinius, a German lexicographer</note>, the Rhetoricians who have treated letters and syllables, such as Vossius in the 4th book of his *Oratory Institutions*, chapter 2; Aristides in the 2nd book of *On Music* <note>Aristides Quintilianus</note>; and what I have written on the subject in the 4th article of the 57th question on Genesis <note>The author, Marin Mersenne, refers here to his own massive work, *Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim* (1623)</note>.

### PROPOSITION LI.

*To know if those who have no tongue can speak, and if the mute can be made to speak; and how to teach them to read and write when they are deaf.*

If vocal trills <note>original: "fredons" — melodic modulations or warbling of the voice</note> can serve to create a language, one can still speak even if the tongue has been cut out, since the passages and the trills are made with the throat. Certainly, it would be difficult to imagine that one could naturally speak without a tongue, if a child from lower Poitou named Pierre Durand did not demonstrate this experience, of which several people from the city of Paris and other places where he has been are eyewitnesses. This invited Jacques Rolland, a Surgeon, to write a book about it titled *Aglossostomography* <note>original: *Agloſſoſtomographie* — from Greek meaning "Description of a mouth without a tongue"</note>, or the description of a mouth without a tongue, which he had printed at Saumur. 

In this book, he says that the opening of the larynx of this child is very small and oval-shaped; that the uvula <note>original: "vulule"</note> which closes it is thin and long; that a small fleshy body, which still appears where his tongue used to be, swells in its middle toward the palate; that his teeth are reversed and lengthened inward; that the buccinator muscles <note>cheek muscles used for blowing and moving food</note> involve themselves easily between the molar teeth; and that all the other parts necessary for the voice have adapted to the necessity of speaking in the absence of the tongue. For the flattening of the palate, the size of the tonsils <note>original: "amigdales"</note>, and the indentation of the muscles he calls *buccinators* narrow the mouth so much that it articulates sounds, because all the parts, being still tender in children, adapt easily to the necessity of speech. We experience this in the idioms of different nations and in the different accents of foreigners, who cannot leave behind their ways of pronouncing and accenting because of the "fold" and the long habit they have contracted from their infancy. But it is not necessary to expand further on this subject, nor to speak of the structure, parts, and use of the tongue, since this Author has treated it very amply in...

# Book One

...the chapters of his book, in which he shows that if the tongue is cut, it cannot be repaired, although one might add to it the small instrument he describes when it is only truncated at the tip. He also shows how it serves to taste, to move and gather food, and to spit, and discusses all its other functions.

Now, if the art of attaching an <term>artificial tongue</term><note>A prosthetic device designed to aid speech or swallowing for those with oral injuries.</note> to the <term>hyoid bone</term><note>A U-shaped bone in the neck that supports the tongue.</note> upon which the tongue rests had been found, one could supplement the defect of the natural tongue, just as one does for teeth and the nose; nevertheless, I do not dare to conclude that the movements of the <term>glottis</term><note>The part of the larynx consisting of the vocal cords and the opening between them.</note> and the <term>epiglottis</term><note>The flap of cartilage that covers the windpipe while swallowing.</note> could not form some speech.

As for the mute, although many believe it is not possible for them to speak otherwise than by the ordinary signs they make with their hands, eyes, and other parts of the body—because they cannot hear any instruction due to being deaf—there is no doubt that they can be taught to move the tongue in such a way that they will form words. One can teach them the meaning of these words by presenting the things they signify before their eyes, or by having them touch them. From this, one can conclude that it is necessary to begin with writing to make the deaf speak, just as one begins with speech to teach others to speak; so that speech and writing are almost the same thing: for one can say that speech is a transitory writing, which consists in movement, and that writing is a constant speech, which is not subject to time or movement.

This can be confirmed by the example of <note>Monsieur Bene may refer to a specific local figure or historical case of a literate deaf person in Arles.</note> Monsieur Bene, who responded in writing to letters sent to him, and who consequently could read all kinds of books, as the city of Arles witnesses. In that city, his children can still be seen, of whom only two sons and two daughters did not speak: he wrote the Genealogy of the Kings, and that of his own house.

Now, the only way to teach the deaf and mute to read and write consists in making them understand that the characters used represent what is shown to them and what they see: for the pronunciation of letters and words—that is to say, speech—does not represent the things signified any more naturally than writing does, regardless of its form. Both depend equally on the will and the institution of men, without which they signify nothing. This is why the deaf can easily understand that each word signifies what they are shown; and because they are deprived of hearing, and consequently their imagination is in no way attached to the objects of that sense, their minds are more capable and stronger for understanding and retaining the characters shown to them. When these characters are joined to all the things one wishes to teach them, they understand that they signify such or such a thing more effectively than those who are not deprived of hearing.

This being established, it is easy to teach the deaf to write all kinds of things, provided they can fall under the sense of sight, or touch, or can be tasted or smelled; but it is more difficult to make them speak, because one cannot show them all the movements of the tongue and the other parts that form speech. Those who hear have no need to see these movements, because they move the tongue and practice little by little until they have perfectly imitated the words they have heard.

<note>original: "Valefius"</note> Vallesius <note>Likely Francisco Vallés (1524–1592), a celebrated Spanish physician known as "The Divine Vallés."</note>

### Harmony.

AFTER having read the first general Preface, in which there are twelve or thirteen very significant matters; that of the six books of Consonances, where one finds seven things to note; that of the book of the Voice, which contains four or five excellent matters for the establishment of the most perfect Language <note>Original: "Idiome." Mersenne often explored the idea of a universal or "perfect" language that could mathematically represent the nature of things.</note>; that of the Instruments, where one finds all the different characters and their names as used in Printing-houses; and that of the Organ, in which many things belonging to the book of the Organ are supplemented; and after having corrected all the errors which are marked at the end of the said Prefaces, or at the end of the third book of Motions, the seventh book of Percussion Instruments (with which I desire that one begins, because the errors of the first four books of Consonances are marked there, which are notable because of the musical notes and the practice), and those which are at the end of the book on the Utility of Harmony, which one may have bound first: after, I say, having done all this, one may read the following Propositions, in order to see at a glance what is contained in all the books of this work. However, the explanation or the proof of several Propositions often contains much more than they promise upon reading them: so that they may compensate for those which give less than what one expects. In any case, the charity and benevolence of the Readers will excuse the defects which may be encountered in any part of this work; it must only be noted that I sometimes change a few words in these Propositions in order to make them more consistent with my meaning; furthermore, the numbering that is sometimes missing from the Propositions in the books is here restored in its entirety. Now, this table of Propositions will supplement what might be desired in the Table of Contents, and will show the relationship that some Propositions maintain with one another when one sees the citation afterward; as appears in the 21st Proposition of the first book following, after which there is: *See the 9th Proposition of the [book on] Utility, etc.* because they both speak of the same thing.

### The Fifty-Three Propositions of the Book on the Voice.

*The printers have incorrectly placed "of Universal Harmony" in the titles of the pages until the eleventh page. See the Preface.*

I. The motive power of the soul is the principal and primary cause of the voice of animals, and has its seat in the tendons. 1.

II. Of all the muscles of the body, those of the chest and the <term>larynx</term><note>The hollow muscular organ forming an air passage to the lungs and holding the vocal cords; the voice box.</note> contribute most immediately to the voice. 3.

III. The <term>glottis</term><note>The part of the larynx consisting of the vocal cords and the opening between them.</note> is the most proximate cause of the voice. 4.

IV. The muscles and nerves of the larynx serve to form the <term>low</term><note>original: "grave"</note> and <term>high</term><note>original: "aiguë"</note> voice. 6.

V. The voice is the sound that an animal makes by means of the <term>vocal artery</term><note>original: "artere vocale"; an archaic term for the trachea or windpipe.</note>, the larynx, the glottis, and the other parts that contribute to forming it, with the intention of signifying something. 7.

VI. The voices of men are as different as their faces, so that one can distinguish them from each other by the voice; and establish <term>Phthongonomy</term><note>original: "Phtongonomie"; a term coined from Greek "phthongos" (voice) and "nomos" (law), intended as the study of character through vocal sounds.</note>, or <term>Phonoscopy</term><note>original: "Phoniſcopie"; the examination or "looking at" the voice.</note> for voices, just as physiognomy is for faces. 8.

VII. The voice of animals serves to signify the passions of the soul, but it does not always signify the <term>temperament</term><note>In 17th-century medicine, "temperament" referred to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an individual.</note> of the body. 8.

VIII. The voice of animals is necessary, and that of men is free. 10. <note>Mersenne suggests that animal cries are reflexive instincts, while human speech is a product of free will.</note>

IX. The voice is the material of speech, and it is man alone who speaks. 10.

X. To determine if man could speak or sing if he had never heard words or sounds. 11.

XI. Assuming that children were raised in a place where they heard no speaking, to know what <term>language</term><note>original: "idiome"</note> they would use to speak among themselves. 11.

XII. To determine if one can find the best language of all those that can express the thoughts of the mind. 12. *See the 47th Proposition of this book.*

XIII. How many kinds of sounds man can make with the mouth and the other organs of the voice and speech. 13.

XIV. If nature had not given voices that express the passions, to know if one could invent the same ones she uses, or more suitable ones. 14.

XV. One can sing <term>Chromatic</term><note>A style of music using many half-steps (semitones) outside the standard scale.</note> and <term>Enharmonic</term><note>A style of music using microtonal intervals, smaller than a half-step.</note> music, and perform the major and minor tone, and even the <term>Comma</term><note>A very small musical interval, used here to describe the minute adjustments singers make to stay in tune.</note> in all the places one wishes. 16.

XVI. To explain how the <term>low</term><note>original: "grave"</note> and <term>high</term><note>original: "aigu"</note> of the voice is made. *Wherein Aristotle's questions on this subject are explained.* 17.

XVII. Whether it is easier to lead the voice from a low sound to a high one, than from high to low. 22.

XVIII. To know whether it is easier to sing by <term>conjunct degrees</term><note>Stepwise motion between adjacent notes in a scale.</note> than by separate or <term>disjunct degrees</term><note>Musical leaps, skipping over notes in the scale.</note>. 27.

XIX. To determine if one can know with certainty which is the low or the high of the sound that one hears. 27.

IX. To explain two other ways that serve to find the internal relations of passages from one Consonance to another. 231.
X. To explain in how many ways one can pass from one consonance to another of a different species by contrary, conjunct, or disjunct movements: where one sees the used and unused passages, the good and the bad. 232.
XI. To determine why the last two passages of the first table, and the first of the second and third table are good or bad: where one sees why the passage from the Major Third to the Unison is not as good as that from the Unison to the Major Third. 238.
XII. To determine if the third passage of the first table is good; which is used to pass from the Major Third to the Unison by the <term>Chromatic degree</term> <note>A semitone interval that changes the pitch of a note without changing its letter name, such as moving from C to C-sharp.</note>, and by the Minor Third: and why one can pass to whatever Consonance one wants when leaving the Unison. 240.
XIII. To determine if the 4th, 5th, and 6th passages of the first table, by which one goes from the Fourth to the Unison, are permitted. 241.
XIV. To determine if it is permitted to pass from the Fifth to the Unison by the 7th and 8th ways of the first table. 241.
XV. Of 2 ways for the Minor Third to go to the Unison by similar disjunct movements, one of which has its Bass making the Fifth while descending, and the treble the Major Third, and the other has its Bass making the Major Third while ascending, and its treble making the Fifth; determine which is the best. 243.
XVI. Why several passages from one Consonance to another are not good, even though they have no bad internal relations: and why it is not permitted to pass from the Major Third to the Unison, as it is permitted to pass from the Unison to the Major Third. 244.
XVII. To explain the universal <term>tablature</term> <note>A system of musical notation that tells a player where to place their fingers on an instrument rather than indicating the pitch of the notes.</note> of Harmonic ratios, from which one can compose all sorts of pieces of Music for 2, 3, 4, and as many parts as one wishes. 245.
XVIII. To explain 2 other sorts of tablature that can serve to understand the Theory while singing. 250.
XIX. To explain all the types of characters proper for singing Music, and show how the Jews, Arabs, Armenians, Samaritans, and other nations can conform to our way of writing and singing Music. 251.
XX. To explain the figures, and the value of notes and other harmonic characters of Europe. 255.

**I.** To explain an easy method for learning and teaching how to read and write Music. 332. *It is the invention of <term>Monsieur des Argues</term>.* <note>Gérard Desargues (1591–1661) was a renowned mathematician and architect; here, Mersenne refers to Desargues's proposal for a simplified musical notation using numbers.</note>
**II.** To explain another method for learning to sing and to compose without ordinary notes, by means of the letters of the Alphabet alone, without <term>mutations</term>. 342. <note>Original: "muances." This refers to the complex traditional system of shifting between "hexachords" (six-note scales) used in Renaissance music education.</note>
**III.** To explain all the characters necessary to easily write and compose all kinds of Music, whether for voices or for all kinds of instruments. 347. *Where one sees two compositions by <term>du Caurroy</term> in 7 and 8 parts, note-against-note; and the Perfect Harmonic Hand of the <term>Gamut</term>.* <note>The "Hand" refers to the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic device used to help singers find their pitches; the "Gamut" is the full range of notes in the musical system.</note>
**IV.** To learn to compose Music correctly in a short time. 351.
**V.** To explain the manner of knowing if a voice is good, and the qualities it must have. 353.
**VI.** To explain the manner used to train voices for the <term>cadence</term>, and to make them capable of singing all kinds of Airs. 354. *Where one sees a warning for Masters who teach singing.* <note>In the 17th century, a "cadence" often referred specifically to a vocal ornament, such as a trill, rather than just the end of a musical phrase.</note>
**VII.** To explain the characters necessary to signify all the particulars of the Airs that one desires to perform with every kind of perfection, and the manner of properly performing <term>cadences</term> and <term>tremblemens</term>. 358. <note>"Tremblemens" were vocal ornaments similar to modern trills or shakes.</note>
**VIII.** To explain the method of making good melodies for all kinds of subjects and letters. 360.
**IX.** To discover the skills that serve to compose good melodies. 362. *Where one sees a specific warning for this subject.*
**X.** Accents are so great in number that it is almost impossible to explain them all. 365.
**XI.** Accents reveal the country one is from, and sometimes the temperament and the mood. 366.
**XII.** The <term>accent</term> is a modification of the voice, by which one expresses the passions of the soul naturally or with artifice. 366. <note>Mersenne views "accents" as the rhetorical and emotional inflections used in singing to move the listener.</note>
**XIII.** Each affection of the soul has its own accents, by which it expresses its different degrees. 367.
**XIV.** One cannot express the Accents of the passions without new characters. 369.
**XV.** All the Accents of the 3 passions need nine different characters to be marked, namely 3 for the 3 degrees of anger, and two other sets of three for love and sadness. 370.
**XVI.** To determine if these Accents can be expressed and performed while singing Music. 371.
**XVII.** To show the utility that <term>Preachers</term> and other Orators can derive from the Accents of each passion. 373. <note>Mersenne connects musical theory with rhetoric, suggesting that public speakers can use musical principles to better influence their audiences.</note>
**XVIII.** <term>Rhythmics</term> establishes and regulates movements, their sequence, and their mixture to excite, increase, maintain, diminish, and appease the passions. 374. *Where one sees 27 examples of movements or metrical feet.* <note>"Rhythmics" (Rythmique) refers to the study of musical meter and time, often modeled on the poetic feet of Greek and Latin verse.</note>

**XIX.** To reduce all kinds of movements into verse, and to explain for this purpose the true French pronunciation of the letters of the Alphabet. 376.

**XX.** To explain all the syllables that are long, common, or short, and to provide rules for establishing <term>French Prosody</term>. 381. <note>Prosody is the study of the rhythm and sounds of language, particularly in poetry.</note>

**XXI.** To explain everything related to feet and <term>measured verse</term>, and particularly the Dactylic Hexameter and Pentameter, and the Sapphic. 384. <note>"Measured verse" (vers mesurés) was a movement in the 16th and 17th centuries that tried to apply the "long" and "short" syllable rules of Ancient Greek and Latin poetry to the French language.</note>

**XXII.** To explain Phalaecian, Iambic, Trochaic, Alcmanian, and Asclepiadean verses. 387. <note>These are specific rhythmic patterns, or meters, borrowed from classical antiquity.</note>

**XXIII.** To explain Anapestic, Paeonic, Major and Minor Ionic, Choriambic, Antispastic, and other meters. 389.

**XXIV.** To explain the attempts made in this century to establish French Prosody and Metric Poetry for the sake of Music. 393. *Wherein one sees an Ode by Horace set to Music.*

**XXV.** To determine the great multitude of movements made by changing the time or the notes of a measure used in singing. 396.

**XXVI.** To explain the use of the preceding variety of movements or times; and to show that practitioners misuse the terms "ternary" and "binary" when they speak of their measures. 398. <note>Mersenne is critiquing how musicians of his time used the terms for triple and duple time.</note>

**XXVII.** To explain <term>Rhythmopoeia</term>, or the method of creating beautiful movements for all kinds of subjects. 401. *Wherein one sees an excellent <term>branle à mener</term>.* <note>Rhythmopoeia is the art of composing rhythms. A "branle" was a popular French folk dance; the "branle à mener" was a specific lead-style version of this dance.</note>

**XXVIII.** To provide examples of all kinds of movements used by the ancients, and to show those of our rhymed verses, and the art of finding them in all kinds of verse. 406.

**XXIX.** To provide examples of the <term>diminution</term> and embellishment of songs, and the art of adorning and beautifying them. 410. *Wherein one sees examples by <term>Messieurs Boësset and Moulinié</term>.* <note>"Diminution" refers to the practice of breaking a long note into many shorter, faster notes as a decoration. Antoine Boësset and Étienne Moulinié were the most famous composers of the French "air de cour" (courtly song) in the early 17th century.</note>

**XXX.** To explain the manner of singing the Odes of Pindar and Horace, and of rendering French verses—both rhymed and measured—as suitable for Music as the verses of Greek and Latin Poets. 415. *Wherein one sees <unclear>an Ode</unclear> by Pindar and another by Horace set to Music; and another example of French measured verse.*

**XXXI.** To explain the Major and Minor Mode, Perfect and Imperfect Time, and Perfect and Imperfect Prolation, with the proper symbols used by practitioners. 420. <note>These terms refer to the complex system of "mensural notation" used before modern time signatures were fully standardized.</note>

**XXXII.** To explain the manner of singing all kinds of measures under all kinds of time, without using the preceding symbols, and to propose what seems most difficult in the Rhythmics of the ancients. 423.

**XXXIII.** To explain the most unique aspects of Saint Augustine’s six books on Rhythmic Music. 424. *Wherein one sees an excellent Paraphrase of the Psalm <note>original: "Super flumina Babylonis"</note> "By the Rivers of Babylon," in French verse, and several remarks on our measured verses.*

**XXXIV.** To determine if it is appropriate to use any species of the Greek <term>Chromatic</term> or <term>Enharmonic</term> Genres to sing rhymed and measured verses with as much perfection as they did. 438. *Wherein one sees the Octave divided into 24 Enharmonic <term>Diesis</term>, and the faults of this 6th book, along with several others that must all be corrected before reading these books, as I have already said in several places.* <note>The Chromatic and Enharmonic genres were ancient Greek ways of dividing the musical scale that used intervals smaller than a semitone. A "diesis" here refers to a quarter-tone or similar microtonal interval.</note>

I. To determine how many species of sounds and musical instruments there are. 1.
II. To explain the matter and the manner in which the strings of instruments are made. 3.
III. To determine if harmonic instruments were made in imitation of voices, or if the intervals of voices were regulated by those of instruments; and if Art can perfect nature, or vice versa; and if one should judge artificial things by natural ones. 7.
IV. Which is the most pleasant sound of all instruments, and which instrument should be used to regulate harmonic intervals. 9. *Wherein one sees <term>Ptolemy’s Monochord</term>.* <note>The Monochord is an ancient scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to measure the mathematical ratios of musical intervals. Claudius Ptolemy was a 2nd-century scholar who defined many of these ratios.</note>
V. To demonstrate all the divisions of the Monochord, and consequently *the entire science of music.* 16.
VI. To demonstrate that the Monochord divided into 8 equal parts contains all the <term>Consonances</term>. 19. <note>Consonances are intervals that sound "stable" or pleasant to the ear, such as the octave or perfect fifth.</note>
VII. To explain the simplest division of a string to make it produce Consonances and the <term>Diatonic steps</term>. 20. <note>The "Diatonic" scale is the standard seven-note scale (like the white keys on a piano).</note>
VIII. To explain the intervals, both Consonances and Dissonances, found in the remainders of the Monochord string after marking the Diatonic steps. 21.
IX. To explain all the Consonances and Dissonances of the Monochord and the <term>Perfect System</term>, whether comparing the whole string to the parts forming the Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic steps, or comparing each step or sound with the entire string or its remainder. In this way, the Monochord and the Harmonic System are considered here in every way that can serve Harmony. 22.
X. To divide all sorts of strings, or straight lines, into as many equal parts as one wishes, without changing the opening of the compass <unclear>by chance</unclear>. 25. *See also the 17th proposition of the 4th book which follows.*
XI. To determine the number of <term>Aspects</term> by which the stars look upon the earth, and the Consonances to which they correspond. 27. <note>In the 17th century, "Aspects" referred to the angular distances between planets in astrology; Mersenne is connecting the "harmony" of the heavens to the "harmony" of music.</note>
XII. To explain the figure of a particular Monochord and all its divisions. 32.
XIII. To explain the difference and distance from one Consonance or Dissonance to another by means of the Monochord; and the manner of dividing the same string half by half to make all sorts of Consonances and Dissonances. 35.
XIV. To explain another Monochord of equality, for dividing the neck of the Lute, Viol, Cittern, and all other instruments played in 12 equal semi-tones, and for making the <term>Diapason</term> and the tuning of Spinets and organs. 37. <note>"Monochord of equality" refers to what we now call Equal Temperament, where the octave is divided into twelve identical steps. "Diapason" here refers to the standard pitch or the range of an octave.</note> *See the 6th and 7th propositions of the 2nd book, and the 9th of the 4th book following.*
XV. To determine how much the intervals of this Monochord of equality are smaller or larger than those of the Monochord following *just* proportions: and if the ear can perceive the differences. 39. <note>"Just proportions" (Just Intonation) is a tuning system based on whole-number ratios, which sounds purer but makes it difficult to play in different keys.</note>

### *17 Propositions of the 2nd Book of Instruments.*

I. To explain the shape, parts, tuning, and temperament of the <term>Lute</term>. 45. *Where one sees two ancient instruments.* <note>The lute was the premier household instrument of the 17th century, possessing a pear-shaped body and a delicate, complex sound.</note>
II. To explain the construction of the Lute and the <term>Pandora</term>: how they must be strung to perfection, and how one may know if the strings are good. 49. *Where one sees the different sorts of knots.* <note>The Pandora, or Bandora, is a large, wire-strung instrument from the lute family, often featuring a scalloped body design.</note>
III. To explain how the neck of the Lute should be divided and the <term>frets</term> placed to play it perfectly: where one sees several remarks on strings and the difference of their sounds. 53. <note>original: "touches"; frets are the gut strings tied around the neck of the lute to mark where the fingers should press.</note>
IV. To explain the <term>Genera</term> and the Species of Music, and all the principal things established by the Greeks in their music. 56. <note>The "Genera" refer to the three ancient Greek systems of tuning: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note>
V. That one uses the system of Aristoxenus on the Lute and other instruments, and what it has of defects and advantages. 58. <note>Aristoxenus was a Greek philosopher who argued that musical intervals should be judged by the ear rather than by strict mathematical ratios.</note>
VI. To explain the <term>temperament</term> of the Lute, the Viol, etc., and to show how much each Consonance or Dissonance is altered. Where one will see the three Genera of Music in their perfection. 62. <note>Temperament is the intentional slight "mistuning" of certain intervals so that an instrument can play in many different keys without sounding dissonant.</note>
VII. That the major and minor tone, the Octave, etc., can be divided into two or more equal parts; and consequently that the <term>Diapason</term> can be divided into 12 equal semitones. Where one has the two mean proportionals, the doubling of the cube, and the frets of each instrument in their proper place. 65. *See page 226.* <note>Diapason is the classical term for the interval of an octave.</note>
VIII. To determine if the <term>Diatonic</term> scale in use is the "Syntonon" of Ptolemy, or that of Pythagoras, Archytas, or Aristoxenus, etc. Where one sees the different Species of the three Genera. 70. <note>Diatonic refers to the standard seven-note scale. Mersenne is comparing modern tuning to the theories of ancient Greek mathematicians.</note>
IX. To explain the manner of playing the Lute to perfection, and how to place each hand or finger as is necessary to play it well. 76. *Where one sees the conditions required to learn to play it, the position of the right hand, that of the left hand; the vibrations, plaintive accents, sighs both simple and compound, and the ornaments of the left hand.* <note>original: "tremblemens, accents plaintifs, ſouſpirs... traits"</note>
X. To explain the characters of <term>tablature</term>, and several particular observations. 82. *Where one sees 16 remarks for playing the Lute and using its neck to perfection.* <note>Tablature is a form of musical notation that tells the player where to place their fingers on the frets rather than which notes to play.</note>

## 27 Propositions of the 3rd Book of Instruments.

**I.** To explain the material, shape, tuning, and use of the <term>Spinet</term>. 101. *See its construction in the 22nd proposition of this book.* <note>The spinet is a small, plucked keyboard instrument, a compact relative of the harpsichord.</note>
**II.** To explain the shape of the Spinet, and the science of the perfect and imperfect <term>Keyboard</term>; and how it must be made to play upon it in the perfect intonation of the <term>Consonances</term>, without using <term>temperament</term>. 107. <note>Temperament is the practice of slightly "mistuning" certain intervals so that a keyboard can play in all keys; Mersenne here explores ways to achieve pure harmony without such compromises.</note>
**III.** To explain the shape, parts, keyboard, and range of the <term>Harpsichord</term>, with two ancient instruments. 110. One also sees a new form of Spinet used in Italy. 113.
**IV.** To explain the shape, material, and parts of the <term>Manichord</term> with all its 49 sounds, and with the octave divided into 25 sounds. 115. <note>The "manichord" is an early name for the clavichord, a keyboard instrument where strings are struck by metal tangents.</note>
**V.** To explain three types of ordinary Spinet keyboards, with the intervals that can be made perfectly in tune on them. 117 and 118.
**VI.** Of what length and thickness the Spinet strings must be to render a perfect Harmony. 120. *Where one sees two numerical tables on this subject.*
**VII.** A deaf man can tune the Lute, the <term>Viol</term>, the Spinet, and other stringed instruments, and find whatever sounds he wishes, if he knows the length and thickness of the strings. 123. *Where one sees the tablature for the deaf.* 125. <note>This refers to using mathematical ratios and visual measurements to set pitch rather than relying on hearing.</note>
**VIII.** That one can know the thickness and length of strings without measuring them, and without seeing them, by means of sounds. 126.
**IX.** To know if one can determine the thickness of an instrument string without comparing it with other strings. 127.
**X.** To determine if one can tune the Lute, Spinet, Viol, etc., without using sounds or ears, by the sole knowledge of the different stretching of the strings. 128.
**XI.** To determine how much drier or more humid the air is each day, by means of sounds and strings. 130. <note>Changes in humidity affect string tension and pitch, effectively turning the instrument into a primitive hygrometer.</note>
**XII.** Of what thickness and length strings must be to make agreeable sounds, which can be judged by the ear: and how one can know the pitch of the strings, when they are too long, too slack, or too short to make sounds that can be heard. 134.

## Summary of Theoretical Music.

**Article I.** Sound is nothing other than a beating of the air, which the hearing perceives when it is touched. Now, the two primary properties of sound consist of its strength and the qualities we call *low and high* <note>original: "graue & aigu"</note>. Its strength is greater when it is produced by a more violent beating of the air; and this beating is more violent when a greater quantity of air is struck at the same time.

As for its depth [low pitch], it is greater when it is produced by slower beats; and consequently it is higher [sharper] when it is produced by faster beats; for example, if one sound is produced in a given time by 50 beats, and another sound in an equal time by 100 beats, this latter sound will be twice as high as the former.

<summary>This page contains a list of corrections (errata) for several books of the treatise and begins a concise summary of "speculative music," defining sound as the physical vibration or "beating" of air.</summary>
<keywords>errata, theoretical music, speculative music, physics of sound, pitch, frequency, acoustics, Marin Mersenne</keywords>

--- Page 41 ---
<meta>This page concludes the supplementary summary of musical theory that the author, likely Marin Mersenne, included to fill empty pages in the printing. It transitions from the mathematical ratios of intervals to the physical properties of sound and air.</meta>

II. When two or more sounds are produced together and at the same time, they are called **Consonants**, when they agree well and please the hearing and the mind. Now, the reason for these harmonies is derived from the union of the said sounds, such that the harmonies are sweeter as their union is closer and greater, as is experienced in the Unison, the Octave, the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, etc.

The Unison is the union or mixture of two sounds made by an equal number of beats of air <note>In 17th-century physics, "beats" refer to vibrations or pulses.</note>; the Octave is the mixture of two sounds, where the lower is produced by one beat and the higher by two; and the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> is the mixture of two sounds, where the lower is produced by two beats and the higher by three.

All simple Consonances are contained and explained by the first 6 numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. For the Octave is from 1 to 2; the Fifth from 2 to 3; the Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note> from 3 to 4; the Diton <note>original: "Diton," meaning two whole tones</note> or Major Third from 4 to 5; and the Minor Third from 5 to 6. Now, these represent the number and the comparison of their beats.

III. The Octave is the sweetest of all after the Unison, because its beats unite most frequently together: for the first beat of the higher sound unites with the first part of the beat of the lower sound, and the second beat with the last part; or rather, its beats unite every 2 strokes; those of the Fifth every 3 strokes, etc.

And when the union is equal on the part of the higher sound, and unequal on the part of the lower, the Consonance that unites its sounds equally on the part of both is sweeter: for example, the beats of the Fifth unite every 3 strokes with respect to the higher sound, and every 2 with respect to the lower. But the Twelfth unites its sounds at every stroke with respect to the lower; that is why it is sweeter.

IV. Since weight cannot make a string rise to the Octave unless it is fourfold, one can say that the higher sound of the Octave is 4 times heavier <note>Mersenne uses "heavier" here to refer to the tension or force required.</note> than the lower sound. But when strings are different in length, and of equal thickness and material, the weight required to make a string that is twice as long rise to the Octave must be <insert>16-fold</insert> <note>original: "16-uple"</note>, because the fourfold weight only brings the double-length string to a Unison with the half-length string <note>original: "souzdouble"</note>; and then the fourfold weight makes it rise to the Octave. <note>The printed word "Octuple" has been corrected by hand to "16-uple".</note>

V. One may say that 230 toises <term>Toise: An old French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or 6.4 feet.</term> are the proper measure of direct sounds, since they travel that distance in the time of one second, whether the wind is favorable or contrary, and whether the sounds are loud or soft. And 162 toises are the measure of reflected sounds <note>echoes</note>, since a syllable pronounced as quickly as possible strikes a wall 81 toises away and then returns to the ear in the time of one second <note>original: "seconde minute"</note>. Now, if sound is produced by circles similar to those made on water, it is certain that the movement of the air carrying the sound is 1870 times faster than the motion of water; from which one can conclude that air is 1870 times easier to move, more liquid, less resistant, and lighter than water.

The proofs of this Summary, along with a great multitude of other speculations and several observations and experiments, will be found in the 19 books, and particularly in the *Treatise on Observations*.

### FIRST
# GENERAL PREFACE
## TO THE READER.

<image-desc>An ornate square drop cap 'C' decorated with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

THIS Preface contains certain remarks which will serve for the understanding of some propositions, or the sequence of the books, which may be arranged however one wishes. Because the printers did not always make the page numbers follow consecutively at the top of the pages, and because they restarted them several times against my intention—as is seen in the 7th book on Instruments, which speaks of <term>percussion instruments</term> <note>These include drums and other instruments played by striking.</note>, of which the first page should have been numbered 413—I did not want to include a table of contents for these books. I feared making it too difficult to use because of the different characters <note>The author is referring to the alphabetical signatures (A, B, C, etc.) used by printers to organize sections of a book.</note> that would have been necessary to signify each particular treatise. For example, it would have been necessary to use the first 8 letters—A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and H—to signify the treatises on sounds, mechanics, the voice, composition, instruments, percussion instruments, and the utility of harmony, etc. Nevertheless, if one desires it, it is not so difficult that it cannot be used profitably; moreover, the book on the utility that Preachers and all people can draw from harmony supplies this table in some way, and everyone can make one for their own use at the end of their copy.

Now, the first notice I wish to give—after having prayed the Reader to correct the printing errors—is only a repetition of what I have said in several other places: namely, that I do not desire that one believe I am persuaded of having demonstrated what I propose in the propositions, even though I often speak affirmatively. One should therefore take everything I have said as a simple narrative, unless one feels constrained by the experiments <note>original: "experiences"; in this period, the word could mean both 'experiences' and 'scientific experiments.'</note> or the reasons I bring forward to embrace what I propose. For example, when I explain sound by the movement of the air, I do not at all prevent one from positing species <note>original: "especes"; a Scholastic philosophical term for the forms or qualities transmitted from an object to the senses.</note> which glide through the air like heat, and in some way like light, though requiring time. And when I have said that the same ratio exists between sounds as exists between the movements of the air or the strings, I leave everyone the liberty to doubt whether sounds—not being homogeneous <note>That is, sounds and vibrating strings are made of different "stuff" or natures.</note> with the strings—can have their ratios and <term>proportions</term> <note>The mathematical relationships, such as 2:1 for an octave, that Mersenne sought to apply to the physical world.</note> transferred to the sounds. However, if one considers the method I use to prove the ratio of the <term>octave</term> and of other <term>consonants</term> <note>Notes that sound pleasing when played together.</note> or <term>harmonic intervals</term>, they do not depend...

not at all on the length or thickness of the strings, because I use nothing other than the movements, or beats of air; so that if there is anything demonstrable in Music, one cannot, in my opinion, proceed with a better method than the one I use in all the treatises of this work. For the number of beats of air <note>original: "batemens d'air." Mersenne is describing what we now call frequency or vibrations.</note> is found everywhere, just as much in strings as in bells, which tremble exactly as many times as the strings when they are in unison. For example, if the string that produces the lowest and deepest sound of my voice trembles and beats the air 40 times in the time of one heartbeat <note>original: "batement de poux." Early modern scientists often used the pulse as a standard unit for measuring short durations of time.</note>, the bell that is in unison will tremble 40 times in the same amount of time, whether it is struck with a hammer or merely touched with the tip of a finger. The same happens to the string of a Lute, which will also have 40 tremblings in that space of time, whether it is plucked very hard or only touched by the foot of a fly, or by the wind, as I show in the 3rd book on movements and in the first 4 books on instruments.

It must be noted in the second place that there are many things in the first book that must be modified following what is in the 3rd, and according to the experiments that everyone can perform at their leisure; and that one can draw several conclusions from the first 3 books which I have not touched upon. For example, one can show that an arrow being shot from inside a boat will appear immobile to one who is outside said boat, assuming it moves as fast as the arrow when it is shot toward the West while the boat goes toward the East; and similarly that a cannonball fired on the earth toward the West would not move at all in the regard of one who remained stable, while the earth turned as fast toward the East, as would happen if the opinion of Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–230 BC), the ancient Greek astronomer who first proposed a heliocentric model where the Earth rotates on its axis and revolves around the Sun.</note> were true. Now, the last propositions of the 3rd book serve for the understanding and correction of the 1st and 2nd, which must not be judged in the final resort before having read said third book on movement, along with its treatise on mechanics.

But it is good to add two things to this book, the first immediately before the 4th proposition on page 165: namely, that one of the excellent minds of this time, giving the reason for the rebound of bows <note>original: "reflexion des arcs," referring to the elasticity that allows a bow to return to its shape.</note> and other bodies, considers first that all bodies we see are filled with a certain very subtle matter <note>This refers to the "subtle matter" or "aether" central to 17th-century Cartesian physics, used to explain forces like gravity and magnetism without a vacuum.</note>, which cannot be seen and which always moves very fast, so that it passes easily through the pores, or the little voids, in the same manner as the water of a river through the holes of a <term>nasse</term> <note>A wicker fish-trap or basket.</note> or a hamper.

In the second place, that bodies which return after being bent have their pores so disposed when they are bent that this subtle matter can no longer pass through as easily as before; from which it happens that it exerts force to return them to their first state. This can happen in several ways: for example, if one imagines that the pores of a bow that is not drawn are as wide at the entrance as at the exit, and that by drawing it one makes them narrower at the exit, it is certain that the subtle matter which enters inside through the wider side makes an effort to exit through the other side which is narrower; and if one imagines that the pores of this bow were round before it was bent, and that afterwards they are oval, and that the parts...

For example, a well-rounded and well-polished ivory ball, of the same size as the lead one, makes 20 turns and as many returns in both sieves, letting them roll from the top of their quarter-circles; but each turn, which lasts one second in the large sieve, lasts less on the small one, following the sub-duplicate ratio <note>original: "raison sous-doublée," meaning the ratio of the square roots.</note> of the times to the spaces.

<meta>This page continues Mersenne’s technical instructions regarding the mathematical division of the lute's neck to achieve equal temperament. so much so that if one divided a line drawn on the Lute, from its bridge to its nut <note>original: "fillet." The nut is the ridge at the top of the neck where the strings cross into the headstock.</note>, into a thousand parts, the second number 944 would give the location of the first fret, and the 3rd, namely 891, would show the location of the 3rd: but because this division is too long and too difficult to perform, even though once it is made on two rules joined at the ends in the form of a compass it could serve forever; it is enough to first mark the first fret signified by B, which one will do by dividing the space between the nut and the bridge into 56 parts, of which 3 parts being removed will show the location of the first fret, as I said on page 202 of the *Instruments* <note>Referring to another section of his massive treatise, *Harmonie Universelle*.</note>. This being done, if one has a proportional compass <note>A mathematical tool used for scaling and calculations before the invention of the slide rule.</note>, it must be opened such that the length from the nut to the bridge is found between the 56 of the equal parts of the 2 arms, because 56 is the difference between 1000 and 944: and then the difference of all the other numbers following down to 500 will give all the other frets: and if the proportional compass is too small, one will take the opening of double 56, namely 112. And because instrument makers <note>original: "facteurs."</note> do not usually have these compasses, it suffices that they divide the half of a rule into 56 parts, starting from the top, which, being joined with a peg to the end of another rule that is also divided, gives them the freedom to open like a compass. I say that if they open these 2 rules such that the opening of 56, taken with a common compass, gives the size of the first fret, the opening of 53 will give the size of the second, that of 49 will give the 3rd, and so on for the others following the small Table that follows, of which the first column contains the 13 numbers of the Scale <note>original: "Diapason." Here referring to the mathematical span of the octave.</note> divided into 12 equal semitones by the 11 numbers, which signify 11 mean proportional lines <note>A mathematical method for determining the divisions of the string to achieve equal temperament.</note> between 1000 and 500, which give the 2 extremities of the Octave. The 2nd column contains the numbers for the makers' compass made of the 2 preceding rules, which they may call the **Scale of the necks**.

Now, the 12 numbers of the 2nd column are nothing other than the differences of those in the first; so that one must always leave the rules open in the same way, and transfer the openings of the eleven numbers one after the other onto the necks, namely the opening of 53 for the 2nd fret: for as for the first, it must be marked as I said above, and having given to the end, or to the points of the rules where 56 is found, the opening of the size of the first fret, the numbers 53, 49, etc., will give the eleven others, if one carries these openings from the first fret one after the other toward the bridge, that is to say, descending. And if there is any maker who cannot understand this, I will demonstrate the Practice to him whenever he wishes.

In the 7th place, I wish to describe here the instrument used to play 5 or 6 Viols by touching the Harpsichord <note>original: "Clavecin."</note> keyboard, because it is very suitable for concerts; for although I spoke of it in the 12th proposition of the 4th book, and in the 30th of the 7th book of *Instruments*, it is appropriate to add that the endless bow <note>term: "archet sans fin." This refers to a continuous looped bow or a rotating wheel mechanism, similar to a hurdy-gurdy but applied to a keyboard instrument.</note> was discovered here by two young men while my books were being printed: namely, by the one I name in the Preface of the said 30th proposition, and by a German, who used gut strings <note>original: "chordes de boyau."</note> whose ends are so well joined with fish glue <note>A strong adhesive made from the swim bladders of fish, commonly used in historical lutherie.</note> that they seem to be continuous. Now, this bow is stretched over two small wooden pulleys that turn on their axes and are perpendicular to the horizon—as are the strings—in the manner of those of a Harp, whose shape it has imitated. Thus, one can see through the strings all those who are behind the instrument, which makes it suitable for seeing everyone singing in the concert, and consequently the one beating the time <note>The conductor.</note>. This is something that should be observed in Organs, so that the Organist might see those singing in the Choir. On this point, it is good to remark that the Organs in the churches of Italy are better arranged than ours, in that they can be seen equally from both sides, both of which serve as ornament and display; whereas one only sees the front of ours, because their bellows <note>original: "soufflerie."</note> are in a room situated behind. However, they place their bellows down in a cellar made for the purpose, so that the wind is carried by a very long wind-trunk <note>term: "portevent." A pipe that carries compressed air from the bellows to the organ’s windchest.</note> which ascends by way of a pillar to the place where the Organ is set between two pillars.

As for the instrument that performs the concert of Viols, and to which one can give the name **Archiviole** <note>A generic term for various types of bowed keyboard instruments attempted during the Renaissance and Baroque periods, such as the Geigenwerk.</note>, or any other name one wishes: the one I am describing has no other body for resonance than a large arm similar to the concave body of the Harp. And when the bow becomes slack, whether for replacement or due to the passage of time, one pulls the pulleys to the right and left by means of screws <note>original: "viz."</note> which hold them attached against a rod or other piece of wood.

This bow glides over a wooden rule that crosses the instrument near the end of the keys <note>original: "marches."</note>, to which are fitted small pieces of wood, brass, or iron, in such a way that they press the strings against the bow as soon as they are depressed to play. But the Frenchman has succeeded even better than the German, because the body of his instrument, being like that of the Harpsichord, resonates much better and produces such a great Harmony <note>term: "Harmonie." Here meaning a rich, pleasing combination of musical sounds.</note> that it leaves the listeners in admiration. His pulleys have their axes parallel to the horizon, and the movement that drives the bow is composed of only a single wheel with a pulley. But it is necessary to attach a piece of rosin <note>term: "colophone." This was done by the excellent maker from Florence, Master **Rameriny**, who placed up to five different tunings on the Harpsichord to accommodate and adjust it to the pitch of all sorts of songs. This can also be done just as easily on the **Archiviole** <note>A "bowed keyboard" instrument, similar in concept to Leonardo da Vinci’s *viola organista* or Hans Haiden’s *Geigenwerk*, where a mechanism bows the strings when keys are pressed.</note> of which we are now speaking; for if one tunes it according to the equality of semitones <note>Mersenne is referring to equal temperament, which allows for playing in any key without the "wolf tones" found in other tuning systems of the era.</note>—which have the advantage of producing a new Harmony because their temperament is different from that of ordinary **Spinets** and **Organs**—and by having seven or eight more keys on the keyboard than usual, one can begin the **C** <note>original: "VT de C sol." But because shorter and thinner strings do not require such large bodies as thicker and longer ones, if one wishes to have a perfect Harmony from the **Archiviole**, its soundboard must be divided into four or five parts, so that the size of each part corresponds exactly to the size of the strings, in order to imitate the different parts <note>The different sizes of the viol family, such as treble, tenor, and bass viols.</note> of ordinary Viols. This will in no way prevent the bow from touching all the strings, to which it must be very close so that they speak <note>term: "parlent promptement." Now, these strings can be made of brass as well as gut, or they can be mixed and twisted together to vary the Harmony and render it more charming and soft.

The eighth remark of this Preface consists of the explanation of **Instruments that never go out of tune**, which are easy to understand through the *Book of Bells* and by what I said regarding **Sounding Cylinders** in the third book of *Movements*. For if one arranges 49 hollow or solid cylinders within the body of a Harpsichord, following the harmonic ratios that I have explained in so many ways, the keys will strike these cylinders and make them sound as softly as one desires. It is easy to mix in small bells of different lengths or thicknesses—for example, in the shape of thimbles <note>original: "dez, ou doitiers."</note> used for sewing—in order to vary the harmony in all sorts of ways. For this purpose, one can make these bodies of gold, silver, brass, and other materials suitable for resonating, to enjoy the mixture of metals through their sounds just as well as through their fusion or casting.

Now, an instrument made of these bodies could serve as a rule, a canon, and an immobile and infallible **diapason** <note>term: "diapaſon immobile." Here meaning a fixed, universal pitch standard, rather than the modern use of "diapason" to mean the range of a voice or a specific organ stop.</note> to regulate and tune all other types of instruments. Each hollow or solid cylinder, being carried or sent throughout the world, would be suitable for communicating the pitch of the organ, the voice, and other instruments, and for making all the musicians of the earth sing the same piece of music in the same pitch, instead of relying on the vibrations of a string, of which I speak in the third book of *Instruments*, proposition 18.

The ninth remark belongs to **organs**, of which each octave can be made of 13 pipes of the same thickness <note>term: "groſſeur." Experience teaches that it is necessary to mix different lengths with different thicknesses to produce pleasant tones, which can occur in an infinite number of ways. However, it seems the best of all is that of the 14th, and then that of the 43rd proposition, although everyone is free to seek others. For example, instead of giving the width of the diagonal to the pipe that descends an octave <note>Mersenne refers to the "double ratio" (2:1), which defines the octave.</note> below the one that has the side of the square for its width, one can give it the width of the geometric mean between the side and its diameter. This divides the double ratio into four equal ratios, just as the said diameter divides it into two equal ratios (that is to say, by the half); so that the thicknesses, widths, or circumferences of these two pipes would be in the same ratio as a quarter of the octave—that is to say, the **Minor Third** composed of three equal semitones.

The tenth remark of this preface adds what I had forgotten in the 31st proposition of the 7th book on Instruments: namely, that **Jacques Mauduit** <note>A prominent French composer (1557–1627) known for his role in the "Academy of Poetry and Music."</note> added the sixth string to the **viols**, which had only five previously, and that he was the first to introduce their ensemble performance <note>original: "concert"</note> in France in place of a violin bass, which people were content to join with the **Oboes**. He also knows the infallible rules and the analysis for finding an infinite number of others like them. **Monsieur de la Charlonye**, Honorary Royal Judge Provost of Angoulême, is also very skilled in the practice and theory of this art, as is **Monsieur de Beaugrand**, Secretary to the King, who has a very subtle and universal mind and of whom I have already spoken elsewhere in this work. The eleventh remark will serve to prevent oblivion from burying the names of those who have been excellent in France in any part of this art, some of whom are still living now. I leave aside the others, of whom I have spoken in the treatises on each instrument, in order to add that Antoine Demurat had no equal in singing, for he had more natural ability than any man in the world, by reason of the goodness, beauty, and accuracy of his voice. Girard de Beaulieu, Bass of the King's Chamber, sang better than any other; and Cornille, both the father and the son, have left posterity almost in despair of ever being able to equal them.

The final remark will serve to conclude this discourse with our Savior, whom the ancient Christians represented in the form of a Shepherd carrying a sheep on his neck and holding a syrinx, or pastoral flute, in his right hand—as can be seen in several figures from *Underground Rome* <note>original: "Roma Soterranea"; a reference to Antonio Bosio's 1632 work documenting the Roman catacombs.</note>, for example on pages 331, 351, 369, etc., which is similar to the one I explain in the 3rd proposition of the 5th book on Instruments. They also represented Him under the image of Orpheus <note>The mythical Greek musician whose music could charm animals and stones; early Christians used him as a "type" or symbol for Christ.</note>, holding a <term>Harp</term> in his hands similar to one of those I describe in the 25th proposition of the 3rd book. By this, they intended to signify that Jesus Christ had come to persuade men to the true worship of a single God, in place of the 360 gods—or rather, idols—that Orpheus, son of Oeagrus and father of Musaeus, had wished to introduce, as Justin Martyr remarks. However, he confesses along with Clement of Alexandria that Orpheus later recognized his error, which they prove by the beautiful verses they cite, in which he exhorts men to join and unite themselves perpetually with God, to whom be all honor and every kind of glory forever.

I am also astonished that so few musicians take account of the principles of <term>Harmony</term> <note>The mathematical and physical laws governing how sounds blend together.</note>, and that no Academy is established for this subject. All gatherings for concerts are held only for singing, whereas many honorable men would desire that, out of the two or three hours employed in this exercise, half of this time be taken to discuss the causes that make pieces of composition agreeable, and why certain transitions from one consonance to another, and certain mixtures of dissonances, are better than others.
