# BOOK ONE
## ON THE NATURE AND PROPERTIES OF SOUND.
### FIRST PROPOSITION.

### DETERMINING WHETHER SOUND IS CREATED BEFORE
*it is received in the ear, that is to say, before it is heard, and whether it is different from the movement of air.*

It is common practice at the beginning of scientific treatises to ask whether the subjects they study have any true object and what that object is; for it is useless to speak if one does not know what one is talking about. It is therefore appropriate, before proceeding further, to know whether Sound—which is the subject or object of Music and of hearing—has a real existence, and what it is. For there are several who believe that Sound is nothing if it is not heard, and that it is a simple impression of the air which should not be called Sound if there is no ear to hear it and distinguish it from other things. Certainly, if this is the case, then hearing must give it the nature of Sound, just as the imagination and the understanding give existence to imaginary thoughts and phantoms, which are called <term>beings of reason<note>In scholastic philosophy, "beings of reason" (Latin: *entia rationis*) are things that exist only in the mind, such as fictional characters or mathematical abstractions, rather than in physical reality.</note></term>. For my part, I consider that Sound is no less real before it is heard than light or colors and the objects of the other external senses are before they are perceived, and that Sounds would not cease to be what they are even if there were no ear. I would maintain this even if I had admitted that Sound was not different from the movement of air.

Nevertheless, it seems that Sound is something other than this movement, since we feel great movements of air, or of water, or of some other similar bodies, which produce no Sound, or which produce one so weak that it is not at all proportioned to the force of the movement. We experience this with stones thrown into the air with slings, with bullets from <term>arquebuses<note>An arquebus is an early type of long-gun or musket used in the 15th to 17th centuries.</note></term>, with artillery balls, and in several other movements that occur when rain and hail fall, and when the water of a deep river flows without making a noise.

On the contrary, there are small movements that make great noises, such as those of the <term>larynx</term>, the <term>epiglottis</term>, and the tongue when we speak, or those of the air that makes <term>Organs</term> and other <term>Flutes</term> sound. Nonetheless, I do not believe that Sound is different from the movement of the body which strikes the <term>Drum</term> or the membrane of the ear; for it is not necessary to add a <term>quality of the third kind<note>According to Aristotelian categories, "qualities of the third kind" (passible qualities) are properties like color, smell, or sound that are thought to act upon the senses.</note></term>, which is commonly called a <term>passible quality</term>, since the movement of the air is sufficient to explain everything that is done by Sounds. For as soon as this movement has struck the membrane of the ear—

<summary>Mersenne argues that sound exists as a physical reality (the movement of air) regardless of whether a person is there to hear it, rejecting the idea that it is merely a mental perception.</summary>
<keywords>nature of sound, movement of air, scholastic philosophy, acoustics, beings of reason, passible quality, physics of sound</keywords>

--- Page 55 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 1 regarding the physical nature of sound. The previous page ended mid-word with "differe-" (different), and this page begins by concluding the sentence describing the anatomy of the ear and the mechanics of hearing.</meta>

ear, which encloses the internal air and the <term>spirits of hearing<note>In the 17th century, "spirits" (animal spirits) were thought to be subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to transmit sensations to the brain.</note></term>. The movement of the external air is communicated to these internal spirits, either by means of the small bone which is attached to the auditory nerve—which strikes another small bone as if on an anvil—or in some other manner, which Physicians ought to treat in greater detail.

As for the difficulty regarding large movements that seem to produce no sound, and small movements that produce great sounds, one may say that the air is not as agitated in those large movements as one might think. For when one strikes the air with a stick, with the hand, or with stones, arrows, bullets, etc., the air yields easily, especially since there is no body to prevent it from escaping. However, the air receives a greater violence through the movement and resistance of the organs used for speech and music than through the movement of any other sort of body, whose noise and whistling is not heard from as far away as speech.

One must therefore conclude that all movements made in the air, in water, or elsewhere, can be called Sounds; especially since they only lack an ear delicate and subtle enough to hear them. The same thing can be said of the noise of thunder and cannons in regard to a deaf person, who does not perceive these great noises: for the movement or trembling that he feels is not called sound except insofar as it is capable of making itself felt by the spirits of hearing. In this way, Sound can be defined as *a movement of the exterior or interior air capable of being heard; I have said, or of the interior*, because of the noises that occur inside the ear. But it is difficult to find precisely what makes the movement of air capable of being heard. For I consider that a string made of gut or <term>brass<note>original: "leton"</note></term> stretched in the air and attached to two walls with nails or pegs fixed in the wall, when touched by a finger, a bow, or a quill, makes almost no noise; yet when stretched over the bridges of a **Lute**, a **Viol**, or a **Spinet**, it makes a great noise. Nevertheless, it is the same percussion of the air. Similarly, the wind split and cut by a piece of wood similar to the <term>fipple<note>The "lumiere" or light of a flute refers to the sharp edge or "lip" of the mouth-hole where the air is split to create sound.</note></term> of a **Flute** makes only a slight whistling, but when followed by the body of a flute, it makes a very great noise. This leads me to conclude that what makes this movement capable of being heard is nothing other than when it shakes a quantity of enclosed air capable of shaking its "prison" and communicating itself to the neighboring external air until it reaches the ear.

From this it follows that bodies which are the most "aerial" are also the most resonant, and that the most "terrestrial" and heavy bodies are less so. Generally, wood is more resonant than metals when used for the soundboards of instruments. Among metals, lead is the least resonant; among woods, fir—being the lightest and most aerial of all—is also the most resonant, while massive and heavy beech is less so. Among fir trees, the one that is driest and most divested of its terrestrial moisture is found to be the most resonant. Now, one must note the term used to express this quality of bodies which causes them to multiply the initial percussion of the air until it is capable of touching the senses of hearing—namely, **resonant**, as if one were to say "sounding once more." For this word expresses the sound that comes to our ear, which is not the primary Sound, but rather the echo multiplied from the first air that touches the string to that which touches the ear—

heard; and what we call *Echo* is the Sound returned and sent back by the instrument that multiplies the Sound, and reflects it just as mirrors reflect light.

We can explain the multiplication of Sound by that of the heat of the air which is heated by a great fire; for just as we do not feel the heat of the fire immediately unless we touch it, but rather feel the heat of the heated air, so too no ear can perceive any Sound other than that which is multiplied and which proceeds from the first. All this does not, however, prevent Sound from being called a *collision* or *beating of air*, which bodies create in the medium that receives the movement, and which is struck or broken and divided by the bodies that produce or receive the movement; for this collision is the cause by which we perceive this movement when it alters or moves the <term>spirits of hearing<note>Early modern scientists believed "animal spirits"—a refined fluid—traveled through the nerves to communicate sensations to the mind.</note></term>, and the cause may receive the name of its effect.

## PROPOSITION II.

->*To determine how movement and Sound are made, and why several very fast and very rapid movements make no Sound that can be heard, such as the movements of several wheels and other bodies that move in the air or in water: and why several very small movements make great Sounds.*<-

This Proposition will serve to answer the objections that can be made against the preceding one, and will show why we hear great Sounds where the movements seem to be very small. Those who say that Sound is different from the movement of the air bring forward several reasons, the first of which is that the object of hearing must be a quality, like those of the other senses, and that movement is a common object of all the senses. The second is that air cannot penetrate walls, through which one nonetheless hears noise. The third is that two men could not hear the words they speak at the same time, because the air cannot receive two contrary movements at once, and there is no appearance that the air is moved across a great space, such as that in which a voice is heard. The fourth is that several small movements of air often make more noise than larger ones, as I said at the beginning. But it is easy to respond to these difficulties, for it is sufficient that the object of each sense be proportioned to the organ and to the power of the soul which is touched by it through the senses, without it being necessary to attach it to quality rather than to quantity—even though one might say that the movement of the air, water, or some other body has the quality of making itself heard. But this consideration adds nothing new to the movement of the air, which is just as much a movement without the ear as when one assumes the ear, although it is not called Sound until it has struck the <term>eardrum<note>Original: "tambour de l'oreille."</note></term>, upon which it imprints a movement similar to itself; this does not prevent it from having the entire nature of Sound, even if it never serves an ear.

It must therefore be said that Sound, being simply considered in the capacity of Sound, is nothing real but a simple consideration and <term>affection of movement<note>An "affection" here refers to a specific mode or state of being that the movement takes on.</note></term>.

If one examines the object of the other Senses, one will find that they are no more characterized by qualities than Sounds; for example, the object of taste and smell consists of the evaporation and exhalation of <term>small bodies<note>In the 17th century, many scientists believed that senses like smell were triggered by tiny physical particles (corpuscles) emitted by objects.</note></term> that come out of the object that one tastes or smells: the object of touch is not different from the quantity of shapes and their properties, such as softness, hardness, smoothness, etc.

As for the second reason put forward, I admit that one cannot hear through walls if there is no place for the air to communicate, or if the walls are not shaken by the Sound made by the person who is enclosed, or who is outside: for if the walls tremble, they will communicate the movement of the interior air to the exterior, or from the exterior to the interior. Now, it is not as difficult as one might imagine for a man enclosed between four walls to impart some sort of movement to them by the strength of his voice, or by some other Sound: for moved air, finding no exit, has great effects, and experience shows that Sound is much diminished by the interposition of a wall or some other solid body; It seems to me, therefore, that we must conclude that walls do not tremble strongly enough when the sound cannot be heard: but I will speak more fully of this difficulty in another place.

The third reason has no force, for we experience that sound is heard even when the wind is contrary, and consequently that the movement of the air caused by the wind opposes the movement we call Sound; and this opposition which hinders the Sound can be so great due to the violence of the winds or other noises that it will not be heard at all.

When two or more men speak at the same time, the air retains the impressions it receives from each of them, just as calm water receives those from stones thrown into it, for we notice that they create different circles, which extend little by little to the edges, and yet are not as distinct or remarkable as if one had thrown a single stone: but the difficulty of these circles deserves a separate discourse. It is for the same reason that the voices of two or more men speaking to each other at the same time are more confused and less intelligible than when they speak one after the other.

As for the space through which the movement of the air or Sound extends, it is not surprising that it is very large given the little resistance the air offers, as we experience with cannon shots, which move it as far as twenty or thirty <term>leagues<note>An old unit of distance; in 17th-century France, a league was approximately 2.4 to 3 miles (4 to 5 kilometers).</note></term>; perhaps even the movement created by the collision of two bodies goes as far as the end of the air, that is, to the <term>firmament<note>The "firmament" refers to the sphere of the stars or the boundary of the atmosphere in older cosmological models.</note></term>, or higher, if it extends higher, just as the circles made by stones thrown into water go to the edges, for it is as easy to explain this movement as it is to explain how a stone thrown into the Ocean causes all parts of the Ocean to move, so that the part of the water that the stone makes rise spreads everywhere to restore the equilibrium of the water; for if it only spread to the neighboring parts, they would be higher than the more distant ones, which would lose their balance and no longer be poised.

And one can say that if the Ocean covered the entire earth, as it did before God separated the waters from it, and if it were calm, a stone thrown into it under the Arctic pole would create circles that would grow—

The last objection supposes a false thing, for since movement and Sound are not different, Sound is all the greater and stronger as the movement of the air is more violent; so that every time a great sound is heard, one must conclude that the movement of the air is great. But if one considers the magnitude and violence of the movement only by the force exerted in the air, or in some other fluid body, one is often mistaken, because the air must be restrained, enclosed, broken, and reflected by the meeting of two solid bodies. For if it is only pushed from one side, and has a free exit on the other, it will make little noise, as happens with an arrow or with arquebus balls <note>An arquebus was an early type of long gun; its bullets travel fast but do not create a "bang" simply by passing through the air.</note> which move through the air and do not make a Sound proportional to their speed. This is because the yielding air suffers little violence compared to air that resists and encounters bodies between which it is enclosed, as is experienced with the movements of a coachman’s whip, which makes a great noise because of the snap of the cord which traps the air.

One may here add several things regarding the extent of Sound, which is called the <term>sphere of its activity<note>The maximum range or distance over which a sound can be heard.</note></term>, and which causes it to be heard from further away, as is experienced with beams and pipes; for when one strikes the end of a beam, or speaks into a pipe, the Sound carries further and more easily than it would without the help of these bodies. But these considerations must be reserved for another place: for it is enough for now to conclude that Sound is produced when the external movement of the air reaches the <term>nerve of hearing<note>The auditory nerve. Early modern scientists believed physical vibrations directly "touched" this nerve to create the sensation of sound.</note></term>, that is to say, that part of the organ of hearing which receives the first strikes of the movement of the external air, to carry them to the spirit <note>In this context, the "spirit" refers to the mind or the seat of consciousness that interprets sensory data.</note> which forms a judgment of them.

The same must be said of water regarding fish, which hear our noises when the circles <note>The author uses "circles" to describe what we would now call sound waves or ripples.</note> of the air strike the surface of the water, which creates other circles reaching the ear of the Fish; just as circles in the water that make a noise imprint them into the air reaching our ears when we hear a noise made in the water. We must further conclude that there is no need for <term>intentional species<note>In Scholastic philosophy, "intentional species" were thought to be non-material "images" or "likenesses" of objects that traveled through the air to the senses. The author is arguing against this old-fashioned, mystical view in favor of a mechanical, physical explanation.</note></term> for Sound, since the movement of the air is sufficient, and we know that it does not carry itself in an instant like light. For there is no reason to say that these "species" would need movement or time to be carried, since they have no contrary forces. That is why I shall not speak of these images or intentional species of Sounds, but only of the movements that make us perceive them: which will bring greater clarity and ease to our discourse, and perhaps greater satisfaction to the Reader.

However, I do not wish to entirely reject all kinds of intentional species, whether of Sound or of other objects, which many propose to establish a more delicate connection between the [sensory] power and the object than that which is made by means of natural, material, and corporeal external qualities, as if it were necessary to strip them of what they have that is too...

### COROLLARY

Since I desire that the perfect Musician be knowledgeable in Philosophy, and that he should know the various imaginings our ancestors had regarding the nature of Sound—so that he may not begin any discourse on harmony in the various companies he encounters without being able to give an account of it—it should be noted for his benefit that Democritus, Epicurus, and several others of their sect believed that Sound, which is produced by the collision or striking of all kinds of bodies, is nothing other than a movement, or a projection of tiny bodies composed of atoms. These exit from the bodies making the Sound, just as rays exit from the Sun, or are created in the air; being struck by the movement of the bodies, they spread in all directions through the pores <note>The author refers to the "pores" of the air—tiny, invisible gaps that thinkers of the time believed existed between particles of matter.</note>, or the small voids of said air, until they no longer encounter any void and are stopped by the small corpuscles or atoms that compose the substance of the air. Thus, according to this opinion, one can imagine a great multitude of tiny invisible bodies, or atoms, flying through the air after it has been struck, which affect all the ears they encounter on their path, in order to bring them news of what has occurred in the air, or in the bodies from which they originated, and of which they are the ambassadors, or the images and representations.

## PROPOSITION III.

->*Determining whether Sound is the movement of the external or the internal air which is within the body that produces the Sound: and whether Sound can be made without the movement of one or the other.*<-

This Proposition seems very difficult to me because it is impossible to perform the necessary experiments on this subject, as will be seen in the following discourse; but to begin with what is most certain and evident: I say first that the external air is sufficient to create Sound, provided that it is agitated or struck with enough force, as happens in all sorts of collisions; for all the noises made by the winds are nothing other than the various agitations of the air, which can occur in several ways, each of which requires a particular discourse. ...that ordinary Philosophers <note>The author refers to "Scholastic" philosophers who followed the traditional teachings of Aristotle prevalent in universities at the time.</note> hold that every mixed body <note>A "mixed body" refers to any physical substance composed of a combination of the four basic elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> is composed of the four Elements—namely earth, water, air, and fire—one may add that the air enclosed within a body similarly produces a Sound, since it is agitated as strongly as the body in which it is enclosed, whether it forms an essential part of said body or merely fills the small cavities that we call pores. Now, this movement of internal air does not change the Sound in terms of its being low or high <note>original: "graue & à l’aigu"</note>, but it modifies and affects it with certain qualities or particular configurations. These allow us to distinguish the Sound of one body from that of another, as I shall discuss elsewhere.

I do not see, however, that it is necessary to add this internal movement to explain the different qualities of Sounds, especially since they can be attributed to the different shapes of the bodies, some of which are more or less polished or rough than others, even if the eye or hand cannot perceive the differences. Experience shows—by means of lenses of crystal and glass, and by concave mirrors, both Spherical and Parabolic—that surfaces which seem very polished and clean are actually uneven and filled with little valleys and mountains. From this, it happens that the Sounds of all kinds of bodies are almost always different in some way, even though they are in unison <note>Playing the exact same pitch.</note> and are as loud as one another. 

Those who say that internal air brings several differences to external Sounds—or who compose Sound from the movement of both internal and external air (the latter being like the image or the "clothing" of the former)—can also add that the water and fire within bodies also contribute to the difference in Sounds, since these two elements are capable of movement. For those who hold that fire is one of the elements composing bodies are obliged by their own principles to confess that fire is more mobile than air, and consequently, it must at least bring as great a difference to Sounds as the movement of air does.

They might even say that the different Sounds made by the same bell, or the same string at the same time <note>A reference to what we now call "overtones" or "harmonics"—the phenomenon where a single vibrating string or bell produces multiple pitches simultaneously.</note>, come from the different elements of which they are composed. They might argue that the lowest and most material Sound, which appears the strongest, is made by the earth; the second by water; the third by air; and the fourth by fire. Or, if they only hear three Sounds, as most often happens, they must attribute the first to earth and water, the second to air, and the third to fire. This being established, they could say that no body moves without making a concert of three or four parts, each representing its own particular element. But I do not wish to dwell on these considerations here, both because I believe Sound needs no movements other than those of the external air, and because there will be many other places where this opinion can be examined more specifically.

As for the movement of both these types of air, no one doubts that it is necessary. For even if some believe that it is not the air that creates the Sound, but rather the bodies moving within the air, they nevertheless admit that it is necessary for them to move. This cannot happen without the external and internal air moving similarly—unless we consider this movement in a vacuum <note>original: "vuide"</note>, which I shall speak of later, or in water, where movement also creates Sound. This is experienced with bells, whose Sound is deeper in water than in air by a Tenth...

### PROPOSITION IV.

->*To determine whether Sound can be produced in a universal or particular vacuum.*<-

We may consider two types of vacuum <note>original: "vuide"</note>, namely the universal and the particular. The first is nothing other than the deprivation of all bodies in the world, which would occur if God ceased to sustain the bodies He created; for nothing would remain but the space in which they exist, which is ordinarily called imaginary space <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "imaginary space" referred to the infinite extension that exists independently of matter.</note>. One can, nevertheless, consider another vacuum slightly less universal than the previous one—namely, a vacuum where air usually fills space. If air were removed from the place it currently occupies, whether by annihilation or by being moved elsewhere, it would leave the concavity of the Firmament entirely void of air.

The second type of vacuum is that which one imagines in the same place as a portion of air, which can only happen by means of a force that separates the air and simultaneously prevents it from reuniting. But no one could achieve this division except one whose strength is greater than the impetus of all created Nature and the inclination it has for its own preservation—for which it is believed that the perpetual union of all its parts is necessary <note>This refers to the concept of *horror vacui*, or "nature abhors a vacuum," a standard belief before the experiments of Pascal and Torricelli.</note>. Now, it is just as difficult to know whether Sound can be produced in a particular vacuum as in a universal one; but because Sound presupposes movement, we must first see if one or several bodies can move within a vacuum. For if such movement is not possible, we must conclude that Sound cannot be made there. Because this difficulty is not yet resolved and the question remains problematic, I say that if some quantity of air moves in the same way within a vacuum as it does when joined with other parts of air, it will produce Sound, even if it cannot be carried to any ear. That is to say, its movement will have everything necessary on its part to be perceived by the ear as the quality of Sound. The same can be said of the internal air of bodies moving in a vacuum. Now, it is not difficult to explain how air or other bodies could have the movement of reflection—that is, a movement composed of "comings and goings" <note>This is an early description of vibration or oscillation.</note>—within a vacuum; for the strings of a Lute placed in a vacuum, being pulled out of their straight line, would tremble at least as strongly as in the air, since their movement would be in no way slowed down <note>The author correctly surmises that without air resistance, a string would vibrate longer, though we now know that without air to carry the wave, we wouldn't hear it.</note>. But since there is no vacuum in nature, and it is perhaps impossible, it suffices to have touched upon this difficulty without it being necessary to examine the others that are customarily proposed: for example, whether a stone would descend perpendicularly toward the center of the earth through a vacuum, or if missiles <note>meaning projectiles, like arrows or stones.</note> thrown into a vacuum would move perpetually, and several others of which we may yet speak in other places.

On the Nature and Properties of Sound. 9

## COROLLARY.

It is easy to conclude from what we have said until now that Sound has no other subject <note>In this context, "subject" refers to the physical medium or material in which sound exists and travels.</note> than the external air, or other fluid bodies that surround sounding bodies—such as water or wine—or the internal air which is part of said bodies: unless one says that Sound is in all parts of the body by which it is produced.

## PROPOSITION V.

->*To explain in what manner the air moves when its motion creates Sound, and what motions do not create Sound.*<-

We live in the air as fish do in water, but with this difference: we cannot leave the air, nor reach its surface as they do. Fish often jump out of the water or stay upon it, but we always have more than fifty thousand leagues <note>A league was a historical unit of distance, roughly 4 kilometers. The author's estimate of the atmosphere extending to the moon reflects 17th-century cosmological beliefs.</note> of air over our heads, for it extends to the Moon, and perhaps to the Firmament <note>The "Firmament" refers to the sphere of the stars in the traditional geocentric model of the universe.</note> and beyond. Now, since we do not see the air—which might be called the water or the sea of men and other animals, and which perhaps differs from water only in being thinner and lighter—it seems we can no best explain or understand the manner in which air moves when it sounds than by the way movements occur in water when bodies move within it and strike it with violence.

For one must not only imagine the movement seen on the surface of the water, when it creates circles that keep increasing from the place where a stone was thrown (which serves as their center) to the edge of the vessel containing it; one must also notice if it makes similar movements all the way to the bottom, and if these circles extend through the entire depth or solidity <note>By "solidity," the author means the three-dimensional volume of the water, rather than it being a solid state like ice.</note> of the water. This can be concluded as much by the Sounds made in the air as by those made in water, for they are heard equally from all sides—though it is more difficult to experiment in water than in air. In the air, rockets and fireworks that make their noise a hundred fathoms <note>A "toise" or fathom, roughly 1.8 meters.</note> high are heard equally from all sides, both above and below.

One can nevertheless perform the experiment in water: for if, among several people swimming underwater or diving, one rings a bell underwater and all hear the Sound—even though some have seven or eight fathoms of water above them and others only one or two—one can conclude that the circles seen on the surface of the water are similarly formed throughout the entire volume of the water. Consequently, both water and air create circles in every part of their depth when they are struck or pressed hard enough to make a noise.

Some imagine that the same portion of air that is struck and creates the Sound divides into an infinity of tiny particles, similar to the atoms of Democritus <note>Democritus was an ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that the world was made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms.</note>, which spread out in a circle to carry the Sound in all directions. But this is not necessary, and there is no reason that can persuade us that the part of the air which is struck detaches itself from the air to which it is...

### PROPOSITION VI.

->*Sounds have the same ratio among themselves as the movements of the air by which they are produced.*<-

If the nature of Sound is not different from the movement of the air, as I have said in the first two Propositions, it is not necessary to prove this sixth; but because several people add a new quality to the movements, I say that it is always true, whatever quality or intentional species <note>The "intentional species" refers to a Scholastic philosophical concept where the "form" of an object is transmitted through a medium to the senses without the physical matter of the object itself.</note> one wishes to add, insofar as it follows the differences of the movement of the air, which makes the Sound loud or weak, low or high, clear or obscure, following the different beats <note>The author uses "beats" (*battemens*) to describe what we now call frequency or vibrations.</note> of the air, as one experiences with the strings of instruments, and with organ pipes, whose Sounds appear lower the fewer times they beat the air, and higher the more times they beat it; so that if one compares two equal or unequal quantities of air, of which one is beaten four times while the other is beaten twice, one will perpetually find that the first Sound will be double <note>In musical theory, a 2:1 ratio (the "double") creates the interval of an octave.</note> the other, and that one will have as many degrees of high pitch as the air from which it comes has been beaten times: but I reserve the experiments of the strings for the book on stringed instruments, and those of the pipes for the book on Organs.

As for the other differences and circumstances of Sound, such as strength or weakness, they come from the same movement of the air being differently affected: for example, when two quantities of air are beaten as many times as each other in the same amount of time, the one that is larger makes a greater noise, which appears thicker, fuller, more massive and more filled; so that one can measure the thickness of the Sound, and say that it has all sorts of dimensions, just like bodies; insofar as it follows, or is, the movement of a body—namely the air, or other bodies whose movement is susceptible to Sound: for if the quantity of air being moved is very small, it renders the Sound small, slender, and thin: if its movement or its beats last a long time, it is long; if they last a short time, it is short, etc.

From this it follows that one can say of a weak and small voice, that it resembles a line, or a thread that has no "sustenance," just as one speaks of a line of water that flows gently through a channel; and that the voice which is strong and well-supplied, even though it be high-pitched, is similar to brass wire <note>original: "fil de leton"</note>, which is firm and hard, and which sustains itself: but I will explain all these differences more exactly in the Proposition that follows, and in the 16th.

## PROPOSITION VII.

### *Explaining how low and high sounds are produced, and what makes them loud or soft.*

Although I have spoken of these two differences in the preceding Proposition, they nevertheless deserve to be explained more fully, because they serve as the foundation of Music, which considers the low and the high of sounds more particularly than their other qualities. But it must be remarked here once and for all that these two terms *low and high*, which the Greeks call *low and sharp* <note>original: βαρὺ (bary) and ὀξὺ (oxy)</note>, signify that the Sound is hollow, deep, and low; or that it is high and pointed, if it is permitted to use these terms. For the French language is not yet so rich and fertile that it does not often need to borrow terms from the Greeks and the Latins, or to employ metaphorical ones when explaining the sciences. The Latins say *Heaviness and sharpness* <note>original: *Grauitas* and *acumen*</note>, and the Greeks *heaviness and sharpness* <note>original: βαρύτης (barytēs) and ὀξύτης (oxytēs)</note>, to signify the depth and the height of Sounds. We can say the "gravity" of the Sound, but we have no correlative word that signifies the contrary to express a "sharp" Sound, for "acuity" is not in common use. This is why we shall henceforth say the "low" (or gravity) and the "high" of the Sound (even though lightness is the opposite of gravity, and blunt the opposite of sharp) in order to accommodate our speech to common usage.

Now, there is no other cause for the gravity of Sounds than the rarity of the beats—that is to say, the small number of shocks and vibrations of the air. For sounds are lower as the number of beats is smaller; and because there are no "low" Sounds except in comparison to "higher" ones, and consequently one cannot establish a "low" Sound if one speaks simply and absolutely, it must only be noted that high sounds are made by a greater number of beats or vibrations of the air. No high Sound exists that cannot be considered low in comparison to one even higher, just as there is no low Sound that cannot be high if compared to one even lower. This reasoning is confirmed by experience with strings, whose Sound is all the more penetrating and high as their vibrations (or their back-and-forth turns) are more frequent, whether one uses a very thick or a very fine string, and whether it moves a little or a lot of air. From this it follows that a high Sound does not come from the speed of the movement, nor a low one from slowness, since it can happen that a movement fifty times slower will produce a Sound fifty times higher than another movement fifty times faster, as I demonstrate elsewhere; this is because a string of a Lute moves fifty times faster at the beginning of its motion than it does at the third or fourth <term>moment</term> after it has been touched. Here it should be noted that I use the word <term>moment</term> <note>The author is defining what we now call a "second."</note> to signify a very short time, which is equal to a second minute of an hour—that is to say, the 3,600th part of an hour—which corresponds to one "moment" or one beat of the heart or pulse, because this measure is suitable for explaining the measures and other circumstances of Music.

Now, this magnitude can be understood in three ways, following the three dimensions of bodies: namely, in length, in width, and in thickness.

Regarding length, one can say that of two strings equal in thickness, the one that is longer—and yet is in unison with the other—produces a Sound that is greater in length, because it strikes more air, by reason that it strikes a longer span of it, as happens with the longer strings of Theorboes <note>A theorbo is a large, bass lute with an extended neck carrying extra "bass" strings that are played open (unfretted).</note> played open, when they are tuned to the unison of the shorter ones. For example, when a thicker string strikes the air, as happens with the thick strings of a Lute, it beats a larger surface of air than a thinner string of the same length; but the density of the air corresponding to said surface is also greater, and consequently solidity always accompanies width.

Now, to return to the strength and weakness of Sound, one must conclude that they have the same relationship between them as the quantities of air that are struck the same number of times, provided the bodies are of the same material. Thus, a string which strikes four times more air in the same amount of time makes a Sound four times louder than one which strikes four times less; consequently, the strings of instruments sound all the louder as they move further from their straight line <note>This refers to the "amplitude" of the string's vibration; the further it is pulled or pushed from its resting position, the more air it displaces.</note>, as we shall demonstrate elsewhere. The same thing must be concluded regarding the Voice, which is all the stronger as the lungs send more air to the larynx.

But I encounter a difficulty here, which consists in knowing why the Sound of a string stretched in the air does not make such a loud Sound, or such a great noise, as when it is stretched over an instrument; and why a hemp string stretched on the same instrument does not make as much noise as a string made of gut or brass <note>original: *leton* (latten), a brass-like alloy used for strings</note>, even though they are all in unison, and equal in thickness and length, and they move as much air as each other. To which I respond that the string stretched in the air has only the "simple" Sound, which vanishes suddenly because there is nothing to hold it; whereas the string stretched on instruments has the preceding Sound (which one can call direct) as well as the resonant and reflected Sound, which is preserved in the hollow of the instrument and sent back by the soundboard <note>original: *table*</note>, which greatly reinforces the Sound. Now, one could explain in the books on instruments why, among several soundboards of equal size and of the same or different material, some resonate better than others, and why there are some instruments that are more muffled <note>original: *sourds* (literally "deaf")</note> and others more resonant; and similarly why different strings stretched in unison sound louder than others, even though they strike an equal quantity of air with equal speed. I will only say here that a portion of the air enters the pores of the hemp string, by which it is struck more softly, and that the quantity of small filaments on the surface of this string, or several other inequalities, render the Sound darker, softer, weaker, and more muffled: to which one...

### PROPOSITION VIII.

*Sound is not communicated in an instant, as light is, throughout its entire extent, but rather over a period of time.*

WE EXPERIENCE that all natural actions do not occur in an instant, nor in an imperceptible moment, and that there are some that require time. For example, heat does not penetrate an object unless it is predisposed to it beforehand; and light extends through its entire sphere of activity in an instant—or if it requires time, it is so brief that we cannot perceive it. However, Sound can only fill its sphere of activity <note>By 'sphere of activity,' the author refers to the physical area through which a sound wave propagates from its source.</note> over a period of time. This duration is longer as the location where the Sound is produced is farther from the ear. This is experienced in several ways, and particularly when one observes the axe or mallet of a woodcutter, or others striking an object: they have already struck a second blow by the time one hears the sound of the first. This occurs when one is five or six hundred paces away, or further.

Now, several experiments would need to be conducted to determine if the "slowness" of Sound corresponds to the distance traveled; for example, whether a Sound produced two thousand paces away is heard exactly two second minutes <note>At this time, "minutes" were often divided into "seconds" (second minutes). This refers to what we now simply call seconds.</note> after it was made, and whether it always maintains the same proportion in its delay. Because winds and the varying conditions of the air carry Sounds faster or slower, nothing certain can be established on this subject. Nonetheless, if one wishes to perform the necessary experiments, one should move half a league <note>A league was a common unit of distance, roughly 4 kilometers or 2.5 miles.</note> away and fire a musket or artillery piece, and then repeat this at a distance of one league, marking the time that passes from the moment the flash is seen until the shot is heard. Alternatively, if one wishes to use four stations, one should first move a quarter-league away, then a half-league, then three-quarters, and finally a full league, to see if each of these four equal distances delays the Sound by the same amount.

This experiment must be repeated several times, particularly when the wind is favorable or contrary, when the air is thick with fog and vapors, or when it is calm, clear, and serene. Afterward, one must observe the difference in the speed of Sound under these various weather conditions and note if Sound travels faster from top to bottom than from bottom to top, in an open field rather than across mountains or valleys, or over the water of rivers and the sea rather than over land, etc. Different locations cause significant differences in Sounds, as was noted during the <term>Siege of La Rochelle</term> <note>The Siege of La Rochelle (1627–1628) was a major military conflict between French royal forces and the Huguenots. It served as a significant site for contemporary scientific and ballistic observation.</note>, the records of which were very precisely kept by one of the Captains.

When one is on the same level <note>The author uses 'Horizon' here to mean a flat plane or level elevation.</note> as the place from which the shot is fired, and there is a valley in between, the shot is heard much better than if one were actually within the valley. On the second of February, between six and seven o'clock in the morning, a battery cannon was fired; the Sound was not heard until three seconds after the fire was applied, even though the Northeast wind carried the Sound, and the weather was se—

I will provide several other experiments with cannons when I speak of the force of Sound and the speed of movement made by cannonballs; for it suffices to note here the great variety in the speed of Sound, the experiments of which are very difficult to verify, especially since one cannot see the fire in broad daylight—which serves as a guide at night—and the smoke that one notices is not perceived as quickly as the flame. As for the night, the air is differently disposed than by day, which is why one cannot conclude that the speed of Sound occurring by day is the same as the Sound occurring at night. One might use another signal for the day: for example, one can raise a piece of scarlet cloth, or some other brilliant color that can be seen from far away. But one can make an objection here against the definition I gave of Sound in the first and second Propositions—namely, that if it is only a movement of the air, it should only be heard when said movement reaches the ear; and there is no appearance that it is faster than the initial movement of the bodies that produce it by their striking. Nevertheless, Sound travels much faster than said bodies, which is demonstrated by the movement of a lute string: its vibrations do not cover a space of more than one or two feet from the start until it comes to rest, yet one hears its Sound from more than a hundred paces as soon as it is touched. From this, it seems one must conclude that this Sound, which travels so fast, cannot be the movement of the air made by the vibration of the string—which has no other speed than that of the string—since they begin, continue, and cease with one another.

[third] species <note>The author is likely referring to "sensible species," a philosophical term from Scholasticism describing how sensory information—like sound or light—travels from an object to the perceiver.</note>; they have the same difficulty to resolve, especially since these species accompany and presuppose the movement of the air, and consequently they cannot travel faster than this movement. Secondly, the air, being very easy to move due to its fluidity and its lack of resistance, moves much faster than the bodies that set it in motion.

Now, one can observe the speed of the air's movement through the motion of musket balls, cannonballs, pall-mall balls <note>original: *boules de pas de mail*. Pall-mall was a popular 17th-century game, a precursor to croquet, where a mallet was used to strike a wooden ball through a high hoop.</note>, and several other bodies that are violently pushed through the air, and which travel as fast as, or faster than, the movement of the air caused by the gunpowder or the mallet. For if the ball flying through the air reaches someone five hundred paces away as quickly as the Sound made by the mallet, one can say that the Sound travels as fast as the ball; and if the musket ball travels faster—as one concludes when seeing birds fall dead from the branches of trees before the noise or the Sound of the shot is heard, even though the ear is close to the said musket—one can observe that the movement of the air occurring at the discharge of the powder is slower than that of the ball. It would further be necessary to examine if the movement of the powder or the mallet is as fast as that of the bullet or the ball, and assuming that the one who strikes lets go of the mallet (which keeps for some time the same motion given to it by the strike), whether it would travel as fast as the ball. This can also be applied to the arm and the hand that throws a stone or some other body into the air; for since these bodies have no other motion than that which they receive from the percussion, it is (it seems) necessary that the mallet and the arm move at least as fast as the missiles. Consequently, if the mallet left the arm, or if the arm left the body, both would move for some time through the air as fast as the ball or the stone; but this difficulty will be explained in the 13th Proposition.

### PROPOSITION IX.

->*Sound does not depend as much on the bodies by which it is produced, as light depends on the luminous body.*<-

It is very easy to prove this by experience, for even though the bodies that produce the Sound no longer tremble at all and remain motionless, those who are so far away that the said bodies stop moving before they hear the Sound they have made, still hear the Sound that is carried through the air while the bodies that made it remain still. And although the woodcutter may be resting, one nevertheless hears the blow with which he struck the tree or the wood, because the air that has been shaken does not stop as soon as the blow. It must be noted, however, that the Sound lasts almost but a moment when the bodies remain motionless, as one experiences with musical instruments: for as soon as one touches and stops the string of the Luth or the Viols <note>The Lute and the Viol (specifically the Viola da Gamba family) were the primary string instruments of the Renaissance and Baroque eras.</note> with a finger, one no longer hears the Sound, because the shaken air only strikes the ear in passing without stopping. The ear cannot easily notice the properties and circumstances of the sound unless it is struck several times, as I shall prove elsewhere.

One can nonetheless say that light cannot subsist in the air without the presence of the luminous body, because it is entirely attached to it just as heaviness is attached to stones; but Sound does not depend on the bodies by which it was made, because it does not serve as their property; for its own subject—namely, the air—is of a different nature, and continues to move long after the rest of the bodies by which it was moved and struck.

Certainly, if the air can only be illuminated when it is rarefied, and if rarefaction cannot happen without local movement, one can conclude that illumination or light is a species of movement; but a more particular consideration of this subject belongs to **Optics**, in which one must see if light is the soul of the air and of other <term>diaphanous</term> <note>Transparent or translucent.</note> bodies, and if it can be called the universal soul of the world, which is in some way similar to death when it is deprived of the said light.

To which I add that if one takes the air to be the body that produces Sound, then Sound depends as much on this body as light depends on the Sun, since it is nothing other than the movement of air, and movement cannot exist without the mobile object of which it is the movement.

### PROPOSITION X.

*Explaining why Sound is more subtle than light, and whether it reflects.*

It is easy to prove that Sound is more subtle <note>In 17th-century science, "subtle" refers to matter that is extremely fine, thin, and capable of penetrating other substances.</note> than light, since it passes through opaque bodies; for one hears Sound that is enclosed within vessels of earth, lead, iron, wood, and all other kinds of opaque materials, even though the rays of the Sun cannot enter there, and the light that is enclosed within cannot escape. From this it follows that a single sheet of paper placed between the eye and the Sun blocks its ray, but it does not block Sound, which passes through walls and penetrates opaque bodies as easily as <term>diaphanous</term> <note>Transparent or translucent.</note> ones, although both decrease its strength and vehemence. But it is difficult to know why light does not pass through opaque bodies as well as Sound does: for it has not yet been demonstrated that the <term>pores</term> <note>Early modern physicists believed all matter contained tiny holes or "pores" through which light and sound particles traveled.</note> and fibers of diaphanous bodies are more aligned with one another than those of opaque ones; and the parts of gold are at least as pure as those of glass. Furthermore, pores do not seem necessary to give passage to light, unless one first grants that light itself is a <term>body</term> <note>A "body" here means a physical substance that occupies space. This reflects the debate on whether light was a particle (body) or a wave/quality.</note> which cannot exist with another body in the same place; which is contrary to experience, which shows that all parts of a crystal or a glass are entirely filled with light that penetrates everything that is perfectly diaphanous, just as oil spread on paper or cloth leaves no part that it does not infect and grease.

This is perhaps what has given some Philosophers cause to believe that light is nothing other than a very clear and very subtle oil, which insinuates itself into all the illuminated parts of every body: but they would have to explain why light leaves no stain or trace after itself as oil does, and why it penetrates only diaphanous bodies, seeing as oil penetrates opaque bodies as easily as diaphanous ones. One can also say that Sound is more universal, for the reason that it moves and shakes all kinds of bodies, and that it carries itself as well into dungeons and darkness as into the brightest places: but I shall speak later of the other comparisons between Sound and light.

As for the reflection of Sound, one perceives it in the Echo of Bells, of Voices, and of other Sounds which respond two, three, or four times, and which teach that Sounds reflect like light when they encounter firm and hard bodies, whether diaphanous or opaque, which resist them, although the ray of the Sun reflects only from opaque bodies. ### COROLLARY.

If one wished to relate all the actions in which the ear is more subtle than the eye, and consequently all the instances where Sound is more subtle than light; it would be necessary to make an enumeration of all that one can hear and learn in darkness and at night, and of all that can enter the mind by means of the ear alone. Consequently, one would almost have to transcribe all the sciences that are found in books and in the minds of all the men on earth, provided that one excepts the science of colors and light. But this work includes several other things that serve this subject.

## PROPOSITION XI.

->*Sound represents the size and other qualities of the bodies by which it is produced.*<-

Experience shows the truth of this Proposition, for the gravity <note>In this context, "gravity" refers to the depth or low pitch of a sound.</note> of Sounds follows the size of the bodies by means of which it is produced, as one sees in the thickest or longest strings of spinets, the lute, and other instruments; in the largest organ pipes, in the largest bells, in the largest cannons, and in all sorts of bodies. So that one can conclude that bodies are always larger when the noise they make is bigger, more hollow, deeper, and more muffled, as happens with the waves of the sea, which make a larger noise than those of brooks and rivers. This happens similarly with deep voices, which testify to the size of the vocal artery <note>The author refers here to the trachea or windpipe.</note> or the size of the glottis, as I will show in the book on the Voice.

Sound also represents other qualities of bodies that make it clearer, or darker and more muffled; cleaner or more confused; harsher or softer, etc. This is because it is very difficult to find two bodies whose qualities are perfectly equal, even if they are of the same material and same size. From this it follows that Sound can serve to notice the difference between all sorts of bodies, even though the other senses judge them equal, as one experiences with several <term>pistoles</term>, <term>quarts d’écu</term> <note>These were common gold and silver coins in 17th-century France.</note>, and other coins, which are so equal in weight, size, and shape that the eye notices no difference, and yet they have their [distinct] Sounds

### PROPOSITION XII.

*To determine the proportion by which Sounds diminish from the place where they are first made until they cease entirely.*

Since all natural agents produce their effects in the form of a circle or a sphere, and since light can serve as our model for speaking of other natural qualities, it must be concluded that Sound spreads equally in all directions, just as a drop of oil does when poured onto a sheet of paper or cloth, or like the ripples created in water when a stone is thrown into it, and that Sound diminishes as the distance increases. Now, the surface area of these spaces increases as the squared ratio <term>raison doublée: a geometric term meaning the square of the ratio of the distances; this describes what we now call the Inverse Square Law</term> of the distance of the Sound from the bodies by which it was first produced; consequently, the Sound diminishes in a geometric proportion, as I demonstrate by this figure, which represents a part of the sphere of activity

that must be attributed to Sound, in which A represents the place where the Sound begins. geometric, and there is no reason that prevents this manner of diminution from applying to Sounds, since they extend and diminish as naturally as the aforementioned light, and they act upon the hearing just as light acts upon the eye, it is reasonable to conclude that they diminish in geometric proportion—that is to say, proportionally across equal spaces. But to understand this diminution, one must note that the actions of natural causes can, first, diminish equally across equal distances; this would happen if a fire heated four times more at four paces than at sixteen, and if its heat always diminished by an equal part over an equal distance. Now, we call this an *Arithmetic* proportion, because its differences are equal. Secondly, they can diminish unequally over equal distances—as when we say that light is four times weaker at 20 paces from a candle than at 10 paces—or equally over unequal distances, such as if the light were only twice as weak at 40 paces as at 10 paces, and as the distances increased in a double ratio, the light diminished only by equal parts. In the third place, they can diminish proportionally through proportional spaces, as would happen to light if it diminished in the same geometric proportion as the intervals; that is, if at 20, 40, and 80 paces it became weaker by 20, 40, and 80 parts than it is at 10 paces. I do not wish to add the fourth manner, <unclear>which</unclear> has no regulated proportion, because one cannot have knowledge of it, even though it might apply to Sounds due to all the fluctuations of the air.

Now, it is easy to judge which manner we should assign to Sounds, assuming that the air is equal and uniform; for since it follows the ratio of the planes through which the Sounds pass, and the distances are in a <term>sub-duplicate ratio<note>A historical mathematical term meaning the ratio of square roots. The author is suggesting that as the distance increases, the intensity decreases in a way related to the surface area of the expanding sound wave.</note></term> of their planes, their diminution belongs to the first part of the second manner.

If someone had an ear good enough to discern how much stronger or weaker a Sound is at all kinds of distances, it would be easy to choose the true diminution. For if they found it half as strong at 20 paces as at 40, and four times stronger at 10 paces than at 40, the diminution would occur in the same ratio as the spaces increased. This, it seems, cannot happen, because equal causes would not act equally, and the weaker would act more powerfully than the stronger, as can be demonstrated by these two lines, each of which is divided into three equal parts.

Now, the same must be said of the *augmentation* of Sounds, which is similar to composition and multiplication, just as diminution is similar to division.

## COROLLARY.

When it has been posited in Theology in what proportion <term>grace</term><note>In this context, "grace" refers to the divine influence operating in individuals for their regeneration and sanctification.</note>, merits, and the other virtues of the **Just** increase, it is very easy to perform the calculation. For if the grace of those who cooperate with all their power increases in geometric proportion—for example, in a double proportion—one must double the first term (which signifies the first grace) as many times as there are actions. For instance, if a **Just** man cooperates twenty times a day with the grace of God, he will have at the end of the day 243,902,008,171,709,440,000 degrees of grace, insofar as this number is the 20th term of a double progression <note>Mersenne uses these staggering numbers to illustrate the power of geometric growth, though his specific calculation here suggests a much higher rate than a simple doubling of 20 steps; he likely refers to a more complex cumulative progression.</note>, which can always be doubled until one has as many terms as there are actions.

By this, **Musicians** may know how much they would merit if they never sang or played instruments without dedicating all their actions to the honor and love of God; and consequently, how much they multiply their sins when they dedicate them to vanity, or perform them with evil intention.

# On the Nature and Properties of Sound.
<meta>catchword: harmo- (likely "harmonique" or "harmonic")</meta>

...150 <term>lines</term><note>A "line" (ligne) was a traditional French unit of measure equal to 1/12 of an inch.</note>, while the pulse beats once, and the Sound of the string reaches as far as forty paces, each of which is two and a half <term>King's feet</term><note>The *pied de Roi* (King’s foot) was the standard unit of length in pre-revolutionary France, measuring approximately 32.5 cm—slightly longer than the modern English foot.</note>; consequently, Sound is faster than the movement of the body by which it is produced, for 150 lines do not even make thirteen King's feet.

And if one removes the space of the diminution of the returns from the first until the 150th, one will not even find six feet for all the movements of the said string: now, forty paces contain more than three times six paces, which is why one can conclude that Sound travels at least three times faster than the movement of the bodies by which it is produced. But the reason for this greater speed of Sound must be taken from the nature of the air, which always moves at the same speed, regardless of the violence it endures at the beginning. For whether it is struck as forcefully as a cannonball or thunder, or whether it is struck as weakly as a Lute string, or by the larynx and the lips, the Sound it makes always travels at the same speed, as long as the air carrying the Sound remains the same; because air has a certain disposition to always move at an equal speed after it has been struck, much like a Lute string, whose vibrations always maintain an equal speed, no matter how strong an impression one may apply to the said string, as long as it has the same tension. Thus, one can call this disposition of the air "tension," since there is nothing that serves us better to explain the uniformity of its movement: though it seems that this solution contains another great difficulty—namely, that the Sounds of all strings ought to be in <term>unison</term><note>In music, unison occurs when two or more notes have the same pitch or frequency.</note> with one another, since they are made by an equal movement of the air, and because Sounds have the same ratio among themselves as the movements by which they are produced, as I stated in the sixth Proposition.

To which I respond that it does not follow that all movements of air are equal in all things, even though they are equal in speed; the air that makes or carries a <term>high</term><note>original: "aigu" (acute or high-pitched)</note> Sound is shaped, figured, or moved differently than that which makes a <term>low</term><note>original: "grave" (deep or low-pitched)</note> Sound, whether the circles of air carrying the high Sound are more frequent and closer to one another, or the small shocks of air strike the eardrum more often—just as the string making the high Sound strikes the air more often than the one making the low Sound. This is true even though the movements of the latter may be much faster than those of the former, as happens when one compares the beginning of a low Sound with the end of a high one, which may be made by a movement a hundred times slower than the low one, as I shall show elsewhere.

It must therefore be noted that the high pitch of a Sound does not come from the faster movement of bodies or the air, but from the frequency or speed of the returns or reflections of the said air, or of the bodies that strike and divide it. This is perhaps why it is said that the object of Music is the <term>sonorous number</term><note>The concept that musical pitch is fundamentally based on mathematical ratios and the frequency of vibrations.</note>, because Sound is higher-pitched the more times the air is struck, and the number of these beats is nothing other than the low and the high pitch. The ear cannot judge the tone it hears unless it has been struck as many times by the air as the air was struck by the string or other bodies. Thus, one can say that the action of hearing is nothing other than the counting of the beats of the air, whether the soul counts them without our perceiving it, or whether it feels the number that touches it: for Plato believes that the soul is a harmonic number...

### PROPOSITION XIV.

->*To determine whether Sound passes through transparent and opaque bodies, and how it is aided or hindered by all kinds of bodies.*<-

I propose this problem to explain how Sound passes through wood, stones, metals, and other bodies, after having assumed the experiments which show that the noise of bodies enclosed within other bodies is easily heard. For if one encloses a stone or some other object in a glass vial, or in some vessel made of wood, tin, stone, or other material, and they are sealed so tightly that the air cannot escape, one easily hears the noise made inside. Furthermore, if one gently strikes the end of a beam that is fixed into the two walls of a hall, one hears the strike at the other end of the beam, even though the walls enclose the beam and prevent the outside air from entering the hall and carrying the Sound to the other end from the outside.

Now, I stated in the second Proposition that Sound made in enclosed places, such as between four walls with no openings, is communicated to the outside by the vibration of the walls. These are so shaken by the internal air that they impress a similar movement upon the external air, which carries the Sound to the ears. If the Sound is so weak that it cannot shake the walls or the other bodies containing it, then it cannot be heard from the outside. But because many cannot imagine that a man's voice, or other noises heard through these bodies, are powerful enough to shake them, one might add that the communication of internal Sound occurs by means of the air held within the <term>pores</term><note>Small microscopic gaps or passages within a solid material.</note> of the wood, metal, walls, and other bodies through which the Sound is heard. Consequently, the internal air of these bodies is often as easy to move as the external air. This is experienced with beams: if one strikes the end so lightly that the Sound cannot be heard in the open air along the length of the beam, it can still be heard at the far end of said beam if the ear is pressed against it—even if the beam is very long and so enclosed that the external air cannot carry the Sound along its sides.

This shows that all parts of the beam have been shaken by the blow, or that the internal air contained in its pores receives the movement from the outside, or perhaps that the Sound is carried by <term>intentional species</term><note>original: "especes intentionnelles". In medieval and early modern philosophy, these were thought to be non-material forms or "images" of a sensory stimulus that traveled through a medium to the senses.</note>, which penetrate all kinds of bodies just as spirits do. However, it would be necessary to test whether all types of wood, when struck at the end, carry Sound as easily as others; and if stones and metals do the same; and finally, to what degree some carry it more easily than others. For if the most porous materials carry it further, or make it more perceptible, even if they are longer and heavier, we must conclude that the air in the pores moves and creates the Sound. Because internal air is part of these bodies, the air in each pore makes the part of the wood separating one pore from another vibrate (assuming that the pores are not continuous, but are separated from one another by means of small membranes,

However, the cavities must be proportioned to the force given to the Sound from the start, which must be large enough to shake the entire mass of air and overcome all other obstacles; for our Sounds do not make the entire **Sphere of the air** resound (though it is very difficult, and perhaps impossible, to know if each Sound fills and shakes it) because it is too vast and they are too weak.

Nevertheless, if one assumes the size of the air and the quantity that a given voice fills, and that voices always shake a quantity of air that is greater as they are stronger, it is easy to conclude what the strength of the voice must be to shake the entire mass of air up to the <term>Firmament</term><note>In 17th-century science, the "Firmament" referred to the expanse of the sky or the heavens.</note>, as I have shown in the 44th **Physical question**.

It seems that if two weights fall upon a bell—for example, two hammers striking a clock—the one that weighs twice as much makes a **Sound** twice as loud. However, it is easy to be mistaken in this matter, for it is possible that the lighter weight will make a louder **Sound** if it is better proportioned to the bell than the heavier one, as I shall demonstrate in the **Book of Bells**. But since it is sufficient here to suppose that two or more **Sounds** can be diminished or increased according to a given ratio, and that the magnitude and strength of the **Sound** follows the quantity of air that is struck (as I have already said), I add that the **Sound** must be four times as strong to have its <term>sensible sphere</term><note>The "sensible sphere" refers to the three-dimensional area around a source in which the sound can be perceived by the ear.</note> doubled. Since the sphere of light maintains this proportion, and we have nothing more perceptible and better regulated in Nature than light, we can align the proportion of other things with its own.

This is why I conclude that just as one must join four candles of the same size to provide as much light when moving twice as far away as one would with a single candle, one must similarly strike four times as much air at the same time to hear the **Sound** from twice as far away. This means that the ratio of the strength of **Sounds** must be the <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>Original: "raison doublée." In early modern mathematics, this refers to the ratio of the squares. If the distance doubles (2:1), the area—and thus the required strength—increases by the square (4:1).</note> of the ratio of the distances. For just as four surfaces of flame (each equal to the flame of a single candle) are needed to fill the base of a cone double in height with as many rays and as much light as the base of a <term>sub-double cone</term><note>Original: "cone sousdouble." A cone with half the height of the larger one described.</note> is filled by a single candle, likewise the strength of the **Sound** that must fill the base of the double cone must be four times as great as that of the **Sound** which fills only the base of the sub-double cone. This is because these two bases are in the duplicate ratio of the height of their cone, as can be seen in this figure, in which **A B C** represents the cone illuminated by a single candle. **A E G** is the cone double in height; the line **A D** is the height of the smaller one, and **A H** is that of the larger one.

Consequently, four times as many rays of light or **Sound** are required to fill the base **E K G** as are needed to fill **B F C**.

## ->Of the nature and properties of Sound:<-

For instance, one must put four lights together, because four equal lights placed together are sustained across a surface that is only double the surface of one of those lights taken separately and in particular. For one must consider light as a body, inasmuch as it is never without a physical body that serves as its vehicle and subject. However, because **Sounds** cannot unite in the same way as light, light serves more to highlight their imperfection or their irregularity than to make one understand their nature and properties; although one can say in general that the strength of **Sound** exists in a <term>duplicate or sub-duplicate ratio</term><note>Original: "en raison double, ou sousdoublée." In the mathematical language of the time, a "duplicate ratio" refers to the square of a value. This is an early description of the inverse square law: if the distance doubles, the intensity of the sound or light is reduced to a quarter, requiring four times the initial strength to compensate.</note> of the distances. That is to say, it must be four times stronger to be heard equally from a double distance, and that the same **Sound** is four times stronger when it is heard from twice as far away.

As for the second part of the Proposition, it supposes that **Sounds** are made by different bodies in various places; because they do not unite among themselves as a single, whole, and total cause, and because they produce their effects separately, one does not hear them further away simply because they are greater in number, even if they are all of equal strength. This does not happen with light; for four separate candles illuminate the same space more strongly than when they are joined together, inasmuch as they have a greater surface area (as is demonstrated in **Geometry**, since four cubes, each of one foot, have much more surface area than the single cube that contains all four of them) and they unite their strengths just as well as if they were all joined together—which does not happen with **Sounds**.

Now, one can here relate several comparisons used by those who explain the 52nd Problem of the 11th Section, and the 2nd of the 19th Section of **Aristotle**<note>The *Problemata* (Problems) attributed to Aristotle was a widely studied text in the Renaissance. Section 11 deals with the voice and Section 19 with music.</note>, and particularly those of the circles made in water when one throws in one or more stones. For even though the circles are stronger and appear more prominent at the beginning when one throws several stones than when one throws only one, they do not extend further just because the number of stones is greater. Similarly, if seven or eight people joined their strength to throw a stone, it would not go 7 or 8 times further than when it is thrown by a single man, even though each of the others has an equal strength.

From this, it is easy to conclude that the union of forces spoken of in **Mechanics**<note>In this period, "Mechanics" referred to the study of simple machines (levers, pulleys) and the mathematical rules governing physical force.</note> is different from the union of **Voices**, since mechanical force increases by the union of several distinct forces as if there were only a single force containing them all. It is likewise different from the union made by grains of wheat or sand, which are seen from further away when all together than when each is seen alone; for one can see a heap of these grains from two leagues away, even though one cannot see a single grain from a hundred paces. But one cannot hear the **Sounds** or the voices of several people from two leagues away, even if the voice of each could be heard from a hundred paces, and even if there were as great a multitude of voices assembled as there are grains in the said heap.

It is nonetheless a certain thing that several equal **Sounds** make more noise and are heard from further away than one of the said **Sounds**, but it is difficult to know by how much this distance is greater, and to perform the experiments that are necessary to decide this difficulty.
