# PROPOSITION XVI.

->*To determine if Sounds have all kinds of dimensions, namely length, width, and depth, and what the other properties, or <term>Accidents</term><note>In the philosophical language of the time, "accidents" refer to the non-essential characteristics of a thing, such as its color, size, or sound, rather than its fundamental essence.</note> of Sound are.*<-

Although the three dimensions of quantity are found only in physical bodies properly speaking, one can nonetheless observe them in physical accidents, particularly when they follow said dimensions, and when they strike the senses differently when the quantity or shape of the bodies is different; this is what happens to **Sounds**, as I have already remarked, for they are thin and slender when the bodies from which they are produced are thin and subtle: but they are thick and massive when the bodies are large and thick, as one experiences with the strings of instruments, and with organ pipes.

Now, the first dimension, which consists of a simple length, can only be considered in Sound in two ways: namely, when it lasts for a short or long time, or when it comes from a very small body, for example from the <term>highest strings</term><note>Original: "chanterelles." The thinnest, highest-pitched string on a lute or similar instrument.</note> of the Lute, and from the smallest strings of the <term>Spinet</term><note>A small, plucked keyboard instrument, a precursor to the piano.</note>; from this it follows that it penetrates easily, because it is subtle like the edge of a knife, and sharp like a needle.

The first manner is the foundation of all the measures and tempos used in Music and in Rhetoric, and consequently in the **Rhythmics** of the Ancients, which varies the tempos in a great multitude of ways, as I shall show elsewhere.

As for the width of Sound, it is more difficult to explain, especially since we have no instruments consisting of different widths that are not at the same time accompanied by different depths; nevertheless, one can say that Sound is wide when the body from which it comes is wide, since it follows the characteristics of the bodies by which it is produced. And then Sound can be called wider when it is stronger, as happens when one sings in the same tone once louder than the other: although this difference belongs rather to the strength of Sound. But one can still find another manner of this width in the thickness of Sounds, which consists of being fuller and more massive in the same tone, which happens when the <term>Soprano</term><note>Original: "Dessus." The highest vocal or instrumental part.</note> and the Bass sing in unison: for the sound of the Bass is much more massive and fuller; this always happens with the voices of Basses, which cannot sing in unison with the Soprano or with the other parts without being fuller and better supplied. This is similarly observed in strings, where the largest has a wider and fuller Sound than the smallest, even though they are in unison. Now, although one might say that this quality of Sound belongs to depth, since it makes it more massive and corpulent, nevertheless, one reserves this depth to explain the <term>gravity</term><note>Original: "grauité." In historical acoustics, gravity refers to the heaviness or low pitch of a sound, the opposite of "acuteness" or high pitch.</note> of Sound, which consists in the slowness of the movement, and which is the reason why we say that the voice of a man singing Bass is hollow, low, and deep, and that he has a good depth of voice.

This is why one can call the Sound deep, or low, and high, or acute, because of the bodies which are large and thick, or small and thin; although one

### Of the nature & the properties of Sound.

...one could say that Sound is all the thicker, denser, and more massive when it is higher in pitch, if we measure this thickness by the multitude of movements, just as we measure the density of bodies and of light by the multitude of parts and rays; for Sound is all the more high-pitched as it is produced by a greater multitude of movements occurring at the same time. But we shall speak further of these dimensions in the treatise on the bodies of the instruments that produce Sound. This is why I turn now to its other <term>accidents</term><note>In 17th-century philosophy, "accidents" are properties or characteristics of a thing that are not essential to its existence but define its current state, such as color or texture.</note>, which are almost as numerous as the external differences of the bodies that produce them, many of whose properties have not yet been recognized.

Now, among the qualities of Sound, all of which depend on the manner in which bodies press, rub, and strike the air, those that give names to **harsh, sour, rough, sweet, clear, muffled** sounds, etc., are the principal ones after the low and the high pitch. As for the others that bear the character of the bodies by which they are produced, one cannot establish a formal science of them because they are almost infinite in number. For if the surface of a body has even a single pore that is not in the surface of another body, they will produce different Sounds, even if they are perfectly similar in all other things; this is because the pore in one causes the body to strike the air differently than if it did not have said pore. The same must be said of the small hollows or bumps found in many bodies, because the effect is always different when the cause introduces some difference into its production.

As for the **roughness** and **sourness** of Sounds, they come from the inequality of the surface of the bodies that strike or divide the air, as happens with the noise made by filing iron or some other metal. For the file breaks the air into as many parts as it has grains and bumps; and when the divided and broken air strikes the <term>spirits</term><note>Following the medical theories of Galen and Descartes, "animal spirits" were thought to be a subtle fluid that traveled through the nerves to transmit sensory information to the brain.</note> of the auditory nerve, it imprints its movement upon them, which gives them as much displeasure as harsh flavors give to the tongue, or as rough, coarse, and poorly polished surfaces give to the touch. From this comes the fact that the pronunciation of words signifying this quality has something unpleasant about it, in order to naturally represent what it signifies, as one perceives when pronouncing (*brute, rude, aſpre [harsh], etc.*) because of the letter R. But I shall speak of pronunciation and the meaning of words in the book on the Voice, where I shall show whether there can be a natural language.

The quality of *roughness* is difficult to explain in Sounds, and particularly in the Voice, because one cannot see how the air breaks or divides itself in the larynx and the glottis, or in the palate and other parts of the mouth of those who have harsh and rough speech. It seems, nonetheless, that all these qualities that make Sounds unpleasant are nothing other than the deformity of the movements of the air. Sound is sweet when it moves uniformly, and it is rough, harsh, and sour when it moves in two or more different ways at the same time. This can be proven by the Sound of two or more flutes or Organ pipes that are slightly distant from <term>unison</term><note>When two notes are "out of tune" or not in unison, their sound waves interfere with each other, creating a "beating" effect that sounds harsh to the ear.</note>; for even though their Sounds taken individually and separately are sweet and agreeable, they are nonetheless rough and disagreeable when joined together, because their movements strike [the ear] differently...

### PROPOSITION XVII.

->*To determine why one hears better at night than by day: and if one can know how much hot air is rarer and lighter than cold air: and how much lighter it is than water.*<-

One must first assume the truth of the experience, which everyone seems to agree upon: namely, that one hears better, more distinctly, and from further away the sounds and noises made at night than those made during the day. However, it would first be necessary to experiment in places far removed from noise, such as deserts, to see if a sound made there would be heard from further away and more clearly. This is because the multitude and confusion of different noises occurring during the day in cities, or in other inhabited places—whether by men, birds, or other animals—prevents one from distinguishing sounds as easily by day as by night. From this, one can derive one of the reasons why one hears more clearly at night than by day. For the ear is less attentive to any particular sound when it is filled with other sounds, a trait it shares with the eye, which sees one of the points of its object more confusedly when it gazes upon a great multitude of things at the same time. The other reason reported by Aristotle in the 33rd Problem of the eleventh Section <note>Aristotle, *Problems*, Book XI, Section 33.</note> is taken from the fact that the eye and the other senses are distracted and occupied by their objects while it is day. From this, it follows that the ear is not as capable of hearing, because the multitude of spirits that serve it at night are dissipated and distributed to the other senses to serve their actions; for the ear is less suited to perform its functions when it has fewer spirits.

But we must see whether, all things being equal on the part of the ear, and the air being no more troubled by day than by night (as might happen in places four or five leagues distant from all types of noise), the night alone is the cause of hearing sounds more easily due to some new disposition of the air. Anaxagoras believed, according to Aristotle's report, that the sun's rays make noise during the day by heating and <term>rarefying</term><note>Rarefaction is the process of making air less dense; Anaxagoras theorized that this process created a "noise" that masked other sounds.</note> the air, and that this noise, filling the ear, prevents it from hearing other sounds. Now, although this opinion is rejected by many, it nevertheless has some appearance of truth if one assumes that illumination occurs through movement, since one can consider sound to exist wherever one encounters movement; and because one cannot demonstrate that the sun's radiation...

But it is easy to prove all these answers false if one examines the experiment of the said thermometer and several others like it. Therefore, one must conclude that the air is thicker at night than by day, whenever it is hotter by day than by night; for if one compares a warm night with a colder day, the air of that night is rarer than that of the said day. From which it follows that one ought to hear sounds more distinctly on that day than at night, if the density of the air is the reason one hears the sound being made more clearly. But because it is almost impossible to recognize whether the thickness of the air is more suitable than its thinness for aiding sounds, I think the best reason why sounds are better heard at night than by day is that the mind is not so distracted at night as by day, and that it occupies itself more strongly with what it embraces. From this it comes that the pain of the sick is more troublesome and harder to bear at night than by day, because the mind attaches itself solely to the consideration of the pain, from which it is not diverted at night by the different multitude of objects—unlike the day, which seems much shorter and more bearable due to the visits of friends and the occupation of the other external senses, which withdraw the mind from the pain.

The second part of this Proposition contains a very great difficulty, namely how much rarer and lighter air is than water, which has not yet been known until now. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the density of air and its physical properties. It moves from general observations about air to specific experimental methods for measuring its weight relative to other substances like water and gold, referencing the principles of Archimedes.</meta>

<header>### Book One</header>

This is experienced in all sorts of bodies, which are heavier as they are more **compact** in themselves, and as they have more parts within an equal space; for example, gold is twice as **dense**, more full, and more compact than iron, and nineteen times denser than water; from this, it follows that it is twice as heavy as the former, and nineteen times as heavy as the latter, and consequently that it would require nineteen times as much water, and twice as large a volume of iron as gold, to weigh equally. And if the air which expands in the **Thermometer** <note>Original: "Thermometre." Here referring to a thermoscope, which used the expansion and contraction of air to indicate changes in temperature.</note> fills twenty parts, each twentieth part will be twenty times lighter than the same air when it is reduced to a space twenty times smaller by **condensation**. Now, one will find the comparison of two different airs—for example, a cold air and a hot air—if one prepares two large boxes, or crates of very light wood, one of which can be closed and sealed so tightly that air can neither leave nor enter: and the other remains always open, and both are of the same weight. For when they have been weighed in a cold and condensed air, such as that outside in winter when it freezes, and when this air has been enclosed in one of the boxes, if they are brought into a room where the air is two or more times warmer, and consequently more **rare** <note>In the scientific language of the time, "rare" or "rarefied" meant the opposite of dense; it refers to air that has expanded and become thinner.</note>, and they are weighed again, one will find that the one in which the dense, cold air is enclosed will weigh more than the one which is open, and whose air is equal in rarity to that of the room.

From this, one will easily conclude how much more one weighs than the other; for example, if the enclosed air weighs one ounce more than that of the room, and each crate contains four cubic feet of air, one can say that the enclosed air weighs two ounces, and that of the room one ounce, assuming that the **Thermoscope** demonstrates that the air of the said room is twice as rare, and consequently twice as light, as that of the outside. And then one can compare the weight of these two kinds of air to water, and to all other bodies, both liquid and soft, as well as hard; for example, if a cubic foot of water weighs 90 pounds, it will be 720 times heavier than the outside air, and 1440 times heavier than that of the inside; and because gold is to water as 19 to 1, it will be 2,736 times heavier than the air of the room.

One can also use another means, namely a large piece of wood, which must be placed in **equilibrium** in the air of the room; for if a piece of lead is twelve times smaller than the piece of wood, and one weighs both in the outside air which is twice as cold and dense, and consequently heavier, these two weights will no longer be in equilibrium. For the piece of wood, being twelve times larger than the piece of lead, will press upon and displace twelve times more air; and consequently, it will be lighter in this air than in the other, by the total weight of the air equal in volume to the said piece of wood. For example, if it takes four cubic feet of air to equal the wood, and this air weighs one ounce, the said wood will weigh one ounce less outside than it did inside, as <term>Archimedes</term><note>The ancient Greek mathematician and physicist. The author refers here to the principle of buoyancy.</note> demonstrates in the seventh Proposition of the treatise he wrote on **Solid bodies** <note>Original: "corps Solides." Referring to Archimedes' work *On Floating Bodies*.</note>, which one weighs in liquid or moist bodies. But I shall speak again of the weight of air and water in several other places.

## PROPOSITION XVIII.

->To determine why one hears sounds from outside better when one is in a room, than one hears those made in the room when one is outside.<-

It is a certain and proven fact that one hears much more clearly the noises made outside when one is in a room, or when one is <unclear>enclosed elsewhere</unclear>, whether one closes or opens the windows, than one hears from outside the noises made inside the room, even though they may be much larger and louder than those outside, which occur in the open air. This is why <unclear>Aristotle</unclear> <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), the Greek philosopher whose "Problems" (Problemata) served as a foundation for scientific inquiry in the 17th century.</note> proposes this difficulty as a definite observation in the 37th <unclear>Problem</unclear> of the eleventh Section, though there are several details that require new experiments: for example, one would need to test how much louder the noise and sounds made inside houses must be than those outside to be heard equally, and by how much noises made in rooms parallel to the outside ground are heard more easily than those made in high chambers and other elevated places.

Now, one might say that sound from outside is heard better from within because the air entering through the windows undergoes several reflections and is reinforced, as if it encountered some place suitable for creating an echo in the room's air, which it moves and to which it imparts a greater <term>vibration</term> <note>Original: "branſle." In early modern science, this referred to the physical shaking or oscillation of air particles that we now call frequency or vibration.</note> because it cannot escape its confining prison; this happens even if the windows are closed, but not as noticeably as when they are open. It should be noted, however, that outside noises are heard less as one moves further from the windows, especially if the distance is off to the side toward the corners of the room.

But when one is outside, noises from inside the house are heard only with difficulty and often with confusion, because the sound inside reflects several times against the walls of the room before exiting, and that which exits in a straight line is in small quantity and has difficulty moving the entire mass of the outside air. Furthermore, those who are outside are most often on a lower level than the room, which prevents the sound from going directly to them. Many other reasons for this effect can be considered, but because they depend on the different circumstances of the place where the sound is made and heard, each person can discover them by considering the layout of each location.

And if one wishes to judge different locations, when they are equally distant and make an equal angle with the straight line that serves as the axis for the voice and the Sound, one will hear equally, provided that reflection does not favor one more than the other.

### PROPOSITION XX.

->*Sounds hinder and harm each other when they meet.*<-

This can be understood in several ways, for a weak and slow Sound can meet with a strong and hurried Sound, as when a man’s voice is weak, or when it meets with a strong voice, or when a low voice meets a high-pitched one; similarly, two or more high or low voices, weak or strong, can meet. Now, voices and Sounds hinder each other in all these ways, as one experiences when two or more people speak at the same time. As for different lights, they help rather than hinder each other; for if one places two candles at the two ends of a room or a table, one sees more clearly in the middle of the two than one sees in the same place if one candle is removed; and if there were a second Sun in the West on the horizon when ours begins to rise, we would see more clearly than we do. Nevertheless, the meeting of different lights has something similar to that of Sounds; for just as a greater Sound prevents us from perceiving the lesser, which it swallows and suppresses, so the greater light hides the lesser from us, as one experiences when lighting a candle in the middle of the day. This happens similarly to all the objects of the other external senses, which can be so preoccupied and affected by one of their objects that there is no more room for others, as is noted with odors which are sometimes so bad, that they

The eye can similarly be so filled with light, the tongue with flavors, and the sense of touch with cold or heat, that the eye will see nothing else, the tongue will be unable to taste any other flavor, nor the touch any other object: for all the senses are so limited that they cannot pass the boundaries prescribed for them. In my opinion, one can say that unison Sounds hinder each other the least of all, particularly if they are equal in strength and in all other things, because this great conformity makes them embrace, unite, and maintain each other rather than destroy each other; although one could say that they hinder each other more in that they cannot be distinguished from one another, due to the perfect union they have together—being similar to two equal lights that mix so perfectly that one cannot discern one from the other. One can say the same thing of two heats, two smells, or two similar flavors, and even of two friends, if we move into the realm of morality, who are so similar in their actions and their wills, when the friendship is very perfect, that they seem almost like the same thing; so that friendship is the cause of equality, or identity, unless identity or equality is the cause of friendship: this is observed in Sounds that form a unison and unite together, because being equal and almost the same thing, they preserve and reinforce each other mutually.

One can also say in this manner that all Sounds that form some musical chord <note>Original: "accord de Musique."</note> hinder each other more than dissonant ones, inasmuch as they blend better together, and it is more difficult to discern them from one another than when they are dissonant; for they unite as much as they can and approach the <term>Octave</term> <note>The most perfect interval in music after the unison, where the frequency of one note is exactly double the other.</note> from which they are distant, or the unison, which is similar to friendship, which is the limit of all the perfections of the world. But if one speaks of the hindrance that Sounds receive from each other insofar as they fight and are contrary, the more they are dissonant, the more they offend the ear and the spirit—which, being a friend of peace and rest (which are the causes of all kinds of good), holds the contrariety and combat of Sounds in horror, unless it be a spirit that takes pleasure in disorder and discord, such as the spirit of the damned, which is in eternal disorder and desires all things to be like itself: from this comes the belief that Music and its consonances can only displease an ill-formed and disordered spirit, such as one who allows themselves to be too easily carried away...

The same thing is observed in Choirs, where the Divine Office is sung in unison, for the strongest voices cover the weakest and prevent them from being heard; and the Sound of drums, large bells, <term>tan mills</term> <note>Original: "moulins à tan." Industrial mills used to grind oak bark for leather tanning, known for being extremely loud.</note>, or paper mills, and generally all kinds of great noises and violent Sounds prevent weaker and smaller Sounds from being heard and distinguished.

### PROPOSITION XXI.

->*Sounds, and consequently voices, can serve to measure the earth, and to make known news of what occurs throughout the world in a short time.*<-

This Proposition is very easy to conceive if one considers that Sound is not carried in a single moment, that it needs time to pass from the place where it is made to the edge of the sphere of its activity, and that one can know the distance from which it can be heard. We find an example of this in <term>Cleomedes</term> <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 2nd century AD) known for his work on the circular motions of celestial bodies.</note> in the second book, where he says that the King of Persia had stationed men from <term>Susa</term> <note>An ancient city of the Persian Empire, in modern-day Iran.</note> all the way to Athens, when he was making war in Greece, so that they might make known to the Persians what was happening in his army. These Messengers were placed on high places and received the voice from one another in such a way that all kinds of news were known within the space of two days, or forty-eight hours. I know that one can use other ways to make news known as quickly as by the voice, for torches can serve for that, which was similarly practiced by the Persians, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The text refers to "De Mundo" (On the Universe), a treatise formerly attributed to Aristotle but likely written later.</note> testifies in the book of the world, chapter 6, where he says that Cambyses, Xerxes, and Darius used torches to know everything that was happening in Asia, as if they had been present everywhere. He means to say that they used Doves at the **Siege of Leiden** to carry news. It is held that those who went to see the performances at the theaters began these messages made by Doves, which they carried in their bosoms, in order to send word to those who remained at home about what was happening at the theater. The Sailors of Egypt practice the same thing, as do those who live between Gaza and Cairo, according to the reports of Belon and Botero. Swallows and Crows can also carry letters, as Marrhen, King of Egypt, showed in Aelian’s *On the Nature of Animals*, Book 6, Chapter 7. But I do not wish to amuse myself by recounting all the ways one can use dogs, cats, other beasts, and birds to carry letters, so that I may return to the **sound** of which we are now speaking. Sound seems to have some advantage over other methods—if not in speed and subtlety, at least because it explains thoughts better, particularly when one speaks. The **Trumpet** can also serve for speech, but the shots of a **cannon** can be heard from much further away; these can be used to warn those who are far removed from all that is happening where one is, as is done at sieges, battles, and other enterprises to give a signal and to command whatever pleases the leader of the army. I leave aside other Sounds, such as those of the **Drum**, <term>Arquebuses</term> <note>An early type of long gun or portable firearm.</note>, Whistles, and Bells, which are used in Cities in times of war to warn the guards of the number of men appearing in the countryside.

Now I say that with all these Sounds, or with whichever one you wish, one can measure the distances of the earth; for knowing from what distance the Trumpet or the Bell can be heard, one will know how far away it is. One can so moderate, soften, and weaken the Sounds that they will measure whatever distance one desires. For example, if the Sound of the Drum is heard from a league away, one could strike it so softly that it is only heard from a hundred paces. It would be more difficult to weaken the Sound of the cannon, because it cannot make a noise unless there is a certain quantity of gunpowder; and if one gives too little wind to Trumpets and Cornets, they will not be able to sound. One can find through experience and reason how much one must diminish the wind or the strike so that the Sound is only heard from a given distance. Those who wish to <term>survey</term> <note>Original: "toiser." To measure or survey distances.</note> by Sounds could establish an art by means of certain instruments, some of which would be heard from six feet, others from 20, from 100, from 1000, and so on.

Now, to send news by means of Sounds, and to know the **speed of the voice**: for example, how many minutes pass from the time the Sound is produced until it is heard at a league, a half-league, a hundred paces, fifty paces, or some other distance, it is necessary to perform several ex-

# Book One

...experiments, and that the one who speaks or produces some sound be seen by the one who is far away, and that he makes some sign with a staff, or with his hand, or in some other manner at the same time that he produces the sound. This is so that the person measuring the speed may know how much time has passed from the moment the signal was given, or from the production of the sound, until the sound was heard by the one far away. The one who speaks, or who produces the sound, can also observe the time if the other person indicates by some sign the moment at which he begins to hear the sound. But the experiment will be easier and more certain if a third person marks the signs and the time, because the one who speaks and the one who marks the time can be hindered or distracted while speaking or making the sign; indeed, the more people there are, the more certain the experiment will be, for they can compare their observations and take a proportional average between those whose results are in dispute.

The movement or beating of the heart could serve as a measure of time, for respiration is more uncertain than the beating of the pulse, since it depends more upon our will. Let us suppose then, for example, that a natural, well-tempered <term>pulse</term> <note>The author is using the human heartbeat as a biological stopwatch, a common practice before the invention of accurate pendulum clocks or stopwatches.</note> beats three times before one hears a sound made five hundred paces away; one could afterwards measure a minute of time by the various beats of the pulse, in order to know how far the place where the sound is made must be to be heard within one minute of an hour. For if one has knowledge of this minute and of the distance, one can conclude how much time is required to make news known throughout the whole world by means of sounds or the voice. I know that the various dispositions of the air, the winds, and the locations on the earth can bring about a great variety in this. But the difference in this speed is often imperceptible within the space of five hundred paces, although one hears the sound with more or less intensity depending on the winds that hinder or help it. I suppose now that the pulse beats three times before one hears a sound made at 500 paces, and that there are 66 beats of such a pulse in one minute of an hour; I say then that the pulse beats at least 18 times before one hears the sound of a cannon, an <term>arquebus</term> <note>An early type of long gun or portable firearm.</note>, a trumpet, a bell, a hammer, thunder, or some other instrument located one league away from us. Consequently, a sound that was strong enough to be heard across the entire earth could only be heard in the time it would take for the pulse to beat 129,600 times—that is to say, in one whole day and eight hours, 43 minutes, and nearly 42 seconds. From this, one can conclude how many days would be needed to hear a sound from the Antarctic Pole to the Arctic; for since there are 14,000 diameters of the earth <note>This figure is likely a printer's error or refers to a non-standard geographic calculation of the era.</note>, each of which has 12,291 leagues, it would take fourteen thousand times as long to hear a sound from one Pole to the other as it would to hear it across the entire diameter of the earth. But sound cannot last so long, nor be so strong that it can be heard from so far away, unless God should wish to produce such a sound; which He will perhaps do when the Angels sound the Trumpet on the great Day of Judgment to call all those who are dead. Now, it is necessary to add the time that messengers spend speaking together and communicating news to one another, and to know how far the posts, or voice stations, are located from each other: these should only be 500 paces apart, so that there are six in every league.

As for the time that messengers spend speaking to each other, one can take one minute...

### PROPOSITION XXII.

->*One can make use of the sounds of every musical instrument, and the different move-*<-
->*ments given to them, to discuss all manner of subjects, and to*<-
->*teach and learn the sciences.*<-

This Proposition is excellent, for it teaches the manner of discussing all things while playing instruments, even if the one who touches them or hears them played is mute. For one can converse with another by playing the Organ, the Trumpet, the Viol, the Flute, the Lute, and other instruments, without anyone being able to understand the discourse except the one who knows the secret, which can be practiced in several ways.

In the first place, if the instrumentalist and the listener use a <term>tablature</term> <note>A system of musical notation that tells a player where to place their fingers on an instrument rather than indicating pitch.</note> that contains all the letters of the alphabet: for each sound will express each letter. For example, the three notes, or the three voices found in <term>G, re, sol, ut</term> <note>original: "G, re, sol, ut." These are the names of notes in the Guidonian hexachord system; here, G is the "gamma" or ground note.</note>, could serve for these three letters R, S, V, etc. And the listener, having his Lute or his tablature before his eyes, will clearly see the words that the player forms with the sounds of his instrument, to which he can respond by playing another instrument. But it is easy to speak together without a tablature if one uses the eight or fifteen sounds of a mode—for example, those of the first mode for the first fifteen letters, and the eight sounds of the second mode for the rest of the letters; or if the twenty joints of the <term>harmonic hand</term> <note>A mnemonic device, also called the Guidonian Hand, where different parts of the human hand represent different musical notes to help singers learn scales.</note> express the twenty letters of our alphabet; for one can omit S, Y, and K, as we shall say elsewhere.

There are a thousand other subtleties and industries that can be found by means of sound; and two or more people can become so accustomed to the sounds of instruments that they will speak familiarly of anything they wish without anyone being able to understand them. One can even express words and entire sentences through sounds, for preludes, the sequence of airs and songs, and the arrangement of modes and the <term>perfect system</term> <note>The "Greater Perfect System" was the foundational scale of ancient Greek music theory.</note> resemble orations and harangues, particularly when the

A musician creates cadences and passages quite appropriately, and uses <term>Rhythmics</term> <note>The study or theory of musical rhythm and poetic meter.</note> according to the subject they are treating. Now, this manner of discourse can be practiced across the entire reach of Sound—that is to say, across a distance of one hundred or two hundred paces and more—for one hears the sound of the Trumpet from much further away. Consequently, Sounds can serve as messengers and secret letters when the person to whom one wishes to write back is only half a league or a league away, from where one can hear Bells or the Trumpet.

One can also make use of the Drum, even though the Sound it makes is not capable of harmonic intervals; for the variety of <term>Rhythmic movements</term> <note>Rhythmic patterns or "feet" borrowed from classical poetic meter.</note> with which it is customarily beaten can serve as characters. For example, one can use the five beats of the fourth <term>paeonic movement</term> <note>A musical or poetic foot consisting of three short beats and one long beat.</note>, which is represented by three shorts and one long (o o o -), for the first four letters A, B, C, D; and the first type of the same movement, which is the previous one reversed (- o o o), for the four letters that follow, namely E, F, G, and H. The "dissolved" <term>Choriambic</term> movement, or <term>Pyrrhic-anapaest</term> <note>A complex rhythmic foot of four short beats and one long.</note>, which is composed of four short movements and one long, can express I, K, L, M, N. Some call this the *French* movement, as the French ordinarily use this movement when they beat the Drum, as seen here: o o o o -. O, P, Q, R can be expressed by the <term>minor Ionic</term> movement, where the first two movements are short and the last two are long, as seen here: o o - -. The Swiss use this when they beat the Drum. Finally, the <term>Choriambic</term> movement, where the first and last movements are long and the second and third are short, as seen here: - o o -, can complete the alphabet by expressing these last four letters S, T, V, X. One can use these same movements on Bells, Trumpets, the Lute, the Viol, the Organ, and other instruments, and adapt them to torches and every kind of signal that can be perceived by the eyes, ears, touch, imagination, and reason.

But one can practice the same thing more subtly by expressing everything one wishes—whether in French, Hebrew, Greek, Spanish, Italian, or any other kind of language—with four different Sounds or movements, which can be varied in twenty-four ways to serve as twenty-four letters. For the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 being multiplied by each other make twenty-four different combinations <note>The author is describing the mathematical principle of factorials: 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24.</note>, which are found in the four aforementioned movements, and in every set of four different things. The reason for this is that as many changes are made in each place as there are things proposed, and each thing can be placed as many times in each row or place as the next lowest number can be changed in its frequency. From this, it follows that three movements can have six different changes, since two change twice; for the third can be placed twice at the beginning, twice in the middle, and twice at the end. And if one adds a fourth movement, it will be found six times in the first place, six times in the second, six times in the third, and six times in the fourth place.

The same thing is observed in the beats of a drum: when the pyrrhic-anapest <note>original: "pyrrhichianapeste." A rhythmic pattern combining the pyrrhic (two short beats) and the anapest (two short followed by one long).</note> movement is played, one sees the French soldiers march; the Swiss, however, march to the ionic minor <note>original: "ionique mineur." A rhythmic foot of two short beats followed by two long beats.</note> movement. But we shall speak more fully of Rhythmics <note>The study of rhythm and meter.</note> and the effects that different movements of sounds have in the treatise on rhythms. These rhythms are common to all sorts of sounds, and consequently to the voice and to speech, which must have different movements according to the different passions that carry us away, or that we wish to display.

From this comes the idea that rhythmic movements are called the soul and the force of sound, just as the various figures of Rhetoric are the soul of an oration. For just as the iron or steel that "arms" a magnet <note>original: "l’aymant." It was believed that placing steel caps on a lodestone (magnet) focused and multiplied its attractive force.</note> multiplies its strength and vigor—unless one believes that they merely demonstrate the magnet's power, which it could not express without their presence—so too does rhythmic movement multiply the force of sound. When it is rapid and light (that is, having many brief durations, such as dissolved choriambs <note>original: "Choriambiques dissous." A choriamb is a long-short-short-long foot; "dissolved" refers to breaking the long beats into shorter ones.</note> or pyrrhic-anapests), it increases the power of the sound so significantly and powerfully that it would be difficult to believe if one had not experienced it.

The second part is also proven by experience, which shows that a vessel made of good metal—such as that used for bells—or a silver vessel, has a sound more penetrating and lively than a leaden vessel. Those who play the Spinet <note>A small, harpsichord-like keyboard instrument.</note> notice that strings of gold or silver produce a different effect than ordinary ones. The same thing could be tested with Trumpets made of gold, silver, steel, and all sorts of metals, or of horn and wood, in order to note the difference in sounds across all types of Trumpets, Organ pipes, Flutes, and Flageolets <note>A small flute-like woodwind instrument.</note>.

It would also be necessary to experiment with every species of string on Lutes, Viols, Lyres, and Harps, and to make these instruments from all sorts of woods, horns, and metals, in order to observe the diversity of sounds. If the shell of a Drum were made of gold or silver, and the skin were that of a Bear, a Tiger, or a Lion, the sound of the Drum would be different from the ordinary one.

The third part is further proven by experience: for when one strikes a body gently, the sound made by the blow does not strike the spirits <note>In 17th-century science, "animal spirits" were believed to be fluids in the body that transmitted sensations to the brain.</note> with such force, and does not excite them as powerfully as when it is louder and more violent. This violence is sometimes so great that the sound causes one to lose their hearing, deprives listeners of their reason and judgment, disturbs or spoils the wine in cellars, causes children to die in their mothers' wombs <note>Reflecting the early modern belief that intense vibrations or "shocks" to the air could physically harm a fetus or affect fermentation.</note>, and breaks the glass in house windows, etc., as is experienced with the noise of thunder, artillery, bells, winds, and storms.

# On the Nature and Properties of Sound.

...as the ratio of the side of a double cube relates to the side of its half-double, the sounds produced by the said strings relate to one another as lines do; consequently, they represent the **squaring of the circle** and the **doubling of the cube**. <note>The "squaring of the circle" and "doubling of the cube" were two of the three great geometric problems of antiquity, involving the construction of shapes using only a compass and straightedge.</note> One must conclude the same for all other types of lines and bodies, even if they are **incommensurable** and **irrational**, <note>Incommensurable magnitudes are those that have no common measure, such as the relationship between the side and diagonal of a square.</note> which can be represented by sounds of the same proportion. But if one hears these sounds together, they create **dissonances** that will be as unpleasant as the strings (or the lines the sounds represent) are irrational. From this, it follows that the dissonances arising from sounds made by strings incommensurable in length are not as harsh as those made by strings incommensurable in power, <note>original: "incommensurables en puissance." This refers to magnitudes whose squares are incommensurable with each other.</note> because the latter are more difficult to comprehend than the former. Now, it is easy to represent all of **Geometry** in this manner by means of sounds, but it is even easier to represent **Arithmetic**, insofar as all numbers are measured by unity, and consequently, they are all commensurable.

One can see in the treatise on the **Lute**—on which the tone is divided into two semitones, and the Octave into twelve equal semitones—how much the **consonances** and **dissonances** of this division differ from those following the harmonic proportion of numbers, which I explain in several places; and how much sounds following **arithmetic proportion** are sweeter than those following **geometric proportion**.

It is also quite easy to conclude that one can represent everything in the world, and consequently all the sciences, by means of sounds. For since all things consist of weight, number, and measure, and since sounds represent these three properties, they can signify whatever one wishes—with the exception of **metaphysics**, which separates all propositions from sensible and intellectual matter, refining them to such a point that they allow us to envision the sovereign beauty of the **Being of beings**. <note>original: "l’estre des estres." A philosophical and theological term referring to God as the ultimate source of existence.</note> From this it follows that the perfect musician can invent dictions and a perfect language that naturally signifies things, and that he can teach the sciences without using any language other than that of a lute or some other instrument, as I shall show more fully elsewhere. And if someone had an ear good enough and learned enough, he could discern and recognize the proportions of all types of lines by means of sounds; consequently, he could explain all the propositions of geometry by playing whatever instrument he wished, or by singing, provided he could do with his voice everything that can be done on instruments. But there is no man who has an ear delicate and subtle enough for this task, unless it be the perfect musician who has not yet appeared.

But the former [the squaring of the circle] has not yet been encountered, or at least it has not been published, although several have come very close, and Molther... <note>original: "Molther." Likely referring to Johann Molther (1591–1633), a German mathematician and physician who wrote on mathematical problems.</note>

To which he adds that we have the **squaring** <note>The "squaring of the circle," or determining the area/circumference of a circle in relation to a square.</note> in more precise terms than those of **Archimedes**, when one takes three times the diameter and the fifth part of the line which subtends a quarter of the circle; this is because the size of the circumference found by this method is 314,142, which differs from what he believes to be exact by only 17. In contrast, the measurement of **Archimedes**, which places the circumference at three and 1/7 times the diameter, <note>The common approximation 22/7.</note> is off by 126. And if one takes his other, more precise measurement, namely three times the diameter and a **ten-seventy-firsts part** (71), <note>original: "vne surdixpartissante 71." This refers to Archimedes' more accurate ratio of 3 10/71.</note> it is off by 74—which is to say four times more than the other method, which only misses by 17 out of 314,159.

### COROLLARY II.

If the ratio of the **vibrations**, or the returns of the string, is the same as that of the length of the strings—as we shall show in the following book—it seems that the number of returns for a string equal to the **diagonal of a square** must be **incommensurable** to the number of returns for a string equal to the side of that same square. Thus, we could provide as many **irrational numbers** between them as there are incommensurable lines; consequently, **Music** can achieve more than **Arithmetic**, equaling **Geometry**. One might respond that each vibration or return is a movement, and that none of the movements of these two strings are commensurable and rational—or at least that there are two which can have no common measure—unless one takes the **power** of these movements like that of the lines, and says they are commensurable in power. <note>In 17th-century mathematics, "commensurable in power" meant that the squares of the lengths shared a common measure, even if the lengths themselves did not.</note> Now, one may also see the 34th Question of the *Physicomathematics*, in which I show whether one can establish a new science called **Psophology**, <note>From the Greek *psophos* (noise). This was a term proposed for the scientific study of sound.</note> and several other difficulties of which I treat in this work, which will serve for the understanding of this Proposition.

### PROPOSITION XXV.

### *To know in what way Sound is different from light, and in what way it is similar to it.*

We have already shown some of the differences and resemblances that exist between **Sound** and **light**; for example, that Sound is not communicated in an instant like light (in the eighth Proposition); that it does not depend as much on the bodies by which it is produced as light depends on the luminous body (in the ninth Proposition). We have also shown in other propositions how Sound is more or less subtle, if it reflects in the air, and if it increases or decreases like light; so it is only necessary here to supply what has been omitted.

I say, then, first, that just as light makes the different colors of bodies appear to us according to the different angles of incidence and reflections it makes upon their surfaces, **Sounds** similarly make the different qualities of bodies appear by means of the movement of the air which touches and strikes their surfaces. One might say that colors are nothing more...

2. **Light** is invisible just like **Sound**, for we see only colored surfaces which represent, as much as they are able, the **Sun** or other luminous bodies. This is proven by polished mirrors, which represent the Sun so perfectly that it is difficult to distinguish the reflection from the true Sun; indeed, if all bodies were equally polished, one would see nothing other than the Sun, no matter where one looked. Now, it is easily proven that light is invisible in itself by the light gathered at the focal points where concave mirrors and lenses of glass or crystal burn; this light cannot be seen at all unless it is reflected by opaque bodies that make it visible. Furthermore, one could just as well say that no **accident** <term>accident: In historical philosophy, a property or quality (like color or sound) that cannot exist on its own without a physical "substance" or body to hold it.</term> is perceptible any more than light is, except by means of the bodies that sustain these accidents and give them the extension <note>meaning physical dimensions or size</note> they can only have through **quantity**. If quantity were taken away, they would perish or be reduced to a single point, unless the Author of Nature performed a miracle similar to that by which He can place and preserve all bodies in the same location, and reduce the entire world into a single point.

It is in this way that **Sounds** make the movement of the air perceptible, and they allow us to notice several qualities of bodies that we could only know through them. If one considers the nature of light very attentively, one will perhaps find that it is nothing other than a movement of the air which carries with it the image of its "first mover"—namely, the luminous body—to make it perceptible to the eye under the name and appearance of color or light; similarly, **Sound** is nothing other than the movement of that same air, which carries with it the qualities of its efficient cause—namely, the bodies that move it—of which it makes us grasp the image under the name and appearance of Sound. And just as one could tell how many pores and rough or polished parts are in the surface of bodies that reflect light if one knew the number of reflected rays and the way each one sinks and immerses into the solid mass of the bodies and reflects back to the eye; likewise, one could know all the inequalities of the surface of bodies that strike the air if one knew all the properties of the movement of the air that strikes the ear in the form of Sound.

### COROLLARY.

It is easy to find the other similarities and differences between Sound and light if one understands what I have said in this Proposition and in the others: this is why I only add that one can imagine that all creatures are similar to movement, as their perpetual changes and alterations testify. ## PROPOSITION XXVI.

->*To explain how the Echo, or the reflection of Sounds, is produced.*<-

I have already shown in the tenth Proposition that Sound reflects; therefore, it is only necessary here to explain how it reflects, and consequently how the Echo is formed. This would be very easy if the reflection of Sounds occurred like that of light, which Geometers regulate in Catoptrics <term>Catoptrics: the branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light, especially by mirrors</term> according to the different angles of incidence of the ray falling upon bodies with flat, concave, and convex planes. But because air is subject to several foreign movements, which often prevent it from traveling in a straight line—which does not happen in the same way to light—it is not possible to regulate Echoes as infallibly as the reflections of light, although we must use them to explain those of Sounds.

For one must always take what is more constant and better regulated to relate it to what is more variable, so that the rule and measure may be certain; since one cannot reason properly if one does not have some assured principle and some firm and unshakable point upon which the discourse is supported, like the balance on its center, in order to examine by right reason everything that falls under discussion. I say then, first, that Sound reflects according to the angles of incidence it makes on the bodies which

### Of the Nature and Properties of Sound.

<note>The author addresses "Orcade," a reference to an Oread or mountain nymph, personifying the Echo as a female spirit.</note> Oread, you will excuse me for not having demanded from her the rent for the woods, meadows, rivers, gardens, houses, and mountains that she occupies. For this bad debtor often left her lodgings, or hid herself to say she was not there. This greatly tormented her creditor for a month, who never ceased looking for her morning, noon, evening, and night, in fair and foul weather; for he always watched her, spying for the opportunity to speak to her. This usurious Nymph has informants everywhere, and great correspondences in the woods, riverbeds, marshes, islands, cellars, churches, bell towers, streets and long stretches of walls, wells, farmyards, manure pits in the middle of farms, wine presses, and courtyards filled with barrels, canals, aqueducts, underground works, arbors, plaster vaults, ruins, large open spaces like ports and pastures, arches of gates and bridges, rocks and the enclosures of hills and high mountains. What I have been able to learn from the Echo is as much as a Mariner could do, searching for a New World with his Compass, whose trembling assures him more than all the guides he could have.

The manner of researching the nature of this image of the voice is twofold: namely, by operation and practice, or by speculation and Philosophical Theory. Theory is drawn from the three principles of generation—namely matter, form, and privation; or from the four causes, or the universals, or the ten Categories <note>These are standard tools of Aristotelian philosophy used to categorize all things in the universe</note>. Practice consists of walks, where two pebbles struck against each other serve to spare the voice, while noting the resonances that act as the preparations, the precursors, and the harbingers marking the lodging and the dwelling of the Echo. And then one uses a geometric plan to trace the figure of the places, using the Geometric pace of five Royal feet <note>original: "pied de Roy," a French unit of length approximately 32.5 cm</note>. One then follows step by step what one seeks in all parts of the Sphere of activity, where there is more or less strength, until one arrives before the reflecting body, to see what the vocal line is, at what point it begins to act, where it ends, what time is most suitable for the Echo, and what the intervals of pronunciation and repetition are—using a watch in hand <note>original: "monstre à la main," an early portable timepiece</note>, or using circular arm swings to mark the difference in pauses and intervals. But at the end of the day, I recognize that it requires another Pan—that is, a man more universal than I in all sorts of other knowledge—to catch this fugitive,

> *Who flees to the willows, and wishes to be seen before [she arrives].*

and who is not known otherwise than by pursuing her in her flight and in her den. As for the quantity and the length of the <term>vocal line</term> <note>the path sound travels</note> of the Echo, I find that to clearly hear a two-syllable word, a distance of twenty-five to thirty <term>toises</term> <note>An old French unit of length, approximately 6.4 feet or 1.95 meters</note> is required, and the location must not be wide open, but enclosed by some continuous wall or ditch. I encountered another echo at one hundred <term>geometric paces</term> <note>A "pas géométrique" was roughly 5 feet</note> which is a bit weak, feeling exhausted by the length of the journey through brushwood, hedges, old ruins, cottages scattered here and there without any order, trees, palisades, gardens, and the farmyards of estates; this sound finally ends in the corner of a building full of openings, which has earth piled against it up to half its height. This echo repeats 4, 5, 6, and seven syllables or more, briefly though distinctly, such as *colintampon*, *Abednego*, *the amerabaquin*, *parafaragaramus*, and *I sing of arms and the man* <note>original: "arma virumque cano," the famous opening line of Virgil’s Aeneid</note>. Our **Echometry** <note>the science of measuring echoes</note> has an advantage not found elsewhere, not even in optics: namely, that it passes not only through transparent mediums, but also through all kinds of opaque bodies. This echo is accompanied by many other Echoes, which speak first according to their shorter distance, borrowing nothing from one another. When the voice is directed to the South, the woods and the dwelling—which is quite resonant—begin the sound; then, depending on the force of the one who cries out along that same vocal line, the other echo from behind the house, which belongs to the river and the willows, repeats. There is one twenty-five <term>toises</term> to the side that says nothing, no matter what noise one makes, having no communication whether one stands parallel to it or tries to cross its path. But if one turns the face to the Southwest between the two Echoes, one hears three or four, each repeating according to its range. There are two that repeat all at once, without one being able to clearly distinguish their intervals. I found an Echo sixty geometric paces along a street that strikes a bell tower eight <term>toises</term> high; it repeats two or three syllables, which it pronounces distinctly and clearly without much force. And if one raises the voice, one awakens another echo in a house built in an L-shape <note>original: "en potance," referring to a gallows or bracket shape</note> in front of a farm. There is yet another in a wine press, with a courtyard and a thatched-roof house, built on three sides near a resonant street; it is sixty-four geometric paces away and repeats three or four syllables, provided they are pronounced quickly, for the interval between the repetition and the pronunciation is imperceptible.

The Echo consists only of a relation, since at least two terms are required for this "image of the voice." Another person with more leisure than I have could expand upon the parallels between Optics and Echometry to show the affinity and the relationship between the two. The action is no less admirable than all else that could be said of the Echo, in which one can examine both the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary source that sets a change in motion; here, the human voice</note>, the way it is formed, and the effects it can produce. Regarding the first, we have no doubt that the human voice is the cause of the **articulated Echo**, after the air from the lungs, having exited, successively imprints upon another air whatever pleases the man, who plays with this Element as well as he does with everything here below.

By this, one sees that from every <term>Category</term> <note>Referring to Aristotle’s Categories, the basic classifications of things that exist</note> one learns what belongs to the Echo: now if one considers <term>Dioptrics</term> <note>The study of the refraction of light through lenses</note> and <term>Catoptrics</term> <note>The study of the reflection of light from mirrors</note>, one will find a great conformity between our lines of action serving the Echo and both the broken or refracted ray, which passes through bodies, and the consideration of the reflected ray. But to create the Echo, a certain strength of voice is required, which, after searching here and there, returns from where it started—if not along the same vocal line, at least within the quarter-circle where the speaker stands. This is what **Aristotle** wished to teach in his second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de l'Ame," referring to Aristotle's "De Anima"</note>, where he represents the reflecting body like a hollow vessel, which is susceptible to everything, or like a ball, which, being pushed against a solid body, returns to the side from which it was thrown, with as much violence as the one who throws it pleases. It is from this shock and this collision of air that the Sound arises, which gave the Indians that **Panic terror** of which **Polyaenus** speaks in his *Stratagems*.

**Pausanias** says that the Megarians gave **Diana** the name of **Guardian** <note>Original: "Gardienne," referring to the title Artemis Soteira (Artemis the Savior/Guardian)</note> for this reason: while the Persians were ravaging Greece and their country, having addressed an Echo during a dark night, they believed it was the enemy responding with mournful cries. They fiercely attacked a resounding Rock, upon which having launched all the fury of their courage and their spears, they were captured the next day and led away as captives; and the others fleeing toward Thebes to **Mardonius** recognized the effects of a deceitful Echo, which gives fear to one while giving pleasure to another who knows how to make good use of it, such as for Music, and to make the voice clearly heard without much shouting.

She says that men would seek her and follow her as much as she had followed and run after them, promising to take her revenge upon the waters, upon which she would cast and grind charms that, by their magical accents, would torment her Narcissus and those who had despised her.

What do you think of this Poetic discourse? One still sees the place in which they immolated <term>Hecatombs</term> <note>A grand public sacrifice, originally of one hundred oxen</note>, the reverberation of which made the sacrifice seem larger than it was. # On the Nature and Properties of Sound.

...to great halls and places of leisure, where one might desire it.

As for Churches, if it serves to help a Preacher be heard, it also interrupts and disturbs him greatly by breaking his speech through its reverberation. Dandinus <note>Likely Girolamo Dandini (1554–1634), a Jesuit scholar and traveler.</note> says that he heard one in a country house in the Milanese territory that repeats up to twenty times; Majolus <note>Simon Maiolus (1510–1597), a bishop and author who wrote about natural wonders in his work "Dies Caniculares."</note> speaks of one in the hall of Pavia which responds as many times as there are windows in the said hall; but it would be desirable if they had provided a description to aid the science of the Echo.

Saint Clement of Alexandria, in the sixth book of his *Tapestries* <note>original: "Tapisseries," referring to the "Stromata" or "Miscellanies," a major work of early Christian philosophy and knowledge.</note>, speaking of the miracle God performed with the sounds of Trumpets and with fire when He gave the Law to Moses, and disputing against the incredulous, alleges several prodigies drawn from natural history to show that the Author of Nature is no less powerful than nature itself. He reports that in England there was a mountain open at the top, and below it a great cavern, in which, when the wind rushed in, one heard a Sound of harmonious chimes by favor of the vents, folds, and sinuosities of the said cavern. And following this, he relates what is found in the history of the Persians: namely, that there are three mountains in a flat plain, situated such that in approaching the first, one hears only confused voices shouting and brawling; at the second, the noise and clatter is even louder and more violent; and at the third, one hears only songs of joy and rejoicing as if they had conquered. It is thus that the air, according to the diversity of the subjects, forms a diversity of prodigies, which the human spirit admires while seeking their causes so as to admire them no longer. You see, therefore, that our Echoes delight in mountains, although cellars have their share, despite what some say—that they serve only as a vehicle to carry them more easily.

As for the time in which the closer Echoes are formed, it is difficult to gain any knowledge of it, for Music has no <term>hooked notes</term> <note>original: "notes crochuës," referring to eighth notes (croavers), which were among the fastest notes in musical notation at the time.</note> fast enough, nor pauses or breaths that can measure them. At 120 <term>geometric paces</term> <note>original: "pas geometriques," a historical unit of distance roughly equal to five feet or 1.5 meters.</note> I found one that responded the word in the time of one minute regulated by a watch; another time I found the same ratio between the pronunciation and the interval of the entire repetition as there is between sixteen and twenty: for when it takes sixteen instants to pronounce the word, it takes twenty others for the interval of the entire repetition, until evening when the air begins to thicken. But when there are fewer trees, houses, and gardens to cross, it returns more quickly, as I have experienced with an Echo of sixty and seventy geometric paces.

The most suitable part of the day for examining the Echo is the evening, at Sunset between five and six o'clock. In October, I find it much better than at other times, for at noon and at one, two, three, and four o'clock, the heated air is too thin and weak, and cannot receive any impression from the Echo; and if it resounds, it is not as well as if it had its necessary temperament and a bit of body; nevertheless, at night and during fogs, there is no way to hear it.

After having moved our Echo through eight <term>predicaments</term> <note>Refers to the Aristotelian "Categories" (predicaments) used in classical logic to classify all things.</note>, I encounter its local difference and its situation from right to left, in which it does not always respond as clearly as it does along the perpendicular vocal line:

## PROPOSITION XXVII.

*To determine what are the distances and lengths of the vocal line of the Echo; if one can know the place from which it responds, and of what length the said line must be to produce an Echo of as many syllables as one wishes.*

If Sound loses no part of its force by its reflection, one must divide its vocal or sonic line into two equal parts, one of which begins at the place where the Sound is made, and ends at the body that reflects it, and the other begins at the reflecting body and ends at the ear that receives the Echo. Thus, if the Sound is strong enough to be heard from a thousand paces in a straight line, the body that creates the Echo can be five hundred paces away. For example, if the entire vocal line is from A to B, when the Sound meets the reflecting surface D E at point C, it will reflect until point B: for the angle of incidence A C D is equal to the angle of reflection B C E; and the Sound coming from point A cannot arrive at point B by a shorter path than through lines A C and C B.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled with letters A, B, C, D, E, H showing the physics of sound reflection. A horizontal line represents a reflecting surface with points D, C, and E. A vertical line extends from C up to H. Lines from A to C (incidence) and from C to B (reflection) create equal angles (ACD and BCE) against the surface DE.</image-desc>

Now, several difficulties are encountered here, the solution to which depends on experience: for example, namely whether the Sound that begins at point A travels faster along the line of incidence A C than it returns along the line of reflection C B, and by how much it goes faster or slower than the other. 2. How far one must be from the reflecting body to hear the Echo. <term>Blancan<gloss>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who studied acoustics</gloss></term> has remarked that one must be twenty-four geometric paces away, or thereabouts—that is to say, forty-eight common paces—to hear the slightest Echoes, which are called <term>monosyllables</term>, because they respond with only a single syllable, for the reason that other syllables return too quickly to the ear and are confused when they meet the others. # Of the Nature and Properties of Sound

It has been experienced that an Echo responds with one syllable at twenty-two geometric paces, <note>A "geometric pace" typically refers to five feet, whereas a common pace is roughly two and a half feet.</note> but one can still perform several experiments to shorten this path.

As for Echoes that respond with 2, 3, 4, etc. syllables, they must be 2, 3, or 4 times further away; and consequently, one that responds with an entire verse,

> *I sing of arms and the man, who first from the coasts of Troy,* <note>original: "Arma virumque cano Troiæ qui primus ab oris," the famous opening of Virgil's Aeneid.</note>

or any other similar Latin or French verse that has fifteen syllables, must be three hundred and thirty geometric paces away, if one allows twenty-two paces for each syllable. If one makes portable Echoes using <term>wooden boards<gloss>ais: planks or shutters used to reflect sound</gloss></term>, one can observe all these distances more exactly, and at the same time determine how many times the voice can make itself heard. <term>Blancanus<gloss>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who studied acoustics.</gloss></term> does not believe that they can respond twenty times to a word of two syllables, as they say the Echo of Milan responds, which is called the *Simonetta*; <note>The Villa Simonetta in Milan was a famous architectural marvel known for reflecting a sound up to 30 or even 40 times.</note> from which it would follow that it was composed of twenty different Echoes, and that the first or nearest being twenty-two geometric paces away (that is to say, forty-four common paces), the last would be 880 geometric paces away, or 1760 common paces, which are worth 4400 <term>Royal feet<gloss>pieds de Roy: a pre-revolutionary French unit of length, approximately 12.8 inches.</gloss></term>, or about a third of a French league: for the league contains 15,000 Royal feet, as I have remarked elsewhere.

Nevertheless, it is not necessary for the distances of the different Echoes to be so great, as I have remarked at the Echo of Charanton, <note>Likely referring to the Protestant temple at Charenton, famous for its acoustics before its destruction.</note> which responded to me ten or eleven times, even though the columns that seemed to create the Echo were very close to one another. Others say they have made it respond 18, 20, and 26 times. But because there is doubt as to whether the Echoes were made by the columns alone (even though they responded from both sides, and when one was in the middle of said columns) or by underground places and neighboring houses, it is necessary to make a portable Echo, by means of which one can know what the distance of the reflecting bodies must be to make them repeat whatever number of syllables one wishes, or as many times as necessary for the satisfaction of the listeners.

But it is difficult to find the place where the Echo makes the reflected voice appear, and whether the ear hears it in the same place where the eye sees the image of its object: for example, if the Sound made at A, which goes to strike C, is heard by the ear at B, as if it were at point I, where the image appears to the eye, as is demonstrated in <term>Catoptrics<gloss>The branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light by mirrors.</gloss></term>. I see no reason that should prevent us from discussing the location of the image of Sounds as we do that of colors: this is why I conclude that the voice, which we call the Echo, seems to come from twice as far as the place where the reflection occurs: for example, if the voice is fifty feet away from the reflecting body it strikes perpendicularly, it will appear to be a hundred feet away, beyond the body reflecting the voice.

And if the voice strikes the reflecting body obliquely, the Echo will appear opposite the line of incidence, as seen in the preceding figure: from this it follows that those who hear the Echo imagine that the Sound is on the side where it is not. One could speak here of all the deceptions created by means of the Echo, but it is very easy to notice them when one understands the science of mirrors, which serve to create the Echoes called "mute," for the reason that there is only a single point from which they can be heard.

->First Book<-

...or they make the reflected voice heard, even though the direct voice is so weak that it cannot be heard.

This occurs when one places the ear at the focal point of a mirror, where the light of the Sun or a candle is most concentrated. For the sound made in the place where the candle is set, which strikes the surface of a spherical concave mirror, reflects between the fourth and fifth part of the diameter of the sphere of which the mirror is a segment. If the mirror is <term>Parabolic<gloss>A mirror shaped like a parabola, which focuses all incoming parallel rays to a single point.</gloss></term>, it reflects at the fourth part of the <term>Parameter<gloss>Also known as the latus rectum; a technical term in conic sections describing the width of the curve through its focus.</gloss></term>, or right side, which I shall discuss in the following Proposition and in the *Book of the Voice*. In that work, the manner of making all types of reflecting bodies will be seen, along with the terms necessary to understand <term>conic sections<gloss>The curves—circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas—formed by intersecting a cone with a plane.</gloss></term>. Therefore, it is not necessary to dwell longer here on the Echo, which can remind us that all parts of our body ought to be resonant Echoes to sing and eternally repeat the praises of God, whose Temple we are, as the Apostle teaches in the *First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter three.* <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 3:16: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God...?"</note>

### COROLLARY I.

One can conclude the speed of Sound by the experiments performed with Echoes. One easily pronounces two syllables one after the other, for which the Echo is heard while the <term>pulse<gloss>Before the invention of precise watches, scientists used the human heartbeat or pulse as a standard measure of a second.</gloss></term> beats once—that is to say, within the time of one second. Now, the voice travels ninety-six <term>geometric paces<gloss>A geometric pace is approximately 5 feet or 1.5 meters.</gloss></term> in this space of time, insofar as it goes and returns twice along the vocal line of a syllable, which is about twenty-four geometric paces. Consequently, one can say that Sound travels one hundred geometric paces in one second, and two <term>leagues<gloss>A league was roughly 2.4 to 3 miles.</gloss></term> in one minute, and so forth; it would travel around the earth in sixty hours, which is worth two and a half days. However, I shall speak more amply and more exactly of this speed in another place.

That is to say, if there were no more space beyond the Stars into which it could pass, it would instead be extinguished near said vacuum. For a Sound made near the same vacuum would vanish or be reflected; and because nothing can be annihilated (since annihilation is as difficult as creation), it follows that Sound and light would reflect back toward the same side of the space in which they were produced. This occurs, however, with this difference: light would reflect an infinite number of times, whereas the reflections of Sound would soon cease, because the moved air restores itself and resumes its rest as soon as it can.

Now, Contemplative Theologians may consider whether the soul, separated from the body, would find God; if it encountered only an intellectual void—that is, if it encountered no other being but itself—would it perform an infinite number of reflections upon itself, like light encountering the vacuum, or would it cease to know? ## COROLLARY III.

Those who undertake to teach the science of the Echo must determine how all sorts of reflective surfaces reflect Sound—particularly regular ones—and consequently demonstrate whether the position of the Voice is perceived at the intersection where the two principal reflected sound rays, which strike the two ears, meet. For this subject, one must consider if Sounds maintain equal angles of incidence and reflection with the reflecting plane, as well as those of inclination with the perpendicular of the point of incidence: whether there is a perpendicular of Sound, and if the plane formed by the sound ray of incidence and that of reflection is the surface of reflection, and if it is perpendicular to the reflecting surface. Finally, it is necessary to consider in the reflection of Sounds everything that is usually established for the reflection of light.
