# Book One

[Sound], if the medium were uniform, would travel along the straight line GH, but it breaks <note>The author uses "breaks" to describe what we now call refraction—the bending of a wave as it enters a new substance.</note> at the point of its incidence N toward the perpendicular CD, and goes to point I, forming the **angle of refraction** HNI and the **refracted angle** IND. Because the image is found on the continued line of incidence, a Sound produced at point G will appear to be at point H, whereas it would have appeared at point S if the medium were uniform. Similarly, if the Sound were produced in water at point I and it broke at the surface of the air at point N when exiting the water, it would be heard in a different place than where it was made; for the **vocal line** <note>original: "ligne vocale"; refers to the path taken by the sound wave.</note> moves as far away from the perpendicular CD when leaving water to enter air as it moves toward the same perpendicular when passing from air into water, assuming it follows the laws of refraction.

I have proposed this so that those who have the convenience of conducting the necessary experiments to resolve this difficulty may know how to proceed. For if one knows the angle of incidence that the Sound makes on the surface of a medium—whether denser or rarer than that in which it originates—and the refraction it undergoes, it will be easy to determine all the refractions for other inclinations of the sound path, provided they follow the analogy that I explain in the following figure. In this figure, line AB represents the surface of the water, or the common boundary of air and water; G and E signify the Sounds made in the air; I and K show the locations and points where the refracted Sounds travel. GNI is the line composed of the incidence and the refraction of the Sound made at G, just as EK is the line composed of the incidence and the refraction of point E. GNC (or HND) is the angle of incidence made by point G upon the surface of the water AB, just as ENC (or FND) is the angle of incidence of point E.

Here it must be noted that there are certain terms necessary for understanding refraction; this is why I explain them through this figure, in which I suppose that line AB represents the surface of the water, or rather the junction or contiguity of air and water where the ray breaks. Thus, the sound ray GNI has two parts: the part in the air, GN, is called the *ray of incidence*, and the part within the water, NI, is called the *ray of refraction*. Therefore, GNI is the broken ray. The surface AB can be called the **refracting surface** <note>original: "rompante"</note>. Point N deserves the name of point of incidence and refraction, since it joins both rays. NM is the refracted ray IN extended to M, just as NS is the ray of incidence GN extended to S. The line CR drawn through the point of incidence and refraction N is called the **perpendicular** <note>In modern physics, this is often called the "normal" line.</note>, just as the line falling perpendicularly from point G onto the refracting surface NB can be called the perpendicular of the object (if one supposes the Sound is produced at point G) or the perpendicular of the ear (if the listener is at that point). We also call the plane passing through the ray of incidence and the perpendicular the **surface of refraction**, because it also passes through the ray of refraction, and everything concerning refraction takes place within it. The angle that the perpendicular CN makes with the ray of incidence GN is called the *angle of inclination*. That which the rays of incidence and refraction make between themselves is called the *angle of refraction*, and that which the perpendicular makes with the ray of refraction is called the *refracted angle*.

Second, that the oblique light ray which falls into a denser medium—for example, from air into water—approaches the perpendicular more closely as it is more oblique, just as it moves further away when falling into a rarer medium—for example, when it passes from water into air. But it is difficult to know the proportion of the oblique falls of the incident rays compared to the proportion of the refractions. For although **Maurolyc** <note>Francesco Maurolico (1494–1575), a mathematician who studied optics and the geometry of the eye.</note> holds that every refraction has the same ratio to every inclination as the first refraction has to the first given inclination, and though he has found through trial that the refraction occurring in crystal is to the inclination (or to the angle of the incident ray with the perpendicular) as three is to eight—which is the ratio of the **Diapason Diatessaron** <note>In music theory, this is the interval of an Eleventh (an Octave plus a Fourth), representing the mathematical ratio 8:3.</note>, that is to say, of the Eleventh—from which it would follow that the greatest inclination, which is 90 degrees, would result in a refraction of 33 3/4 degrees; nonetheless, **Kepler** <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), known for his laws of planetary motion, also made significant contributions to the study of optics.</note> has conducted other experiments which show that refractions are not entirely proportional to inclinations, although they are close enough from the first degree of inclination up to 30, and they increase from 30 up to 90 degrees, which results in a refraction of 48 degrees.

But since one of the most excellent minds of this century <note>This likely refers to René Descartes. His *Dioptrique* (1637) first published the law of sines (Snell's Law).</note> has found the true proportion of refractions to inclinations, I wish here to note the analogy, so that when it is found that experiments correspond to it, all learned men may pray him to provide the reason and the science for it. He has thus found that there is the same ratio of the **Sine** GO, of the angle of incidence GNO, to the **Sine** PE, of the angle of incidence PNE, as there is of the **Sine** IR, of the refracted angle NIR, to the **Sine** KQ of the refracted angle NKQ, which he will demonstrate in his *Dioptrics* when it pleases him. I place here only the table of refractions that occur in water, which he calculated when the incident ray makes an angle of thirty degrees, and its angle of refraction is 11 or 12 degrees, after having considered this table.

### PROPOSITION XXX.

->*To determine by how much Sound is lower in water than in air; and if one can infer from this how much air is rarer than water.*<-

It is certain that an instrument sounding in air and in water produces different Sounds, and that the sound it has in water is lower by a **Major Tenth** <note>A musical interval spanning an octave and a major third.</note> than that which is made in the air. All experiments show this evidently when they are performed with a bell; its Sound, having two degrees of gravity <note>In this context, "gravity" refers to the depth or lowness of pitch.</note> in the air, has five in the water. This occurs because of the density, or coarseness, of the water, which offers greater resistance to the movement of the body producing the Sound, or which prevents the parts of the bell from vibrating as fast as they do in the air.

And because the high and low pitch of Sound depends on the fast or slow movement of the liquid bodies <note>In 17th-century science, "liquids" often referred to all fluid media, including air.</note> that serve as the vehicle for Sound, one can conclude that the speed of the movement of air is to the speed of the movement of water struck by the same instrument as five is to two. Furthermore, the rarity <note>The opposite of density; "rarity" describes how thin a substance is.</note> of air is to that of water as 125 is to 8. This is because we find through experiment with all other bodies that produce Sound that their solidities exist in a **tripled ratio** <note>In modern terms, this means the ratio is cubed (5³ = 125 and 2³ = 8).</note> to their Sounds, as I shall discuss elsewhere. From this, it follows that bells which produce an **Octave** <note>An interval where the frequency ratio is 2:1.</note> are in an eight-fold ratio to one another, because their Sounds follow the ratio of their diameters, which, when tripled, gives the eight-fold ratio of their solidities. Consequently, the ratio of the Tenth, which is five to two, being tripled, will give that of 125 to 8. This is slightly larger than the fifteen-fold ratio of fifteen to one. This is enough to make "good minds" <note>A 17th-century term for scholars or intellectuals.</note> consider whether it can be said that water is only fifteen times denser than air, and whether the proportions reported by others for these two Elements are false—such as that of **Aristotle**, who makes it ten-fold; or others who make it a hundred-fold; and that of **Kepler**, who makes it 1,533,304,682. By Kepler's calculation, the air of a room twelve feet in every direction would contain no more matter than an eighth part of a cubic inch.

I know that several objections can be raised against the Proposition I have explained: for example, that an inch of water, when exhaled <note>Turned into vapor or steam.</note>, can fill a room of several feet, and that vapors fill the space with a great quantity of air, etc. But it must be answered that water, when rarefied, is lighter than the air that constrains it to rise, even though it is not as **diaphanous** <note>Transparent or translucent.</note>; for the qualities of transparency do not follow the density of bodies. I leave aside several other objections to bring forward one that is stronger and more suited to this subject than the others: namely, that the Sound of a bell which has five degrees of gravity should be less grave in liquids less heavy than water. For example, when the spirit of wine, which is called *eau de vie* <note>Brandy or concentrated alcohol.</note>, is lighter, and consequently rarer than water, the Sound that the bell makes...

<header>Book One</header>

...in that liquid <note>referring to brandy</note>, the sound should be sharper <note>higher in pitch</note> than the one it produces in this liquid <note>referring to water</note>, so that the Sound of brandy would form a Fifth <note>A musical interval where the higher note vibrates 1.5 times faster than the lower one.</note> with that of water, when the weight of the latter is to the weight of the former as three is to two.

The same must be said of the Sound produced in turpentine oil, and in other liquids that are lighter or heavier than water. This does not actually occur, for the Sound remains almost always in unison, or rises at most by only a semitone. This does not contradict what I have said, because the density of water is perhaps only in a triple ratio of sixteen to fifteen compared to the density of brandy. Now, it is easy to perform several experiments on Sounds in all sorts of liquids and environments, which is why I shall say no more of it. I only add that a bell cannot ring in oil, nor in milk, and that it makes the same Sound in wine as in water—or at least the difference is not perceptible.

## COROLLARY I.

One can perform several other experiments to determine the ratio of the density of water to that of air, in order to compare them with the preceding ones. Now, it seems they can all be reduced to three methods: namely, the method used to weigh air to judge its density by its weight; the space it fills; and the resistance it offers both to the rays of luminous and sonorous bodies, and to the movements impressed upon it. As for the method of weighing it, some believe that its weight is to that of water as the weight of bodies weighed in air is to the weight of those same bodies weighed in water. For example, that air is rarer <note>less dense</note> and lighter than water in the same ratio that gold is lighter in water than in air; and because water of an equal volume to gold is nearly twenty times lighter, and consequently gold weighs less by a twentieth part in water than in air, it would follow that water would be almost as rare as air.

Now, this method is not sound; for besides there being no appearance that water is so rare, it would follow that it would have all sorts of proportions to the rarity of air depending on the different bodies one weighs in air and in water. One would have to conclude that there would be no proportion between the rarity of air and water when a body that weighs something in air weighs nothing in water. But I have explained a better way to weigh air in the seventeenth Proposition.

The second method considers the proportions of the spaces that air and water fill; for if a cubic inch of water can fill a bladder of a hundred cubic inches when it is converted into vapors or air, it must be said that water is a hundred times denser and heavier than air. This follows the experiment that Bacon <note>original: "Baco"</note> says he performed in his *Novum Organum* <note>original: "nouuel Organe," refers to Francis Bacon's 1620 work on scientific method</note>, page 286, where he remarks that a portion of brandy being reduced to vapor fills a bladder a hundred times larger than the said portion.

The third method consists in the proportion of the resistances of air and water. Now, this resistance is first noticed in the rays of light, which seem to have more difficulty entering water than air; from this, it follows that they refract more in water. I leave aside for now the Sounds of which I have already spoken, in order to notice the other resistance made by air and...

## ->COROLLARY II.<-

If one can judge the proportion of the density of these two elements by the movement of heavy bodies that descend through them, I add a very exact observation that can serve to find it, namely that a lead musket ball which descends thirteen feet in the air in two beats of time <note>likely referring to a specific measurement of time like a half-second or a pulse</note> descends in the water in five beats, for having made a channel two or three inches wide & 13 feet high, the lead ball falls through the air in one second, and in water in two and a half seconds; so that it could descend 80 feet in the air while it descends twelve feet in the water. But it is difficult to know if one must follow the simple ratios of the times of these falls, or their squared ratio <note>original: "raiſon doublée"; in the 17th century, a 'doubled ratio' meant the square of the ratio</note>, or cubed ratio to determine the proportion of the said densities.

When the lead ball is hollowed out in such a way that it weighs three times less than the solid one, they descend just as quickly in the air as one another, but the hollow one descends in the water in five seconds. On which it must be noted that the experiments can only succeed with spherical bodies: for other shapes hinder them wonderfully in the water; for example, a quadruple <note>original: "quadruple"; likely a gold coin or a weight of that name</note> descends only in 12 seconds, and a lead plate of the same width in 8 seconds. A square parallelogram of wood from China <note>possibly cinnamon or another dense imported wood</note> half a foot long and one inch wide, descends in 5 and ½ seconds; and as many shapes as one can imagine hasten or delay the movement in the water quite sensibly.

One can also consider the speed of movements made by bodies descending in water, whether by their weight or in other ways; and similarly those of bodies submerged to the bottom of the water when they return to its surface, in order to note if those heavier than water descend, and the lighter ones rise, by increasing their speed in the same proportion as the movements they have in the air; for example, to know if the pith of an elderberry <note>original: "moüelle de ſureau"; the soft, buoyant tissue inside the stem of an elder tree, commonly used in early physics experiments</note> which rises from the bottom of the twelve-foot-high channel to the top, having risen the first foot in a given time, rises four feet in two times—that is to say, if bodies lighter than water increase their speed in a squared ratio, following the square roots of the times, as happens with the speed of heavy bodies descending in the air.

Be that as it may, it is difficult to conclude anything about the density of water and air based on the descent [of bodies] within them, because one encounters as many different proportions as the weights have different shapes. From this, it is easy to conclude that bodies must have the same shape to be able to draw any conjecture regarding their movements.

### COROLLARY III.

One can imagine several other means to find the ratio of these densities, particularly by the compression of water and air. For if one takes two hollow spheres, or two syringes, so tightly sealed that nothing can escape, and one is full of water and the other of air; if one squeezes the two spheres and other vessels until they burst, one will see how much more condensation <note>meaning compression or reduction in volume</note> the air has endured than the water. For example, if the vessel containing the air has been so pressed before breaking that its cavity held a hundred times less space than before it was pressed, and the cavity of the water vessel decreased by only one-hundredth part, one would conclude that air is 99 times rarer <note>less dense</note> than water.

### COROLLARY IV.

The experiment performed in water to know whether Sounds are refracted <note>original: "se rompent"; referring to the "breaking" or bending of waves, known today as refraction</note> like light, or contrary to light, cannot give us enough certainty to conclude how it is. This is because the Sound produced between two waters <note>meaning completely submerged</note> appears so weak that it seems one can make no other judgment of it than that of its weakness and its gravity <note>meaning its low pitch or weightiness</note>.

Now, when I say *between two waters*, I mean that the bodies making the Sound are so surrounded by water that it touches them on all sides and at every point of their surfaces. For if they sound in the air that is under the water, they do not change the pitch <note>original: "l’aigu"; the highness or treble of the sound</note> of their Sound at all; this is because the ear, whether plunged into the water or free in the air, always hears the same pitch of the Sound produced in the air, whether the air remains joined with the whole mass of the other air or is separated from it—as happens when one plunges a vessel full of air into water, wine, oil, milk, or some other liquid, or encloses it within four walls. From this, one must

### COROLLARY V.

## PROPOSITION XXXI.

->*To know whether a high sound is more pleasant and more excellent than a low one.*<-

This question can be decided by experience and by reason, but one must take the low and the high from the same genre; that is to say, on the same instrument, or within human voices, for it would be a different difficulty if one wished to compare the high voice of a man and the low sound of a Viol or a Lute.

One can therefore understand this difficulty by the comparison of the low Sound and the high Sound of the same instrument—for example, the Lute, the Viol, the Spinet, or one of the organ stops <note>original: "jeux d'Orgues"</note>, or the human voice. And the comparison of voices can be made in two ways: namely, the low voice of one who sings the Bass, and the high voice of a child, or the low and high voice of the same person. But one must not compare a good voice with a poor one, for the quality of the low voice must be equal to that of the high, so that the comparison may be perfect. One must therefore first compare the voice of the same man in order to know if he sings more pleasantly in the lower register than the higher, when he has an equal ease in singing both. For example, I suppose that his voice has the range of an Octave without being strained, and consequently that his middle voice being at G <note>original: "G re sol vt"; a note in the Guidonian hexachord system</note>, he can easily rise to C <note>original: "C sol vt fa"</note> or to D <note>original: "D la re sol"</note>, and descend to low C <note>original: "C fa vt"</note>. The question is whether the low C will be more or less pleasant than the high C; one can also ask the same thing of the middle G compared to the same high C, for the former is low in comparison to the latter. And then we will compare the low or middle voices of the Tenor <note>original: "Taille"</note> with those of children and Trebles <note>original: "Dessus"</note>.

As for the voices of the same man, it seems that the middle one is the most natural and the most pleasant, and that after it, those which are in the higher register are more pleasant than those which are low and which approach silence, especially since they have less of a raspy <note>original: "rauque"</note> quality, and they are all the more vivid and awake as they have a greater speed in their movements. And this reason proves not only that high voices are more pleasant than low ones, but also more pleasant than middle ones: although

Nevertheless, Aristotle holds the contrary view in the 7th Chapter of the 5th book of *The Generation of Animals*, stating: "the low voice seems to be nobler by nature, and in melodies, the low is better than the high." <note>original Greek: "ἡ δοκεῖ γενναιοτέρα εἶναι φύσεως ἡ βαρυφωνία, καὶ ἐν τοῖς μέλεσι τὸ βαρὺ-τῶι συντόνωι βέλτιον"</note> That is to say, the low voice <term>grave: the low-pitched or "heavy" voice</term> seems to be the most noble, that the low sound is better than the high sounds <term>aigu: high-pitched or "sharp" sounds</term> in concerts; and that the low voices in songs are more excellent than the high ones, insofar as that which surpasses others is more perfect, and the depth of the voice consists in an excess of magnitude; "for perfection lies in superiority, and low pitch is a kind of superiority," <note>original Greek: "τὸ γὰρ τέλειον ἐν ὑπεροχῆι. ἡ δὲ βαρύτης ὑπεροχή τις"</note> for what is great is preferable to what is small, just as a great good is preferable to a lesser one.

This can be confirmed by considering the greater strength of those who have a larger voice, and consequently larger and ampler body parts, which are in some way represented by the voice. The voice depends on these parts and acts as a mirror of the soul and the body. From this comes the fact that deep voices have more majesty, weight, and strength to impress and produce powerful effects upon the listeners, being similar to the sound of thunder and the cannon, which shakes and astounds walls and men more forcefully than lesser noises do.

And if one compares an excellent Bass <term>Basse: the lowest vocal part</term>, such as that of Monsieur Moulinié <note>Étienne Moulinié (1599–1676) was a prominent French composer of the Baroque era</note>, with an excellent Treble <term>Dessus: the highest vocal part or soprano</term>, such as that of Monsieur Bertaut <note>Jean-Louis Bertaut was a renowned singer in the French royal court</note>—both being Singers of the King's Music—one will find some who take more pleasure in hearing the Bass than the Treble. However, one must not follow the judgment or feeling of men in this matter, since it is as inconstant as their moods; the Bass pleases the same listener more at one time, and the Treble at another, depending on how they are predisposed. This is why, leaving aside the differing judgments of men—which arise from different dispositions of the body or the mind—one must consider the depth or highness of the Sound in itself to find which is the most pleasant or excellent. For regarding the strength of the Sound, the low is the strongest when it is driven by a proportionate force, and consequently, it makes a stronger impression on the bodies it encounters within the reach of its action.

But because that which has more strength is not always the most pleasant—even if it is the most excellent in its kind—since the sound of thunder, though great, strong, and powerful (and therefore excellent), is not pleasant and harms the hearing and causes deafness, we must here distinguish the quality of being *excellent* from that of being *pleasant* in Sound. We must see what makes it pleasant, for the more it possesses the quality that makes it pleasing, the more pleasant it will be.

Now, what makes it pleasant must be taken not only from what it has within itself, but from its relationship to the ear or the imagination, which receives the pleasure of Sounds. Because experience shows that a low sound does not please everyone equally, one must believe that men have dispositions within themselves that contribute more to certain pleasures than others. These are similar to the dispositions of smell and taste, which cause what is pleasant to one to be unpleasant to another; for some love the flavor of the orange and the lemon, while others hate it or do not love it as much; and one person takes pleasure in smelling the carnation <note>original: "oeillet"</note> who hates the scent of the lily and the rose.

This is why we must consider the disposition and the imagination of the listener, even though we neglected it when judging the excellence of the Sound, not being

<meta>This page continues the debate regarding the aesthetic and philosophical superiority of different vocal ranges, moving from the previous page's defense of the "grave" or low voice (based on Aristotelian views of nobility and strength) to a discussion of the "middle" and "acute" or high-pitched voices.</meta>

# On the nature and properties of Sound.

The question here is not about the "best" Sound considered simply and absolutely, but rather Sound compared according to the preferences of different listeners; though in this matter one might follow the feeling and opinion of the great multitude, particularly those who have a "good ear." Many hold that the Sound which is in the middle of the <term>grave: low-pitched or "heavy"</term> and the <term>aigu: high-pitched or "sharp"</term> is the most pleasant of all, both because it is less forced—being more natural and vigorous—and because it signifies a well-balanced temperament, giving a beautiful air and tone to speech.

Nevertheless, one encounters a greater number of men who take more pleasure in high Sounds than in middle ones; and we experience that the <term>Dessus: the soprano or highest part in a musical composition</term> in concerts are much more pleasant than the other parts. The Soprano alone ravishes the listener when it is well sung; so much so that it seems Composition was invented to showcase the excellence of the Soprano, and to make one taste its goodness by comparison with the other parts, which give it brilliance, just as black and other dark colors do when they are placed opposite white. It must therefore be concluded that the high Sound is the most pleasant, provided it does not exceed the capacity of the ear, as is experienced in the solo performances <note>original: "recits"</note> of young children whom one prefers to hear over any other concert. This is because the high voice represents to us the innocence, delicacy, and youth of children, who are more full of life, or closer to the source of life, and who sing more delicately and sweetly than those who sing the other parts; or perhaps because the high Sound flatters the ear and gathers the spirit more effectively.

For the high voice, being made by <term>battemens d'air: vibrations or "beats" of air</term> which are more continuous and less interrupted than those of other voices, approaches more closely the works of nature which are continuous. It moves further away from silence and nothingness than do the low voices: now, all creatures flee from the void and from nothingness, and each loves "being," in which the high Sound participates more than the low. For the high includes the low, which it surpasses as much in its "degrees of being" as it does in its quality of height—which is like form and light in regard to the low, which is similar to matter and darkness. From this it follows that when the Soprano joins the other parts, it brings to them a great light whose rays penetrate even into the hearts of the listeners; indeed, when it sings all alone, it appears like a flash of light that eclipses the previous voices and penetrates to the deepest part of one's thought. So much so that if one hears the other voices after the Soprano, and it falls silent for a little while, it seems as if one is leaving the light of the Sun to re-enter the darkness.

### COROLLARY.

Since one is forced to admit that there are almost no absolute demonstrations in <term>Physique: natural science or the study of the physical world</term>, I do not doubt that one could also hold that low Sounds are the most excellent, whether by reason of the larger bodies that produce them, or the rest and unity which they more closely approach, or for other reasons that one can imagine; therefore, everyone is free to believe what they wish. On this subject, one may see other similar difficulties that I propose in the penultimate Proposition of the *Book of Songs*, and at the beginning of the *Book of Composition*. <note>The author refers to other sections of his own treatise, likely the "Harmonie Universelle" by Marin Mersenne.</note>

# Book One

<margin>Position.</margin>Now, since it is highly likely that Sound is nothing other than the movement of the air, or of other bodies, it is now necessary to speak of this movement in order to understand the nature of Sound more perfectly.

### PROPOSITION XXXII.

->*Determining whether there is movement in nature, and what is necessary to establish it.*<-

I am not speaking here of movement taken in a general sense, as is done in Physics, but only of <term>local movement: the change of position of a body from one place to another</term>, which alone produces Sounds. Now, although it is very evident that there are many different movements in nature, many difficulties are nevertheless proposed against its existence; these so embarrass the mind that one is almost forced to oppose them with experience alone for their solution. 

For example: if there is movement and it is continuous, as one imagines it to be, it follows that a tortoise goes as fast as the Eagle, since at each moment of time the Eagle does not travel any more distance than what corresponds to that <term>indivisible: a point of time or space that cannot be further divided</term>; and consequently, the eagle will never be able to reach the tortoise, who will be one step ahead. For while the eagle covers half of that step, the tortoise will advance a little, and a little more still while the eagle covers half of that half—that is, a quarter of the step—and so on through other parts unto infinity. <note>This is a variation of the famous "Achilles and the Tortoise" paradox by the Greek philosopher Zeno, used here to question the nature of continuous motion.</note> 

That is to say, the human mind is not capable of understanding how it is possible for one continuous movement to be slower than another. This has forced the Spanish Philosopher <note>Rodrigo de Arriaga (1592–1667) was a prominent Jesuit theologian and philosopher whose "Physical Disputations" were widely studied in the 17th century.</note> Arriaga, in his sixteenth physical disputation, and several others, to say that the slowness of movement is nothing other than an interruption caused by many "rests," even though the senses cannot perceive them; and that these rests are either longer or greater in multitude as the movement becomes slower. 

For example, if the movement of the tortoise is a hundred thousand times slower than that of the eagle, the number of rests between the parts of the eagle's movement will be a hundred thousand times less than those in the movement of the tortoise. He also supposes this in the natural movement of stones and other heavy bodies that fall toward the center of the earth. 

And although this imagination is not free from great difficulties—such as that of the radius of two <term>concentric circles: circles that share the same center, like a target</term>, which moves through the larger circumference in such a way that it seems necessary for the aforementioned rests to be as large on the outer circle as on the smaller one—nevertheless, some persist in this thought. They prefer to posit <term>physical indivisibles: the smallest possible physical units</term>, some much larger than others, which can change place entirely or only in part in a single moment, rather than embracing the continuity of movement or the infinity of parts or points that make up the length of a space. 

However, I much prefer to follow the idea of an infinity of imaginary points, or parts, which constitute the continuum in lines as well as in movement; this allows one to respond that the eagle travels much more distance in the same amount of time than the tortoise, just as happens with the part of a radius further away from its center.

Whatever the case may be, it is not necessary to know the ultimate truth of this matter to determine what pertains to the speed or slowness of movement, since it suffices to know that speed causes the moving body to pass more...

faster in the same space, or that it travels more distance in the same time, than that whose movement is slower: just as it happens that a body is rarer when it fills a larger space, and denser when it fills a smaller one. This must be noted carefully, because **speed** in some way resembles **density**, just as **slowness** resembles **rarefaction**, or vice versa. <note>The author is drawing an analogy between the "thickness" of matter (density) and the "intensity" of motion (speed), a common concept in 17th-century natural philosophy.</note>

As for the things necessary to establish movement, it is very difficult to regulate them. This is because if we take different locations in relation to some fixed point in the world—for example, in relation to the North Pole—it is not necessary for a body to move to change its location, provided the Pole itself moves. Thus, if the location of the Sun were determined by its distance from certain points on the earth, it would change location even if it were stationary and the earth turned around it, as the followers of **Copernicus** imagine; consequently, one could say the Sun would have a movement. But if we establish the movement of each body based on the space it leaves, and which it filled before—and if we imagine that this space is entirely immobile—it will be easy to understand the change of this location, provided we add that it does not happen in a single moment, but over a span of time. 

Several theologians teach that spirits separated from matter—for example, **Angels** and rational souls—can change location and leave France to find themselves in China in an instant. This means they spend no time passing through the Provinces between France and China, because their changes of location can occur through "interrupted instants." <note>This refers to the Scholastic debate on whether angels move through space continuously or "jump" from one point to another without crossing the distance between.</note> This is easy to understand, insofar as the intellect does the same thing when it thinks of the earth and immediately afterward of the stars, without thinking of what lies between them. But I am not speaking now of this type of movement, which does not properly belong to <term>Physics: the study of natural bodies and their motions</term>, and which can neither produce **Sounds** nor be perceived by the senses.

This being settled, I take local movement here to be the action by which a body leaves the space it occupied and passes successively to another space distant from the previous one. This remains true whether the extent and size of the world be finite or infinite, and whether there be a "high" or "low," or a "right" or "left," or not. We must nevertheless add that it suffices for local movement that the same parts of the moving body do not always touch the same parts of the space, even if the body, considered as a whole, does not change the space containing it. This ensures that balls spinning on their immobile axis between two pivots are not exempt from the movement of which we speak. 

Now, we have no need of external bodies to experience and understand local movement; for even if there were only one man in the world, and everything else were annihilated, he would feel quite well the movement his hand would make from his feet to his head, and that which he would make with other parts of his body. The same would happen to an indivisible spirit, imagined as reduced to a single point, which would perceive its own movement even if there were no other created thing in nature. Here, one must suppose that movement can occur in spaces that some call **imaginary**, and which they believe to exist from all eternity, though they are perhaps nothing other than...

### PROPOSITION XXXIII.

*Considering the movements of all bodies in general, & the space in which they occur.*

We cannot know if the spaces beyond the stars are finite or infinite, nor if they are empty or filled with some dark or luminous bodies; for it may be that the space containing the visible part of the world, from the earth to the stars, is but a point compared to the rest of the world beyond, and that this vast region contains other stars, each of which might be a hundred thousand times larger than the firmament <note>In traditional cosmology, the "firmament" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars that was thought to enclose the universe.</note>. For the power of God is infinitely greater than our imagination, and there is no creature that can be compared to Him with more reason than one that would be infinite. But since it is not possible for us to know if He has made such a creature, nor even if it is feasible—and since we have no more knowledge of the space and the bodies one might imagine beyond the firmament than a man raised in a forest, from which he never departed and where he never heard mention, would have of the ebb and flow <note>original: "flux & reflux"</note> of the sea—it suffices to consider what concerns us, and the movements we perceive.

Now there are particularly two kinds of movement: those that seem straight to us, and others that seem circular. For example, it seems that the bodies called **heavy** <term>heavy bodies: "corps pesans," or objects with mass that naturally tend to fall toward the Earth's center in Aristotelian and early modern physics</term> descend straight toward the center of the earth, and that they similarly travel straight when one throws them up, down, or to another side. As for the others, they seem circular, as one notices in the movement of the Sun and the Moon. However, because **Astronomy** & **Physics** have not yet provided a demonstration to show whether it is the earth that turns, or if it is the Sun, and since everything perceptible to our senses can be explained by either of these movements, we will only touch upon this difficulty as much as necessary to examine several rare experiments discussed in the book that follows. It must only be noted that there is neither "up" nor "down" in this world, properly and absolutely speaking, since what is "up" in relation to one is "down" in relation to another. For example, we imagine that our **Antipodes** <note>Those living on the opposite side of the globe.</note> are down beneath our feet, and they think the same thing of us; and one could say that the center of a circle or a sphere is its "highest" place, and the circumference is the "lowest." Whatever the case, it is enough that we understand one another when we speak, so that words do not convey anything other than what is in the idea and the mind, and so that we avoid all difficulties that arise only from different understandings of terms. But before beginning the second book, I wish to finish this one with a Proposition that will serve as a passage to the third book for those who do not delight in the difficulties of **Physics**, and who want only what serves precisely for **Music**, so that they may leave the second book without any prejudice, or

### PROPOSITION XXXIV.

*To demonstrate whether a string stretched by a peg, or by a weight, is equally stretched in all its parts, and if the force that tightens it communicates its impression sooner and more strongly to the parts near it than to those further away.*

This Proposition is more difficult to determine than many imagine, for the parts of the stretched string <term>string: In this era, musical strings were usually made of gut or brass; here, the author is treating them as a physical model for studying tension.</term> that are closer to the weight, or to the peg, seem more stretched than those further away, insofar as the force that tightens the string passes through the parts closest to it before arriving at those further away, and has all the more vigor as it is closer to its origin.

And we find by experience that strings usually break in the parts close to the weight that stretches them; this happens, it seems, because they are more tightly stretched in those places than toward the middle, where they never break. To this, one adds that strings yield and sag more easily in the middle than in any other place, as seen on instruments, and on the ropes used to pull boats along rivers. These reasons, and all others that can be brought here, make the Proposition difficult; and we experience that strings are easier to break when they are long than when they are short, and consequently that they endure a greater tension. In effect, the length of bodies is the reason they act more powerfully, or yield more easily; for if one pushes a pike against another body, one will overturn it more easily than if one pushed with a shorter stick of equal thickness, even if one pushed with equal force. From this, some conclude that force increases in proportion to its distance from its source, just as one notices with the power of seeds, which are weak at their beginning and increase their vigor as they move away from the matrices <note>original: "matrices"; a 17th-century term for the "womb" or origin point where something is formed or held.</note> in which they were enclosed and, as it were, mortified.

And we see in mechanics that force is greater the further it moves from its center: for if one encounters the arms of a wheel, or a windmill, or the movement of the arm toward the hand, one experiences that the force is much greater than at the axle, or at the center of said wheels, or toward the shoulder, where the movement of the arm begins. To this, one can relate the movement of stones and other missiles, or thrown bodies, which have more force and more effect when they are distant and have already traveled a long way, than when they are near the arm, the bow, or the arquebus <note>An early type of portable gun or musket.</note> by which they are pushed. Consequently, one can say that the string is more tightened in the parts distant from the force than in those closer to it, since forces increase in proportion to their distance from their beginnings—just as one observes with rivers, which are but brooks at their sources, and even with the rumors that are spread; which gave rise to the Proverb

One can also say that if the string were equally stretched in all its parts, a single force would equally stretch a string a thousand leagues long and a string one foot long, which seems incredible; and that if the longer one were equally stretched by an equal weight, then being moved away from its straight line, it would make as many turns and returns <note>Meaning cycles of vibration or oscillations.</note> as the shorter one which is equally moved, which does not happen; for the string AB being pulled to G, takes twice as long to return to F as the string AF, which being pulled as far as E, or as far as the string AB, returns twice as fast, and consequently twice as often to H, as the string AB returns to F.

Nevertheless, one can say that the strings of instruments are equally stretched in all their parts, insofar as they produce a <term>unison: the sounding of the same pitch by two different strings or parts of a string.</term> when the bridge is placed in the middle; and that the tuning peg, or the weight, can send all its force through all parts of the string at the same time, just as a weight at the top of a lance weighs just as much at the same time upon the hand holding the lance by the bottom end as upon the top end; and just as the movement one imparts to a staff by pushing or pulling it is imparted equally to all parts of the staff at the same time; this is why a single weight stretches a string of a thousand leagues as easily as one of a foot, which I will explain when responding to the fifth objection.

And if it is objected that the unison demonstrates only that each half of the string is equally stretched, because the two ends are equally tightened—given that the upper point where the string is attached makes the same impression on the string as the weight that stretches it, so that the impression of both weakens as it approaches the middle—one can answer that if one takes a length near the middle that is equal to another length taken near one of the ends, these two lengths will be in unison, even though the two bridges that determine the length of the middle section provide no new tension to the string, and only support it in the same position they find it: consequently, the string is equally stretched in all its parts.

The reason for this is that A B resists just as much and stretches twice as much when it is pulled from point F to G as the string A F when it is pulled from point H to I; and like the string A H, which is pulled from point L to K, which stretches twice as less as the string A F, and four times less than the string A B, although it resists equally.

For the elongation <note>The stretching or lengthening of the string under tension.</note> of strings has the same ratio as their lengths; and it is just as difficult to elongate a string of four feet by a certain measure as it is to elongate one of one foot by a quarter of that measure. But we shall say in another place how much these elongations decrease the thickness of the strings: for it is enough to have shown here that the strings of musical instruments are equally stretched in all their parts.

As for the objections brought against the equality of this tension, one can respond to the first that the force which tightens the string is communicated to every part at the same time; otherwise, when the force surpassed the resistance of the string, it would break at the end to which it is applied before it had communicated its force to the middle or to the other end. This is contrary to experience, which shows that the string is stretched in all its parts before it breaks, however great the force applied to it may be: for the string is just as hard at one end as at the other, and produces an equal Sound in all its parts regarding the <term>bass and the treble: referring here to the pitch or "gravity" and "sharpness" of the tone produced.</term>

We can therefore compare the force of the weight, or of the <term>tuning peg: the wooden or metal pin turned to tighten the string.</term> which tightens the string, to the motion imparted to the stick of which we have spoken, the middle of which is moved as soon as the end to which the force is applied; and to the ray of the Sun, which illuminates the diameter of its sphere at the same time.

The second objection is taken from the breaking of strings, which occurs at the place where the weight or force is attached. But this break can happen in that place by reason of the elongation of all the parts of the string, which meets near the weight, or the effort given to the string when knotting it, or in unstrutting <note>likely referring to the physical stress of winding or unwinding.</note> it, or due to other circumstances observed in different experiments. This does not happen with tuning pegs that stretch the strings without it being necessary to untwist or knot them. From this it follows that they break more often near the <term>bridge: the part of the instrument that holds the strings up from the soundboard.</term> than near the pegs, where they are better preserved. Now, one can here consider several kinds of tensions: for a string can first be stretched with a peg, a winch, a screw, or another instrument, as happens on the <term>Lute: a plucked string instrument with a rounded body and a neck.</term> and on other necked instruments; secondly, it can be stretched and pulled by a weight attached to one of the ends, as would happen if one stretched the strings of a Lute or a <term>Harp: a multi-stringed instrument where the strings are stretched within a triangular frame.</term> with weights to tune them; this can be done by a deaf person <note>This suggests that the physics of weight and tension are so predictable that one could tune an instrument by calculation and weight alone, without needing to hear the pitch.</note>, as I demonstrate in the third book on stringed instruments.

In the third place, the string can be tightened at the same time by two pegs placed at the two ends of the string, by turning them both equally, or by two weights attached to the two ends, which pull it equally.

from one side to the other. In the fourth place, being stretched by two pegs; or attached on one side to the bridge, and on the other to the peg, it can receive a new tension by a weight attached in the middle, or in some other place on the string stretched horizontally. This can similarly happen when it is tightened by two weights attached to the two sides.

One can finally stretch it at whatever point or part one wishes, by means of a **movable bridge**, <note>A small block placed under the string that can be slid back and forth to change the vibrating length and pitch.</note> to which one can give all sorts of heights, as one experiences on the **Monochord**; <term>Monochord</term> <note>A scientific and musical instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundboard, used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships of musical intervals.</note> now, the bridge has the same effect by raising the string as the weight does by lowering it.

This being established, we must see the effect of these different tensions in order to respond to the second objection, and first, the effect of the first two ways of tensioning, which are greatly different. For when the string is tightened with a **peg**, <note>A tuning pin, like those found on a violin or harpsichord.</note> it seems that it suffers no more strain and does not suffer more on the second day than the first, because the peg gives it no new impression, and only keeps it in the same state; but when it is tightened by a **weight**, it suffers always, inasmuch as the weight acts as strongly on the second and the hundredth day as the first. This is why the string often breaks near the weight, whereas it breaks near the peg when it is stretched by a peg.

Furthermore, when the string is stretched with a weight, if one puts another weight in the middle, or at some other part of the string to pull it down—such as weight E, which is attached to three different points of the preceding string A B—the weight C rises and gives freedom to weight E to lower the string more and more, until it breaks, if weight E is strong enough to break it. And if it is not strong enough, and yet is greater than weight C, it carries it away and lifts the string off the plane or the support on which it was stretched. But when it is tightened with a peg, it only yields in the middle until it can no longer suffer being elongated, inasmuch as the peg always holds firm without yielding to the weight that one puts in the middle, or at some other point of the string, or to the bridge which has the same effect by raising the said string as the weight does by lowering it.

Now, all the parts of the string, which is tuned up to a certain tension and remains in that state, contribute equally in suffering the tension; so that they reduce themselves to an equilibrium of resistance and suffering, in which they remain until one of the parts disunites and separates from the others, and causes the breaking of the string.

Nevertheless, it seems that the weight gives as equal a tension to the string as the peg, since its power extends to both ends of the string at the same time, there being no other distinction except that it breaks near the weight, or far from the peg, as some believe—though there is nothing certain in this matter, for it breaks often enough near the peg and far from the weight. This happens whenever and wherever it is weaker towards the peg, or far from the weight, than in any other place. So, I estimate that there is no other reason for the breaking of strings in certain places rather than others, except that they are weaker; it being, it seems, impossible to find a string that is without inequality in all its parts, of which some are weaker than others, whether it be made of **brass**, iron, or other metal, or of silk, hemp, **gut**, <note>Animal intestines, usually from sheep, dried and twisted to make musical strings.</note> etc., as I have shown.

to the discourse on the material of **harmonic strings**. <note>Strings used for musical instruments, which Mersenne studied extensively to understand the physics of music.</note>

When a string is equally stretched from both sides, many believe it must break in the middle, because the impression from the two **pegs** <note>Tuning pins or pegs used to tighten strings.</note> or the two weights reaches the middle of the string—where they meet—sooner than any other place. Others say that if it is equally strong in all its parts, it cannot break when equally stretched from both ends; otherwise, it would break into an infinite number of pieces, as there is no reason why it should break in one place rather than another. But experience shows that it breaks almost always at one of its ends, as I stated in the eighth question of the *Preludes to Harmony*, <note>original: "Preludes de l'Harmonie," a work by Mersenne published in 1634 regarding the mathematical foundations of music.</note> unless it happens to be weaker in the middle than elsewhere.

Nevertheless, the points where strings break when pulled in different ways are so irregular that it is almost impossible to draw certain and necessary conclusions from them. For experience shows they often break in the middle when used to pull boats on the water, even though they are very loose in that spot—where they seem to be less under tension, if one measures the degree of tension by the stiffness of the rope. One could say this rupture happens in the middle because of the weight of the entire rope gathering there, or because the middle soaks more often and longer in the water, which causes it to rot and consequently weakens it more than the other parts; but I will speak further of this rupture when responding to the third objection.

As for the tension the string receives by suspending a weight in the middle, or at some other part, or by using a **bridge**, <term>bridge</term> <note>A support that holds the string up; in Mersenne's experiments, moving a bridge or adding a weight to the middle of a horizontal string was a way to test tension and pitch.</note> I have already spoken of this in the explanation of the preceding figure. This is sufficient to understand how much more it is stretched by a weight or a bridge placed in the middle than by any other means. But several things can be considered in this manner of tension: for example, knowing what weight must be suspended in the middle, or what the height of the bridge must be, to stretch it as much as a given weight suspended at one of the ends (whether the string is vertical or horizontal). This can be discovered by the equal stretching of the string, and more easily by the **Sound** <note>Mersenne was one of the first to scientifically link the pitch (sound) of a string to its physical tension and length.</note> of one or the other side of the string when raised in the middle by a bridge or lowered by a weight, and by the Sound of the same string (or another equal one) stretched by one or both ends with weights or pegs; however, this tension requires a specific discussion.

As for the third objection, I reply that the **displacement**, <note>original: "abaissement," referring to the distance the string moves when pushed or pulled down.</note> which occurs more easily at the middle of the string, is due to it being further from the bridges in that spot than in any other. The bridges represent the supports for two **levers**, <note>Mersenne is applying the laws of mechanics to acoustics, treating the string as a flexible lever.</note> insofar as all parts of the string are more or less stiff in proportion to their distance from said bridges, as seen in the preceding string to which weight E is attached. For the same logic applies to the string (or the lever A F, or B F) regarding the displacement F G, as applies to the lever A H and A L regarding the displacements H I and L K.

This is why it is easier to move the string at the middle than at any other point; just as one moves a lever of double length twice as easily as one of half length, so too one displaces a string of double length (with equal tension) twice as easily as one of half length.

# Book One

Now these greater sags <note>original: "abaïssemens," referring to the downward curve or sagging of a string under its own weight or tension.</note> coexist very well with the equal tension in the parts of the string, just as the easier movement of a longer **lever** <note>original: "leuier." Mersenne frequently uses the lever as a foundational model for understanding mechanical advantage.</note> coexists with the force it has equally in all its parts, even though they obey with more difficulty and offer more resistance when they are closer to the weight or the support <note>The fulcrum.</note>, for which I shall provide the reason in the discourse on the strength of the pegs of the **Lute** and other necked instruments, as this strength relates to the lever.

One can also consider the weight of the entire string, which appears more in the middle than at other points, insofar as it forms a smaller or larger arc in the middle depending on whether it is more or less heavy or stretched. The center of this arc meets the line that cuts the string perpendicularly through the said middle. But I will explain this arc and everything pertaining to it in another discourse, for I now wish to respond to the **fourth objection**, which consists of knowing whether a string that is longer breaks more easily than one that is shorter.

The fourth objection contains a proof contrary to the others; for its purpose is to show that the longer string is the most stretched with an equal force, whereas the other objections were made to prove that the string is more stretched when it is short. And the reason lies in knowing if the string breaks more easily when it is longer, as happens in the examples reported there, which show (it seems) that the larger the bodies, the more effect they have, and that the power <note>original: "vertu"</note> and force that pulls or pushes is all the greater as it moves further from its origin up to a certain limit, which bounds the **sphere of activity**, or the proportion of the moving force and the mobile body.

This can be confirmed by the longest **Cannons**, which have a greater range and trajectory; and by the **Blowguns** <note>original: "Sarbacanes"</note> that children use to push pins and small arrows much further than they do with shorter ones, even though they seemingly push their breath or wind with an equal force in both the long and the short ones.

Indeed, the larger and more massive the bodies that act or suffer, the more force they have to act and resist, as is experienced with large **vessels** both at sea and on rivers; for they strike what they encounter much harder than small boats do, even though both move at an equal speed, because the force of the wind is better impressed upon large mobile bodies than small ones. This is because all impressions and qualities communicated to bodies are received according to the capacity of said bodies, each receiving only as much as it needs and is capable of. This is why one does not throw a straw <note>original: "festu"</note> as far as a stone, even though one exerts as much effort to throw one as the other; this is because straw and other such things are not capable of so great an impression as heavy ones, or because there is a greater proportion of the surface of the straw to its weight than the surface of a stone or some other heavier body to its weight. From this comes the fact that the air resists the surface of the straw much more than it is forced by its weight, whereas it is much more forced by the weight of other bodies than it resists their surfaces. This concludes similarly for the natural descent of heavy bodies toward their center.

### On the Nature and Properties of Sound:

To this one can add that we push much more air when throwing a light body than when it is heavy, since a light body contains more air in its **pores** <note>In 17th-century physics, "pores" were the tiny spaces within a material. It was believed that light objects like cork or sponges were less dense because their pores were filled with air.</note>; now air does not "desire" <note>Mersenne uses the language of "desire" (desire) to describe the natural tendencies or physical properties of matter, a common phrasing in natural philosophy before the modern concept of inertia was standardized.</note> to be moved within air, nor to be thrown from one place in the air to another. We experience something similar in water, for those swimming submerged <note>original: "entre deux eaux," literally "between two waters," meaning to be underwater but not at the bottom.</note> cannot throw a portion of water from one place to another except with great difficulty. Now, we are always swimming and living within the air, and air is perhaps nothing other than **rarefied water**. But this reason of resistance seems to contradict the objection, since a longer string should resist more than a shorter one, and consequently, it should be more difficult to break than the shorter one—if the resistance of the length increases in the same proportion as the other aforementioned effects which distance themselves from the force or source of the movement. Yet this is contrary to experience.

Certainly, it is very difficult to resolve this difficulty. I respond only that I do not believe a string breaks more easily simply for being longer, unless it is because of the greater **swing** <term>vibration: original French *branle*, referring to the back-and-forth oscillation or swaying of the string</term> and the greater shock it suffers; or because a long string is more likely to contain weak or uneven parts where the break occurs. Most examples, like that of the longer **pike** <note>A long wooden spear used by infantry. Mersenne uses it as a standard example of how length affects the flexibility and "swing" of an object.</note>, etc., can be explained by the greater swing that larger bodies make. One could also say the longer string receives a greater impression due to its greater quantity <note>Referring to the mass or volume of the string material.</note>, though it would seem to follow that it would break two, three, or four times more easily when it is two, three, or four times longer—which does not happen.

Now it is difficult to relate this greater swing to any principle of **Mechanics**, unless it be the **screw**, for the swing—not lengthening the pike—cannot be related to the **lever**. But if we add a new principle—namely, a greater movement—we find that the swing adds a new motion to the one the stick or pike received from the arm; and two or more movements acting together produce a greater effect than when they are alone. But if the pike or another body has a greater effect (even without a swing) than a half-pike or a smaller body, we must admit that **quantity** increases the force, even if the force moving said bodies is equal. This may happen because there is less surface area in large bodies than in small ones in proportion to their quantity and weight. Or rather, one must answer that a pike, a boat, or other bodies are never pushed with a greater effect unless they are pushed harder, and that we are mistaken when we believe they are pushed with an equal force that increases proportional to the size of the body. Just as a ship cannot be moved as fast as a small boat by an equal wind, the full pike and larger bodies cannot be moved at an equal speed by an equal force—even if we cannot notice this inequality in the force of the hand of the person pushing or pulling all sorts of bodies.

The objection contains several other things regarding the principle and extent of forces and **seeds** <note>original: "semences." In this context, it refers to the internal "germs" or fundamental principles of natural properties or movements.</note>; to the force of rays, to the radii of wheels and other mechanical engines; to the manner of...

As for balls and other bodies that travel further when the tubes and <term>blowguns<note>original: "sarbatanes." These were long tubes used to fire projectiles by breath, often used as a physical model for cannons in 17th-century ballistics.</note></term>, or other similar bodies, are longer, we shall perhaps speak of them in the book on the *Music of Cannons, Drums, and other noises used in war*.

The fifth objection contains two things, the first of which is true, and the second is false: for there is no doubt that the same weight, or the same force, stretches a string equally regardless of its length—even if one end were attached to the **firmament** <note>The "firmament" refers to the heavens or the sphere of the fixed stars; Mersenne is using a cosmic scale to emphasize that physics remains consistent regardless of distance.</note> and the other to a nail in a floor or a **Monochord**—and consequently even if the first were 16,030,000 **leagues** <note>A league (lieuë) was a unit of distance, roughly 4 kilometers. Mersenne is imagining a string stretching millions of miles into space.</note> long and the second only one foot long. This is because weight breaks a long string as easily as a short one, as we have remarked above and elsewhere. The second part of the objection draws a conclusion from equal tension to the equality of the **vibrations** <note>original: "retours," referring to the back-and-forth movement or oscillations of the string.</note> of the string; the falsehood of this will be demonstrated in another place.

Now, one can conclude from this whole discourse that the strings of musical instruments are equally stretched in all their parts, and that the breaking that occurs near the **bridge** <note>original: "cheualet."</note> or elsewhere comes from the strings being weaker or more worn in the places where they break, or by reason of different accidents encountered in different instruments, the different material of the strings, and the different manner of tension; I reserve the discussion of these for the treatise on instruments, in which it will be easier to examine all the different encounters and properties of strings.

## NOTICE.

I will speak more particularly of everything concerning the force and movement of strings in the third book, after having considered in the second the movements of the greatest bodies of the universe, such as the **Earth** and the **stars**, and several things touching the movement of heavy bodies toward their center, and of violent movements made by means of wheels and otherwise. To this, it will always be easy to add many other things, both by experience and by reason, given the great multitude of different movements observed in nature. Now, the book that follows contains the examination of what **Lord Galileo**, a most excellent philosopher, proposed in his *Dialogues on the Systems of Ptolemy and Copernicus*, and several other things that deserve to be considered by the best minds in the world, so that they may establish some principle in this subject which might provide a multitude of advantageous consequences for **Physics**. If any conclusion is found in this first book that is not sufficiently well deduced, or some similarity that does not please, everyone is free to leave them or to adapt them as they like; which I desire to be understood for all the other books.

would then fall through a semicircle equal to the quadrant of the circle of the Moon’s heaven, as I shall demonstrate later.

I come now to the proportion of the speed of heavy bodies, which always go on increasing their speed as they approach the earth, following all the experiments I have been able to make with bodies heavy enough to overcome the resistance of the air—for example, with balls of lead and of wood.

Now, what **Galileo** remarks in response to **Scheiner** is true: namely, that this speed increases according to the odd numbers that follow unity <note>This refers to Galileo’s "Law of Odd Numbers," which states that the distances traveled in successive equal intervals of time by a falling body follow the ratio 1, 3, 5, 7, etc.</note>; so that if in a given time the moving body covers one space, it will cover three in the second interval of time, five in the third, seven in the fourth, etc. This is because the spaces covered by the moving body from the place where it begins falling are to one another in the <term>duplicate ratio<note>The "duplicate ratio" of times means the ratio of their squares ($t^2$).</note></term> of the times in which the fall occurs: that is to say, the spaces are to one another as the squares of the times.

This being established, he says he has tested that a hundred-pound cannonball falls from a height of one hundred <term>brasses<note>The *brasse* (fathom) was a unit of length based on the reach of a man's arms, roughly 5 to 6 feet. Here, the text specifies 3,000 brasses make one mile.</note></term> in 5 seconds of an hour; the same happens to a ten-pound ball, and to any other body that has enough force to cleave the air. And because the spaces increase according to the squares of the times, one will find the fall for the time of one minute of an hour if one multiplies the hundred brasses by the square of 12 (because a minute contains 12 intervals of 5 seconds); that is to say, by 144, one will have 14,400 brasses for the fall of one minute of an hour. And by the same rule, the square of 60 minutes multiplying 14,400 gives 51,840,000 for the fall of one hour, which is worth 17,280 miles. And to know the fall of 4 hours, he multiplies 17,280 by 16, which is the square of 4; from which comes 276,480, which is greater than the radius of the concave of the Moon, which is only 196,000, or 56 terrestrial semi-diameters <note>The author uses 56 earth radii as the distance to the Moon, a common estimate in the 17th century based on Ptolemaic and Copernican calculations (the modern average is about 60).</note>, since the radius of the earth is only 3,500 miles, each of 3,000 brasses, as his adversary supposes. Against him, he concludes that the cannonball will descend in less than four hours: and if one does the exact calculation, it will fall in 3 hours, 22 minutes, and 4 seconds. For since it covers one hundred brasses in 5 seconds, it will cover 588,000,000 (which are worth 56 terrestrial semi-diameters) in the aforementioned time, as he proves by multiplying the third term by the square of the second, to get 14,700,000,000, which being divided by the first term, namely by one hundred, the square root of the quotient gives 12,124 for the seconds the ball employs to fall—that is to say, 3 hours, 22 minutes, 4 seconds. The reason for this calculation is founded on the fact that the square of the given time is to the square of the sought time as space is to space. That is why if one multiplies the third number by the square of the time (which is the second number) and divides the product by the first number, the quotient will give the square of the sought number, the root of which will be the said sought number.

Now, we had found another means of computing the times when the spaces are given, before having seen the preceding one; for knowing that the spaces are to each other in the duplicate ratio of the times, it is easy to infer that the times are to each other in the <term>subduplicate ratio<note>The "subduplicate ratio" refers to the ratio of the square roots.</note></term> of the spaces; and that if the spaces are to each other as the squares of the times, the times are to each other as the square roots of the spaces: upon which we found the rule that follows.

Just as the root of 100, namely 10, is to 5 seconds, so the root of 588,000,000, namely 24,248 7/10, is to 12,124 7/20, which makes 3 hours, 22 minutes, 4 seconds, 21 thirds. But as for Galileo’s experiment, I cannot imagine where the great difference comes from...

# On the Movement of Bodies.

...is found here in Paris and its surroundings, concerning the time of falls, which has always appeared much shorter to us than his: it is not that I wish to reproach such a great man for a lack of care in his experiments, but I have performed them several times from different heights, in the presence of several judicious persons, and they have always turned out the same way. This is why, if the <term>fathom<note>The original French uses *brasse*, a unit of length roughly equal to the reach of a man's arms.</note></term> that Galileo used is only one foot and two-thirds—that is to say, 20 inches of the <term>King’s foot<note>The *pied de Roy* (King’s foot) was the standard French unit of length, slightly longer than the modern English foot.</note></term> used in Paris—it is certain that the ball descends more than a hundred fathoms in 5 seconds. Now, it seems that the said fathom is only that long, since we give 5,000 feet to one Italian mile, which contains 3,000 fathoms; and the size he gives for the circumference of the earth, namely 22,000 miles, approaches that which we give it, namely 7,200 leagues, which are worth 21,600 miles; whether he uses this number because it is easier, or because he gives 400 miles more than we do to the circumference, to which we give 64,800,000 fathoms, or 108,000,000 King’s feet; and if he made the circumference equal to ours, his fathom would only be 19 7/11 inches.

This being established, Galileo’s hundred fathoms are 166 2/3 of our feet: but our experiments, repeated more than 50 times, joined with the <term>duplicate ratio<note>The "duplicate ratio" refers to the law that distance is proportional to the square of the time ($d \propto t^2$).</note></term>, constrain us to say that the ball covers 300 feet in 5 seconds, which is to say 180 fathoms, or almost twice as much as he states. Thus, it should cover the hundred fathoms, or 166 2/3 feet, in 3 seconds 18/25, which makes 3'', 43''', 20'''', <note>3 seconds, 43 thirds, and 20 fourths. In this period, time was subdivided into 60ths: seconds, thirds, and fourths.</note> and not 5 seconds. For we have tested very exactly that a lead globe weighing about half a pound, and a wooden one weighing about one ounce, fall 48 feet in 2 seconds, 108 feet in 3 seconds, and 147 feet in 3 and 1/2 seconds. Now, 147 feet equates to 88 1/5 fathoms; and if there is a miscalculation, it comes rather from us giving too little space to the said times than the contrary, for having let the weight fall from 110 feet, it fell in exactly 3 and 1/2 seconds; but we take 108 to regulate the proportion, and men cannot observe the difference in time in which it falls from 110 or 108 feet. As for the height of 147 feet, it was half a foot short; which makes the duplicate ratio very exact, insofar as the weight must cover 3 feet in a half-second, following this speed: 12 feet in one second; and consequently 27 feet in 1 1/2 seconds, 48 feet in 2 seconds, 75 feet in 2 1/2 seconds, 108 feet in 3 seconds, and 147 feet in 3 1/2 seconds. This corresponds very well to our experiments, according to which it will fall 192 feet in 4 seconds, and 300 in 5 seconds, during which Galileo only places 166 feet or 100 fathoms, according to which it must cover one fathom in a half-second, and 4 in 1 second, which are nearly 6 2/3 feet, instead of 12
