### PROPOSITION II.

*If a weight, having fallen through a given distance, no longer increased the speed it acquired at the last point of that distance, and continued at that same speed, it would cover a distance double the first in an equal time; from which it is inferred that the falling stone passes through all possible degrees of <term>slowness<note>Original: "tardiveté." Galileo argued against the idea that objects jump to a certain speed instantly; instead, they pass through every infinitesimal degree of speed starting from zero (rest).</note></term>.*

Galileo uses the triangle ABC to explain the degrees of speed of falling weights; and for this purpose, he divides the side AC into five equal parts—AD, DE, EF, FG, and GC—and draws lines parallel to the base BC, namely DH, EI, etc., so that one might imagine that the parts marked on AC represent equal units of <term>time<note>In this geometric model, the vertical axis represents the duration of the fall, while horizontal lines represent the instantaneous speed at those moments.</note></term>, and that the parallels represent the degrees of speed which increase and grow equally in equal times. Thus, A is the point of rest, and the moving body at A acquires the speed DH at time AD; and consequently, at the second unit of time DE, the speed is increased by IE, and likewise for the other lines KF, etc. But because this speed grows continually from moment to moment, and not by pauses or jumps from one specific time to another, it is certain that the degrees of speed from the rest at A until the acquisition of the degree HD in the time AD are infinite, following the infinity of the instants of time AD, or the points of line AD.

This is why one must imagine an infinity of lines drawn through all the points of the line AD, which make up the surface of the triangle ADH; by which we understand all the distances the moving body will cover with a movement that is always increasing uniformly. And for this purpose, one must complete the parallelogram AMBC, and extend the lines from each point of A to each point of MB, so that just as BC of triangle ABC signifies the degree of the greatest speed, and the surface of the triangle is the sum of all the speed with which the moving body passed through such a distance in time AC, in the same way, the parallelogram is a mass and a sum of as many other degrees of speed, each of which is equal to the greatest speed BC. This sum is double the sum of the triangle, just as the parallelogram is double the same triangle. From this, he concludes that if the moving body, which used the degrees of speed of the triangle, has passed through all that distance, it would, if using the speed corresponding to the parallelogram, cover double the distance in the same time by a <term>uniform movement<note>Original: "mouvement egal." This refers to motion at a constant speed, as opposed to "uniformly accelerated" motion.</note></term>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the laws of motion. It shows a rectangular frame with corners labeled M (top-left), A (top-right), C (bottom-right), and O (bottom-left). A vertical axis AC on the right is divided into segments by points D, E, F, G, and C. From these points, horizontal lines DH, EI, FK, GL, and CB extend to a diagonal line AB. The points where these horizontals meet the diagonal are labeled H, I, K, L, and B. The diagram represents the geometric derivation of the distance traveled under uniform acceleration, comparing the area of the triangle ABC to a corresponding rectangle.</image-desc>

But we will perhaps explain this more clearly by drawing from the line BC (which signifies the maximum speed) the two lines CO and BN to double the parallelogram, for BD is equal to BA. Now it must be noted that all the speeds of HD, IE, etc., are found joined in BC, so that the speed BC is composed of all the preceding ones, just as the line of times AC is composed of all the other lines. But the surfaces comprised by the small triangles AHD, AIE, etc., increase as the square of the times; for those that have double the side result in a quadruple ratio. This I demonstrate in triangle AIE, which represents the distance covered during time AE, for it is quadruple the triangle AHD, which is covered in time AD (which is half of time AE); consequently, the surface...

## Second Book

*A K F* is 9 times larger than *A H D*, just as the space covered by the moving body at time *A F* is 9 times greater than that covered at time *A D*: so that if time *A E* and speed *E I* are to time *A F* and speed *K F* as 2 is to 3, the spaces *A I E* and *A K F* are as their squares, 4 and 9. And if one takes the space covered during specific parts of said times, the first part being 1, the second will be 3, the third 5, and the following 7, 9, etc., according to the sequence of all <term>odd numbers<note>This refers to Galileo’s "Law of Odd Numbers," which states that the distances traveled in successive equal intervals of time by a falling body follow the ratio 1, 3, 5, 7, etc.</note></term>; just as are the surfaces *A H D*, 1; *H D I E*, 3; *I E K F*, 5; *K F L G*, 7; *L G B C*, 9.

Now, if the speed *B C* no longer increased, and the fall continued uniformly, it would no longer be necessary to increase *B C*, but it would only be necessary to continue the lines of increase from *A B* from *C* to *O*, so that *C O* represents a time equal to *C A*, and the space the moving body would cover is signified by the parallelogram *B C N O*, which has the same degree of speed at both *B C* and *N O*, and which is double the triangle *A B C*; from which it is easy to conclude that the space covered by a moving body in uniform motion is double that which is covered by an accelerated motion <note>This is the "Mean Speed Theorem," demonstrating that an object moving at a constant speed (equal to the final speed of an accelerated body) covers twice the distance in the same amount of time.</note>.

I show the same thing again through numbers, for the benefit of those who do not know Geometry: and I say that if the moving body covers 3 feet in half a second, it will have acquired such an <term>impetuosity<note>Original: "impetuosité," a term used before "momentum" or "kinetic energy" were formally defined to describe the "force" of a moving object.</note></term> that, by not increasing it further, it will cover 6 feet in another half second: which one will understand by considering the path it travels immediately before and after the end of the half second in very short times: for example, I consider the path the weight travels in each <term>tierce<note>A historical unit of time: 1/60th of a second.</note></term> of this half second, which contains 30 of them; in the first of which it covers 1/25 of an inch; in the 2nd, 3/25 of an inch; in the 3rd, 5/25; in the 4th, 7/25, and so on according to the odd numbers up to the 30th, or last tierce, during which it covers 59/25 of an inch, just as it would cover 61/25 in the following 31st. Now, since this speed always grows in arithmetic proportion by always adding the same number to the preceding number, I conclude that if one takes the middle of the 30th and the 31st tierce, which is the end of the half second, one will also have the middle of 59/25 and 61/25, which is to say 60/25 of an inch, or 2 2/5 inches; which the moving body covers in one tierce taken partly before and partly after the end of the half second, namely 30 <term>fourths<note>Original: "30'''" (quatrièmes), representing 1/60th of a tierce, or 1/3600th of a second.</note></term> before and as much after. And if one multiplies 2 2/5 inches by 30 tierces, which are in half a second, one will have 72 inches, which is to say the 6 feet that had to be found in half a second: which shows that it covers one foot in 5 tierces, and that it acquires exactly this speed at the last instant of the first half second, or at the first instant of the following one.

The same thing will be found by half-tierces, while the weight covers 1/100 of an inch, for it will cover 119/100 in the 60th half-tierce, and in the 61st, 121/100, and consequently it will cover 120/100, or one inch and 1/5 in 15 fourths before and after the end of the half second: now if one multiplies 1 1/5 inch by 60 half-tierces which are in half a second, one will have 72 inches, or 6 feet.

From which it is easy to conclude that the speed of weights goes toward infinity, as much toward the end as toward the beginning of their fall; and that one can decrease the speed in a given ratio if one goes back toward the beginning, just as one increases it by descending toward the end: for example, the weight covers 1/3 of a <term>line<note>Original: "ligne," a unit equal to 1/12th of an inch.</note></term> in 50 fourths, and one line in the 50 that follow. It covers 1/90,000 of an inch, or 1/7,500 of a line in one fourth, and if it continued at this speed it would cover only one foot in 5 minutes. In 20

### COROLLARY II.

*Where it is shown in how much time a stone would fall from the Stars, the Sun, and the Moon, down to the surface, or to the center of the earth.*

I suppose that the stone follows our proportions <note>The author is referring to the Law of Falling Bodies (often associated with Galileo), which states that the distance an object falls is proportional to the square of the time elapsed.</note>, which show that it falls 12 feet in one second, and 300 feet in five seconds. From this, it follows that it will fall from the surface of the earth to the center in 19 minutes, 56 seconds, 25 thirds, 9 fourths, and 36 fifths <note>Following 17th-century mathematical notation, "thirds," "fourths," and "fifths" are sexagesimal subdivisions of a second—each one being 1/60th of the previous unit.</note>, as we said in the first corollary; from the Moon, which is at a distance of 56 radii <note>original: "demidiam." (demidiametres). A "half-diameter" is the radius of the Earth.</note>, to the center of the earth in 2 hours, 29 minutes, 14 seconds, 25 [thirds], 48 [fourths]: and down to the surface in 2 hours, 17 minutes, 54 seconds, 6 thirds, 54 fourths. When these are subtracted from the previous number, there remains 1 minute, 20 seconds, 18 [thirds], 54 [fourths] for the time of the fall that occurs from the surface of the earth down to its center.

The weight would fall from the Sun, located 1142 radii away, to the center of the earth in 11 hours, 13 minutes, 56 seconds, 48 [thirds]; and down to the Moon, located 56 radii away, in 10 hours, 57 minutes, 12 [seconds], 54 [thirds]; which being subtracted from 11 hours, 15 minutes, 56 seconds, 48 [thirds], there remains 16 minutes, 43 seconds, 54 thirds for the fall from the Moon to the center of the earth. And from the Sun to the surface of the earth, the fall occurs in 11 hours, 13 minutes, 38 [seconds], 57 [thirds]: which being subtracted from 11 hours, 13 minutes, 56 [seconds], 48 [thirds], there remains 17 seconds, 51 [thirds] for the fall from the surface of the earth to its center; and for the fall from the Moon to the surface, one has 16 minutes, 26 [seconds], 3 [thirds].

Finally, the weight will fall from the stars, located 14,000 radii away, to the center of the earth in 39 hours, 19 minutes, 41 [seconds], 57 [thirds], 54 [fourths]: down to the Sun in 37 hours, 4 minutes, 24 [seconds], 37 [thirds], 21 [fourths]: and from the Sun to the center in 1 hour, 38 minutes, 17 [seconds], 20 [thirds], 33 [fourths]. From the stars to the Moon in 39 hours, 14 minutes, 58 [seconds], 30 [thirds]: and from there to the center in 4 minutes, 43 [seconds], 27 [thirds], 54 [fourths]: and from the Sun to the Moon in 1 hour, 33 minutes, 33 [seconds], 52 [thirds], 39 [fourths].

And if one desires the exact time of the fall from the firmament, one has 39 hours, 19 minutes, 41 [seconds], 58 [thirds], 12 [fourths]. Down to the surface, 39 hours, 19 minutes, 36 [seconds], 54 [thirds]. From the surface to the center, 5 seconds, 4 [thirds], 15 [fourths], that is to say, 1/19th of the whole fall from the Stars to the center of the earth.

This demonstrates a strange speed for weights, assuming they always maintain the same progression; for this last number shows that a stone would cover 1145 leagues <note>The author estimates the Earth's radius to be 1145 leagues. A league was a variable measurement of distance, usually around 2.5 to 3 miles.</note>, which is to say the entire radius of the earth, in the time it takes the pulse or the heart to beat six times; this is almost incomprehensible, and is why several people deny that this progression of speed continues all the way to the center. To this, one might add that weights might perhaps not descend from the Stars at all, upon which they might remain just as they do upon the earth. But we can conclude nothing about what would happen, since we can perform no experiment on this.

### PROPOSITION III.

-> *To determine the figure of the movement of heavy bodies that would fall from the top of a Tower, or from any other height one might wish, assuming that the earth moves and completes a full rotation on its axis every day.* <-

It is not necessary to explain the helix <term>helix: a three-dimensional spiral path</term> that the weight would make if its movement were uniform like that of the earth, since we have already shown its deformity <note>In this context, "deformity" refers to the irregularity or deviation of the path from a simple geometric curve</note> and its inequality, which I assume now so as not to use any repetition. But so that this proposition might be more pleasing, I wish to examine Galileo’s thoughts on this subject, of which he speaks starting on page 156 of his *Dialogues* <note>Referring to Galileo's "Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems" (1632)</note>: this is why I describe here the circle BI with center A, which represents the earth, and I extend the radius <term>demidiametre: literally "half-diameter," the standard term for a radius in this period</term> AB as far as C, so that BC is the height of the Tower; this Tower, being carried by the earth along the circumference BI, describes with its summit the arc CDN. I then divide the radius AC in half at point E, from which I describe the semicircle CIA, through which Galileo says it is probable that the stone falls, if its movement is composed of the circular [movement] of the earth and the straight [movement] which is proper to the stone: which he proves thus.

Now, these points always move further and further from the top of the Tower; this is why the straight movement of the stone along the Tower shows itself to be increasingly augmented and more violent <term>violent: in early modern physics, "violent motion" referred to any motion that was forced or accelerated, as opposed to "natural motion" at a constant speed</term>. And because the angle DCI is infinitely acute, the distance from the surface CFD, or from the top of the Tower, is very small at the beginning; consequently, the movement of the stone is all the slower as it is closer to C, or to rest, and it moves faster toward the center A than in any other place.

Now we must examine this beautiful thought of Galileo’s, in order to see if the movement of the stone, which seems perpendicular to us, can be circular and equal to that of the earth, just as the semicircle BIA is equal to the quarter circle CN. We had already considered this same line before having seen his *Dialogues*; but since he places the fall of weights in the squared ratio of times <note>The Law of Falling Bodies: the distance an object falls is proportional to the square of the time elapsed</note>, as we have done, to which the ratio of the versines <term>Sinus verses: versines, a trigonometric function equal to 1 minus the cosine of an angle</term> of equal arcs is nearly similar—principally at the beginning of the fall when they are small—it is easy to show that the fall of stones cannot occur through the semicircle BIA: which I demonstrate by the other figure that follows, namely A, 90, L, in which the arcs represent the time, and the versines the space of the fall. We have said above that if the weight fell in six hours from wherever it might be, it would be necessary for it to have various degrees of speed according to the various distances from the center from which it was let fall; and consequently, being at the Moon, distant by 58 terrestrial semi-diameters, or 66,666 leagues <term>league: a unit of distance; here likely referring to the "great league" used in 17th-century French geography</term> from the center of the earth, it would travel 820 leagues in 36 minutes of an hour, since the earth would travel 9 degrees in 36 minutes. Now, the versed sine <term>versed sine: a trigonometric function (1 - cosine) used in early physics to calculate the vertical distance fallen during circular motion</term> of 9 degrees is 1,230, the radius being 100,000; therefore, if the radius is 66,666, the versed sine will be 820 leagues; and if the radius is equal to the semi-diameter of the earth, that is to say, 1,145 5/11 leagues, the versed sine of 9 degrees will be 14 1/10, and therefore the weight ought only to travel 14 1/10 leagues in 36 minutes: and nevertheless it will fall, according to our experiments and the squared ratio <note>The "squared ratio" refers to the law of falling bodies, $d = at^2$, where distance is proportional to the square of time</note>, 3,732 leagues and 1,200 toises <term>toise: a traditional French unit of length, roughly 1.949 meters</term> during the said time.

<header>On the Movement of Bodies.</header>

### PROPOSITION V.

*To explain the utilities and the practical applications that can be drawn from the preceding propositions for Mechanics, and for several other things; and particularly how one can measure all sorts of heights by the fall of weights, and how one can easily find the distance of a fall in a given time, and the time required when the distance of the fall is known.*

If heavy bodies always follow the proportion of which we have spoken, when they fall from all sorts of heights—as occurs at the heights we have upon the surface of the earth—one can tell from what height they fall, provided that one knows the time of their fall, and the first space <note>In this context, "space" refers to the distance covered in the first interval of time</note> of said fall. For example, if one knows that a ball has taken 30''' <note>original: "10'''"—this appears to be a transcription error in the original or the OCR for 30'''. Mathematically, 30 thirds of a second (half a second) fits the calculation for 3 feet when compared to the 2-second/48-foot example</note> to travel 3 feet, it must be concluded that it fell 48 feet in 2'', and if it takes 3 1/2'', that it fell 147 feet. Thus, a man enclosed in a room, or standing in the middle of a well, a quarry, etc., and seeing the falling weight pass before his eyes, can tell from what height it fell if he observes the speed of its fall and what path it travels in 30''' <term>30 thirds: in early modern science, a "third" (indicated by ''') is 1/60th of a second</term>, or in another period of time. And if he knows the depth of the place where the fall occurs, he will know the time it needs to complete its journey.

From this, one can derive a new way of measuring heights and depths; for if one knows the time of the fall, or at least the path it travels at the final moment of its fall, one will know the height of the tower, the vault, the well, or other places from which it falls. However, it is not appropriate to use this method of measuring heights [regularly], because one can easily be mistaken over a great height by 3 or 4 feet, or <term>toises: an old French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or 6.4 feet</term>, and more—given that between 108 and 147 feet, there is only a half-second of difference.

Nevertheless, if someone wishes to make use of it, I place here a table for their benefit, by which it is easy to know the time of the fall of a given body when one knows the place from which it falls, and the place from which it falls when one knows the time of its fall. For one must only double the ratio of the times to know the spaces, or take the square root <note>original: "sous-doubler la raison"—literally "sub-double the ratio," a contemporary term for finding the square root in geometric proportions</note> of the ratio of the spaces to know that of the times. Now, the first column contains 30 half-seconds, so that one may know the space the weight covers in falling in each of the first 30 half-seconds—that is to say, in the first half-second <column-break/> minute, in the second half-second, or in the others that follow until the thirtieth half-second. For this time suffices for all the heights and depths that may be encountered, insofar as we have no towers, wells, mines, etc., whose height is more than 2,700 feet, or 450 toises. The tower of Utrecht <note>The Dom Tower (Domtoren) of Utrecht, which was then and remains the tallest church tower in the Netherlands</note>, which is held to be one of the highest in the world, is only one <term>stade: an ancient unit of length (stadium), here used to mean 125 feet</term>, or 125 feet; and the deepest quarries and caverns from which coal, slate, etc., are drawn, are at most only 250 toises, or 1,500 feet.

The 2nd column contains the odd numbers, which show the proportion of the falls that occur in each half-second; for all the odd numbers (which constitute the differences of the square numbers) give the individual falls—

But I have drawn these up for half-seconds, because weights descend quite notably in a half-second, that is to say in the 120th part of a minute; although one could make others for thirds, and fourths, and for thousandth parts of seconds, etc., by always following the same order and the same proportion of numbers. <note>The "proportion of numbers" refers to the Galilean law where the total distance fallen is proportional to the square of the time.</note>

The 3rd column keeps the same proportion as the 2nd, insofar as it proceeds from the multiplication of the 2nd, for the weight descends 3 feet in the first half-second. But if one makes a table where the unit is the first space covered in a given time—for example, if instead of 3 feet one takes half a <term>toise: an old French unit of length, approximately 1.95 meters</term>—the 2nd column will give the distance of the fall made in each time interval, without it being necessary to use the 3rd column; so that the 2nd number of the said 2nd column, namely 3, will show that the weight falls 3 half-toises, and the [next] number 5, that it falls 5 half-toises.

The same thing happens if one divides each second into 12 parts, to know the height from which the weight falls in each 12th part of a second, as one sees in this small table, which shows that it falls from one inch high in the first twelfth; from 3 in the second twelfth part, from 5 in the third twelfth, etc., and consequently that it falls 4 inches in 2 twelfths, 9 in 3, and 36 inches in 6 twelfths, that is to say 3 feet in the first half-second; so that this small table ends where the large one that follows begins, and which contains thirty half-seconds, that is to say 15 seconds, which are worth 1/4 of a minute of an hour, or the 240th part of an hour.

The 4th column <note>The 4th column likely appears on a subsequent page in a larger table, but is explained here for clarity.</note> shows how far the weight descends in all the half-seconds taken together: for example, how far it falls in 2, 3, or 4 half-seconds, that is to say in one, one and a half, or two seconds. For if one only wants to know the whole seconds, one must always take double the numbers in the first column. One will thus know that it descends 300 feet in 5 seconds, because 300 feet is in the 4th column, opposite the 10 in the first, which is worth 10 half-seconds, or 5 seconds: and the 30th or last number of the 4th column shows that it descends 2700 feet in 15 seconds, or in 30 half-seconds, which are marked at the end of the 1st column, whose numbers continually follow the natural order, and mark the time of the falls.

Those of the 2nd column, being added together, make the squares: for 1 and 3 make the first square number, namely 4; 1, 3, and 5 make the 2nd square, 9; 1, 3, 5, and 7 make the 3rd square, 16, and so on to infinity. Each of these gives the fall of each half-second when one takes them for half-toises; if one wants the falls in <term>Royal feet: "pieds de Roy," a pre-metric unit approximately 32.5 cm</term>, the 3rd column contains them: but those of the 4th column add up the spaces that are separated in the 3rd.

I add another use for <term>Mechanics: the study of machines and forces</term>, namely that one can know the force of <term>percussion: the impact or strike</term>, or the blow, if it depends on the speed of the movement of the striking bodies; thus one can know the height from which hammers must fall to produce whatever effect is desired; and consequently, from where they have fallen when one sees their effect. Finally, one can receive several other satisfactions from this <term>speculation: theoretical study</term> by comparing the different speeds of falls with other movements in nature; for example, if one determines the speed of a cannonball, an arrow, or any other <term>missile: any object thrown or projected</term> that one wishes, or the flight of birds, winds, lightning, etc. One will easily find the heights from which weights must fall to go as fast as the said missiles and other moving bodies, or to go slower according to a given ratio. ### COROLLARY.

I leave aside several other applications that anyone can infer from these experiments, to which others may be added; and I shall be very pleased if they are continued after me, so that many secrets of nature may be discovered, and the reason for this proportion of speeds may be found, or it may be determined at what point each weight begins to decrease its acceleration while falling, and where it finds the point where some believe they no longer increase their speed <note>A reference to terminal velocity, the point where air resistance prevents further acceleration.</note>, and from there travel to the center <note>The center of the Earth.</note> at a uniform rate; although I touch upon these difficulties elsewhere. Now, since we have discussed the fall of weights so precisely, it is appropriate to examine another excellent idea that Galileo attributes to Plato, and which he himself seems to follow and embrace with great satisfaction, since it depends on falls and experiments with which he agrees; this is why I add the following proposition.

## PROPOSITION VI.

->*To determine if the heavenly bodies fell from the same place by a straight motion, which then changed into the circular motion they have now, as Galileo imagines along with Plato, to whom he attributes this opinion; and to provide the method for calculating their falls, their distances, and their circular movements.*<-

If I am found to be too bold in carrying Harmony <note>The author, Marin Mersenne, often linked the "Harmony of the World" (laws of music and math) to the laws of physics and astronomy.</note> to the heavens, and in speaking of sounds or the movement of the stars, one must consider that God has placed us in this world to be spectators of His handiwork, and to consider its efforts and movements, in order to admire the wisdom and power of the Maker, and to love His goodness, upon which we absolutely depend.

Now, since we know that the planets move—whether one considers the stars to be mobile or immobile—and that they are the largest visible bodies in the world, we shall first see if they could have acquired the speed of their circular movements (by which they roll around the Sun or the Earth) through the force of straight motion. By this means, a great man of our time <note>Referring to Galileo Galilei.</note> imagines that the planets fell from the same place to the locations where they are now, and where their Author changed their straight motion into a circular one of the same speed, so that it might be eternal, or last until His providence caused it to cease.

This is therefore what we have to examine; and for this subject, we must take the size of their circles and the speed of their movements, in order to see if this comes as close to accuracy as he asserts, and if the size of the circles is justly proportioned to the speed of movement, following the ratio of the <term>impetuosity: the momentum or "force" acquired by a body during its acceleration</term> acquired through straight motion.

As for the diameters of the circles of the planets, we shall take those of

The Earth, following this hypothesis, completes its revolution in 365 days, 6 hours, and 9 minutes relative to the <term>fixed stars: the background stars that appear not to move relative to one another</term> around the Sun; and in 1 second, it travels 5,135 feet and 1/7. Venus completes its revolution in 5,393 hours around the Sun, and travels 6,000 feet and 19/22 in one second. Mercury completes its revolution in 2,111 hours, 15 minutes, and 36 seconds; and in one second, it travels 7,615 feet and 1/7.

Now let us see from what distance from the Sun these bodies fell to have acquired the momentum of motion by which they cover the spaces we have mentioned in the span of one second. We will place all others at their mean distance from the Sun, because it would be useless to make them aphelion or perihelion, given that one cannot bring them closer to one body without moving them further from another. Now, the coincidence of Mercury’s aphelion and Saturn’s perihelion is quite fortunate, because they are both in the same sign of Sagittarius toward the end, and that of the Earth is very close at the beginning of Capricorn.

...fourth, and the spaces they cover in this time are in a ratio of 25 to 16, because they will travel 4 leagues 2,793 feet in 72 43/100 seconds, and 2 leagues 9,932 feet in 57 342/500 seconds.

This being established, it is easy to find the distance of the place where Saturn was formed, for it is distant from the Sun by 12,871,863 leagues 4,112 feet; that of Jupiter by 7,421,956 leagues 8,276 feet, as is demonstrated by adding the <term>radius: half the diameter</term> of its circle—namely 7,421,951 leagues 10,476 feet—to the path it traveled in a straight line to acquire the speed of 4 leagues 12,800 feet.

The location of Mars is distant by 2,087,087 leagues 234 feet; that of the Earth by 1,374,568 leagues 13,439 feet; that of Venus by 988,742 leagues 8,333 feet; that of Mercury at <term>aphelion: the point in an orbit furthest from the Sun</term> by 621,324 leagues 9,498 feet. From this, we derive the same proportion of which we have spoken; for the distance from Saturn to the Sun contains 20 and 7/10 times that of Mercury at aphelion; that of Venus 13 times; that of the Earth 9 and 2/5 times; that of Mars 6 and 1/6 times; and that of Jupiter one and 3/4 times, slightly less. But it is necessary to explain the manner of calculating these times and spaces, so that everyone may examine the truth of the calculation.

Now, this calculation is very brief and easy; for if one wishes to find that Saturn travels 1,730 feet in one second, one must divide its entire circumference, reduced into <term>King’s feet: a standard French unit of length before the metric system, roughly 32.5 centimeters</term>, by the number of seconds it takes to complete its entire revolution, in order to avoid the fractions encountered in other methods of calculation. And then, to know in how much time it acquired this speed, we assume our experiments to be very certain, which have shown us that a moving body travels 12 feet in one second, 48 feet in 2 seconds, 108 feet in 3 seconds, etc. <note>This follows the rule that distance is proportional to the square of time: 1²×12=12; 2²×12=48; 3²×12=108.</note> From this, we conclude that when it falls from 108 feet, it must necessarily travel 12 feet in the first second of its fall, 36 in the second, 60 in the third, etc., so that the difference in the path it travels in each second is 24 feet, since there is a difference of 24 from 12 to 36, and from 36 to 60, and because the path of the descent increases in arithmetic proportion by the continual addition of the same number, 24. Consequently, if one wishes to know the time required for a moving body to acquire, through its fall, a speed capable of covering 60 feet in one second, one must divide 60 by 24 (which is the difference of the path it travels in each second) to get 2 1/2; and at that instant, it will have acquired a <term>momentum: the driving force of a moving body</term> capable of covering 60 feet in one second, if it were to increase its speed no further. Now, if we suppose that Saturn travels 1,730 5/12 feet in its circle every second, we must divide this number by 24, and the quotient will give 72 43/100 seconds—namely, the time necessary for it to acquire a speed capable of covering 1,730 feet in one second, provided it increases its speed no further.

But it should be noted that I am assuming the planets do not travel further in falling than heavy bodies do here on Earth; for we cannot perform experiments that constrain us to conclude that they descend faster than terrestrial bodies, which descend almost as fast as one another when they have enough force to overcome the air so that it brings them no sensible hindrance, as we have said elsewhere.

Let us see then, according to these hypotheses, from what distance from their circle they have fallen, and how much of a path they traveled before turning in a circle; this will be found by using a rule that may be called the <term>square rule of three: a calculation used to find a value that varies with the square of another, essential for gravity</term>, and by saying: if in one second the moving body travels 12 feet, how many will it travel in 72 43/100 seconds?

For example, here I square 1 and 72 <sup>43</sup>/<sub>100</sub> to get 1 and 5,199 <sup>78049</sup>/<sub>100000</sub>, and then I multiply 5,199 by 12 to get 62,393 feet <sup>31947</sup>/<sub>40000</sub>, which is the distance sought. <note>The author is demonstrating the inverse-square law relationship between time and distance in falling bodies, a principle established by Galileo.</note>

If the first number had been something other than 1, it would have been necessary to divide 62,393 by the square of said number. Now, I prove the truth of this rule by doubling the number 62,393 to get 124,787 <sup>11947</sup>/<sub>20000</sub>, which Saturn will travel in 72 seconds of circular motion that no longer increases its speed. This is because if it travels 62,393 feet in 72 seconds of accelerated and unequal movement, and if it continues at that same speed, it will travel double that—namely 124,779 feet—in an equal and uniform movement over 72 seconds. Thus, by dividing 124,787 feet <sup>11947</sup>/<sub>20000</sub> by 72 <sup>43</sup>/<sub>100</sub> seconds, the quotient must give the number of feet it travels in each second in its orbit; this occurs similarly in the division where the quotient is 1,730 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>10</sub> feet, which Saturn travels in 1 second in its orbit.

From this, one can derive yet another means to know how far Saturn has fallen to have acquired its speed; for if one multiplies the number of seconds, 72 <sup>43</sup>/<sub>100</sub>, by the feet it travels in 1 second—namely 1,730 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>10</sub>—one will have 124,789 <sup>21947</sup>/<sub>20000</sub>, which when divided by 2 gives 62,393 <sup>31947</sup>/<sub>40000</sub>, as before. Now, even if one follows the experiments of Galileo regarding the time of falls, they do not greatly favor his thought. For if one sets the annual orbit at 200 terrestrial semi-diameters, and the <term>mobile: the moving object</term> falls 100 <term>fathoms: *brasses*, a French unit of length roughly equal to 5 or 6 feet</term> in 5 seconds (which is 4 fathoms in 1 second, and 16 in 2 seconds), it will travel 12 fathoms in the 1st second, 20 in the 3rd, and so on for the others, always adding 8 fathoms. And then, if these 100 fathoms are 166 <sup>2</sup>/<sub>3</sub> feet, so that the fathoms are to the feet as 5 to 3, one will find that Saturn travels 1,384 <sup>11</sup>/<sub>12</sub> feet, which gives 830 <sup>227</sup>/<sub>240</sub> fathoms in 1 second. When these are divided by 8, which is the difference in the path the mobile makes in each second, one has 103 <sup>4174</sup>/<sub>5000</sub> seconds for the time the weight will travel 4 <term>leagues: *lieues*, a unit of distance varying by region but often around 2 to 3 miles</term> 11,879 <sup>11</sup>/<sub>12</sub> feet. For if one multiplies 103 <sup>4174</sup>/<sub>5000</sub> by itself, one will have 10,781 <sup>3</sup>/<sub>4</sub>, which multiplied by 4 gives 43,126 fathoms, worth 4,611,879 feet—that is to say, 9,484 feet more than in our calculation. And Jupiter will have been created at 8 leagues 11,046 feet from its orbit, which only exceeds the preceding calculation by one league and 2,295 feet; this is not significant when considering distances of several million leagues.

### COROLLARY.

This opinion does not prevent God from having let the Planets, and even the Stars, fall from different places, and from having changed their straight movements into circular, or Elliptical ones, or into any other shape that pleased Him. Thus, I have not concluded that He did not do it, but only that it was not possible following the hypotheses in question. That is why everyone is still free to imagine whatever they wish about it, and to invent other hypotheses that preserve and explain everything that can happen in the various movements of celestial bodies. Now, after having explained what concerns the perpendicular fall of weights, it is necessary to examine the oblique fall that occurs by means of planes inclined to the horizon.

### PROPOSITION VII.

->*To explain the movements of weights on planes inclined to the horizon, with the proportion of their speeds; and to determine if a falling weight passes through all possible degrees of slowness.*<-

We have shown in the previous propositions that weights descending perpendicularly toward the center always increase their speed in every fall that can be tested; the same thing happens to a weight moving on a plane inclined to the horizon. Now, before presenting our experiments, it is appropriate to note that <term>Galileo</term> <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), the Italian physicist and astronomer whose work on motion laid the groundwork for classical mechanics.</note> made use of this speculation when he stated near the beginning of his *Dialogues* that Jupiter and the other planets fell in a straight line, passing first through all <term>degrees of slowness</term> <note>This refers to the concept that an accelerating object starts from a state of rest (infinite slowness) and passes through every intermediate velocity.</note> until reaching the speed they were meant to maintain in their circular motions; this is what we examined in the previous proposition. To this, he adds that a falling weight acquires an <term>impetuosity</term> <note>original: "impetuosité." In 17th-century physics, this term was used to describe what we now call momentum or kinetic energy.</note> capable of carrying it back up through as much space as it descended, provided that all types of impediments are removed. For example, a ball falling to the center would rise just as high on the other side of the center, with only the air being able to diminish this ascent. He confirms this with a weight attached to a cord <note>A pendulum.</note> which, when pulled away from its perpendicular line, returns just as far on the other side, except for the resistance of the air and the cord; and by the siphon, in which water rises as high as it has descended. However, I will deal with these matters in another place; for here we must consider the descent of bodies on inclined planes, such as plane CA and DA on the horizontal plane AB. Now, this descent occurs for the same purpose as it does along the perpendicular CB, since weights descend to reach the center of the earth. And because the weight, having arrived at point A, is just as close to the center as when it has descended to B, it acquires the same impetuosity both at A and at B, which is so great that it could make the weight at A and B rise back up to C; for although the line CA is longer than CB, it would nonetheless rise just as easily, because it would face less opposition.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a right-angled triangle labeled with points C at the top apex, B at the bottom right corner forming the right angle, and A at the far left on the horizontal base. An inclined line CA represents a plane. Another line DA starts from a point D on the base AB and meets the top C. A point T is marked on the line CA, with a perpendicular line BT drawn from the right angle corner B to the point T on the incline.</image-desc>

Now we must examine these thoughts of Galileo and consider that if it is true that the weight acquires an equal impetuosity whenever it has approached the center by an equal distance, it will only fall as far as T on the plane CA during the time it falls perpendicularly as far as B. This point T is found at the spot where the perpendicular line drawn from point B meets the plane CA—namely, BT. This must always be done to find the other points on the inclined plane where the weight must be located when the position of the perpendicular descent is given, or to find the said position on the perpendicular line. For example, a line drawn perpendicularly to CA at point A, and consequently parallel to line TB, being drawn until it meets the extension of the perpendicular CB, will give the location of the weight falling perpendicularly.

Similarly, on the inclined line DA, the weight falling from D to B will fall along the incline from D to I, which is the place where the line drawn from B intersects DA at <term>right angles</term>; and when it has fallen to A via the line DA, it will be at the point on the extended line DB where it is intersected by the line drawn from point A parallel to IB, which intersects DA at right angles.

From this it further follows that the time of the perpendicular fall is to the time of the oblique fall as the oblique path is to the perpendicular; for example, the time of the fall of the weight from C to B is to the time of the fall of the same weight from C to A, as CB is to CA: or in this second figure, the time of the fall from A to C is to the fall from A to B as AC is to BA, and consequently A will fall to D in the same time as it falls to B.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing an inclined line AB and a vertical line AD. Point C lies on the vertical AD between A and D. Point E is located above point B. Now, in triangle ABC, the angle B being 30 degrees, the line AC is half of BA, which serves as the radius, and AC is the <term>sine of 30 degrees</term> <note>In trigonometry, the sine of 30° is 0.5, meaning the side opposite the angle is half the hypotenuse.</note>, just as angle D of triangle ABD has; and therefore its sine AB is half of the radius AD, which is four times CA; and BA is the <term>mean proportional</term> <note>A value $x$ such that $a/x = x/b$. In this geometric context, it relates the lengths of the different paths of descent.</note> between AC and AD, since it is double AC and half of AD. And if we suppose that AC is 3 feet, the weight will cover it in half a second, and the 3 other parts which are from C to D in another half second, as we have demonstrated in the preceding propositions: now we suppose that it falls in the same time along the line AB as along the perpendicular AD, it will therefore reach AB in one second—that is to say, twice as much time as it employs to descend from A to C: from which it follows that there is the same ratio of the time of fall AB to the time of fall AC, as there is of the line BA of 6 feet to the line AC of 3 feet, for the line AB is double AC, just as the time of fall AB is double the time of fall AC: which was to be demonstrated.

Furthermore, since the times are in <term>sub-duplicate ratio</term> <note>original: "raison sousdoublee." In modern terms, this means the ratio of the square roots of the distances.</note> of the spaces, the ratio of the time of the fall through AC to the time of the fall through AD is as the root of the space AC, 1, to the root of the space AD, 2. There is also the same ratio from the line AC to BA, and from AB to DA, for AB being the mean proportional between AC and AD, it is to the said lines as the roots of the spaces AC and AD are to one another.

From this one can infer that the speed along the inclined line AB is in some way equal to the perpendicular speed AC, because the time increases in the same proportion as the space: for just as a man who travels 10 leagues in a day goes no faster than one who travels 20 leagues in 2 days, so too the moving body that covers AC of 3 feet in half a second will go no faster than that which covers AB of 6 feet in a second.

But the principle upon which these speculations are founded is not demonstrated—namely, that a weight falling along the incline AB always maintains such a speed relative to another body allowed to fall at the same time from point A along the perpendicular AD, that the line drawn from one body to the other (namely EC or BD) will form a right angle on the incline AB. Although there is a strong appearance that it is true, I shall give my opinion on this at the end of this proposition, after having considered whether the weight passes through an <term>infinity of degrees of slowness</term> from A to C, or to B.

# Second Book

Now it is certain that a weight descends all the more slowly as the plane is more inclined <note>In this context, "more inclined" means more nearly horizontal, or further from the vertical.</note>; for example, it moves more slowly on **A B** than on **C A**; so much so that one can provide a plane so slightly inclined to the horizon that the moving body will only travel 15 <term>Royal feet</term> <note>The "pied de Roy" (Royal foot) was a pre-metric French unit of length, approximately 32.48 cm, slightly longer than the modern English foot.</note> in a year, or in a hundred years, or in as long as one might wish: which demonstrates an extreme slowness. Let **B A** be a line inclined to the horizon by 7,967,056,942,080,000,000 <term>perches</term> <note>A unit of length; its value varied by region but was often around 18 to 22 feet.</note>, each of 15 Royal feet; if one removes three zeros from the said number, one will have the number of leagues a weight would travel in a hundred years. If the angle **A B D** is a right angle, and the line going from one moving body to another—namely from **A** to **D**—is perpendicular to the incline **B A**, it is certain, by the supposition, that when the body falling through **B D** is at **D**, the body falling at the same time from **B** to **A** will be at **A**. But to find the inclination of **A B**, that is to say the angle **B A C**, and the length of **B C**, one must know that **A B** is the <term>mean proportional</term> <note>A geometric mean: a value x such that a/x = x/b.</note> between **B D** and **C B**, and therefore as **D A** is to **B A**, likewise **B A** is to **B C**. Now, **B D** is to **B A** as 7,967,056,942,080,000,000 is to 1; therefore **A B** has the same ratio with **B C** as it does with **B D**; so that **B C** is only $\frac{1}{7,967,056,942,080,000,000}$ of a perch, or $\frac{1}{44,161,421,456,000,000}$ of an inch; which the moving body travels from **B** to **C** in a little less than 18 eighths and 29 ninths of time <note>The author is using sexagesimal divisions of time beyond seconds: thirds ($60^{-3}$), fourths, etc., down to eighths ($60^{-8}$) and ninths ($60^{-9}$) of a minute or hour.</note>: for if it travels one inch in 5 seconds, it will travel $\frac{1}{142,614}$ etc. of an inch in 18 eighths.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram located on the right side of the page. It illustrates an inclined plane AB. A vertical line descends from point B to point C, forming a right-angled triangle ABC. A line AD is drawn perpendicular to the incline AB, extending downwards to point D. Point E is marked on the line AB, close to point B.</image-desc>

The demonstration of this number is done as follows: I multiply $\frac{1}{441,614}$ etc. of an inch by the square of 5 seconds to have $\frac{25}{441,614}$ etc., the square root of which is $\frac{5}{210,384,000}$, or $\frac{1}{42,076,800}$ of a <term>third</term> <note>A "third" (tierce) is 1/60th of a second.</note>, by dividing 8,834,108,313,604,000,000,000 "ninth-minutes" of an hour, which are in these Julian years, by 7,967 etc. For the quotient gives 1,108 ninths and $\frac{660,912,177,556}{7,907,056,942,080}$: and if one divides the numbers of this fraction by 1,635,945,984, one will have $\frac{404}{487}$: so that one will have the same time of 1,108 ninths etc. by two different ways, one of which proceeds by the ratio of spaces being the duplicate of that of times, and the other by the proportion of **A D** to **B A**, and of **B A** to **B C**; for the spaces **D B** and **B C** are in a duplicate ratio of the ratio of **D A** to **B A**: but the times being in a sub-duplicate ratio of the spaces, the time of the fall **B D**, which occurs in a hundred years, must be in the same ratio with the time of the fall **B C**—that is to say with 1,108 ninths and $\frac{404}{487}$—as the line **A B** is to **B C**, that is to say as 7,967 etc. is to 1.

And to know the inclination of the plane **A B**, one must say: if **A B** as a radius of 7,967 etc. gives **B C** as 1, the sine of the angle **B A C**, how much will **A B** as 100,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 give? One will have 125,517, which subtends an angle of $\frac{1}{2,317,156,306,344,352}$ of a minute of a degree, that is to say 4 tenths and 21 elevenths, which give the inclination of the plane **B A**, upon which the weight being at **A** will have acquired a speed capable of traveling 30 feet in a hundred years. Now, having fallen to **C** via the perpendicular **B C**, it will have only the same speed; consequently, it passes through all degrees of slowness before having acquired a certain degree of speed, given that one can incline the plane **A B** even less: and even if one takes the speed of the moving body when it is at **E**, which I suppose to be 3 and $\frac{3}{4}$ feet from **B**—for **B E** is a quarter of **B A**—it will only reach **B E** in 50 years, and will only travel 15 feet in a hundred years if it continues at this same speed, which will also cause the speed of the perpendicular fall **B C** to diminish in the same proportion.

Now we must here record the experiments that we have performed very precisely <unclear>which</unclear> follows, so that one may follow what they yield. Having therefore chosen <unclear>a</unclear> height of five <term>Royal feet</term> <note>The "pied de Roy" (Royal foot) was a pre-metric French unit of length, approximately 32.48 cm.</note>, and having had a plane hollowed out and polished, we <unclear>there</unclear> gave it several types of inclinations, in order to let a lead ball and a very round wooden one roll the whole length of the plane. On the plane inclined by twenty-five degrees the ball falls one and a half feet; it should fall two feet, 1 1/2 inches. On that of thirty degrees it falls two feet: it should fall 2 1/2 feet, for it would travel six feet in the air while it falls 2 1/2 feet on the plane, whereas it should only fall five feet. On the plane inclined by 40 degrees, it should fall three feet, two and a half inches; and the very precise experiment gives only two feet, nine inches, for when one places the ball at two feet ten inches from the end of the plane, the ball which moves perpendicularly falls first; and when one distances it by two feet eight inches on the plane, it falls last; and when one distances it by two feet and nine inches, they fall exactly at the same time, without one being able to distinguish their sounds <note>This was a common method of measuring simultaneous arrival before the invention of the stopwatch: listening for a single "thud" or "click" as the two objects hit their targets.</note>.

On the plane of forty-five degrees it should fall three and a half feet and a little more, but it only falls three feet, and will not fall three and a half feet unless the other falls five and a half feet through the air.

On the plane of fifty degrees it should travel three feet ten inches; it only travels two [feet] and nine inches. This we have repeated several times very precisely, for fear of having failed, because it falls in the same time from 3 feet—that is to say 3 inches more—on the plane inclined at 45 degrees. This seems very strange, since it ought to fall all the faster as the plane is more inclined. And nevertheless, it goes no faster on the plane of 50 degrees than on that of 40: where it must be noted that these two inclinations are equally distant from that of 45 degrees, which holds the middle between the two extremes, namely between the infinite inclination made in the perpendicular line and that of the horizontal. However, if one considers this prodigious effect, one can say that it happens because the motion of the ball, being too violent in the inclination of 50 degrees, cannot slide and roll on the plane, which makes it jump several times; from which follows as much rest as jumps, during which the ball that falls perpendicularly always advances on its path. But these jumps do not happen in the inclination of 40, and only begin after that of 45, up to which the speed of the ball always increases in such a way that it can always roll without jumping. Now, while it travels three feet ten inches on the plane inclined at fifty degrees, it travels six and a half feet in the air, whereas it should only travel five.

->COROLLARY I.<-

I doubt that <term>Mr. Galileo</term> <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642). The author is questioning whether Galileo actually performed the experiments he described in his theories on motion.</note> has performed the experiments of falls on the plane, since he does not mention them at all, and the proportion he provides often contradicts experiment. I wish for several others to test the same thing on different planes with all the precautions they can devise, so that they may see if their experiments match ours, and if enough light can be shed on the matter to create a <term>Theorem</term> <note>A mathematical rule or scientific law.</note> in favor of the speed of these oblique falls. These speeds could be measured by the different effects of the weight, which will strike all the harder as the plane is less inclined relative to the horizon and as it approaches the perpendicular line.

->COROLLARY II.<-

Those who have seen our experiments and assisted in them know that one could not proceed with more accuracy, whether regarding the plane—which is quite straight and well-polished, forcing the moving body to descend straight—or regarding the roundness and weight of the balls, and the falls themselves. From this, one may conclude that <term>experiment</term> <note>Original: "l’experience." At this time, "experience" often meant experimental observation.</note> is not capable of generating a <term>science</term> <note>The author suggests that raw data alone, due to physical variables, cannot easily be turned into a perfect mathematical system.</note>, and that one must not rely too much on reasoning alone, since it does not always correspond to the truth of appearances, from which it often deviates. This will not prevent me from speaking of the equally inclined plane as it ought to be, so that heavy bodies may press upon it and weigh equally on each of its points. If anyone wishes to conduct more accurate experiments, they must use an inclined plane longer than ours; for example, a plane of 48 feet, on which the time of the fall will be much more perceptible—and if one had one of one hundred or 200 feet, it would be even better.

He concludes that while theory and experiment often diverge, using longer planes might provide more perceptible and accurate data.</summary>

### PROPOSITION VIII.

> *To demonstrate whether a weight can descend via an inclined plane to the center of the earth, and the method of describing a line so inclined that the weight always rests upon it and presses against it equally at every point.*

It is certain that a plane intended to support the same portion of a weight at all its points must be equally inclined toward the horizon. Those who imagine that our ordinary planes—for example, that plane **AB** is equally inclined to the horizon **BC** in all its parts—are mistaken. This is because <image-desc>A small geometric diagram of a right-angled triangle. Vertex A is at the top, vertex C is at the bottom right (the right angle), and vertex B is at the bottom left. A point E is marked on the hypotenuse AB.</image-desc> point **A** is inclined differently than point **E**, and point **B** differently than **E**. Consequently, there are as many different inclinations as there are different points on our ordinary planes. From this, it follows that one can easily be mistaken in <term>Mechanical treatises</term> <note>Works on the mathematical principles of machines and motion.</note> that assume the existence of inclined planes; for although the difference between the inclinations and their various parts is not very great, it can nonetheless hinder the truth of demonstrations, which consists in the <term>indivisible</term> <note>A 17th-century mathematical concept referring to the infinitely small components of a line or shape, a precursor to calculus.</note>. If the planes were very long, the error would be noticeable, and a weight supported by one of the points might roll or slide over the others. This will be admitted once the following discourse is understood, which shows the difference in inclinations of a plane continued in a straight line (as ours are) and teaches how to describe all sorts of planes equally inclined to the horizon, so that weights always press upon them equally—or how a single weight weighs differently on planes that continue in a straight line, as ordinary planes do.

Now, two things must be remarked upon here: namely, that every straight line is inclined toward the horizon; and that this inclination is diverse, according to the various parts of the line. Furthermore, the inclination of a plane is the angle comprised between the horizontal line and the plane or the inclined line. This being assumed:

Let **EF** be a straight line placed upon the circle representing the earth or the <term>horizon</term> <note>In this context, the horizon refers to the tangent line or plane relative to the Earth's curved surface.</note>. Since it touches it at point **D**, it is cut at that point at right angles by the perpendicular line **DO**, and therefore it is horizontal at that point. Outside of that point, it is necessarily inclined because it is no longer cut at right angles by the perpendicular line; for any perpendicular other than **DO** makes an angle at the center of the earth with the said line **DO**. Consequently, the angle formed on the line **EF** is less than a right angle.

Let **10 O** be a perpendicular falling from point **10** of the line **EF** to the center of the earth. I say that the said line **EF** is inclined toward the horizon at this point according to the measure of the angle made by the said perpendicular **10 O** with the perpendicular **DO**—namely, by 10 degrees. Because the angle **OD 10** is a right angle, the angle **O 10 D** will be the complement of **10 OD**, and thus 80 degrees, which is the inclination of the said line **EF** with the perpendicular. The complement of this is the inclination with the horizontal line, which will be 10 degrees; and such will be the angle **X 10 O**, made by the said line **EF** with the line **X 10 Z**, which is the horizontal, being parallel to the line **280, 100**.

Now, the further one moves from the horizontal point **D**, the greater the inclination will be—

## Book Second

...because the angle formed at the center of the earth always increases.

From this, it follows that weights placed on the aforementioned line will always roll until they reach point **D**, and they will do so more quickly the further they are from it (excluding <term>impetuosity</term> <note>In 17th-century mechanics, "impetuosity" refers to the momentum or "force" acquired by a moving body.</note>). This is because when they are at that point, the perpendicular line will pass through the <term>center of gravity</term> of the body—specifically through **C**—and will cut it into two equal parts. However, if it is as far away as point **10**, it will be cut unequally, and the part toward **D** will be larger and heavier than the other; consequently, it must necessarily pull the body toward the said point **D**.

But we must examine by how much one of these parts is heavier than the other, according to the various inclinations. For this purpose, I draw the line **10 C A** perpendicular to the straight line **E F**, which cuts the cylinder into two equal parts; then I draw the radius **C B**. I state that the angle **A C B** is equal to the two angles **C 10 B** and **C B 10**, which are equal to each other because their bases are equal; therefore, it will be double one of them. Now, since **A 10 B** is 10 degrees, **A C B** will be 20 degrees and will measure the arc **A B**. Once this arc is found, I state that the ratio of the circumference of 360 degrees to the arc **A B** of 20 degrees is the same as the ratio of the area of the entire circle (which I suppose to be 154 feet, taking a diameter of 14 feet) to the area **A C B**, which will be 8 ^5/_9 square feet, with a thickness of one foot if the cylindrical body is one foot thick.

For the <term>isosceles triangle</term> <note>The original term is "equicrure," literally "equal-legged."</note> **C B 10**, I draw the line **C I** perpendicular to the base, or the <term>chord</term> <note>The straight line segment "soustendue" (subtended) across the arc.</note> of 160 degrees **B 10**. Therefore, **C I** will be the sine of the complement of the angle **I C 10** (or **I C B** of 80 degrees), for which the lines **B I** and **10 I** are the sines. Now, since the radius **C 10** is 7, **C I** will be 1 foot, 5 inches, minus ^1/_{22}; and **10 I** will be 6 feet, 10 inches, 8 lines, and a little more. These, when multiplied by 1 foot and 5 inches, yield 9 feet and 109 ^1/_2 inches; when these are added to the area **A C B** (8 feet ^5/_9, or 80 inches), we obtain 18 feet, 45 inches, and 48 lines for the area of the figure **A 10 B**. When these are subtracted from the semicircle of 77 feet, there remains 58 feet, 98 inches, and 96 lines for the smaller section **10 B**. Consequently, the other section will be 95 feet, 45 inches, and 48 lines—that is to say, 36 feet, 90 inches, and 96 lines greater than the other.

Note that the "feet" we speak of here are cubic, but the inches and lines are square, with a thickness of one foot.

Regarding the weight, I assume the cylinder is made of iron, of which a cubic foot weighs 576 pounds. Thus, an inch (at one foot of thickness) weighs 4 pounds, as there are 144 inches in a foot; and a line weighs ^1/_{36} of a pound—that is, 3 <term>gros</term>, 40 <term>grains</term>, or 256 grains <note>The "gros" and "grain" were traditional French units of weight used before the metric system; a "gros" was 1/8th of an ounce.</note>. In this way, the cylinder will weigh 88,704 pounds. The larger section, which alone does not press upon the inclined plane, weighs 54,901 ^1/_3 pounds, and the smaller weighs 33,802 ^2/_3 pounds, the difference being 21,098 ^2/_3 pounds.

When the inclination is 20 degrees, the larger section contains 65 feet, 103 inches, and 114 lines, which makes it 37,855 pounds heavier than the other. Once this difference is given, if one wishes to find the smaller section, one must take half of the said 65 feet, 103 inches, and 114 lines (which is 32 feet, 123 inches, and 129 lines) and subtract it from the semicircle of 77 feet to obtain 44 feet, 20 inches, and 15 lines. If one adds the said 32 feet, 123 inches, and 129 lines to 77, one will have the larger section: 109 feet, 123 inches, and 129 lines.

When the inclination is 30 degrees, the excess of the larger section will be 93 feet and 111 inches, which weighs 58,012 pounds more than the smaller section, which is 30 feet and 16 ^1/_2 inches.

# Book Two

But if one wished to make a plane that always maintained the same inclination, it would have to intersect all the lines originating from the center at the same angles, and it would form a sort of **helix** <note>In this context, the author is describing what we now call a loxodrome or a rhumb line—a curve that crosses all meridians of longitude at the same angle.</note> similar to that made by a **ship** that always sailed by the same course, and which intersected all the **Meridians** at the same angles. By this course, it could never arrive at the **Pole** where all the meridians meet, because it could not intersect them all at the same angle at a single point. Likewise, this plane would intersect all the perpendiculars at the same angles, and for the same reason, it could never arrive at the center of the earth, it being impossible for a line to intersect an infinity of other lines at the same angle in a single point.

Furthermore, although the said plane always approaches the center, it nevertheless does not go there, but rather turns to the side; and therefore it will never arrive, but will turn perpetually around it. For if one imagines the said plane as close to the earth as the present figure shows, even though it were extremely close to the center in relation to the whole earth, one sees by the said figure that it can still be brought much closer. And when it has been led to within a **line** <note>A 'line' (ligne) was a French unit of measurement equal to 1/12 of an inch, or about 2.25 millimeters.</note> of the center, it will still be easy to make it approach closer, by taking the space of a foot which corresponds in all things to that of a line, and whose supposed spaces have the same ratio with them as 144 to 1 <note>This refers to the square of 12, as there are 144 square lines in a square inch.</note>; for one has as much right to make a large figure represent a small one, as to make small globes that represent the entire earth with its rivers, its mountains, and its forests. And within the said space of a foot, one could still lead the plane to within a line of the center, which would be only 1/144th of a line; and if one wishes to go further, one could still make the said space a foot in diameter, and lead the plane unto infinity. And although there would be much work to calculate the said spaces, and how many turns this line or plane would make around the center, or how close it would be at each turn, it is nonetheless not impossible; but it would be necessary to find the **secants** and the **tangents** of the **thirds, fourths, and fifths** <note>In early mathematics, subdivisions of a degree were measured in minutes, seconds, thirds (1/60th of a second), fourths (1/60th of a third), and so on.</note>, and perhaps also of the seventh and eighths, which are the last to complete 90 degrees; this would produce marvelously large secants. And then it would be necessary to add all the said secants from the first up to that of a seventh or eighth near 90 degrees.

Now, to guide the said inclined plane, I suppose that the circle described here is the **Equator** on the globe of the earth cut into two parts, so that the perpendicular lines going to the center are the meridians, according to the order in which they are marked on the earth, and which here divide the circle, or the Equator, into 360 degrees of **longitude**.

Similarly, each perpendicular (or meridian) is divided into 9 equal parts, each of which contains 10 degrees of **latitude**, through all of which parts pass small circles, which make the **parallels**. Now this line must be so guided from point **D**, that it intersects all the meridians and parallels at the same angles. And if the plane is inclined by 45 degrees, when the curved line describing the said plane arrives at 10 degrees of longitude, namely at point **A**, it will have 9 degrees 57' of latitude, and it will be 3' short of being at the tenth parallel, or at 10 degrees of latitude. And when it has arrived at the said parallel, it will then have passed the 10th Meridian, and will be at 10 degrees 3' of longitude. Being at point **b** at 20 degrees of longitude, it

Now, one will find the longitude at whatever degree of latitude one wishes—for example, at the fifteenth degree—by gathering the **secants** <note>A secant is a trigonometric ratio. In early modern navigation and cartography, summing secants was the standard method for calculating distances on a sphere, a process that eventually led to the development of the Mercator projection.</note> of every minute from the **Equator**, which is taken as the **radius**, up to the fifteenth degree; these will be 900 secants in total, excluding the said radius, which amount to 9,104,428. I divide this by the radius, which is here 10,000, to get 910, which makes 10 d. 10' of longitude. This is so exact that it would be difficult to perceive the difference between the true spaces and these. Nevertheless, when one approaches the center of the earth, because the secants of the minutes are very different from one another, it will be necessary to add the secants of all the **seconds**, and then of the **thirds** and **fourths** <note>Just as a degree is divided into 60 minutes and a minute into 60 seconds, early mathematicians continued the sexagesimal (base-60) division into "thirds" (1/60th of a second) and "fourths" (1/60th of a third) for extreme precision.</note>, until their difference is not perceptible, if one wishes to proceed exactly. Thus, the latitude being given at this inclination of 45 degrees, one need only divide the secants of the minutes (or half-degrees if one does not care for such an exact measure) by the radius, and one will have the minutes (or half-degrees) of longitude. But if a quantity of minutes of longitude is given, for example 600', which are 10 degrees of longitude, one must multiply 600' by the radius to get 6,000,000, which is the sum of the secants of 9 degrees, 57' of latitude.

At other inclinations it is not so easy to find the longitude and the latitude; but the longitude being given, one must use the following proportion: As the **radius** is to the **tangent** of the angle of inclination, so are the minutes of longitude to the sum of the secants of the minutes of latitude. For example, I want to know at how many degrees of latitude the plane will have reached at point 10 deg. when it is at point 4, which is 40 degrees of longitude; I say as the radius 100,000 is to the tangent of 10 degrees of inclination 17,633, so is 40 degrees or 2,400' of longitude to 4,231,9200, which is the number of the secants of 7 degrees 2', or the latitude sought.

The latitude being given—for example, the plane being at point 7 at a latitude of 10 degrees—I seek in which **Meridian** <note>In this context, the "meridian" refers to the specific line of longitude the object has reached.</note> it is, and say:

As the radius 100,000 is to the tangent of the complement of the angle of inclination of 10 degrees, which is 567,128, so is the sum of the secants of 10 degrees of latitude, which is 6,030,618, to the minutes of longitude; the sum will be 3,420' <gloss>15325 / 1,000,000</gloss>, which are 57 degrees, 0', 7", 56'", 22"" of longitude. One can do the same for other inclinations.

Now, to know how far the plane is distant from the surface of the earth at each degree of latitude, one must take the proportion of 90 degrees to 1,145 **leagues** <note>The "league" (lieue) was a unit of distance; here the author estimates the Earth's radius to be 1,145 leagues.</note>, which is the distance from the surface to the center of the earth. ### PROPOSITION IX.

*Explaining another easier and more Geometric way to describe a plane of equal inclination; and determining what shape is made by the movement of Globes that roll on ordinary planes; and whether rolling is faster than flowing or sliding.*

Given the circle in which, and by means of which, one wishes to describe a <term>plane of equal inclination</term> <note>A path or surface where the angle of descent remains constant relative to the center, resulting in a spiral-like curve.</note>, it is easy to trace it using as many points as one desires; these points will be closer to one another the more parts the circle is divided into. Now, I describe the plane A B C D E F G H I K L M N by means of a division into 6 parts, which is done by drawing the 6 rays <note>original: "rayons," referring to the radii of the circle.</note> T A, T O, T Q, etc. And then, having drawn the line A O, I divide it in the middle by drawing the ray T S, which gives B as the second point of the plane. Afterward, I transfer the <term>compass opening</term> <note>The distance between the two points of a compass, used here to maintain a specific measurement.</note>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram within a circle with center point T. Radii are drawn at specific angles, and a polygonal spiral-like path is constructed by connecting points A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, and N situated on these radii. Dotted lines illustrate the radii and the construction method using distances from the center.</image-desc>

T B onto the ray T P, in order to draw the straight line from B to P, which gives the 3rd point of the plane, C; and then I transfer the opening T C onto the ray T Q, so that the line C Q marks the 4th point of the plane, D, and I continue always until all the points E, F, etc., up to N are marked. These can be continued unto infinity; and if one wishes to have them closer together so that the line of the plane is described more accurately, one can draw as many rays as desired between T A and T S, and between those that follow, so that the straight line, which always touches two rays while cutting the one in the middle, is shorter. Now, what I have said of the hexagon can be adapted to the triangle, the square, the dodecagon, and to all regular figures inscribed in the circle.

But one may remark several things here, and particularly that a weight would move perpetually through this equally inclined plane without ever being able to arrive at the center of the earth, around which the plane would always turn without reaching it; and consequently, that this plane is found in no place in nature, which does nothing in vain, and which gives a limit, or a center, to every thing. In the third place, sea vessels that hold their course by <term>rhumb lines</term> <note>Also known as loxodromes; these are paths on a sphere that cross all meridians at the same angle, allowing a ship to maintain a constant compass heading.</note>, or by <term>loxodromes</term> AB, C, D, etc., which cut the meridians at right angles, will travel along a line similar to the one described here. They will maintain the same inclination as weights descending along an equally inclined plane. I leave aside many other conclusions that can be deduced from this line in order to explain the second part of this proposition, which consists of knowing what figure is described by a ball rolling on a plane. I say "rolling," because if it only <term>slides</term> <note>The author distinguishes between 'glisser' (sliding without rotation) and 'rouler' (rolling with rotation).</note>, it describes as many straight lines as there are points in its semi-circumference, of which the longest and highest is perpendicular to the end of its axis A.

But when it rolls, the point of contact that supports it on the plane describes a <term>half-ellipse</term> <note>While the author uses the term "half-ellipse," the path described by a point on a rolling circle is technically known today as a cycloid.</note> with every turn it makes. Thus, a ball that travels one hundred times the length of its circumference while rolling describes one hundred half-ellipses. Similarly, every point on the ball describes parts of an ellipse, as experience shows by rolling a pulley, or some other round body, and marking the movement with a pencil on a slate placed beside the body as it completes a full turn.

Now it must be noted that the line of equal inclination is not only described by means of right angles made upon the meridians, but also by all other sorts of angles, provided they are always equal to one another.

As for the final part of this proposition, it is very difficult to resolve, and it is not easy to test by experience. This is because one would need to have a perfectly polished plane, so hard that it could not yield at all to the moving object, which would need to possess the same qualities. In such a case, it is probable that sliding would be as fast as rolling. However, because no plane is found without <term>pores</term> <note>The author uses "pores" to refer to the microscopic roughness or friction of a surface.</note> that hinder the moving object, and because a rolling object touches the surface almost only at a single point, we cannot have instances of rolling that are not faster than sliding. But it is not easy to know by how much one is faster than the other.

I only note here that the <term>projection</term> <note>The trajectory or flight.</note> of a cannonball that occurs without rolling can be compared to sliding. But because the air can hinder it more when it always strikes the same side of its surface than when it travels while rolling, it is probable that the ball goes further and faster when it rolls—though this difficulty deserves a more particular discourse and examination. It may happen that balls no longer roll when the <term>impetuosity</term> <note>A 17th-century term for momentum or kinetic energy.</note> with which they are thrown is too great, such as when they are fired by artillery or muskets. Nonetheless, it seems they would have much more effect if they rolled, because they would join the force of a <term>brace</term> <note>original: "vieil brequin" (vilebrequin), a hand-cranked drill. The author suggests the spinning ball acts like a drill bit.</note> or a screw to their momentum.
