### COROLLARY VIII.

Since I have shown the manner of describing a plane equally inclined to the horizon, it is reasonable that after calculating the parts of the cylinder, which weigh differently upon planes according to their different inclinations, I should examine the 9th proposition of the 8th book of the *Mathematical Collections* of <term>Pappus</term> <note>Pappus of Alexandria (c. 290 – c. 350 AD), a great Greek mathematician whose works preserved much of ancient geometry.</note>, which consists of knowing what force is necessary to support a given weight on a straight plane inclined to the horizon at a given angle. ## PROPOSITION X.

->*The plane being inclined to the horizon at a given angle, to determine the force which*<-
->*can support the given weight on the said plane.*<-

I would not have included this proposition here if it had been available in French, and if the booklet where it is found were common; though it deserves to be in many places because of the great utility that can be drawn from it. Now, common sense dictates everything that is supposed in this demonstration: namely, that equal weights weigh equally at equal distances, which similarly applies to other equal forces that push, pull, press, or strike from equal distances. For example, equal weights *a* and *d* weigh equally at equal distances *cf* and *cg*, and consequently remain in <term>equilibrium</term> <note>A state of balance where opposing forces cancel each other out.</note>. It is only necessary to observe that the <term>powers</term> <note>In 17th-century physics, 'puissance' (power) often refers to an applied force or agency.</note> which can apply their strength in all sorts of slants and ways can use them such that one pulls, pushes, and presses upward or to the left, just as strongly as the other does downward, or to the right side, etc. Thus, if this one pulls as strongly downward as that one pulls upward, no movement will occur. This had to be observed because forces are applied from all sides, whereas weights apply their force only toward the center of the earth.

When the power applies its force perpendicularly upon the plane, it resists entirely, so that it cannot pass through nor slide upon it. But when it applies it obliquely, it does not resist entirely; that is why...

All these things having been posited, let the weight *a* be placed upon the inclined plane *l 2* in such a way that it is not attached to it at all; it is certain that it will fall if it is not held back: consequently, whether the lever *c n* pushed by the <term>power</term> <note>original: "puissance." In early physics, this refers to the force or effort applied to a system to maintain balance or create movement.</note> *k* acting from the distance *c h* resists the falling weight *a*, or some power equal to *k* holds it back, it will remain on the plane *l 2* in such a way that it can neither rise nor descend.

For should it descend first, if possible, along the plane *n l*, while the lever *c a* (which is pushed by *K* from the distance *c h*) resists it; then the lever *c h* and the power *K* would rise, as the lever *c a* descends with the weight *a* and the distance *c f*; which is absurd, since they remain in <term>equilibrium</term> <note>A state in which opposing forces or influences are balanced.</note> by the 6th and 7th [propositions] of the 1st [book] of the *Equilibriums of Archimedes* <note>Refers to the treatise "On the Equilibrium of Planes" by Archimedes (c. 287–212 BC), which laid the foundations for statics.</note>, and consequently the weight *A* will not descend while it is held by the power *K* by means of the lever *h c a*.

And because the lever *h c a* pushing *a* sends its force along a line perpendicular to the lever, let *a o* be perpendicular to the lever *a c*, and parallel to the plane *l 2*; the lever *h c a* pushing the weight *a* sends its force along a line perpendicular to the lever: let *a o* be perpendicular to the lever *a c*, and parallel to the plane *l 2*; the lever *h c a* pushing the weight *a* sends its force along the straight line *a o*, or along the plane *l 2*. And because the power *K* acting through the lever *h c a* by pushing the weight *a* through the point *a* holds it back, it follows that another power equal to the power *K* acting in the same manner upon the weight *a* will also hold it back; so that there will be no need for the lever, but only for the power which will perform the same action as the lever. And the same thing will always happen, whether the same power pushes through point *a*, or whether it pulls the line *a o* while being at some position on the said line, for example at *o*: whether the line *a o* being wound around the pulley *o p*, like a cord, the power or the weight *y* are suspended, for whatever the case may be, the weight *A* will always be held still on the plane *l 2*, so that it can neither descend nor rise. The power *K* is thus found to stop the weight *A* on the given plane *l 2* inclined to the horizon *l m* by the given angle *m l 2*; which is what had been proposed.

### COROLLARY II.

If some excellent geometer undertook the examination of this book by Cardano, and the others he has produced, it would be one of the finest labors that could be seen. This would be particularly true if he demonstrated the truth of what Cardano put forward as true without demonstration—for example, that it is more difficult to overturn a cube than a <term>tetrahedron</term> <note>A triangular pyramid; the simplest of the Platonic solids.</note> of equal size and weight—and the error of what he put forward against the truth, such as when he said, along with Tartaglia <note>Niccolò Fontana Tartaglia (c. 1499–1557), an Italian mathematician who often feuded with Cardano over algebraic discoveries and mechanical theories.</note>, that a tilted <term>balance</term> returns parallel to the horizon. In reality, it always tilts further until it is perpendicular to the horizon, because of the center of the earth, where all heavy things aim. On this point Guidobaldo <note>Guidobaldo del Monte (1545–1607), an influential author on statics whose *Mechanicorum Liber* refined the study of balances and pulleys.</note> also failed, when he said that it remains at whatever inclination one places it. But there are several difficulties in this matter, because one can make balances that remain inclined in certain positions, outside of which they will descend lower; so many accidents can occur here that they deserve for the most learned mathematicians to make specific treatises on them.

### COROLLARY III.

One could perhaps explain why a ball rolling on an inclined plane goes slower than when it falls perpendicularly, by the preceding demonstration. One could say that the part of the ball supported by the plane acts as a kind of counterweight, which prevents the fall of the ball as much as it can; the ball rolls all the more slowly as it is more supported, as I have shown in the other propositions. Here it must be noted that it is not the same thing for a weight to be weakened by the said counterweight as for it to be made of a lighter material. For example, if the weight of a lead ball of one pound is so diminished by the support of the plane that it weighs no more than one ounce (that is, 16 times less), and a wooden ball of the same size also weighs only one ounce, it does not follow that the wooden ball will not descend faster perpendicularly than the lead one does obliquely; for the wooden ball has no counterweight or plane to hinder it or turn it from its straight path. But it suffices to consider here whether the hindrance of the plane is perpetually analogous and proportional to the slowness or the speed of the oblique fall of the ball that rolls or slides upon it.

## COROLLARY IV.

It must be noted that I always assume a ball or a cylinder upon the planes, because it is too difficult to determine the parts of other bodies—for example, <term>cubes</term> and <term>tetrahedrons</term> <note>A tetrahedron is a triangular pyramid, a solid shape with four triangular faces.</note>—which are supported by the said planes; and because these bodies cannot roll and slide as smoothly as balls do. However, one could examine what the inclination of the plane must be to make them roll or overturn, and to make them cease their sliding; this sliding would always maintain the same ratio as it increases in speed as the rolling of a ball, since they descend for the same cause and toward the same end.

## COROLLARY V.

Since we cannot demonstrate that weights always maintain the same proportion of speed while descending all the way to the center [of the Earth] as that which we observe at all sorts of heights, it is not out of place to examine if they might change, and what that change might be. This is so that those who wish to go further may find some kind of opening into this subject. This is why I add the two following propositions before beginning other discourses on the different movements of nature, which depend on those that lead to the center of the earth, or which follow their proportion.

## PROPOSITION XI.

*To determine if the speed of falling heavy bodies increases according to the ratio of the sections of a line cut proportionally: wherein one sees the properties of this section, and the manner of cutting a line in <term>mean and extreme ratio</term> <note>original: "moyenne & extreme raiſon." This is the classical geometric definition of the **Golden Ratio**.</note> unto infinity.*

The learned <term>Vendelin</term> <note>Godefroy Wendelin (1584–1667) was a Flemish astronomer who conducted early experiments on gravity and falling bodies.</note> was the first who made me think of this proportion for the fall of heavy bodies; for having asked his opinion on this speed, he conjectured that it followed, perhaps, the proportion of the line cut in mean and extreme ratio, which he calls *divine* <note>original: "diuine." The "Divine Proportion" was a common Renaissance term for the Golden Ratio, popularized by Luca Pacioli.</note>, as do many others, by reason of its admirable properties, of which we shall speak later. But since we have already regulated this speed through our experiments, I place here a table in which one will see the comparison of falls that occur in the <term>squared ratio of the times</term> <note>original: "raiſon doublee des temps." This refers to the law of falling bodies, where the distance fallen is proportional to the square of the elapsed time ($d \propto t^2$).</note>, and of those that would occur according to the section of the said line.

For this purpose, the first column shows by its numbers the path taken by the lead ball, which descends in each half-second of an hour—or in 30 <term>thirds</term> <note>original: "tierces." In early modern timekeeping, a "third" was a unit of time equal to 1/60th of a second.</note>, for example: 3 signifies that it descends 3 feet in the first half-second; 9, that it descends 9 feet in the next half-second; and so on for the others up to 51, which signifies that it travels 51 feet in the eighth half-second. 

The second column adds the preceding numbers together to show the total fall over the preceding times; for example, the second number, namely 12, signifies that it travels 12 feet in one second, and the 27 which follows shows that it travels 27 feet in a second and a half, etc., up to the last number, 192, which teaches that it travels 192 feet in 4 seconds.

The third column contains the numbers of the section continued in mean and extreme ratio, such that if the ball travels 5 spaces in the first half-second, it will travel 8 in the next, and then 13, 21, etc. <note>These are numbers from the Fibonacci sequence, which approximates the Golden Ratio.</note>, which are added together in the fourth column.

I suppose then that A C is divided proportionally at point B, and that the small segment A B is 5, and the large B C is 8, and consequently that the entire line A C is 13; for these numbers behave in the same way as what we have said above, namely that the square of B C is equal to the rectangle formed by the whole A C and the smaller segment B A, as one sees by multiplying 5 by 13 to get the rectangle 65, to which the square of 8 is equal—namely 64—if one subtracts one unit from the former. One can still calculate the proportion of these lines otherwise: for example, if one divides 10 into $6\ 1/5$ and $3\ 4/5$, the latter multiplied by 10 gives 38, and the former multiplied by itself produces $38\ 11/25$, so that the difference between the rectangle and the square is $11/25$, and the square is the larger. If one divides the same 10 into $6\ 2/11$ and $3\ 9/11$, this last number multiplied by 10 gives $38\ 2/11$, and the rectangle is the larger by $3/121$, and one will perpetually approach their true ratio without, however, being able to reach it. This is also experienced in the roots of <term>surds</term> <note>original: "nombres sourds," literally "deaf numbers," a historical term for irrational numbers like the square root of 2.</note>, or irrationals, which one approaches little by little unto infinity by means of <term>fractions</term> <note>original: "nombres rompus," or "broken numbers."</note>, without ever being able to meet them exactly.

Now the segments of the line A F produce a type of proportion which consists in this: that there is the same ratio of A B to B C as from B C to C D, and the same ratio from C D to D E as from D E to E F; and by conversion, there is the same ratio from F E to E D as from E D to D C, etc. I leave aside a thousand other remarks that one could make about the segments of this line compared among themselves, or with the whole line, in order to finish the discourse on these movements.

## PROPOSITION XII.

### *To know whether falling weights always increase their speed, or if they decrease it, and if there is some point of equality where they begin to descend at a uniform speed.*

I do not believe that human reason, devoid of experiments, can resolve this difficulty; although many imagine that the Earth attracts heavy bodies, and that they go faster toward the surface of the Earth than when they are lower down between the surface and the center, for the reason that the entire Earth pulls them toward the center when they fall through the air onto its surface, and that it no longer acts in its entirety when they descend beneath it, inasmuch as all the parts that are above the weight pull them back toward themselves as much as they can. For example, if the weight reached as far as the middle of the Earth's semi-diameter, all the Earth that is to the side of five hundred seventy-two leagues—that is to say, the semi-diameter passed—would pull back the

...the weight follows its path toward the center <note>of the Earth</note>, and the speed of its motion would decrease little by little, until having arrived at the center it could no longer pass further, for the reason that the two hemispheres of the earth would then pull it equally from one side and the other. But because we do not know if bodies descend only because they are attracted, or if they have some heaviness <term>peſanteur: the quality of being heavy or the force of gravity</term> in them independent of this attraction, we can conclude nothing from it that satisfies the best minds; for the experiments that could be made in wells and the deepest mines do not decrease the speed noticeably enough for us to perceive it; and the earth has no holes that go deep enough for this purpose; unless it has some abysses which one cannot approach, and which cannot serve for this purpose.

There are others who believe that weights encounter a point of equality <note>What we now call "terminal velocity"</note> in falling, at which they no longer increase their speed: which seems probable, both because there is little appearance that they would travel such a great distance in so little time as that which we calculated previously—given that the air cannot, it seems, yield as fast as would be necessary to make room for the falling weights—and because very light weights, such as **elderberry pith** <note>The soft, spongy center of an elderberry branch, used here as a extremely light test material</note> of the size of an arquebus or musket ball (which weighs 360 times less than the said ball), go almost as fast as the lead ball at the first moment of their fall: but shortly after they go much more slowly; for the said pith takes more than 3 seconds to fall from 48 feet high, from where the lead ball falls in 2 seconds.

Now these two things are very considerable: for as to the first, we experience that arquebus and cannon balls striking water bounce back, because the water cannot yield fast enough, and it is so pressed and violated by the speed of the motion of the balls that it becomes hard like stones, or at least hard enough to repel them, or to hinder them. Upon which one could determine at what speed a given body must go, and at what angle it must strike the water to be repelled, or to penetrate it: and then one would find the speed at which a given weight must descend to so press the air that it can no longer yield, and that it repels the said weight, or to cleave it in such a way that it always yields equally, to make the rest of the fall of equal speed.

Some have imagined that one would find this point of equality, from which falls begin to be uniform, if one placed the **scale pans** <note>original: "baſſinets"</note> of a balance underneath, and if one always increased the weight of one of them, until the body falling into the other could no longer carry away the weights: for example, if a lead ball of eight ounces carried away the pan where there is one pound, when it falls from 12 feet, and it carried it away with two pounds when falling from 48 feet, it is certain that it would have increased the speed it had when falling from 12 feet; and if it carried away more than two pounds when falling from 96 feet, the space of 48 feet would not yet be its point of equality. And if after having fallen from 96 feet it carried away the pan that has three pounds, and falling from higher it no longer carried away more than three pounds—for example, if it could not carry away three pounds and one ounce—one could say that its motion no longer increases past 96 feet. But besides the fact that these experiments are almost impossible, by reason...

# Book Two

<meta>catchword: knowledge</meta>

Since a falling weight does not always land exactly in the center of the **scale pan**, as is required, it might perhaps be difficult to find a height great enough to limit the increase in speed of a falling body, even if it were twelve times lighter than lead (such as many types of wood which we will discuss later). Nevertheless, if someone wishes to conduct the experiment, they can find heights of 144 feet, from which balls of wood or wool will fall conveniently enough into the scale pans, provided that the pans are very large.

If one were to attach a string to one of the arms of a balance, and the falling ball were also attached to the other end of the string, it could—as it falls—give a perpendicular jolt to the ball <note>original: "boule," referring here to the weight or mechanism on the scale</note> which would lift the pan on the other arm. However, the balance would need to be placed high up so that the weight could descend, and one would have to account for the weight of the string itself. Now, this <term>point of equality: the state we now call "terminal velocity," where the resistance of the air equals the force of gravity</term> would be reached much sooner and at a closer distance the lighter the falling weight is. For example, **pith** <note>The soft, spongy tissue found in the center of plant stems like elderberry</note> might reach it at perhaps 12 or 24 feet. Because a piece of pith the size of a lead ball weighs only one grain, one could join several pieces of elderberry together to reach the weight of an ounce or a pound, so that it could move a pan loaded with a noticeable weight—for example, one or two ounces or pounds.

Now, even if the point of equality for a weight—for example, this pith—were found, it does not necessarily follow that we would have found the point for others, such as balls of wood or lead. This is because different bodies encounter different impediments in the air according to their different **pores** <note>The author suggests that the internal structure or "porosity" of a material affects how air flows around or through it, influencing resistance</note>, which can disrupt the consistency of the proportions. There are several things to consider regarding the resistance of the air that are not sufficiently known to us. Thus, it does not follow that the point of equality for falling lead must be 360 times further away than that of the pith, even though the pith weighs 360 times less, or that it would take a piece of pith 360 times larger to weigh as much as the said lead ball. Similarly, one cannot conclude that it descends 360 times more slowly, since experience shows the contrary; for the time it takes to fall 48 feet is not triple the time of the falling lead.

One could similarly use water to find this point of equality, because bodies whose weight is almost equal to water—such as wax and several types of wood, and even stones that float on water as does the one I possess (even though it has no visible pores and is quite heavy)—sink very slowly to the bottom when one adds just enough iron filings or similar things to make them descend through the water. For after observing the ratio of speeds and weights in that element <note>water</note>, one could conclude something similar for the air, particularly if one knew the ratio of its density and weight to that of water, which I discussed in the **First Book of Sounds**.

Now, one can consider the struggle that takes place between weights descending in water as well as in air, against the parts of these two elements which rise in equal volume as much as the weights descend. We can compare these two contrary movements to those of the two arms of a **balance**, where one carries the other, such that one always rises as much and as quickly as the other descends. Here it must be noted that the weight which descends slowly is similar to the arm of a balance which is only so slightly stronger that it has difficulty tipping the other. However, it is even more difficult to determine how much faster the given arm of a balance descends with a light weight than with another heavier one—or how much more quickly a branch double or triple the length of another branch descends with the same weight, or with a larger or smaller one according to a given ratio—than it is to know how much faster different falling weights go compared to one another. This, therefore, is what we must work on to find the proportion of all kinds of movements.

### COROLLARY II.

One can adapt this entire discourse to <term>oblique planes: surfaces tilted at an angle, also known as inclined planes</term>, or those inclined toward the horizon, since the balls that descend upon them—whether by rolling or sliding—maintain the same proportion in their speeds as when they descend perpendicularly. 

The reason why an **arquebus** bullet <note>An arquebus was an early type of long-handled firearm, a predecessor to the musket</note> which pierces a wooden board that has been raised perpendicularly to the horizon without any support, pierces it without making it fall, can be understood because the air cannot yield as quickly to the board as it can to the much smaller bullet (which is heavier relative to its size). This is why the board remains standing; and if it were to fall, it would be toward the side from which one fired rather than the other, because of the <term>recoil: the "contrecoup" or reactionary force of the struck air</term>. However, different experiments may lead to other reasons or strengthen this one. I add only that recoils are very significant in <term>percussions: the impact or striking of one body against another</term>, as are <term>contretemps: literally "counter-times," referring to the timing of opposing forces or rhythmic interference in motion</term>.

Now, after having considered the movements of weights made toward the center of the earth, whether perpendicularly or by straight planes inclined to the horizon, we must examine those made toward the center via circular lines, in order to compare them to one another.

### PROPOSITION XIII.

It is certain that a ball cannot flow or roll toward the center along a convex circular line when it is not held at all. For example, a weight placed at point L cannot flow along L O D, because it will fall perpendicularly toward the center, from which the circular line L O B moves away. But if one attaches the weight B to the string A B, and one pulls this string to A L, so that the weight B is at point L, and the string, being attached at point A, is free on the side of the weight, this weight will descend from L to B via the quarter-circle...

For example, the motion of a lead ball, whose weight is twelve times that of a ball made of <term>charme: hornbeam, a dense hardwood</term> of the same size, lasts 4 times longer than the motion of that hornbeam ball when they are pulled from the same distance. The lighter one makes 40 swings, while the heavier one makes only 39; that is to say, it gains one swing in every 40. And if the cord is 6 times thicker, it gains one swing in 200, and the size of its swings decreases more than those of a more slender cord, just as those of the wooden ball do. I leave aside several other considerations of which I spoke in the second Latin book, *On the Causes of Sounds* <note>original: "De Causis sonorum"</note>, and elsewhere.

### PROPOSITION XIV.

*To explain how much faster the ball goes when falling or rising through a quadrant of a circle, how much heavier it is in one place than in another, and how much longer or shorter the cord must be to make each of its swings and returns in more or less time, according to the given ratio.*

I suppose that the cord A B is three feet long, and that the ball B is a lead ball of 8 ounces, or half a pound. I say first that it descends faster as it moves from L toward B, because it approaches closer to B, which represents the center of the earth <note>In the physics of this period, the resting point of a pendulum—the point closest to the ground—was treated as the point closest to the center of the world, where the "natural" pull of gravity is strongest.</note>.

Secondly, if the speed of the fall through the quadrant <note>A quadrant is a quarter of a circle, or a 90-degree arc.</note> follows the speed of a vertical fall, and assuming the said quadrant is divided into 27 parts: if the weight descending from L covers the first part in a given time, it will cover the next three parts in an equal amount of time (which will be the 2nd interval of time); in the 3rd interval, it will cover the next 5 parts; in the 4th, the next 7 parts; and in the final interval of time, the remaining 9 parts until it reaches B <note>This is an application of Galileo's law of odd numbers, which states that the distances covered by a falling body in successive equal intervals of time follow the ratio of odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, etc.</note>.

But I doubt this similarity of ratios, until experience shows that a ball rolling on a horizontal plane, thrown with violence, keeps this proportion in the different parts of its path. For example, when it travels one hundred paces, if one divides the time of its journey into 4 equal parts and its path into 16 parts, it must cover 7 parts of its path in the first interval of its motion, 5 in the second, 3 in the third, and only one part in the fourth interval. Consequently, if one divides a line drawn the length of a **pall-mall court** <note>original: "jeu de pas de mail," a popular 17th-century game where a ball is struck with a mallet through a hoop, similar to croquet or golf.</note> into 16 equal parts, each of which is 20 **Royal feet**, and the ball, struck by the mallet, travels 320 feet, or 53 **toises**, in its entire course—which I suppose lasts one minute of an hour—it will travel 140 feet in the first 15 seconds (that is, in the first quarter-minute), 100 in the second quarter, 60 in the third, and 20 in the last quarter. Those who wish to find the ratio of the diminution of violent motions may invent other methods, and see if the ratio of different weights, and of different lengths and inclinations used for the lever, the scales, and other parts of **Mechanics**, can assist this speculation.

### PROPOSITION XV.

->*To provide the manner of making Clocks and Watches in less than a quarter*<-
->*of an hour, which divide the day, the hour, and the minutes into as many equal parts*<-
->*as one might wish, and to show the utility of these Clocks.*<-

Even though those who perfectly understand the theory and practice of Gnomonics <term>Scioterique: the art of making sundials to tell time by shadows</term> can make Dials or Sun-clocks in a very short time and at little expense; nevertheless, the thread or the cord used to mark the first or second minutes is more suitable for this. Furthermore, one can easily carry a thread or a string three and a half feet long wherever one wishes, of which each swing with its return will mark exactly one second of an hour—that is, the 60th part of a minute, or the 3600th part of an hour. And if one wants each swing of the cord to last only half a second, one need only take a quarter of its length, which is very easy by folding it in four.

Now, when I say that each swing of the cord three and a half feet long lasts one second, I mean that the path it makes from point K, where the weight B was raised, to point L is one swing <note>original: "tour," meaning one oscillation or "beat."</note>, and its return from L to K is the second swing, and so on; so that the swing K L and the return L K last two seconds. Although it must be noted that the weight falling from K does not rise all the way to L, but only between L and O; otherwise the weight would move forever and become a perpetual clock, as might perhaps happen if the movement occurred in a vacuum without the hindrance of the air. Physicians might similarly use this method to recognize by how much the pulse <note>original: "poux."</note> of their patients will be faster or slower at various hours and various days, and how much the passions of anger <note>original: "cholere," referring to the humor of yellow bile associated with a quick temper.</note> and others hasten or delay it; for example, if a cord three feet long is needed to mark the duration of today's pulse by one of its turns, and if two are needed—that is to say, one turn and one return—to mark it tomorrow, or if a cord only 3/4 of a foot long is needed to make a turn in the same time that the pulse beats once, it is certain that the pulse beats twice as fast.

I leave a thousand other uses that can be drawn from this proposition, for it suffices to see the Table alongside, of which the first column signifies the seconds, the second shows the proportion that the different lengths of the cords must keep to each make their returns in the number of seconds directly opposite in the first column; and the third column gives the length of the cords; for example, if one wants to make a Clock that marks a quarter of a minute of an hour by each of its turns, the 15th number of the first column, which signifies 15", will show in the 3rd that the cord must be 787 1/2 [feet] long to make its turns each in a quarter of a minute: or if one wants to take a smaller example, because it would be difficult to attach a cord at such a height, if one wants the turn to last 2 seconds, the 2nd number of the first column shows the second number of the 3rd column, namely 14, so that a cord 14 feet long attached to a nail will make each of its turns in 2".

Now, after having considered perpendicular, oblique, and circular movement, it is necessary to see if one hinders the other when they meet, after having remarked that the weight E, guided to the top of the quarter circle B, does not descend through the said quarter B C D E, but through the line B S T Q, as I have often experienced; this happens because the weight presses more on the cord, and consequently causes it to stretch, following the proportions that can be observed in the curved line B S T Q, which is the quarter of an ellipse. One must not take the measurement of this on the dotted line of this figure, but from experience, which gives the distances of this line from the quarter circle. And if one wishes to describe the three other quarters of the ellipse, one will find its two centers by means of its two semi-diameters A Q and A B; for one leg of the compass, opened to the largest semi-diameter A B, being placed at point B, the other leg carried onto the semi-diameter A Q will give one of the centers M; and then being transported onto the other semi-diameter, which is found by extending Q A beyond A, one will have the other center, which serve to describe the entire ellipse. Now, it is certain that if the cord were made of a material that could not stretch, it would guide the weight through the quarter circle: but stretching, it describes a part of an ellipse, as I have said, or a line that closely approaches it. Let the ratio that must be found be like the line A B to C, and let B A surpass C by as much as one wishes. Let the center of the circle, from which a secant must be drawn, be D, so that the secant is to the tangent as C is to B A. Afterwards, one must take the third proportional of B A to C, namely A I, and make it so that the diameter F E is to G E as B I is to I A; and then one must draw the tangent G H: for this being established, one has what was required to be done, since G H is to G E as A B is to C, inasmuch as B I is to I A, so F E is to G E, and because C is the mean proportional between B A and A I, and G H is the mean between F G and G E, it follows that as B A is to C, so F G is to G H, and G H is to G E, which was to be demonstrated.

The other diminution of speed unto infinity by the diminution of the weight of the moving body is represented by the line **A D** drawn from point **A**, which makes a smaller angle than **B A E**, and intersecting the parallels at points **M**, **N**, **O**, it shows the degrees **F O**, **H N**, and **K M** <note>These segments on the shallower line AD represent the slower acceleration of a "lighter" object.</note> acquired at times **A F**, **A H**, and **A K** to be smaller than the other degrees acquired at the same times—those being as if from a heavier moving body, and these from a lighter one. Now, it is certain that as line **E A** moves toward **A B**, and as the angle **E A B** narrows, the speed of the moving body decreases unto infinity, and consequently these two causes create a double diminution unto infinity. This cannot prevent the wheel from making the projection by returning the moving body to its surface; otherwise, the spaces through which that which is thrown must descend would have to be so short that, however slow the fall of the moving body might be due to an infinite diminution, it could still lead itself back there. Therefore, the diminution of the spaces would have to be so infinite that it surpassed the double infinity of the diminution received by the speed of the falling body. Now, one magnitude cannot decrease more than another which is decreasing doubly toward infinity.

### Book Two ###
<meta>catchword: It is necessary</meta>

the two straight lines meeting at an angle similar to angle B A E, or B A D, or another infinitely more acute, but always rectilinear: and that the decrease of the spaces, by which the **moving body** <note>original: "mobile"</note> must return to the circumference of the wheel, is proportioned to another kind of decrease comprised between the lines that touch at an angle infinitely more acute and narrower than any right angle, as one sees at the arc A N E, cutting the parallels that determine the degrees of speed, however small they may be: now, the parts of these parallels comprised between the arc and the tangent A B make up the quantity of the spaces, and of the return to the wheel, and go on decreasing in a greater proportion than the parallels of which they are a part.

As for the parallels comprised between the straight lines, they always decrease in the same proportion; for example, if A H decreases by half at point F, H I will be double F L, and subdividing F A by half, the parallel drawn from the point of this division will be half of F L, and if one continues the division unto infinity, the parallels that follow will always be half of those which precede: which does not happen for the lines comprised between the tangent and the circumference of the circle: for if one makes the same subdivision in F A, assuming that the parallel drawn from point H is double that which comes from point F, this latter will be more than double the following one; and if one continues toward A, the preceding lines will contain those which immediately follow 3, 4, 10, 100, 1,000, 100,000, and 100 million times, and more until infinity: so that this line will be much shorter than is necessary to make the thrown bodies return, or rather, to make them maintain themselves always on the surface. I propose yet another doubt, namely whether the decrease in speed that comes from the decrease in the gravity <note>original: "pesanteur"</note> of the moving body always occurs in the same proportion, like that which comes from proximity to the place of the fall; or whether it occurs according to the proportion of the lines comprised between the secant and the circumference, or according to a greater proportion. And after having remarked that the speeds of falls do not follow the proportion of weights—seeing as a ball of elder wood <note>Elder wood pith was commonly used in early physics experiments because it is extremely light.</note> 30 or 40 times lighter than a lead ball moves hardly twice as slowly—he concludes that the projection <note>The outward centrifugal force caused by rotation.</note> cannot occur if the speed decreases very little, even though the weight increases a lot, since it does not occur even if one assumes that they decrease in the same proportion. This would also happen even if the speed decreased much more than the gravity: for example, according to the proportion of the parallels comprised between the tangent and the circumference, and even if the moving body had only the least gravity that one could desire for descending: for the decrease of gravity according to the proportion of the parallels comprised between the tangent and the circumference has as its ultimate goal the nullity of weight <note>Zero weight or weightlessness.</note>, just as the parallels have as the ultimate goal of their decrease the point of contact, which is an indivisible point: now, gravity cannot decrease to this extremity, because the moving body would no longer weigh anything; but the space of the return of the moving body thrown to the circumference is reduced to this extremity when the moving body is placed on the circumference at the point of contact, because no space is needed to arrive there; so that the inclination <note>original: "propension"</note> to go downward is always sufficient to lead the moving body back to the circumference, from which it is separated by the smallest space of all, or rather by nothingness.

# On the Movement of Bodies.

It is now necessary to examine these beautiful thoughts of Galileo <note>original: "Galilee"</note>, so that the mind may find resolution and attach itself to some truth if we can discover it; which we will attempt to do in the proposition that follows, for fear that this one might be too long and too tedious.

## PROPOSITION XVII.

->*To examine whether the Earth, turning like a wheel at a given speed, would throw stones along its tangent, or otherwise; wherein one sees the admirable properties of various angles of contingency; and the examination of Galileo’s reasons.*<-

I begin this proposition with the admirable property of the circle, which consists in making an angle so small with the straight line that touches it that it is impossible to imagine one as small composed of two straight lines: for the greatest of all the possible <term>angles of contingency</term> <note>Also called an "angle of contact," this is the "angle" between a curved arc and the straight tangent line touching it. In early modern mathematics, it was often debated whether this was a true quantity or infinitely small.</note> of the circle with its tangent is infinitely less than the smallest that can be made of two straight lines. There are even angles comprised of curved lines greater than angles composed of a curved line and a straight one, which are nevertheless smaller than the smallest composed of two straight lines. This will be understood by noting that straight lines and curves can be considered in four ways, the first of which is when two straight lines meet, and then they make the greatest angle of all. The second, when a straight line meets a curve, the angle of which is always less than the preceding one.

The third is when two convex circumferences meet, as is seen in angle B R C or A R C of this figure: for this angle is double the angle made by the tangent, since D R B is half of it: but the angle C R A is less than the angle C R B of A R B composed of the convex surface of the smaller circle B R and the concave surface of the larger A R: now this sort of angle is the smallest of all the angles that can be imagined; and there can be an infinity of them depending on whether the arcs are part of a larger or smaller circle, the angles of the second and third type always being proportionately larger as the circles are smaller.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two overlapping circular arcs meeting at a single point labeled R. A tangent line passes through R, with points labeled D, C, and G along its length. Points A and B are located on the arcs themselves. The diagram illustrates the various "angles of contingence" formed between curves and tangents as described in the accompanying text.</image-desc>

As for those of the fourth manner, they are determined by the difference between circles, because circles being nearly equal, like A R and B R, and touching each other internally, form the smallest possible angles when the circles are the largest possible and have nearly the same center; and if the smallest imaginable circle touches the largest possible circle, it will produce the largest angle of all.

Now, although one may create an infinity of angles in these two ways, the greatest of those possible will always be less than the smallest of those that can be composed of two straight lines: for this angle is so small that the Earth could not distance bodies from its surface before they had time to return to it, by reason of the small space that <term>subtends</term> <note>To extend under or be opposite to an angle.</note> such a small angle, near which said space is taken, even if the Earth turned as fast as the <term>prime mover</term> <note>original: "premier mobile"; in pre-Copernican astronomy, the outermost sphere of the heavens that carries all others with it in its daily rotation.</note>.

And if it is replied that a ball could at least run across the surface of the

### Book Two

<meta>catchword: almost</meta>

...earth toward the East, since it will not distance itself at all from the center, and the earth will push it from that side; it is evident that this ball cannot go faster than the earth, and that, having the same movement, it will always remain in the same place. Here one may note that if some terrestrial body approached the earth, for which it had no natural inclination <note>original: "inclination"; in 17th-century physics, this refers to a natural tendency toward a center of gravity.</note>, the earth could give it some sort of impetus <note>original: "impreſſion"</note>, which would make the movement of this body appear to us toward the East if it went faster than the earth, or toward the West if it went slower.

This being established, we must examine through numbers what Galileo <note>original: "Galilee"</note> sought to demonstrate through lines—namely, that the distance a body, cast by the daily motion of the earth, must cover to return to its surface is so small that it has more than enough time to arrive there.

I say first that the earth covers 360 degrees in 24 hours, and 15 seconds of a degree in one second of time <note>original: "1\" d'heure"; literally "one second of an hour," meaning a second of time.</note>, if one assumes the motion attributed to it by Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samos, an ancient Greek astronomer who proposed a heliocentric model.</note>. Secondly, if the circumference of the earth is 64,800,000 <term>fathoms</term> <note>original: "braſſes"; a unit of length equivalent to about 5–6 feet.</note>, one minute will be 3,000 fathoms, and 15 seconds will be 750. The tangent of this would be 72,722 ½, and the secant 100,000,000 6/10; or the tangent 7,272,251 and the secant 10,000,000,265, which exceeds the radius of 10,000,000,000 by only 265. And if one reduces the diameter of the earth to 412,363,636 inches, it [the ratio] will be as 1 inch, 1 <term>line</term> <note>original: "ligne"; a traditional unit of length, 1/12th of an inch.</note>, and 1/3—that is, the distance a stone would move away from the surface in one second—compared to the aforementioned whole radius to 265. Now, the stone will fall 144 inches in this second, as experience teaches, and therefore it will travel 133 times more distance than is necessary to reunite with the earth.

Regarding what Galileo adds—that light bodies do not decrease the speed of their motion in proportion to their lightness, and that he has tested that a body weighing 30 or 40 times more travels barely twice as much distance in the same time—I wish to note here the reality of the matter, following the most exact experiments we have conducted and repeated very often from different heights.

Two balls, one of lead and the other of white wood, descend just as quickly as one another from a height of 147 feet, even though the wooden one is 12 times lighter; or if there is any difference in the falls, it is not perceptible <note>original: "ſenſible"</note>, although some claim to have found through experiment that, with weights in a similar proportion, the lighter one travels 3 feet less than the heavier when falling from the same height. However, when a body is so light that it barely has the strength to overcome air resistance, one then recognizes the differing speeds of the falls. I provide two examples: one of a ball of <term>elderberry pith</term> <note>original: "moüelle de ſureau"; the soft, spongy tissue inside elderberry stems, used for its extreme lightness in early physics experiments.</note>, which, being equal in size to a lead ball weighing five <term>drachms</term> <note>original: "gros"; an old unit of weight equal to 1/8 of an ounce.</note>, weighs only one grain. That is to say, the weight of lead is to that of this pith as 360 to 1, such that balls of this pith, equal in size to musket balls, could serve as grains for weighing, instead of those made of brass or silver. The other example is a ball fifteen times lighter than the elderberry pith, such that it is 5,400 times lighter than lead. Now, it descends 3 times slower than the lead, for it travels only 48 feet in 6 seconds, whereas the lead does so in 2 seconds. As for the elderberry pith, it descends from the same place in 5 seconds, such that its speed is to that of the lead as 2 is to 5, which is the ratio of a <term>Major Tenth</term> <note>A musical interval used here as a mathematical ratio (5:2). The author, likely Marin Mersenne, frequently used musical terminology to describe physical proportions.</note>; and nevertheless it goes...

# Of the Movement of Bodies.

...almost as fast at the beginning of its movement; from which I will conclude in another proposition that heavy bodies do not always increase their speed while descending, and that having descended to a certain place toward the center, they begin to descend more slowly, or to maintain the speed they have acquired up to that point, without increasing it further.

If one takes the distance that a thrown body must be from the surface, one will find the same proportion, while the earth covers one second of a degree in 4 <term>thirds</term> <note>original: "4''' d'heure"; a "third" is a division of time equal to 1/60th of a second.</note> of an hour, which is worth 50 fathoms on the earth—that is to say, 1,000 inches, or 83 1/3 feet.

The tangent of one second is 4,848,100, and the secant is 1,000,000,000,012, which exceeds the radius by 12; therefore, as 1,000,000,000,000 is to 12, so the radius of the earth of 4,948,363,636 is to 1/16 of a <term>line</term> <note>original: "ligne"; a traditional unit of length equal to 1/12th of an inch.</note>, or almost 1/17 of a line. Consequently, the stone would distance itself by 1/17 of a line in 4 thirds of an hour, during which a weight falls 5/8 of an inch, or 7 1/2 lines, even though it only needed to fall 1/17 of a line—that is to say, about 131 times less.

And if one wishes to take the difference between the tangent and the part of the secant which is between the tangent and the circumference, the tangent of 15 seconds is 27,442 times greater; for if the tangent is 7,272,251, the part of the secant is 265. But the difference between the tangent of one second and the part of the secant is 404,003 times greater, for the tangent being 4,848,100, the part of the secant is only 12.

One can by the same means find the projection that would occur in a <term>fourth minute</term> <note>original: "quatriesme minute d'heure"; a "fourth" is 1/60th of a "third," or 1/3600th of a second.</note> of an hour, in which the earth would cover 15 fourths of a degree, which are worth 50 lines on the surface of the earth; for the excess of the secant over the radius is 205 parts, where the radius has 1,000,000,000,000,000 and the tangent 20,200,400,000; now this excess amounts to 1/5,000,000 of a line—that is to say, one part of a line divided into a million parts.

But a stone would fall 1/7,000 of a line in one fourth minute of an hour, which is 133 times more than would be required. This matches exactly the difference in the space it covers in one second—namely 144—and the distance from the surface where the stone would be in one second of time, for it would only be distant from it by one inch and 1 1/2 lines.

By this, one sees that the decrease in time always follows the decrease in distance from the surface in the same proportion, such as that of 1 to 133, if one supposes that the weight falls 12 inches in 1 second. It is therefore certain that the proportion of the tangent to the excess of the secant increases greatly, as Galileo <note>original: "Galilee"</note> has demonstrated, since in 15 seconds of space on the earth the proportion is 27,442 to 1, and in an arc of 1 second it is 404,008 to 1—that is to say, nearly one hundred million times greater. But in return, the <term>sub-double proportion</term> <note>original: "proportion sousdouble"; likely referring to the law of squares in falling bodies, where distance is proportional to the square of time.</note> of the spaces to the time wonderfully diminishes the spaces the mobile body must cover. This is capable of always keeping the decrease in distances in equal proportion to the decrease in distances made by the mobile body in the time during which it moves away along the tangent. Although if one considers these proportions, one finds they do not increase as much as it seems, given that the arc of 15 seconds being 15 times greater than that of 1 second, the said proportion of 404,008 to 1 is almost fifteen times greater than that of 27,442 to 1; and the arc of 1 second being 240 times greater than that of 15 fourths, the proportion of 98,538,536 to 1 is a little more than 240 times greater.

From this, it is easy to conclude that if one increased the speed of the Earth as **Galileo** <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), whose *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* is likely being critiqued here.</note> wishes, and if, for example, one made it turn one revolution in 12 hours, the body would move away from the circumference by 1/101,087,007 of a line in 2 fourth-minutes of an hour, at which time the falling body would only cover 1/1,687,500 of a line, so that the path it would cover in 2 fourth-minutes would be 30 times greater than what would be necessary. If one found bodies so light that they only covered 12 feet in 12 seconds, they could not reach the surface, for if 1/144 of a line were required to return to it, it would only cover 1/144. ### COROLLARY.

Although one can deduce many things from this proposition which pertain to the projection <note>In this context, "projection" refers to the centrifugal effect—the tendency of objects to be thrown off a rotating body.</note> of all kinds of wheels, it is nonetheless more appropriate to examine in a new proposition what proportion there is between the projection of a large wheel and that of a small one, so that we do not confuse the difficulties.

### PROPOSITION XVIII.

*Explaining the difference in projections that can be made by the different speeds of the same wheel, and of two or more wheels of different sizes.*

Since we have compared the earth to a large wheel, we must examine whether the projection of what is placed, or what falls upon rotating wheels, is thrown further as they become larger, or as they turn faster. On this matter, it is reasonable to look at the views of Galileo <note>original: "Galilee"</note>, since he is the first to have spoken of it, and who said that the same wheel flings stones further the faster it turns, because the cause of the projection increases in the same ratio as the speed; but if one increases the size of the wheel, and it does not make more turns in the same time than the smaller one, the cause of the flinging, or projection, does not increase according to the speed of the circumference. He believes he proves this by the experiment of projecting a stone with sticks <note>original: "bastons"</note> that are split at one end to hold the stone; for one can throw it with a stick one fathom <note>original: "brasse" — a unit of length usually measured by the span of a man's outstretched arms, roughly 6 feet.</note> long, even though one cannot do so with a stick of six feet, even though the movement of its extremity is twice as fast as that of one fathom.

This he relates to the different manner of projection; for the stone does not leave the stick as long as it is moved uniformly, but when it goes faster, one must restrain the arm to curb its speed so that the stone escapes and moves with the impetus it has acquired. This cannot happen with a large stick, because its length and its flexibility do not obey the arm so easily as to stop promptly enough; it continues to accompany the stone and retains it by diminishing its movement little by little. This he confirms by the sudden stop that a large stick encounters, which makes it release the stone—much like the jolt a boat makes against the sand makes it "leave" those who are inside, who fall toward the side it was traveling. And this leads him to grant that everything on the earth would be overturned if it encountered some similar obstacle while turning.

This being established, he endeavors to prove that a large wheel does not have more force to throw a body than a small one, even if they complete their turns in the same time, and even if the circumference of the large one moves a thousand times faster.

# Of the Movement of Bodies.

The resistance that a body offers to movement arises from its natural inclination <note>The author uses "natural inclination" to refer to what we now call gravity or inertia.</note>, or from some other quality that makes it resist movement; for the inclination it has to move downward is equal to the resistance it has to going upward. This is experienced in the balance scale, where two points equally distant from the center remain in equilibrium because the weight of one resists that of the other, which cannot make it rise. However, it seems that its resistance to upward movement does not consist of weight alone, since a weight of one hundred pounds cannot lift one of four pounds when the arms of the balance are not equal; this is practiced every day with the **steelyard balance** <term>original: *Romaine*; a type of scale with arms of unequal length, using a sliding weight to find the mass of an object.</term>.

It is therefore necessary to relate this different force to the different movements of the weights, and to say that the same weight has all the more force the further it is from the center of the steelyard, because it moves much further in the same time that the other moves very little; so that the speed of the smaller weight precisely compensates for the gravity of the larger one. For if one attaches a weight of one hundred pounds to the shorter arm, and one pound to the longer arm—provided the longer arm is a hundred times the length of the smaller—the single pound will travel a hundred times more distance in its descent than the other weight does in its ascent.

From this, he concludes that one has as much difficulty resisting a moving object of one pound that moves with a hundred degrees of speed, as another of a hundred pounds whose speed has only one degree. I come now to his demonstration.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two concentric arcs centered at point A, representing wheels of different sizes. A vertical line A-B-C connects the center to the tops of both wheels. Tangent lines B-F and C-D extend from the top points. Points G and E on the arcs represent the positions of moving objects (stones), with lines G-F and E-D illustrating the distance the objects would need to be "pulled back" to remain on the circular path versus following the tangent path of projection.</image-desc>

Let **B G** be the circumference of the medium wheel, and **C E** that of the largest. Let the semi-diameter **A B C** be perpendicular to the horizon, and through points **B** and **C** let the tangents **B F** and **C D** be drawn. Let the two parts of the arcs **B G** and **C E** be equal, and let the wheels be turned at the same speed on their center **A**. If two moving objects—for example, two stones—are carried by the circumferences **B G** and **C E** at an equal speed, so that while stone **B** travels along arc **B G**, stone **C** completes arc **C E**, I say that the circumference of the smaller wheel has much more force to throw stone **B** than that of the large wheel to throw **C**. Because the projection <note>In this context, "projection" refers to centrifugal force—the tendency of an object to be thrown outward from a center of rotation.</note> must occur along the tangent, when the stones leave points **B** and **G**, they will travel along the tangents **B F** and **C D**. Now, stone **B** cannot remain on the wheel if its own weight does not pull it back by the length of the **secant** <term>A line that intersects a curve at two points; here it represents the distance between the circular path and the straight line of projection.</term> **F G**, or the perpendicular drawn from point **G** to **B F**. But stone **C** only needs to pull back by the length of the secant **D E**, or the perpendicular led from point **E** to **C D**, which is much less than **F G**, and always becomes smaller as the wheel becomes larger.

And because these distances must be covered in equal times, when the wheels are turned from **B** to **G** and from **C** to **D**, the retraction of stone **B** along **F G** must be faster than the other, **D E**. Consequently, a greater force is needed to retain stone **B** on its wheel than stone **C** on its own. One could also say that the speeds of the wheels being equal, they give an equal impetus to the stones along the tangent, but because the tangent does not move away as much on the large wheel, it supports the movement of stone **C** and gently satisfies the "appetite" <note>The "appetite" of a stone refers to its physical tendency or impetus to continue in a straight line.</note> it has to move away. This does not happen with the smaller wheel, where the tangent moves away significantly. Thus, it would perhaps be necessary to increase the speed of the large wheel as much as the size of its diameter to make it throw its stone just as...

# Book Second

Let us now see what truth there is in this discourse; and because it is quite long, we must place the examination of it in the following proposition.

### PROPOSITION XIX.

->*To determine what force the Earth would have to throw stones and other bodies if it turned in twenty-four hours, and what the force of other wheels is.*<-

It is difficult to conclude without experiment <note>The original French *experience* can mean both "experience" and "experiment," but in this scientific context, it refers to empirical testing.</note> that the projection <note>The act of being thrown outward.</note> from wheels occurs along the tangent, and that the force of larger wheels is greater than that of smaller ones. It seems that one might have as much right to say that if it occurs in this way, the movement of the Earth would have 17,181,818 times more force to throw bodies than a wheel two feet in diameter turning in 24 hours. This is because, in a similar arc, the tangent or the perpendicular is that much larger, and that much further from the surface, as the diameter of the large wheel is greater than that of the smaller one. Let A C be the radius <term>original: *demidiametre*; half the diameter.</term> of the Earth, being 17,181,818 feet, and A B that of a wheel of one foot. The arc E C will be 17,181,818 times larger than B I, and the tangent E D just as many times larger than B O. The same thing will happen at distance D E, or at the perpendicular E L with respect to distance I O; so that the Earth would throw a stone that much further as its radius is larger, because it moves that much faster, even though it makes no more turns than the small wheel.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating circular motion and tangential projection. Two concentric circles of different radii are centered at point A. A small arc BI belongs to the inner circle (radius AB), and a larger arc EC belongs to the outer circle (radius AC). Tangent lines BF and ED extend from points B and E respectively. Points and lines are labeled A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, O to mark intersections and specific lengths for mathematical comparison.</image-desc>

And the path created by the largest tangent cannot satisfy the appetite for movement <note>This refers to the "impetus," a medieval and early modern concept that objects "carry" a certain amount of force that keeps them moving until it is exhausted.</note> of the stone, because the stone no longer touches the wheel as soon as it has left the point of contact. In this way, we have no need here for distances with tangents, nor for the aforementioned perpendiculars, for the projection would be very small if the stone did not go at least as far as the radius of the wheel. Instead, we must only consider the horizontal lines B F and C D, along which the stone must travel—though it does not follow them entirely. For when point B of the wheel reaches G, the stone will not arrive at F (where the tangent of arc B G ends); otherwise, its movement would increase as it went, since the tangent B F is more than double the tangent B O, even though the arc B G is only double the arc B I. This contradicts experiment, which shows that violent movements <note>In Aristotelian physics, "violent motion" is any movement forced upon an object that goes against its "natural" tendency (like falling toward the Earth).</note> decrease and never move faster than the movement of their causes.

This is why it is better to take the horizontal line B F parallel to the sine of the arc <term>original: *sinus de l'arc*; a trigonometric line segment related to the angle of the arc.</term> made by the wheel while the stone is moving, until the wheel has made an arc of 45 degrees. This agrees in some way with the movement of the stone, which at the start moves almost as fast as the wheel, just as the sine of a small arc is perceptibly as large as its arc; so that the movement of the stone becomes slower than that of the wheel

...just as sines become smaller than their arcs: not that I mean to say that these decreases are entirely similar, otherwise the stone would not have to pass the length of the wheel's diameter, since the sines no longer increase when they approach the <image-desc>A geometric diagram of a circular quadrant. This being established—namely, that the stone must follow the length of the sine rather than the tangent (which follows even from the opinion of Galileo, who maintains that it falls back onto the wheel, which cannot happen unless it follows the tangent <note>Galileo discusses this in his *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems*, arguing that gravity usually overcomes the "throwing" force of rotation.</note>, and who says its weight only needs to pull it back by the perpendicular drawn from point E to the tangent CD of the large circle, or by the perpendicular drawn from point G to the tangent BF of the smaller circle)—one must only measure the line CL made by the stone pushed by the large wheel, while it makes the arc CE, which I suppose to be 7 degrees; and then the line BK, which the stone makes while the smaller wheel makes the arc BG of 14 degrees. From this, it follows that this [smaller] wheel will make two turns for every one turn of the large one, so as to move at an equal speed; and nevertheless, it will not have more force to throw [the stone] than the large one, because at the same time that the large one drives the stone from C to L, the smaller one drives it from B to H. Now, the line LC is equal to the sine of 7 degrees EM, which is 12,186 parts where the radius AC has 100,000; and in the smaller wheel, it is 24,372 parts where its radius AB is 100,000. Now, the line BK is equal to the sine of 14 degrees NG (which is the arc made by the smaller wheel), which is only 24,192 parts, and which consequently is less than the line CL—that is to say, the projection <note>The distance an object is thrown.</note> from the large wheel—so that it has twice as much force as the smaller one, even though it makes half as many turns.

This will be seen even better if we take wheels with greater differences. For example, if the arc of the large wheel CE is two degrees, and if it is six times larger than the smaller one, then the line LC will be 20,940 parts, that is, six times larger than the sine of two degrees; and the arc of the smaller wheel BG being 12 degrees, the line BK will contain only 20,791—that is, 149 parts less. And if the large one were a hundred times larger, while it made the arc CE of 18' <note>18 arc-minutes; there are 60 minutes in one degree.</note>, the small one would make the arc BG of 1,800', or 30 degrees. And while the stone was thrown from C to L, whose distance is equal to the sine of 18' ME, which is 524 parts (where AC has 100,000, or 52,400 parts where AB has 100,000), the stone would be thrown by the small wheel from B to K, whose distance is equal to the sine NG of 30 degrees, which has 50,000 parts of radius AB. So, when the small wheel, making a hundred times more turns than the large one to go just as fast, would throw the stone as far as 500 parts, the large wheel will throw it as far as 524 of those parts—that is, about 1/20th further than the small one, which might throw it 20 paces, for example, and the large one 21, even though Galileo asserts that the small one will throw it further.

# Book Second

in Physics; as I have demonstrated in several places in this work, I come to experiment, in order to observe the manner in which nature acts in these movements, and to draw a decision from it.

Having taken two wheels in a sesquitertial ratio <note>original: "raison sesquitierce"; a ratio of 4 to 3.</note>, of which the larger has a diameter of three and a half inches, and having made them complete 20 or 22 rotations in one second of an hour, the larger one threw the ball (which fell upon it from the height of a finger) about two feet, and the small one a foot and a half: but when they make only 10 rotations in a second, they do not throw it at all; for they only begin to throw it half a foot when they make 12 or 13 rotations in the said second. This projection is horizontal, and almost as fast at the beginning as the movement of the wheel, although after the space of this half-foot, or two feet, it suddenly falls to the ground; this is strange, considering that violent movements <note>In the physics of this era, "violent motion" referred to motion caused by an external force, as opposed to "natural motion" like gravity.</note> that go fast are accustomed to carry the body very far. This can serve to decide the difficulty that I propose in another place: namely, whether the same body can be thrown along the same line—for example, parallel to the horizon—such that by going faster at the beginning, it nevertheless does not go as far as when it is thrown by some sort of method <note>original: "industrie"; implying a mechanical setup or specific technique.</note> so that it goes more slowly at the start.

But I return to the wheels, in order to note further that another large wheel which turns the two previous ones makes no projection of the ball that falls upon it when it turns three times in a second, which is the fastest movement one can give it with the arm, which makes it go as fast as the smallest wheel doing 10 and a half rotations. Perhaps it would make the same projection as the small one if it went as fast as when it makes 20 or 22 rotations, which would happen if it made 6 rotations in one second of an hour. Regardless, the experiments are very difficult, for by letting several lead balls of the same size fall on the same wheel, which goes very fast, sometimes the projection covers two feet, other times one foot, or half a foot, and at other times no projection occurs at all. This prevents me from concluding on this subject until other experiments made on a larger scale have given more light; therefore, I pass to other difficulties.

...top of their masts, because weights always fall at the foot of the mast, even though the ship moves faster than the weight descends; the reason for this we shall explain after having examined whether the perpendicular motion of stones, etc., is hindered by circular motion, and whether these two movements are opposed.

To which I first respond that if one takes "perpendicular" to mean that which leads the moving body from the place where it falls to the point where it arrives by the shortest line, and if one imagines a fixed point at the place from which it fell, then the path of the stone descending from the top of the mast <term>top of the mast<gloss>original: "hune"; the platform or "crow's nest" near the top of a ship's mast</gloss></term> to the foot of the mast while the ship moves is not actually perpendicular. This is true even though it seems to be perpendicular to those who drop the weight and to those who are inside the ship, just as it is easy to experiment with in a running carriage <note>original: "carrosse"; a horse-drawn coach.</note>. For the person inside, who throws a ball upward, believes that it rises and falls back perpendicularly, and indeed he receives it back in his hand just as if the carriage remained immobile—even though it travels very fast and the ball thrown upward as straight as one can imagine ought to have fallen behind the carriage. But a person standing on the ground, watching the movement of the ball, notices very easily that it does not go straight, and that it leans toward the horses all the more as they go faster. The same thing happens to the ball that falls from the top of the mast, and to the one thrown upward in a boat that is moving.

From this, it is easy to conclude that the movement of these bodies is not truly perpendicular, and that it is not possible for us to perceive whether the Earth moves by watching these falls; they will always appear perpendicular to us, just as they do to those in a carriage or in a sea vessel. Secondly, I say that the circular motion of the Earth would in no way hinder the movements that appear perpendicular to us, as is experienced in a vessel that moves without rocking from one side to the other from the moment the weight falls until it reaches the bottom. For the weight falls along the same line as a plumb line <note>original: "filet d'un plomb"; a lead weight on a string used to determine a vertical line.</note> attached to the top of the vessel, even though it is exposed on all sides to the exterior air and to all sorts of winds. Now, the movement of the vessel, and of everything that moves on the surface of the water or the Earth, is circular, since the Earth is round.

Now, it seems to many that if the daily motion <note>The "daily motion" refers to the rotation of the Earth on its axis every 24 hours.</note> of the Earth is assumed, it must prevent the perpendicular fall of stones. For although these two movements do not seem contrary, like those that go up and down, nevertheless, the movement parallel to the horizon—which does not seem contrary to the fall of the weight—prevents it from going toward the center of the Earth. The weight would never descend toward the center if the movement of the horizontal projection were eternal, as might perhaps happen without the resistance of the air which opposes it. From this, one might conclude that if the circular motion of the Earth were eternal and as fast as that of a ball coming out of the mouth of a cannon, it ought to prevent the fall of all kinds of weights, if the Earth imparted its motion to them; since this does not happen, it seems to demonstrate that the Earth is immobile.

And if one responds that the weight always approaches the center, however imperceptibly, no matter how much violence the horizontal movement might do to the perpendicular, one can reply that the force carrying the cannonball <note>original: "boulet"; a projectile or ball.</note> is so great...

And if circular motion hindered the perpendicular fall even slightly, it would be hindered less the closer the stone was to the center (where circular motion is slower). Consequently, it would fall faster as it approached the center, whether continuing its fall begun at any place above or below the surface of the earth, or just beginning it. But this manner of falling would not favor the one that ought to occur in 6 hours along the semicircle we spoke of previously.

Now, one may conclude from this entire discourse that if the Earth turned in 24 hours, or in more or less time, it would in no way hinder the descent of weights, which would always be perceived as just as perpendicular as they are when assuming the Earth is immobile.

Let us now see the reason why weights seem to fall perpendicularly, both in boats and carriages and in all other similar places. Regarding this, I say first that it is not because the vessel pushes the stone, for it is not necessary for the vessel to touch it; given that when thrown upward in the open air, it falls back into the hand that threw it, even though the boat, carriage, or horse carrying the thrower moves at the greatest possible speed. One might say the hand pushes the ball just as the vessel would, since it seems to have started from there, because the vessel and everything it contains forms a solid, which sinks into the water only as much as an equal volume of water is heavier, as we shall show elsewhere with Archimedes <note>A reference to Archimedes' Principle of buoyancy.</note>.

In the second place, I say that the hand or the boat communicates their motion to the weight that descends, whether by pushing it (when one makes it fall from the top of the mast toward the prow) or by pulling it (when it falls toward the stern). For, supposing the vessel travels 18 feet in one second, it will travel one and a half feet in 5 tierces <term>tierces<gloss>A "tierce" is a historical unit of time measurement, representing 1/60th of a second.</gloss></term>, during which time the weight only falls one inch.
