### PROPOSITION XXI.

*Explaining why a stone dropped from the top of a ship's mast, or from a carriage, etc., or thrown upward, falls on the same spot of the vessel or carriage, whether they remain stationary or move at whatever speed one might wish.*

It is certain that one catches in one’s hand a stone thrown as straight upward as possible while in a boat or a carriage, even if they travel as fast as the post <note>The "post" refers to the speed of relay horses used to carry mail, the fastest land travel of the era.</note> or birds; which would likewise happen if they traveled as fast as an arquebus <term>arquebus<gloss>original: "arquebuſe"; an early type of long gun</gloss></term> ball, for experience compels us to abandon the bias <note>original: "preoccupation"; the author refers to the common-sense intuition that objects should be "left behind" by a moving vehicle.</note> that prevents many from believing it.

Now, it seems that Galileo <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), the Italian scientist who used this experiment to defend the idea that the Earth could be rotating without us feeling it.</note> derives the reason for this experiment from the ease with which a ball moves on a horizontal plane, when he asks us to imagine a copper ball on a plane as polished as marble, and that all resistance from the air be removed; for it will have no more inclination toward motion than toward rest, because it is always equally distant from the center [of the Earth], and if it is pushed, its motion will be eternal, if the plane is not bounded, there being no cause to slow, hasten, or prevent its motion. This being established, he says that water is a very polished horizontal plane when it is calm, and that ships floating on it, once pushed, are disposed to move perpetually; which must also be concluded for the stones and other things carried by the boat, which acquire an impetus <term>impetus<gloss>original: "impetuoſité"; in 17th-century physics, this referred to the "power" or momentum a body retains once set in motion.</gloss></term> capable of making them follow the vessel, all hindrance being removed—namely, air resistance and the inclination to go downward, which can impede circular motion. But the air offers very little resistance to a very heavy stone, as is experienced in strong winds; and if the air is carried at the same speed as the ship, it will not hinder the stone at all.

As for the inclination to go downward, he says it is not contrary to the circular motion that occurs around the center, and that perpendicular motion toward the center does not destroy the other, because the only contrary motions are those where one approaches the center and the other moves away from it; now, circular motion in no way prevents perpendicular motion from bringing the weight closer to the center, and the heavi-

### Book Second

...the weight having no other goal than to lead it toward the center, the imprinted virtue <term>imprinted virtue<gloss>original: "vertu imprimee"; an early scientific term for what we now call momentum or impetus</gloss></term> only wants to lead it around the center, so that no hindrance remains.

One can also provide other causes for this experiment, namely that the movement of the stone is very slow at the beginning of its fall, and therefore the movement of the vessel can easily imprint its momentum upon it. For example, when a lead ball falls from the crow's nest <term>crow’s nest<gloss>original: "hune"; the platform near the top of a mast</gloss></term> of a ship 48 feet high, which travels at 5 English miles per hour, it is certain that the ship travels 14 feet while the ball falls. Now, the experiment repeated more than a hundred times shows that it falls from this height in 2 seconds <note>The notation 2'' refers to seconds</note>, and consequently it will only descend one third of a line <term>line<gloss>original: "ligne"; a traditional unit of length equal to 1/12 of an inch</gloss></term> in the time of 50 thirds <note>The notation '''' refers to "fourths" or "thirds" of a second in base-60 time divisions common in the 17th century</note>, as I showed in the second proposition. Thus, it very easily receives the impression of the vessel which travels faster than it does when it begins its fall, for it only moves 1/810,000 of an inch in 20 fourths; and if it continued to descend in this manner, it would only cover one foot in a quarter of an hour, while the vessel would cover more than half a league. From this, it happens that the ball falls on the same spot of the vessel where it would fall if it remained immobile, as shown by all the experiments, which deserve for me to explain the reason. I say, then, that if one imagines a vessel moving as fast as an arrow, and that inside it there is an arrow set as it is on a crossbow—for example, that someone holds it in their hand above the crow's nest—it will go as fast as the ship even though they let it go. If the ship stopped shortly after one had let go of the said arrow, it would continue its movement, which would carry it as long and as far as if it had been shot with a crossbow.

Similarly, if the ship hastens its course as soon as the ball is dropped, it is certain that it will not fall in the same place where it would have fallen if the ship had remained immobile, or if it had continued the same movement (which is the same thing here). It is therefore evident that the fall occurs in the same place in a vessel that moves as in one that rests, from whatever height the weight may fall, provided that the one who drops it, or the place from which it falls, is on the vessel or on one of its parts; otherwise, it falls in another place. For example, if the ship or the carriage moves 12 feet in a second, the weight or the stone that someone outside the carriage throws 12 feet high toward the door will fall behind the carriage, because it has not received its impression; but if the person inside the carriage throws the same stone 12 feet high, he will receive it back in his hand, and it will always seem to him that it rises and falls in a straight line, whereas the path is actually oblique, as it indeed appears to all those outside the carriage. Thus, all those inside are mistaken if they do not correct appearance with reason, as do those who believe they prove the immobility of the Earth by the perpendicular fall of stones, since they would appear just as perpendicular to us even if it turned around its axis, or around the Sun, whether in 24 hours or in a moment, and even if it had no attractive virtue, no more than the carriage. This is what Christian Philosophers <note>The author is likely addressing contemporary Scholastic theologians who used the Bible to argue against the Copernican (sun-centered) system.</note> must notice, so that they do not make the truths of Holy Scripture ridiculous to the Pagans by bringing forth reasons that show nothing other than their ignorance, or the weakness of their...

# On the Movement of Bodies.

...their imagination and their mind: for it is much better to be content with the divine revelation alone of the truths proposed to us, than to add reasons which can be proven null by experiments or by other stronger and better reasons. For example, supposing it were a truth of faith that the Earth is so stable and immobile that it moves neither around its axis, nor around the Sun, nor by any other movement—not only according to the appearances of the senses, but also according to the truth—it is not appropriate to confirm its stability by the perpendicular fall of stones, or by the equal movement of missiles <term>missiles<gloss>original: "missiles"; here referring generally to any projectile thrown or fired, such as stones or arrows</gloss></term> toward the East and the West. For it can be clearly shown that the same thing would happen even if the Earth were mobile and had the two or three movements that several have imagined. <note>The author is referring to the Copernican theory. He warns that using the "perpendicular fall" as proof of a stationary Earth is dangerous because, as Galileo argued, a stone would still appear to fall straight down on a rotating Earth due to shared momentum.</note>

It is not that it is not very good to use reasons to show that our faith has nothing impertinent in it, and nothing that is not worthy of the Divine Majesty or within His power, when these reasons are of such a quality that no consideration can be produced to weaken them. However, it is as dangerous to use the former kind as it is useful and laudable to use the latter, as St. Thomas <note>original: "S. Thomas"; referring to Saint Thomas Aquinas</note> did in several places of his *Summa against the Gentiles* <note>original: *Somme contre les Gentils*; the *Summa contra Gentiles*, a major theological work intended to defend Christian doctrines against non-believers using reason.</note>.

### COROLLARY.

It is easy to conclude that the violent movement of missiles is not caused by the movement of the air succeeding one another <note>This refutes the Aristotelian theory of "antiperistasis," which claimed that air pushed from the front of a projectile rushed to the back to keep it moving.</note>, since a lead ball that falls across from the door, or behind a carriage, falls perpendicularly without following it, provided that the person who lets it fall is outside the said carriage. This clearly shows that the air moved by the vehicle is not the cause of the ball following it, but only the impression it has received <note>Referring to "impressed virtue" or momentum.</note>, which is perhaps not at all different from the movement it continues perpetually when it meets no hindrance. Now, we must further examine a consequence that Galileo <note>original: "Galilee"</note> draws from the fall of heavy bodies.

### PROPOSITION XXII.

*To determine if an artillery ball fired horizontally from the top of a tower arrives at the ground as soon as an equal ball falling perpendicularly from the top of the same tower.*

If a stone thrown while on horseback—when the horse walks at an even pace or runs at full gallop—always falls back into the hand of the one who throws it straight up, as quickly as it would fall back when the horse is not moving, there is some appearance of truth that a ball fired horizontally from the top of a tower or from any place whatsoever arrives at the ground as soon as another ball falling perpendicularly from the same place. It is this, in my opinion, which persuaded Mr. Galileo <note>original: "sieur Galilee"</note> that this experiment ought to occur; but having performed it, I found it was far from being true, and that a crossbow bolt fired point-blank <term>point-blank<gloss>original: "de point en blanc"; firing a weapon directly at a target without adjusting for the drop of the projectile</gloss></term> at its proper range takes twice as long to make the path...

# BOOK THREE
## ON THE MOTION, tension, force, weight, and other properties of Harmonic strings, and other bodies.

After having spoken of the movement of the principal bodies of this Universe, particularly that of the earth, it is necessary to examine more particularly those movements belonging to the strings of instruments, and to other bodies that produce Harmony: which we shall do in the Propositions of this book, where we will also treat the force necessary to support a given weight on an oblique plane inclined to the horizon.

### PROPOSITION I.

->The ratio of the number of vibrations of all kinds of strings is inverse to their lengths.<-

**L**ET the preceding string AB be attached to the two bridges <note>Small wooden blocks that support the strings on a musical instrument, defining the vibrating length.</note> of the **Monochord** <note>A scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used since antiquity to study the mathematical relationships of musical intervals.</note> at the two points A & B; and the string AF be attached at points A & F. I say that string AB, being pulled to point G, will return only once to point F, while the string AF, pulled to point I, will return twice to point H, as experience shows; so that AF will always return twice while AB returns only once: consequently, the number of vibrations <note>original: "retours," referring to the oscillation or the completion of a cycle of movement back and forth.</note> of AF is double that of AB, just as the string AB is double the length of string AF: from which it follows that the number of movements or vibrations of a string increases in the same ratio as its length decreases, and consequently that the ratio of the said vibrations is inverse to the ratio of the lengths of the string.

The reason for this inequality of vibrations is derived from the equality of tension, for point G of string AB moves as fast toward F as point I of string AF moves toward H; this proves that string AB is as tense, and as forceful <note>original: "violente," here meaning the physical force or kinetic energy of the snap back to equilibrium.</note> at point G as string AF is at point I: but because point G has twice as much distance to travel to reach F as point I has to reach H, it follows that point I will go to H, and return from H toward point I, while G goes to F; and that it will strike the air of the line AF twice, while G strikes the air of the line AB only once.

The same must be concluded for other strings, however large or small they may be; for example, for the string AH, which is one-fourth <note>original: "souzquadruple."</note> the length of string AB, its vibrations will be four times the number of vibrations of string AB: and if it were a hundred times shorter, they would be a hundredfold, and so on consecutively to infinity, or at least to the limits of brevity and length of the

## COROLLARY VI.

It follows further from this Proposition that musicians have until now taken the ratios <term>ratios: "raisons," the mathematical relationship between two notes</term> of Music in reverse, for they believed that the low sound of each interval is the greater term of the ratio, and that the high sound is the lesser, because they only considered the material of the sound <note>the physical length of the string</note>, or rather its efficient cause, whereas they should have considered its nature and its form, as we do: hence it comes that they said the low sound of the Octave contains twice the high <note>referring to the string length ratio of 2:1</note>, whereas the high contains twice the low <note>referring to the frequency or vibrations, which the author argues is the true measure</note>, and they called the most agreeable proportion of sounds "harmonic division," whereas it is only "Arithmetic," as we will demonstrate very clearly in the thirty-sixth Proposition of the book on Consonances: and consequently one can say that the true ratio of sounds, or of their intervals, is the inverse of that which all musicians have followed until now.

## PROPOSITION II.

*To explain the different velocities of the parts of each turn and return of the strings used for musical instruments, and in what proportion they diminish.*

It is certain that the first return of a string of a Lute, Viol, and other instruments is larger than those that follow after, otherwise they would last perpetually, and the string would never come to rest: for example, the string AB fixed at points A and B being pushed or pulled from point E to point C, if it is let go and it returns to point D, it is certain that it will not return as far as C, but only as far as F, that is to say, to some point less distant from E than C is. Now I have often experimented that if the line of the first turn CD is 20 parts, the first return DF is only nineteen parts, although I have also sometimes observed a greater ratio of the first turn to the first return, for example, the ratio of eleven to twelve, so that the first turn is a sesqui-eleventh <note>original: "sesquionziesme," a ratio of 12:11</note> of the first return, as I explain at greater length in the seventeenth Proposition of the first book on Instruments, in which one sees the table of diminutions of each turn and return, from the first to the last, of which I have also put another table in the thirty-second Proposition of the second Latin book on the causes of Sound <note>original: "liure Latin des causes du Son," referring to the author's work *Harmonicorum Libri*</note>. But before speaking of it here more fully, it is necessary to explain the different velocities of each turn and return. Regarding which I say first that the string never goes faster at any place on the line of its periods CD than when the hand lets it go from point C where it had been pulled, because it is never more strained <note>original: "violentée," referring to the tension or potential energy at the point of furthest displacement</note>: which must also be said of bows used to shoot arrows, for the string ACD forms a bow, even though it makes the angle ACD in this figure.

In the third place, it is certain that the turn of the string from C to D is natural from C to E, to which it returns as to its center, or its line of direction A E B; and that the rest from E to D can be called violent <note>In the physics of this period, "natural" motion was movement toward a natural place of rest, while "violent" motion was movement forced away from it.</note>, because it moves away from its center E. This is why it resists as much as it can this violence it received from the beginning of the impression made upon it by pulling it as far as C: so that each turn or return of the string is composed of two species of movements, although one can take it as a single one, because the violence of the pulling <gloss>traction</gloss> or the pushing <gloss>impulsion</gloss> from E to C is the cause of both.

Now I find here three very significant difficulties: namely, whether the string does not always go faster from F to E, since we experience that heavy bodies <note>original: "corps pesans," referring to falling weights or masses</note> go faster the closer they approach their center, and we say that E is the center of the string, whose point is considered like a stone falling toward the center of the earth, E.

The second difficulty consists in knowing why the string does not stop at E, since it seems it has no other purpose than to return to its center, and nevertheless it leaves it two thousand times before coming to rest there.

And the third belongs to the cause of the returns, or the reflections of the string, for it is very difficult to know what constrains it to return from C to E; but these difficulties deserve specific Propositions. This is why I stop here only at what is contained in this Proposition, and I say that it seems probable that the velocity of point C, which returns to D, always diminishes until it reaches D, following the different spaces it

### Book Three

<meta>catchword: it</meta>

One must use the same experiments that I have employed to find the number of returns <note>This refers to the frequency or cycles of vibration.</note> of each instrument string; but instead of needing only a brass <gloss>leton</gloss> or gut <gloss>boyau</gloss> string of one hundred King’s feet <note>original: "pieds de Roy." A pre-revolutionary French unit of length, approximately 32.5 centimeters.</note> in length, one must take one a thousand feet long. This must be stretched so that its tension <gloss>traction</gloss> from E to C is ten feet, and that it employs ten seconds of a minute for each turn and return—that is to say, the tenth part of a minute <note>Mersenne’s math here is unusual, as ten seconds is the sixth part of a standard 60-second minute; he may be proposing a decimal division for his experimental timing.</note>—so that having divided its line of return C D into ten equal parts, one has the leisure to observe the time it takes to make each tenth part. For if it makes the first part in the first second, and the three following parts in the second second, it will follow the proportion of heavy bodies <note>original: "corps peſans," referring to objects in freefall.</note> that descend toward their center; but if it passes twice as fast through the first part as the second, etc., it will follow the proportion of the violent motion of missiles <note>In the physics of this period, "violent motion" (as opposed to "natural motion") referred to the movement of projectiles or objects pushed by an external force.</note>, etc. Now, the **Tuileries gallery** <note>The Grand Gallery connecting the Louvre and the Tuileries Palace in Paris, famous for its great length, making it ideal for experiments on sound and motion.</note> is quite convenient for conducting this experiment. One may still doubt whether the decrease in speed that occurs from E to D follows the same proportion as that from C to D, because the movement E D is "violent," since it moves the string away from its center E—which it approaches through the movement C E—and whether the part E D of the return C E D lasts longer than the part C E.

Experience and reason lead me to conclude that point C of the string always goes on decreasing its speed from C until D; for since it only returns by reason of the force <gloss>violence</gloss> that stretches it, it must return all the more quickly as it is more tightly stretched. I demonstrate this in this manner: when one pulls it only as far as F, or to whatever point one wishes between F and E, it takes as much time to make its turn as when one pulls it as far as C or beyond. This could not happen unless it moved more slowly as it is pulled less, and consequently less forced <gloss>violentée</gloss>. Now, this force is less as the point C approaches closer to E, at which point it is no longer forced; from which it follows that it must go less quickly in proportion as it advances toward E, at which it would rest if the air surrounding A C B did not still push it toward D, or if it had not taken on too great a momentum <gloss>branſle</gloss> to return to its line of direction.

From this we can conjecture the answer to the second part of this Proposition: namely, that the returns decrease in the same proportion as the forces <gloss>violences</gloss>, so that if the force of the string A D C is less by a nineteenth part (following the table of the seventeenth Proposition of the first book of *Instruments*), the return D F will be smaller and slower by a nineteenth part than the turn C D, and so on for the other turns and returns, if their decrease continues according to geometric proportion. But experiments are so difficult that without a string of a thousand feet, one cannot be certain; and one is never so certain of the places where it returns at each turn that one does not doubt whether it has passed beyond, or if it has precisely finished its comings and goings at the points marked. Thus, it is always necessary that reason supplements something in the experiments, which alone cannot serve as principles for the sciences that require a perfect accuracy that the senses cannot perceive. For example, one cannot demonstrate through the senses that a **Spinet** <note>A small, rectangular or wing-shaped keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note> string is two or three times longer, thicker, or more stretched than another; for if it lacks only a hundred-thousandth part over two feet, it...

## PROPOSITION III.

->*To know whether strings and other projectiles that have returns rest at the points of their reflections, and what the cause of these reflections is.*<-

This difficulty is one of the greatest in Physics <note>During the 17th century, "Physics" referred to the broad study of natural philosophy and the laws of the physical world.</note>, and it seems it cannot be resolved or known by experience nor by reason. This is because he who denies this rest can say that the eyes are deceived by experience when a very long string stretched by both ends, or another shorter one attached at the top end and free at the bottom, seem to rest; he will say that they move, albeit very slowly. Now, there are several movements that relate to this one: namely, that of heavy bodies <note>original: "corps pesans," referring to objects with mass subject to gravity.</note> that one throws perpendicularly upward, and which seem to rest a little while when they have arrived at the equilibrium of violent motion and natural motion <note>In Aristotelian physics, "violent motion" is movement caused by an external force (the throw), while "natural motion" is the object's inherent tendency to return to its natural place (falling toward the Earth).</note>. That is to say, when the force they have to descend is found to be equal to the force pushing them upward; for there can be no movement where there is an equality of resistance, and where one side pulls as strongly as the other.

The same difficulty is raised regarding balls that one throws against walls, which must also rest at the point of their reflection <note>The "point of reflection" refers to the exact moment the ball hits the wall and reverses direction.</note>, according to the thought of those who do not believe that two contrary movements can be continuous, and who only place a contiguity between the two parts of the same tree, of which one is dry and the other green, or one is dead and the other lives. I leave aside a thousand things that make several turns and returns, such as steel blades and everything that possesses a spring <gloss>ressort</gloss>, in order to consider the reasons on both sides. One side proves that there is no rest at the points of reflection, because if the preceding string rested at D, it should always rest there, there being no apparent cause that pushes it back toward E and F. On the other hand, if it does not rest at all, it seems that it must always go faster in every part of the line C D than in any part of the line D F; that is to say, it must observe the same proportion in its total movement as a stone that is thrown: which nevertheless does not happen, for

# Book Three

experience shows that a weight attached to a string, which has the freedom to go here and there, moves much more slowly when it approaches the points of its reflections <note>In this context, "reflections" refers to the turning points or the furthest extent of a vibration or swing where the direction of motion reverses.</note>, than when it moves away from them and passes through its line of direction, as I will show later.

And if one attaches a string a thousand feet long by both ends, whether horizontal or perpendicular to the horizon, and notices the same difference in speeds, and the great slowness of its movements toward the points of reflection—at which it moves with an infinite slowness <note>This refers to an infinitesimal speed approaching zero.</note>, just as a stone does at the beginning of its fall, whether perpendicular or oblique to the horizon, which I will treat in another Proposition—it seems that one would not be mistaken in saying that it rests for a moment. This moment occurs when the force that pushed it is in equilibrium with the natural spring <term>spring (ressort): the internal elastic potential or "snap-back" quality of the string's material</term> which pulls it back to its center E. For if the force that pushes it, and perpetually agitates it from one side to the other, acted continuously, its movement should always be weaker and slower in proportion as it approached its rest; consequently, it would be faster toward each point of its preceding reflection than toward the center E, where it nonetheless appears faster than at any point of the preceding reflection, at which it begins anew a movement as distinct and new as if one had touched the string again.

Now, assuming that this point of reflection is a true rest, and that it comes from the equilibrium of the two aforementioned forces, it follows that the force which retains the string as much as possible at this point is overcome little by bit, and that the said string goes faster at point E, where all external force is extinguished, than at any other place; and that immediately after this greatest speed, the movement begins to slow down until it arrives at the point of equilibrium and reflection. From this it follows that one must speak differently of the first turn of the string pulled to C than of the first return and the others; and that since the force of the hand that releases it at C in no way retards the inclination <note>Original: "pante." This refers to the natural tendency or "slope" of the motion toward the center.</note> it has to return to its center E, it hastens as much as it can according to the violence that the tension or traction has caused it. But if the violence <note>In 17th-century physics, "violent motion" was movement caused by an external force, contrasting with "natural motion."</note> is extinguished at all points of reflection, and nothing remains but the said inclination, one must say the same thing of each return as of the first turn; and if the experience of a sufficiently long string fixed at both ends shows that it goes more slowly when leaving point C than when it arrives at E, one must conclude that it imitates the return of heavy bodies toward their center, which we have discussed elsewhere.

But since I see no reason strong enough to demonstrate whether it rests during its reflections, I come to the second part of the Proposition, which consists in seeking the cause of these reflections; for it is very certain that the string returns several times to its center E, whether it rests at the point of reflection or moves continuously. It is also certain that the cause of this reflection is within the string, since the external air cannot have this force, given that the air itself is at rest when the string is released at C. Now, it is known that the parts of the string extend and perhaps open their pores when it is pulled to C, and that these parts retract and close their pores when it returns to E; but it is not known what constrains them to close again, for if one says that this return of the parts is caused by the force of the internal air which was condensed during traction, and which returns...

And when one has considered all the principles of each movement, and when one wishes to know what determines them toward one kind of movement rather than several others, one will be constrained to have recourse to the first independent Author <note>A reference to God as the "Prime Mover" or ultimate source of physical laws.</note>, who determines all principles as He pleases, and to what He pleases.

Now, what seems most certain in this is that the string, the bow, etc., that one bends is in a perpetual movement which opposes the contrary force of the traction, and consequently that one must seek no other reason for the return than this movement, which makes itself apparent as soon as the hindrance is removed, just as does the movement of a stone toward its center <note>Following Aristotelian physics, it was believed that heavy objects like stones had a natural inclination to move toward the center of the Earth.</note>; for one can say that it is always moving, since it makes a perpetual resistance and impression upon the hand that holds it: which can easily be applied to the string pulled to C, or to any other point one wishes away from point E.

### PROPOSITION IV.

->*Explaining why the string which returns from the place where it was pulled passes several times beyond its center without stopping there.*<-

We seek a very obscure reason for a very evident effect, namely why the string A B, pulled or pushed as far as C, passes beyond its center E, since it has no other intention than to stop there—similar to a stone that would fall to its center, where it should, it seems, stop without passing beyond, and without going here and there as does the string of which we speak. One would not easily imagine that it ought to pass beyond its center E, given that the speed with which it leaves C is instituted by nature only to make it resume its straight position A E B, if the effect did not constrain us to change our opinion. For there is little appearance that nature, which is so prudent, or rather which so necessarily follows the conduct of its Author (who can do nothing in vain), gives a greater jolt to the string than that which is necessary to restore it to its proper place. Otherwise, one would accuse nature of the same imprudence as a man would show, who, having no other design than to stop at his house, went so abruptly and so fast that he could not stop there without passing much further, and without going back and forth several times, and consequently without traveling a hundred times more distance than is necessary.

Now, it seems to me that to give the reason for this Phenomenon, it would be necessary to know the different games of the air <note>Refers to the behavior or dynamics of the surrounding air as it interacts with the moving string.</note>, and the different impressions it makes on the string that it repels, for it can add a new force to it...

...even if their movement is too small to be perceptible, I am far from wanting to demonstrate what I prove through experience. This experience will be followed by all those who perform it, because the understanding must be convinced by evident reason to be compelled to embrace a demonstration. I wish for this to be noted once and for all, so that one does not believe that I always use the word **demonstrate** or **demonstration** in a mathematical sense. Those who know the difficulty encountered in demonstrating anything in Physics will easily conclude this; for in Physics, it is very difficult to establish other maxims more advantageous than well-regulated and well-conducted experiences. These experiences perpetually show that each cycle or return <note>original: "tour ou retour." This refers to a single back-and-forth vibration of the string.</note> of the string—stretched and fixed at both ends, like that of a **Viol** or another instrument—lasts just as long as every other; so that the difference in duration between the smallest and the largest vibration is not perceptible.

Now, reason favors this experience, because the violence <term>violence (violence): in early physics, this refers to the external force or "impetus" applied to an object to move it out of its natural state of rest.</term> or the impression made upon the string is all the greater as the path of its return is longer. This is why it moves all the faster as the space it covers is larger. For example, if it travels one foot on the first return and one line <note>A "line" (ligne) was a historical unit of measurement equal to 1/12 of an inch, or about 2.26 millimeters.</note> on the hundredth, it will go 144 times faster on the first return than on the hundredth, where it will be subjected to much less force; and when the force ceases, it will come to rest.

And if there is no rest at the point of reflection <note>The "point of reflection" refers to the furthest point of the string's swing before it changes direction.</note>, and its entire movement is produced by the first impression, one must say that the return it makes from each point of its reflection toward its center is always forced, and that it is at most only half-natural, since it is by the same movement that the string goes as far as the center and beyond the center. From this one can conclude that each side of every cycle and return lasts just as long as the other, and that—with the external impression alone being established as their cause—the string always moves faster toward each preceding point of its reflection than at any point on its following line of return, as I have already remarked. Thus, if the sound is produced only at the center, one must admit that it is not produced by the greatest speed of movement—but we shall speak of this difficulty later.

As for the number of returns of each string, it is very large before it comes to rest; for it is certain that it always moves as long as one hears its sound. The sound of thick **Lute** strings is perceived by the ear for a sixth part or a third of a minute—that is, while the pulse of a healthy man, without emotion, beats ten or twenty times. Thus, it only remains to note how many times the string strikes the air in a second <note>Mersenne refers to "second minutes," which we simply call seconds today.</note> to know how many times it strikes it before coming to rest, or rather, before it is no longer perceived. In this period, a "first minute" referred to what we call a minute, and a "second minute" referred to a second.</note>, as I will show hereafter; from which it must be concluded that the ear is marvelously subtle, since it notices movements that are a hundred thousand times smaller than the hundred-thousandth part of a **line** <term>line (ligne): a traditional unit of length equal to 1/12th of an inch, or about 2.25 millimeters.</term>, and consequently that it surpasses the subtlety of the eye by more than a hundred thousand times. But if one takes the fraction that explains the last return of the string marked in the table of the aforementioned seventeenth Proposition, one will have much more reason to admire the brevity of these returns; for with unity serving as the numerator, the denominator has sixty zeros after the unit, so that it is necessary to use our new Arithmetic to express this prodigious fraction, saying that the 1584th return of the **Lute** string, which it makes toward the end of its tremors, is only the **nineteenth-illion** <note>original: "dix-neufilion." Mersenne is using a custom naming system for extremely large numbers; here he refers to a value with 60 zeros.</note> of a line, which is expressed by this fraction:

Those who do not understand this manner of numbering up to infinity without getting confused, and without any difficulty, can see the demonstration of it in the first chapter of the third book of *The Truth of the Sciences* <note>original: "la Verité des Sciences," a work published by Mersenne in 1625 defending scientific knowledge against skepticism.</note>, where I provide the method for counting the number that would be written from the North Pole to the South Pole in characters as small as those of this fraction.

### COROLLARY.

The final returns of the string are so small that if everything in the world—for example the earth, the walls, and everything we see and touch—were to move by similar turns and returns, we could not perceive it in any way; so that all the bodies of the world can create a perpetual harmony, even though no one hears it, and we have reason to humble ourselves in our ignorance, which we cannot remedy until it pleases God to deliver us from the obligation we have to the stupidity of the senses.

### ADVERTISEMENT.

Before pursuing everything pertaining to Movements, sounds, weight, and the other qualities of strings and other bodies, I wish to place here a discourse on the force necessary to sustain, pull, or push a given weight upon all sorts of planes inclined to the horizon, composed by **Monsieur de Roberval** <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval (1602–1675), a renowned French mathematician and physicist at the Collège Royal.</note>, Professor of Mathematics at the **Royal College of France**; one will easily judge by this sample how much one may hope for from a mind so judicious and so excellent. Now, I divide it into four Propositions to accommodate it to my subject, although one could put it into as many Propositions as there are Scholia and Corollaries.

### PROPOSITION V.

->*Explaining the easiest way to count every vibration and return of any Lute, Viol, or Spinet string, etc., and determining the limits of the eye’s and ear’s sensitivity.*<-

I am not including the Treatise on Mechanics here as previously mentioned, because it is longer than I expected; for this reason, I am reserving it for a separate book. Now I come to the explanation of this fifth Proposition: first, one must determine the desired sound of the string before asking for the number of its returns <note>vibrations</note>, because it makes a greater number of them in the same amount of time as the sound becomes higher in pitch. Suppose, then, that one wishes to know the number of returns of a **Spinet** or **Lute** string when it is in unison with **Chapel pitch** <term>Chapel pitch (ton de Chappelle): a standard reference pitch used in French churches, which Mersenne defines here by the dimensions of an organ pipe.</term>, taken from an open four-foot pipe or a stopped two-foot pipe producing **G-re-sol** <note>A pitch corresponding to G.</note>, below which the deepest or lowest voices in France can only descend by a **Fifth** to reach **C-sol-ut** <note>A pitch corresponding to C.</note>.

Now, anyone can carry this pitch with them by means of a hollowed-out key or a **Flageolet** <term>Flageolet: a small, high-pitched flute-like instrument.</term>, which rises to the Octave, the Fifteenth, or any other interval one wishes above the aforementioned **G-re-sol**, because it is enough to remember that this pitch is higher than the Chapel pitch by a given interval to then express it with the voice or otherwise.

This being established, I say first that the string making the pitch of **G-re-sol**—which is nearly the lowest my voice can descend—strikes the air 168 times; that is, it passes 168 times through its center or its line of direction in the time of one second <note>original: "seconde minute." In this era, "first minutes" were minutes and "second minutes" were seconds.</note>, or it returns 84 times toward the person who pushes or pulls it. Secondly, a string seventeen and a half feet long is sufficient for conducting the experiment, since it does not vibrate too quickly and allows leisure to count its returns, as can be seen with a **Lute** or **Viol** string of the thickness used for the frames of **Rackets** <note>Mersenne often compared musical strings to the thick gut strings used in tennis rackets.</note> (which are made of twelve sheep intestines). This string returns only twice in the time of a second when stretched with half a pound, four times when stretched with two pounds, and eight times when stretched with eight pounds. Now, if one sounds a part of the string only ten inches long, when it is tightened with four pounds, it rises to unison with Chapel pitch; and when it is tightened with eight pounds, being twenty inches long, it rises to the same pitch; and finally, when it is only stretched by the force of half a pound, it makes the same pitch by taking only five inches of length.

From this, it must be concluded that the vibrations are in a **sub-duplicate ratio** <term>sub-duplicate ratio: a square root relationship. Mersenne is describing what is now known as "Mersenne's Law," where frequency is proportional to the square root of tension.</term> of the weights or forces tightening the string, and consequently that the forces are in a **duplicate ratio** <term>duplicate ratio: a squared relationship.</term> of the air-strikes or vibrations of the string. This is why it is not enough to tighten a string twice as hard to make it move twice as fast; rather, one must stretch it four times as hard. I leave aside several other conclusions that I deduce in Proposition 16 of Book 1, and in Propositions 7, 8, 12, 15, 16, 17, and 18 of Book 3...

stringed instruments, and I come to the second part of this Proposition, which is much more difficult than the first. For the limits and the beginnings of natural actions are usually unknown to us, and the manner in which they occur surpasses the human mind; it is enough to demonstrate this in the movement we are discussing here, which is often too fast or too slow to be perceived. Now, it is certain that the ear does not perceive many movements that the eye discovers, which is experienced with a string seventeen feet long; the ear cannot notice its vibrations <note>French: *tremblemens*</note>, which the eye sees very well, because they do not strike the air strongly enough or often enough to produce a sensible noise, or because the sound is not enclosed and reflected by an instrument—just as it happens that the sense of touch does not perceive many levels of heat before they are reflected.

But to begin with the eye: I say that it does not perceive movements when they are too fast or too slow, and it does not see bodies when they are too small or too poorly lit, just as the ear does not hear sounds that are too weak or too distant. And perhaps bodies can be so intensely illuminated, and sounds can be so vehement, that these two senses will perceive nothing at all.

Regarding movements, the ear can only feel them by means of sounds, while the eye can only perceive them by noticing the movements. And just as one cannot judge by the eye whether movements are strong enough to be felt by hearing, likewise the ear cannot judge whether the movements that make sound are large enough or slow enough to be seen. Now, if one takes a <term>Monochord</term> <note>Monochorde: a single-stringed scientific instrument used to measure musical intervals and string tension</note>, or the strings of a <term>Spinet</term> <note>Epinette: a small, plucked keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</note>, one will experience that the eye is unable to discern the number of movements of strings that are at <term>Chapel pitch</term> <note>ton de Chappelle: the standard reference pitch used in 17th-century French music</note>, and that the imagination becomes confused when it must count more than ten returns in a second; so that the number ten <note>French: *nombre denaire*</note> limits its greatest capacity, as one will experience constantly. But if one takes strings that rise an <term>Octave</term> or a <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>Quinzieſme: an interval of two octaves</note> above the aforementioned pitch, the eye will no longer be able to see the movement of the string and will judge that it is at rest, whereas the ear will judge that it is moving.

It is not the excessive speed of the strings' movement that prevents the eye from perceiving it—since it sees and notices other movements a hundred times faster, for example, those of arrows and other missiles, as I shall say later—but because each turn and return is too short, and they follow one another too closely to be noticed. The ear, on the contrary, cannot notice the turns unless they follow one another quickly enough. From this it follows that it does not hear the eight returns made by a string seventeen and a half feet long in one second, and that a string must strike the air at least twenty times in a second to make itself heard, and that it must strike it only forty-two times for its movement to be visible to the eye—without, however, the eye being able to count its returns once they exceed ten.

I leave aside the determination of the speed and slowness of movements that cannot be perceived—for example, the movement of clock hands, that of a lit brand <note>A piece of burning wood or ember</note> being swung in a circle, that of the stars, and a thousand other things that appear in different places without one being able to notice the movement by which they changed place—so as not to stray from my subject, and to reserve these remarks for another place.

I only add that millstones can serve to determine the maximum speed that the eye can perceive, just as clock hands serve to find the maximum slowness. Furthermore, the speed of missiles <term>missiles: in this period, any object propelled through the air, like an arrow or a stone</term> must in some way correspond to the distance of those same bodies, which can be so great that they can no longer be seen—as happens with a cubic foot object that cannot be seen from a league away. It would therefore be necessary to find the analogy between distances and the speeds (or slownesses) of movements for all kinds of sizes; this is a subject that deserves specific speculation and experiments.

### COROLLARY.

It matters very little if the experiments regarding the number of returns <note>French: *retours*, referring to the cycles of a vibration</note> that I included in the 17th and 18th Propositions of the third book on Instruments do not correspond to those in this Proposition. For instance, I previously stated on page 143 that the French Basses <note>Likely referring to the *basse de violon*, the predecessor to the cello</note> descend as low as a sound of 48 beats to create a unison with an open four-foot pipe, yet in this Proposition I have assigned 84 vibrations <note>French: *tremblemens*</note> to the same pipe—which is to say almost twice as many. This discrepancy exists because I have sometimes taken the octave above and other times the octave below. Furthermore, I have not proposed my experiments so that they may be followed as an absolute rule, but only so that everyone takes the trouble to perform them themselves. One should adjust their own ear, and whatever organ pipe or other instrument they wish, to the number of vibrations they choose. It is sufficient that the same number of vibrations always produces the same tone, regardless of the different dispositions of the ear, the voice, or the instruments, as I also remarked in the sixth Corollary of the aforementioned 18th Proposition. I wish for this to be noted for all other experiments: it is enough that each person can verify or rectify them following the manner I prescribe, or according to whatever other method they judge to be more appropriate and easier.

### PROPOSITION VI.

->*To determine at what moment and in what place during the cycles and returns of the string the sound is produced: and whether the sound is sharper at the beginning of the vibrations than at the end.*<-

These two difficulties are very great, both because it is difficult to subject them to experiment and because reasoning seems to oppose the experiments that are performed, as we shall see later. I say first, then, that the sound is not made by the first movement from point C to E, or at least that it is not perceptible, for it is not heard if one places a finger or some other object at the center point E to prevent the first passage of the string. Neither is it produced by the rest of the first cycle from E to D, for the same reasoning applies to both parts. Nevertheless, reason seems to dictate that the sound should be made by this first cycle more than any other, since the string strikes the air with more speed and violence then, given that it traverses the entire line C-D in the same time that each subsequent vibration traverses a shorter distance. Now, I am speaking here of sound that is defined by a certain degree of pitch <note>French: *graue, ou d'aigu* — literally "low or high"</note>, for one can hear a certain whistling of air during the first return, particularly when there are some pores or sensible inequalities in [the string]...

But as for the sound that constitutes the pitch <note>original: *ton*</note> of the string, it only begins to be produced at the first return from D to E, which encounters the air that was following C on the first turn, and pushes it back with violence from D to E; so that the air at E finds itself enclosed between the air following from C to E, and that which is pushed back from D to E. From this, it follows that the sound is higher-pitched <note>original: *aigu*</note> the more frequently the string strikes the center E, and that its degrees of pitch increase in the same proportion as the number of returns: so that if the string strikes E a hundred times, it produces a sound that has a hundred degrees of height; and if it strikes it so infrequently that the air has leisure to escape, or to restore itself between the first turn and the first return, it produces no sound that can be heard.

### PROPOSITION VII.

->*To explain the different centers, and the different forces of each return of the strings.*<-

It is certain that each return has its own different center, if one considers the center of each arc produced at each return: for example, suppose that the string A B is pulled as far as C, and that it returns to D, and consequently that the concave of the arc A C B changes into the convex of the arc A D B, as indeed happens in each turn and return of the string; K will be the center of A C B, or of A D B which is equal to it, by transposing K to the opposite side. But the arc of the return A F B has its center at M, which is to say twice as far away as K, so that the center is further away as the peak of the return is closer to the center of the line of direction E. Now, although the returns never distance themselves as much as the arc A C B or A D B distances itself from E, I have nevertheless used this distance so that it may be better understood: for even though Lute <note>original: *Luth*</note> strings are three, four, or five feet long, they are not moved more than a line <note>original: *une ligne*; a historical measurement approximately 2.25mm or 1/12th of a French inch</note> away from their center E when they are played; this is why the centers of their arcs are extremely far from E, since these arcs differ very little from the line of direction A E B: for example, the arc A G B has its center at point Q. Similarly, E is the center of the arc R C S, therefore R E S is the string, and D is the center of the arc R F S. But if one took the center of this string from the points of attachment <note>original: *l'arreſt*</note>, namely from A or B, the point C or D would not have the same center as the point E, as can be seen in triangle A C D: from which one can conclude that E, and consequently all the points of the string A E B, change through an infinity of centers when the string changes from a straight line into a curve; for example, point E being pulled to C no longer depends on center A, otherwise it would have to rise from D to C along the arc D T C, or along the arc E F Y while rising. Now, each part of the string stretches, and consequently weakens and becomes more delicate in proportion as the arcs are larger and have their centers closer. And when the strings return to pass through their line of direction, the extended parts contract again and make the string thicker, restoring it to the same state it was in before. Nevertheless, the momentum <note>original: *impetuoſité*</note> it imprints upon itself at each return is so great that it is constrained to pass much further forward than its center E.

As for the force of the strings, it is certain that it is all the lesser as they move less distance from E, and as their center is further away, as is easy to see in this figure, in which the arc A F B has all the less...

### PROPOSITION VIII.

->*To determine all the ratios that exist between the length of bodies and their sounds.*<-

It is certain that a string equally tensioned on a Lute, or on another instrument, produces a sound that is lower-pitched <note>original: *graue*</note> the longer it is, and higher-pitched <note>original: *aigu*</note> the shorter it is, because its vibrations <note>original: *tours & retours* — literally "turns and returns"</note> are slower or faster. Consequently, if of two equal strings, one is equal to the diameter and the other to the side of a square, one will have two sounds in the same ratio as the strings, and therefore they will be incommensurable <note>referring to the mathematical relationship where the ratio cannot be expressed as a simple fraction, such as 1 to the square root of 2</note>. Now, this is always true whatever length one gives to the strings, such that if one is a hundred times longer than the other, it will produce a sound a hundred times lower; this must be understood as two strings equal in thickness and in tension: and consequently, the sounds of the strings have the same ratio between them as the lengths of said strings.

But if they are different in thickness <note>original: *groſſeur*</note>, and if one considers them as cylinders of the same height whose bases are unequal, it is certain that the ratio of their bases must be in the squared ratio <term>double ratio: in 17th-century mathematics, the "double ratio" refers to squaring the ratio</term> of their sounds. For all experiments show that the diameter of the base of the string which produces the Octave below against another string of equal length and tension is double the diameter of the base of that thinner string. From which it follows that the thick string contains four times the material of the smaller one, since cylinders of the same height are to each other as their bases, for the base of the thicker one is fourfold that of the thinner one, because the bases are in the squared ratio of their diameters.

Now, it must first be remarked that the equal tension of which I speak here must be understood as an equal force that stretches both strings, so that one does not confuse the equality of force with the equality of the strain <note>original: *violence*</note> suffered by the strings; because it is certain that the thicker string is not as strained by a weight of one pound <note>a unit of weight used here to represent a measure of force</note> as the smaller one is, and this difficulty requires a specific discussion.

Secondly, this speculation can serve for stringing all sorts of stringed instruments with strings of the same length but different thickness, by an equal force applied to each string: for example, the one whose base is sixteen times larger (or the diameter four times larger), when stretched with the weight of one pound, will be the Fifteenth, or the Double Octave <note>original: *Diſdiapaſon*</note> below the one whose base is one-sixteenth as large (or the diameter one-fourth as large). This is marvelous, because it seems that a string double in thickness should produce the Octave below, just as a string double in length does; and nevertheless, one must put four strings together and make only one of the four to produce the Octave below, whereas if one extended them in length, they would make the double Octave; thus one must compensate for the double space gained by redoubling the matter: but we will speak of this difficulty in another Proposition, for it suffices to know in this one that it is necessary to double the ratio of each interval of sounds...

to obtain the strings <note>original: *chordes*</note> that produce them, for which I provide the practical application in the third book of instruments, Proposition seven.

In the third place, beyond the experience of strings of every sort of material, one finds the same ratios between pieces of parchment so thin that they can be taken for simple surfaces, or for widths without depth. For a piece of parchment four times as wide, stretched by the same weight as one a quarter as wide of the same height, produces the Octave below. Now, the piece four times wider is only double in diameter when it is twisted into a round shape like a string. If one stretches metal strings in width, the one double in diameter will be found to be four times in width, like the parchment. And if one twists four strings together, they will produce the Octave with one of the four.

Now, even though this discourse is true for strings stretched on instruments, or in whatever other manner one might wish, it does not follow that other cylindrical bodies, or those of another shape, have the same ratio with sounds as strings do, as many have believed until now. This I show through very exact experiments that we have performed several times in the presence of excellent Geometers and Musicians, whose ears are very learned and delicate; and if anyone doubts it, I will show him the same experiments, which deserve a particular Proposition.

### PROPOSITION IX.

#### *To know if, two or more sounds being given, one can find the sounding cylinders that produce the said sounds: or if, the cylinders being given, one can know their sounds: where one will see many marvelous experiments.*

HAVING had several cylinders of different thicknesses <note>original: *grosseurs*</note> and lengths drawn from the same material through different holes of draw-plates <note>a "filiere" is a tool used to pull metal into wires of specific gauges</note>, and having first compared those differing in length and equal in thickness, we found that the one four times the length only produced the Minor Seventh <term>Septiesme mineure; a musical interval consisting of ten semitones</term>, which seemed to many to be only a whole tone, without there being almost any way to correct the imagination; because the same cylinder produces two or three different sounds at the same time, one of which is heard better from afar than from nearby, and the other is heard better from nearby than from afar, so that it seems to make a different sound when it is brought close to the ear than when it is far away.

Now, the two sounds they produce are most often different by a Fifth, or its octaves <note>original: *repliques*</note>, or by a Fourth, or an Octave and its repetitions, which brings such great difficulties to these experiments that unless one has a great love of the truth, it is very difficult to verify them. Be that as it may, I put here the most accurate ones that could be done or imagined, leaving aside the various phenomena encountered therein due to the different sounds each body makes at the same time; for I have always believed that one must particularly focus on the dominant sounds that are heard better and which appear stronger than the others. Two cylinders of the same thickness, whose lengths are in the ratio of forty lines to seventeen—that is to say, almost as five is to two—produce the Octave. Here it must be noted that I provide their lengths in lines, of which 144 compose the King’s foot <note>the *pied de Roy* was a pre-metric unit of measurement, approximately 32.48 cm</note>, because I used them, and they make

Two other cylinders, whose diameter is one line and a half, are in a ratio of 86 lines to 37 when they produce the **Octave**, which is to say that their lengths are nearly seven to three. Here it must be noted that I provide the lengths and the thicknesses of these cylinders so that one does not imagine there is an error in my experiments, even though cylinders of other thicknesses or lengths might, perhaps, have other ratios to produce the **Octave**, since the first ratio of five to two differs from this second one of seven to three, already showing something similar: so that it appears that all the different lengths and thicknesses maintain different ratios in their sizes to produce the **Octave** and the other intervals of sounds; and that the ratio of the length of the thickest cylinders approaches closer to that of harmonic intervals <note>Harmonic intervals refer to the standard ratios found in music theory, like 2:1 or 3:2.</note> than does the ratio of the thinnest ones.

Now, if the latter thickness of the two cylinders is kept while the length is at a ratio of two to one, they produce the **Triton** <note>The Triton is a restless, dissonant interval of three whole tones, also called the augmented fourth.</note> together: which happens similarly to the two cylinders where one is double in length and which have base diameters of two lines, and to several others of different thicknesses: so that this is almost the most certain thing I have observed in different lengths: namely, that a double length always produces the **Triton**, or the **false Fifth** <note>original: *fausse Quinte*; another name for the Triton.</note> below against the half-length: which is strange, considering that when the double length is only lengthened by one inch—that is, by a third of the smaller or a sixth part of the larger—it makes the sound descend as much as the three preceding inches did. For when they are equal in length, they produce a **unison**; three inches added to one of the two makes it descend to a **Triton**, and another inch being added makes it descend to the **Octave**, which is to say as much as the three preceding feet <note>Mersenne seems to use "feet" here to emphasize the scale of change, though the measurement was in inches.</note>, which one would never have guessed by reason alone; this is why one must place little trust in natural things if reason is not supported by experiments. Regarding this, it must be noted that the longest cylinder very often seems to rise a **Fourth** higher than the smaller one, even though it is a **Fifth** lower: <note>The words "ce qui est" are crossed out in the original.</note> ~~what is~~ this is so difficult to discern that it would not be possible to decide if reason did not aid the ear, as we experience with our cylinders made of pure **rosette** <note>A high-quality, refined grade of copper.</note> or pure red copper.

From this it happens that a cylinder four, five, or six times the length does not appear to descend to the Octave of its fraction, etc., even though its sound is much lower, because of a great multitude of sounds that it produces at the same time, and which blend together; the deepest of these is a thick **droning hum** <note>original: *bombus*; a Latin term for a buzzing or booming sound.</note> or noise that one hears when bringing it close to the ear, which is often at the Octave, or at the repetitions of the Octave of the higher sound it produces: so that by imagining this higher sound, one believes that it rises higher than the shorter cylinders. I leave aside a thousand phenomena that experiments reveal on this subject, in order to explain the ratio of sounds and the different thicknesses of cylinders of the same length, which are all half a foot long: but the diameter of the base of the largest is ten lines, that of the second is five lines, that of the third is 3 1/3 lines, that of the fourth is 2 1/2, and that of the fifth is nearly two.

But the fifth cylinder rises a **fifth** higher than the fourth, whereas it ought to descend lower, following the ratio of the preceding ones.

As for cylinders differing in thickness and length, it is very easy to proportion them such that they will make whatever sound one wishes; for if their lengths and their thicknesses are in the same ratio as the intervals of sounds, they will produce them: for example, if one desires the **Octave**, two cylinders of which one is double the other, as much in length as in height, will make a very accurate **Octave**, as experience teaches; for having had two cylinders cast, one a foot long and the other half a foot, I found that they made an **Octave** when the diameter of the base of the larger one was double the diameter of the smaller, regardless of how thick the cylinders were.

The same thing must be said of all the other intervals, so that two cylinders will make a **fifth** if the diameter of the base of the thicker one is <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A sesquialter ratio is 3:2, where one value is one and a half times the other.</note> to the diameter of the base of the smaller one, and if its height is similarly sesquialter to the other: and if one maintains the ratio of other intervals, as much in the length as in the thickness of the cylinders, or of all other kinds of bodies—square, triangular, etc.—they will always produce the sounds that one desires.

### COROLLARY.

I will not speak here of the proportion of organ pipes, because I provide specific discourses on them in the *Book on Organs*; nor of everything belonging to the bodies of wind instruments, insofar as I am making an entire book on them: so that it suffices to remark upon some phenomena of cylinders in the Proposition that follows, after having shown that one cannot establish anything certain in Music by the length of cylinders alone, as is easy to conclude from all our experiments.

But a cylinder of an inch and a half, or two inches, no longer produces any sound that can be judged. Here it must be noted that a cylinder four inches high, with a base diameter of ten lines <note>A "line" (ligne) is a historical French unit of measurement equal to 1/12 of an inch, or about 2.25 millimeters.</note>, still produces a sound one can judge, for it rises a **Fifth** higher than one of half a foot; so that the lengths of these two cylinders follow the ratio of the sounds, although we have not observed the same thing in the thinner ones: this shows that one must not be satisfied with a few experiments to establish a general truth, and that many must be performed across all sorts of volumes.

Now, although this thick cylinder four inches long sounds well enough to judge, it does not follow that one an inch long and four times thinner than the previous one can sound, for one sixteen times thinner and an inch and a half long no longer makes a sound that can be judged.

And all our experiments lead me to conclude that it must be at least two inches long to make a distinct sound, however thin and slender it may be: for if it is very thick, it will not ring; and whatever height it has, it will not ring unless it is at least four times the diameter of its base: this is why metal cubes ring no better than a stone of the same shape.

As for the uncertainty of sounds that comes from the excessive length of cylinders, it begins with those that are half a foot high and two lines in diameter, and continues in all other thinner ones, because they make certain trembling and confused noises, from which it is very difficult to catch the tone; the tone only begins to be distinct enough in cylinders half a foot high whose base diameter is four lines.

Let us now see why cylinders do not follow the ratio of strings, which are also cylinders, regarding which we must first note that they do not produce their sounds by the mere beating of the external air, as strings do, but by the trembling of the **internal air** <note>Mersenne believed that "internal air" trapped within the microscopic pores of solid objects was responsible for transmitting sound through the material.</note> which is within their pores, which is shaken by the shuddering of all the parts of the copper, as one perceives by touching the cylinders and the **Bells**, which are the same thing when ringing: and because the parts shudder differently, and consequently the internal air does not move uniformly in all parts, it happens that one hears several different sounds from the same body, depending on the places where it is struck, or according to the different shudders of the various parts of the resonant body. From this it comes that strings, and all other sorts of bodies, make three or four different sounds at the same time which accord together, as I remark in the fourth book on **Stringed Instruments**, and elsewhere: which is worthy of very great consideration, for it seems that the harmony of chords is imprinted in the nature of each thing, which employs itself to praise its **Author** <note>The "Author" refers to God, reflecting Mersenne's view of science as a way to understand the divine order of creation.</note> as soon as it is touched: for all sonorous bodies normally produce the **Octave**, the **Fifth**, the **Fourth**, and the **Thirds**; which appears particularly in the largest bodies: for example, when one strikes the blade of a Damascus sword, or some fairly wide vessel made in the fashion of a lamp, whose edges are very thin, or when one gently touches one of the thick strings of the **Viol** with the bow, one hears all these consonances at the same time, because the internal air of these bodies trembles in one part five, four, three, and two times, while it trembles only once in the others.

## COROLLARY I.

I have not been able to find certain proportions between square plates, or parallelograms, and their sounds: which is why I do not speak of them in the Proposition; although I have had some cast from different types of tin, and have experimented with those made of iron. I have nonetheless often remarked that a square plate of iron or fine tin, when it is eight times the size <note>original: "octuple"</note> of another, descends almost to the **Octave**: which similarly happens to a plate eight times smaller in width and of equal height. But a plate double in height with equal width only descends by a **Major Third**. One can also compare these plates according to their different thicknesses; which should, it seems, correspond to the different thicknesses of cylinders. I also leave aside the comparison of cubes, whether hollow or solid, because they do not produce sounds that can be judged or that are suitable for harmony, as I have experienced with solid and hollow cubes of Cornish tin: although if one made cubic anvils of different sizes, it is likely that the blows of heavy hammers could be so great that they would make them resonate; and that the anvil eight times larger would descend to the **Octave**, since this ratio succeeds in all other bodies, whether solid or hollow.

## COROLLARY II.

Since all bodies that create harmonic intervals are in a triple ratio <note>In 17th-century mathematics, a "triple ratio" (raison triplée) refers to a cubic ratio ($x^3$), matching the relationship between a three-dimensional object's volume and its linear dimensions.</note> of their simple ratios, and regarding these bodies, one can say that the ratio of the **Octave** is eight to one, or quadruple because of their surfaces which are in a double ratio <note>A "double ratio" (raison doublée) refers to a squared ratio ($x^2$).</note> of the terms of the harmonic interval—as I remark in the 10th Proposition of the *Book of Consonances*—it is reasonable to provide a table here containing all these ratios. This is so it may serve those who wish to make wooden **Regals** <note>A Regal is a small, portable pipe organ that uses reeds to produce sound.</note>, or other instruments made of cylinders, or of parallelepipeds <note>A three-dimensional solid with six parallelogram faces, such as a rectangular block.</note>, or of other material, to find all their consonances and other just intervals. This will assist in making the **claque-bois** <note>Literally "clack-wood," an early French term for a xylophone or percussion instrument made of wooden bars.</note>, which I discuss in the 26th Proposition of the third book of instruments. This in no way prevents the true ratio of the **Diapason** <note>original: "Diapaſon." This is the Greek musical term for the Octave.</note> from always being two to one, since it occurs whenever one body strikes the air only once while the other strikes it twice, whether the body striking it once is shorter and thinner, or longer and thicker. ### COROLLARY III.

The numbers in the first column all have only unity for their difference; but the number two is the difference between the differences of the numbers in the second column: for example, the difference from one to four is three, and five is the difference from four to nine; now, the difference from three to five is two, and so on for the others. The difference of the differences of the numbers in the third column is 6: for example, the difference from 1 to 8 is 7, and that from 8 to 27 is 19; now, 12 is the difference from 7 to 19. Similarly, from 27 to 64 there is 37, which surpasses 19 by 18, which is 6 greater than 12. Just as the difference from 64 to 125 is 61, which surpasses the preceding difference of 37 by 24, which is 6 greater than 18. I leave aside a thousand other considerations that one can make regarding these numbers, because they do not serve harmony <note>Here, "harmony" refers to the science of music and sound.</note>, although they have great properties in <term>algebra</term> and elsewhere.

Chinese wood <note>original: "Le bois de la Chine," likely referring to a dense tropical hardwood like rosewood or padauk</note> is in unison with the Octave, but it has a much clearer and more resonant sound, so much so that it is almost like that of metal: ebony is in unison with hornbeam, just as beech and pear are in unison with willow. This clearly shows that it is not possible to distinguish woods solely by their sounds; for although there may be some small differences between the aforementioned unisons, and the sound of some may be more or less clear, soft, dry, etc., nevertheless the ear is not capable of noticing it sufficiently to judge the difference between woods by their sounds alone.

Here, it must first be noted that I used <term>parallelepipeds</term> <note>These are six-sided solid figures where every face is a parallelogram, essentially rectangular blocks or prisms.</note> of the same length and thickness, which were all very dry: the length of which is five inches and seven lines, and the side is half an inch <note>In the pre-metric French system, a "line" was 1/12th of an inch. As for the other woods, they descend lower than the fir in the following manner.

Alder, willow, and wild cherry by a semitone.
Hornbeam, ebony, oak, and beech by a <term>Minor Third</term>.
Sycamore and maple by a <term>Major Third</term>.
Walnut by a <term>Fourth</term>.
Pear and service tree <note>original: "cormier," the wood of the Sorb tree, known for its hardness.</note> by a <term>Fifth</term>.

Resonant tin and fine tin rise higher by a whole tone than iron, with which common tin is in unison: lead makes no sound that can be judged. Now, I set the sounds of these cylinders in musical notes for the benefit of Practitioners.
