### COROLLARY I.

One can see in the nineteenth Proposition of the third book on Instruments the difference found between the sounds of the tin plates reported there and those of the preceding cylinders; and similarly between the sounds of bells made of the same metal, of which I speak in the fourteenth and fifteenth Propositions of the Book of Bells: where one will find several differences showing that bells of different metals reduced to cylinders do not have the same sound, and that a lead bell makes a sound, even though it makes none when it is cylindrical in shape.

### COROLLARY II.

After having hardened the iron and steel cylinders with a very hard and strong <term>temper</term> <note>the process of heating and then rapidly cooling metal to change its physical properties, such as hardness or elasticity</note>, I was unable to notice any difference between the sounds of the tempered cylinders and those that were not, even though the latter were much softer and more mild; and the steel cylinder, which it seemed ought to rise higher and make a sharper sound than the iron, was found almost in <term>unison</term>, being only lower by a <term>comma</term> or a <term>diesis</term> <note>these are very small musical intervals; a comma is roughly 1/9th of a whole tone, and a diesis is a small interval used in ancient Greek tuning systems</note> than the iron.

Whence it must be concluded that sounds cannot serve much for the knowledge of the different qualities of bodies, because they do not change perceptibly enough to make them distinguishable; for so great a hardness as that of tempered steel, so different from common iron, yields nothing perceptible regarding their sounds, and so many woods of different natures are in unison with one another. This is why, instead of being astonished by the meeting of two men whose vocal tones are so similar that they cannot be distinguished, one must rather admire that so few such cases occur. We should attribute this rarity and its cause—founded in the different configuration of the organs—to the providence of God, who wished to remove the cause of many quarrels and other troublesome accidents that could arise from the resemblance of voice and speech; even though we have the eye and other senses to discern men and other bodies from one another by qualities other than their sounds.

## PROPOSITION XII.

->*Determine the weight of all the species of wood and metals that served in the previous experiments.*<-

Now, I have compared them to a fir cylinder equal in size, by means of which one will know the ratio of the weights of each species of our woods reduced to cylinders equal to the weights of the metal cylinders, just as one knows the ratio of their sounds, if one understands the preceding Propositions.

From this, one must not conclude the true ratio of the weight of these metals, because some fill the mold or the sand better than others, and consequently they vary in thickness, even though the eye does not perceive it; for example, lead is thicker than copper because it melts better. Furthermore, the copper has been drawn through a <term>drawplate</term> <note>a tool used to reduce the diameter of wire or rods</note>, the iron has been hammered, and the other metals have been cast. From this, it happens that their natural weights cannot be sufficiently known and determined; so it is necessary to have recourse to water, in which being weighed, after having weighed them in the air, they each show their exact weight, as I remark elsewhere <note>this refers to hydrostatic weighing, a method for determining density pioneered by Archimedes</note>.

The scales of Monsieur Petit, Engineer <note>Pierre Petit (1594–1677), a prominent French mathematician and physicist who collaborated with Mersenne and Pascal</note>, which I used to weigh the preceding bodies, are so accurate that the sixth part of a grain easily tips them; so that those who wish to perform experiments regarding weights can have recourse to them, in order to have everything that can be desired on this subject.

### PROPOSITION XIII.

*One can determine the length of strings and the difference of their sounds by the difference of weights suspended from said strings; and the difference of weights suspended from the strings by the difference of sounds and the length of the strings.*

This Proposition can serve to find the weight if one is given the sound and the length of the string, and to find the sound or the length of the string if one is given the weight. Consequently, if one knows the sound or the noise of a cannon, of thunder, of the wind, of earthquakes, of a drum, of a <term>gnat</term> <note>original: "moucheron"; Mersenne was fascinated by the high-pitched "buzz" of insects and sought to calculate their wing-beat frequency</note>, of organs, of bells, etc., one will know what weight is required to create another sound or noise equal to the sound given by all sorts of bodies by means of the tension of strings.

Similarly, if the weight is given, one will know how low or high the sound is; and what sound can be made by the weight of an <term>écu</term> <note>a French crown coin</note>, of a grain, of a <term>mite</term> <note>original: "ciron"; then considered the smallest possible living creature</note>, or of a weight that is as much smaller than a mite as a mite is smaller than a pound or the weight of the entire earth. Even though the difference in sounds coming from imperceptible weights may not be audible, I am speaking here of the <term>ratio</term> <note>original: "raison"; here meaning the mathematical relationship or proportion</note> which follows the truth of proportions; but one must always suppose that the weight stretches the string strongly enough to make it sound.

Now, this Proposition has two parts; but because the second is the converse of the first, the same proof will serve for both. I say, then, that the ratio of each musical interval, when <term>doubled</term> <note>In 17th-century mathematics, to "double a ratio" meant to square it (multiply it by itself). For example, doubling the ratio of 2:1 results in 4:1.</note>, gives the weight by which the string, being stretched, produces the desired sound. I shall explain this with examples.

Suppose one wishes to know what weight should be used to make a string rise to the Octave. One must first know its tension—that is, by what weight it is stretched when it produces the sound upon which the others are tuned. Let us suppose it produces the note <term>C</term> <note>original: "l’vt de C fa, vt"; a reference to the note C in the Guidonian system of solfège</note>. I say that one will know the weight necessary to make it rise to the Octave if one knows the weight that brings it to that C. For if we suppose the weight to be four pounds, it will require sixteen pounds to raise the same string to the Octave, because the ratio of the Octave, which is two to one, produces a quadruple ratio when doubled. As one sees in these two double ratios, $^2/_1$, $^2/_1$, which must be multiplied in this manner: two times two makes four (for to multiply a ratio, one must multiply the greater and the lesser terms by themselves) and one times one is one. Now $^4/_1$ is the doubled ratio of $^2/_1$, and consequently 4 and 1 are in a quadruple ratio. This shows that the weight which puts the string at the Octave below must be one-fourth of the other weight.

One will similarly find the weight that must be added to the four pounds (which give the first sound to the string) to produce the Fifth, the Fourth, the Whole Tone, and the other intervals. For if one multiplies the ratio of the Fifth, which is three to two, one will have the "double sesquiquartal" ratio, since three times three is nine, and two times two is four. Now nine and four are in a double sesquiquartal ratio, for nine contains four twice, and 1/4 of four. Conse-

Consequently, if instead of four pounds one suspends a new weight from the string which is in a <term>double sesquiquarter ratio</term> <note>original: "raison double sesquiquarte"; a ratio of 9:4 (or $2 \frac{1}{4}$ to 1)</note> to four, it will produce a Fifth higher. But one must use the rule of proportion to find this weight, and for this purpose, one must find the two radical numbers of the double sesquiquarter ratio, or two numbers that contain this ratio; now, nine and four are its radical numbers, although one could use eighteen and eight, thirty-six and sixteen, and all others that have the same ratio. Secondly, one must arrange the terms in this way: if four gives the proposed sound, which is as four, what will nine give? One finds the sound nine. Now, there was no need to use this rule here because the numbers of this ratio show both the weight and the sound.

I take, therefore, six pounds for the first sound of the string, which will serve to determine the sounds and the weights; if one wishes then to know the double sesquiquarter weight of six, one must say: if four gives nine, how much will six give? One will have thirteen and a half pounds, which will make the string rise to the Fifth, for all weights have a relationship to the first, and are as much greater or smaller as the first is heavier or lighter. One must also use this rule for the other sounds and the other weights. Now, the following table contains the weights that make the string rise through all the harmonic intervals of the Octave, according to the experience I have had of it in the presence of many people. The weight of six pounds is the foundation, insofar as I have used it; this does not prevent one from taking whatever other weight one wishes to mark the unison of the string, or the first sound to which the others are compared.

The first number of the first column, namely six, shows the weight by which the strings are set to unison; the one that follows, namely twenty-four, signifies that the weight which makes the Octave above is four times six. The other numbers show the weights that make each harmonic interval; and the numbers of the third column signify the <term>ratios</term> <note>original: "raisons"</note> of each interval, whose name is seen in the second column.

<note>The table above contains several printing or calculation errors in the original, notably the repetition of Roman numerals (XXIX for XXXIX) and inconsistent digit counts in the large values. These numbers represent the weight in pounds required to reach the specified number of octaves above a base note.</note>

It must nevertheless be noted that experiments cannot be conducted so precisely on strings that something is not lacking, especially since they stretch when they are tensioned with a greater weight. From this, it follows that a quadruple weight <note>original: "poids quadruple"</note> does not make the string rise to the exact **Octave** unless one adds a sixteenth part of that quadruple weight; for example, four ounces added to four pounds. Likewise, a weight in a **double sesquiquartal** ratio <note>A ratio of 9/4 or 2.25. In Mersenne's terminology, "double sesquiquarte" refers to the ratio of weights needed for certain intervals.</note> does not make it rise to the **Fifth**, unless one adds a nineteenth part. For example, instead of two pounds and six ounces (which is the double sesquiquartal ratio of one pound), one must add two pounds and eight ounces—that is, two ounces more, which constitutes the nineteenth part of two pounds and six ounces.
<margin>1/380 parts.</margin>
<margin>Now 1/19 exceeds 1/20 by [some] parts.</margin>

One can continue this same progression until one has found a number that corresponds to the weight of the solidity of the **Firmament** <note>The "Firmament" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars in the traditional geocentric model of the universe.</note>. If one wishes to know what sound and what **Octave** the string would produce if the weight of such a Globe were suspended from it, assuming that each cubic foot of the Globe weighs one hundred pounds, or as much as is required.

Now, although I have adapted this discourse to **Octaves**, one can also take the **Fifths**, the **Fourths**, the **Diesis**, the **Comma**, and all the other intervals for which I have given the weights and ratios in the other table. For one must only continue the double ratio, the sesquiquartal <note>original: "sesquiquarte"; the ratio 5:4</note>, the **superbipartient seven** <note>original: "sur sept partissant neuf"; the ratio 9:7</note>, or the others I have marked, to find the weights that produce the **Fifth** or the **Fourth**, double, triple, and hundredfold, etc., unto infinity. One can also find the weights necessary to produce two, three, or four **Commas** or **Diesis**, etc. Consequently, one can know how many **Diesis**, **Tones**, etc., the weight of the earth (or any other weight larger or smaller) will create by tensioning the string.

But if one wishes to find how much one must diminish a weight of six pounds to make the string descend by an **Octave**, or by any other lower interval, one must use the same progression by **fractions** <term>fractions: original "nombres rompus," literally "broken numbers"</term>, which will always signify a smaller part of six pounds, and consequently a lesser weight; for the more the fractions are increased, the more they diminish the whole number they divide, as I have shown in the book *The Truth of the Sciences*, in the second chapter of **Theoretical Arithmetic**, and in the third book, chapter 2.

One will know the sound that a string would make when stretched with an ounce, a dram, or some other small weight, assuming nonetheless that these small weights stretch it strongly enough to make it sound; consequently, if one knows the weight of a fly, or of a mite <note>The "ciron" (mite) was a common 17th-century reference for the smallest visible living creature, often used in philosophical debates about infinite divisibility.</note>, one could say what sound it would make being attached to a string. But there is no need to draw up a table of these small weights, for experience shows that an ounce, and even a pound, is not heavy enough to make the aforementioned string sound when it is already stretched with six pounds.

Nevertheless, if one proportioned the string to the weight, and if one could find a string that had the same ratio to the fly or the mite as the string I used had to the weight of six pounds, the mite would produce a sound; but it would have to be as slender as the legs of a fly, or those of a mite, whose hearing one would need to possess to perceive such weak sounds. For if it has ears, it can hear the noise it makes while walking as clearly as we hear the noise we make; and perhaps it hears the **consonances** and **dissonances** that occur within the pores of the body when the blood and other humors move and alter from moment to moment by a continual combat, or by the mixing or encounters that occur within the parts of the body where small animals are found.

But this consideration is beyond our practical use, though it may serve to remind us that God has imprinted a light in our understandings that surpasses all kinds of sensations and experiences, which we can use to proceed to infinity. For if one can state the ratio of a mite's foot to the body of the same mite, one will know what sound it would make being suspended from a string as slender as its foot; and that a weight four times less than the weight of a mite suspended from the same string would produce the **Octave** below, just as a weight four times that of the mite would produce the **Octave** above.

And one does not know if there are not yet other animals within the mite, which are as small in its regard as it is in ours: this ought to prevent the hasty judgment of those who believe that everything they do not see, or which they cannot perceive, does not exist, or cannot be. I leave aside a thousand other things that could be proposed in order to conclude this discourse, which proves that one can know the length of the string by the weight, as seen in the two preceding tables; for example, the weight of thirteen pounds and <gloss>1/2</gloss> being given, one knows that the string set to **Unison** with the one that has six pounds suspended must be shorter by a third—that is to say, of two strings that make a **Unison**, each being three feet long, one must be shortened by one foot to make the **Fifth** above, which it would make while remaining the same length as the first if it were stretched with thirteen <gloss>1/2</gloss> pounds <note>Mersenne is applying the law that pitch is proportional to the square root of the tension. Since 6 pounds multiplied by 9/4 equals 13.5 pounds, his math is perfectly consistent.</note>: one must conclude the same thing for other intervals.

## NOTICE.

I have explained many things regarding the movement, the tension, and the force of strings from the sixteenth Proposition of the first book on Instruments until the end; from the sixth until the twentieth of the third book; and in the eleventh Prop. of the fourth book, which could have been inserted here in the form of Corollaries. For example: the manner in which the deaf can tune stringed instruments using the **tablature for the deaf** <note>tablature: a form of musical notation showing instrument fingering rather than pitches. Mersenne suggests a visual or tactile method for those who cannot hear.</note>; and the method for counting the number of vibrations <note>original: "tours & retours" (turns and returns)</note> of their strings, along with several other Propositions found in the aforementioned books; this is why I do not repeat them here.

## COROLLARY.

If one could find instruments that multiply the force of sounds in the same proportion that telescopes <note>original: "lunettes de longue veuë" (long-view glasses)</note> multiply the size of visible objects, one would hear the sound made by mites <note>original: "cirons"</note> and other small animals as they walk, and a thousand other kinds of tiny noises that occur day and night in all living bodies, and within ourselves. Just as one sees the eyes and feet of mites, the hair and feet of mites or cheese-worms, and the little "serpents" or worms found in vinegar <note>vinegar eels: tiny nematodes (Turbatrix aceti) that live in unfiltered vinegar, a popular subject for early microscopists.</note> by means of small magnifying glasses—which would enlarge objects even more if their glass had the **Hyperbolic** <term>Hyperbolic: A non-spherical lens shape that mathematicians of the time believed would eliminate optical distortion (aberration).</term> figure necessary to perfect the science of **Dioptrics** <term>Dioptrics: The study of the refraction of light through lenses.</term>.

## PROPOSITION XIV.

*To determine why a greater weight, or a greater force, is required to bring a string of double length to **unison**, than to bring a string of double thickness to the same **unison**: and whether the **unison** is a certain testimony of the equal tension of all types of strings.*

I assume the experiment which shows that a quadruple weight <note>i.e., four times the weight</note> brings a string of double length to the **unison** <term>unison: two sounds of the exact same pitch.</term> of a sub-double string <note>a string half as long</note>, and that a double weight brings a string of double thickness to the same **unison**. That is to say, when four pounds are attached to the end of a string two feet long, it produces the same sound as a string one foot long of the same thickness to which one pound is attached; and that a string one foot long, but double in thickness, to which a weight of two pounds is attached, also produces the same sound. From this, one can conclude the sounds produced by all kinds of weights compared to all kinds of lengths and thicknesses of strings, following the ratios we have explained elsewhere.

Now, a quadruple weight is necessary to bring the string of double length to **unison**, because the string of double length has two things that must be compensated for: namely, the double length and the double amount of air that is struck. Since a double weight is needed to compensate for the double air, and then another double weight to compensate for the double length, it follows that a quadruple weight is required for the compensation of both.

# Third Book

But it is only the thickness of the **string** <note>original: "chorde"</note> that must be compensated for in one that is simply double in thickness; this is why one must only double the force. From this, it appears that a great force is required to overcome the extension or length by tension. Now, the string that is double in thickness has no other extension than the <term>sub-double</term> <note>Meaning half the length.</note>; consequently, no force is needed to compensate for its extension by tension. And although one might say that its double thickness requires a double weight, and that the air surrounding it—which it strikes—must also be overcome by another weight, nevertheless, the **concave** of the air struck by the string double in length is larger than the concave of the air struck by the one double in thickness. For these two concaves of air form concave cylinders, just as the strings form solid cylinders, which strike the concave surface of the air with their convex surfaces.

Now, the bases and the heights of equal cylinders are reciprocal; and cylinders whose bases and heights are reciprocal are equal, according to the fifteenth Proposition of the 12th [Book] <note>Mersenne is referring to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book XII, which deals with the volumes of cylinders and cones.</note>. Consequently, the concave of the air struck by the string double in thickness is not equal to the concave of the air struck by the string double in length, since the diameter of the cylinder double in thickness is not double the diameter of the cylinder double in length; for the surfaces of cylinders are as the diameters of their bases. Nevertheless, it seems one must conclude that the struck air should only be considered according to the length of the axis, and not according to the thickness of the cylinder—which is to be understood when it is not enclosed in a pipe and is free, as when it is struck by a string. However, I shall speak again of this difficulty at the end of this Proposition. This is why I come to the second part, which speaks of the **equal tension** of strings, which I shall treat through reason and experiments. It seems first, then, that **unison** gives us an equal tension only when the stretched strings are equal in material, length, and thickness; for if the string is longer or thicker, it must be stretched more strongly than the shorter or thinner one to make a unison with it. This occurs similarly in the human voice: for the **Bass** <note>original: "Baſſe"</note> must exert himself more to sing in unison with the **Soprano** <note>original: "Superius"</note> than to sing in unison with another Bass.

Now, experience shows that the string double in length, pulled by four forces, is much more tense than the sub-double pulled by two forces; for the middle of the former is harder and bends with more difficulty than the middle of the latter. Nevertheless, the former should bend more easily and be softer if the string double in length had only an equal tension.

As for the string double in thickness, I find more difficulty there; for experience does not show so evidently whether it is equally or unequally stretched by two forces when the sub-double in thickness is stretched by one force. Although it seems one must conclude in favor of equal tension, not only because they are in unison, but because the one double in thickness resists the force doubly, so that unison shows equal tension—not only between strings equal in all things, but also between strings unequal in thickness, provided they are equal in length.

Furthermore, one can consider cylinders of wood not only when they are cut with the <term>straight grain</term> <note>original: "droit-fil"; refers to wood cut parallel to the longitudinal fibers</note>, but also when they are carved across and horizontally, to see how much stronger the former are than the latter, whether they are placed perpendicular or parallel to the horizon. Now, cylinders can be carved in several ways: for one can cut the wood following the diameters of the circles that appear on the cross-section of the wood, or across the diameters by cutting the circles into segments; this is easily imagined by visualizing the surface of a cut tree trunk, where the circles show the new wood the tree produces each year—for some believe the tree has as many circles as it has years. One must also see if wood cut horizontally has parts that are weaker as their circles move further from the center of the tree and closer to the part called the <term>sapwood</term> <note>original: "aubie"; the softer, living outer layer of a tree trunk</note>, which is the weakest and softest of all. Now, these circles and their diameters do not appear equally on all kinds of trees, which is why one would have to choose species of wood that have more distinct and manifest circles, to see if the cylinder is stronger when it is cut along the length of the diameters or across the diameters; and whether the northern side is weaker or stronger than the southern side, and by how much one is stronger than the other.

If one observes all these particulars, one will find the ratio between the strength of upright wood and cross-grain wood; and after having performed the experiment on walnut, the <term>service tree</term> <note>original: "cormier"; a very hard wood traditionally used for tool handles and machinery parts</note>, and other species of wood, one will see if the strengths of fir or oak wood, taken with the grain or at an angle, maintain the same ratio as other species of wood. I have found through experience that fir wood of the same size, when straight-grained, carries twenty times as much or more than when it is cross-grained. Now, before finishing this Proposition, it is not out of place to consider the force of presses, even though it is much weaker than the force of hammer blows and weights falling from above: for a man is not strong enough to crush and flatten an iron cylinder the thickness of two or three <term>lines</term> <note>A "line" (ligne) is an old unit of measurement, about 2.25mm</note> with the strongest vises used by locksmiths, even though they can flatten the same cylinder with a single hammer blow. But the force of an artillery shot is even greater than hammer blows: to which one can relate the force of thunder and of mines that throw towers to the ground and cause mountains to leap and burst; for these terrifying forces come from the same cause as the force of hammer blows—namely, from the movement and pressure of the air, of which the greatest speed is the cause of the greatest force.

### COROLLARY I. ###

...of the press, for which I suppose the handle is two feet long from the center of the screw to the point where the hand is applied, so that each turn it makes contains twenty-four inches <note>Mersenne’s calculation here is unusual; for a 2-foot (24-inch) handle, a full rotation would normally be about 150 inches. He may be calculating based on a specific mechanical ratio or a partial turn.</note>; if the hand has the strength of two hundred pounds, it will press as strongly on what is beneath it as if it were loaded with a weight of four thousand four hundred pounds. Now, the force of the press will be even greater as its handle is made longer; for example, if it is seven feet long, the press will have the force of fifty-two thousand eight hundred pounds: for the <term>semi-diameter</term> <note>the radius</note> being seven feet, it makes twenty-two feet <note>original: "vingt-deux pieds"; Mersenne arrives at this by multiplying the 7-foot radius by 22/7 (an approximation of Pi), though this technically describes only half the circumference.</note>, that is to say two hundred sixty-four inches for each turn. Now, two hundred sixty-four multiplied by two hundred gives fifty-two thousand eight hundred, and shows that one man having the strength of two hundred pounds, by himself, exerts as much violence on what is under the press as two hundred sixty-four men would do without the press: for if each man has two hundred pounds of strength, two hundred sixty-four will have as much pressing force as fifty-two thousand eight hundred.

One can also by this same means determine the force of the <term>brace</term> <note>original: "vieil brequin," a crank-shaped handle used for drilling</note>, of bits, and of other instruments used for piercing, for they pierce all the more easily as the circuit of their handles is greater: for example, if the iron of the brace or the <term>auger</term> <note>original: "terriere," a large wood-boring tool</note> is one <term>line</term> <note>original: "ligne," a historical unit of measurement equal to 1/12th of an inch</note> wide, and its handle makes two feet at each turn, that is to say two hundred eighty-eight lines, one man alone, by means of the brace, will do as much as two hundred eighty-eight men who do not use this instrument.

But the reason for the strength of this instrument, and of several others, can be drawn from the *Treatise on Mechanics* which is at the end of this book.

### COROLLARY II. ###

If one remembers the ratio according to which weights fall toward the center of the earth, of which we spoke in the first Proposition of the second book: and that their effects must be all the greater as they move faster, it is easy to conclude from what height they must fall to produce the desired effect: for example, since the weight having fallen from 4 feet high has only one degree of speed at the first foot; it has three at the end of the fourth foot, because it covers three times as much ground, and consequently it goes three times as fast at the second moment of its fall as at the first, and five times as fast at the third as at the said first; this is why it must break a string five times stronger by its fall of 9 feet than by that of one foot, and a string three times stronger falling from four feet than by falling only one foot high. This can be applied to piles that one drives into the ground, and to all resistances that can be overcome. But I have explained these speeds so clearly and in so many ways in the second book, that it is not appropriate to say anything else of it here: especially since I touched upon this force of weights in the fifth Proposition of the said book, which shows several uses that can be drawn from the speed of falls.

# PROPOSITION XVI.

->*The gravity of sounds is greater as the bodies from which they come are less brittle, and as their parts are better bound and united to one another, provided there is no other obstacle. Wherein many things are seen concerning the Principles of Chemistry.*<-
<note>In 17th-century acoustics, "gravity" refers to the lowness or depth of a pitch, while "acuteness" refers to high pitch.</note>

**E**xperience shows the truth of this Proposition in all kinds of bodies; for dry wood, which has lost its moisture, sounds higher than that which is green; and those who have dry hands make a more ringing noise by striking them against one another than those who have damp hands. Gold, silver, lead, and mercury render a graver and duller sound than iron, copper, or bell metal, because the parts of gold, silver, and lead are better united than the parts of other metals, by reason of the great quantity of quicksilver <note>original: "vif argent," or mercury</note> found in the former, and the small amount encountered in the latter. Some believe that the gravity of sound depends on the quantity of mercury found in sounding bodies; this is something Chemists should consider, in order to know why one body sounds higher than another, and whether this proceeds from the greater quantity of fixed or volatile salt, of sulfur, or of mercury found in the body, or from the multitude of pores and the different particles of air mixed within the body. This same speculation will serve to find the source of the hardness and weight of each body, and to know what makes stones, metal, or wood more brittle, more friable, and more "sour" <note>Mersenne uses "aigres" (sour/bitter) here to describe a quality of metal that is brittle or prone to cracking</note> than others.

Some hold that metal which has a greater quantity of stony sulfur, such as iron and copper, has a sharper sound, and consequently that gold renders a graver and duller sound than other metals because it has no stony sulfur except in potency. From this it follows that the more quicksilver a metal has, and the less stony or fixed sulfur, the heavier it is; from which they conclude that brass <note>original: "airain"</note> has a sharper sound than copper, inasmuch as one mixes two parts of calamine <note>a zinc ore used in the production of brass</note> with three parts of red copper to make yellow brass <note>original: "leton"</note>; which calamine has a quantity of stony sulfur, which it adds to that of the copper, which is called pure copper, or "rosette" <note>refined copper, often named for the rose-like shape it took during cooling</note>.

It is therefore necessary to see, according to these Principles, if each metal has a sound that is sharper the more sulfur it contains, and if the gravity of sounds follows the same ratio as the quicksilver and the weight they contain. But to understand this reasoning, which is drawn from the Principles of Chemistry, one must suppose that every compound <note>original: "mixte"</note> is composed of three Principles, which are called salt, sulfur, and mercury, to which one may add water and earth to have five Principles. Of these, water or "phlegm" is the first, inasmuch as it is the most volatile and consequently least internal to the compound. The second is called spirit, inasmuch as it is the most penetrating and most volatile, and is recognized by its acidity. The third is sulfur, or oil, which is more fixed than the two preceding ones, but more volatile than the two others; it is always flammable, unless it be fixed and inseparably united with all the other elements by a long depuration and "coction" <note>a term for the "cooking" or maturation process in alchemy</note> in the composition of the compound, as it is in gold. The fourth...

# Of the movements and the sound of strings.

The fourth Principle is salt, which is caustic and more fixed <note>In early chemistry, "fixed" refers to a substance's ability to resist the heat of fire without evaporating or changing.</note> than the three preceding ones. The fifth is earth, whose nature is to be dry. Chemists say that water, or "phlegm," is neither hot nor cold, and that it is susceptible to these two qualities depending on whether the air in which it is found is hot or cold.

To this they add that water is always humid, heavier than earth, and lighter than spirit or salt. Sulfur, which produces high-pitched <note>original: "aigus"</note> sounds, is always hot by its nature and the lightest of all the elements; it is the cause of the diversity of odors and colors in mixed bodies, particularly when it is fixed. And depending on whether it is fixed or volatile, perfect or imperfect, transparent or opaque, it forms the perfect or imperfect metals, precious stones, or other mixtures. It appears in the form of oil in plants, and in the form of fat in animals. Finally, the spirit of life, the radical moisture <note>The "radical moisture" was believed to be the fundamental fluid that maintained life and prevented the body from drying out.</note>, and the balsam of nature—which is found in minerals, vegetables, and animals—is attached to this sulfur. This is why their nature is more or less vigorous and hard according to the nature, quality, and excellence of the sulfur they contain; and when it is separated from them, mixed bodies decay, metals lose their malleability, precious stones their luster, plants their growth, and animals their life. From this one can conclude that the highest-pitched sound comes from the same Principle as the primary vigor of each thing.

Salt is hot, the heaviest, the least porous, and the most compact of all the other Principles. Now, there are three kinds of salts: namely, mineral, vegetable, and animal. The first appears in the form of vitriol and alum; the second in the form of alkali; and the third in the form of sea salt—each of which is fixed, volatile, or common. The first is analogous to sea salt; the second to sal ammoniac <note>original: "sel harmoniac," ammonium chloride.</note>; and the third to saltpeter. These three salts provide the various flavors, the freezing points, and the solidity of bodies; and when they are separated from bodies, fixed salt takes a square shape, saltpeter takes that of a cone, and sal ammoniac that of filaments. Spirit is a liquid body that is called mercury in minerals, and "subtle moisture" in plants and animals. In all bodies, it differs only by the mixture of oily or salty elements, for which it serves as matter and nourishment; but it is not fluid in bodies unless it dominates them, for it is held in check by sulfur and salt. It gives transparency and weight to bodies and makes them lucid.

Now, when these three Principles—namely salt, sulfur, and mercury—are joined inseparably after having rejected water and earth (which is the driest of all the other Principles and the lightest, except for oil, and is neither hot nor cold except by accident), a universal medicine is formed, which they call a Panacea, inasmuch as when it is mixed with purgatives or astringents, it increases their virtues.

They believe that Aristotle knew these three Principles when he spoke of celestial heat, the vital Principle, the spirit, and the essence of each thing; and that Plato called them "seminary virtue" <note>A term referring to the creative power or "seed" within matter.</note>; some call them the simple Principles of the seed. Paracelsus calls them *the soul of the world, balsam, mummy, star, quintessence, elixir, fifth element, crystalline matter, radical or primigenial moisture, vital sulfur, prime matter, heat, melissa, etc.* Those who call themselves Kabbalists have named salt the *prime matter*, which is unctuous, glutinous, tenacious, fixed, and permanent: the very pure salt made of earth and water, the substantial point that spreads through all parts of the substance, like the

The third Principle, namely **mercury**, is called the *middle Principle*, *ethereal body*, or *body-spirit* and *spirit-body*, which unites matter and form: it is the *heaven* and the *influence* of the Chemists, which binds and unites superior things with inferior ones. But many deny that these Principles are the excrements of the useful ones, insofar as phlegm is just as much attached to salt as to spirit, and that earth is a Principle of composition just like salt. **Soot** is also not useless, for it contains a little phlegm, more spirit, a little oil, much salt (but volatile), and a quantity of earth (but very light); so that soot can be resolved into all these Principles. ## PROPOSITION XVII.

->*The density and rarity of bodies is, it seems, the cause that the sounds they produce are different regarding the low and the high: here it is spoken of the Principles of Chemistry, and of those of the hardness and heaviness of bodies.*<-

Density of bodies is understood in two ways: for it can signify the thickness of bodies, as when we say a piece of wood or iron is half a foot thick; secondly, it signifies a greater multitude of parts in the same place, which makes a body more compact and compressed: and it is in this meaning that this Proposition must be understood, a dense body being nothing other than that which has much matter in little space, just as a "rare" <note>In this context, 'rare' refers to 'rarefied'—the opposite of dense.</note> body is that which has little matter and few parts in much space; for example, grains of incense and benzoin <note>Benzoin is a balsamic resin obtained from the bark of several species of trees, historically used in perfumes and medicine.</note>, or other aromatics, are dense before they burn, for they occupy very little space: but when they burn and are converted into smoke, they have little matter in much space: for a few grains of incense can fill a room of four toises <note>A 'toise' is an old French unit of length, approximately 6.4 feet or 1.95 meters.</note> square, so that one can say a grain of incense occupies a place a thousand times larger when it is in smoke than when it is not burning.

We see the same thing in boiling water, and in all other liquids that are reduced to smoke; but I do not want to amuse myself with these considerations, nor research more exactly how much water, wine, tallow, incense, etc., can be condensed or rarefied, both because these are not bodies suited for making the sound we are discussing, and because this deserves a discourse of its own. I only add that bodies struck in water, wine, milk, and brandy have their sounds lower <note>original: "graues" (grave). In music theory, this refers to a low pitch.</note> than those they make in air, and consequently that sounds are not so high <note>original: "aigus" (acute). This refers to a high pitch.</note> in a thick and cloudy air as in a calm and purified air. From which it follows that the sounds of musical instruments are lower in Winter than in Summer, although we do not perceive this difference, insofar as if the sounds receive some alteration by reason of the different seasons and alterations of the air, our ears are similarly affected and altered, and therefore they are not capable of perceiving or judging this difference, for the understanding needs the organ <note>The physical sense organ, in this case, the ear.</note>, and we are not exempt from these alterations.

Nevertheless, if nature or art gave us a sound by means of which one could regulate all other sounds, one could test whether the sound of instruments or human voices are higher in Summer than in Winter, and by how much, assuming that this first sound were invariable to the changes of the air:

...but I know of none that can serve this subject, and the same difficulty is encountered in all other sciences, since we cannot establish a weight in nature for the <term>Isorropic<note>From the Greek *isorropia*, referring to the study of static equilibrium or the balancing of weights.</note></term>, nor a color for Perspective, nor a measure for <term>Geodesy<note>The science of measuring the Earth and surveying land.</note></term>: now these defects of nature must invite us to the search for a truth more excellent and firm than that of created things, which is found in God alone, to whose glory we must refer all our thoughts and actions.

But I return to the density of bodies, in order to see if the sound is all the more high-pitched as the body is more dense or more rare, which must be understood not only of bodies of the same nature, but also of those of different species. Now it is very difficult to establish a general and universal Proposition on this subject: for if one says there is the same ratio of the high to the low as there is of dense bodies to rare ones, one finds dense bodies like gold and lead, which have a lower sound than brass and iron, which are rarer—or less dense—than gold.

Some hold that a distinction must be made between metals, stones, and wood when one wants to speak of their sounds by reason of their densities, and that an infallible sign of the greatest union or density of parts must be established, on which all do not agree, although all give first rank to gold, which is the most massive, even though it does not have a high-pitched sound.

Others believe that the natural coldness of bodies is an infallible sign of their density, because matters that cool down, thicken and descend, and those that rarefy, expand and rise upward, as do the vapors of the earth and water: from which they conclude that what is dense is cold, dry, heavy, opaque, full of shadow, obscure, black, and similar to night; that it loves rest, that it is sluggish, mixed, hard, rough, obtuse, raw, narrow, and bitter. They say also that density is the cause of pain, fear, melancholy, avarice, lying, laziness, hatred, cruelty, diseases, death and all that belongs to the side of privation and imperfection. 

On the contrary, they hold that rarity makes bodies hot, moist, light, sublime, diaphanous <note>Transparent or translucent.</note>, shining, clear, white, fast, simple and extended, soft and sweet, and that they are similar to day, to light, and to movement; and consequently that rarity signifies or gives boldness, joy, pleasure, liberality, truth, subtle inventions, love, mercy, humility, health, life, and everything that approaches closer to <term>act than to potency<note>Aristotelian philosophical terms: 'Act' refers to the fulfillment or reality of a thing, while 'potency' refers to its latent potential. Here, rarity is associated with higher, more realized states of being.</note></term>. 

But all these properties need a longer discourse: this is why I return to sounds, and say that one must experiment to see when dense bodies have a low sound, in order to notice the conjoined quality that takes away their high-pitched sound, and to give the sound when one knows the density, without there being any necessity for another exception than that of bodies which go against the general law of density and pitch.

The same thing happens to pipes that need wind, for the stronger and faster the wind is, the thicker, heavier, and harder it is; and one can so push and enclose the air that it will be as hard and as difficult to penetrate as walls. For example, air enclosed in a perfectly inflated and closed ball carries great burdens without the air yielding in any way, and could carry an entire house if its covering did not break, because the air enclosed within is hard enough to resist: from which one could conclude that...

## On the movements and the sound of strings.

...that the movement by which it is pushed is faster, for this movement thickens and hardens it, and consequently makes it heavier, as is experienced with an inflated ball, which weighs more than when it is empty. <note>This refers to early pneumatic experiments showing that compressed air has more mass than air at normal pressure.</note>

I leave aside several difficulties regarding the density of bodies—for example, to what density each body can be reduced, such as air, water, etc. It is observed through experiment that <term>spirits of wine<note>The original French is "eau de vie," referring to distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note></term> can be so rarefied that it occupies a hundred times more space than it does in its natural state; but it is not known if it can be condensed as much. Some say that they condense it to such a degree that it is as hard as crystal, and that they can convert air into icicles.

But the principal of all the difficulties regarding this proposition consists in knowing from whence comes the greater density or rarity, the greater weight or lightness, and the greater hardness of bodies; for if one knows the primary causes of these qualities, one will similarly know from whence comes their low or high sound. Some believe that these primary causes are nothing other than the abundance of spirit and of the **quintessence**, and that the more spirit a body has, the heavier, harder, and denser it will be; this is experienced in the <term>Dead Head<note>original: "Caput mortuum." A term used in alchemy and early chemistry to refer to the useless residue or "dregs" left over after distillation or sublimation.</note></term> of the Chemists, which weighs almost nothing after the salt, sulfur, and mercury have been extracted from it. To this they add that salt, which is the primary matter of bodies, gives them solidity, and that it coagulates, fixes, and congeals them as much as it can by its amalgamating virtue, by which fluid and volatile things become fixed and permanent: for example, when rain falls, it becomes solid in plants by means of the earth; this does not happen when it falls into water, in which the salt is not brought into action; from which it follows that the more salt there is in a body, the harder, denser, heavier, and more solid it is, as is experienced in bones, which have much more salt than the other parts of the body.

This agrees with what we have said above: namely, that a dense and compact body has much matter, or salt, in a small space.

But this knowledge is not enough to understand the density and weight that cause the sound to be low or high, and why it differs according to the mixture of the other parts of the compound, for the form they call **sulfur** tempers the coagulation of the salt, and gives the final action to the matter, making the compound perfect. This is why it would be necessary to know how much sulfur and mercury are with the salt of each body, for it is very certain that the sound is rendered different by the different quality of the mercury, or of the water that enters into the composition of bodies (some call it the <term>Middle Principle<note>original: "Principe metoyen." In alchemical theory, Mercury was seen as the mediating element that linked the stability of Salt with the volatility of Sulfur.</note></term>, insofar as it unites the sulfur and the salt, and gives them vigor) in order to observe if the highest sound comes from the greatest density of bodies, when it is created by the assembly of parts that are of the nature of air or water. This can be experienced in glass, which seems to testify by its color and its diaphanous quality that its density comes from a multitude of parts of air or water. Nevertheless, the metal of which bells are made and steel have very high sounds, although they are very far from the nature and qualities of glass, which has hardness like them—for it is as hard as or harder than iron or steel, since they cannot bite into it; but I will give the reason for the hardness of bodies in another place. ### PROPOSITION XVIII.

->*To explain the different qualities of bodies that make the sound lower or higher, clearer or duller, louder or softer, etc.*<-

The principal qualities that contribute to the diversity of sounds consist particularly in the hardness and density of bodies, and their contrary qualities; for it is experienced that the metals which are the hardest are accustomed to making sounds that are higher <note>original: "plus aigus"</note>, clearer, and more resonant, as is easy to conclude by the aforementioned cylinders of which we spoke in the ninth, tenth, and eleventh Propositions. I leave aside several other qualities—for example, <term>friability<note>The tendency of a solid substance to break into smaller pieces or be reduced to powder.</note></term>, which causes bodies to break easily, and dryness and rarity, which usually make the sound higher, etc. I have spoken of these at great length in the forty-first and forty-second Propositions of the second Latin book on the *Causes of Sound*, which deserve an entire volume to explain the reasons for all the properties and qualities of bodies found in the forty-second Proposition. This is why I come to other difficulties that will serve to understand what has been said of the movement of bodies; moreover, many things can be concluded regarding these qualities by reading the books on Instruments, particularly the sixteenth Proposition of the first and the nineteenth of the third book, and the *Book of Bells*; from which one can draw much light to understand what makes voices harsh, hard, clear, dull, etc.

It is certain that the greatest density of bodies does not always make the sound lower <note>original: "plus graue"</note>, since gold, which is denser than lead, makes a higher sound; but when the greatest hardness is joined to the greatest density, it usually makes the sound higher. Generally speaking, each body makes a sound that is all the higher as it <term>vibrates<note>original: "tremble." Early scientists used "trembling" or "shaking" to describe the rapid oscillations we now call vibrations.</note></term> more quickly, as is easy to conclude by the number of vibrations made by strings. ## COROLLARY.

It must be noted that the hardest bodies do not always produce the highest-pitched sounds. I have found through experimentation that a string made of gut, of the same length, thickness, and tension as one made of brass, sounds higher by an <term>Eleventh<note>An eleventh is a musical interval spanning an octave plus a fourth.</note></term>. Similarly, strings made of hemp, equal to those of brass, also sound higher, even though they are softer and less heavy. Consequently, the observation made by <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), a Greco-Roman mathematician and astronomer whose work *Harmonics* was a standard text for music theory in the Renaissance.</note></term> in the third chapter of his first book on Music is not always true—namely, that bodies produce a higher sound when they are denser, or when the ratio of hardness of one to the other is greater than the ratio of their densities. 

For example, after stating that bronze sounds higher than wood because it is denser, he adds that bronze, though less dense than lead, sounds higher because the ratio of the hardness of bronze to that of lead is greater than the ratio of the density of lead to the density of bronze. However, experience shows that a hemp string is rarer and softer than a bronze one, and yet it sounds higher; and a cylinder of fir wood equal to one of bronze sounds higher, though it is softer and rarer. If someone were to argue in favor of Ptolemy that this is because it is lighter, it is easy to find bodies that are less dense, less hard, and less light, yet do not sound as high as other bodies that are denser, harder, and heavier. Thus, it is very difficult to prescribe the exact combination of all the qualities necessary for a body to produce a higher sound according to a given ratio without encountering an exception.

## NOTICE.

I am expressly omitting several discourses that could be made regarding the preceding observations on the length, thickness, and tension of strings. A summary of these can be seen in the seventh Proposition of the third book of <term>*Instruments*<note>Referring to another section of the author's monumental work, *Harmonie Universelle*.</note></term>. For instance, if one considers the different tensions or thicknesses of strings, one can set the ratio of the Octave at 4 to 1, or 8 to 1, if one considers the volume of air struck by the different lengths. On this subject, one may consult the tenth Proposition of the first book of <term>*Consonances*<note>Another part of the same treatise, focusing on the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note></term>. I also leave aside the reasons for these different tensions and thicknesses so that those who take pleasure in speculation—and who are more satisfied finding reasons through their own industry than by encountering them elsewhere—will not lack for exercise.

Now, this delay occurs because the air resists more when it is more compressed; but it is difficult to know how much more it resists at each moment of the fall. I know that an excellent Philosopher has imagined that the weight, perpetually pressing the air, always increases its speed, so that if after the first moment in which the stone moves, God took away its weight, it would still descend by the force of the movement it had imprinted on itself in the first moment; and that if it were in a <term>vacuum<note>The author refers to "le vuide," a concept hotly debated in the 17th century; many followed Aristotle in believing a true vacuum was impossible.</note></term>, it would always travel at a constant speed. But because gravity always accompanies the first movement, it increases its speed by one degree at each moment: from which it follows that the stone travels no more distance in the first three moments than in the fourth. This being settled, he concludes that it reaches a certain point of equality, after which it always descends at the same speed. This he proves because the air, which resists more and more in proportion to how much it is violated, does not resist as much in the first moment as the speed is increased as it does afterward. For example, the speed increases by one degree at each moment, and the air resistance does not grow by a degree; but because its resistance always grows, it eventually becomes so great that it is equal to the impulse, or to the force of gravity, and consequently, it prevents gravity from adding a degree of speed at each moment from then on, so that the movement remains equal. 

But a very excellent <term>Geometer<note>Likely referring to a mathematician like Pierre de Fermat or Gilles de Roberval, who were contemporaries applying rigorous mathematics to physics.</note></term> has demonstrated that this point of equality cannot be reached, following the previous reasoning. For since the resistance of the air cannot grow more than the speed of the fall, let us suppose, for example, that at the beginning of the movement the speed is one, if the air did not hinder it; and because it does hinder it, let us say it is only one-half, by reason of the said resistance, which will also be 1/2. Now, at the 2nd moment, when gravity adds another degree to the speed, it would be 3/2 if the air did not hinder it again; but it will not hinder as much in proportion as the first time, because the air is already in motion, nor more than in the same proportion—that is to say, it will not decrease half of the speed, which instead of 3/2 would be no more than 3/4. At the 3rd moment, gravity will add one degree to the speed, which would be 7/4; and if the air takes away half, only 7/8 will remain; and so on for the other moments, the impediment of the air will be 15/16, 31/32, 63/64, 127/128, 255/256 and so on to infinity. By this, one sees that these numbers, increasing to infinity, will always be less than unity; and consequently, the air resistance will never take away as much speed as it acquires through gravi-

It is also certain that of two given weights of the same material and shape, the larger must fall first, because the air does not resist it as much in proportion as it does the smaller one. ### COROLLARY I.

If musket balls fired perpendicularly upward maintain the same proportion in the speed of their fall as those we let drop from 144 feet high—that is to say, if the distances they travel are in the <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>The "duplicate ratio" is an early mathematical term for a squared relationship ($t^2$). Mersenne is applying Galileo's law of falling bodies.</note> of the time they spend in their fall—they will fall back nearly as fast as <unclear>they</unclear> <unclear>went</unclear> up, so that if the ball leaving the <term>arquebus</term><note>An early type of long-gun or portable firearm, predecessor to the musket.</term> travels one hundred <term>toises</term><note>A pre-metric French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or about 6.4 feet.</note> in a second and a half, the ball will also travel one hundred toises in the final second and a half of its fall. And if a cannonball rises perpendicularly 1,800 toises (as much as it does in its greatest horizontal range), it will travel 118 toises in the final second of its fall and will take 30 seconds to descend, which is to say as much as it takes to rise. This could serve to determine the proportion it maintains in the decrease of its speed from bottom to top, and to compare the force of the Earth's attraction with the impulsive force of cannons, which seem to oppose each other.

### COROLLARY II.

Bodies descending toward the center of the earth increase their speed in the duplicate ratio of the times, as I have shown in the first Proposition of the second book, because <term>gravity</term><note>Mersenne uses "pesanteur," which refers to the weight or heavy quality of an object that causes it to fall.</note> always adds new movements at every moment of the fall. For example, when a weight descends one foot in one moment, it descends 4 feet in 2 moments; because if it were stripped of its gravity at the instant it reached the end of the first foot, it would continue to descend at the same speed it had acquired at the end of that foot, and consequently, it would travel twice as much distance—that is, 2 feet in the 2nd moment, as I have shown in the second Proposition of the second book on movements—and would continue at the same speed to the center, or beyond, even if its gravity were not restored to it. 

But as soon as gravity is restored to it, it would hasten its course: for example, instead of having only traveled 3 feet in 2 moments—namely, one foot in the first moment while possessing gravity, and 2 in the second—it will travel 3 in the second [moment], then 5 in the 3rd, 7 in the 4th, etc., because gravity always adds a new degree of movement in each moment. From this, it follows that the weight travels 9 feet in 3 moments, 16 in 4 moments, and so on, following all the squares, as I said in the first Proposition of the second book on Movements. Now, it must be assumed here that movement, once imprinted upon a moving body, never ceases unless it is removed by some impediment, as we have already remarked. One can adapt this reasoning to the attraction of the earth, or to the <note>original: "desir, & à la propension"</note> desire and inclination that bodies have to reunite with their whole.

If the weight always increases its speed in falling, according to the duplicate ratio...

## P R O P O S I T I O N XX.

->*Explaining the movements of a weight attached to a string, and their circumstances and uses.*<-

Although I have spoken very amply about this type of movement from the thirteenth Proposition of the second book of *Movements* up to the sixteenth, it nevertheless deserves that I add some considerations to make its use more profitable and more universal. From this, one can conclude the same thing as one would for a stone falling through an opening made through the diameter and center of the earth: namely, that if weight B always traveled as fast as it does when passing through point E while descending, it would cover a space equal to its entire semicircle KEL in the same amount of time it took to cover the quarter-circle KE while descending, or EL while rising...

->On the movements and the sound of strings.<-

An 8-ounce weight oscillates for at least a full hour when it is attached to a string or a thread of 3 and a half feet, which makes exactly 3,600 oscillations <note>Original: "tours & retours," referring to the back-and-forth swings of a pendulum.</note> in one hour; consequently, the 3,600th part of the straight line I H, and of the circular line I B, is the final return, or the final fall that brings the weight B to rest. This is to say that the final fall of B is only the one thousand two hundredth part of a line <term>line: a historical unit of length, roughly 2.25 millimeters or 1/12th of an inch</term>, for I H is 3 lines long, or 1/4 of the inch M B.

### COROLLARY I.

If one assumes A E to be 3 and a half feet, a string of this length provides the "minute-clock," which I explained in the fifteenth Proposition of the second book of *Movements*; this is very convenient because it divides the minute of an hour exactly into 60 parts to create second-minutes <note>Essentially what we call "seconds" today.</note>, which are almost the shortest duration of time that can serve accurately enough for observations requiring attention and precision. However, if one wishes to mark the half-seconds that the weight employs to descend from C, or from D to E, one could use another sub-quadruple <note>Meaning a string one-fourth the length of the first.</note> string marked A $\gamma$; this would give each half-second by each of its swings, and consequently a quarter of a second by each half-swing from 3 or from $\delta$ to $\gamma$. When observing, it would be appropriate to have these two clocks, so that one counts the swings of the thread A $\gamma$ while the other counts those of A E, whose number is always half that of the former.

### COROLLARY II.

The movement of weight B descending from K, or from L to E, is sufficient to disabuse those who believe that the speed of a weight descending perpendicularly does not increase as it falls; for the experiment is so evident in the fall of B through the quarter-circle L B that there is no way to contradict it. Now, this increase in speed proceeds solely from the speed it would have in falling through the perpendicular A B. Thus, the weight travels the part of the circle C D in almost the same time it would take to travel the perpendicular H I. And because experience shows that the weight falling from A to E descends at least as fast from $\gamma$ to E as from A to $\gamma$—since it travels 3 times more distance in the second moment of its fall than in the first, as we have shown in the first Propositions of the second book of *Movements*—it follows that it descends that much faster from D to E than from O to D, just as it would descend faster through the perpendicular line corresponding to the arc D E than it would through the one corresponding to O E. This is seen even better in the figure for the fourteenth Proposition, where I treated this matter. From this, it is easy to conclude why the string A B must be four times the length of A $\gamma$ to make its returns in double the time; that is to say, why it must be in a duplicate ratio <note>A ratio of the squares.</note> of the times to have returns of longer duration, or in a sub-duplicate ratio <note>A square root ratio.</note> of the times to have shorter returns according to the given ratio. However, one must observe what circular motion can change in these ratios, for the air hinders circular motion differently than perpendicular motion; and these elongations do not always follow the same ratio down to the center of the earth, since one must treat them exactly the same as...

# COROLLARY III.

Galileo remarks that there are an infinite number of points in the string <note>Original: "chorde," referring here to the string of the pendulum.</note> A B, each of which has the inclination to return to the perpendicular line when the string is pulled away from it. He says that because all these parts have the faculty of returning there more quickly—or through a smaller circle—the closer they are to point A, they prevent the movement of the weight O from making perpetual rotations and returns, even if one imagines it in a vacuum without the hindrance of air. This is perceived by attaching another weight to some point on the string A B, or A O, for example at point ε; for this weight seeks to move along the circle ε γ. The same must be concluded for all the other points of the string A O, and this is seen more clearly in a chain made of iron or other heavy material than in a string.

# COROLLARY IV.

The circular fall of weight B, and that which we spoke of beyond the center of the earth, seem to show that the speed of the projection of heavy bodies thrown upward or horizontally decreases in the same ratio. For the movement that makes B rise from E to O is similar to that of projection. Consequently, what cannot be tested in the movement of ordinary missiles—for example, in that of cannonballs and musket balls, or in that of arrows and stones thrown with a sling or by hand, because of their excessive speed—can be observed by means of a string 30 or 40 feet long. This string makes its swings and returns so slowly that they can be divided into 3 or 4 sensible parts, in order to notice how much faster the weight goes in each part.

For example, if one hangs a thread from a soaring vault of 126 feet or more, such as that of St. Pierre of Beauvais, which is 144 feet high, and if one pulls the weight attached to the thread so that it is raised perpendicularly by one <term>toise: an ancient French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or 6.39 feet</term>, it will make each of its swings in 6 seconds. Consequently, it will rise for half of each swing in the time of 3 seconds, such that one can mark the path it travels in each second and determine how much larger one of the three parts of the arc will be than the others. This is done to know the proportion of the decrease it maintains in the speed of its <term>violent movement: in early physics, motion caused by an external force (like a throw), as opposed to "natural" motion like falling</term>, or in that of its natural movement which it makes in the other part of its circle.

# COROLLARY V.

I leave aside the other uses that can be drawn from the swings and returns of any string one might choose, because they are almost infinite; for example, they serve to know the speed of the voice and of other noises, and that of the Echo; the speed of cannonballs, of the flight of birds, of the running of horses, and of all bodies that have some sensible movement. But because the weight, being pulled as far as K or L, employs as much time to descend through the quarter-circle to E as another weight does which descends from...

## COROLLARY VI.

The same reasoning that shows that the different falls of heavy bodies toward the center of the earth occur in the square of the ratio <note>Original: "raison doublee," a mathematical term referring to the square of a ratio.</note> of the times, similarly proves that the lengths of the strings <term>strings (chordes)</term> <note>In this context, the author refers to the length of the pendulum cord.</note> used to measure time must be in the square of the ratio of the times one wishes to measure. Now, the reason for the long duration of the period of the swings and returns of each string depends on the inclination of the planes upon which one can imagine the weights attached to the string move. For if one considers the quadrant of their descent as being composed of an infinite number of different planes, one will find that the plane approaching the tangent line is so little inclined above the Horizon, and has so little slope, that a ball rolling upon it would not travel the space of one foot in an entire day, as is easy to conclude by what has been said in the seventh and eighth Propositions of the second book, the speculation of which can be applied here.

## NOTICE.

It is necessary to adjust everything I have said regarding the Echo from the twenty-sixth to the twenty-ninth Proposition of the *Book of Sounds*, following the more specific observations I have made since then in different locations, which are explained in the Proposition that follows, and which provides several things that had not been previously noticed.

## PROPOSITION XXI.

->*To determine the exact measurements of the vocal lines of the Echo, and the benefits that can be drawn from them for Philosophy and Mechanics.*<-

Now, this measurement of the Echo, or of the reflection of the voice and other sounds, is so certain that all experiments confirm it. Regarding this, one must first remark that the Echo is always of an equal speed in all kinds of weather, whether it be foggy, or the air be clear and serene, or the wind be favorable, contrary, or blowing across: for we have experimented several times, and in several places, with all these varieties.

<margin>*</margin>In the second place, that winds or other atmospheric conditions <note>Original: "impreſſions de l'air."</note> contrary to the Echo weaken it, or render it useless because it cannot be heard, even though they in no way hinder its speed.

In the third place, that the preceding measure of the Echo is rather too long than too short, and consequently that the distance of 69 1/3 Royal feet <note>The "pied de Roy" or Royal foot was a pre-metric unit of length, approximately 32.48 cm.</note>, (or to avoid the fraction) 69 feet, is sufficient for one syllable pronounced in the seventh part of a second: so that it is necessary to reform the measures of the Echo, of which I spoke from the twenty-sixth Proposition of the *Book of Sounds* onward, following this Proposition, inasmuch as I had not yet made sufficiently exact observations.

In the fourth place, it seems that one can conclude the speed of the voice and other noises by means of the Echo; for since it repeats the seven syllables, *I will bless the Lord* <note>original: "Benedicam Dominum"</note>, or any others one might wish, and sends them back within one second, the last syllable *num* travels 485 Royal feet going out, and as many returning within the time of one second—that is to say, 162 <term>toises</term> <note>A "toise" is a traditional French unit of length, roughly equal to 1.949 meters or 6 feet.</note> or thereabouts. In this manner, one can choose this number of toises for the speed of reflected Sounds, which I have always found to be equal, whether one uses the sound of trumpets and arquebuses <note>An early type of portable long gun.</note>, or that of stones, and whether the voice is deep or high-pitched. This must be carefully noted in order to abandon the different opinions, or rather the errors, concerning the greater speed of loud and high-pitched Sounds compared to weak and deep ones, and other circumstances, which I explain here following the great multitude of tests I have performed in the presence of many people, and which everyone can perform to disabuse themselves.

In the fifth place, one can conclude the number of syllables pronounced in a given time that can be repeated by the Echo of a league <note>A "lieue," roughly 4 kilometers.</note>, or of any other length one might wish: for since there are 2,500 toises in a league, and experience teaches that the voice always travels at an equal speed to the extremity of its range—which similarly happens to all other kinds of noises—it follows that the Echo of a league can repeat 208 syllables, by giving the distance of 12 toises to each syllable. Now, one would employ a little more than nine seconds to pronounce these 208 syllables at the same speed as the 7 preceding ones.

By this, one can examine all the Authors who treat the Echo and other things belonging to the voice: for example, that which Boissard reports in his *Topography of Rome*, page 34, of which we have already spoken in the thirty-seventh Proposition of the *Book of Sounds*, namely that the Echo of the tower of Metellus near Mount Aventine repeats 8 times the entire first verse of the *Aeneid*:

And because the site of the Echo must be distant by 162 toises <note>A pre-metric French unit of length, approximately 1.95 meters or 6.4 feet.</note> to repeat a 14-syllable verse a single time, and 8 times as much, that is to say, 1196 toises, to repeat this verse 8 times in a row without one overlapping the next, it follows that the last wall, or the other body which reflects the 8th or last time, is distant by 1296 toises <note>The author's arithmetic here (162 x 8 = 1296) corrects the previous figure of 1196.</note> from the one who speaks, whether in a straight line or through various turns, which the voice can take through a great multitude of different reflections. Or, if we take only 11 toises for the repetition of each syllable (that is to say, the smallest distance of all possible ones), the verse of 14 syllables, which repeats only once, requires an Echo distant by 154 toises; and repeating 8 times in a row, the reflecting body must be distant by 1232 toises, which is to say nearly half a league. Consequently, the voice must be strong enough to be heard as distinctly and as loudly from a league away as it is heard in the 8th repetition of the verse, because the voice of the Echo travels one league when counting its journey out and its return—something that cannot happen with the ordinary voice of men, whether by day or by night. For experience teaches that the Echo of 14 syllables is so weak by the final syllables that one has difficulty hearing it, or shouting loudly enough to make this Echo respond from 154 toises away.

In the sixth place, one can measure the width of city moats <note>Original: "fossez."</note>, or other such accessible or inaccessible places by means of the Echo. For example, if the city walls respond with only one syllable pronounced in 1/2 a second from the edge of said moats, they are at most only 12 toises wide; and if one is so far away that the Echo responds with 7 syllables pronounced in one second, and there are 60 toises from the place where the Echo is heard to the edge of the moats, they will be 21 toises wide.

I leave aside a thousand other uses that can be drawn from Echoes, in order to explain the second part of this Proposition, which consists in finding Echoes in all sorts of places.

I say, then, that one finds Echoes in all sorts of places where there is some wall from which one can move away by 12, 24, 48, or more toises; and if one can move as far from the surface of the earth by climbing upward, and the vocal line <note>The path of the sound wave.</note> falls perpendicularly, one will also hear Echoes. I said perpendicularly, because the voice that falls obliquely upon a polished plane does not return to the speaker, since it reflects at angles equal to those of its incidence, as I explained in the *Book of Sounds*, Proposition twenty-seven and twenty-eight. But because walls are not polished, it can happen that the Echo returns to the speaker even if the plane of the wall does not entirely receive the perpendicular vocal lines, just as happens with light which splashes back in all directions upon encountering a rough and uneven body. Now, experience will show all of this so clearly to those who wish to try it that it is not necessary to speak of it further.
