## COROLLARY II.

One can know how much stronger one voice is than another by means of the Echo; for if one has only the strength to make 4 syllables repeat, and the other 8, the latter will be twice as strong, and so on for the others. Here it must be noted that many cannot persuade themselves that a loud voice does not travel faster than a weak one: but they will abandon this opinion at the first experiment they make, whether the sound is produced solely by the beating of the air, or by the images of the voice that are called *intentional*. <note>A term from scholastic philosophy, "intentional species" were thought to be the forms or "images" of things that traveled through a medium to the senses.</note>

The same thing happens with circles in water, which do not form any faster when the water is struck harder.

Many more conclusions can still be deduced from our trials; for example, that the sound of the Echo which returns is just as fast as that which goes out, and that the voice travels as fast at the end of its course as at the beginning. This seems marvelous, whether sound is made by *encyclies* <note>From the Greek word for "circular," referring here to the expanding spherical waves of sound.</note> or circles that one imagines in the air—similar to those made in water—or by means of atoms and small bodies that one imagines coming out of the mouth or meeting in the air; or whether the air, once shaken, takes on a natural movement of its own that always has an equal speed, as happens with the vibrations of strings which are always equal, etc. For why is it that the greatest winds in the world, even when contrary, do not hinder the speed of sounds? And why does the violent impression made by cannon shots or the whips of carters not move the air faster than the slightest impression of the voice? If noises filled the air in an instant, as light does, we would use that to explain them; but since they employ more time to spread through the air the further away they are, I do not know how this difficulty can be explained. Regardless, it is certain that our observations are true and very exact, which will be admitted once they have been performed.

I leave aside several difficulties that can similarly be resolved by experiment: for example, whether a cannonball travels faster or slower than a musket or pistol ball, and how long it takes to go up and come back down when fired perpendicularly, etc. This is easy to observe by means of our clock, <note>In the 17th century, "horologe" or clock referred to early mechanical timing devices, often pendulums or specialized timers for physics.</note> which can serve to know how many toises it travels while ascending, provided that one perceives the beginning and the time of its return, or its fall. ### COROLLARY III.

Although I have experimented with Echoes in several places, it is nevertheless not out of place to mark the principal ones in this Proposition, namely the house of Monsieur d’Ormesson <note>Olivier Lefèvre d'Ormesson (1616–1686), a prominent French magistrate and friend of the author.</note>, situated in the valley of Montmorency, and those of Monsieur de Verderonne, where I have quite accurately measured the distance necessary to make as many syllables respond as one wishes to all kinds of bodies <note>In this context, "bodies" refers to physical structures like walls or cliffs that reflect sound.</note> that are arranged to send back and reflect the sound to the place where it was first produced. Here it must be noted that I do not undertake here to make Geometric demonstrations, but only to explain our observations and to draw from them some conclusions that might serve the finest minds to go further. Now, we made 14 syllables respond at night at d’Ormesson, by moving far enough away, although by day it can only respond with 7, with the same strength of sound that one makes from half the distance; from which one can conclude that daylight hinders almost half the extent and the range of the voice.

### COROLLARY IV.

If sound is made or spreads through circles of air similar to those made in water when it is struck, and if it is permitted to judge the density of air and water by comparing the speeds of their circles, one will find that water is at least a thousand times denser than air, insofar as the circle of water extends at most only one foot from its center to its circumference, while the circle carrying the sound extends a thousand feet. This is easy to test by means of our seconds-clock <note>Mersenne was a pioneer in using pendulums to measure time in seconds for scientific experiments.</note>; for the circles of water only advance and grow by one foot in the time of one second, in which the voice travels nearly a thousand feet; and if one follows the square or the cube ratio <note>original: "raiſon doublee ou la triplee"</note> of one to a thousand, water will be a million or a trillion times thicker and more corporeal than air. But it is not certain that sound is made by the said circles of air, and even if that were certain, one would still have reason to doubt whether it...

it would be necessary to compare those of water with those of air, because it is certain that the sound made under water is not carried by the visible circles we see on the surface; otherwise, the sound would take as much time to travel from the bottom of the water to the ear as the circles take to spread across an equal space. This does not happen, since it seems that sound made under water is heard as quickly as that made in the air, whether one plunges the ear under the water where the sound is made, or whether it remains in the air, as we have experienced. From this, one can conclude that sound is produced, both in the air and in water, by a movement and by unknown circles, and that the quality of this impression is no less invisible than that of missiles <note>The author is comparing the invisible force of sound to the "impetus" or force driving a projectile like an arrow or cannonball.</note>. For if sound is produced by circles similar to those in water, how can it be that contrary winds—which seem to be made by other contrary circles—do not delay the sound at all? This is also difficult to explain by the images called **intentional species**, since it is admitted that they must be accompanied by movement and by the circles of the air <note>original: "especes intentionnelles." This refers to a Scholastic philosophical concept where objects emit "species" (forms or images) that travel through a medium to reach our senses.</note>.

### COROLLARY V.

When making the experiment of the Echo, or other things consisting of observing time and regulating the **seconds**, one must only pull the weight attached to the cord to an angle of 45 degrees from its perpendicular—that is, from the line perpendicular to the plane on which one stands while making the observation. This is because if one pulls it until it makes a right angle with the said perpendicular, its swing lasts a little more than a second; so, whoever pulls it to this angle will be assured that the voice travels at least as fast as a second, and even a little faster <note>The author is describing a simple pendulum used as a timer. He is noting that the period of a pendulum varies slightly with the amplitude of the swing, a problem later solved by Huygens's discovery of the cycloidal path.</note>.

### COROLLARY VI.

Since there are places that gather the voice better, and which return a greater quantity of **vocal lines** to the ear than others, it is certain that one can find places so disposed that the second or the third [reflection], though further away, will repeat louder than the first—just as one can set up three mirrors, where the second or third further away reflects a greater quantity of rays than the first closer one.

But I do not believe it is possible to create Echoes that respond in another language, nor in other syllables than the very ones pronounced. There is no "spring" <note>original: "ressort," implying a mechanical device or hidden mechanism.</note> which can be released to form new syllables through the movement of the air that makes the sound, since this movement of air is imperceptible when it reaches the reflecting places. These places always return only the same syllables they receive, whatever form or figure one might give them. Consequently, one cannot create as many varieties with the Echo as with mirrors or with glass lenses, unless nature teaches us other phenomena than those noticed until now.

One can, nevertheless, ensure that the syllables and words answered by the Echo belong to two or more **languages**, as I show in the 7th Corollary, which can serve to inspire new inventions by means of Echoes <note>This refers to clever wordplay where the end of a word in one language sounds like a full word in another, such as shouting "Amour" (Love) and having the echo return "Mour" which sounds like "Mors" (Death) in Latin.</note>.

## COROLLARY VII.

*Explaining the way to create Echoes that respond in a language other than the one they receive.*

There are several languages that share similarities, where certain syllables or words have such a correspondence that the Echo can respond in a different language than the one used when speaking to it. This is perhaps what led some authors to claim that Echoes can respond in French to someone speaking Spanish. This will be easier to understand through the following example—which was used at Tournon <note>Tournon-sur-Rhône, home to a famous Jesuit college during the 17th century.</note> during the funeral honors rendered to Henry IV <note>King Henry IV of France, assassinated in 1610.</note> in the Church of Saint Julian on July 30, 1610—rather than through a long discourse. The final syllables of this Greek Anapestic <note>Anapest: a poetic meter consisting of two short syllables followed by one long syllable.</note> and Acrostic <note>Acrostic: a poem where the first letter of each line spells out a word or name; here it spells out ERRIKOS SEBASTOS BORBONIOS (The August Henry Bourbon).</note> Epitaph form this French quatrain as the Echo's response:

> , Alas, who does not groan for so valiant a Hero?
> , Henry, dead in Paris, lies here beneath the stone,
> , I am mistaken; here are only bones; up, to rest his soul,
> , But living in Louis, giving peace to all. <note>original: "Louis." Referring to the young King Louis XIII, successor to Henry IV.</note>

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| E | Why flows this gloomy silence forever? <note>original: "αἰ ἆς" (ai as) sounds like "Helas" (Alas).</note> | Alas |
| R | From where comes this speech? The tomb is full of groaning. | Who does not groan? |
| R | This speech, which your sound calls out, is it not love? | A Hero |
| I | Ah, how much violence has come to them? | so valiant? |
| K | Who has found what his name was? | Henry |
| O | What terrible things he suffered, at Paris. | dead in Paris |
| S | Is he a savior? Alas, alas! Who will rejoice? | lies here |
| B | The King! He is in your fields, but [leave] me. | under the stone, |
| O | Is there no light at all for this whole life? | I am mistaken, |
| R | On the path I travel, what tomb stops you? | here are only bones: |
| B | Go now: does sorrow hold you unswervingly? | up, to rest |
| O | Hear the voice; leave it and let me be. | his soul, |
| N | If you are dead here, you must show us how to live. | But living |
| I | Where? Not in the libations, but in Louis. | in Louis |
| O | What good is it for all those who do good? | to all |
| S | I continue as the good son, giving peace. | the peace giving. |

Now, although one must stretch the spelling a bit, as they say, the coincidence is nonetheless clever; it is enough that there are some responses that are not forced—such as the first "alas"—to show that a man who understands only French can grasp the meaning of the Echo's words, even though it responds in Greek.

experience, without relying on our own [measurements], which I do not provide as so strictly regulated that one might not notice a few toises <note>The toise was a pre-revolutionary French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or about 6.4 feet.</note> more or less when it comes to the distance from the place where the noise is made to the place that reflects it. I have said "more or less" because it is certain that although the voice travels 81 toises going out and just as many returning within the time of one second <note>original: "seconde minute." In this era, "minute" could refer to a small division of time; "second minute" is what we simply call a second.</note>, it may nevertheless happen that one will notice a few toises more or less in certain experiments, depending on the thinness or density and other alterations of the air. This will be observed in Echoes that occur across ditches full of water, ponds, rivers, and marshes, compared to those over dry land.

If the speed of Echoes—that is, reflected sounds—followed that of sounds that travel straight without reflection, one would have to stand 115 toises away (that is, 34 toises further) from the walls that return the sound. This is because sound travels 230 toises in one second, according to the experiment we conducted over 1152 toises, which it covered in the time of five seconds. But it may be that this difference in speed comes from the fact that direct sound does not travel as fast in the first hundred toises as in those that follow, and that it only covers 162 toises in the first second, and 247 1/2 toises in each subsequent second. We shall provide the resolution to this after having experimented with both direct and reflected sounds; for if a distance of 81 toises produces an Echo of 7 syllables pronounced in one second, and it requires increasing this distance by 123 1/2 toises to hear the Echo or repetition of 14 syllables pronounced in two seconds, one must conclude that direct and reflected sound travel at the same speed, and that they do not travel as fast at the beginning as they do afterward.

### COROLLARY IX.

When I said that a string of 3 and a half feet marks the seconds by its swings or returns <note>The author is describing a simple pendulum used as a timer. At this time, the relationship between pendulum length and time was a major area of study for scientists like Mersenne and Galileo.</note>, I in no way prevent one from shortening the string if it is found to be too long, or if each of its swings lasts a bit too long for one second, as I have sometimes noticed according to different clocks—whether common ones or those made for a specific purpose. For example, the same common clock, with which I have often measured an entire hour with 3,600 swings of the 3-and-a-half-foot string, has at other times not made its hour so long; for it was necessary to make the string only 3 feet long to have 900 swings in one of the quarters of an hour of said clock. And I have experimented with a wheeled watch <note>original: "mōstre à rouës." A mechanical watch or portable clock.</note> made specifically to mark only seconds, finding that a string of about 2 and a half feet made its swings equal to the said seconds. This in no way hinders the truth or the accuracy of our observations, as it suffices to know that the seconds I speak of are equal to the duration of the swings of my 3-and-a-half-foot string; so that if someone can divide the day into 24 equal parts, he will easily see if my second lasts too long, and by how much it is too long.

### PROPOSITION XXII.

*To explain several circumstances and properties of Motions, both natural and violent, whether oblique or perpendicular: wherein one sees the examination of the thoughts and experiments of Galileo on this subject.*

Although I have already spoken of the natural Motions that occur on inclined planes in the second book, nevertheless the thoughts of Mr. Galileo, joined with our observations, deserve this Proposition.

Now, he says at the end of his *Dialogues* <note>Referring to Galileo's "Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences" (1638).</note> that if a quadrant <note>original: "quart de cercle"</note> is arranged like A B E, a perfectly round and polished ball descends and rolls at the same time—that is to say, just as quickly from B to E via the quadrant as from point C, or D, or any other point one might wish, however close it may be to point E, or at least that the difference in time is not perceptible. This must be examined before proceeding further.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a quadrant of a circle labeled A B E. A horizontal diameter is marked with points A, I, and B. A vertical radius drops from the center I through points H, G, and F to the bottom point E. Points C and D are marked on the arc between B and E. Horizontal lines connect these arc points to the vertical radius IE (at points G and F) and to a vertical line dropped from B (at points K, L, and M).</image-desc>

I say then, first, that having arranged a sieve <note>The author uses "crible" (sieve), likely referring to the circular wooden frame of a sieve used as a smooth track for the ball.</note> according to his intention, all experiments show that the ball descends sooner from C, or from D, or from any other lower point, to E, than from point B, and that the difference in time is sensible enough to be perceived. Upon which it must be noted that inequalities that might be on the sides of the sieve, or on the ball, cannot hasten the movement of the ball, which they would rather delay. Now, the sieve used for our experiments is 21 inches in diameter, or thereabouts, and 16 inches in the curvature of its quarter, represented by the quadrant B E.

Secondly, I say that a ball of pure gold, whose diameter is about 5 lines <note>A "line" was a traditional French unit of length, approximately 2.25 millimeters or 1/12th of an inch.</note>, and weight half an ounce and half a *gros* <note>The "gros" was a unit of weight equal to 1/8th of an ounce, roughly 3.82 grams.</note> less two and a half grains, makes ten turns and as many returns on the edges of the sieve before coming to rest at E, when it rolls from point B. When it rolls from 45 degrees, it makes 8 turns and as many returns; when it descends from 10 degrees, it makes 5; and when it descends only 2 degrees, it makes two; this is always understood for each side.

Thirdly, when it descends from 90 degrees—that is, from point B to E—it climbs back up the other side as far as 70 degrees; and when it returns there for the second time, it climbs to 45 degrees; and then it climbs to 45, 35, 30, 20, 15, 10, 5, and 2 degrees on the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, and 9th return that it makes on the left side.

But when the ball is heavier, such as one of lead, whose diameter is one inch, it makes a greater number of turns and returns, for this ball makes 12 on each side. Conversely, the elderwood ball <note>original: "boule de sureau." Elderwood is very light and pithy, often used in early physics experiments to show the effects of air resistance.</note> of the same size as the gold one, and weighing only one and a half grains, makes only 4 turns and as many returns before coming to rest when falling from B to E. Although it climbs to 55 degrees on the other side, it makes only 2 returns when falling from 10 degrees, and only one when descending from 2 degrees.

I leave it to the <term>Geometricians: Early mathematicians and physicists who used geometry to describe the laws of nature.</term> to determine by how much each degree increases or decreases the said returns, for experiments are too coarse for this subject.

In the 4th place, these returns are similar in several ways to those of weights attached to a string that goes from one side to the other, of which I have spoken previously: for the ball descends by <term>natural motion: The movement of an object toward its natural place, such as a heavy object falling toward the earth.</term> and rises by <term>violent motion: Motion produced by a force that pushes or pulls an object away from its natural state.</term> within the sieve, just as it does when suspended by a string, and it takes as much time to rise as to descend during each turn it makes; that is to say, the turn composed of its descent and its rise, being divided into two equal times, leaves the descent on one side and the rise on the other. But if one compares one of the last turns with one of the first—for example, that from C to E with that from B to E—one will find that the former occurs sooner than the latter. This also happens with the string, whose smaller returns occur sooner than the larger ones, although it seems that their times are not as different as those of the returns of balls rolling in a quadrant. It must nonetheless be noted that there is a way to make the difference of these times perceptible in the string, as I have done several times; even though one does not usually perceive this difference in the coarse experiments that are made, following which one must understand what I have said in other places: namely, that all its returns occur in equal time <note>The author is discussing "isochronism"—the idea that a pendulum takes the same time to swing regardless of the width of the arc. While Galileo suggested they were equal, the author correctly notes that very precise experiments show slight differences.</note>.

In the 5th place, it appears likely that the violent movements of <term>projectiles: original: "missiles," referring here to anything thrown or shot, like stones or bullets.</term> that are thrown by hand or otherwise, decrease in the same ratio as natural movements increase, since the ball rising in the quadrant of the sieve, or in that made by the string, decreases its violence and its movement in the same ratio as it had increased its natural movement from B to E; and a stone thrown straight upward by hand takes as long to rise as to descend. From this, one can draw several very useful conclusions for <term>Mechanics: The study of machines and the laws of physical motion.</term>, which deserve a particular treatise.

I add only that if all sorts of projectiles decrease their speed in the same ratio as natural motion increases its own, one can say how high they must rise, provided that one knows the time they take to cover the first part of their path. For example, since experience teaches that a <term>harquebus: original: "arquebuſe," an early type of portable firearm.</term> ball, which carries one hundred <term>toises: An old French unit of length, approximately 1.95 meters or 6.4 feet.</term> from point-blank range, covers the said hundred toises in the time of one and a half seconds, it would take 21 and a half seconds to rise; let us assume nonetheless that it takes only 21 seconds to facilitate the calculation: I say that it will rise perpendicularly 832 toises and one foot, as is easy to conclude by the 5th Proposition of the 2nd book, where one sees the demonstration in a particular table. Consequently, the ball will rise only 12 feet in the 21st or final second, for the ratio of the speeds of violent motion is the inverse of that of natural motion. One can also say how far a stone thrown upward will go, if one knows the speed of the hand that releases the stone: although one must first know the resistance of the air compared to the stone; for between two balls, or other projectiles of different size but the same material, the larger one overcomes the air more easily, for the reason that its...

The surface touches less air in relation to its <term>solidity: In 17th-century physics, "solidity" refers to the volume or three-dimensional mass of an object.</term> than the surface of a smaller ball in relation to its own solidity. For example, a ball one inch in diameter, weighing one ounce, has a surface of 1; a ball with a diameter of 2 inches has a surface of 4. Consequently, this larger ball is hindered by the air by a factor of 4, while the smaller one is hindered by a factor of 1. However, the <term>motion: Here, "motion" refers to the momentum or "impetus" imparted to the object.</term> impressed upon the larger ball is as 8, while that in the smaller one is only as 1, since these impressions are made throughout the entire solidity of the balls. From this, it follows that the larger ball, even if thrown at the same speed as the smaller one, can nevertheless travel further. This must also be applied to bodies of the same size, where some are lighter than others. Now, the larger body having 8 degrees of force and only 4 degrees of opposing resistance, it still has 4 degrees of force remaining, whereas the smaller one has only one degree of force and an equal amount of opposing resistance. This can disturb and hinder what I have said regarding the speed and length of <term>violent movement: Motion caused by an external force, such as a throw or a shot.</term> compared to <term>natural movement: The inherent tendency of a heavy object to fall toward the Earth.</term>

Now, I have only said that this reasoning for the decreases in speed seems plausible, because all phenomena perhaps do not correspond to these decreases. For example, bullets and balls from firearms and other missiles thrown upward do not produce as great an effect when falling back down as they do when leaving the <term>arquebus: An early type of long-gun or musket.</term>, the cannon, or crossbows, as many believe. One can see, however, if balls rolled on a horizontal plane maintain the aforementioned ratio as they decrease their speed; but these difficulties deserve entire treatises of their own.

The second thing noticed by <note>original: "Galilee"</note> Galileo consists of the movements that occur on planes placed within a quadrant or a semicircle. He asserts that a ball descends as quickly by the plane AE as by the plane CE, or DE, or any other one chooses, even if it covers only one degree. Regarding this, we have conducted many experiments that do not satisfy us; therefore, it is enough to see those explained in the 7th Proposition of the 2nd book, from which one can draw the solution to this difficulty, until we encounter machines large enough to make the difference in time perceptible.

He adds that the ball descends through the entire diameter of the circle in the same time as it descends on any inclined plane one chooses to place within the semicircle or the quadrant. For example, it descends as quickly from A to B, in this 2nd figure, as from C, or D, or E to B.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram labeled "2 figure" illustrating chords as paths of descent. A circle features a vertical diameter AB (A at top, B at bottom). Multiple lines representing paths are drawn from points C, D, and E on the upper arc down to the bottom point B. On the right arc, points F, G, and H are indicated. A horizontal tangent line at point B extends to the right, where the letter K is placed.</image-desc>

The reason for this is that it has less inclination to descend the closer it is to the center, and the more it is supported by the plane. I leave the other reasons explained in the aforementioned 7th Proposition, to which one may add that the part of the ball by which it is carried and supported by the plane can be considered as the counterweight to the part that is not supported, by which it seeks to fall.

The 4th thing he remarks upon consists of the ratio of falls through the quadrant and by the planes applied to it. For he maintains that the ball rolls sooner from G to B through the entire quadrant of the circle than through the plane GB, or HB, or any other plane one might choose, even if it covered only one degree.

# Book Three

He finally adds that a ball descends sooner from G to B via the two planes GH and HB than via the single plane GB, even though the latter is shorter; he must also conclude the same for three, four, or however many straight planes one wishes, because they more closely approach the curvature of the quarter-circle. For example, it must descend faster over the six sides of a 24-sided <term>polygon: The text refers to "plans" or sides of a geometric shape inscribed in a circle.</term> inscribed in the circle than via the three sides of a 12-sided polygon, and so on for the others. From this, it follows that it must fall faster via the quarter-circle GB than from A to B, since it falls from C, D, or E to B in the same time as from A to B. It must also fall faster from G to B via the two planes GH and HB than from A to B for the same reason. Now, one can calculate, following his principles and our observations, by how much sooner it falls when rolling over two or several planes than over a single one as far as B. As for the fall via the quarter-circle, it occurs in exactly the same time as a perpendicular fall made along a straight line equal to the said quarter-circle taken within the diameter. For example, if the diameter is 14 feet, the quarter-circle will be eleven feet <note>original: "le quart de cercle en aura onze" — This uses the common 17th-century approximation of Pi as 22/7.</note>, and consequently, the ball will be 3 feet short of completing the entire diameter in the same time it takes to roll through the quarter-circle; that is to say, it must begin to descend 3 feet lower than the top of the diameter to equal the time of descent via the quarter-circle. This seems marvelous, considering that it does not descend faster perpendicularly than circularly, since it covers an equal path in the same time, even though it approaches the center more closely by the perpendicular of eleven feet than by the eleven feet of the quarter-circle, which, having only 7 feet in height, is exceeded by 4 feet by the perpendicular height. But if it always descended in the same time through every part of the quarter-circle, however small it might be—for example, through the last degree—it would take just as long to approach the center the length of one line as it would eleven feet, etc., just as it does when descending on straight planes. On this matter, one can hope for the enlightenment that <note>original: "le sieur Galilee"</note> Mr. Galileo will provide in his book on *Movement* <note>Galileo's *Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze* (1638) dealt extensively with these problems of motion.</note>.

### COROLLARY I.

Those who wish to observe the speed of the <term>arquebus: An early type of portable long gun or musket.</term> ball, of which we have spoken, must use the same powder in both quality and quantity if they wish to find the same time for its speed from <term>point to point: The original "de blanc en blanc" refers to the distance between two targets or marks.</term>; otherwise, its range may be faster or slower than ours. For example, coarse powder that is beaten for 4 hours, and which is made from 3 pounds of <term>saltpeter: Potassium nitrate, the primary oxidizing ingredient in gunpowder.</term> of two boilings, half a pound of <term>hazel: The original "coudre" refers to the wood of the hazel tree.</term> charcoal or alder, and as much sulfur, will not produce as great an effect as the fine powder made from saltpeter of three boilings and which is beaten for 6 or 8 hours <note>The "boilings" refer to how many times the saltpeter has been refined to remove impurities.</note>.

Now, an experiment made with several charges of powder equal in quantity but unequal in quality would not be useless for considering the different forces, speeds, and effects of each sort of powder; and one would see if these effects correspond to those of the wheel instrument commonly used to test the strength of different powders.

### COROLLARY II.

->*On the decrease of violent motions.*<-

All experiments teach us that the speed of violent motions <note>"Violent motion" was a term used in early physics to describe motion forced upon an object against its "natural" tendency, such as a stone thrown upward.</note> decreases in the same ratio as that of natural motions increases; so that if one divides the path taken by the <term>missile: any object thrown or projected, such as a stone or a bullet</term>, for example, a stone or a ball thrown upward, into six parts corresponding to six equal parts of time, or the duration of their movement, and if the time is six seconds [minutes] <note>In this period, "secondes minutes" referred to what we now simply call seconds—the second division of the hour.</note>, the missile will cover eleven parts of its path in the first second, nine in the second, seven in the third, five in the fourth, three in the fifth, and one in the sixth; this can be observed in a ball that one causes to roll on a horizontal plane. But when the missile rises perpendicularly, its gravity [weight] shortens its path slightly; for example, if one imagines that the surface of the Earth were the center of several back-and-forth returns of a ball that would reflect many times very high, if it were of such a hard material, and if it fell perpendicularly on a plane so hard that neither gave way at all, the ball would reflect almost as high as the place from which it descended, and would perhaps decrease the height of its reflections in the same proportion as a weight attached to a string [a pendulum] decreases its swings, or as the string of a <term>Lute: a popular pear-shaped string instrument</term> decreases its own [vibrations]. Now, the first return of a weight suspended from a string decreases at most by only a sixtieth part, so that if a ball fell from a height of a thousand <term>toises: an old French unit of length, roughly 1.95 meters or 6.4 feet</term>, it would rise back at least 834 toises the first time. From this I conjecture that the weight of an arquebus ball hardly decreases its perpendicular range, unless the perpendicular encounter with the air hinders it much more than the circular [oscillation]. One can further apply this reflection and return to a stone that one might throw upward if one were at the center of the Earth, for it would return almost as high toward the Antipodes as it had been thrown from our side. To this must be added the returns of balls that occur on the edge of the <term>sieve: likely a reference to a rimmed circular experimental apparatus mentioned earlier in the work</term> of which we have spoken, and all other violent motions that can be related to these turns and returns.

### COROLLARY III.

This proportion of the decrease of violent speed and the increase of natural speed being established, it is not surprising if one does not see musket balls fired perpendicularly fall back, since they travel at least 60 toises during the last second of their fall; this is why, when one conducts the trial, it would be appropriate to arm oneself in <term>musket-proof: armor capable of resisting a musket shot</term> gear, or to place oneself in a location where one cannot be wounded. Now we shall treat this subject more fully after having justified several experiments which are necessary for the deduction of several very useful conclusions, both for Theory and for <term>Mechanics: the practical application of the laws of motion and machines</term>.

### PROPOSITION XXIII.

->*To explain several things that can be drawn from everything that has been said in this book.*<-

Even though it is very easy to conclude many things from what we have said in this 3rd book, I nevertheless wish to give examples to facilitate the method; and for this subject I say first that it is easy to tell the number of <term>gut strands: the material made from animal intestines used to manufacture musical strings</term> of which each string of a Lute, Viol, or another instrument is made, by the sound it makes: for after having considered the sound of a string that has only one strand, one knows the ratio of its tone with that of other strings of whatever thickness one wishes, whether they have the same or different length and tension, provided that one knows the said tension and length: for example, if a single-strand string one foot long and stretched by one pound produces the *ut* of *C sol* <note>In the Guidonian system of music notation used at the time, "ut of C sol" corresponds to the note C.</note>, and a string two feet long stretched by seven pounds descends an Octave, it is certain that it is composed of three gut strands, because if it were only stretched by four pounds, it would have only one strand, since the tension is in the <term>duplicate ratio: a mathematical term meaning the ratio of the squares (e.g., if the sound frequency doubles, the tension must quadruple)</term> of the sounds, when the strings are of equal thickness: and because besides this double length, the thickness is triple, one must still triple the weight or the tension of the single-strand string to have the tension of seven pounds.

In the second place, one can say in some manner that a string of a known length, thickness, and tension, is such or such a sound, for example, that a string of twelve strands four feet long, and stretched by four pounds

### Of the movements and sound of strings.

...is the chapel pitch <note>The "ton de chapelle" was a standard reference pitch used in 17th-century French sacred music, typically higher than the "ton de chambre" used for secular music.</note>, etc. or the **C** of the *C-sol* <note>original: "vt du C sol." In the Guidonian system of solmization used at the time, this refers to the note C. The author is identifying a specific pitch by its frequency.</note>, or the "forty-eight" sound, based on the forty-eight times that this string strikes the air in the space of one second; and the string which strikes the air sixty times in that second can be called the ***third minute*** <note>A "third" (tierce minute) was a historical unit of time representing 1/60th of a second, following the division of an hour into minutes and then seconds.</note>, since each of its cycles or beats lasts one third-minute.

One can similarly conclude the same for the strings <note>The author refers here to the weighted cords or pendulums used in timekeeping.</note> we use to make second-clocks, for they can bear the name of the time they measure, and that of the sounds they would make if the beats of the air, which they produce by their back-and-forth cycles, could affect our hearing: for example, the string that completes each of its cycles in one second would descend six octaves lower than one that completes sixty-four cycles in the same time.

In the third place, one can say that the eye "sees" sounds and concerts when it sees the number of beats of each string; though this sight belongs more to the understanding than to the eye. And if one perceives the number of beats with the hand, one can say that one "touches" the sounds, and that every sense is a species of touch and of sight. One can finally conclude that all sorts of air-beats produce some sound, whether the air strikes or is struck; and that the determination of these sounds <note>That is, the pitch or frequency.</note> depends on the number of said beats.

In the fourth place, the speed or slowness of the movement is indifferent to the low or high pitch of the sounds, because the movement of a **Lute** string which approaches its rest is extremely slow, even though it produces a sound just as high-pitched as at the beginning of its movement, which was a thousand times faster; so that it is only the greater or lesser number of beats—or the back-and-forth cycles of the string against the air, or the air against the string—which contribute to the high and low pitch of sounds.

I leave aside several other considerations that will be found in the books on Instruments, in order to give notice of what is contained in the **Treatise on Mechanics** which follows, and which I had promised at the end of the fourth **Proposition**: but I have since judged that it was more appropriate to have it serve as the conclusion to this book.

It should therefore be noted that I place it here instead of the fifth **Proposition** of the second book of **Movements**, which must be understood and adapted according to what is explained and demonstrated in this Treatise. In it, one will find many things that serve to determine the strength of **Lute** strings and other instruments: for besides the knowledge of the power that can pull, push, or support a given weight on a plane inclined to the horizon, when the angle of inclination is known (whether the power that pulls or supports is parallel to the plane or not), one will see what force two strings or two supports must have to sustain a given weight. Consequently, one will see the effect of weights attached to the string of the first **Proposition** of this book, or weights pressing or pulling the given string at a given point, so that everything I have said on this subject must be adapted according to the demonstrations that will be seen. I leave aside the manner of making a machine that can overcome any sort of resistance, unless it be infinite, and several other marvelous speculations which can be reduced to practice, and which can serve to explain the weights necessary to break all sorts of strings, or to make them bend as much as one wishes, at whatever point on the string one wishes to attach them. But before beginning this Treatise,

### NOTICE.

One can favorably explain Aristotle's opinion on the generation of the low and high <note>original: "graue & de l’aigu"</note> of sounds, of which we spoke in the book on Sounds and the Voice, and several times elsewhere, because one experiences that a rod makes a noise or whistling that is all the more high-pitched as it is moved more quickly through the air: and it would seem possible to determine the speed of projectiles <note>original: "missiles"</note> in each part of their path by the difference in the high and low of their sounds, if one could notice it: which must also be concluded from the different speed of descending bodies, following the great and laborious demonstration seen in the 12th Proposition of the book on Dissonances. But experience teaches that one does not hear the noise of projectiles when they go too fast or too slow; for example, one does not hear the sound of an arquebus <note>An early type of long gun.</note> ball while it covers 160 *toises*, even if one has an ear close to the place through which it passes, nor when it goes as slowly as stones thrown by hand: which seems strange, and which deserves research into the cause, in order to know what the speed of each projectile must be to notice its sound: perhaps too great a speed makes a noise so high, and too great a slowness one so low, that they are beyond the range of hearing: whatever the case, the modification of sounds regarding the low and high always comes from the different number of active or passive beats of air. Now if there is anything in the preceding books that conflicts with what is demonstrated in the *Treatise on Mechanics* which follows, it must be corrected according to the demonstrations found there, and if anyone performs more exact experiments than ours, he may follow them, our intention never having been that one follow anything other than the truth, wherever it may be found.

## On the Movement of Bodies.

->Book Second<-

Because the falling weight does not always land exactly in the center of the scale pan, as is required, it might perhaps be difficult to find a height great enough to limit the increase in speed of a falling body, even if it were twelve times lighter than lead, as are several types of wood which we shall discuss later. Nevertheless, if anyone wishes to perform the experiment, they may find heights of 144 feet, from which balls of wood or wool will fall quite conveniently into scale pans, provided they are very large.

If one were to attach a string to one of the arms of the balance, and the falling ball were also attached to the other end of the string, when it fell, it could give a vertical <term>jerk<note>The original term "secousse" refers to the sudden momentum transferred when the string goes taut.</note></term> to the ball, which would lift the scale pan of the other arm. However, it would be necessary to place the balance high up so that the weight could descend downward, and to add the weight of the string to it. Now, this <term>point of equality<note>A term for terminal velocity, where the resistance of the air equals the weight of the object, preventing further acceleration.</note></term> would be reached all the sooner and closer the lighter the falling weight; for example, <term>elder pith<note>The soft, spongy core of the elderberry stem, used in early physics for its extreme lightness.</note></term> would perhaps reach it at 12 or 24 feet. And because a piece of pith the size of a lead ball weighs only one grain, one could join several pieces of pith together until they reached the weight of one ounce or one pound, so that it could move the scale pan loaded with some detectable weight—for example, one or two ounces or pounds.

Now, although the point of equality for one weight (for example, this pith) might be found, it does not necessarily follow that one would have found it for others, such as balls of wood or lead. This is because bodies encounter different <term>impediments<note>original: "empeschemens"; referring here to air resistance.</note></term> in the air according to their different pores, which can disrupt the consistency of proportions. There are many factors to consider in air resistance that are not sufficiently known to us. Thus, it does not follow that the point of equality for falling lead must be 360 times farther away than that of pith, even though it weighs 360 times less, or that one would need a piece 360 times as large to weigh as much as said lead ball. Similarly, one cannot conclude that it descends 360 times more slowly, since experience shows the contrary; for the time of its fall from 48 feet is not triple that of the lead's fall.

One could similarly use water to find this point of equality, because bodies whose weight is nearly equal to water (such as wax, and several kinds of wood, and even stones that float on water, like the one I have, even though it has no visible pores and is quite heavy) go very slowly to the bottom when one adds only enough iron filings or similar things to make them sink in the water. For after having noted the ratio of speeds and weights in this element, one could conclude something similar for the air, particularly if one knew the ratio of its density and weight to that of water, of which I spoke in the first book of *Sounds* <note>Referring to the author's previous work on acoustics and fluid dynamics.</note>.

### COROLLARY I.

If falling weights lift a scale pan that is heavier the faster they go, one can tell from what height they fall by seeing the weight they cause to trip; and one can know the speed of a cannonball or a <term>harquebus<note>An early type of long gun or matchlock firearm.</note></term> shot by the weight it causes to rise. This would greatly serve to increase our knowledge...

# Notice to the Reader.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'S' featuring intricate floral scrollwork and foliage motifs.</image-desc>

Regarding the subject of the fourth axiom, we noticed after printing that a few words could be interpreted differently than we intended, and might therefore cause some difficulty, which we shall endeavor to resolve entirely here. Firstly, when we represent <term>cords<note>The original "chordes" refers to the strings or lines used in mechanical diagrams to represent forces.</note></term> marked by dotted lines along the arms of the balance in the figure on the fourth page, we mean for these cords to be <term>contiguous<note>Meaning touching or sharing a boundary; here it implies the cord is flush against the arm.</note></term> and as if united to those same arms, upon which they may nevertheless slide freely. This should be understood in the same way for all the other figures. Furthermore, in the same figure, the solid line FG, mentioned on the fifth page, line 24 and following, must be contiguous and as if united to the arm BC, upon which it may nevertheless slide freely if it is not stopped. The same line FG must be considered without weight, so as not to load the balance. And when we say that this line FG is pressed perpendicularly against the firm surface HG, we do not mean that it is attached to the same surface like a <term>peg<note>original: "cheuille"; a wooden pin or bolt used for fastening.</note></term>; but only placed against it by the end G, so that it cannot move back toward G when pulled by the cord CF by the force of the power D. The same should be understood on page 6 and others.

Moreover, the most noteworthy errors that occurred during printing are in the following sheet; these must be corrected diligently before reading the Treatise, which is only a <term>specimen<note>original: "eschantillon"; indicating that this published work is a preview or excerpt of a larger project.</note></term> of a larger work on Mechanics which cannot appear in print quite so soon.

# TREATISE ON MECHANICS.
## OF WEIGHTS SUPPORTED BY <term>powers<note>The original French uses the term *puissances*. In 17th-century physics, this specifically refers to what we now call "forces."</note></term> on planes inclined to the Horizon.
### *Of the powers that support a weight suspended by two cords.*

->By G. Pers. de Roberval, Royal Professor of Mathematics at the College of<-
->Master Gervais, and in the Chair of Ramus at the Royal<-
->College of France.<-

FOR the demonstrations in this Treatise, we assume the knowledge of the definitions and principles of Mechanics as they are found in Archimedes, <term>Guidobaldo del Monte<note>original: "Guid-Vbalde." He was an influential Italian mathematician whose 1577 work *Mechanicorum Liber* was a standard text in Roberval's time.</note></term>, <term>Luca Valerio<note>original: "Luc Valere." An Italian mathematician (1553–1618) famous for his work on finding the centers of gravity of solids.</note></term>, and in other Authors: to which we shall add what follows by way of explanation, and for greater understanding.

### DEFINITION.

The line of direction of a weight, or of a <term>power</term>, is a straight line drawn from the center of gravity of the weight, or from the center of the power, toward the place to which the weight or the power aspires—whether by pulling, pushing, or resisting, whether moving freely, or by flowing and sliding. Thus, the line of direction of a weight hanging freely is that which is drawn from the center of gravity of the same weight to the natural center of heavy things, which for terrestrial things is the center of the earth. But for weights that slide on surfaces, and for powers that can be directed toward all parts of the Universe, the lines of direction can also be directed likewise: as happens with cannonballs and other bodies thrown by violence, with birds that fly, animals that pull or push with or without instruments, and other similar agents; for this reason, their lines of direction can have an infinity of positions, which can only be determined for each case in particular.

### AXIOM I.

When a power, or a weight, pushes against a surface opposed perpendicularly to the line of direction of the same weight or power; the surface, being firm enough, will resist the power or weight entirely, which will be unable to escape, flow, or slide upon the surface. But if the power or the weight pushes against a surface opposed obliquely to the line of direction of the same weight or power; then the power or the weight will slide upon the surface, flowing toward the side where the obtuse angles are. And when a power or a weight flows and slides on a surface, if it encounters another surface opposed perpendicularly to the line

<summary>This page introduces Roberval's treatise on mechanics, defining the "line of direction" for forces and weights and establishing his first axiom on how surfaces resist or deflect motion based on the angle of impact.</summary>

<header>Treatise on Mechanics.</header>

of direction of flowing and sliding, this surface will prevent the <term>power<note>As noted previously, "power" (puissance) in this context refers to what we now call force.</note></term>, or the weight, from flowing and sliding further, and will stop it entirely, provided that it be firm enough.

### AXIOME II.

As much force or power is required to push as to pull, resist, stop, lean upon, sustain, and to hold back: provided that it be through the same distances and through the same lines of direction. For example, if to pull a weight on a plane inclined to the horizon requires a power of 1000 pounds, it will require an equal amount to push the same weight on the same plane. And if, in the first following figure, to hold back the weight E suspended freely by the line B E, a power of 10 pounds is required, an equal power will be needed to sustain the same weight E from below. And if a power of 10,000 pounds pushes perpendicularly against the surface of a wall, and the wall resists the power, it will be with 10,000 pounds of resistance; for if the wall has less resistance than 10,000 pounds, it will be overturned.

### AXIOME III.

In whatever place one puts the same power within its line of direction, it will pull or push equally. It shall be the same for a weight. As in the second of the two following figures, whether the power suspended at point B on the arm A B is at B itself, or at D, or at E—its line of direction being B D E, and the power always the same—it will always pull the same on the balance B C. Some doubt, not without reason, whether the same <term>heavy body<note>original: "corps pesant." In modern terms, we would distinguish between the mass of the object and the weight (the force of gravity acting upon it).</note></term> would weigh the same being closer to, or further from, the center of the earth, than it does here on its surface. But even if it weighed unequally, nothing would go against this Axiom, in which the question concerns the same weight <note>The force itself</note>, and not the same heavy body. And if the same body weighs more in some place than in another, on that occasion it represents different weights. It is the same when the power of some agent, such as a cannonball, slows down in various parts of its line of direction: for then, although it is the same agent, it is no longer the same power.

Assuming then that the balance B C is in equilibrium, in the second figure, if instead of the arm A B one substitutes the arm A D; the balance D A C, whose arms A D and A C are inclined toward each other at the angle D A C, will remain likewise in equilibrium, provided that the power which was suspended at B is placed at D, or suspended at the same point D by the cord D E. One can likewise substitute for the arm A C the arm A O, assuming that the line of direction of the weight, or of the power C, is C O. And thus one may substitute such other arm as one wishes which goes from the center A to the lines of direction B E or C O, whether extended or not. And whether the powers are placed upon the ends of the arms; whether they are suspended from the same ends by cords; or whether they are placed above the ends on firm lines; provided that they always pull or push through the same lines of direction, they will always pull or push equally, and will create equilibrium in the same way as before.

<summary>This page establishes the equivalence of pushing and pulling forces and introduces the principle that a force acts identically regardless of where it is applied along its line of direction. Roberval also makes a sophisticated distinction between the mass of an object and the variable force of weight.</summary>

### SCHOLIUM.

From this third Axiom one can easily demonstrate that in an <term>inclined balance<note>A balance scale where the beam is not perfectly level with the horizon.</note></term>, when the arms are equal, the weights equal, or the <term>powers<note>As established previously, "power" (puissance) refers to force.</note></term> equal, and the lines of direction of the powers, or of the weights, are parallel to one another; there will always be equilibrium, just as if the balance were horizontal. For in the second figure of the two following, let there be an inclined balance B C, of which the center is A, the equal arms A B, A C, and equal powers placed by their centers at the ends of the arms B, C, or suspended at the same ends by their lines of direction, of which lines one is B E, the other O C prolonged toward C, if need be; and let these lines B E and O C be parallel to each other. Let there also be the line D A O perpendicular to the two lines of direction, which D A O represents a horizontal balance, of which the arms A D and A O will be equal in the triangles A B D, A C O, by <note>original: "26. Proposition du 1. d'Euclide"</note> Proposition 26 of Book 1 of Euclid. Since then, by the third Axiom, the power B, or another suspended at point B on the arm B A, weighs as if it were suspended at point D on the arm A D: and the power C, or another suspended at point C on the arm A C, weighs as if it were suspended at point O on the arm A O: and since the powers B, C are equal, and the arms or distances A D and A O are also equal; the powers B, C will counter-balance and be in equilibrium, by the <note>original: "premier Axiome des Mechaniques d'Archimede"</note> first Axiom of the Mechanics of Archimedes. It will be the same if B, C are equal weights; provided that their lines of direction are parallel to each other, which does not happen with weights that hang freely, whose lines of direction are inclined toward the center of the earth: and for this reason one can demonstrate that in an inclined balance having equal arms and equal weights, the arm that is tilted down carries away the other until the balance is perpendicular to the horizon: which one will find demonstrated in our Mechanics.

## AXIOM IV.

Equal weights, and equal powers pulling or pushing through equal distances, will pull or push equally: provided that the lines of direction of the weights and powers are similarly inclined (that is to say, they make equal angles) with the distances through which the weights and powers pull or push. And this is true, whether the weights pull against one another, or the powers against one another, or the weights against the powers. As in the third figure, which is in the following Proposition, if the power or the weight K pulls on the distance C H through the line of direction H K; and another power equal to K pulls, or pushes on the distance C A through the line of direction A O; the distances C H and C A being equal, to which the lines of direction H K and A O are similarly inclined, namely perpendicularly, the equal weights, or the equal powers, will pull or push equally. Likewise if on the equal distances C A and C D equal powers or equal weights pull through the lines of direction A F and D G, making the equal angles C A F, C D G, they will pull equally.

Thus, the cord DC held by the line GF will always be prevented from slipping and sliding on the arm AC, and the balance will be maintained in equilibrium. ### AXIOM V.

A balance that no longer rests upon its center supports nothing anymore, and therefore, in this state, serves no purpose; and the power, or the <term>arrest<note>original: "arrest"; a fixed stop, anchor, or block that prevents movement.</note></term>, which relieves the same balance, supports the load that the balance previously supported. As if, in the second figure of the Scholium of the fourth Axiom, power D weighs upon the end of arm A D along the line of direction B D E toward E, and another power or an arrest located at B pulls or holds the same power D from the other side, along the same line of direction, and with as much force as power D can have weighing upon balance A D: then power D will be supported by the power, or by the arrest B, according to the second Axiom; and by common knowledge, the same power D will no longer weigh upon balance A D. This balance, being no longer loaded, will no longer rest upon its center (for in <term>pure Mechanics<note>The study of ideal machines where the weight of the parts themselves, like the lever arm, is ignored to simplify calculations.</note></term> we consider the balance as being weightless in itself). And even if the same balance were removed, power D would remain in the same state, supported by the power or by the arrest B, as it was previously supported by the balance A D. It would be the same if D were a weight instead of a power.

These things being established and explained in this manner, we shall divide this little Treatise into three Propositions, of which the first will be: Given a plane inclined to the horizon, and the angle of inclination being known, to find a power which, pulling or pushing along a line of direction parallel to the inclined plane, supports a given weight upon the same plane. The second: To find the same when the line of direction by which the power pulls or pushes is not parallel to the inclined plane. And the third: To find two powers capable of supporting a given weight suspended from two given cords.

### PROPOSITION I.

### COROLLARY I.

From the preceding Proposition, one can infer that there will be the same ratio from the <term>hypotenuse<note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.</note></term> L N to the base L M, as from the weight A to the power which can prevent it from sliding along the arm of the balance C A, and which by the same means will prevent it from pressing upon the inclined plane L N z: this will be demonstrated if one represents the distance C A N as an inclined plane: for it will be shown that the force required to sustain the weight at this inclination must be to the same weight as the perpendicular F A is to the hypotenuse C A; that is to say, as L M is to L N, because of the similarity of the triangles L M N and A F C. Now the same power produces no other effect than that which was produced, in the second figure of the <term>Scholium<note>An explanatory note or comment on a mathematical or scientific text.</note></term> of the fourth Axiom, by the power K, which pulling by the cord A C, prevented the weight A from sliding on the arm C A, and from pressing upon the plane L N z: which one will recognize if the demonstration is made as above, taking C A for the inclined plane.

### COROLLARY II.

If the weight A is hung from a firm line such as C A attached at point C, around which it can move freely with its weight: it is clear that the weight will not come to rest until the line of <term>suspension<note>original: "appenfion"</note></term> C A is joined to the line C L perpendicular to the horizon: but if the same weight with its line is pulled by force from the place of its rest, and positioned as it is in the figure at A; to maintain it in this state, pulling by the line of direction A O perpendicular to C A, one requires a power equal to the weight Q, which is to the weight A as C F is to C A, just as has been demonstrated; inasmuch as the line C A being firm, represents the arm of the balance B A. By the same means, the weight A no longer pulls with all its power against the line C A to which it is hung; but its power in this position is to its total power—<gloss>namely</gloss> that which it would have if it pulled through the line C L—as A F is to A C, by the first Corollary.

### COROLLARY III.

A weight falling by <term>force<note>Original: "violence." ### COROLLARY IV.

It is also clear that the <term>power<note>In this period, "power" (puissance) refers to the force applied to move or support a weight.</note></term> which supports a weight on an inclined plane is not to the weight itself as the angle of inclination is to a right angle; which, however, <term>Cardan<note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath. The author is critiquing Cardano's incorrect theory that the force needed to hold a weight on a slope is proportional to the angle of the slope.</note></term> intended to say in the 5th book of *Proportions*, Proposition 72. For there is a smaller ratio of the angle of inclination MLN to the right angle M, than of the perpendicular MN to the <term>hypotenuse<note>The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.</note></term> NL, and therefore the power that Cardan assigns us is less than what is required. 

And experience itself is entirely against Cardan. For example, at an inclination of thirty degrees, experience shows us that to support a weight, one requires a power that is half of the same weight: and yet according to Cardan it would suffice if the power were one-third of the weight, since an angle of thirty degrees is one-third of a right angle. Likewise, according to Cardan, at an inclination of 60 degrees, to support fifteen pounds one would only need ten pounds, and nonetheless experience will show that thirteen pounds, or very nearly, are required. 

Now experience agrees entirely with our demonstration, which we have tested, and which everyone can also test easily enough, having the proper instruments as we have. As for <term>Pappus<note>Pappus of Alexandria (c. 290 – c. 350 AD), a Greek mathematician. His "Mathematical Collection" was a primary source for Renaissance mechanics.</note></term>, who in the eighth book of his *Mathematical Collections*, ninth Proposition, wishes to demonstrate this Proposition (if it be true that it is by his own hand), he has succeeded very poorly, having produced only a <term>paralogism<note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note></term> instead of a demonstration: and experience in many cases is much more contrary to what he concludes than to what was concluded by Cardan.

### COROLLARY V.

One can also clearly see that less force is required to make a weight ascend by an inclined plane than by the perpendicular. But conversely, this weight will travel a longer path, and consequently will take more time to ascend by the inclined plane than by the perpendicular. And the time taken by the inclined plane will be to the time by the perpendicular as, conversely, the power pulling by the perpendicular is to the power pulling by the inclined plane.

It establishes that the force required to move a weight on a slope is proportional to the slope's dimensions, not its angle, and introduces the fundamental trade-off between force and distance (the Law of Simple Machines).</summary>

# Treatise on Mechanics.

For to make weight A rise perpendicularly from M to N, a <term>power<note>Original: "puissance." In early modern physics, this refers to the force or effort applied to a machine to move a load.</note></term> slightly greater than the weight itself is required; and to make it rise to the same height by the inclined plane LN, a power slightly greater than weight Q is required, which is less than weight A, according to the <term>ratio<note>Original: "raison." In 17th-century mathematics, "reason" or "ratio" refers to the proportional relationship between two values.</note></term> of line MN to line LN. But in compensation, the path LN along the inclined plane is longer than the path MN along the perpendicular. And since time is in proportion to the distance of the paths, it will take more time by the inclined plane LN than by the perpendicular MN, and the ratio will be as LM to MN—that is to say, as the weight A is to the power which supports that same weight on the inclined plane LN. Likewise, when two planes are unequally inclined, more force will be required to support or to lift a weight on the one where the angle of inclination is greater than on the one where the angle of inclination is smaller; but conversely, more distance and time will be required to climb to a certain height by the plane with the smaller angle of inclination than by the one with the greater angle of inclination. This is easy to demonstrate. Thus, in general, to make a weight rise on inclined planes, more time will be required in proportion as the power is lessened; which is found in all the ordinary instruments of Mechanics.

I am aware that in Practice, when it comes to making a weight rise by an inclined plane, many difficulties often arise from the nature of the material which oblige us to employ much more force than what is required by the preceding demonstration to support the same weight on the same plane. This may be because the plane is never perfect and resists the heavy body through its inequality <note>By "inequality," the author refers to surface roughness or friction.</note>, which for its part is also unequal; or because the wheels have difficulty turning, or the cords do not bend easily—not being perfectly flexible, nor without weight as we consider them in Theory—or for some other reason. But here our intention has only been to consider Mechanics in its purity, and as it would be if matter had no resistance of its own; the rest—namely, the difficulties that arise from the nature of matter—belong to another consideration. Furthermore, our Proposition is to find a power that can support a weight on an inclined plane, which we have satisfied. And when it comes to making the same weight rise on the plane, one must add to the power we have found enough force to overcome all the difficulties that will arise from the nature of the material.

# Treatise on Mechanics.

[The wedge] receives the same demonstrations as the inclined plane: but it has this convenience of being able to be assisted by the power of the Hammer, which is almost incomprehensible, and such that all other powers are almost nothing in comparison to it. Thus the wedge, assisted by the hammer, is the strongest instrument we have in Mechanics.

### PROPOSITION II.

> *When the line of direction by which a power supports a weight on an inclined plane is not parallel to the same plane; the inclination of the plane being given, and the weight; find the power.*

This Proposition has two cases, and a determination that must be explained before all else. To do this, let weight A be placed on the inclined plane L N z: let there also be the inclined <term>balance<note>Original: "balance." Here referring to a theoretical beam or lever used to calculate the equilibrium of forces.</note></term> C A N perpendicular to the same plane, and the horizontal balance C F, with the line A F perpendicular to C F, Y A O parallel to the plane L N z, and N M perpendicular to the horizontal plane L M, all as in the third figure. Further, from point N on the inclined plane L N z, let the perpendicular N T be raised, meeting the horizontal plane at point T, and let the same line T N be extended as far as A, the <term>center of gravity<note>Original: "centre de pesanteur." The point at which the weight of an object is balanced in all directions.</note></term> of the given weight A, so that the line T A can, when necessary, represent a cord, or a firm line. 

Now it is clear that if the line of direction by which a <term>power<note>Original: "puissance." In this context, the force or effort applied to hold the weight in place.</note></term> supports weight A is the line A F, which is the line of direction of the same weight, the power must be equal to the weight, by the second Axiom; and in this state, weight A being entirely supported by power F, it will no longer press upon the inclined plane L N z, according to common knowledge. It will also not press, all the more so, on the same inclined plane if the line of direction by which the power supports it is placed between A F and A Y, dividing the angle F A Y. For example, if the power pulls weight A by the line of direction I A, far from supporting the weight on the inclined plane, it will on the contrary cause it to descend and separate from the same plane, making it come below itself to support it freely by the line of direction of the same weight, which is clear enough in itself. 

Thus, the power that is to support weight A on the inclined plane L N z must not pull through a line of direction placed between A F and A Y. Nor must the line of direction of the power be A Y, nor between A Y and A T: for in this state the power would cause the weight to slide and descend on the inclined plane instead of supporting it, which is also clear; as if the power pulls through line A Z. Now we suppose that the plane offers no hindrance to line A Z, nor to others like it that cross through the same plane: and if this penetration shocks the imagination of those who do not wish to detach themselves from matter, let them imagine that the plane is open along the line L N z, specifically to provide passage for the cords we need to pull from beneath the plane; this is what we have done with the planes we use when we wish to have the pleasure of seeing experience make manifest to the senses those truths that reason had discovered and concluded beforehand. It must be understood likewise that the plane L N z offers no hindrance to the balance C A N. Finally

# Treatise on Mechanics.

...when the <term>power<note>Original: "puissance." In historical mechanics, this refers to the force or effort applied to a system.</note></term>, acting along line AT, pulls the weight perpendicularly against the plane LN 2, it certainly makes it press more firmly against that plane, but it does not take away its tendency to slide. Therefore, as this tendency remains in the weight without anything resisting it, the weight will slide—provided the plane is perfectly smooth—regardless of how great the power pulling it along the perpendicular line AT might be. This power contributes nothing toward making the weight move up or down the plane, as it uses all its force to make it press harder against the surface. We shall demonstrate this more fully in the fourth <term>Scholium<note>Original: "Scholie." An explanatory note or comment following a mathematical proof.</note></term> that follows. 

It remains then to examine two positions of the power. The first is when its <term>line of direction<note>The straight line along which a force is applied.</note></term> is between AF and AO, dividing the angle FAO, as if the line of direction were AQ and the power were at Q, or passing over a <term>pulley<note>Original: "poulie."</note></term> at E; this position constitutes the first case of the Proposition. The second position, which constitutes the second case, is when the line of direction is AR and the power is at R, or passing over a pulley at S. 

However, these two cases differ only in their geometric construction, for the demonstration is the same in both. Furthermore, if line QA is extended toward A as far as one wishes to point Z, and RA to point I, pushing weight A toward Q along the line of direction ZA is exactly the same as pulling it along line QA; likewise, pushing along line IA is the same as pulling along RA, according to the second <term>Axiom<note>A self-evident rule or principle used as a foundation for a logical argument.</note></term>. Thus, a single demonstration will serve for both pulling and pushing.

We must determine the value of this power Q or E. From point C on the line QA, let the perpendicular line CB be drawn; it will fall between points Q and A because the angles AQC and QAC are acute. This perpendicular CB will be "given" <note>In geometry, "given" means the value is known or can be determined from the existing setup.</note> because the triangle CAB is given—the line CA being fixed by the construction, angle B being a right angle, and angle CAB being the complement of angle BAO. Let it also be established that just as the given line BC is to the given line CF, so the given weight A is to the power Q or E, which shall then be known. I maintain that this power Q or E, found as we have just described, is the one required.

For let there be a power O which, pulling along the line AO parallel to the inclined plane LNz, sustains the weight A on the same plane, or on the <term>balance<note>Original: "balance." There is, therefore, the same ratio of power O to weight A as there is of line CF to line CA, according to the first Proposition. But the power Q or E, pulling along the line QA oblique to the arm of the balance CA, pulls in the same way as it would at the distance CB (representing the arm of the balance), according to the third <term>Axiom<note>A self-evident principle used as a starting point for the proof.</note></term>, to which distance CB the line of direction QBA is perpendicular. Since the power Q or E pulls perpendicularly upon the distance CB, and the power O also pulls perpendicularly upon the distance CA, and since the proportion is reciprocal—from power O to power Q or E, and from distance CB (by which power Q or E pulls) to distance CA (by which power O pulls)—the powers will pull equally. This is according to the sixth and seventh Propositions of the first book of the *Mechanics* of Archimedes <note>Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), whose work "On the Equilibrium of Planes" established the law of the lever.</note>, or by what can easily be deduced from them, as we have done in our own *Mechanics* in two entirely different ways. 

But the power O, pulling at the distance CA, maintains the balance CA in equilibrium with the weight A placed on the inclined plane LNz, and prevents it from sliding down the plane, according to the first Proposition. Therefore, the power Q or E, pulling at the distance CB or CA, will likewise maintain the balance CA in equilibrium and prevent the weight A from sliding. And since the cord QA is attached to the <term>center of gravity<note>The point where the weight of the object is balanced in all directions.</note></term> A, it will "unload" the balance, which by this means no longer presses upon its center and becomes unnecessary according to the fifth Axiom. Consequently, the power Q or E, pulling by the cord QA, sustains the given weight A on the plane LNz, whose angle of inclination NLM is given; and the power Q or E is determined, which is what was required.
