Therefore, etc., as before.

### SCHOLIUM I.
<note>A "Scholium" is an explanatory note or remark added to a mathematical or scientific proof to provide further context or practical application.</note>

In this Proposition, and particularly in the second case, there is one thing that might at first appear strange to many: which is that the position of the line RA could be such that the perpendicular CI would be equal to CF, or less than CF in any given <term>ratio<note>Original: "raison." The mathematical relationship between two quantities.</note></term> one might wish. Consequently, the weight A could be equal to the power R or S, or even less than that same power in whatever ratio one chooses. Thus, a greater power than the weight A would be required to sustain the same weight upon the inclined plane LNz when pulling or pushing along a line of direction that is not parallel to the plane itself. 

But as reason has concluded it, so will experience make it apparent to the senses of those who wish to test it, and who have the proper instruments to do so. The matter only appears strange because it has not been considered before and is not commonly practiced. Nature, through a blind knowledge, always leads us to pull or push along lines of direction parallel to the plane upon which we move a weight; this is because along these parallel lines, less force is required than along others, which shall be proven momentarily. Add to this that there is usually more convenience in the practice of pulling or pushing along lines parallel to the plane than along others which are not parallel to it.

## COROLLARY.

Since in the first case of this <term>Scholium<note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary added to a mathematical or philosophical text to clarify a proof.</note></term> it has been demonstrated that the <term>power<note>In early modern physics, "power" (puissance) refers to what we now call force or effort applied to a system.</note></term> is greater as its line of direction approaches the line AF, which is the limit beyond which the powers are useful on that side, according to the determination of the second Proposition; and that the power which pulls through AF must be equal to the weight, by the second Axiome; it is clear that the other powers will always be less than the same weight. But in the second case of this same Scholium, since it has been demonstrated that the power is greater as its line of direction approaches the line AT perpendicular to the inclined plane; which line AT is the limit beyond which the powers are useless on that side, by the determination of the second Proposition; it is clear, by <term>common knowledge<note>Original: "commune cognoissance." This refers to a "common notion" or axiom that is self-evidently true.</note></term>, that on that side, the line AT is the one through which the greatest power of all would be required, in order to, by pulling through it, support the weight A on the inclined plane LN 2.

### COROLLARY.

Since it is the same to push by the **line CA** as to pull by the **line AT**, it is clear that there will be no finite power which, pushing by the **line CA**, prevents the **weight A** from sliding on the **inclined plane LN 2**. Therefore, even if there were another plane parallel to the **plane LN 2**, such as the **plane 21-22**, between which and the **plane LN 2** the **weight A** were compressed by whatever force one might wish, if the planes were perfectly flat, the weight would not fail to slide, insofar as the **plane 21-22** by pressing produces the same effect as the power which would press along the line of direction **CA**, which does not prevent the weight from sliding. And even if the two planes were not inclined, but perpendicular to the horizon, the same effect would follow with even greater reason.

### ADVISORY.

It is true that in practice there is no way to experience what we have just demonstrated in this fourth Scholium, and in its Corollary, because we have no **perfect plane**: and the inequalities that are encountered in ordinary planes create small eminences and cavities, which being inserted into one another, prevent the sliding, which cannot happen without <term>collision<note>The physical impact or "bumping" of the microscopic irregularities on two surfaces as they move against each other.</note></term> and the breaking of the small parts of the bodies that touch. This collision brings resistance, and therefore some power is required to overcome this resistance, which would not happen on a perfect plane. And the more the inequality of the surfaces is great, or the surfaces are pressed one against the other, the more there are parts inserted into one another, and more deeply, and therefore the collision is that much greater, and the resistance to sliding greater, to overcome which one needs that much more power. Also, experience shows us that two bodies of which the surfaces are unequal, coming to be rubbed one against the other by a continual collision, the eminences are broken, the

In the following discourse, we take for "two cords" not only those which are actually and in fact separate; but also a single cord which forms an angle: for the two portions contained between the angle and each of the two ends of the cord represent two different cords tied together at the vertex of the angle. ...either by one power and the other by another, or by supports in two different places; the other ends of these cords meet and form an angle, at the vertex of which is hung a given weight, and the position of each cord is given: one asks for each of the powers, assuming that the two together sustain the weight; or, what is the same thing, one asks what resistance each of the supports brings in sustaining the weight by the given cords.

Let there be, then, the weight A, of which the line of direction <note>The vertical line through the center of gravity along which the weight acts.</note> is AF, and let one of the given cords CA be held by the support, or the power C; and let the cord CA make with the line FA the given acute angle CAF; and let the line CF be drawn perpendicular to the line of direction AF, which CF shall be prolonged toward F as much as necessary. This being established, the other cord, which along with cord CA sustains the weight A, must be in the same plane as the triangle CAF, otherwise the weight would not remain in that state: which we assume to be known. It is also necessary that the other cord be, with respect to the line of direction AF, on the other side of the line AC—such as AQ, AO, or AR, etc. For if the two cords were on the same side of the line AF, the weight would not remain still, but would change position and come to rest directly under the cord closest to the line of direction. And if the cord were FA itself, it would sustain the weight entirely on its own, without need for another: which we also assume to be known. Furthermore, the other cord will form with cord CA an acute angle, a right angle, or an obtuse angle.

Let it first make a given acute angle, which shall be angle CAQ, the cord being AQE, and its power Q or E; and the other power being C or K pulling by the cord ACK. From point Q, let the line QD be drawn perpendicular to the line of direction AF, and the line QG perpendicular to the cord CA: and let QD be prolonged until it meets the cord AC at point 4. Also let CB be perpendicular to the cord AQ. Now, by the 2nd Proposition, we have seen that if CA is the arm of a balance <note>The author uses "balance" here to mean a lever or a physical beam used to calculate forces.</note> upon which the weight A is held by the cord CA so that it does not slide along the arm CA: and that as CB is to CF, so the weight A is to the power Q or E pulling by the cord QA, this power Q or E will hold the balance CA in equilibrium; and the cord QA being attached to the center of the weight A, the balance will remain unloaded, and the weight A will be sustained partly by the power Q or E, and partly by the plane LN 2 perpendicular to the balance CA; or in place of the plane LN 2, by the cord CA, according to the <term>Scholium<note>original: "Scholie"; an explanatory note or commentary.</note></term> of the 4th Axiom. Thus, by this means, the power Q or E is found.

By the same means, and by the same discourse as the 2nd Proposition, if QA is taken for the arm of a balance, upon which the weight A is placed and held by the cord QA so that it does not slide on the arm QA: and that as GQ is to QD, so the weight A is to the power C or K—this power C or K pulling by the cord CA will hold the balance QA in equilibrium; and the cord CA being attached to the center of the weight A, the balance A will remain unloaded, and the weight A will be sustained partly by the power C or K pulling by the cord CA, and partly by the cord QA. Now, since the angle GAQ is given, and the cords AQ and AC, with the angles CAF and QAD, the perpendiculars CB, QG, CF, and QD are given, and their ratios also given; and consequently the ratios of the given weight A to the powers Q or E, and C or K; which powers, as a result, will be given; and they sustain the weight A by the cords QA and CA, which is what was requested.

### COROLLARY I.

From what has been demonstrated in this <term>Scholium: A marginal note or explanatory comment used in historical texts to clarify a mathematical proof.</term>, it is clear that the weight is <term>homologous: In this geometric context, it means that the line representing the weight and the lines representing the forces have the same proportional relationship as the sides of the triangles being discussed.</term> to the line drawn from one power to the other: namely, in the first and third cases, to the line C Q; and in the second case, to the line C 3. Furthermore, the powers are reciprocally homologous to the lines drawn from those same powers to the point where the perpendiculars of the triangle meet. For instance, in the first case, where the weight is A and the powers are C and Q, and the intersection point of the perpendiculars is V: power C is homologous to the line Q V, and power Q is homologous to the line C V. In the second case, where the weight is A and the powers are C and 3, and the intersection point of the perpendiculars is A: power C is homologous to line 3 A, and power 3 is homologous to line C A. And in the third case, where the weight is V and the powers are C and Q, and the intersection point of the perpendiculars is A: power C is homologous to line Q A, and power Q is homologous to line C A. This is easy to observe through the demonstration in the same Scholium. Thus, the first power is homologous to the line drawn from the second power to the intersection of the three perpendiculars of the triangle; and conversely, etc.

### COROLLARY II.

By the demonstration of the same Scholium, it further appears that the weight is always less than the two powers combined, as the weight is homologous to one side of a triangle, and the two powers are homologous to the other two sides <note>This refers to the triangle inequality theorem: the sum of any two sides of a triangle must be greater than the third side.</note>. And even when one of the cords, such as R A, cannot meet the line C F extended toward F, it will still be demonstrated that the weight will be less than the two powers combined; indeed, in this case, it will even be less than power C alone, since the perpendicular R H (to which the weight is homologous) is less than the perpendicular R P (to which power C is homologous).

### COROLLARY III.

There is another noteworthy thing here: namely, the reciprocity of the triangles C A Q and C V Q. These are such that V is the intersection point of the perpendiculars of triangle C A Q; and conversely, point A is the intersection of the perpendiculars of triangle C V Q. Angle C A Q is acute, while C V Q is obtuse, and the two together equal two right angles <note>Meaning they are supplementary, adding up to 180 degrees.</note>. For when the weight is A, being homologous to line C Q, the powers C and Q are homologous to lines Q V and C V. And when the weight is V, also being homologous to line C Q, the powers C and Q are homologous to lines Q A and C A. Thus, the cords of one triangle form the lines homologous to the powers of the other reciprocally; which is demonstrated.

## SCHOLIUM II.

In the preceding <term>Scholium: An explanatory note or remark added to a mathematical or scientific text to clarify a proof.</term>, we showed that in all cases where the two cords supporting the weight—being extended, if necessary—meet with line CF, which is perpendicular to the line of direction AF, one on one side and the other on the other side of point F; the weight and the two powers were <term>homologous: Meaning 'corresponding' or 'proportional.' In this context, it means the magnitude of the force is proportional to the length of the side of the triangle.</term> to the three sides of a triangle. But in this second Scholium, we will demonstrate in general that whatever the arrangement of the weight and the powers supporting it on two cords—provided the cords are not in a straight line with each other—the weight and the two powers are always homologous to the three sides of a triangle. 

To perform this demonstration in general, there are three cases: the first is when the angle formed by the cords is acute; the second, when it is right; and the third, when it is obtuse. In the first case, let the cords be CA and AQ, forming the acute angle CAQ; let there also be the weight A, its line of direction AF, the perpendiculars CF, CB, QG, QD, and the rest as in the first case of the third Proposition, and let lines FB and GD be drawn. I assert that the triangles CFB and QDG are similar, and that to the three sides of whichever of the two one chooses, the weight A and the two powers C and Q (which support the same weight A on the cords CA and QA) are homologous. 

For since the angles CFA and CBA are right angles, the four-sided figure CFBA <note>The author is describing a cyclic quadrilateral, a shape whose corners all touch the edge of a circle. This allows him to use specific geometric rules about angles.</note> will be inscribable in a circle; therefore, angle CBF will be equal to angle CAF, and angle FCB equal to angle FAB. By the same reasoning, the figure QDGA will be inscribable in a circle; thus, angle QGD will be equal to angle QAD, and angle GQD equal to angle GAD. Consequently, since angle CBF of triangle CBF and angle GQD of triangle GQD are equal to the same thing—namely to CAF or GAD—it follows that angles CBF and GQD are equal to each other. By the same means, angle FCB of triangle FCB will be equal to angle QGD of triangle QGD, both being equal to angle FAB or QAD. Thus, the two angles CBF and FCB of triangle CBF being equal to the two angles GQD and QGD of triangle QGD respectively, these two triangles CFB and QGD will be similar. 

Therefore, BC will be to CF as QG is to GD; and BC will be to BF as QG is to QD. But as BC is to CF, so is weight A to power Q by the third Proposition, and by the same Proposition, QG is to QD as weight A is to power C; therefore, QG will also be to GD as weight A is to power Q; and BC will be to BF as weight A is to power C. It is therefore clear that in triangle CBF, the weight A being homologous to line CB, power Q will be homologous to line CF, and power C will be homologous to line BF. And that in triangle QGD, the weight A being homologous to line QG, power C will be homologous to line QD, and power Q homologous to line GD.

In the third case, let the cords *CA* and *AR* support weight *A* and form the obtuse angle *CAR*, with the rest of the construction being as in the third case of the third Proposition; let lines *HP* and *FI* be drawn. I assert that the triangles *RHP* and *CFI* are similar, and that the weight *A* and the powers *C* and *R* (which support the same weight *A* on the cords *CA* and *AR*) are homologous to the three sides of whichever of the two triangles one chooses. For it will be easily demonstrated that triangles *RHP* and *CIF* are similar because the four-sided figures *RHPA* and *CIAF* can each be inscribed in a circle; therefore, the angles *HRP*, *HAP*, *CAF*, and *CIF* are all equal to one another. But as *RH* is to *RP*, so weight *A* is to power *C*; and as *CI* is to *CF*, so weight *A* is to power *R*, all by the third Proposition; hence *RH* is to *HP* as weight *A* is to power *R*, and *CI* is to *IF* as weight *A* is to power *C*. It is therefore clear that in triangle *RHP*, weight *A* being homologous to side *RH*, power *C* will be homologous to side *RP*, and power *R* homologous to side *HP*. Likewise, in triangle *CFI*, side *CI* being homologous to weight *A*, *CF* will be homologous to power *R*, and *FI* homologous to power *C*. Therefore, in all cases, the weight and the two powers are always homologous to the three sides of a triangle. This triangle is formed by the two perpendiculars falling from the same power—one upon the line of direction of the weight, the other upon the cord of the other power—and by the line drawn from one of these perpendiculars to the other. Furthermore, if from any point taken on the line of direction of the weight, one draws a line parallel to one of the cords up to the other cord, the triangle formed by this parallel, the line of direction, and the cord will be similar to the aforementioned triangle, and consequently its sides will be homologous to the weight and the two powers; this a <term>Geometer: A mathematician or scholar of geometry.</term> will easily prove, along with several other properties that we shall leave aside.

### COROLLARY.

It follows that not only are the two powers together greater than the weight, but also that the weight taken with one of the powers will be greater than the other power; this is because the weight and the two powers are homologous to the three sides of a triangle, any two of which, taken as you wish, are greater than the third <note>This is a reference to the triangle inequality theorem: the sum of any two sides of a triangle must be greater than the third.</note>.

### SCHOLIUM III.

The <term>powers: In this context, "powers" (puissances) refers to the forces or tensions applied to the cords to balance the weight.</term> remaining in the same locations, and the weight always being the same, and within the same <term>line of direction: The vertical path along which the force of gravity acts on the weight.</term>; when the angle comprised by the cords which support the weight is larger, larger powers will be required to support the same weight by those same cords.

This is easily demonstrated following the preceding Proposition, the first Scholium, and its Corollaries. For in the case where both cords can meet with the line *CF* extended toward *F*, the larger the angle comprised by the cords, the further the point of the meeting of the perpendiculars will be from point *F*; and consequently the lines drawn from the powers to this meeting point will be longer. For example, if the powers are *C* and *Q*, and the angle comprised by the cords is *CAQ*, the meeting of the perpendiculars will be *V*, and the lines drawn from the powers to the meeting point will be *CV* and *QV*. However, if the powers are still *C* and *Q*, but the angle *CVQ* is larger than the angle *CAQ*, the meeting of the perpendiculars will be at point *A*, which is further from point *F* than point *V* is; and the lines drawn from the powers to the meeting point will be *CA* and *QA*, which are longer than the lines *CV* and *QV*. Now, the line *CQ* is always <term>homologous: Meaning "proportional" or "corresponding in ratio."</term> to the weight; and the lines drawn from the powers to the meeting point of the perpendiculars are reciprocally homologous to those same powers. Therefore, the angle of the cords being larger—and consequently the lines drawn from the powers to the meeting point being larger—**the powers will also be larger.** 

But in the case where one of the cords does not meet the line *CF* extended, such as when one of the cords is *CA* and the other is *AR*, the angle *CAR* is necessarily obtuse <note>An angle greater than 90 degrees.</note>; therefore, the larger this angle becomes, the more acute <note>An angle less than 90 degrees.</note> the angle *CAI* will be, and the shorter the perpendicular *CI* will be; and consequently there will be a greater ratio of *CF* (which always remains the same) to *CI*. But *CF* is homologous to the power *R*, and *CI* is homologous to the weight; therefore, there will also be a proportionately greater ratio of the power *R* to the weight; and thus the power *R* will be that much larger. Similarly, the larger the obtuse angle *CAR* becomes, the more acute the angle *RAH* will be, and the shorter the perpendicular *RH* will be; and consequently there will be a greater ratio of *RP* (which always remains the same) to *RH*. But *RP* is homologous to the power *C*, and *RH* is homologous to the weight; therefore, there will also be a proportionately greater ratio of the power *C* to the weight; and thus the power *C* will be that much larger.

---

### COROLLARY.

Since, in whatever position the weight and the powers may be, the powers being outside the line of direction of the weight must be larger as the angle comprised by the cords is large; and since the larger the angle, the closer the cords come to forming a single straight line between them, it is clear by common knowledge that the largest powers of all will be those required when the cords form a single straight line between them, in whatever position the weight and the powers may be, provided that the same powers are outside the line of direction of the weight, one on one side and the other on the other, of that same line of direction.

## SCHOLIUM IV.

### PROBLEM.

Of two <term>powers: In 17th-century mechanics, "powers" refers to the forces or tensions applied to cords to balance a weight.</term> that support a given weight, one being given; the position, or the location of each of the two; and the <term>line of direction: The vertical path along which gravity pulls a weight downward.</term> of the weight being given by its position between the locations of the two powers; find the other power; and the location where the weight must be placed in its line of direction to be supported by the two powers on two cords.

Let **C** and **R** be the locations of the two powers, of which power **C** is given as large as one wishes; let there also be a given weight as one wishes, of which the line of direction is **F A**, given by its position between the locations of the two powers **C** and **R**: it is necessary to find within the line **F A** the location of the given weight, and the other power **R**, so that the two powers **C** and **R** support the same weight hanging on two cords at the location that will have been found. Let the line **CR** be drawn, and from the two points **C** and **R** on the line **F A**, let perpendicular lines **CF** and **RP** be drawn: and let it be done so that as power **C** is to the given weight, so the perpendicular **RP** (namely, that of the unknown power upon the line of direction) is to some line parallel to **CF**, such as **R 9**. Let also the line **R-9-8** be equal to the two perpendiculars **RP** and **CF** taken together; and let us suppose that **R 9** is less than **R 8**; then from center **R**, and with the <note>original: "interualle" - here meaning the radius</note> of the line **R 9**, one shall describe the circle **H-9-5-6**; and from point **C** one shall draw a line that touches the same circle at point **H** below the line **CR**; at which point **H** let the line **RH** be drawn perpendicular to the line **CH**. Now the line **CH** extended, if necessary, will intersect **F A** (because the radius of the circle **R 9** is less than **R 8**); let it therefore intersect it at point **A**, and let the cords **RA** and **CA** be drawn, from which the given weight is hung at point **A**; and on the cord **RA** extended, if necessary, let the perpendicular **CL** be drawn; and let it be done so that as **CL** <note>The original text uses "CI" in the ratio, but "CL" in the construction; CL is the geometrically consistent term.</note> is to **CF**, so the given weight is to the power **R**. It is clear by the preceding proposition that the powers **C** and **R** will support the given weight **A** just as it is on the cords **CA** and **RA**. If the line **R 9** found as above were equal to both **RP** and **CF** together, that is to say, to the line **R 8**, the line which from point **C** would touch the circle would be **C 8** parallel to the line of direction **F A**; and therefore the Problem would be impossible. For otherwise, if it were possible, let the weight be at **A**, arranged in its line **F A**, and supported by the powers **C** and **R** on the cords **CA** and **AR**: therefore, as it was demonstrated in the preceding proposition, power **C** will be to weight **A** as **RP** is to **RH**; but by the construction, power **C** is to the same weight **A** as **RP** is to a line equal to both **RP** and **CF** taken together, that is to say to **R 8**, therefore **RH** would be equal to **R 8**, which is absurd, the weight **A** being in the line **F A**, according to the proposition.

If **R 9** is larger than **R 8**, the Problem will still be impossible: otherwise the absurdity would be that **RH** would be larger than **R 8**.

## COROLLARY II.

It is also clear that the <term>cords: The strings or ropes from which the weight is suspended.</term> will never come into one and the same straight line, whatever the powers C & R might be. For insofar as the line CA touches the circle below the line CR, it will always happen that point A, which is in the line FA (which passes between C & R, by supposition), will be below the line CR, and therefore the cords will form the angle CAR below the line CR: which will happen the same in any other position of the power R, O, or Q, etc.

### <term>SCHOLIUM: An explanatory note or remark added to a mathematical or scientific proof.</term> VI.

At the beginning of the third Proposition, we supposed that the angle CAF was acute: which we did because, of the two angles that the cords make with the line of direction FA <note>The "line of direction" refers to the vertical path along which gravity pulls the weight.</note>, one must always be acute; otherwise, both would be obtuse, or one right and the other obtuse, or both right. Now, both cannot be obtuse, the cords being perfectly flexible, as we suppose them to be. For if one of the cords were AY making the obtuse angle FAY, and the other cord AT making the obtuse angle FAT, the weight being A and the powers Y and T, then by common knowledge, far from the powers and their cords supporting the weight A, they would instead pull it down. It will be the same if one of the angles is right and the other obtuse. Therefore, the whole difficulty comes down to this: namely, whether both angles that the cords make with the line of direction FA can be right angles, in which case the two cords would form a straight line with each other, by the 14th Proposition of the 1st book of Euclid <note>Euclid’s Elements, Book 1, Proposition 14 states that if two adjacent angles equal two right angles, the remaining sides form a single straight line.</note>, which is impossible.

For, if it were possible, let one of the cords be CF, the other QF, the weight F, and the powers C and Q, the two angles CFA and QFA being right angles to the line of direction FA, and let the powers C and Q support the weight F on the straight cord CFQ. Then, by the preceding 4th Scholium, given the weight F and its line of direction FA, along with the locations of the powers C and Q, one could find a place on the line FA where the weight F, being placed, would be supported on two cords by two powers, one of which would be as great as one wished—even greater than the two powers C and Q taken together, which are claimed to support the weight A. Let this place be V, at which the weight, being placed, is supported on the cords CV and QV by two powers, one of which (let us call it 4 <note>Likely a label for a specific force, possibly a misprint for a letter like 'H'.</note>) is as many times larger than the two powers C and Q taken together as one wishes. Now, the cords will form an angle below the line CQ by the 2nd Corollary of the preceding 4th Scholium, which angle let be CVQ. Therefore, the powers 4 and Q which support a weight by the cords CQ and QV (which form an angle at point V) would be much greater than the powers C and Q which support the same weight on the cords CF and FQ positioned in a straight line; which is absurd, by the <term>Corollary: A proposition that follows naturally from one already proved.</term> of the 3rd Scholium of the 3rd Proposition. And therefore it is also absurd that any two powers C and Q, whatever they may be, could support the weight F on the straight cord CFQ. Thus, the angles that the cords make with the line of direction of the weight can be neither both right, nor both obtuse, nor one right and the other obtuse; it remains

By the same reasoning, it will be demonstrated that a weight cannot be supported by a perfectly flexible straight cord, regardless of the forces pulling on the ends of the cord, and regardless of the position of that same cord—provided that it is not aligned with the <term>line of direction: The vertical path along which gravity pulls a weight.</term> of the weight. For example, if the cord is C A T, the forces are C and T, and the weight is A; the forces C and T, no matter how great they are, will be unable to support the weight A upon the straight cord C A T.

### COROLLARY.

If a cord is straight and perfectly flexible, and if one places a weight or any force upon it, the cord cannot remain straight; instead, either the forces holding the ends of the cord must give way, whatever they may be, or the cord must stretch, or it must break, unless it is infinitely strong. This is what experience shows us every day with cords, even those that are not perfectly flexible, such as those of musical instruments. Even though these strings are tightened with as much force as one likes, an extremely small force makes them bend, and thereby sound <note>By "sound," the author refers to the vibration caused when a string is plucked or bowed, which requires the string to be displaced from its straight rest position.</note>. The same thing is seen with <term>tightrope dancers: Referred to in the original as "Danceurs de chordes."</term>, whose rope bends as soon as they step upon it, even though it is tightened with great force and is not naturally very flexible. We also see the same thing with the horses that pull a boat up a river; although they are often numerous and strong, they cannot make the rope by which they pull become a perfectly straight line. To prevent tightened cords attached to <term>anchor points: The original uses "arrests," referring to fixed points or stops.</term> from breaking every time they are pulled, nature has made all—or most—of them capable of stretching; thus, by yielding to the force that pulls them, they are better preserved. When they reach a state where they can no longer stretch, they break at the slightest pull.

### SCHOLIUM VII.

From the above, one can learn how to construct a very simple instrument by means of which a single force can support a very great burden. Let C and Q be two pulleys over which the cord K C Q E passes. At the two ends of this cord, let the weights K and E be hung, and let there be a force F pulling the cord C Q along the line of direction F A, perpendicular to the same cord C Q. It is clear that if the cord is flexible at the points of the pulleys C and Q, and is of such a nature that it cannot stretch, the force F pulling it toward A will cause it to bend. Consequently, by making it pass over the pulleys, it will cause the weights K and E to rise a certain distance. However, this distance is often very small, and at the beginning, the force descends much further than the weights rise. For this reason, to raise the weights very high, one would have to do it in several stages. Therefore, this instrument would serve best in cases where it is only necessary to pull or tear away <note>The author suggests this setup is ideal for "uprooting" or "tearing" (arrachant), where a massive initial force is needed to break something loose rather than moving it a long distance.</note> a body that is attached to another, since its principal force lies at the very beginning, which is what is required for such a task. To prevent the cord C Q from stretching—which could especially undermine the strength of the instrument—one could make it out of a chain.

I will say further that at the junction F, there being two rings, one could join them by a third ring made in the shape of a wedge with the point facing upward—let this wedge be very long and sharp—and at its lower part, let a cord be attached by which the power pulls from F toward A, which will help greatly. And when C is a fixed point and Q a pulley, if one takes a lever whose <term>fulcrum: The author uses "arreſt" here to describe the pivot point of the lever.</term> is C, to which lever is attached the wedge-shaped ring that is at F, and let the lever be as much longer than CF as possible toward Q, then since the power weighs or pulls perpendicularly on the end of the lever that is toward Q, this will create a nearly invincible force for tearing things out. This is even more effective if the power used to pull the end of the lever employs a wheel and axle, or a screw, as is seen in some <term>presses: Likely referring to wine or oil presses that use massive mechanical advantage.</term>. But it is necessary, before pulling, to have the cord CQ tightened as much as possible, so that it cannot, by stretching, elude the greatest vigor of the instrument, which vigor is at the beginning. It is also necessary that the pillars supporting the pulleys and the fixed points be seated upon a firm foundation that cannot sink, so that the pulleys or fixed points cannot change place. Therefore, this instrument will be of no use on a vessel floating on the water. Furthermore, it can serve just as well being positioned flat as being elevated above the Horizon, and it does not matter if the power pulling the cord CFQ along the line of direction FA pulls toward A, or on the contrary toward point B; for the same effect will always follow.

## SCHOLIUM VIII.

We have observed, regarding the subject of a weight hanging from two cords, a thing that has pleased us greatly; it is such that when the weight is thus supported by two powers—the ratios being as demonstrated in the 3rd Proposition—the weight cannot rise or fall without the reciprocal proportion of the paths of the weight and the powers being changed, contrary to the common order. 3rd Prop. or as C Q is to the lines Q C and Q V, according to the first <term>Scholium: An explanatory note or remark added to a mathematical or scientific text.</term> of the same Prop. if below the weight A, along its line of direction, one takes a line such as A P, it will happen that if weight A descends as far as P, pulling the cords with it and causing the <term>powers: The forces or efforts applied to move or balance a weight.</term> K and E to rise, there will reciprocally be a greater ratio of the distance the powers travel while rising to the distance the weight travels while descending, than of the weight itself to the two powers taken together; thus the powers would rise more in proportion than the weight would descend in carrying them, which is against the <note>original: "l'ordre commun"</note> common order. If above the weight A, along its line of direction, one takes a line such as A V, and the weight rises as far as V, the rising cords also being carried by the powers K and E which descend, there will reciprocally be a greater ratio of the distance the weight travels while rising to the distance the powers travel while descending, than of the two powers taken together to the weight: thus the weight would rise more in proportion than the powers would descend in carrying it, which is again against the common order, in which the weight or the power that carries the other always travels a greater distance in proportion than the weight or the power that is carried. Now, that the ratios of the distances that weight A and its powers would travel in rising and descending are such as we have just described, and against the common order, the proof of this will be found in our *Mechanics*, for it is too long to be included here. Therefore, weight A, by subsisting and remaining in its place according to the arguments of the 3rd Prop., also remains within the common order, which is what we wished to remark.

### SCHOLIUM IX.

When a weight is hung freely from a cord, and one wishes to move it to the side to a designated place which it can reach while remaining suspended from its cord, one can easily find the required power, for which even the position will be assigned. For let weight A, having been freely hung by a cord attached at point C, be moved as far as A, the cord being C A. If one then asks for the <note>meaning the "minimum force"</note> least power of all those that can move the weight to the designated place A, it is clear that it will be the one pulling along the line A O 3 perpendicular to the cord C A, which power will be O or 3, as was demonstrated in the Scholium of the 2nd Prop. For the same force is required as to support the weight on the inclined plane L N 2, in place of which the cord C A is substituted by the Scholium of the 3rd axiom; or, what is the same, the same force is required as to hold the <term>balance: Here referring to a state of equilibrium in a mechanical system.</term> C A in equilibrium, pulling by the cord A O 3, which power is less than if one pulls by another cord, such as cord A Q or A R. But if the location of the power is assigned, such as Q, O, or R; then the power Q, O, or R will be found by the 3rd Prop., seeing that there are two cords C A and Q A or R A supporting weight A. It can also be demonstrated without looking further that the power O, or 3, is the least of all those that can support weight A in its current state. For let there be another power Q, or R, of which we have so often spoken. Thus weight A is to power O as A C is to C F, and weight A is to power Q as B C is to C F; and weight A is to power R as C I is to C F, by the 3rd Prop. But the ratio of C A to C F is greater than that of C B to C F, or of C I to C F, since A C is longer than C B or C I; therefore the ratio of weight A to power O is greater than that of the same weight A to power Q, or R; and consequently power O is less than power Q, or R.

->THE END.<-

# Preface to the Reader.

The books on the **Voice** and on **Songs** which follow may inspire many fine minds to treat the same subject more fully and precisely; and the rough sketch I have drawn of it will serve to add luster to more perfect works. For there is almost no Proposition in these Treatises from which one could not create an entire book. For example, if one wished to express all the monosyllabic <term>words of a single syllable</term> utterances, and those of which I speak in the 44th Proposition of the book on the **Voice**, and if one wished to give them meaning following the primacy and excellence of the things that constitute being, it would require more than a hundred reams of paper. Regarding this, one may look at the German, Greek, and Latin monosyllables that Stevin <note>Simon Stevin (1548–1620), a Flemish mathematician who argued that languages with many monosyllables, like Dutch, were superior for expressing complex thoughts.</note> placed at the beginning of his *Geography*, to show a sample of the idiom of the age, which he calls *sage* <note>original: "sage" (wise). Stevin believed in a lost "Age of Sages" where knowledge was perfect.</note>, and whose language would be restored by our 47th Proposition. As for the utterances in the 48th Proposition, they could not be contained in as many reams of paper as there are grains of sand in the sea. The 43rd Proposition similarly deserves a particular treatise, as do the 50th, 51st, 52nd, and 53rd.

I have omitted several things concerning the **Voice**; for example, that those who cannot speak because of holes which sometimes form in the upper palate <note>Mersenne is referring to cleft palates or injuries to the roof of the mouth.</note> may recover their speech by plugging the said holes with a piece of linen or cotton; that there is a way to correct stammerers, and to make them lose their stuttering if they accustom themselves to speaking as slowly as those who sing. There are a thousand other difficulties regarding the **Voice** and hearing of which one could make entire volumes: for example, that one can create an artificial tongue to repair the defect of a natural one that has been cut, just as one makes use of silver or ivory teeth, etc. And if one wished to discourse upon all the ways of deceiving the eye and the ear, of which I speak in the final Proposition, it would be necessary to explain the whole of **Perspective** <note>In the 17th century, "Perspective" often referred broadly to the science of optics and how light—and by extension, sound—travels.</note> and compare it to the accidents and properties of sound and the ear.

The book on **Songs** contains many more very useful and remarkable things, for the tables of **Combinations** <term>combinatorics; the mathematical study of counting and arranging sets</term> can be applied to an infinity of things, and will greatly assist those who have operations to perform which require the said tables, of which the one in the eighth Proposition is very laborious. The 9th Proposition teaches how to sing everything comprised within *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la* <note>The traditional "hexachord" system of musical notes used before the modern "Do-Re-Mi" system was fully established.</note>. The 10th shows the Art of making **Anagrams**. The 13th, 14th, 15th, and 16th show how one can read and write letters whose deciphering is impossible unless one uses the powers <note>original: "dignités." In early mathematics, this referred to the degrees or powers of algebraic variables.</note> of **Algebra**; and the others teach in how many ways all sorts of **Songs** can be varied in whatever manner one might take them. As for the 13th Proposition, it shows the manner of composing whatever idiom <note>language or dialect</note> one might wish; for example, if it were true that the mother and universal tongue, from which the others depend, had all its roots consisting of three letters—as occurs in **Hebrew**—the 4th number of the table of all possible utterances, which I have placed in the said Proposition, shows that there are 10,648 roots, or primitive words, in that language, which...

# BOOK ONE

->*OF THE VOICE, THE PARTS WHICH SERVE*<-
->*to form it, of its definition, its properties,*<-
->*& of Hearing.*<-

<image-desc>An ornamental drop-cap letter Q, decorated with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

SOME believe that the number of the Muses was taken from the number of parts that help to form the voice, of which one of the most necessary is called the *lung*, which pushes the air it had drawn in; this is what we call *inhaling* and *exhaling*. The windpipe <note>original: "aspre artere." From the Latin *aspera arteria*, an old anatomical term for the trachea, so named because of its rough, cartilaginous rings.</note> is the second part, which serves as a channel and conduit for the wind. The larynx follows after, the opening of which is called the *glottis*, or *reed* <note>original: "languette." Literally "little tongue," referring here to the reed of a woodwind instrument.</note>, which resembles the reed of flutes. The fourth is the palate, the concavity of which makes the air, or the sound, resonate. The fifth is called the *uvula* <note>original: "gargareon." A term derived from Greek used in early anatomy for the uvula.</note>; and the sixth is the tongue, which forms speech through its movement. In the seventh place, the four front teeth serve to form the voice through the different encounters of the tongue which strikes them. Air is the eighth thing, without which all the other parts would be of no use. And the mouth is the final part, whose lips form most of the letters that we call Consonants, and particularly those that the Hebrews call *labials*, as we shall say elsewhere. As for the name of the Muses, it took its origin from Music, and Music took its own from the Greek verb *to seek* <note>original: "μάω" (maō). Ancient etymologists often linked the Muses to this root, suggesting they represent the search for knowledge.</note>.

Now, to understand briefly and clearly everything that belongs to the Voice, one must first explain its efficient cause <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; essentially, the "maker" or "trigger" of an action.</note>, and the instruments and organs that serve to form it. Secondly, what its formal cause or its definition is; and then what its properties are, its effects, its ailments, and several other things that will be seen in the following Propositions.

## FIRST PROPOSITION.

->*The faculty or motor power of the soul is the principal and first cause of the voice*<-
->*of animals, and has its seat in the tendons.*<-

I do not wish to amuse myself by explaining the number of faculties and powers of the soul, for I suppose that one understands ordinary Philosophy; I will only say that the soul of animals has the strength and the power to move all the parts

### BOOK FIRST

of the body which it informs, just as it has the power to see, to hear, and to perform its other functions, and that this power is called motor, or moving.

Now it must be noted that I have said, *of animals*, so that one may know that I am not treating here of the voice of Organs, or of other voices that are formed by wind without the intervention of living and animated organs, although the greater part of such voices depends on the motor faculty of man, who imitates the voice of animals by means of air, wind, wheels, weights, and several other springs; but these imitated voices only have the name of "voice" by borrowing it from those we treat in this discourse.

I also said that this virtue of the soul is the first and primary cause of the voice, for although the soul is the source and origin of all the animal's actions, nevertheless one usually takes the nearest and most immediate cause for the first and primary cause: but it must be noted that there are two motor powers in the animal, one of which is called *natural*, because it depends on no knowledge, and consequently performs its functions without knowing them, as is seen in the movement of the heart and the arteries, and in that of respiration.

This power is no different from the vital faculty found in oysters, and in other fish and shelled animals: the other power is the *animal* faculty <note>In the 17th century, "animal" often refers to the *anima* or soul; thus, the "animal faculty" is the power of the soul to govern voluntary movement and sensation.</note>, which is common to us and all sorts of animals, and which is subdivided into three others, namely into that which leads, that which pushes, and that which carries out, which one can call *directing, impelling, and executing*.

Fancy <note>original: "phantaſie." In early modern philosophy, this refers to the faculty of the mind that receives and processes sensory images before they reach the intellect.</note> is that which directs by the knowledge it has of the object; that which excites and inclines particularly toward action is called *appetite*; and the motor faculty, which is named *executrix*, puts our desires into execution, and is the efficient cause of all our movements.

As for fancy and appetite, they are rather moral causes than physical and natural ones, and have a different subject than the motor faculty, for fancy is in the brain; and the sensitive appetite, of which we speak, is in the heart; but the motor faculty is in the muscles, or, following the opinion of *Aristotle*, in the joining of the bones, which he calls the beginning and the end of movement, which occurs by pushing and pulling; which he perhaps believed because the concave and the convex of the bones that meet are similar to the hinges and straps of doors, where the former serves as the convex, which remains immobile, and the latter as the concave which turns upon the hinges.

Now the muscle pulls the bones when it contracts and withdraws, but when it extends they return to their place. From this it comes that *Galen* <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), an influential Roman physician and philosopher whose anatomical theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, in the book he wrote on the causes of respiration, compares the motor faculty to a Rider, the muscle to the horse, and the reins to the tendon, which the muscle uses to move the bones, just as the Rider uses the bridle to make the horse walk; and when the muscle extends, it pushes the bones.

Those who say that the animal spirits <note>original: "esprits animaux." These were thought to be a very subtle, vapor-like substance that traveled through the nerves to facilitate movement and thought.</note> serve as the seat and subject of this faculty—because the animal is deprived of movement when these spirits cannot descend and communicate through the nerves—have not considered that this power cannot reside in a subject that has no life, since it is living; and no one doubts that animal spirits have no more life than blood, since they are nothing other than a purified and subtle blood, similar to the vapor produced by boiling.

We must therefore conclude that the muscle is the proper seat and the subject of the motor faculty of the soul, though there is no agreement on the specific part: nevertheless, the most learned Physicians hold that the tail of the muscle (which they call *mys* <note>Original Greek: μὺς, meaning "mouse," from which the word "muscle" is derived because the movement of a muscle under the skin was thought to resemble a mouse running.</note>, because it is similar to the tail of a mouse, and which forms the tendon that ends at the extremity of the bone) is the seat of this faculty. For it is not in the nerve, which serves only as a canal to carry the animal spirit <term>animal spirit: In 17th-century physiology, these were subtle fluids or "vapors" that traveled through the nerves to communicate the soul's commands to the body.</term>, nor in the arteries that accompany it, because they serve only to carry the vital spirit: and the flesh serves only to fill the empty spaces; consequently the tendon, or the fibers, serve as the proper subject, or the principal seat of this faculty.

Although one might say that the proper subject of the motor faculty is the soul, or the animal itself, which is the being to whom all actions are attributed; but I am speaking here of the organic and instrumental seat and subject.

### PROPOSITION II.

*Of all the muscles of the body, those of the chest and the larynx serve the voice most particularly and most immediately.*

Anatomists have noted 425 muscles in the human body, namely 64 in the head and neck, 45 in the trunk of the body, 51 in each hand, and 56 in each foot: now those of the chest are greatly necessary for the voice, because the chest must expand so that air may be drawn into the lungs, and it must narrow to expel the vapors; this is why it has 32 muscles for inspiration <note>The act of breathing in.</note> which occurs when the chest expands, and 32 for expiration <note>The act of breathing out.</note>, for it has 16 on each side that expand the ribs, and 16 others that close and restrict them.

The eight muscles of the epigastrium <note>The upper part of the abdomen.</note> also serve inspiration, and consequently the voice, as Du Laurens <note>André du Laurens (1558–1609) was a famous French physician and anatomist to King Henri IV.</note> teaches in the fifth book of his *Anatomy*, where he holds that the internal intercostal muscles tighten the chest, and the external ones open it, and that the former serve expiration, and the latter inspiration. To which he adds that the external ones are stronger and larger, especially since the dorsal muscle, or sacro-lumbar, has twelve tendons that make it stronger. From this, it seems one can conclude that inspiration is more necessary to man than expiration, since nature has provided more carefully and more powerfully for the inspiration of air.

But of all the muscles of the chest, the diaphragm is the most necessary for ordinary breathing, just as the others are more necessary for violent breathing, which causes the chest to swell extraordinarily.

As for the origin of this muscle, which almost entirely by itself performs natural respiration (which is nearly imperceptible), some say that it begins at its middle near its nervous circle; and others say that it takes its origin from the entire circumference of the chest, and that it ends at the said nervous circle as its center, and consequently that it has its tail in the middle, and its head toward the sternum and the extremities of the false ribs.

Its shape is similar to that of a Ray <note>The "Raye" or stingray, a flat-bodied fish, used here to describe the broad, thin shape of the diaphragm.</note>, and it is covered by the pleura <note>The membrane surrounding the lungs.</note> in its upper part, and by the peritoneum <note>The membrane lining the abdominal cavity.</note> in the lower. It is pierced in two places to make room for the esophagus which descends downward, and for the vena cava <note>A large vein carrying deoxygenated blood.</note> which ascends to the heart. It is called the diaphragm because it divides the irascible soul from the concupiscible <note>The "irascible soul" was associated with spirited emotions like anger and courage (located in the heart), while the "concupiscible soul" was associated with basic desires and appetites (located in the liver).</note>, that is to say, the liver from the heart, and the natural parts from the vital parts, and serves to ventilate...

# Book One

the hypochondria <note>The upper region of the abdomen, just below the ribs.</note>, to press the intestines and to prevent excrement from rising upward. Finally, it is called *phrenes* <note>Original Greek: φρένες, a term used for both the diaphragm and the mind or heart.</note>, as if it were the seat of wisdom, because when it is inflamed, one is in a perpetual delirium due to its great sympathy with the brain. Now, this delirium and the symptoms of frenzy prove that this muscle is necessary for the voice, especially since when it is affected, respiration is shallow and frequent, and the voice is shrill, because its inflammation prevents the thorax from expanding and contracting, causing this muscle to pull upward and making the thorax narrower. The pleura <note>The membrane lining the cavity of the chest and covering the lungs.</note>, which covers all the ribs, also serves the voice, for it folds over when it reaches the sternum, and then goes straight to the spine. This fold is called the *mediastinum*, which holds the heart suspended and divides the thorax into two parts; it is so arranged that one part of the membrane is about three fingers' distance from the other, in order to leave a free space for the heart; but the space that the heart does not need creates a cavity to serve as an echo for the voice, and to produce the resonance that accompanies and follows deep voices when they finish singing or speaking.

The second part of this proposition obliges me to speak of the larynx, which is the proper instrument of the voice and serves as a natural flute for animals. It is at the head of the trachea, or "rough artery" <note>The *aspre artere* (trachea) was so called by early anatomists because of its cartilaginous rings, distinguishing it from "smooth" blood vessels.</note>, and is cartilaginous so that the air, being struck and beaten, is fit to form the voice. It is composed of three cartilages, namely: the thyroid or shield-shaped cartilage (which protrudes more in the throats of males than females and is called the anterior); the cricoid or ring-shaped cartilage, which always keeps the artery open; and the arytenoid or posterior cartilage, where the glottis is located, the opening of which creates the deep or shrill voice.

This glottis is covered by the epiglottis, for fear that the food we take might fall into the larynx and suffocate us. As for the larynx, it has fourteen muscles that open and close it in various ways according to the different voices of the animal. There are four "common" muscles, the first two of which are called *bronchi* <note>In 17th-century anatomy, these "bronchi" muscles refer to the sternothyroid muscles, which connect the breastbone to the larynx.</note>, which originate from the sternum and rise along the sides of the trachea until they are inserted into the lower parts of the thyroid, which they tighten while widening the upper parts. The other two are opposite the former and come from the hyoid bone to go to the lower parts of the said thyroid, pulling it upward by tightening the upper parts of the larynx and widening the lower ones.

The two other common muscles serve swallowing rather than the voice, which is why they surround the esophagus on all sides.

But it has ten "proper" <note>In this context, "proper" means muscles specific to that organ alone.</note> muscles, the first of which tightens the front and lower part of the thyroid in order to widen the upper part of the larynx. The second ends at the arytenoid and opens the glottis. The third is carried to the same cartilage to open the posterior parts of the same glottis and to close the anterior ones. The fourth performs an action contrary to that of the third, and the last, which is the smallest of all, opens the duct. Now, the small branches of the recurrent nerve are spread throughout all these muscles, which is why the voice is lost when this nerve is cut.

The epiglottis <note>A flap of cartilage at the root of the tongue, which is depressed during swallowing to cover the opening of the windpipe.</note> lies over the glottis in the shape of an ivy leaf, whose base is at the upper internal part of the thyroid cartilage, and the tip points toward the palate. It is cartilaginous so that it may lower easily when food descends to the stomach, for fear that it might enter the vocal artery <note>The "vocal artery" refers to the trachea or windpipe; early anatomists often called it the *aspre-artère* or "rough artery."</note> and the lungs, and so that it may rise promptly to strike the air with force when it is pushed by the lungs, which act like animated bellows to form the voice. Nevertheless, the epiglottis never closes so tightly that it does not let some small amount of moisture pass into the artery when one drinks, and it is always a little open during both inspiration and expiration.

As for the glottis <note>The part of the larynx consisting of the vocal cords and the opening between them.</note>, it is composed of a cartilage, a muscle, and a membrane, so that the voice is produced by a voluntary movement, of which the muscle is the principle; for the muscle constricts and closes it, or enlarges and opens it, according to the voice that one forms.

The cartilage strengthens it, for fear that it might be overturned by the force of the wind, and the membrane is the reason why it opens and closes easily.

This membrane gives smoothness to the glottis and covers the muscle, so that it is in no way offended by the frequent agitation of the air, and so that the glottis does not rupture when it is full of wind, or suffer discomfort from smoke, dust, cold, or any other accident. It is fatty and moist in order to lubricate the glottis; for we would have difficulty speaking if it became parched, as happens to those who are afflicted by a burning fever or a long journey, who can hardly speak, or who have a voice similar to that of cranes and geese, until they have moistened their membrane. It must not, however, be watered too much, for fear that the voice becomes hoarse like that of those suffering from catarrh <note>A "caterreux" is someone with an excessive buildup of mucus, usually from a cold.</note> who have a rheum.

The moisture of this membrane is unctuous, which is not so quickly dissipated and exhaled as if it were of the nature of water, as happens to the moisture of reeds <note>Referring here to the reeds used in musical instruments.</note> which must often be moistened and wetted, because the moisture is soon lost and evaporates immediately.

The opening of the glottis has almost the shape of an oval, but its extremities are a little more pointed, and it is of the same size as the larynx: It usually corresponds to respiration, because those who need a greater respiration also need a larger opening; this is particularly noticed in that of oxen.

The glottis begins at the <term>arytenoid cartilage</term> <note>A pair of small three-sided pyramids which form part of the larynx, to which the vocal folds are attached.</note> and ends at the <term>scutiform</term> <note>Meaning "shield-shaped"; another name for the thyroid cartilage.</note>, for which the <term>cricoid</term> <note>The ring-shaped cartilage of the larynx.</note> serves as an immobile base: but it must be noted that its opening extends from the front parts to those in the back, and not across, so that the wind which forms the voice goes straight to the top of the palate, to be converted into speech by means of the tongue.

This glottis has small cavities that retain the wind, and which serve it to resist more easily the movement of the 44 muscles of the thorax; now, although the epiglottis is lowered by the weight of food, it is also lowered by a specific muscle, and raised by another; though birds are deprived of it, so that they receive no hindrance in taking their nourishment, which often consists of small grains that they swallow so quickly that they could not enter their throat if they had an epiglottis that had to be lowered at

### PROPOSITION IV.

*The muscles and nerves of the larynx are necessary to create low and high voices.*

We have already said many things about these muscles, to which must be added that the scutiform cartilage <note>original: "cartilage scutiforme." This is the thyroid cartilage, named for its shield-like shape (from the Latin *scutum*).</note> is moved by two muscles, one of which pulls it upward and narrows the slit of the glottis in order to make the voice high-pitched; from this comes the fact that the larynx rises when we sing the Soprano <note>original: "Dessus," the highest part in early vocal music.</note>. Other muscles pull the same cartilage downward and open it to make the voice low; this occurs when the larynx descends while singing the Bass. There is another movement across the width and breadth of the scutiform cartilage by means of several muscles that open and close it, performing the same movement upon the glottis. There are still other muscles inserted into the cricoid <note>A ring-shaped cartilage forming the lower part of the larynx.</note> which open and close the arytenoid <note>A pair of small cartilages to which the vocal cords are attached.</note> and give these same movements to the glottis.

As for the nerves that serve the voice, they are inserted into the six muscles of the larynx, to which they communicate the animal spirit <note>In early modern medicine, "animal spirits" were believed to be a subtle fluid that traveled through the nerves to produce movement and sensation.</note> from the brain to perform their functions; for when the left branch of the sixth pair of nerves <note>Following the anatomical tradition of the time, though modern anatomy identifies the vagus nerve as the tenth cranial nerve.</note> has descended, it sends two branches to the larynx—namely the left and the right—which are called the recurrent nerves. I do not wish to speak of the other nerves that come from elsewhere into the muscles of the larynx, because anatomists have not yet explained how they serve the voice.

Now it must be noted that the qualities of the voice can be reduced to three differences: for it is weak and strong, clear and hoarse, or low and high. The strong voice is made by the violent movement of the muscles of the thorax, the clear voice by the well-tempered moisture of the cartilages, membranes, and muscles of the larynx, and the hoarse voice by the excessive moisture or dryness of the same parts.

As for the low and high voice, it is produced in three ways, which can be explained by the instruments that make sound lower or higher in proportion to whether they are larger or smaller, as is seen with the flute; for when one opens the hole that is near the mouthpiece, it makes the sound higher because it is shorter, its length being taken only from its mouth <note>original: "lumiere," referring to the labium or opening of a whistle-type instrument.</note> or from its reed to the first hole that is kept open.

The other cause comes from flutes being narrow and slender, or wide and thick; and the third is taken from the opening of the holes and the mouth or opening of organ pipes, for the sound is all the more high-pitched as the hole is more open.

But it is difficult to apply these three causes, or those encountered in stringed instruments, to the manner in which the larynx and the glottis produce low and high voices. For it does not seem reasonable to say that the lengthening or shortening of the vocal artery <note>The trachea or windpipe.</note>, which occurs when its rings move further apart or closer together, is the cause of the low and high pitch of the voice, especially since this artery only serves to carry the wind from the lungs to the larynx. It acts like the foot of an organ pipe, which carries the wind to the register in the body of the pipe without being able to vary the pitch of the sound; for no matter the length of this foot, the pipe always produces the same sound.

# On Universal Harmony.

Ptolemy compares the vocal artery <note>original: "artere vocale." In early modern anatomy, the trachea or windpipe was often called the "vocal artery."</note> to the flute in the third chapter of the first book of his *Music*, between which he places this difference: that the position of the one who plays the flute remains firm and immobile, and that the parts of the instrument's body that are open or closed are mobile, by reason of the holes which are closer or further from the reed or the tongue <note>The vibrating element of the instrument.</note>; and that the place of the artery which is struck remains immobile; but that he who plays, or who beats the air, is mobile and knows how to find the place in the artery from which he sends the wind, whose distance from the external air is in the same ratio as the intervals of the sounds that are produced. That which is not easy to understand may yet be true; for if he means that the wind pushed from a deeper or shallower part of the artery causes the sound to be more or less high-pitched, he says the same thing as those who believe that the length or brevity of the same artery makes the difference between the low and the high; but he does not speak at all of the opening of the glottis, which makes the voice more or less high, although it is difficult to explain how this different opening creates all the diversity of voices, which are comprised within a double or triple Octave—that is to say, within the Fifteenth or the Twenty-second <note>Musical intervals representing two and three octaves, respectively.</note>, to which many voices rise, making all the sounds of the Twenty-second. There is nothing that can better serve the explanation of this difficulty than the reed of the regals <note>A small, portable pipe organ that uses reeds to produce sound.</note>, which are called "human voices" <note>Referring to the "Vox Humana" organ stop, designed to mimic the human voice.</note>; for in proportion as one opens this reed by pulling the movement upward, the voice becomes lower; and when one pushes it lower to close the reed, it becomes higher. Similarly, when the glottis opens further, it makes the voice lower, and when it closes, it makes it higher. But I shall treat this matter again in the 16th Proposition, which will supply what is missing from this one.

### PROPOSITION V.

->*Voice is the sound made by the animal by means of the vocal artery, the larynx, the glottis, and the other parts of which we have spoken, with the intention of signifying something.*<-

Sound serves as the "genus" <note>The general category in a formal definition.</note> for this definition: For the voice has this in common with all kinds of noises, that it is a sound. These words, *that the animal makes with the vocal artery, etc.*, distinguish the sound of animals from the sounds of inanimate bodies, and from those made by animals without using the mouth, such as the noise made by clapping hands; and because there are sounds so similar to the voice that they cannot be discerned from it, I have added, *with the intention of signifying*, for the "difference" <note>The specific characteristic that distinguishes a species within a genus.</note> of this definition; so that when the animal makes some sound without this intention, it does not deserve the name of voice, even though it makes it with the instruments of the voice. And if the animal intends to signify something by sounds other than the voice, they are called signs, and not voice. Nevertheless, they may be called voice because of this intention: from this comes the saying that a mute speaks by signs, and that all creatures make voices that announce to us the power and declare to us the goodness of God, because He intended in making them that they should serve us for this purpose.

## PROPOSITION VI.

->*The voices of men are as different as their faces; so that one can recognize and distinguish people from one another by the Voice; and consequently one can establish <term>Phthongonomy</term> <note>From the Greek roots for "voice" and "law"; the science of determining character from the sound of the voice.</note>, or <term>Phonoscopy</term> <note>From "voice" and "observation"; the identification of individuals by their vocal qualities.</note> for the Voice, just as <term>Physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of judging character from facial features.</note> is established for Faces.*<-

Experience teaches the truth of this Proposition, for the voice gives us more light to know someone than touch does; from this comes the fact that Isaac was deceived by touching Jacob, whom he recognized by his voice <note>A reference to the biblical story in Genesis 27, where the blind Isaac is tricked by Jacob’s tactile disguise but notices the voice does not match.</note>. And if one encounters men who have voices so similar that no difference can be found, there are similarly faces that one cannot distinguish from one another.

Now I speak here of the natural voice which is not disguised; for I shall later give a particular discourse on voices that are counterfeited, and which are imitated so perfectly that they can deceive the ear just as well as the resemblance of handwriting or faces deceives the eye.

Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note> recognized the capacity of the chest by the voice when he said that those who have a strong voice, and who can continue it without interruption, have a large thorax. This he confirms by the example of those who command attention in public places by using an iambic dipody <note>A rhythmic unit in poetry consisting of two iambs (short-long feet).</note>, which is found in these two phrases: <note>original: "ἀκούε λᾱὸς, ou ἀκουε πᾱς"</note> "Listen, O people," or "Listen, everyone"; which he calls "speaking the foot" <note>original: "πόδα λέγειν"</note>, following the explanation of Joseph Scaliger <note>A famous 16th-century French scholar.</note>, who compares this rhythmic unit to that of the words "now listen" <note>original: "or escoutez"</note>; and who corrects the explanation of Mercuriale <note>Girolamo Mercuriale, an Italian physician known for his work on gymnastics and health.</note>, who understood this passage as the voice used to call wrestlers to the race or the combat. Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist.</note> speaks of another "foot" <note>A measurement of distance.</note> that had to be left between the place intended for the playing of trumpets and the place where houses were built.

Those who relate all things to the providence of God notice it in the diversity of faces, which prevents us from being deceived in trade, and ensures that those who have similar faces are recognized by their speech. And although all parts of the body are perhaps as distinct in each different body as faces and voices are, nevertheless these two parts of man strike our senses more sharply and make a more vivid impression on the mind. To this one may add that the face and the voice are the mirrors of the soul, which supply in some fashion the window that Momus <note>In Greek mythology, the god of satire and mockery, who complained that man was poorly made because he lacked a window in his chest to reveal his secret thoughts.</note> desired to have facing the heart.

## PROPOSITION VII.

->*The Voice of animals serves to signify the passions of the soul, but it does not always signify the temperament of the body.*<-

Experience teaches the first part of this Proposition; for birds, dogs, and other animals make a different cry when they are angry, when they lament, or when they are sick, than when they rejoice and are well; and the voice is more high-pitched in sadness and in anger than outside of these passions; for bile <note>Referring to the "four humors" of ancient medicine; yellow bile was associated with a hot, dry temperament and anger.</note> makes the voice high-pitched; melancholy and phlegm make it deep; and the sanguine humor <note>The humor of blood, associated with a balanced and cheerful temperament.</note> makes it temperate. From this comes the comparison of the high pitch to fire, the deep pitch to earth and water, and the temperate pitch to air.
