# On Universal Harmony

...principal discourse; and he describes a spiral line in the <term>Harmonic Hand</term> <note>Also known as the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic device used in the Middle Ages to help singers learn to sight-sing.</note> of Guido d'Arezzo <note>Original: "Guy Aretin"; a 11th-century music theorist who revolutionized musical notation.</note>, where Saturn <note>Original: ♄</note> governs the second voice, the Moon <note>Original: ☽</note> the 3rd, Mercury <note>Original: ☿</note> the 4th, Venus <note>Original: ♀</note> the 5th, the Sun <note>Original: ☉</note> the 6th, Mars <note>Original: ♂</note> the 7th, Jupiter <note>Original: ♃</note> the 8th, Saturn the 9th, the Moon the 10th, Mercury the eleventh, Venus the 12th, the Sun the 13th, Mars the 14th, and Jupiter the 15th. For he describes the Planets following the order they hold from the circumference to the center, and arranges the voices from the center to the circumference; that is to say, he descends from Saturn to the Moon, and ascends from UT <note>The original name for the note 'Do' in the solfège system.</note> all the way to LA: So that the lower voices relate to the superior Planets, whose heavens are larger, and the higher voices to the inferior Planets. To which he adds that the voices attributed to a very benevolent Planet, such as Jupiter and Venus, make perfect Consonances with the lowest voice, or the first; that those which meet a moderately benevolent Planet, like the Moon and Mercury, make imperfect Consonances; and those which meet a malevolent Planet, that is to say Mars and Saturn, make Dissonances.

He says further that Saturn governs the second voices which are hoarse, low, and heavy; Mars the sevenths, which are harsh, hasty, and unseemly, and that these two voices never agree with the first: that the Moon governs the middle voices, and particularly the 3rd; Mercury the cheerful voices, full of joy, and particularly the 5th; Venus the soft and lascivious voices, and particularly the 6th; Jupiter the sweet and constant ones, such as the 8th; and the Sun and the Moon those which have a particular grace.

Certainly this speculation should not be neglected because of the similarity found between Consonances and benevolent <term>aspects</term> <note>In astrology, the angular distance between planets that determines their influence.</note>, and between Dissonances and those called "bad" aspects. But it is by no means necessary for the Musician to know the properties of the Planets to compose good songs: for one can compose all sorts of musical pieces without knowing the Planets, which have no particular influence on the voice. And experience shows that du Caurroy, Claudin, Guédron, Boësset, Moulinié <note>Famous French composers of the late 16th and early 17th centuries, known for their courtly songs and polyphony.</note>, and other Composers, have made very good pieces of music and good airs, even though they did not know Astrology. As for the different voices of animals, one would have to make particular observations to know how much the voice of some is higher than that of others when they are in anger, or carried away by some other passion, and to see what can be known of their temperaments, or the degree of their passions by their different cries, or by their natural voices, whose intervals can be noted: for example, the cuckoo makes a <term>Minor third</term> while singing, of which the first syllable is higher than the second: and the lowing of cows is composed of the <term>Major tenth</term>, of which the first part is the lowest, and the second is the highest. The 2nd part of this Proposition is evident, for there are those of a hot and bilious temperament who have a voice as low and as strong as those with a cold and earthy temperament: and one finds singers whose Bass is equal, yet who have very different temperaments; so that one must conclude that the low or high pitch of the voice is not an infallible sign of temperament, nor of the strength of the man or the animal; and many have a strong and large voice who are weaker than those who have a weaker and higher voice. From this it follows that the gravity of the voice signifies nothing other than a larger opening of the <term>glottis</term> <note>The part of the larynx consisting of the vocal cords and the opening between them.</note>; and that the strength of the voice is only a sign of the size of the <term>thorax</term>, or that of the <term>lungs</term>, or of the strength of the muscles of the <term>larynx</term>. Nevertheless, one can say that the largest and strongest voices are often accompanied by a greater physical strength, of which they are like the symbol and the mark.

## PROPOSITION VIII.

*The voice of animals is necessary, and that of humans is free; that is to say, that man speaks freely, and that animals cry out, sing, and use their voices by necessity.*

We experience the freedom we have to speak, or to be silent at any moment, even when passion makes us speak; unless that passion is so strong that it robs us of the use of reason: for the tongue, the <term>larynx</term> <note>The "voice box" containing the vocal cords.</note>, and all its muscles along with the other parts that serve the voice, obey the spirit as promptly as the foot and the hand: so that one can say that the tongue is the hand of the spirit, just as the hand is the hand of the tongue, inasmuch as the tongue writes the thoughts or the words of the spirit, just as the hand writes the words of the tongue.

As for animals, many say they do not cry out by necessity, since there seems to be nothing more free than the song of birds, such as the nightingale, the goldfinch, and others; and nevertheless, it must be admitted that they sing only by necessity, whether pleasure or sadness drives them to sing, or they are excited to it by some natural instinct, which leaves them no freedom to be silent, or to stop once they have begun to sing. And when they hear a Lute, or some other harmonious sound, and they sing in competition with one another, the sounds they imitate, or which excite them to sing, strike their imagination so forcefully that they cannot remain silent; for their <term>sensitive appetite</term> <note>The faculty of the soul that responds to physical sensations and desires, shared by humans and animals.</note> being heated by the impression of the imagination, necessarily commands the <term>motor faculty</term> <note>The biological ability to move one's body.</note> to move all the parts necessary for the voice.

## PROPOSITION IX.

*The voice is the matter of speech, and only man can speak.*

The first part of this Proposition is so evident that there is no need to prove it, since we use the voice to form speech, just as sculptors use wood and stones to make images: for images or statues are made by the different shapes given to the material from which they are made: and discourse is a harmonic perspective, for which the voice serves as a canvas to receive all sorts of images, since words are the images of the notions of the mind.

It must therefore be said that [speech] is the form, the ornament, and the perfection of the voice, which can be formed and figured into words only by man, just as words can be formed into discourse only by the mind: for parrots and other birds that speak do not know what they are saying, and learn their lesson without knowing what it signifies; so that their jargon is not worthy of the name of speech, if we take it in the same sense as the Latins take *verbum* <note>Original: "verbum"; Latin for "word," often implying a word that carries rational meaning or "the Word" in a philosophical sense.</note>, which must

### PROPOSITION X.

->*Whether man could speak or sing if he heard no sounds or words.*<-

The solution to this difficulty depends on an experiment which is nearly impossible; for it would require raising a child from the first day of his birth until 20 or 30 years of age in a place where he could hear no sounds—which cannot happen, since even the slightest movements create sounds. It is similarly difficult to raise him without his hearing any speech; and even if such an experiment could be performed, since it has not yet been attempted that I know of, we cannot judge the results to draw a solution to this doubt. This is why we must rely on reason alone, which dictates that a man would not speak at all if he had never heard words, because he would not imagine that words could serve to explain the thoughts of the mind and the desires of the will. And even if he did imagine it, he would not know which expressions he should use to make himself understood. One may therefore conclude that man would not speak if he had not learned to speak. Nevertheless, since birds sing naturally, and since man can imagine that high and fast sounds are made by a more sudden movement, and that they have different shapes and consequently can represent different things, one could say that man would still speak even if he had never heard speech, provided that he had someone to whom he could address his words.

If the objects that make an impression on our senses caused us to form words <note>The original uses "dictions," meaning specific words or linguistic utterances.</note> conforming to said impressions, those who received the same impressions would imitate the same sounds; but we usually give names to things by chance, and subsequently other words to other things with which they have some resemblance. This is why we cannot judge the words that would be pronounced by children who have not been taught to speak using our vocabulary, which in my opinion possesses more artifice than those they would form themselves.

### PROPOSITION XII.

### PROPOSITION XIII.

->*To determine how many species or kinds of sounds man can make with the*<-
->*mouth, and the other organs of the voice*<-
->*and of speech.*<-

The great variety of sounds that man makes proceeds from the diversity of the organs and instruments of the voice, or from the different ways they can move to strike the air: for when the larynx or the glottis gives a free passage to the air without it stopping in the mouth, one cannot hear this movement of air, because it produces natural respiration—which one only hears when it is forced or vehement, as happens to those who sleep, or who blow with their mouths open. This is ordinarily called <term>exsufflation</term> <note>From the Latin *exsufflatio*, meaning a breathing out; here it refers to the warm, open-mouthed breath.</note>, which is done simply, or with a rattling of the throat, which Basses in Music sometimes use to supplement the natural voice which they lack, and which is not deep enough. Now, this exsufflation receives several distinctions according to the force and speed with which it is made. 

The second noise is made by the wind, or by the air that one pushes while the mouth is closed; one can call this <term>sufflation</term> <note>Meaning a "blowing" or "hissing" breath through pursed lips, which Mersenne notes is cooler than the open-mouthed breath.</note>, which is used to blow and light a fire, or to cool broth that is too hot, for this breath cools the air, just as exsufflation warms it. The third is **whistling**, which is used to imitate the sound of flutes and flageolets, and the song of birds; some use this with such artistry that there is no less pleasure in hearing them than the song of birds or the instruments they imitate, as those who have heard **Fauverole** <note>Presumably a well-known performer or whistler of the era.</note> and several others can testify. 

The fourth noise or sound can be called **voice**, or **cry**, which is common to humans and animals, and which is made without forming syllables; and the fifth is the voice joined to syllables, which forms **speech** and **song**. Now, if one wished to specify every kind of sound that can be made by means of the mouth and the other organs of the voice, it would be necessary to describe every way in which birds sing and all sorts of animals cry out; for men counterfeit and imitate the roaring of lions, the lowing of bulls, the neighing of horses, the sound of all sorts of organ stops, and that of all other instruments. Thus, one would have to explain all the noises and sounds of nature to know all that the human voice can do, which contains the nature of all other sounds, just as human nature comprises that of all other creatures: so that one can apply what is sung on the day of **Pentecost** <note>The Christian feast celebrating the Holy Spirit descending upon the Apostles, enabling them to speak in many languages.</note> to the human voice, namely,

### P R O P O S I T I O N XIV.

*If nature had not provided the voices with which we express the passions, to know whether we would invent the same voices that she uses, or if we could invent better and more suitable ones.*

If we possessed a natural language, <note>The "natural language" refers to a long-standing philosophical quest to find the original tongue of humanity (often thought to be Hebrew or an "Adamic" language) where words perfectly reflected the essence of things.</note> one could ask the same question: namely, if we could re-establish it, assuming it were lost. And because we confess that we would not know how to find a natural language now—even though we are in the same condition we would be in after having lost it—we must similarly admit that the art and reason we possess could not provide us with the same voices that serve us naturally to explain our **passions**, <note>In the 17th century, "passions" referred to all powerful emotions or states of mind, such as joy, sorrow, anger, or fear.</note> if we had lost the use of them. For who could guess that tears and sobs, accompanied by cries and wailing, are the most proper signs to represent sadness, or that laughter is more proper to signify joy than several other signs one might devise? For what purpose is there in shedding streams of tears to bear witness to pain? Pricks that draw blood would be much more suited to that. But because we are treating here more particularly of the voice than of other external signs, I do not believe one can demonstrate that the voices we call natural—which serve as a language for the passions—are more fit to express them than several other voices that could be established for this purpose.

And if one observes the voices with which animals express their passions and affections, one will judge them just as indifferent for signifying the said passions as our words are for signifying our concepts, or the other things of which we wish to speak; for the syllable *kik* has no more proportion to the flight of chicks—though the hen uses it to make them escape—than the syllable *glo*, which she uses to call them back. The same thing can be said of the other voices used by all sorts of animals, for which I do not know why they determined themselves to these rather than to other sorts of cries and voices, unless it be that having found them easier, they retained them without inventing others. For if one says that Nature did not make their organs capable of forming other articulations, that is what would need to be proven; and if birds had never been taught to speak, one might similarly imagine that nature had deprived them of the organs necessary for speech, which would nonetheless be quite false.

Certainly, although we do not know why the voices of animals, or those of men, naturally signify the passions (due to the various difficulties I have brought forward, or others one might imagine), there is nonetheless a great appearance that they are natural, and that they have within them something more suited to signify the passions than others that could be invented. This is all the more probable because it is held most certainly that the Author of Nature, or intelligent Nature, determines the animals and conducts them in such a way that they have no liberty in their actions. ...one might reply that the young are taught by their fathers and mothers while they are in the nest, or even in the shell; it must nevertheless be that the first father and the first mother formed these voices without having learned them, and consequently that they are as natural to them as eating and drinking. This remains true unless one says that Adam taught whatever voices he wished to each kind of animal to express its **passions**, <note>In this context, "passions" refers to the "passions of the soul"—intense emotional states like fear, joy, or anger that were believed to trigger physical responses.</note> or that one attributes their first institution to God, who distinguished their languages so that the different species might be distinct by their voices, just as they are by their external form and their other qualities.

But it is not necessary for us to use these solutions, since we know by experience that the chickens or chicks, whose eggs are hatched in the ovens of Egypt, <note>This refers to artificial incubation, a practice famous in the early modern period as a marvel of Egyptian ingenuity, where eggs were hatched using the heat of specialized kilns rather than a brooding hen.</note> have the same voices as those who have heard their fathers and mothers; from which we must conclude that these voices are natural to them. Now, one would have to find the proportion of their voices to their passions to prove that they are more suitable than other voices.

One can say in general that the harshest and roughest voices are the most suitable for signifying the passions of annoyance and displeasure; and that the softest voices are suitable for amorous passions, and that great cries better represent great pains and sadness. In truth, it is very difficult to be satisfied on this matter, for the reason that we do not know the nature of animals, nor that of their passions; from this it follows that we cannot know which voices are most suitable to express them. However, if one had very exactly noted all the voices they use, one could establish something on this subject, which is large enough to occupy a **Philosopher**. <note>A "Philosopher" here refers specifically to a Natural Philosopher, the precursor to the modern scientist, who studied the laws of the physical world.</note>

If the parts of the animals, by contracting, create the voices by which they signify their sadness, and the expansion of the same parts or others creates the voices they use to express their joy, and if this contraction and expansion cannot happen without forming these voices, then we must admit that they are natural, even if we do not know the reasons for it. This must similarly be confessed if the Author of Nature <note>A common Enlightenment-era title for God as the designer of the universe's mechanics.</note> gave them these voices to express their passions; for what God gives to each thing at the beginning of its creation and production is customarily natural, because it is in conformity with the principles and nature of each thing. Thus, we need only find the conformity of the voices, or the language of each animal, with the passions it expresses, to resolve the difficulty of this Proposition.

### COROLLARY.

It is not enough to say that a thing is natural to an animal, or to any body, if one does not show why it is natural to it; but because this demonstration presupposes a perfect knowledge of the animal, or the body—which man cannot have in this world—we must lift our spirit to God instead of occupying it any longer with these considerations, and admire His providence and His wisdom, which is so eminent in every creature that it is impossible for us to comprehend it, until He has removed the seal that closes this mystery to us, and has enlightened us with the **light of glory**. <note>The "light of glory" (lumen gloriae) is a theological term referring to the supernatural capacity given to the soul in heaven to see God and understand the mysteries of creation perfectly.</note>

### PROPOSITION XV.

->*That one can sing Chromatic and Enharmonic music, and produce*<-
->*the major and minor tone, and even the comma, in all*<-
->*places as one desires.*<-

It is very easy to prove this Proposition; for if one follows the sounds of an instrument, or of the perfect system—particularly those of the Organ, which contains the three genres of Music <note>The three "genres" refer to the ancient Greek classifications of melody: Diatonic (whole and half steps), Chromatic (using semitones), and Enharmonic (using even smaller intervals called quarter-tones or diesis).</note>—one will sing all the intervals of the Chromatic and the Enharmonic. Once the voice has become accustomed to these intervals, it will sing them as easily as those of the Diatonic. The same must be said of the intervals found within the species of the three genres; for there are no intervals to which the human voice cannot accommodate itself, provided they do not exceed its reach and range. And if Practitioners take the trouble to instruct some children with an Organ divided into these intervals, they will have the satisfaction of making them sing the Enharmonic. One can also compel singers to produce the said intervals, provided they are willing to sing what they know; for if one takes the same song a <term>diesis</term> <note>A very small musical interval, specifically an Enharmonic diesis, which is roughly a quarter-tone.</note> higher or lower than they do, this diesis will be heard throughout.

Furthermore, one can demonstrate the places where the <term>minor tone</term> or the <term>major tone</term> <note>In the tuning systems of this era, not all "whole steps" were the same size. A major tone (ratio 9:8) is slightly larger than a minor tone (ratio 10:9).</note> occurs; for if one person holds a steady note while another sings by conjunct degrees, if he begins by singing a minor third and then a fourth, he will produce a minor tone; and if he rises to the fifth, he will produce a major tone; and if he passes to the major sixth, he will produce a minor tone. Similarly, if he first sings the minor third and then the major third, he will produce the minor semitone; this also happens when one passes from the minor sixth to the major sixth, or from the major to the minor.

And finally, if he passes from the minor semitone to the major, he will produce the Enharmonic diesis. Now, one can further prove that the voice is capable of all these intervals by the experience found in church singing and in concerts, in which the voices rise or fall little by little, as is perceived at the end, where they are often found to be higher or lower by a semitone. They did not arrive there all at once, but imperceptibly; so that if they dropped at each measure, one can say they divided the semitone, or the interval by which they descended or ascended, into as many parts as there were measures.

The same thing is experienced with the <term>reeds</term> <note>The "tongue" or "lan-guette" is the vibrating metal part of a reed pipe in an organ.</note> of Organs, whose tongue, being opened or closed, rises or falls as little as one wishes. This happens similarly with other pipes that can be widened or narrowed at the end with a <term>tuning tool</term>, and whose <term>mouth</term> <note>Original: "lumiere," referring to the opening where the air escapes to produce sound.</note> can be so slightly increased or diminished by means of the "ears" <note>Metal flaps on either side of an organ pipe's mouth used for fine-tuning.</note> that shade it, that one can produce a quarter of a <term>comma</term>, <note>A comma is a tiny interval, the smallest difference between two notes that is typically perceptible to a trained ear.</note> which can be divided into as many parts as one desires. This can also be done on stringed instruments, of which we shall speak elsewhere.

But since God has given us a voice so flexible that it can pass through all these degrees, it is reasonable that we employ them to His praise; and that when we perform the intervals of Consonances or Dissonances, we think of the intervals and distances that separate us from the Concert of the Blessed, whose desire musicians ought to express through Psalm 144: *I will extol thee, my God, O King; and I will bless thy name for ever and ever.* <note>original: "Exaltabo te Deus meus Rex, & benedicam nomini tuo in sæculum & in ſæculum ſæculi."</note>

## PROPOSITION XVI.

*Explaining how the low and high pitches of the voice are produced; that is to say, in what manner the voice rises or falls when speaking or singing, wherein the questions that Aristotle proposed on this subject are explained.*

If we did not have the example of reeds <note>The author uses "anches," referring to the vibrating tongues found in instruments like oboes or organ pipes, to explain human anatomy.</note> to help us understand the movements of the little tongue of the larynx, which the <term>Anatomists</term> <note>17th-century medical scholars who studied the structure of the body.</note> call the <term>glotte</term> <note>The glottis: the opening between the vocal folds in the larynx.</note>, it would be difficult to know how a man's voice can have a range of 3 or 4 <term>Octaves</term> <note>An interval spanning eight notes of a standard scale.</note>. This is because the width of the <term>vocal artery</term> <note>original: "artere vocale." In this period, the trachea (windpipe) was often called the "rough artery" or vocal artery.</note> and the larynx alone are not enough. We see this in the ordinary pipes of <term>Organs</term>, which cannot be widened enough to produce an Octave—even if they are made six or seven times wider or narrower—unless they are also lengthened at the same time. Experience teaches us that among several pipes of the same height, one that is twice as wide only drops by one tone, and if it is four times as wide, it only drops by a <term>Major Third</term> <note>An interval of four semitones, such as C to E.</note>, as I noted in the treatise on Organs. Now, it must be noted that the length of the "artery" (the trachea) does nothing to make the voice lower or higher—that is, deeper or more shrill—as I have already stated in the fourth Proposition. This is despite what the Anatomists imagine, for the trachea serves the tongue of the larynx no more than the foot of an organ pipe serves the pipe itself. The foot merely carries the wind from the bellows to the "mouth" where the <term>bevel</term> <note>original: "bizeau." The slanted edge in a whistle or organ pipe that cuts the air to create sound.</note> is found that cuts the air. The trachea only carries the wind from the <term>lung</term> to the larynx; the "tongue" of the larynx always remains at the same pitch as long as it has the same opening and the wind is pushed with equal force. Thus, the pitch would not change even if the trachea were six feet long or only an inch long, as is demonstrated by the foot of a pipe, which does not change the pitch no matter how much its length is reduced.

I said above, *provided that the wind is pushed with an equal force*, because the same opening and the same tongue of a pipe can produce several different tones by means of the different force of the wind pushed by the mouth or by bellows. From this, one can similarly conclude that the same opening of the tongue of the larynx can serve several different tones when the wind is pushed with greater violence, although it is not certain whether the said opening always narrows for each higher pitch and widens for each lower and deeper pitch.

Now, it is not necessary here to repeat what we said about the parts, uses, and composition of the "tongue" or glottis in the third Proposition. That is why I limit myself in this section only to explaining the movements it makes, or the shape it takes, when creating low and high voices. I say that it is necessary for the tongue to be more open for low sounds than for high ones; or, if it keeps the same opening while making two or more different voices in terms of pitch, the wind must be pushed differently—namely, stronger to make the voice high, and weaker to make the voice low. If the tongue of the larynx is similar to the reed of <term>flutes</term> <note>Likely referring to recorders or reed-pipes here.</note>, and if it

The vibrating part of an instrument, here used as an analogy for the vocal folds.</note> creates sound by its vibrations, just as the strings of other instruments do, and that it makes them more or less low or high depending on whether it vibrates more slowly or more quickly; so that if the ratio of the low sound to the high is double—that is to say, from 2 to 1—it is certain that the reed vibrates twice as fast when making the high sound, and consequently that it vibrates a hundred times in making the high sound when it vibrates fifty times in making the low sound.

But if it <note>The "languette" or glottis.</note> is not similar to the said reed, or to the <term>tongue</term> <note>The small metal strip that vibrates in a reed pipe.</note> of the <term>Regals</term> <note>A small portable organ that uses reed pipes to produce a buzzing, brass-like sound.</note>, and if it does not vibrate as many times to produce the <term>Unison</term>, but rather remains firm and stable like the tongue of those <term>Organ pipes</term> which have no reeds—such as those of the <term>Principal</term> <note>original: "monstre." For sound is nothing other than the movement or the vibration of the air, called a **high sound** when it is fast—that is, when it vibrates many times in a short time—and called **low** when it vibrates slowly. For the same thing happens when the air is cut, broken, or struck by a tongue, or by another moving body, or by an immobile body, as one experiences at the holes in walls and rocks, which make a sound or a whistling that is higher the more times the air vibrates upon entering; this happens when it is pushed with more impetus and vehemence, or when it enters through a smaller opening which divides it into a greater number of parts and cuts it more finely. And because it does not matter at all for the purpose of singing to know whether the tongue of the larynx vibrates and beats the air as many times as the reeds of flutes, or if the air divides itself as many times while exiting to create the voice, it is not necessary for us to dwell longer on this subject; although a more exact investigation into the manner in which the voice is rendered lower or higher—and of the movements of each muscle, and the other parts of the larynx and its tongue—would be worthy of the study of an <term>Anatomist</term> and a Philosopher, in order to know the greatest and least opening this tongue can have while singing, and what the different shapes of the exterior body and the interior cavities of the larynx are when all sorts of voices are heard.

But we must here explain a great difficulty, namely: how sound is modified regarding high and low pitch when one strikes another body. For example, when one strikes an anvil with a hammer, or some other body, or when one claps the hands together; for these beatings make sounds, of which some are lower and others higher, and yet it seems that the air does not vibrate, and that it is only pressed or broken for a short time, returning immediately to its ordinary state. To which I respond that the air never makes any low or high sound except through its vibrations, by its little waves, or by its flux and reflux, or by circles or other movements which have the same effect as the said vibrations; for since we experience in wind and string instruments that the sound is made low or high in this manner, it is reasonable to maintain uniformity in other noises, even though we cannot judge their high or low pitch because their movements are not enclosed in a pipe or in some other body by which they might be preserved uniformly, and they are sometimes so low or so high that they surpass the range of hearing, which often cannot judge the tone unless it compares it

### COROLLARY.

->*Wherein the Problems of Aristotle pertaining to low and high voices are explained.*<-

<term>Aristotle</term> <note>Referring to the "Problemata," a collection of scientific questions attributed to Aristotle, though likely written by his followers.</note> has proposed several difficulties on this subject, in order to explain the reason why the voice of man and animals is low or high; for he asks in the tenth Problem of the eleventh Section, why cold falling water makes higher sounds than when it is hot: in the 13th, 15th, and 50th, why those who cry have high voices, and those who laugh have low ones: in the 14th, why children and other animals have high voices when they are young: in the 16th, 36th, and 62nd, why women, the elderly, and <term>eunuchs</term> <note>Men castrated before puberty, who retained high-pitched singing voices.</note> have high voices, and others have low ones: in the 17th and 61st, why we have lower voices in winter than in summer: in the 18th, why the voice becomes lower through drinking, vomiting, and cold: in the 21st, why those who have worked and are weak have higher voices: in the 24th, why calves have lower voices than oxen, given that in all other species of animals the young have higher voices: in the 32nd and 53rd, why those with troubled spirits have low or thick speech: in the 40th, why animals have higher cries when they are stronger, and yet the same thing happens to man when he is weaker: in the 56th, why those who are sober have high voices in winter, and drunkards in summer. Now, it is very easy to respond to all these questions, and to all others that can be made on this subject, if one follows our foundations; for the true reason why the sounds or voices of animals and men are lower or higher is taken from the fact that they strike the air more or fewer times, whether the air struck has a large or small extent, and whether it is condensed or <term>rarefied</term> <note>Thinned out or made less dense.</note>, as experience shows with the strings of instruments, whose sounds make a Unison even though they strike more or less air, and whether the air is coarse or subtle, provided that the number of their beats is equal in equal time, as has been proven in the Books on Stringed Instruments and elsewhere.

I say then to the first difficulty, which consists in knowing *why cold water makes a higher noise than hot*, that if this happens (as I suppose for now, because I do not wish to dispute the experience here) that the reason must be drawn from the greater <term>impetuosity</term> <note>Force or speed.</note> of the fall of cold water, which, pressing the air, causes it to make more reflections or returns in the same time—although the difference in the weights of hot and cold water is not so sensible as Aristotle noted, for if one experiments, one will find that the most accurate scales remain in balance when one puts as much hot water in one of the pans as cold in the other.

And then I have no doubt that <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Specifically referring to the Aristotelian view of falling bodies, which held that heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones.</note> believed that the different speeds of the movements made by heavy objects in descending are perceptible when the differences in weight are perceptible, even when the distance of movement does not exceed 50 feet; which is nevertheless false, and contrary to experience, which shows that a stone of one hundred pounds does not descend faster than one of an ounce, as I have stated more fully in another place. Nevertheless, it does not follow that the sound is not higher when the body that strikes the air is heavier, even though it does not descend faster; for just as with two bodies of equal weight and traveling at an equal speed, the one that is harder or more pointed causes more pain and strikes harder, so too does it make a higher sound, even if its hardness is not so great as to noticeably exceed that of the other body. Thus, it is not necessary for the weight or hardness of cold water to be noticeably greater than that of hot water to make a higher sound, since we experience with several <term>pistoles</term>, <term>escus</term> <note>Historical gold and silver coins used in France and other parts of Europe.</note>, and other pieces of money, that some make higher sounds than others, even though they are of the same weight and the same material. The same thing happens with glasses, whose sounds are so different—even though they are of the same size and weight—that among several thousand it is difficult to find two that are in <term>Unison</term> <note>Sounding at the exact same pitch.</note>.

Now, if anyone does not believe that hot water makes a lower sound than cold, it is easy to test it, unless one fears they do not have an ear as good as Aristotle, or those who proposed this experiment to him, to be able to notice the difference in these sounds; for I am not judging the fact now, as I said before. And then, this is not the place to examine if hot water is lighter, and from where this lightness might come; nor if it is true that a lit torch with which one strikes someone causes them less harm than when it is extinguished, as he says, though I do not believe he has tested it, or that it is true. This is why I pass to the second difficulty, to which the greater part of the others can be related.

I ask, then, why those who cry have a higher voice than those who laugh, which he says similarly of children, women, the elderly, <term>eunuchs</term> <note>Castrated men, historically known for having high-pitched singing voices.</note>, those who have worked, and those who are weak. To which it must be answered that the primary high voice of those he proposes must be taken from the <term>reed</term> <note>original: "languette." This refers to the vibrating part of the larynx or an instrument's mouthpiece.</note>, or the opening of the <term>larynx</term>, which is narrow, and not from a stronger or weaker impulse of air; for when one plays a <term>cornet</term> <note>A wind instrument made of wood or ivory, common in the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</note>, an organ pipe, or some other wind instrument, the sound does not always become higher when one gives them more wind, or pushes the air harder—although some are found that rise to the <term>Octave</term> and the <term>Twelfth</term> <note>Intervals in music; the Twelfth is an octave plus a perfect fifth.</note>, as the <term>Trumpet</term> does—but that does not happen to many others, which rise at most only by a half-tone, even if one gives them much more wind.

Certainly, I am astonished by the solution of Aristotle, who says that those who cry and who are sad have a high voice because, being weak, they push very little air, which goes all the faster because it is in a smaller quantity—given that a small quantity of air has its movement as slow as a larger quantity, when the force that pushes the air is increased in the same proportion as the quantity of air. This is experienced with the string of a <term>Lute</term>, which, being double in length, makes a Unison with the <term>sub-double</term> <note>original: "souz-double." In this context, it likely refers to a string of half the length or a specific proportional relationship in string physics.</note>, even though it moves twice, and perhaps 4 or 8 times more air than the sub-double, because the greater tension increases its force, as I have demonstrated in the book on stringed instruments. We observe that many have a higher-pitched voice when laughing than when crying, and in joy rather than in sadness; thus, it is not appropriate to seek the reason for a proposition that is not constant. One should be satisfied to know that the voice of those who laugh, and of others, cannot be deeper unless they open the <term>reed of the larynx</term> <note>The author uses the term "anche" (reed), comparing the vocal cords and glottis to the reed of a woodwind instrument.</note>, or if they push a large quantity of air more slowly than those who have a high-pitched voice, as I show more fully in the *Book on Organs*.

As for laughter and tears, I shall speak of them in another place. It must also be remarked that <term>Aristotle</term> is mistaken when he says in the 13th Problem that those who are warm produce a deeper sound when they blow into flutes, and those who are cold produce higher sounds; for the sound of flutes is modified by the size of their <term>mouthpieces</term> <note>Original: "lumieres," referring to the aperture or "window" of a flue pipe or flute where the air vibrates.</note>, or by their holes, and they have the same sound whether the wind pushed into them comes from a warm place or a cold one. But this difficulty belongs to the Organs and other wind instruments, which I treat elsewhere.

He makes the same errors in the 26th Problem, and in others, where he always supposes that a smaller quantity of air is moved faster, even though the force moving it is weak, and that the force moving the largest multitude of air is very strong—because, he says, the small amount of air is like a line, and the larger quantity of air is like a body. From this, one would have to conclude that of two organ pipes, one of which is two feet long and the other one foot, the one that is only one foot long would have a deeper sound than the other when it is four or eight times wider—since a hollow cylinder one foot long, whose diameter is quadruple or eightfold that of a hollow cylinder two feet long, contains much more air, as is demonstrated in <term>Geometry</term>. And yet it is a very certain thing that this cylinder or pipe which contains more air has a much higher sound than the cylinder or pipe two feet long. Moreover, it is very certain that <term>eunuchs</term> <note>Castrati or male singers with high-pitched voices were common in the musical landscape of this era.</note> and others push a large quantity of air when they speak very loudly, more so than the most robust men whose speech is weak, and yet the latter have a thicker and deeper voice than the former.

Now, it is not necessary to examine his other questions, since he always relies on the same principles, the falsehood of which is evident. For example, he says that voices are deeper in winter than in summer because the air is thicker and less suited to movement. But if we follow experience, our Basses will not agree with what he says, for they are just as hollow and deep in summer as in winter, since they always sing the same pieces of music at the same pitch. And furthermore, if the air is coarser (about which those do not agree who hold that it is thicker in summer), the strength of the stomach and the lungs is similarly greater in winter, as we experience, and as he himself admits in other places following <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The ancient Greek physician often cited as the father of medicine.</note>, who remarks that the bellies of animals are warmer in winter than in summer; so that this force, which depends on heat, compensates for the thickness of the air. It must therefore be concluded that the high or low pitch of sounds and voices has no cause other than the greater speed and frequency of the returns, reflections, or the ebb and flow of the air, without the quantity of said air being able to bring any change to the pitch, as I have demonstrated elsewhere.

I add, nevertheless, that if he intends to speak of these returns or beatings of the air when he says that the sound is higher as the movement of the air is faster, then he is right. Now, one can perhaps conjecture from his 19th Problem that he...

held this opinion, although he falls into another error, since he supposes in this Problem, and in the 20th, that voices seem to be higher-pitched when one is further away from them; for if one sings or tunes an instrument to <term>unison</term> <note>Two notes at the exact same pitch.</note> when one is very far from other instruments, one finds that the song and the instrument make the same unison with the instruments or voices that one approaches.

Moreover, the reason he gives for this experience is not good; for even if the air moving in a distant space were in smaller quantity, and had much diminished from the place where the sound began, the same distance could be the cause of its movement being slower, as he confesses elsewhere. Consequently, the distant sound should rather be deeper than higher-pitched, since the highness of a sound is made by the speed of movement, and not by the quantity of air, as I have said previously. But perhaps those who reported the experiment to Aristotle took a weaker voice for a higher-pitched one, for that which is weak is compared to that which is thin and slender.

As for the cows and calves, of whom he says that the voices are deeper than those of bulls and oxen—and which he treats more amply in the 7th chapter of the 5th book of *On Animals*—if that is true, it must necessarily be that the wind from their lungs is pushed more weakly, or that the opening of the larynx of calves and cows, which is called the <term>glottis</term> <note>The opening between the vocal cords in the larynx.</note>, is larger than that of oxen and bulls, which is false. It would then be necessary for Aristotle to prove that a small quantity of air is moved slowly by the calves, though he always supposes the contrary in his other questions, where he maintains that the movement of a small quantity of air is fast, even though it can be very slow when the force moving it is very weak. It must, however, be noted that one inspires all the more air as the heart is warmer, since inspiration occurs to cool it, or to furnish it with the matter for its <term>spirits</term> <note>In early modern physiology, "spirits" were subtle fluids thought to circulate through the body to facilitate movement and sensation.</note>; and consequently, the voice which is made by the expiration of this same air is stronger or thicker than that of those whose heart is less warm, and who expire a smaller quantity of air, assuming that the instruments of the voice are equal.

Now, one can conclude from this entire discourse that the voice of animals is always higher-pitched as their <term>reed</term> <note>Original: "anche." The author compares the vocal apparatus to the reed of a musical instrument.</note> is smaller, whether the opening of the glottis is diminished by <term>fluxions</term> <note>An old medical term for an excessive flow of humors or inflammation.</note>, by fear, by sadness, and by other passions, or by nature, by old age, or by whatever other manner one wishes. But I desire that the reader note that I would be pleased if someone could verify that Aristotle did not fail in all the places where he spoke of voices; for even though many believe he is not the author of the *Problems*, he who shows the truth of their solutions or their hypotheses will greatly oblige me.

### PROPOSITION XVII.

->*To know whether it is easier to lead the voice from a deep sound to a high one, than from a high to a deep one.*<-

### On the Voice.

...than the low ones, as Aristotle says in Problem 20, for they are more composed and more multiplied; this is why he remarked that the lowest voices must recite the song representing rest, which he calls a <term>soft and calm melody</term> <note>original Greek: μελος μαλακον, και ηρεμαιον (melos malakon, kai hremaion)</note>, because they approach rest and silence, and they are made by a weak and soft beating of the air, as one sees in the 50th Problem of his 19th Section. Now, it is easier to move from the complex to the simple through analysis and division than from the simple to the complex through <term>synthesis</term> <note>The process of building up or combining elements.</note> and composition, or multiplication. Furthermore, we most often experience that singers are forced to "re-warm" <note>A term for readjusting the pitch after it has drifted.</note> their voices at the end of their <term>motets</term> <note>A polyphonic choral composition, usually on a religious text.</note> or hymns, because their voices have naturally lowered without them noticing, and without them being able to recognize it for certain without the help of an organ pipe or some other instrument that puts them back in their proper tone. The high pitch has need of external help to be preserved in its movement, just as we have need of the supernatural help of God to maintain us in the movement of His Love. This shows that movement from high to low is more natural to the voice than the contrary movement, which forces the body of the <term>larynx</term> <note>The voice box.</note> to rise too high; this causes us more difficulty and pain than when it descends, since the descent is more natural to it, just as happens with other heavy bodies.

Moreover, assuming that the moving voice does not extend and rise as far as a shriek, nor descend as far as a rasp—which are the extremes that offend the ear and fight against the melody—one finds that the low voice is the most agreeable. We notice this with the Lute, where the <term>chanterelle</term> <note>The highest-pitched string on a lute or violin.</note> does not provide as much melody and is not as sweet as the bass strings, whose movements are not made with as much violence and speed as those of the said chanterelle. From this comes the fact that we feel strained, as if we were carrying on our shoulders those who struggle to climb and to sing high notes. Now, if the low voice is more pleasing, it is likely that it is easier to reach than the high voice, which is less pleasing; and even if the high voice were more pleasing, nevertheless the strain and labor necessary to produce this voice diverts and diminishes the pleasure of the ear, for when the pleasure does not outweigh the pain, it cannot be great.

One can also consider here whether it is more difficult to open the <term>glottis</term> <note>The opening between the vocal cords.</note> than to tighten it beyond its natural state; and whether the muscles of the <term>thorax</term> <note>The chest or upper trunk of the body.</note> and the larynx, and the lungs, exert themselves more to sing from high to low than from low to high. But because it seems that these are the same thing, or at least that there is no great difference, and that the experiences of singers are not so certain nor so uniform that we can draw a reliable judgment from them; and even because he who relies only on experience never penetrates the secrets of Nature and truth, to which reason alone opens the door—and because practice cannot lead us to universality, since speculation alone finds truths that can never fall into any material organ—besides the fact that experience is subject to the senses, from which one cannot always draw a true judgment (and less so in Music than in anything else, due to the different passions and inclinations of men, who rarely agree on what concerns the excellence of the diversities that adorn Music), one must have recourse to reason rather than to experiments. For there do not occur so many disagreements between those who abstract themselves from all that is corporeal and who seek a principle purified of all mixture, as there do between the <term>Practitioners</term> <note>Performers or musicians who play by ear or habit rather than theoretical understanding.</note> who are blind in their art and have not so much certainty as they have routine, which sometimes hits upon a good result only by chance.

# Book One

We must therefore follow the reason that seems to dictate to us that it is more pleasant to sing while ascending than while descending, especially since one goes, as it were, from death to life, and from nothingness to being. This is because the high-pitched voice has more movement, and its high pitch is produced by beatings of air that are more frequent and follow each other more closely; this approaches a "continuous" state, whose being and consistency are firmer and more uniform than those of a low sound. The parts of a low sound are more separated, and consequently closer to their own ruin and nothingness—a state which all beings flee with all their strength. We experience this in concerts, where the <term>Sopranos</term> <note>Original: "Dessus." In this period, the highest vocal part in a polyphonic composition.</note>, both in voices and instruments, awaken the attention much more and are much more pleasant—as if approaching closer to heaven and to life—than the <term>Basses</term>. Now, we take more pleasure in approaching that which is more perfect and more full of life than that which is more imperfect and closer to death. From this it follows that we love and cherish children more than the elderly, who are similar to great, heavy sounds and to winter, just as children are like spring or summer, and like heat or fire. Low voices are like the darkness, sought only by owls and goblins; but high voices are like light and the day, which serve as an ornament to Nature, just as high sounds do for Music. Music loses all its charm when it does not have good Sopranos; the low voices serve almost no other purpose than to make the high ones noticed, allowing them to enter the ear and the mind with more diversity and pleasure.

This is, in my opinion, part of what one can imagine to prove one side or the other of this <term>difficulty</term> <note>In the context of 17th-century philosophy, a "difficulty" refers to a formal problem or question posed for debate.</note>, which should, it seems to me, be resolved in the manner that follows. However, I do not wish to prejudice those who will produce better reasons for either side; I wish this to be understood for all other difficulties where the solution does not consist of true demonstrations, but only of conjectures or probable reasons, which are subject to being contradicted and challenged.

One can move from low to high, or from high to low, in two ways: namely by <term>conjunct degrees</term> <note>Moving step-by-step up or down the scale (e.g., Do-Re-Mi).</note>, or by <term>disjunct degrees</term> <note>Moving by leaps or intervals larger than a step (e.g., Do-Sol).</note> which are separated. This is why we must see which is the easiest or most difficult; and because the <term>Octave</term> contains two separate sounds that one can only sing by leaping from one to the other, we will begin with this <term>Consonance</term> <note>An interval or chord that sounds stable and harmonious.</note>.

I say, then, first, that it is easier to ascend to the Octave than to descend to it, because it is easier to divide a thing into two parts than it is to add as much again to it, or to double it. For example, it is easier to divide

the line AB into two parts through the middle, than to add the equal line BC to it: for one sees both ends of the line AB that one wishes to divide in two; but one sees only one of the ends of the equal line that must be lengthened, namely B, and the eye and the hand are so occupied in tracing the line BC that one almost no longer remembers the two ends of AB, nor consequently the length of line AB.

The same thing happens when one rises to the Octave, because it is easier to divide the air of the mouth into two parts than to add as much again to it, because we already have that which we are dividing, but we do not have what must be added. Now, it is easier to dispose of and order what we have and what is present to us, than what we do not have and what is absent.

## On the Voice.

But to understand this more clearly, one must remember that the high voice is like the <term>chanterelle</term> <note>The highest-pitched string on a lute or similar stringed instrument.</note> of a Lute, or like the thinnest and shortest string, and the low voice like the thickest or longest. This is because the larynx and the <term>glottis</term> <note>The opening between the vocal folds in the larynx.</note> are wider and more open for low sounds than for high sounds. Because high sounds are produced by the division or reduction of low ones, it follows that it is easier to move upward to a high pitch than to descend to a low one; this can be applied to other sounds which we ascend toward, as we did with the Octave; see Aristotle in Problem 13.

As for <term>conjunct degrees</term> <note>Moving from one note to the very next note in a scale, rather than leaping.</note>, there are those who maintain that it is easier to descend than to ascend, following Aristotle's remark in Problem 33 of the 19th section. This is because it seems that the high sound is the beginning of the low, and that the middle sound—which the Greeks call the *Mese*—is the leader and, as it were, the Prince of the <term>Tetrachord</term> <note>A scale of four notes; the "Mese" was the central, stabilizing note in ancient Greek musical theory.</note>: <note>Original Greek: ἡγεμὼν ὀξυτάτη τῷ τετραχόρδου—"the highest leader of the tetrachord."</note> for the low sound is the most noble and the most resonant: <note>Original Greek: βαρὺ δυνατώτερον, καὶ ὀξυφωνότερον—"the low is more powerful, and [the high] more clear-voiced."</note>. But this difficulty will be explained in the proposition where we shall see whether the low sound is more excellent and pleasant than the high. It must nevertheless be noted that Aristotle teaches the opposite in Problem 47, where he says that the voice often falters and ends on a high note by ascending higher than it should, because the high pitch is easier to sing. Yet he holds the opposite in Problem 37, where he teaches that it is difficult to sing high notes because of the great tension and violence one must apply to them. He seemingly forgets what he said in the eleventh section: that the voice appears higher at the end than at the beginning because it is smaller and weaker. Now, it is easier to do a smaller thing than a larger one, since the former requires less strength than the latter, just as it takes less time to travel a short distance than a long one. He confirms this in Problems 6 and 20 of the eleventh section, and in 13, 14, 15, 16, and several others, in which he attributes the cause of high voices to the weakness and infirmity of those who speak or sing, as we saw in the 17th proposition.

But it suffices to note that Aristotle is not very consistent in this matter, and that there are many others who hold that it is easier to sing while descending than while ascending. For example, they say it is easier to sing *la, sol, fa, mi, re* than *re, mi, fa, sol, la*, because the *la* produces three <term>vibrations</term> <note>Original: "tremblemens." The author is describing the frequency of sound waves. In the ratio of a Perfect Fifth (3:2), the higher note vibrates three times for every two vibrations of the lower note.</note> while the *re* produces two. From this it follows that one of the vibrations of *la* does not align with the vibrations of *re*, for the second vibration of *la* does not coincide with any part of the vibrations of *re*. However, the *re* has no vibration that does not coincide with one of the preceding vibrations of *la*. Furthermore, the vibrations of *re* always align on the second beat, but those of *la* only align on every third beat at the same time. One of these vibrations in every three-beat cycle remains, as it were, separate, without uniting with any part of the vibrations of *re*, such that the string or the voice of *la* produces at least three hundred vibrations in every moment of time that do not align.

Similarly, it is argued that it is more pleasant to sing *fa, mi, re* than *re, mi, fa*, because *fa* has four vibrations that do not align with any of the vibrations of *re*, but *re* has only three vibrations that do not align with the vibrations of *la*. Now, it is more pleasant to finish with sounds that approach closest to unity, as low sounds do; this is why the final cadence of songs is almost always made by descending. # Book One

The reason I have provided for the **Octave** <note>The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</note> also suggests that it is easier to diminish the **glottis** <term>glottis</term> <note>The opening between the vocal folds in the larynx that controls the pitch of the voice.</note> which produces the low sound, in order to make a higher one—both in **conjunct degrees** <note>Moving from one note to the next step in a scale (e.g., C to D).</note> and in leaps. For example, it is easier to diminish the opening of the glottis and the air by a ninth or tenth part to rise from *ut* to *re*, or from *re* to *mi*, than it is to add a similar portion of opening or air to descend from *mi* to *re*, or from *re* to *ut*. One must conclude that it is easier to ascend than to descend, whether by steps or by intervals. Furthermore, the argument drawn from the vibration of the *la* <note>The note A in the solfège system.</note>, which is not found in any vibration of the *re* <note>The note D.</note>, is not valid, because the *la* is finished by the time one pronounces *re*. This is why it does not matter if one vibration has no relation to the others, since the said vibration is finished when the others begin.

But one must respond to the arguments of the opposing party and say, in the first place, that everyone flees from "nothingness" <note>The author uses "nothingness" (le neant) to represent silence, lack of existence, or the bottom of the scale.</note> and everything that approaches it, as much as they can. Now, this flight comes from the same principle that makes us seek what helps to maintain and preserve us in our being. For although low sounds are simpler in their movements, nonetheless, because they are larger, they require a greater force due to the larger quantity of air that must be pushed. This is experienced when one wishes to sound the large pipes of **Organs**, for the lungs cannot supply the quantity of wind necessary to make them speak. Likewise, when one sings the **Bass**, one cannot sustain the voice for as long as when one sings higher; this is why one is more often forced to catch one’s breath. And the low sound of the Octave contains twice the high, and is compared to an obtuse angle in the eighth problem, just as the high sound is compared to an acute angle.

Now, although it seems more natural to go downward, and voices lower themselves on their own when one sings for a long time, it does not follow that it is more pleasant, nor even easier, to descend than to ascend. This is because this natural inclination to go downward is an imperfection that leads us back toward nothingness. As for ease, experience teaches that it is easier to sing while ascending than while descending, particularly when one employs **passages** <note>Melodic runs or flourishes between notes.</note> or **trills** <term>fredons</term> <note>Rapid vocal ornaments or "shaking" of the voice.</note>. To this, one must add that just as Nature, and even the Arts and sciences, begin with the simplest and easiest things, one should also begin with low voices rather than high ones, since they are the simplest and easiest, following the opinion of others. And when the pitch drops while singing for a long time, this comes from certain voices that cannot conform to the tone they have taken, which is too high for them; this is why they always descend until they have met their natural tone, and they carry the others along so much that they force them to descend.

Finally, the argument that low tones are more pleasant than high ones assumes something that has not yet been determined, of which a specific discourse must be made. However, we can respond that many maintain that high sounds are more pleasant than low ones, and that they receive more pleasure from hearing the **Treble** <term>Deſſus</term> <note>The highest part in a polyphonic composition, equivalent to the soprano.</note> sing than the **Bass** or the other parts.

### PROPOSITION XVIII.

->*Concerning whether it is easier to sing by conjunct degrees than by separate or disjunct degrees.*<-

This difficulty deserves to be clarified, even though it seems it can be decided by the common opinion of practitioners <note>Practical musicians and singers of the time.</note>, who hold that it is easier to sing by **conjunct degrees** <note>Moving from one note to the very next in the scale, like C to D.</note> than by **disjunct degrees** <note>Leaping over notes, like C to G.</note>, without even excepting the **Consonances** <note>Intervals that sound "pleasant" or stable, such as the Octave or Fifth.</note>. Nevertheless, if one remembers that when singing by conjunct degrees, it is more difficult for the imagination to subtract or add the movements necessary to produce the tones and semitones than when singing by consonant disjunct degrees, it will be difficult to follow their opinion and the experience which seems to favor them with reason. For it is more difficult, for example, to take the eighth or ninth part of a whole, and to increase or decrease it by an eighth or ninth part, than to increase or decrease it by half—since a half is easier to find, and a whole is divided more easily into two or three parts than into eight or nine. Now, when one sings by conjunct degrees—for example, *ut, re, mi* <note>The first three notes of the scale: C, D, and E.</note>—if *ut* corresponds to eight string vibrations, *re* will have nine, and *mi* ten; therefore one must increase *ut* by an eighth part to make *re*, and *re* by a ninth part to make *mi*. And if one rises from *mi* to *fa* <note>Moving from E to F.</note>, one must increase *mi* by a fifteenth part of *mi* to make *fa*.

But to rise to the **Octave**, one must increase the low sound by half, and if one wishes to descend by an Octave, one must decrease the sound by half. Similarly, if one wants to rise to the **Twelfth** <note>An interval of an octave plus a fifth.</note>, one must triple the sound, and the imagination must retain two-thirds. It seems this difficulty can be resolved in two ways. The first is that since the Octave contains the musical scale, it is easier to rise to the top by steps than by leaping and passing through without steps; for there is less space from *ut* to *re* than from one of the sounds of the Octave (or other Consonances) to another. The second is that one might say long-standing habit and the great practice we have in singing by conjunct degrees has rendered them easier and more natural than the Consonances. As for the larger **Dissonances** <note>Intervals that sound "clashing" or unstable.</note>, they are more difficult to sing, both because of the distance between their sounds and the difficulty those sounds have in uniting. Furthermore, there is less trouble in opening the **glottis** <term>glottis</term> <note>The opening between the vocal folds that determines pitch.</note> by conjunct degrees than by intervals, because there is less difference between these openings. For example, one only needs to open or close the glottis more or less by an eighth or ninth part when singing *ut re* or *re ut*; but when making an Octave, one must open or close it twice as much as before. Finally, any passage made from one extreme to the other without a middle point is more difficult than one made by passing through the middle.

This happens particularly with the sounds of strings, organs, or small children, who often produce an octave above or below the sound which we thought was in **unison** <note>Two or more sounds at the same pitch.</note> with the aforementioned voices or sounds.

Now, one of the means to recognize this depends on another voice, or another sound, which must be placed at the **Fifth** or the **Fourth** <note>Musical intervals: a Fifth spans five scale degrees (like C to G), and a Fourth spans four (like C to F).</note> of the sound or voice that is in doubt; for if one intends to produce a Fifth below, and yet the sound is an octave lower than imagined, the sound one thought was a Fifth will turn out to be a Fourth. Conversely, if one intends to produce a Fourth, one will produce a Fifth; and because the Fourth is harsher and rougher than the Fifth, it can easily be discerned. Furthermore, if the sound were a **Fifteenth** <note>An interval of two octaves.</note> lower than imagined, one would produce an **Eleventh** instead of a **Twelfth** <note>An Eleventh is an octave plus a Fourth; a Twelfth is an octave plus a Fifth.</note>. This can be explained by numbers in this manner: if the sound is 3 instead of the 6 one imagines, it would be necessary to strike 4 to create a Fifth with 6; and because one has taken 6 for 3, one will produce a Fourth and not a Fifth; by which the rest of the discourse may be understood.

The other manner depends on the strings; for if we believe, for example, that we are producing a Twelfth, and yet we produce an Eleventh—that is to say, if the sound is a Fifteenth lower than we imagine—when we strike the string that deceives us, it will not make the other string tremble as sensibly as it would if it were making a Twelfth and not an Eleventh. The same thing must be said proportionately of the Fifth and the Fourth. I said *proportionately*, for when the string that makes the Twelfth is struck, it makes the string at the Twelfth tremble more strongly than the one at the Fifth, as I have proved elsewhere.

I leave aside the third manner, which is the most subtle, because it is easy to understand it through the discourse I have made concerning the number of vibrations of each string in the *Book of the Spinet* <note>The spinet is a smaller, rectangular member of the harpsichord family.</note>.

### PROPOSITION XX.

-> *One can learn to speak well and to pronounce well by means* <-
-> *of Music.* <-

Since speech consists of beating the air, and since one speaks well when one accents and pronounces words <note>original: "dictions"</note> as is required, it is not difficult to understand how Music can serve in speaking well, for it treats of **accents**. We shall show in the 47th Proposition that the perfect Musician can invent the best of all possible languages, and can make it spoken to perfection. Now, if one considers what it is to speak well, one will find that it is nothing other than to pronounce distinctly, and to make syllables long or short according to their nature, or the designation of those who invented the words and who prescribed their pronunciation and usage. To this, one must add accents; for even though one pronounces very distinctly and observes the measure of the syllables, it often happens that the speech is unpleasant because of the bad accent given to it. Music also shows how much each syllable must be raised, and how much the last one (upon which the accent is usually made) must be more acute or more grave than the first; so that there is nothing of importance in words that is not subject to the rules and the science of Music, as is easy to conclude from all that has been said in the preceding books. And if one encounters many Musicians who speak poorly or who have bad accents, they are capable of correcting themselves, since they know how one must proceed. But we shall speak further of this matter in the discourse on the profit that Orators and Preachers can draw from Music.

### PROPOSITION XXI.

->*Explaining how the voice can be increased and weakened.*<-

We showed in the 16th Proposition how the voice is rendered more grave and more acute; we must see in this one the ways that make it stronger or weaker, the first of which consists in pushing more or less air. Experience teaches that a sound is greater and stronger as the quantity of air that one strikes is greater: for example, when one touches the strings of a **Lute** <note>A plucked string instrument popular in the Renaissance and Baroque eras.</note> or another instrument with more force, they sound louder, because they beat and cleave a greater quantity of air. This happens similarly to the tongues of **reeds** <note>The vibrating element in instruments like the oboe, here compared to the vocal folds.</note> and the **larynx**; for when one speaks louder, one pushes more air, which exits with more violence, just as water does through a channel when it is more heavily burdened or more pressed; for even though the opening of the channel always seems to be filled, it is nevertheless more "full" when the water exits with greater violence. From this one can conclude that all places that are hollow and concave reinforce the voice, insofar as they preserve the movement of the air for a longer time, or because they cause a greater quantity of air to move and tremble longer. And since opposites come from opposite causes, it must be admitted that the voice is all the weaker as the place where it is made is less concave and more solid. From this it follows that the soundboard <note>original: "table"</note> of Lutes resonates better when it is thinner and more delicate, and that the sounds become duller when it is thicker; and consequently that soundboards of gold, silver, ivory, boxwood, or other solid and massive wood, are not as good as those of cedar, fir, or other woods that are lighter, more porous, and less dense <note>original: "rare," meaning the opposite of compact or dense</note>; which gives them a certain kind of concavity, and a vibration that brings grace and strength to the sounds. And if we had no palate, and the sound were made simply by the glottis <note>original: "languette," referring to the vocal apparatus</note> without being held and preserved in the mouth, it would appear much lesser and weaker. As for the other ways of reinforcing the voice, which depend on the reflection made by means of bodies formed and shaped as ovals, parabolas, or hyperbolas, we shall speak of them later.

There is yet another way that serves to reinforce the voice, namely the continuity of the bodies that serve to make the sound, or which preserve it over a long distance, as is experienced with beams, at the end of which one hears the slightest taps with which they are struck at the other end, and with the vaults and arches of bridges, which carry the voice and other noises through the entire arch much further than they would go without this help. I leave aside a thousand other ways by which the voice can be aided, because they can be related to the preceding ones, or because they must be treated in another place.

### COROLLARY.

One can consider several things on this subject, particularly that God has not given us two or more openings of the larynx, or several arteries to make two or more sounds at the same time, because they would have been useless to us, and one might have hindered the other; and further, the harmony of two or more parts that a single man could have made is not necessary for him. God willed that this pleasure should depend on others, so that the harmony of voices might invite men to a harmony of manners, and to a reciprocal friendship, which is represented by the Consonances <note>In music theory, these are intervals that sound stable and pleasant together.</note>. He has also not given us a voice so strong that it can be heard by everyone, so that each person may have spaces in the air where he can exercise his voice without it being hindered by other noises, by which the air would always be moved if voices penetrated its entire extent. I leave aside a thousand other considerations that can serve as a subject to admire the wisdom of the Sovereign Artisan <note>A reference to God as the master creator.</note>.

### PROPOSITION XXII.

->*To determine if a single man can sing two or three different parts at the same time, and if he can ascend or descend higher by some kind of artifice than he does naturally.*<-

Although it seems that the same man cannot sing two different parts at the same time, because a single part so occupies the mouth, the throat, and the other organs of the voice that he can pronounce nothing except what he is singing; nevertheless, experience teaches that one can sing one part with the throat and another by whistling, as does the son of Pierre d'Avignon, who for this reason is considered one of the rarest men in the world. But no man has yet been seen who utters two words, or who sings two notes at the same time while pronouncing a syllable—for example, C and D <note>original: "VT & RE," the historical names for the first two notes of the hexachord scale</note>; for those who speak from the throat or from the back of the mouth to make people believe they are far away, or to imitate an echo, cannot utter other words at the same time, because the tongue and the other organs of speech cannot have two movements at once.

As for whistling, it depends solely on a lesser or greater pressure of the lips, which does not prevent the throat and the tongue from moving, as is easy to experiment with at any time; for there are few who cannot whistle while singing, provided they are not obliged to utter words, although that can easily be acquired through long practice.

Now, since the whistling of the lips is not tied to the low or high pitch of the voice, or of the syllables being pronounced, one should not be surprised that it performs the Treble <note>original: "Dessus," the highest vocal part</note>, because the highness of its sounds is determined by the opening or the pressure of the lips, and by the different multitude of air vibrations <note>original: "battemens de l'air"</note> created by the meeting of the lips. I have noticed that one whistles more easily at the Octave and at the Twelfth of the voice or the words being pronounced than at other intervals, but everyone can conduct their own particular experiments on this subject. To which I add that one can also perform a third part with the breath from the nose by means of a flute, or even several parts if one pushes the breath from the nose into several flutes at the same time; but besides the fact that it is very difficult to accustom oneself to performing these parts, they are much less pleasant than when each man sings his own.

The other part of the Proposition seems more difficult to resolve; for although experience shows us that La Fueille <note>likely a reference to a contemporary virtuoso known for this feat</note> ascends eight or ten tones higher than usual by means of an ivy leaf that he places on his tongue, which serves him like a flageolet <note>a small, high-pitched wind instrument similar to a recorder</note> or another instrument whose sound is very sharp, nevertheless we have found no similar industry for descending eight or ten tones lower than the deepest tone of the natural voice. And when one ascends by means of this leaf, one cannot pronounce words, for it only causes the movements and vibrations of the air or breath pushed from the lungs to be more frequent as the tones one reaches become higher. Thus, one would have to slow the movements and create a smaller multitude of vibrations in the air to descend lower than the natural tone of the voice, as happens when one uses the Serpent <note>a bass wind instrument shaped like a snake, used to support the lower voices</note> or some other Bass wind instrument.
