## PROPOSITION XXIII.

->*To determine how halls or galleries must be built to hear distinctly at one end everything said at the other, even if they are very long and the voices are very weak and small; wherein one sees the proportions between the circle and the Ellipse, whose measurements are reported.*<-

This Proposition contains one of the most beautiful secrets of Mechanics and of Catoptrics <term>Catoptrics: the branch of optics dealing with reflection, which the author here applies to the reflection of sound</term>, which will lead us to what must be determined here regarding sounds and voices. I say, therefore, that the vault of the hall or gallery must be made in an oval—that is to say, it must have the shape of an *Ellipse*—inasmuch as the sounds that strike the elliptical vault, when the speaker is in a certain given place, are all reflected to the other extremity, at the point which is opposite in a straight line to the previous place. These two points, or these two places, are called the two *foci* <note>original: "focus"</note> of the *Ellipse*, of which I have already explained some properties elsewhere.

But the principal property serving this purpose consists in the fact that all the rays starting from one of the *foci* and falling upon the surface of the Ellipse are reflected to the other *focus*. This resembles the *focus* of a parabola in that both gather all rays into a single point, although this occurs in different ways: for the rays falling on a parabola must be parallel to its axis, which is not required for rays falling on an *Ellipse*, for it is enough that they come from one of its *foci*.

Now, the figure that follows will make this discourse understood and will show how to measure all kinds of Ellipses, the proportions of which I set down here as demonstrated by Archimedes.

1. Every circle is to the Ellipse as the square of the diameter of the circle is to the rectangle formed by the diameters <note>the major and minor axes</note> of the Ellipse.

2. By the 5th and 6th propositions of *On Conoids and Spheroids* <note>original: "des conoides, & des spheroides," a treatise by Archimedes</note>, every circle having its diameter equal to the major diameter of the Ellipse is to that Ellipse as the square of the major diameter of the Ellipse is to the rectangle formed by the two diameters.

3. Now, as the square of the major diameter is to the rectangle of the two diameters, so the major diameter is to the minor; and as the square of the minor is to the rectangle comprised of the two, so the minor is to the major.

4. Therefore, as the minor is to the major, so the circle formed by the major diameter is to the Ellipse.

5. And as the minor is to the major, so the circle formed by the minor diameter is to the Ellipse.

6. Therefore, if one knows the area of the circle, one will know the area of the Ellipse, and vice versa.

Now, I wish further to provide the method that must be used to find the solidity <note>volume</note> of the spheroid, which some improperly call the *solidity of the Ellipse*; this I shall do in the discourse that follows.

->*How to measure the Ellipse, or the oval, whose major diameter is equal to the semi-diameter of the firmament, and any other proposed Ellipse.*<-

I have shown in the preceding discourse how to find the area, or the capacity <note>volume/area</note>

...capacity <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of the "capacity" or area of the Ellipse</note> of the Ellipse; which can also be done using numbers. For, having found the areas of the two circles—the one having the major diameter of the Ellipse for its diameter, and the other having the minor diameter—if one multiplies the area of one by the area of the other and takes the square root of the product, the root found will be the area of the Ellipse. And if one takes the square root of this root, one will have the side of a square equal in area to the Ellipse. As for the circumference <note>original: "circuit"</note>, it cannot be found [precisely], any more than that of the circle, the Parabola, or the Hyperbola; but let us see how we must find the volume <term>solidity: the historical term for three-dimensional volume</term> of the spheroid.

First, the cone is one-third of the cylinder which has the same height and the same base, as Euclid demonstrated in Book 12, Proposition 10.

Now, the cylinder is produced by the plane of the circular base multiplying the height of the cylinder.

Therefore, having the minor diameter of the spheroid, one will have the area of the circle made from that same diameter; which, being multiplied by half the height of the major diameter, will give the cylinder, of which one-third will be the cone, which will have the same height as half the spheroid, and the same base.

Now, half of the spheroid is double this cone; therefore, the entire spheroid is equal to four times the cone, according to the 29th proposition of the *Conoids* <note>Referring to Archimedes’ treatise *On Conoids and Spheroids*</note>. This I demonstrate by this figure, in which AB and CD are the diameters of the Ellipse. Now, the circle of which CD is the diameter is to the Ellipse as CD is to AB; and the circle which has AB for its diameter is to the Ellipse as AB is to CD. Finally, the cone which has for its base the circle of which CD is the diameter, and AE for its height, is one-quarter of the spheroid ABCD.

Straight lines connect point F to points C, D, and E, forming geometric triangles within the ellipse's quadrants.</image-desc>

I now wish to perform the calculation for the Ellipse whose major diameter is equal to the semi-diameter of the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars in historical cosmology</note>, and the minor diameter is half of that. Let diameter AB, then, be 14,000 terrestrial semi-diameters <note>radii of the Earth</note>, and CD be 7,000. Now, I suppose here that the Earth has a circumference of 7,200 leagues, each of which is 15,000 Royal feet <note>original: "pieds de Roy," a pre-metric French unit of length</note>: therefore, the semi-diameter of the Earth is 1,145 and 5/11 leagues.

The surface area of this Ellipse is 1,010,290,909,090 [square leagues]; of which the solid content <note>volume</note> is 1,527,481,860,087,258,982,520 leagues, which are worth 22,914,227,701,308,888,473,800,000,000 Royal feet.

We have found thus far that the area of the circle made from the major diameter of the Ellipse is to the area of the Ellipse as the major diameter of the Ellipse is to the minor; and that the area of the circle made from the minor diameter of the Ellipse is to the area of the Ellipse as the minor diameter is to the major. Consequently, if the major diameter is double the minor, as it is in the preceding Ellipse, the area of the circle made from the major diameter is double the area of the Ellipse.

To which I add that the mean proportional <term>mean proportional: a value between two numbers such that the ratio of the first to the mean is the same as the ratio of the mean to the second; the geometric mean</term> between the two diameters of the Ellipse is the diameter of the circle equal in area to the Ellipse, so that one need only find the content of this circle to know the content of the Elliptical area. But we must find the points of the Ellipse called the *foci* <note>original: "foyers," or "focus"</note>, inasmuch as light and sounds reflect from one to the other, creating one of the most admirable effects in all of nature.

## PROPOSITION XXV.

### *To determine at which points on the major diameter of the Ellipse the foci meet—that is to say, the points where the rays of light and sound reflect when they originate from one or the other of the said foci.*

This proposition contains the fruit and the principal effect of the Ellipse, which is particularly useful for sounds; for if the person speaking, or playing an instrument, is at point G, the sound that travels from G to the surface BCA or BDA will reflect to point F, and the sound made at point F will reflect to point G. Consequently, if sound follows the reflection of light, and the ellipse is perfectly polished, it will be heard as clearly from G at F, or from F at G, as if one were standing right next to the speaker, even if the oval were as long as the radius of the heavens <note>original: "semidiametre du firmament"—a poetic way of describing a massive, cosmic distance</note>. However, because sound is nothing other than the movement of air, which diminishes little by little, we should not speak of sound in exactly the same way as light, since light is not hindered and diminished by the resistance of air as sound is.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of an ellipse with horizontal major axis AB and vertical minor axis CD. The center is marked E. Foci are marked F and G on the major axis. Lines connect F and G to point C on the upper vertex, and to point D on the lower vertex.</image-desc>

Now, it is very easy to find these points, as one only needs to take half of the major diameter AE with a compass and place one of its feet at the end of the minor diameter <note>Point C or D</note>, and the other on the major diameter; for it will show the two foci <term>foyers: literally "hearths" or "focal points" where energy converges</term> on either side, namely F and G; for DF and DG are equal to AE. To this I add that all lines drawn from one of the foci to the surface, and from the surface to the other focus, are equal to the major diameter: for example, the line FDG <note>The combined path from F to the boundary at D and back to G</note> is equal to diameter AB, and so it is with the others.

The shape of this Ellipse shows what form must be given to a hall or gallery where one wishes to be heard from a great distance, even when speaking very low, and even if the sound is very small and weak; this is why I wish to show further in the following proposition how the vault <note>The curved ceiling</note> must be constructed when one has two specific locations between which one wishes to hear all kinds of sounds.

One must bisect AB at point D, and the line C in the middle; and after having drawn the line DA out to E, one must make DE equal to half of C; and having drawn DF perpendicular to BE, one must describe from center A a circle, of which half of C is the radius <note>original: "semidiametre"</note>, which intersects the line DF at point F, for DF will be half of the minor diameter of the Ellipse.

### PROPOSITION XXVII.

*How Architects must build vaults to give them the figure and form of the Ellipse, in order to assist sounds, and to carry them further by artifice than they are carried naturally in open air, or in buildings that do not have the shape of the Ellipse, wherein it will be seen that Artisans do not make the true oval with their compass.*

Even though things that are beautiful and excellent, and which bring great utility, are customarily difficult, it is nevertheless easy to trace all kinds of Ellipses with a specialized compass, which one might call an <term>Elliptical compass</term>, or with two strings; for since all the lines that come from the *focus* and strike the concave surface of the Ellipse to reflect back to the other *focus* are equal to the major diameter, if one attaches a string to one of the *foci* and leads it through all the points where the circuit of the Ellipse must be traced, such that its other extremity always touches the other *focus*, the Ellipse will be described, as one sees in this figure, in which EC, EB, and EA represent the same string marking the points through which the Ellipse must be drawn.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of an ellipse used to demonstrate the "string method" of construction. A horizontal axis is marked with points E and F (the foci). Points G and H are located on the far left and right ends of the major axis, respectively. A vertical line passes through the center, marked with point I at the bottom.</image-desc>

From this it is apparent that Artisans do not make true ovals or Ellipses with their standard compasses, which describe only two portions of a circle for the two sides, and two others for the two ends of their oval; for the true Ellipse is not made of parts of one or several circles, but of other parts which are proper and particular to it, and which may be called "Elliptical."

But I wish also to explain other ways of describing the Ellipse, which I take from the second book of the *Conics* by Monsieur <term>Mydorge<note>Claude Mydorge (1585–1647), a prominent French mathematician and physicist who worked extensively on optics and geometry.</note></term> (whom one may call the <term>French Apollonius<note>A reference to Apollonius of Perga, the ancient Greek geometer known as the "Great Geometer" for his work on conic sections.</note></term>, since he has restored the science of <term>Conic Sections</term>), so that Architects may choose whichever method they please.

Now, I shall say many other things about these figures in the treatise on the **Echo**, which will teach how Architects ought to build places suitable for hearing all the voices of those who speak inside or outside, even though they may be one or two leagues away: and also in which places one should position Concerts to receive the greatest contentment one can imagine. Let us see, meanwhile, the manner of describing Ellipses.

### PROPOSITION XXVIII.

*Explaining other methods used to describe the Ellipse.*

The fifth general method from the second book of the *Conics* <note>original: "Coniques"; a study of the shapes resulting from cutting a cone, such as circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas.</note> by Mr. Mydorge <note>Claude Mydorge (1585–1647) was a prominent French mathematician and a friend of Descartes.</note> is one of the easiest; now, one must know the two *foci* <note>original: "focus". The points used to determine the curvature of the ellipse; in a whispering gallery, these are the points where sound collects.</note> A & B, and the two vertices, for the line joining the two *foci* is the major diameter, which must be extended to G, so as to make HG equal to HA. Then, one must describe arcs of a circle from center B of whatever size one wishes, provided that the diameter of the smallest is larger than AH, and that of the largest is smaller than BH, as do the arcs or circles described by the opening of the compass BF; one must then describe other arcs from point G, whose each diameter is equal to the distances from G to each circle, and the point of the compass which touches the aforementioned arcs at points F will show the locations through which the Ellipse must be drawn, as seen in the figure.

Now, if one takes the minor diameter for the diameter of a circle, the perpendicular lines drawn from said diameter to the circumference, and transferred onto the major diameter, will show the points through which the Ellipse must be drawn.

And if one wishes to extend the parabola, one must still find other mean proportionals, in order to have other points, for example, point 9, 10, and the others even unto infinity.

### COROLLARY.

It should be noted that all the demonstrations and descriptions of conic lines depend almost entirely on the right-angled triangle, as is seen in the parabola B A C, whose points are found by means of the triangle B C E and C F H. Likewise, mean proportionals are found by the same right-angled triangle, which has been rightly called the master of Geometry.

Now because the shape of the hyperbola is greatly useful for making voices louder and more intelligible, and because it can serve in several places where the Ellipse and the parabola would be useless, its description must be taught.

### PROPOSITION XXX.

*Explaining the manner in which it is necessary to describe all sorts of hyperbolas to strengthen the voice and musical concerts.*

Among several manners that serve to describe the hyperbola, the fifth general method from the second book is very easy, and relates to the second method of the preceding proposition; but one must know the vertex and the two foci <note>original: "focus"; the points that determine the shape of the curve.</note> of the hyperbola. Let the vertex be H, the focus be A, and the interval HG be equal to HA; let HA be extended toward I, in order to divide it into as many parts as one wishes. This being done, one must describe arcs through each point of the division, the radius <note>original: "semidiametre"</note> of which is the interval from B to each point; for the

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the construction of a hyperbola. A horizontal axis is marked with points A, H, G, and I. Point A is labeled as a focus (foyer) and H as a vertex (sommet). A vertical line segment passes through H. Various circular arcs are drawn from points A and B, intersecting at points labeled F, which define the hyperbolic curve. points where these arcs are cut by other arcs described from center A—whose radius is the interval from each point marked on HE to G (for example, the arcs described from B, the radius being BE, and the others being described from point A, the radius being GE)—show the points F, through which the line of the hyperbola passes. It is easy to find an infinity of other points through which the line must pass. Now it should be noted that the line HB is the transverse diameter, and HI the axis.

I leave aside several other general and particular methods that can be seen in the second book, in order to add here a good portion of the terms that are necessary to understand the sections for the benefit of those who do not understand Latin.

### PROPOSITION XXXI.

*To explain the terms of Conic sections which can serve Architects, and which are necessary to understand their properties.*

It is difficult to understand these terms without seeing figures; nevertheless, I will bring as much clarity to them as I possibly can. I say first, then, that a cone is similar to a sugarloaf <note>A traditional form for refined sugar, which was sold in tall, solid conical blocks.</note>, or to the solid mass of rays that come from a base to a point of the eye, and that which comes from the section of a plane made through the axis of the cone is called a triangle.

Secondly, the axis of the cone is the line that descends from the vertex to the center of its base; it is this axis that describes the cone by the movement of one of its extremities, while the other remains immobile; and if this axis is perpendicular to the base, the cone is "right," otherwise it is "scalene" <note>In modern terms, an "oblique" cone, where the top point is not centered directly over the base.</note>.

<header>Book One</header>

Thirdly, the section of the cone is the line created on the surface of the cone, and is the common intersection of the plane and the conical surface, such that the conical line is the portion of the section of the cone; and the straight lines that terminate on either side within the section, or within the portion, are called *straight lines within the section*, or within the portion.

Fourthly, the diameter of a section of the cone or of its portion is the straight line described within the said section, which it divides in two, and is called the *intersected line* <note>original: "entrecoupee." This refers to the diameter or abscissa in early modern geometry.</note>. And the ordinates <note>Lines drawn from the curve to the diameter, usually parallel to each other.</note> to the diameter are all the others that are divided, or parallel to those that are divided.

Fifthly, the *axis of the section* is the line that divides the ordinates into two equal parts. The *vertex of the section* is the end of each diameter that is in the section, or in the portion of the section, which is called the *supreme point* in the axis.

Sixthly, the *parameter* <note>original: "parametre." Also known as the latus rectum; a constant that defines the proportions of a conic section.</note> is the straight side, or the straight line drawn from the vertex of the section parallel to the ordinates, whose power is measured according to the said parameter, which is called the *right parameter* when it is drawn from the vertex of the axis. As for the different sections or cuts of cones: that which follows after the triangle produced <note>The "axial triangle" formed by cutting the cone through its peak.</note> is made by a plane that cuts the cone parallel to the base, and generates the *circle*: if the section of the cone is parallel to one of the sides of the triangle cut through the axis, it is called a *parabola*: when it is cut in such a way that the diameter of the section, being extended, meets one of the sides of the extended triangle, it is named an *hyperbola*: and finally, when the diameter of the section cuts or meets the two sides of the triangle beneath a vertex in such a way that the cutting plane is not parallel to the horizon, nor sub-contrary <note>original: "sous contraire." A specific geometric orientation where a section is cut at an angle opposite to the base but producing a circle.</note> to the base, it is called an *ellipse*.

I leave aside several matters concerning cones that I have explained in the 16th chapter of the 4th book of the *Truth of the Sciences* <note>Mersenne refers to his own 1625 work, *La Vérité des Sciences contre les septiques ou pyrrhoniens*.</note>, where one may see several figures serving this subject, in order to pursue the other difficulties of the voice.

### PROPOSITION XXXII.

*To explain by which movements of the organs the passages and trills used in singing are made.*

It is a certain thing that the reed of the larynx—that is to say, its tongue or its opening—contributes more immediately to passages <note>original: "passages." These are rapid melodic runs or melismas.</note> and trills <note>original: "fredons." This term was used for various types of vocal ornaments and shakes.</note> than the other parts, inasmuch as it is necessary to mark the degrees and intervals one makes while sustaining the passage; this can only happen through the different openings of the tongue <note>The vocal folds or glottis.</note>, as I have shown when speaking of low and high sound. From this it follows that those who have the said tongue more mobile are more suited to making passages and trills, and that those who have it too hard and too dry cannot make them. Now, passages or trills can be made either in the throat by means of the reed, as I have said, or with the lips; but this latter manner is deformed and condemned by those who teach how to sing well. But of all the Nations that learn to sing and who make passages from the throat, even the Italians—who make a particular profession of Music and of recitatives—confess that the French make the best passages, the beauty and sweetness of which it is not possible to explain unless the ear hears them; for the warbling or the murmur of waters and the song of nightingales is not so pleasant; and I find nothing in nature whose comparison could make us understand these passages, which are more ravishing than trills, for they are the quintessence of Music.

# On the Voice.

We can say nothing else regarding the parts that assist in this <term>diminution</term><note>The practice of breaking a long note into many shorter, faster notes; also called "passages" or "divisions."</note> and this ornament of the voice, except that it is necessary for the muscles and cartilages that produce the voice to be very obedient. Furthermore, the "spirit" brought by the <term>recurrent nerves</term><note>The recurrent laryngeal nerves, which control the muscles of the larynx.</note>—which come from the sixth pair or conjugation of nerves—and that which is supplied by the arteries within the vocal organs, must be very prompt and in great abundance. Thus, one may say that those who easily perform "passages" have a softer <term>reed</term><note>original: "anche." The author compares the vocal apparatus to the reed of a woodwind instrument.</note>, since they open and close it more easily than others.

There are those who believe that the epiglottis, which covers the larynx, serves to create <term>fredons</term><note>Rapid vocal ornaments, similar to trills or warbles.</note>, but it is more likely that it serves only to prevent portions of the food and drink we consume—which enter the stomach through the esophagus—from entering the "vocal artery" <note>The trachea or windpipe.</note> and descending into the lungs, which could not happen without causing us great distress.

Others say that the <term>uvula</term><note>original: "columelle." Literally "little column."</note>, which is attached toward the back of the roof of the mouth and descends in the shape of a small cone, serves to create these "passages." When it is overly relaxed, as sometimes happens due to "fluxions" <note>An accumulation of fluid or inflammation, such as a sore throat or congestion.</note> and an abundance of humors, it hinders the voice. However, I shall speak of the ailments and defects of the voice in Proposition 35, and of its medications and remedies in Proposition 36.

## COROLLARY.

The Greek musicians did not speak of the <term>fredons</term> and "passages" used today to ornament and "embroider" songs, unless it is that we no longer understand their terms. This seems to suggest they did not use them, for they were so prolific and curious in creating specific and particular terms that they invented almost nothing to which they did not give a unique name.

## PROPOSITION XIX.

->*To determine whether speech is more excellent than song, and in what ways they differ.*<-

Song is very different from speech, for it requires neither consonants nor vowels, as one experiences on the Organ and on the instruments used to make all sorts of songs heard; even though they pronounce no letters, one can nevertheless create an entire language of as many words as one wishes by means of these songs. This can be easily concluded from what we demonstrated in the *Book of Songs*. Consequently, speech has no advantage over song except for common usage and the institution of men, who willed that words composed of vowels and consonants should signify their thoughts and external objects. Thus, there is no other difference between speech and song, except that song seems more suited and natural for signifying passions and other things, particularly those consisting of movement.

For the singing of a semitone <note>A half-step, the smallest interval in Western music.</note> is suited to expressing sadness, and that of the <term>ditone</term><note>A major third.</note> is suited to explaining joy. If one were to examine the nature of all intervals, one would find the conformity they may have with every thing, such that they could be used instead of our ordinary words to make ourselves understood and to express the nature of things. But they would be inconvenient, because it would be necessary to sing while speaking, and those who do not have a voice suited to making the intervals of sounds would be unable to explain their...

### PROPOSITION XXXIV.

->*To determine if the method used by the French in singing is the best of all possible methods.*<-

If I were to conclude affirmatively without examining this difficulty, foreigners might say that those of my nation had bribed me to praise them, and that it is a very sweet and laudable thing to fight for one's homeland. But since I have proposed to subject all difficulties to reason and experience, we must first consider that the Italians believe they sing better than we do, and that the Greeks yield to neither. Secondly, to judge this difficulty, it would be necessary to have heard the most excellent musicians of China, Persia, and other provinces, as no one can judge voices they have not heard; for even though the Italians and the French imagine their <term>cantors</term><note>original: "Chantres." Refers to professional singers, often those trained in church or court settings.</note> to be the most excellent in the world, those who possess judgment believe nothing of the sort unless they are convinced by reason, since the experience of it is too difficult, owing to the challenge of hearing the best voice of every province. This would have to be done in the same place and at the same time, because one cannot compare absent sounds, the imagination of which is easily lost.

In the third place, our climate is not the most temperate in the world, and the air of our France does not surpass the goodness of that enjoyed by other Kingdoms; for that of Greece and several other Eastern countries is much purer than ours, and consequently, it seems more suitable for voices. This is perhaps why the Greeks produced the musical effects mentioned by ancient authors, by reason of their excellent voices, which had more power over the passions—both because they were stronger and clearer, and because they were more accurate, and they performed <term>passages</term><note>Rapid, decorative runs of notes that "divide" a long melody into smaller, faster parts.</note> and <term>fredons</term><note>Vocal ornaments similar to trills or warbles.</note> that were more ravishing and better defined than ours. Now, if one must judge the method of singing by reason, it must be confessed that the one which has the most power over the listeners is the best; for this delicacy of "passages" that the best masters teach has no other greater effect than a certain "tickling" of the ear, which seems to pass into the spirit and the heart, particularly when they are sustained and last a long time.

It must nevertheless be admitted that of all those heard singing in the lands of our neighbors, such as in Spain, in Germany (both Upper and Lower), and in Italy, one encounters none who sing as agreeably as the French, insofar as the others do not perform their "passages" as delicately; and although they have voices that are stronger, clearer, more distinct, and more resonant, they are nonetheless not as sweet or as charming—though individuals may be found in every nation who equal or surpass the French, for nature sometimes produces extraordinary individuals, now in one Kingdom and then in another, who surpass all their peers. But I speak here of what is ordinary,

# Of the Voice.

ordinary, and wish to leave the comparison of the voices of all nations, and of their songs, to those who are able to hear the best voices and the best songs of Italy, France, and the other Provinces.

However, if one wishes to judge which is the best method of singing, and in what the goodness of the voice consists, one must establish rules that are accepted by all <term>cantors</term><note>original: "Chantres." Refers to trained singers, typically in a liturgical or professional context.</note> and proven by reason; and he who executes them best while singing will surpass all other voices, for which he will be the rule and the exemplar, and he who approaches them most closely will sing the best. But we shall speak of these rules in the treatise on Songs, and elsewhere. And because these rules have not yet been well established until now, it seems that we have not yet sung with all possible perfection, even though voices may have had the best method, and they may have applied themselves very perfectly to the execution of the Songs that have been composed.

### PROPOSITION XXXV.

->*To determine what are the vices and imperfections of the voice; and if one can make Music be sung by a bad and inflexible voice.*<-

This proposition has two parts, the first of which is difficult to determine, inasmuch as what one person believes to be a vice and imperfection in the voice, another will perhaps estimate to be a perfection. From this it follows that many think they have a good voice which is nonetheless bad; and the brilliance or the strength of the voice—or that which pleases some—wounds the ear and the imagination of others. So, one must first determine if the voice has vices, and afterwards what they are, before coming to the second part. Certainly, since voice and speech were given to us to explain ourselves and to converse with one another, the voice must not wound or inconvenience the listeners; otherwise, it would destroy the end for which it was given. From this I conclude that the voice which wounds or inconveniences the hearing is <term>vicious</term><note>In this context, "vicious" (vitieuse) means "defective" or "full of faults," rather than morally wicked.</note> and bad, and that there is no way to cure it except by stripping it of the quality that makes it disagreeable and difficult to endure. This happens to a voice that is harsh, sour, and rough, which offends the hearing as much as rough and rugged objects offend the hand over which they move; the reason being that the spirits serving the organs of hearing and touch are displaced from their position and disturbed in their movements. For the sweet and uniform voice is similar to smooth and polished bodies, the touch of which receives contentment. Now, the other senses operate similarly through a kind of touch, though it be more delicate and invisible; so that we can say of all of them what we experience in one, for nature is uniform in her operations. And if one encounters someone who prefers harsh and rough sounds to sweet ones, he is like one who prefers <term>Dissonances</term> to <term>Consonances</term><note>Dissonances are clashing musical intervals; Consonances are harmonious ones.</note>; for rough voices are filled and composed of Dissonances, even though it is difficult to notice the intervals because of their smallness and frequency. Or, if they have no Dissonances, the small parts of the sound of which they are composed are separated and interrupted by the roughness of the <term>columella</term><note>original: "columelle." Literally "little column," likely referring here to the uvula or the physical surface of the throat and larynx.</note>, which is rugged, either because it has been spoiled and eroded by some wound or disease, or because it has had this imperfection since the time of the formation of its parts.

The harshness of the voice can also come from the dryness of the parts that form it,

# Book One

and from defluxions <note>A 17th-century medical term for the flow of "humors" or fluids, often from the head to the throat, thought to cause illness or irritation.</note> that make them uneven; for the voice and the sound follow the conditions and qualities of the bodies that strike the air. One can also include the shortness of the voice among its vices, for short voices testify that the breathing is too short and too frequent; to which is related the trembling voice, which has no firmness nor constancy, by reason of the weakness of the muscles or the nerves which tremble while moving the cartilages of the **trachea** <note>original: "l'artere." In early modern anatomy, the *arteria aspera* or "rough artery" was the standard term for the windpipe.</note>. As for the hard and rigid voice, it derives this vice from the hardness of the **reed** <note>original: "l’anche." Here the author compares the vocal apparatus to a woodwind instrument; the "reed" likely refers to the glottis or vocal folds.</note>, or from other parts which give an infinity of different qualities to the voice, which one may call a "brazen voice" when it imitates the trumpet, and similarly it can receive the denominations of all the bodies whose sound it imitates. The cracked, muffled, and dark voice derives its imperfection from a quantity of phlegm and other humors which hinder the organs of the voice, which happens particularly when the **uvula** <note>original: "columelle."</note> is cut or damaged; so that after the conformation of the organs, which all have different qualities, the various vices of the voice come from the humors. The hoarse voice is the most ordinary of the faulty ones; it contracts this vice through the defluxions that fall from the brain into the throat, and onto the cartilages of the larynx, or by the swelling and relaxation of the uvula, or by the great efforts proceeding from the voice which one has used by shouting too loudly and for too long; as the Royal Prophet testifies happened to him in Psalm 68:

> *I have labored crying out, my throat has become hoarse;* <note>original Latin: "Laboraui clamans, raucæ factæ ſunt fauces meæ." This is Psalm 69 in modern numbering.</note>

which is interpreted as referring to our Savior being on the cross. From this it follows that fear, fright, excessive wakefulness, and other causes that cool the parts of the body can be the cause of the voice becoming hoarse, just as the common people believe happens to those who have "seen the wolf," which is nonetheless false, unless they are first seized by a great fear; for those who keep wolves for their pleasure, and who see or touch them often, do not have a hoarse voice at all; so that one can place this falsehood among the popular errors, even though Pliny, Solinus, and their followers <note>original: "Symmiſtes." A term for those who share the same mysteries or opinions; disciples.</note> have written of it. I leave aside several other imperfections which can almost all be related to the preceding ones, of which inflexibility is not the least, for it prevents the grace and vigor of discourse.

The second part of this proposition consists in showing if an inflexible voice can sing Music; which seems impossible, since such a voice can make no regulated interval, unless by chance. Nevertheless, **Josquin** <note>Josquin Desprez (c. 1450–1521), one of the most famous composers of the Renaissance.</note> showed that an inflexible and bad voice can sing its part; for having promised **Louis XII**, whose musician he was, to make him sing his part, even though he had a discordant and very bad voice, he made a composition in four parts, and made the King admit that he could sing in Music.

It must nonetheless be remarked that it is necessary that the voice hold firm on one tone, or on one string, and that it be constant; for if it varies so much that it has no resting point, it is not possible for it to sing its part, even if it were uniform, unless in varying it made certain tones whose differences could be noted, and that this variety kept some sort of uniformity; for one cannot regulate what is unregulated and disordered except by means of that which is regulated and ordered, just as one cannot solve the difficulties of irrational numbers and of algebra except by rational numbers and by equations: which shows that every sort of diversity depends on the unity to which all things must return as to their source and their origin. I give, therefore, the piece of Music of which I have spoken, in order to join the example to the discourse.

Now, there is no voice so poor that it cannot sing this **Tenor** <note>original: "Taille." ### PROPOSITION XXXVI.

#### *To know which remedies one can use to cure the defects and imperfections of the Voice, and to preserve it.*

The defects of the voice that are natural are usually more difficult to cure than those that arise by accident; for example, it is very difficult to cure **stammerers** <note>original: "begues."</note>, and those who stutter, hesitate, or **speak thickly** <note>original: "parlent gras." Likely referring to a rhotacism or "lisping" quality.</note>, although histories assure us that **Demosthenes** <note>The famous Greek orator who reportedly practiced speaking with pebbles in his mouth to overcome a speech impediment.</note> overcame the natural defect of his tongue. Now, there are several ways to preserve the voice, which must be discussed before giving the remedies to remove its imperfections. One of the means of preserving or increasing the voice consists of exercise and physical labor, which one should perform before a meal until sweating; another is to read and sing often, as is done in church choirs; and the third consists of abstinence from all sorts of immoderate pleasures, and particularly that of women, as **Quintilian** and **Cornelius Celsus** <note>A Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work *De Medicina*.</note> remarked in the twenty-fifth [chapter] of his seventh book, where he reports the custom of **infibulating** <note>original: "infibuler." A historical practice of using a metal ring or clasp to prevent sexual activity, believed by some ancients to prevent the voice from dropping during puberty.</note> children to preserve their voices. As for the choice of meats, it is not necessary to speak of it, since the different conditions of life oblige us to use those we encounter; one must only note that leeks and onions serve the voice because they cleanse the throat; which similarly occurs if one uses crushed cabbage seed mixed with sugar, or juice of licorice, or **syrup of tobacco** <note>In the 17th century, tobacco was considered a medicinal herb and its syrup was used to treat respiratory congestion.</note>. It is also believed that a lead plate placed on the stomach makes the voice clearer and more pleasant; but I leave aside all these extraordinary remedies, and several methods which actors and preachers may use to preserve their voices, in order to prescribe the remedies that serve to cure its illnesses, and particularly for the **cold** <note>original: "rheume."</note> and other **catarrhs** <note>original: "fluxions." Excess bodily fluids thought to flow from the head to the throat.</note> that diminish the voice and make it hoarse, rough, and unpleasant. Now, the **herbal tea** <note>original: "tisane."</note> made from barley and licorice with a little sugar is excellent for curing these catarrhs; and if one cannot use this drink, one can take a decoction of figs, or syrup...

## PROPOSITION XXXVII.

### *Explaining how one can learn to sing all kinds of degrees and intervals without a master.*

This proposition promises nothing that is not very easy, for he who wishes to learn to sing without a Master <note>A professional singing teacher.</note>, and who does not want anyone to know he is learning to sing, needs only a string <note>original: "chorde."</note> stretched over a piece of wood three feet long and one or two inches wide; for this, all kinds of portable sticks can serve, in which one can so hide and cover the said string that no one will be able to see it. For the small bridges <note>original: "cheualets."</note> that one will slide under the string following the diatonic degrees <note>The standard scales consisting of whole steps and half steps.</note>, or those of other genres, will guide the voice as one wishes; or if one wants only a single bridge, it will show all possible intervals and degrees, the ratios of which will be noted by means of the numbers written beneath the string, or with a compass <note>A tool for measuring and dividing lengths precisely to find musical ratios.</note>. Now, this stick can also serve several other uses, for those who travel can note the range of the voice of all kinds of people, and how low <note>original: "graue."</note> or high <note>original: "aiguë."</note> it is. Concert masters can use it to give the pitch, and to note the differences in the chapel pitches <note>original: "tons de Chappelle." Pitch was not standardized in the 17th century; it varied significantly between different cities and cathedrals across Europe.</note> across all of Europe. And orators, both sacred and profane, can guide their voices by means of this string, both to take the true tone of their voices when they begin, and to raise or lower it in the course of the discourse, according to the dignity of the subjects they treat. One can similarly use the Lute <note>A plucked string instrument popular in the Renaissance and Baroque.</note> and all other stringed instruments, of which the Spinet <note>original: "Epinette." A small keyboard instrument related to the harpsichord.</note> is the principal and the easiest, because its keys are so arranged that one can make any interval or degree one wishes with a single hand, or even without the hand, for it is enough to depress the keys of its keyboard, whether with the foot, or with the mouth, or in any other way one wishes, following the devices and mechanisms which I have...

But the Organ is the most suitable of all instruments for learning to sing, for the reason that its tones hold for as long as one wishes, in order to give the voice leisure to adjust itself and to accustom itself to all sorts of tones and intervals.

Now, those who learn Music in this manner will make their intervals more accurately than those who have learned from Masters, provided that the keyboard and the pipes are arranged like those I have explained in the treatise on the Organ, in which the major and minor tones and semitones, the sharps <note>original: "dieſes." In this context, it refers to sharps or small melodic intervals used to achieve "just intonation" or perfect tuning.</note>, and all the consonances are in their proper precision and perfection; and consequently, he who has learned to sing without a Master will teach how to intone accurately better than any other. But he will not be able to give grace to the songs and the passages that depend on vocal runs <note>original: "roulemens de gorge," literally "rollings of the throat." There is another way of learning which is more Philosophical, but it is more difficult, for it consists in making the air that exits the opening of the larynx vibrate as many times as the string that makes the sound one wishes to imitate—something which one does without knowing it when singing in unison with another sound; and when one does it by science, one will sing more rationally.

### PROPOSITION XXXVIII.

->*How it may be that birds learn to sing, and to speak, and if they*<-
->*take pleasure in singing.*<-

It is no more difficult to know how birds can learn to sing than it is for men who cannot see, and who have no knowledge of what must be done to imitate sounds, or the voice of the Masters, or of the Instrument that teaches them; for the movement of the muscles, of the larynx and its glottis <note>original: "languette," literally "little tongue." In 17th-century anatomy, this often referred to the epiglottis or the structures of the larynx that produce sound.</note>, and the beats of the air made by strings and wind instruments are not known to the person learning to sing. Thus, he does not know what he is imitating, since he does not know the number of air movements necessary to achieve unison, or to rise and descend as the Master does.

One can say almost the same thing of children who learn to walk, to jump, to dance, and to perform acrobatics <note>original: "voltiger." This refers to athletic feats, vaulting, or tumbling.</note>, inasmuch as they do not know which muscles must be moved to imitate the steps and movements of their Masters, since they do not even know if there are muscles, nor in what number are those that help to make all sorts of steps. And because one has as much or more trouble learning to walk and to dance as to sing, it is difficult to know which is more or less natural to man. From this, one can conclude that we say nothing in this proposition that is not common to both man and beasts, and that the difficulty is equal in both, since we experience that birds can as easily learn to speak and to sing as children, and that all animals learn to walk sooner than man. But I do not wish to dwell on the other advantages they have over us, although they are very great, in order to consider the manner in which one learns to sing; which is done by the imitation of several unknown movements, for it is not enough to...

We must therefore say that birds and children learn to speak or sing only by moving the larynx and the other parts serving the voice in all sorts of ways, until they have by chance encountered the opening of the little tongue <note>original: "languette." Likely referring to the epiglottis or the rhythmic movement of the vocal apparatus.</note>, or have pushed the air necessary to create the sound, or to form the speech and song they wish to imitate. One must simultaneously admire how the imagination guides the voice, and how it moves all the muscles serving speech without even knowing them; this testifies that there is some intelligent nature within us, far more excellent than ourselves, which guides all these movements through a very certain science <note>In the 17th century, "science" referred to a precise, certain form of knowledge, often seen as divinely implanted.</note>, and upon which our muscles and all our other parts entirely depend. However, experience shows that there are children who imitate all kinds of songs so easily that they repeat them perfectly as soon as they have heard them; and when this occurs, one can conclude that they are very well-suited for singing Music. Now, although one may not know the muscles or their movement, it must be admitted that the imagination possesses an admirable industry and promptness for imitating all kinds of sounds that do not exceed the range of the voice. This occurs whether the sounds serving as models and originals strike and affect the nerve of hearing and that of the voice—which responds by a form of echo, just as a string does when it is in unison with one that is touched—or whether the intervals of sounds used in singing are natural to both man and birds. But it is difficult to explain the manner used by the imagination to move all the parts necessary for speech, and how it can know the sound it imitates: unless one says that God has placed the principles and the seeds of all knowledge in the said imagination, which only needs the presence of the object to excite and awaken its power and notion; or that it has a perpetual movement that necessarily follows the external movements of objects in animals, and follows them freely in men.

Now, if one believes we have said nothing to satisfy this difficulty, one may first consider that we can know nothing infallible when it comes to the manner in which the actions of the external or internal senses are performed; for it surpasses the reach of the human mind, because we have no previous experiences or notions that can make us conceive how life joins with things that have no life, and the soul to the body, or how the powers of the soul act upon the parts of the body, or how the invisible and the spiritual can act within the visible and the material.

Secondly, if someone is found who has a mind so fortunate and subtle that he can explain this manner of learning to speak or sing more clearly or more truly, we shall follow his sentiments without making any account of what has been said until now: this I similarly mean for all the other difficulties in this work, regarding which I shall always prefer the truth to my opinions, since truth is the image of the **Eternal Word** <note>original: "Verbe eternel." A theological term for the Logos, or the divine reason of God.</note>, for whom and by whom we are created.

In the third place, we must see if it can be said that the imagination, the soul, or its powers, have knowledge of all the movements necessary for speaking and singing, and that they know the number and power of the nerves and muscles, just as the Master or the Father of the family knows the number and strength of his

The other part of this proposition, which consists of knowing whether birds take pleasure in speaking and singing, is not, it seems, so difficult. For although it is very hard to explain or to know how the soul finds delight in physical objects, or how sensations bring pleasure into the imagination, we nevertheless experience that the impression made by external objects on our organs brings us pleasure and contentment whether we want it to or not. This occurs with certain pleasures that many would wish to be rid of, because they go against the law of God, or deprive us of other greater and more solid pleasures. And when one approaches places where concerts are being held, if the ear receives the impression of the chords, it is not within the listener's power to prevent the contentment the ear receives from them; for the "tickling" of the movements <note>The physical vibration of sound waves acting on the ear.</note> brings pleasure with it. When the impressions of each object are proportioned to the sounds and bring them some kind of perfection, they receive a natural contentment, and it is not within the power of our free will to prevent it. For each part of the body has a particular pleasure when it attracts and turns something into itself, or when it performs some other action, since God willed that pleasure be joined to action. Now, everything that can be said of the parts of the human body and the pleasures they receive can be applied to birds, since they are not devoid of passions, of which pleasure is one of the principal ones—though contentment should be attributed more to the soul and its faculties and actions than to the parts of the body that serve as its organs for receiving all the pleasures that flow from objects through the senses until they reach the imagination.

# Book One

One can similarly object to the assumption made about land animals—namely, that they cannot speak or sing—for many things are believed impossible until experience has convinced us otherwise; experience shows in many instances that what was judged impossible is actually very easy. Indeed, horses have been seen to make various cries and appear to laugh at the command of their master. To this, one might add that perhaps we do not yet know the proper method to use to teach oxen, dogs, and other animals to sing and speak. Perhaps we would succeed if we chose the right hour of the day or night, and if we employed the instruments and all the necessary circumstances for this purpose. For since their temperament, their organs, and their **imaginations** <note>In the 17th century, the "imagination" was considered a physical faculty of the brain that processed sensory images and directed the muscles.</note> are not entirely alike, it is probable that one must use different methods to teach land animals than those used to teach birds; even among birds, some are more difficult to teach than others.

One can nevertheless believe that there is some difference in several birds, whether in the imagination or in other organs, which prevents them from being able to speak. As for the imagination, we can only recognize its imperfections by its effects, because it cannot be subjected to our senses or to our experiments. Consequently, one can only have recourse to the parts that compose and move the **larynx**, and to the tongue which serves to form speech, in order to observe if land animals (or certain birds) lack some nerves or muscles that are found in those that speak and sing—such as the parrot, the crow, the blackbird, the sparrow, and several others—or if those who cannot speak have a tongue that is too long, too short, too thin, or too thick.

**Fabricius** <note>Girolamo Fabrici d'Acquapendente (1533–1619), a pioneering Italian anatomist who studied the vocal organs.</note> described the larynx of man, sheep, pig, horse, ox, monkey, and hen in his treatise on the larynx, but he did not provide enough light to understand what these animals lack to be able to speak or sing. Indeed, I do not believe that **Anatomists** can notice this, for the reason that the parts used for the voice have several movements that can only be recognized in the living animal when it cries, sings, or speaks. From this it follows that they are often mistaken when they say that such and such a muscle cannot serve such and such a movement; for these parts have several uses in living beings that are known only to him who is their first and principal author <note>A reference to God as the creator of the biological "machine."</note>.

Now, all these difficulties are the reason why I cannot determine anything certain on this matter. For if it is said that beasts have cartilages and muscles that are too hard and too heavy to move the tongue and to open the **glottis** <note>The opening between the vocal folds in the larynx.</note> as is required to speak and sing, one can reply that cows show the opposite. They produce a <term>Major Tenth</term> <note>An interval spanning an octave plus a major third; a significant vocal range.</note>, which is suitable for singing, and they could likely produce smaller intervals through which they seem to pass gradually while ascending. Furthermore, it is not necessary that their speech be formed any faster than their cry. In effect, if they moved their tongues as required when they cry, they could form some words. One would therefore have to show that it is impossible for them to strike the air coming out of their larynx with their tongue to prove they cannot speak; the same could similarly be said of the elephant and all other animals.

### Of the Voice.

One can nevertheless conclude that land animals and birds that have never been heard to speak are not capable of speech, and that they lack something found in those that do speak. For among many birds raised in the same place—all of whom hear the instruction given to the parrot and to those being taught to speak—one does not notice the others making any effort to form words, even though they all have their own particular song and warbling. The same occurs with land animals, some of whom have a great multitude of different tones and cries which they use to express their **passions** <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "passions" refers to internal emotions or physical drives like fear, joy, or hunger.</note>.

Certainly, if one considers that the rooster’s crow has three or four syllables, and that there are many other birds whose song is articulated, one finds it impossible to know why they cannot form other syllables. For it seems they possess a tongue and other parts of the **larynx** <note>The voice box.</note> just as suited for speaking as those of the magpie—though I believe notable differences would be found if one performed an anatomy of them as exact as that of the human larynx and tongue. But the manner of forming speech will be better understood through Proposition 43, which will show by which movements of the tongue and other parts of the mouth all the letters of the alphabet are formed, and consequently why several animals cannot speak. Some attribute this to the excessive length, width, or thickness of their tongues, which we shall discuss in the aforementioned proposition. For this reason, I move to the second difficulty: namely, whether one can say that the voices of birds and other animals are speech, and if there is a way to understand them.

As for the first part, there is no doubt that the jargon of birds and the cries of animals serve them as words, which one may call the language and idiom of beasts. Experience shows that those of the same species understand each other as well by their different voices as men do by their words, and that their cries are at least as varied as their passions. If one had observed closely enough all the voices made by animals of each species, one could establish as many natural languages to express everything they feel as there are species. For it has been noted that animals of each species have as many different cries to call and warn others as they encounter different types of food; consequently, a bird that finds wheat uses a different song or voice than when it finds millet or some other sustenance. They have still others to express their desires, anger, and sadness, which can easily be observed in dogs, in the hen leading her chicks, and in many other animals. For example, **Fabricius** <note>Hieronymus Fabricius ab Aquapendente (1533–1619), a famous Italian anatomist who studied the vocal organs of animals.</note> noted that a hen defending herself against a dog first made her young ones retreat and flee by the syllable *Kik*, and that when the dog had gone, she called them back with the syllable *glo*, as can be seen in the third treatise he wrote on the speech of beasts, Chapter 5. There, he also explains the different voices of dogs in general. However, one would need to use musical notes and different tempos to accurately explain these voices, particularly when they are composed of high and low tones. This care belongs to those who manage aviaries, parks, and other royal grounds where all sorts of birds and wild or tame beasts are kept; for they can easily record the **tablature** <note>A system of musical notation.</note> of their cries and all their voices, which serve to express the different degrees of their passions.

Now, once this **tablature** <note>A systematic chart or record used to organize observations, similar to a musical score.</note> has been made, it is easy to reach an affirmative conclusion regarding the second part of the second difficulty: namely, that man can understand the chatter and the language of all sorts of animals. There is no need to resort to the fables told about **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A first-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note>, **Tiresias** <note>The famous blind prophet of Greek mythology who was said to have learned the language of birds.</note>, **Melampus** <note>A legendary healer and seer who, according to myth, could understand animals after his ears were licked by snakes.</note>, and **Democritus** <note>The ancient Greek "atomist" philosopher who studied the natural world.</note>. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> is right to mock them in the 49th chapter of his 10th book for saying that one learns the language of all kinds of birds if one eats a serpent born from the blood of those birds; for there is no other natural way to understand their chatter except through the long and careful observations of which I have spoken. All the rest is fabulous and cannot be believed by a man of good judgment, unless he first experiences it for himself.

As for the whistling and the human speech that is taught to birds, it is certain that they do not know the meaning of it, and they signify nothing else by these words than their own joy; unless one believes that they recite what they have learned to please their listeners and to endear themselves to their master. This is not probable, however, since they only speak at certain intervals of time, even when their master desires it and does everything possible to make them speak. From this, one can probably conclude that they only recite what they have learned when nature and their mental impressions excite and drive them to it. Nevertheless, those who train birds may know several circumstances of these matters that are not known to others; this is why they must be consulted if one wishes to know how birds should be taught to speak or whistle. This includes knowing the hours of the day or night that are most suitable for making them learn their lessons, and how they must be covered and placed in darkness so that external objects do not distract them, giving them the entire night to meditate on the lessons of the master **bird-trainer** <term>oiseleur: historically a bird-catcher, here referring to one who trains and keeps birds.</term>.

### COROLLARY I.

One can say that birds that speak have tongues, beaks, and other parts used for the articulation of sounds that are more suitable than those that do not speak at all. Even though the others might be able to speak if the necessary means were used for that purpose, these means have been neglected because there is too great a difficulty in teaching them. Having encountered birds that quickly learn everything they are taught, many have believed that the others were not capable of forming words. This is similar to what happens with many children who are abandoned to ignorance; though they are not entirely incapable of learning the sciences, they are so slow and have so little inclination for letters that one loses patience before the necessary time has been employed. We see this by experience in those who are placed for five or six years in various colleges and under different tutors, who can conceive nothing until they meet some new master who overcomes the difficulty through his own diligence and labor.

### COROLLARY III.

Since we experience such a large number of imperfections in animals and in ourselves, which cannot be corrected, and since there is nothing in all this world that is perfect, and which does not have far more imperfections than perfections, it is reasonable that we detach our affection from everything that falls under the senses, in order to direct it toward God, from whom we hope for the liberty of the children of grace, and the light which will dissipate our ignorance, our infirmities, and our imperfections.

### PROPOSITION XL.

*> Explain how Balaam’s donkey and the serpent of Eden spoke; and in what manner God or the Angels can speak.*

There is nothing easier to explain this difficulty than to say that an Angel moved the tongue of **Balaam’s donkey** <note>A reference to Numbers 22:28, where God opens the mouth of a donkey to rebuke the prophet Balaam.</note>, and that a devil moved that of the serpent to make them speak, since speech is nothing other than the beating of air made by the tongue in the mouth; although some have imagined that animals spoke before **Adam** was driven from paradise, because they read that the serpent spoke.

And it is perhaps from this that the fables of other animals took their origin, of which **Pliny**, **Plutarch**, **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author whose work *On the Nature of Animals* collected various animal myths and observations.</note>, and other historians make mention, to which one may add the horse of **Achilles** which **Homer** calls **Xanthus** <note>original: "Xante". In the *Iliad*, this horse is briefly given a human voice by the goddess Hera to prophesy Achilles' death.</note>, and whom he made to speak; and the one spoken of by **Oppian** <note>A Greco-Roman poet who wrote about hunting and natural history.</note>. **Livy** <note>original: "Tite-Liue". A Roman historian known for recording "prodigies," including reports of speaking oxen.</note> also reports that an ox spoke; and **Philostratus** gives the same privilege to the ship and to the elm tree in the *Life of Apollonius* <note>Referring to the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana; the "ship" is likely the *Argo*, which in myth possessed a beam of wood that could speak.</note>.

Now, I do not wish to absolutely deny that one could teach donkeys, horses, and oxen to speak, because I do not see reasons strong enough to prove that this is impossible; for it is not enough to say that their mouths are too wide, that their lips cannot assist in the pronunciation of the consonants **b, m, and p** <note>These are "labial" consonants, which require the use of the lips; the author is questioning if animal anatomy truly prevents these sounds.</note>, that the cartilages and muscles of their <term>larynxes</term> <note>The organ in the throat used for breathing and producing sound.</note> and their tongues cannot move and flex as is necessary for speech because of their hardness—since one could say even more regarding the larynx and the other parts that birds use to speak, if we did not have the contrary experience. For they have no lips nor teeth, and their palate is so small that it would be difficult to imagine that the **Magpie** <note>original: "la Pie".</note> could speak if one had not heard it.

As for their larynxes, they do not have as much resemblance to those of humans as do those of terrestrial animals; and several birds which seem just as suited for speech as the magpie or the crow, such as the eagle, the hen, etc., do not speak at all;

# Book One

That is why I would not entirely blame those who would maintain that God gave the property of speech to Balaam’s donkey <note>original: "l’asneſſe de Balaam." But this consideration deserves another place. Furthermore, it suffices to say that God or the Angel formed the speech of the said donkey in order to make Balaam come to his senses, and to make him think about what he was going to do, without it being necessary to inquire why God was not content to make the Angel appear to Balaam (whom He could have prevented from cursing the people of God), nor why He did not prevent the demon from forming speech in the serpent. For it is impossible for us to penetrate the true reasons for these things until God teaches them to us in paradise, the hope of which should make us embrace His commandments and follow His will with every kind of affection and ardor.

## PROPOSITION XLI.

->Explain how those who counterfeit and imitate spirits to frighten children,<-

There are several manners of speaking that are very different, by reason of the different tubes and other instruments that one uses. For example, if one speaks into a cracked pot, one represents noises that cause fear at night, and which some charlatans use to represent the return of spirits. But the manner used by those who counterfeit the language of spirits is done without any instrument; for those who weaken their words so much that they are judged to be far off, even though they are present, do not form the speech with any instruments other than the tongue. And one is not accustomed to speaking without a tongue, although there is perhaps a way to make an artificial tongue to form the voice in automatons <note>original: "automates." Early mechanical machines or clockwork figures designed to mimic the movements and sounds of living beings.</note>.

Now, it is much easier to speak without opening and without moving the teeth, than without opening the lips; without the movement of the lips, we cannot form the letters called *labials* <note>Consonants produced using the lips.</note>, namely these five consonants: B, M, P, and V <note>The author lists four, though the text mentions "these five." ### PROPOSITION XLII.

->*To know if the whistlers <term>Whistlers: original "sibilots," referring to those who mimic the high-pitched or hissing sounds attributed to ghosts.</term> who use the artifice of which we have spoken to imitate that which is*<-

The common proverb serves as a refuge for many people, namely that the actions of men must be judged according to their intention, *Whatever men may do, the intention judges them all* <note>original: "Quicquid agant homines intentio iudicat omnes."</note>, although Judges look rather at the action than at the intention, since the latter is invisible, and is known only to God, or to him who performs the action, whereas the former is known and proven by witnesses. From which it follows that one can resolve this difficulty in two ways, namely by judging the action by the intention, or without regard for the intention; if one followed the judgments of God, who considers the interior more than the exterior, one would sometimes not punish actions that appear evil, and at other times one would punish those that seem good. As for the judgments of men, although they sometimes increase the penalty of criminals because of the bad intention they had in committing the crime; nevertheless, they look more particularly at the external action insofar as it disturbs the state and the public order, breaks the Edicts of Princes, or of the Republic, and contravenes the laws and customs that are received and approved. This being established, I say first that these whistlers who counterfeit the spirits and souls of the deceased to frighten those who hear them, or to mock the appearance of spirits or the immortality of the soul, commit a mortal sin against God, and that they are unfaithful, or at least that they put themselves in danger of losing their faith; for even though many false things are recounted regarding the appearance of spirits, and though they have never seen the effects of it, nevertheless it seems that they wish to undermine the foundations of immortality. This being established, it is very easy to conceive how souls or Angels can appear to us in bodies formed of air, or other materials, and through effects whose causes are as unknown to us as the Angels themselves.

But those who speak only in this manner to rejoice with their friends, whom they warn of this stratagem before using it, and who never use it with bad intention, nor with scandal to those whose belief and faith can be easily shaken by reason of the weakness of their minds, do not offend God mortally; and if they had learned this manner of speaking in the throat with the intention of showing what the human voice can do, or to draw some other light for Physics <note>In this period, "Physics" (la Physique) referred broadly to the study of the natural world and the laws of nature.</note> or for Medicine, they would be worthy of praise, since the discovery of a truth that can serve to raise oneself to God, or to use it usefully and honestly, is worth more than all the treasures of the world, when they serve only to fulfill the desire of the greedy. ### PROPOSITION XLIII.

#### *To explain which movements of the tongue or other vocal organs are needed to form vowels, consonants, and syllables.*

It is as certain that the tongue and other vocal instruments use different movements when pronouncing syllables and letters, as it is difficult to explain them, because we cannot see these movements; for although we experience that the tongue moves forward and retreats, that it swells to approach the palate, and that it lowers to form vowels, we do not know by how much it swells or by how much it lengthens. But so that we may explain all these difficulties more methodically, one can divide all letters into vowels and consonants, and subdivide the consonants into five orders, as the Hebrews do: namely, into labial letters, which they call <term>Bumap</term> <note>original: "Bumap." A mnemonic for the Hebrew letters Bet, Vav, Mem, and Pe, which are produced using the lips.</note>, because B, M, V, and P are pronounced with the lips; from this comes the belief of many—though they are mistaken—that parrots and other talking birds cannot pronounce these letters because they have no lips.
   The other letters are called <term>dentals</term>, or <term>zastsarast</term> <note>original: "zastsarast." A mnemonic for the Hebrew dental/sibilant sounds: Zayin, Sade, Samekh, Resh, and Tav.</note>, because z, t, s, and r require the teeth to be pronounced; this must nevertheless be understood of men, for birds who have no teeth pronounce them as well as labials, as experience shows, and consequently these parts are not necessary for these letters. The third order belongs to the letters of the palate, which the Hebrews call <term>gicak</term> <note>original: "gicak." A mnemonic for the Hebrew palatal letters: Gimel, Yod, Kaph, and Qoph.</note>, because g, i, c, and k are pronounced with the palate of the mouth; the others take their name from the tongue, which they call <term>dathlenath</term> <note>original: "dathlenath." A mnemonic for the Hebrew lingual letters: Dalet, Tet, Lamed, Nun, and Tav.</note>, because d, t, l, and n are formed by the movement of the tongue; and the fifth are named <term>gutturales</term> <note>Sounds produced in the throat.</note>, which they call <term>ahchang</term> <note>original: "ahchang." A mnemonic for the Hebrew guttural letters: Aleph, He, Het, and Ayin.</note>, because a, h, ch, and gn are pronounced from the throat, for they have four letters of aspiration. But since these five orders of letters do not always need all these parts, I will divide them only into vowels and consonants, of which the former have as much need for the movement of the tongue and palate as the latter; and because <term>Organs</term> <note>Mersenne refers here to the pipe organ, comparing its mechanical "voice" to the human one.</note> do not have a tongue that has the same movements as those of humans, birds, and other animals, they cannot form vowels, as I will say in the treatise on Organs.
   Now it must first be noted that vowels are not formed by the simple opening of the <term>larynx</term> <note>The voice box.</note> and the <term>glotte</term> <note>The glottis, the opening between the vocal folds.</note>, which has no other power than to form low and high sounds, loud and soft, clear and hoarse, etc.; for the sounds would make no vowel if one had no tongue, of which the simplest lowering at the tip forms the first vowel A, when it extends and sustains the sound; the O is made almost by the same position of the tongue, for it retreats and swells...
