...very little toward the middle of the palate. But the lips do not have as much of an opening to make the *a* as they do to make the *o*, because they necessarily narrow, and it is not possible to form the *o* with the same opening of the lips used to form the *a*. From which it follows that the lips are necessary to form vowels, since the mouth must open as much as it can to form *a*, and the two lips must form an oval shape to form *o*. As for the *e*, the tongue swells and approaches very close to the palate to form it, and the lower lip lowers further than for the *o*, and from being curved it returns to its natural position, so that the lips are more open for the *e* than for the *o*, although the teeth always have the same opening. The tongue touches the palate to form *i*, and the lips make their opening wider than for the pronunciation of *o*. Finally, the tongue makes almost the same movement in forming *u* as in forming *e*, although it touches the palate a little less than when it pronounces *i*. As for the lips, they retain the shape with which they form the *o*, and narrow their oval.

But it is not necessary to dwell longer on the explanation of these movements, since everyone can observe them in themselves or in others; this will be much more successful if one sings while pronouncing the vowels rather than speaking, because the movements of the lips are more noticeable. This should also be noted for the formation of the **Consonants**, which we will speak of after considering why there are only five vowels in all kinds of idioms and languages.

Certainly, there is no other reason for this number, except because all other vowels participate in these five; for if there is any other possible, it is between *a* and one of the other vowels, namely between *a* and *e*, or between *a* and *o*, *a* and *i*, *a* and *u*, etc. From this, it follows that one can form the same vowels in several ways, as happens with the three or four French *e*s, one of which is pronounced with a wider opening of the lips and a greater lowering of the tongue, because it approaches the *a*; it can be written with this character *ë*. The other can be called *masculine*, because its pronunciation is firmer, owing to the acute accent given to it, and is written thus: *é*. And the last is the *feminine*, which is heard very little, and which is pronounced like the <term>schwa</term> <note>original: "ſchewa." In Hebrew grammar, a vowel sign indicating a very short "e" sound or a vocal rest.</note> of the Hebrews.

But I leave aside several other considerations that one could make regarding vowels; for example, which was the first invented, and which is the easiest to form; whether they signify something naturally, or if they are indifferent (as are words of several syllables) to signifying whatever one wishes, since I will speak of this elsewhere. One must only note here that vowels existed before consonants, because children begin their articulation with the vowels they use to cry, and particularly with the letter *a*, because it is the easiest to pronounce.

As for the consonants, they are made by the compression of the air, which is variously struck, broken, or pressed by the tongue, the teeth, and the lips; for the *b* is formed by the lips, which press together and open almost at the same time; the same happens with *m* and *p*. The letter *f* is formed by the pressure of the upper teeth biting slightly on the lower lip; and because the pronunciation of this letter begins with a vowel, namely with *e* <note>In many languages, including French, the name of the letter 'f' is pronounced 'effe', starting with a vowel sound.</note>, it is called a <term>semi-vowel</term> <note>original: "demi-voyelle."</note>, as are *l, m, n, r*, and *s* for the same reason. Now, it should be noted that all our consonants are not necessary, for one can use *cs* instead of *x*, *c* instead of *k*, and *ph* instead of *f*. One can also abandon *h*, since it...

The letter *h* serves only as a breath <note>original: "aspiration"</note>, which can be substituted by the Greek rough breathing mark, which is formed like a reversed comma in this manner ‘ ; and one can also set aside those letters that have nearly the same pronunciation, namely *g, t,* and *p*, which are pronounced almost like *c, d,* and *b*. For those who use a harsher tongue, and who have a stronger breath and voice, such as the Swiss and the Germans, pronounce *p* for *b*, *f* for the consonant *v* <note>original: "u consone"</note>, *t* for *d*, and *c* for *g*; this bears witness to a great internal heat. Those who speak with a lisp, and whom the Greeks call *traulos* <note>Greek: *traulos*, meaning one who lisps or has a speech impediment</note>, also change *tr* into *dl*; for instead of pronouncing *travail* <note>French: work/labor</note>, they say *tl*, or *dlavail*: but this pronunciation is one of the defects of the voice.

As for the different pronunciations observed among the majority of our neighbors, Charles V <note>Charles-Quint (1500–1558), Holy Roman Emperor</note> used to say that the language of the Germans is suited for war, because it is fit for threatening and reprimanding; that Spanish is suited for love and for speaking to God, by reason of its gravity and majesty; that Italian is suited for eloquence and for entertaining the Gods; and that French is Noble, and suited for endearments and for making compliments, according to the report of Fabricius <note>likely referring to the anatomist Girolamo Fabrici (Hieronymus Fabricius)</note>.

But I return to the manner in which **Consonants** are formed: the *c* is made by the touching of the tongue to the lower teeth; for all consonants change their sound according to the greater or lesser effort of the parts that form them. For example, when the lips press together very little they make *m*; if they press the air a little harder they form the *b*; and if they press it very hard they make the *p*: and all of this is done by the movement of the lower lip rising against the upper one. All the other consonants are formed by the movement of the tip of the tongue, which makes *l, n,* and *r* by pulling backward, although this withdrawal is very small; it moves forward a little for *c, g,* and *t* by the movement the tip makes toward the teeth; it strikes the palate to make *l*, and to make *r* it strikes the palate and the upper teeth; it moves in almost the same way by bending against the palate for *l* and for *n*, but it pulls and bends a little more for *n*. Finally, *s* is formed by the tongue pressing the palate all along its length, in order to make the whistling sound <term>sibilance</term> that one hears in the pronunciation of this letter. If anyone desires a longer discourse on this matter, he may read Girolamo Fabrici in the treatise *On Speech* <note>original: "Hierosme Fabrice au traité de la Locution"</note>, though I would rather advise him to experience within himself all the movements made by the lips, the tongue, and the other parts of the mouth while pronouncing all sorts of letters, from which one can draw more satisfaction than from the reading of books. As for the teeth, they are not necessary for speaking, for those who have lost them all pronounce all sorts of words <note>original: "dictions"</note> very well, inasmuch as the gums serve them as teeth.

## COROLLARY.

When one presses the teeth against the top of the larynx while pronouncing vowels and consonants, one feels different movements, and that each letter requires a particular movement of the muscles to be formed; consequently, many other movements aid in the utterance <note>original: "prolation"</note> besides those of the lips, the teeth, and the tongue, of which we have spoken.

But it is not possible to explain all these movements, because they are not sensible enough for us to notice them; for Anatomists cannot discern them in the larynx and other parts of a dead body, nor even in a living body, even if one could perform an anatomy <note>dissection</note> upon it while the letters were being—

From this, it follows that it is not possible to make machines speak through mechanical springs by using certain and general rules. If some clockmakers produce sounds similar to the crowing of a rooster or some other animal, this is achieved by chance encounter rather than by art. This is why I have no doubt that the head of Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar rumored to have created a mechanical talking head or automaton</note>, which people speak of, is a myth. The books he left behind do not testify in any way that he was industrious or learned enough to create such a machine, which I believe should be reserved for angels, or for men who see the principles of nature within themselves—if such men exist in the world, which I do not believe.

### COROLLARY III.

Since there are men who imitate all kinds of birds and musical instruments, although these sounds are not made using our vowels—as can be observed with trumpets, organs, and all types of whistles—it is certain that there can be vowels other than our own. For why can we not say that the voice which imitates the sound of an organ pipe or a flute is a particular vowel, distinct from the five ordinary ones? Thus, one could say there are as many vowels as there are different instrument sounds. Those who know how to imitate them could create a language that would perhaps come closer to the conditions and properties required of a natural language <note>A "natural language" in this context refers to a hypothetical language where sounds perfectly reflect the essence of the things they name</note> (which some believe possible and claim to have found) than any other. Experience also shows there are men who pronounce a vowel that falls between *A* and *E*, possessing qualities of both.

### PROPOSITION XLIV.

*To explain why some people speak through the nose, whether there is a way to remedy it, and what sounds can be made with the nose.*

Several reasons can be given for this speech defect, which is called speaking through the nose, or nasalizing <note>original: "nazarder"</note>. One reason is that the passages <note>original: "conduits"</note> are obstructed <note>original: "oppilez"</note> or too narrow, as experienced during colds or catarrhs <note>a buildup of mucus in the nose or throat</note>. These cause an obstruction that makes one speak through the nose because the breath from respiration struggles to exit. Now, when one presses one of the nostrils, or both, the same thing is experienced. It is also held that if the uvula <note>original: "luette"; the fleshy piece hanging at the back of the throat</note> is eroded or damaged, it causes one to speak through the nose. This cannot be remedied when the narrowing of the passages is the cause, or when there is some other natural reason for this vice. But when <note>The original text uses a nasal abbreviation 'quãd' for 'quand'</note> the obstruction comes from a cold, or from some other fluxion <note>a discharge or flow of bodily fluids</note> or accidental cause that does not destroy the physical makeup <note>original: "temperament"</note>, shape, or position of the parts used to avoid nasalization, it can be remedied by the same means used to cure the aforementioned fluxions.

Now, it should be noted that one cannot recognize from the external shape of the nose whether someone nasalizes, as the nose appears very narrow and compressed in many who do not nasalize at all, because they have wide enough cartilage and other internal parts. Hence, those who judge the internal from the external are often mistaken; for we see many whose heads and other mem-

As for the sounds that come from the nose, the first is that of breathing, where strong inhalation produces snoring. One also finds those who play wind instruments with the nose—for example, the flageolet <note>A small flute similar to a recorder</note> and other flutes—or who sing music in two parts, one with the mouth and the other with the nose. Some also imitate the sound of the organ stop called the *nazard* <note>original: "nazard," a pipe organ stop with a distinctively nasal quality</note> by pressing one nostril with one hand and tapping with the other hand against the other nostril. I omit several other inventions that can be used by pressing the said nostrils, or by lengthening them by means of certain instruments that extend them as much as one wishes; and likewise the method of reconstructing severed noses, about which Taillacotius <note>Gaspare Tagliacozzi (1545–1599), a pioneer of plastic surgery who developed techniques for rhinoplasty using skin from the arm</note> has written an express book. I will only remark upon what is said regarding the severed part of a nose that has been reconstructed from the arm of some man: namely, that this part added to the nose separates and dies when the person from whose arm it was taken happens to die, as if this part added to the severed nose were still connected to the arm of the one from whom it was taken. For if this is true, it is the subject of a long discourse, consisting of finding the source of this sympathy of parts; and whether the part cut from the arm of another man lives by the life or the soul of the severed nose, or by that of the arm. Now, this difficulty is common to the scions <note>The "rejettons" or shoots used in plant grafting</note> that one grafts upon wild rootstocks, and to several other things that must be treated elsewhere. One may also see the 14th problem of section 33, where Aristotle asks why the deaf have a habit of speaking through the nose, where he explains what pertains to sneezing.

### PROPOSITION XLV.

->*Whether different climates or the locations of the earth are the causes of different voices and different manners of speaking.*<-

It is commonly observed that Northerners <term>Septentrionnaux: people from northern regions</term> have stronger voices and more vehement breathing than Southerners <term>Meridionaux: people from southern regions</term>, although one finds many—both in Germany and in other places closer to the North—who have voices that are weaker and higher-pitched than those of the South; so that one cannot establish a general rule on this subject. Now, the reason for the stronger and rougher voice of Northerners must be taken from their greater internal heat, which needs to breathe a larger quantity of air to refresh and temper the heat of the heart; for this air, being pushed back and held by the lung, makes the voice all the stronger as it is in greater quantity, provided that the organs of the voice contribute to it proportionally. One might also say that the air of the North, being coarser, stronger, and thicker, makes voices deeper and stronger, since temperaments follow the climates, and natural actions follow the temperament: for air is one of the principal nutrients, or one of the principal things that preserve life. But the air of the South is more subtle and hot, from which it follows that Southerners have less internal heat, and that their voices, which are formed from this air, are higher-pitched, because the air moves more quickly. And if one considers the speed of the vertical sky at the equator, one will find that it moves much faster in comparison to the sky of the Northerners than their voices are deep and strong compared to those of the Southerners. It must nonetheless be admitted that different voices come rather from the

different temperament <note>original: "complexion," referring to the balance of bodily humors</note>, and from the different constitution of the organs of the voice, rather than from different types of air. For experience shows that the voice is not noticeably deeper or stronger in thick air than in thin air, and those who travel toward the North or the South always maintain the same voice.

As for the different manners of speaking, these depend more on education and custom than on temperament; for if one takes a child from France to Italy, once he has learned to speak, he will speak like an Italian. The same would happen if he were taken to Tartary or to China. And lest anyone object that a child acquires a particular disposition at birth that determines him to speak in one way rather than another, I say that a child who is taken at two or three years of age from France to Italy, or to Persia, and who returns at twenty or fifty years of age, will have as much difficulty speaking French as if he had been born in Persia. Furthermore, a Frenchman living in Persia can so instruct his Persian children that they will speak French as well as those in Paris, and they will speak as little Persian as if they had never seen Persia. This can be confirmed by several experiences of the Dutch, and of many others who teach French or other foreign languages to their children before they know the language of the country. From this I conclude that different climates contribute nothing to the different manners of speaking, which arise solely from custom; and consequently, all types of languages are indifferent to all types of countries. This can be witnessed by the Spanish in America, whose children always speak Spanish, provided they do not corrupt their tongue by mixing it with that of the Barbarians <note>A common 17th-century term for non-European peoples</note> and the Savages.

Now, this does not prevent some from having the tongue, or other parts that contribute to forming speech, more suited to pronouncing certain syllables than others; but since this occurs within the same climate, it is not necessary to attribute the cause to the difference of the sky, the air, or the earth.

### PROPOSITION XLVI.

->*Whether one can know the temperament, the passions, and the affections of men*<-
->*by the voice, and by the different manners of speaking,*<-
->*and of laughing, and from whence laughter comes.*<-

Since there are men who boast of knowing the temperament and the passions of men by the features of the face and by the lines of the hands—which serve as the subject of Physiognomy <note>The practice of judging character from facial characteristics</note> and Chiromancy <note>Palm reading</note>—it is likely that one can say the same of the voice, of speech, and of laughter. This is particularly true of the voice, which testifies that a man is of a hot temperament <note>In humoral theory, a "hot" temperament was associated with energy and passion</note> when he has a strong voice, as Aristotle supposes in the 3rd problem of the eleventh Section <note>original: "3 probleme de l'vnzieſme Section" of Aristotle's *Problems*, a work investigating various natural phenomena</note>. This is because he who has a very hot stomach and heart draws in much air to cool them, and consequently exhales and pushes much air out of the lungs, which makes the voice large and strong. From this, one can conclude that he who sustains the same voice for a long time has large lungs, just as one concludes that organ bellows are very large when they take a long time to fall and contain much air.

One cannot, however, absolutely conclude that he who has the strongest and most robust voice is of a hotter temperament, for experience shows...

...to see that many are weak who have a strong voice, and that many are robust who have a weak and small one. As for the deep voice, about which Aristotle poses several problems in the eleventh Section <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Problemata*, a collection of questions on natural history and medicine</note>, it testifies that the glottis <note>The opening between the vocal folds in the larynx</note> is very wide, and consequently a high-pitched voice is a sign that the glottis is small and narrow. This is why those who weep have a high-pitched voice, because they do not open the glottis as wide as those who laugh. A similar thing happens to children, whose throats are narrow, as well as to women and the elderly. Aristotle says the cause of this difference is that all those with deep voices exhale and expel a large quantity of air that moves slowly, whereas those with high voices push out a small quantity of air that moves with great speed. To this he adds that voices are deeper in Winter than in Summer, because the air is thicker and coarser and consequently moves more slowly, and because the long sleep of Winter weighs down all parts of the body. This can also happen due to phlegm <note>original: "pituite," one of the four bodily humors associated with cold and moisture</note> and the "fluxions" <note>An old medical term for the flow of bodily fluids</note> that fall into the windpipe <note>original: "artere," here referring to the trachea</note>, which make the movement of air more sluggish, as he notes in the eighteenth problem.

Indeed, we find from experience that one speaks with a thicker voice when one has a cold. This shows that the fluid falling upon the lung or into the larynx delays the movement of air, since a sound is never deeper unless the movement that produces it is slower. This must be understood as a movement composed of "turns and returns" <note>A reference to the vibratory nature of sound waves</note>, as I have explained elsewhere. He also says in the 32nd problem that those who are afraid have a high-pitched voice because cold seizes them and weakens their heart, so that they exhale very little air; this is why they are pale, which shows that heat leaves the upper parts of the body—the same parts to which heat rushes when one feels shame.

I omit several other things he assumes: for example, that those who hesitate and stammer when speaking, such as stutterers, are "melancholic" <note>Possessing an excess of black bile, thought to make one analytical but prone to sadness or over-imagination</note>, and their tongues cannot keep up with the speed of their imagination. Because they have difficulty speaking, they speak very loudly, for they cannot overcome the obstacles that trouble them without using great force. He attributes all these defects of the tongue to weakness in the 30th problem; however, I have spoken of these vocal defects elsewhere and have explained several problems from the eleventh Section in the corollary of the 16th proposition. Therefore, I will not dwell longer on this subject, adding only that everyone can observe several details that will help establish **Phoniscopy**—that is, the science of the voice—which I have treated very extensively in the thirty-fourth Physical Question.

The second part of this proposition concerns the different manners of speaking, without regard to different languages. We experience that many melancholics speak slowly, and that those of a hot and choleric <note>Associated with yellow bile; characterized by a quick, fiery temperament</note> temperament speak quickly and abruptly, because "earth" predominates in the former, and "bile" (which is of the nature of fire) in the latter. As for different accents, everyone owes these to their country and to custom; therefore, one can conjecture nothing certain about temperaments from accents. A Norman raised among Gascons will have the accent of the Gascons if they have not learned the language of their own province; likewise, Gascons transported in their childhood to Normandy have no other accents than those of the Normans. This is an experiment very easy to perform if one doubts it.

But I will speak more fully of speech in the *Book of Accentual Music*, where one will see how the Musician can understand the tone and the mode necessary to move the <term>passions and affections</term> <note>In the 17th century, these terms referred to the various emotional states—such as joy, anger, or sadness—that art aimed to evoke.</note> of his listeners.

The last part of this proposition speaks of laughter, the cause of which is not easy to find. However, be that as it may, it seems that one can know the nature of men by their manner of laughing; for laughter being a natural movement, it teaches us the nature from which it is produced. From this comes the fact that *Prosper Aldorise* <note>Prospero Aldorisio, an Italian author who wrote on physiognomy and laughter in the early 17th century.</note> gave the name <term>Gelotoscopy</term> <note>original: "Gelofocopie," a pseudo-science meant to determine character from laughter, from the Greek "gelos" (laughter).</note> to the book he wrote on laughter. He says that the efficient cause is the heat generated by the union of "hot spirits"; to this he adds that this union of spirits occurs in the admiration of a new thing that was not at all expected. The source of these <term>spirits</term> <note>In early modern medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that circulated through the body to carry out vital, animal, and natural functions.</note> resides in the left side of the heart, and they agitate the <term>diaphragm</term> which separates the vital parts from the animal parts <note>The "vital parts" usually referred to the heart and lungs, while the "animal parts" referred to the brain and nervous system.</note>. The eyes become clearer and brighter when one laughs, by reason of the flames that the heart sends to them; the spirits that have gathered and united in the brain to admire [something] so excite those of the heart that one can die from laughing too much, because the heat of the spirits having left the solid parts and the humors, they can no longer sustain life. Finally, the respiration is vehement because the heat of the heart pushes and pulls the lungs with violence; from this it happens that the air being inhaled and exhaled generates the laugh.

Now, there are as many different kinds and manners of laughing as there are different mixtures of sound and voice, all of which can be related to the five vowels *a, e, i, o, u*. They participate in these more or less according to the size of the laugh, which often brings out tears, and which sometimes causes coughing, sneezing, yawning, jumping, and dancing. Laughter that makes the vowels *a, e, i, o, u* heard is produced from bottom to top; of these, *a* is formed at the beginning and *o* in the middle of the palate of the mouth; *e* is made in the palate by an oblique movement, and *u* is formed near the teeth. *a* and *u* are formed by the widening of the <term>larynx</term>, which narrows to form *i*.

Now, since a greater heat is required to move the lobes of the lungs when the laugh is made in *a*, one can say that those who form *a* while laughing have more heat than those who form *o* and *i*, and that *i* signifies a greater heat than *u*. The vowel *a* testifies to the humidity and the ease with which the <term>glottis</term> <note>original: "languette," literally "little tongue," referring here to the vocal apparatus within the larynx.</note> opens, and consequently that one is <term>sanguine</term> <note>One of the four temperaments, associated with blood; characterized by being warm, moist, and cheerful.</note>; but *e, o, and i* show its dryness, and that those who form these letters while laughing are of a cold and dry temperament. Likewise, the vowel *u* signifies that one is cold and moist; the vowels *i and o* show that one is hot, dry, and <term>bilious</term> <note>Associated with yellow bile; a temperament characterized by being hot, dry, and prone to anger.</note>; *e* signifies <term>melancholy</term> <note>Associated with black bile; a temperament characterized by being cold, dry, and pensive.</note>, and *u* signifies <term>phlegm</term> <note>Associated with the humor of phlegm; characterized by being cold, moist, and slow.</note>, and that those who form these letters while laughing are subject to the diseases that come from these humors, or are suited to the virtues which these same humors favor. This is why I conclude that *a and o* signify boldness and liberality when they are made with a quick movement, and that *e and u* signify avarice. Furthermore, those who form *a and o* are loved by those who form *e and i*, who seek heat to perfect and preserve themselves; and those who form the same letter love each other reciprocally by reason of their resemblance. Those who form *a and e* have a more lively and sharp spirit; those who form *e* have more memory and less imagination, and are more stubborn. The vowels *i and u* testify to a short life, and the others to a long life; so that the "spring" of the life of one who forms *a* lasts 25 years, which he gives similarly to the Summer, Autumn, and Winter of life.

# Book One

But everyone can judge whether this Author is right, and whether what he says is not true; at the very least, he provides the subject and occasion to observe the different manners of laughing, and to see if there is a means to conjecture something of the <term>temperament</term> <note>In 17th-century medicine, "temperament" referred to the balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which determined a person’s health and personality.</note> and the inclination of men by their laughter. We must research the causes and the object of this laughter, so that this natural affection of man may be known, and so that we may know if the faculty of laughter is so specific and essential to him that it cannot belong to any other animal. As for the **object of laughter**—that is to say, the thing that provokes one to laugh—it usually requires two conditions: it must surprise, being something pleasant that is not ordinarily seen; and furthermore, the one who laughs must be so disposed that he has nothing in his body or mind that prevents him from laughing. This must be noted to avoid several examples and difficulties that might be proposed against this; but it is difficult to find the true cause for why the said object makes us laugh, especially since laughter seems to belong to the <term>animal part</term> <note>The "animal part" refers to the "animal soul" (from the Latin *anima*, meaning life or breath), which governed the senses and movement shared by humans and animals, as opposed to the "rational soul" unique to humans.</note>, and consequently, animals should likewise laugh. This does not happen, even though one notices some who weep, as does the **stag** when it is caught, there being no more reason to laugh than to weep. Indeed, one notices some species of laughter in animals when they rejoice, so that one might attribute laughter to them, since there are those who grant them some degree of reason.

But it is not necessary to speak here of animals, since these discourses belong to men, who are so different in mind and temperament that it is very difficult to find a single, uniform cause and object that makes them laugh. For even though that which surprises us and that which is not ordinary makes us laugh, we nevertheless laugh at certain encounters and certain objects that do not surprise us. And although many believe that the **object of laughter**, or the **ridiculous**, consists of an ugliness or deformity without pain <note>This definition of the ridiculous as a "deformity or error that does not cause pain" is a classic concept derived from Aristotle’s *Poetics*.</note> of the body, the mind, or external things, to which wonder is joined—produced by some sort of novelty in the thing or the manner in which the thing is expressed—nevertheless, this opinion is not without difficulty. Whatever the case may be, the thing laughed at must be pleasant, and it must surprise us with some sort of novelty, and there must usually occur some movement that does not suit the thing being laughed at. From this comes the belief of some that the object of laughter, or the ridiculous, is a deformity that does not wound, or which can serve no other purpose than to provoke laughter; to which all ridiculous things can be related, whether the deformity is found in the ridiculous thing itself, or in its actions, and in the manner of doing them. Now, it is a certain thing that the object of laughter must be joyful, since laughter is like the **flower or the perfection of joy**, which can be called a species of laughter. A more exact search for this belongs to Philosophers and Physicians, who must consider why the heart and the <term>diaphragm</term> move with such great violence when one laughs that it seems one must "burst," as they say, and that one is often constrained to clutch the belly to repress the excessive violence of the movement. They must also note why the lips tremble so much while laughing, and from whence comes the vehemence of the movement of all parts of the mouth and the face: for one cannot explain all these movements and all their causes without reporting several things from **Anatomy** and **Physics** <note>In this period, "Physics" referred to "Natural Philosophy," the study of nature and the physical universe, rather than the modern specialized field.</note>, which would be tedious here.

F iii

One may consult the two treatises on laughter written by the anonymous author of the *Games* <note>Likely referring to a contemporary collection of social or courtly intellectual exercises.</note>, whose style is excellent and whose mind is subtle; as well as the work by Joubert <note>Laurent Joubert (1529–1582), a famous French physician who wrote a celebrated treatise on laughter.</note> and others, to consider whether a wise man should laugh, and if laughter is an act of folly. This was the belief of certain savages who, upon being brought to Europe, were astonished to see men laugh, and doubted whether they were of a different nature than those who do not laugh at all. However, I find this story difficult to believe; for it seems highly unlikely that entire nations could be found where no one laughs, unless they are all so dull-witted that they lack the spirit to laugh, or their knowledge and science are so excellent that they no longer have anything to admire—if, indeed, the subject of <term>admiration</term> <note>In this period, "admiration" meant a sense of wonder or surprise at the unexpected, rather than just high regard.</note> is a necessary condition for laughter and for establishing what is ridiculous, a point on which not everyone agrees.

## COROLLARY.

One may see what I have said concerning the science of the perfect Musician in the fifth question of the *Preludes to Harmony*, and what I have said elsewhere regarding the knowledge he must have of <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of judging a person's character or temperament from their facial features or physical appearance.</note>, the voice, and sounds, in order to choose songs suited to rouse his listeners to whatever passion he desires; and particularly the discourse on the <term>temperament</term> <note>The specific balance of "humors" or qualities in a person's makeup that dictates their health and personality.</note> he ought to possess, which I treat very extensively in the fourth question of the said *Preludes*.

## PROPOSITION XLVII.

->*To know whether one can invent the best language of all possible ones.*<-

If one could invent a language where words had their natural meaning—so that all men understood the thoughts of others by their pronunciation alone, without having learned their meaning (just as they understand that one rejoices when one laughs, and that one is sad when one weeps)—this language would be the best of all possible ones. It would make the same impression on all listeners that the thoughts of the mind would make if they could communicate immediately between men as they do between the Angels. But since the sound of words does not have such a direct relationship with natural, moral, and supernatural things that their pronunciation alone can make us understand their nature or their properties—given that sounds and movements are not characters inherently attached to the things they represent until men have agreed upon them and assigned them whatever meaning they wished—one must conclude that even the names Adam gave to the animals are, by their nature, as indifferent to signifying stones or trees as they are to animals. This will be admitted if one judiciously examines the <term>Hebrew</term> or <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Chaldean here refers to Aramaic, which was often grouped with Hebrew in early linguistic studies.</note> words believed to have been spoken by Adam. Since letters, syllables, and their pronunciation are arbitrary and signify nothing other than what we intend, we must see if the art and wit of men can invent the best possible language; this cannot happen unless one first supposes that the best language is that which explains the notions of the mind most briefly and clearly. Furthermore, since words with fewer letters or fewer syllables are the shortest, the language composed of the briefest words will be the best, as it will reach...

### Book One

...more quickly to the goal one proposes for languages, which consists of explaining and putting outward what one has in the mind.

This being supposed, I say that the best of all possible languages must be composed of all the <term>words</term> <note>original: "dictions." In this context, it refers to any articulate sound or word formed by letters.</note> that can be made from a single letter, and then those of two, three, and four letters, until it has a large enough number of words to express all things that can be known and spoken of. However, it is not necessary to show the number of words that can be made of one, two, three, or four letters, etc., because the tables showing the number and diversity of songs in the *Book of Songs* <note>Mersenne refers to his own work on musical theory, where he used mathematical permutations to calculate all possible melodies.</note> also serve to reveal how many words there are in the 22 letters of the alphabet, considered in every possible manner. For example, the first number in the general table of 22 notes shows that there are only 22 one-letter words; the second number shows that one can make 484 words of two letters; and the third shows that one can make 10,648 words of three letters. Consequently, one could create a language where no word exceeds three letters in length, which would possess 11,154 entirely different words.

But because there are many combinations of consonants in the aforementioned table that cannot be pronounced, one must use another method to create only pronounceable words, so that nothing is superfluous. I do this in two ways: first, by assuming there are only 16 consonants—namely *b, d, f, g, h, k, l, m, n, p, q, r, s, t, x, z*—for the letters *c* and *k* can serve in every place where one puts *c*, and *z* in every place where one puts *s*. This being established, if one uses a vowel taken from the five ordinary vowels, I say first that one can make 160 words of a single vowel and a consonant; and that by taking 2, 3, 4, or 5 vowels with a single consonant, one can make as many different words as are seen in the following table, all of which can be pronounced, as one experiences in this word *a, e, i, o, u*, which has five vowels. Indeed, one can make three hundred thousand similar words,

| | |
|:---|:---|
| One consonant | |
| With 1 vowel, | 160 |
| With 2 vowels, | 1,200 |
| With 3 vowels, | 8,000 |
| With 4 vowels, | 50,000 |
| With 5 vowels, | 300,000 |
| **Total Sum** | 359,360 |

just as one can make fifty thousand of four vowels and one consonant, which would be similar to these two words, *aérée* <note>airy</note> and *aiisée* <note>easy; an archaic spelling of "aisée."</note>; and consequently, one can make an entire language from a single consonant accompanied by five vowels, provided it requires no more than three hundred fifty-nine thousand, three hundred and sixty words.

And if one desires a larger number of words, and wishes to use two consonants (whether similar or different), one can make 3,840 words with a single vowel and two consonants, of which 160 will be useless because they cannot be pronounced, such as *bba* or *abb*. There would be 38,400 with two vowels, of which 800 would be useless, such as *bbaa* or *aabb*. With three vowels, there would be 320,000, but 4,000 would be useless, similar to *bbaaa*. And if one uses 4 vowels, one would have 2,400,000 words—that is to say, more than two million—which exceeds the multitude of words in the most fertile language in the world; for only twenty thousand would be useless. And if one adds five vowels, one would have 16,800,000, of which one hundred thousand are useless.

# On the Voice.

29 characters: for besides the five ordinary vowels, there are five others, because the vowel *e* is pronounced in three ways. First, as the <term>shva</term> <note>original: "şçeva." A Hebrew vowel sign (◌ְ) indicating a very short, neutral sound, often called a schwa in modern linguistics.</note> of the Hebrews, which is similar to the two dots we call a *comma* <note>The author likely refers to the vertical arrangement of the two dots in the shva mark.</note>; this corresponds to the "feminine e," which is barely heard, as seen at the end of the <term>word</term> <note>original: "diction." In this context, it refers to any articulate sound or word formed by letters.</note> *Françoise* [French] or *commande* [command]. The second is pronounced with an acute accent, as happens at the end of the word *malgré* [despite]. The third is pronounced between the first two, as seen in the first syllable of *fête* [feast], which is ordinarily written with an *s*, *feste*, even though it is not pronounced at all; this *e* is also found in the words *accez* [access], *progrez* [progress], and in a thousand other similar ones. The three other vowels are composed of two letters, although one hears almost only one: the first is *au*, which the French ordinarily pronounce like a double *oo*, or rather like a long *o*; the second is *ou*, which the <term>Canadians</term> <note>A 17th-century term for the Indigenous peoples and early settlers of New France (modern-day Canada).</note> and other <term>savages of America</term> <note>original: "sauvages d'Amerique." A period-specific term for Indigenous North Americans.</note> often use at the end of their words; and the third is *eu*, as seen in the second syllable of the word *Dieu* [God]. Consequently, it is necessary to establish these ten vowels—*a, e, é, ê, i, o, u, au, ou, eu*—so that there is no word that cannot be written exactly as it is pronounced.

As for diphthongs and triphthongs, they are composed of the preceding vowels; that is why I do not add them here, such as *œ*, *æ*, and the others I reported in the 13th article of the 50th question on Genesis. There are 19 consonants necessary to pronounce all sorts of words, namely: *a, b, c, d, f, g, h, i, K, l, l, m, n, ñ, p, r, s, z, t* <note>Note that in 17th-century printing, 'i' often represented the consonant 'j', and 'a' may here represent a specific breathing or a transcription error in the original list.</note>. Several things must be noted here: first, that *c* only serves to pronounce syllables written with *ch*, which is a strong aspiration. What is ordinarily written as *ca* but pronounced *Ka* should be written with *K*, which is pronounced strongly with all vowels. When it is pronounced *ça*, as if written *sa*, it must be written with *s*, which is pronounced the same way with all vowels, at the beginning, middle, and end of words. For we use *z* in all places where *s* is pronounced softly and weakly, as in the word *aize* [ease] instead of *aise*. The *K* also serves in place of *q* joined to *u*, which is placed after it when one must pronounce words similar to the Latin conjunction <term>wherefore</term> <note>original: "quare."</note>. Furthermore, there are two *l*s and two *n*s, some of which are pronounced more firmly and others more softly. This is why some are called "hard," as in the words *l'amour* [love] and *navire* [ship], and the others "soft," "fat," or "delicate," as seen in the words *œillet* [carnation] and *magnifiques* [magnificent]. For the letter *l* which we usually double, and the letter *n* before which we place a *g*, are pronounced softly. Now, their characters must be distinguished (since they have a different sound), as the Spaniards do by placing a bar over the *ñ* to signify that it must be pronounced sweetly and softly, just as the French syllable *gnon* is pronounced in the two words *compagnon* [companion] and *mignon* [darling].

This being assumed, one can see how many different words of one, two, three, and four letters, etc., can be made in the following Table A. This table shows in how many ways the 19 consonants can be varied by taking them one by one, two by two, three by three, four by four, and five by five. But because these conjunctions of consonants cannot serve to make words unless vowels are mixed in, the second Table B shows how many words can be made from a single consonant when one is permitted to use one, two, three, four, or five vowels taken from the ten vowels listed above.

Now, even though I have only included the <term>words</term> <note>original: "dictions"</note> of five consonants with as many vowels, I nevertheless wish to provide the method for finding all the other words that can be composed of 19 consonants and 10 vowels. I shall explain this using the example of ten consonants and as many vowels. I say, then, that if the word has 20 letters—namely 10 consonants and 10 vowels—one must continue the multiplication of the consonants by 19 until one has 10 numbers <note>Mersenne is calculating $19^{10}$.</note>, having performed 9 multiplications, the product of which will be 6,131,066,257,801. Afterwards, one must add 10 zeros to this number, on account of the 10 vowels; and finally, one must multiply this number by the ordinary <term>combination</term> <note>In this context, Mersenne is referring to what we now call a multinomial coefficient, specifically $\frac{20!}{10! \times 10!}$, which calculates the number of ways to arrange the letters.</note> of 20 things divided by the square of that of 10, the quotient of which will be 184,756, and the sought-after number will be 11,327,512,775,262,815,560,000,000,000.

But if there were only 8 vowels, one would only need to add 8 zeros to the aforementioned number, and multiply that number by the ordinary combination of 18 divided by the product of the combination of 10 (which is 3,628,800) multiplied by the combination of 8 (which is 40,320), on account of the 10 consonants and the 8 vowels.

Finally, if the words consisted of 30 consonants and 20 vowels, one would have to continue the multiplication of the consonants by 19 until one had 30 numbers—that is to say, one would have to perform 29 multiplications—and add 20 zeros to the product because of the number of vowels. Then, one would have to multiply this number by the ordinary combination of 50 things (which is the total number of letters in the word), among which there would be 30 of one kind and 20 of the other; but one must multiply the ordinary combination of 30 things by that of 20, and divide that of 50 by the product to obtain the number of these words, and the quotient will be the multiplier sought.

If one wishes to be content with only vowels to create an entire language, it is very easy to know how many words one will have; for 10 being multiplied 9 times will give all the words of one, 2, 3, and 4 letters, etc. And because each multiplication adds a zero, one will have 10,000,000,000—that is to say, 10 <term>billions</term> <note>In Mersenne's time, a "billion" could refer to different scales, but here he explicitly specifies a 1 followed by 10 zeros ($10^{10}$ or ten thousand million).</note> of vowels—which exceeds the number of all Greek, Latin, Hebrew, and Arabic words. This is easy to show by comparing these words with the others, even though the largest of these words made of vowels has only 10 letters, while several Greek or Latin words have 22 letters, as seen in the word *Constantinopolitanorum* <note>Latin: "of the people of Constantinople."</note>. But since I have shown that the best language is the one that has the shortest words—inasmuch as it explains thoughts and notions of the mind more promptly—and since it is certain that words cannot signify naturally, but only by artifice (that is, by virtue of the will and the institution of men), we must see if the shortest possible words can be put into use throughout the world, and by what means that might happen, after noting that the preceding words can still be varied, and consequently multi-

Now it is very easy to determine how much any chosen number of accents increases the number of previous <term>words</term> <note>original: "dictions"; Mersenne uses this term to refer to any pronounceable combination of sounds, whether they have meaning or not.</note>, for if, for example, one pronounces each word with 10 different accents to signify 10 different things, one must simply multiply the number of words by 10. ### PROPOSITION XLVIII.

->*To explain how many possible and pronounceable words there are, whether one uses the French Alphabet and letters, or Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, Chinese, etc., and consequently to provide all possible languages.*<-

I have shown in the preceding proposition that 19 consonants and 20 vowels are required to pronounce everything that can fall within the imagination; this is why it is necessary to bring forth the table of 19 consonants and that of 20 vowels, and to provide the method for finding the number of words that can be composed from them. And because one can find words that will have some consonants repeated two or several times, the table that follows goes up to 30, so that one may know the number of words that would be composed of 19 consonants, where one might be repeated 11 times, or one 5 times and another 6 times, etc.

If one wished to find the words of 40 or 50 consonants, it would be necessary to multiply the last number by 19, until one had performed the 40th or 50th multiplication <note>Mersenne is describing the calculation of powers, such as $19^{40}$ or $19^{50}$.</note>. And if one wishes to use more than 10 vowels in the words, one must multiply 10 by itself as many times as one places vowels. For example, if one uses 10 vowels, one must perform 10 multiplications if one repeats one or several vowels multiple times; for example, if one repeats each of the 10 vowels twice, one must multiply 10 by itself up to 20 times; this is so easy that it is not necessary to provide a table for it.

This is why I come to the examples, which will serve better for the understanding of this proposition than would longer discourses. But it must first be noted that the numbers ranging from unity to 30 show how many different conjunctions of a number of consonants taken from 19 there can be, which are equal to the number in this first column on the right hand: for example, the number 2 shows that they can be joined in 361 ways <note>$19 \times 19 = 361$.</note>; and 3 shows they can be joined in 6,859 ways <note>$19 \times 19 \times 19 = 6859$.</note>; and consequently that there can be as many <term>radical words</term> <note>Root words or base forms.</note> of 3 consonants, without there being any vowel.

## COROLLARY.

Although I do not believe that one can have a language that signifies naturally <note>Mersenne is weighing in on the "Cratylism" debate: whether words have a natural, inherent connection to the objects they describe, or if language is purely a human convention.</note>, nevertheless because one encounters Philosophers who hold the contrary, & because the perfect Musician must know all that can be said on this subject, I wish to show in the following propositions what can be called natural in languages, & how one can imitate the nature of things through words.

### PROPOSITION XLIX.

*Whether one can, or whether one should give a single name, or several to each individual, & if there are more things than names, or words; & what makes one Language more excellent than another.*

Since we have demonstrated how many <term>words</term> <note>original: "dictions"</note> can be made, it is necessary to consider if they suffice to name all things natural & supernatural, & if a single word suffices to serve as a name for each individual. To which I respond, first, that it is very certain that the words of all the languages that have been, or that are still in use throughout the whole world do not suffice to give each thing a name that is its own and particular, as one experiences with all the individuals of herbs & of trees; for each nation is content to give them the name of their species. For example, all the individual plants of the herbs that are called *betony*, *vervain*, *rosemary*, *etc.* <note>original: "betoine, uerueine, romarin"</note> have no other names than those just mentioned: for the French, the Latins, & the Greeks do not distinguish the individuals of these species from one another at all, except by pointing them out with a finger, or by some other sign, or by these demonstrative pronouns, *this herb*, *etc.* for example, *this betony*, *this rosemary*, *this betony* <note>original Latin: "hæc betonica"</note>, *etc.* It happens

As for the number of <term>words</term> <note>original: "dictions"</note> that can be formed from the 10 vowels and the 19 consonants of which I spoke in the 48th proposition—particularly when it is permitted to create words from 30 consonants and 20 vowels—it is marvelously large, for it contains 73 characters <note>In this context, "characters" refers to the number of digits in the resulting figure, indicating its scale.</note>; now, it only takes 46 characters to express the number of grains of sand that would fill the entire solidity of the firmament—that is to say, the entire world known to us, as I demonstrated regarding the first verse of Genesis, in the 16th reason. For since the 47th character makes this last number 10 times larger, and the 48th and 49th characters increase it a hundredfold and a thousandfold, it is evident that this language has a hundred thousand times more words than there would be new grains of sand in all this world, and in a hundred million worlds larger than ours: and consequently much more than all the men and all the animals of the world have hairs, even if there were as many men and animals as there would be grains of sand in all these worlds.

And if it is said that God can always produce new individuals unto infinity, the number of which will surpass that of the said words, I say similarly that one can always add new words by increasing the number of their letters.

I respond in the second place, to resolve the other part of the proposition, that one must have several names for each individual if one wishes to express all its properties; but because we cannot know them for several reasons that could be brought forward, it suffices to have as many names or different terms as we recognize different properties in them.

Where it must be noted that those who believe that the different names by which all nations have named species signify the different properties they envisioned in said species, have no other foundation than their imagination, or some imaginary relationship to the <term>primitive language</term> <note>The "primitive language" refers to the concept of the original tongue spoken by Adam, which was believed to perfectly describe the essence of things.</note>. <header>Book One</header>

composed of all possible <term>words</term> <note>original: "dictions"</note>, whose roots, or radical words, are in a large enough number to provide different names for every property of every species, or of every individual; and if one supposes that Adam (whom Christians and Jews recognize as the first man) had perfect knowledge of all the sciences, and of the properties of each thing, one can imagine that he gave as many names to each species—for example, to each animal—as he recognized different properties within it. Consequently, the different words in all languages that signify the same thing are derived from the names he invented and imposed from the beginning of the world, or during the span of nine hundred and thirty years that he lived.

To which one may add that he gave at least a thousand names to each species in order to derive from them all the different names that all the nations of the earth give to the said species, in each of which Adam was able to observe a thousand different properties, whether absolute or relative. For one can give as many different names to water as there are other bodies in nature to which it can be compared, whether in hardness or in weight; for example, if one compares it to gold, it must be given a name explaining that it is nineteen times lighter than the said gold, and compose other names expressing how much more or less light or heavy it is than all other bodies, of which one can say the same thing as of water. From this, it follows that as many different words would be needed to signify the relative properties of each body as there are different things in nature.

But because we have no testimony of this imposition of names, and since Adam could not have pronounced a hundredth part of the said names in all the time he lived—and even then, he would not yet have pronounced a hundredth part of them even if he had lived until the present day and had imposed a hundred thousand of them in every minute of an hour—it is evident that he did not find all the words, nor did he impose all the names that can serve to explain all the properties of species and individuals.

This can be confirmed by the few words of the <term>Hebrew language</term>, which are so vague and so general that Holy Scripture often uses the same word to signify very different things. From this, one can conclude the simplicity of the first inhabitants of the earth, who, having need of only a small number of things, invented only a small number of terms. Perhaps they judged that the best language of all possible ones is the shortest, and that which has need of the fewest words; just as <term>Mathematicians</term> have judged that the best way to use weights is to take those that follow in a <term>triple progression</term> <note>A mathematical system (1, 3, 9, 27...) that allows one to weigh any whole number amount using the fewest possible weights by placing them on either side of a balance scale.</note> from one pound up to 2,187 pounds, even though one has only eight kinds of weights, the demonstration of which depends on <term>Mechanics</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Mechanics" referred to the branch of physics dealing with machines and balances.</note>.

Indeed, all things are usually all the more excellent as they are simpler, as taught by the <term>Theologians</term>, who place only one idea, or a single act of knowledge, in God, by which He knows and names all things. They also hold that the most excellent <term>Angels</term> <note>According to Scholastic philosophy, higher angels require fewer "species" or mental concepts to understand the universe than lower angels or humans do.</note> have a smaller number of ideas, or species, which serve them as names to express the nature and properties of each thing.

One can similarly prove that the excellence of a language consists in having few <term>words</term> <note>original: "dictions"</note> through the practice of Arithmetic and Algebra, which use only ten different characters to express everything within their power and scope.

And if one could express all the things we need with ten words, or <term>terms</term> <note>original: "dictions"</note>, or with as many words as there are letters in the alphabet, one could conclude that this language would be the simplest of all those that have existed until now; and because I have shown elsewhere that ten things can be varied a billion times, it follows that one can express a billion things with ten words, or even with ten letters or characters.

### PROPOSITION L.

->To determine if the sounds of the voice—that is, the vowels, consonants, syllables, and words—can have such an analogy and relationship with the things signified that one could form a natural language.<-

If letters signify something naturally when they are pronounced or written, it seems that one could compose words from them to create a natural language, since languages are composed of words, and words of letters, as if from their basic elements. Indeed, many have remarked that there are specific letters suited to express sweetness or harshness, as well as other qualities of bodies, actions, and passions. For the two vowels **a** and **o** are suited to signify that which is great and full; and because **a** is pronounced with a wide opening of the mouth, it signifies open things and the actions one uses to open and to begin some work. This is why Virgil began his *Aeneid* with the word *Arma* <note>Latin for "Arms" or "Weapons"</note>, and why he judged that this vowel signifies the love that opens the hearts of lovers to pour themselves into one another, as one sees in these words: *Phillida amor ante alias* <note>Latin: "Phyllis, love before all others"</note>, in which there are five **a**'s in succession.

As for the vowel **e**, it signifies things that are slender and subtle, and it is suited to express mourning and pain because the mouth narrows while pronouncing it. This is why Virgil uses this letter several times when describing misery:

> *Alas, what land, what seas can now receive me in my misery, etc.* 
> <note>original Latin: *Heu quæ me miſerum tellus, quæ me æquora poſſunt, Accipere, &c.*</note>

It is also suited to represent an echo, as seen in these words: *the hills resound with the shout* <note>original Latin: *colles clamore reſultant*</note>.

The vowel **i** signifies things that are very thin and very small; from this comes the word *minime* <note>Latin for "least" or "very little"</note>, which has two **i**'s and one **e**, and which consequently is more suited to signify humility than any other word. It also expresses that which is penetrating, like a lightning bolt:

> *She herself hurled the swift fire of Jove from the clouds.*

The vowel **u** signifies dark and hidden things, following the nature of its pronunciation. I leave aside many other things that could be said about vowels, of which I have already spoken elsewhere, in order to add something about consonants, which are suited to express the things they represent, or with which they have a relationship. For example, **f** is suited to represent wind and fire; from this comes the Latin word *flo* <note>original: "flo", meaning "to blow"</note>, and many other similar ones.

The letter **s**, and **x** (which is composed of **c** and **s**) are suited to signify things that have some sort of harshness, like winds and storms, particularly when it is added to **r**, as in the word *stridor* <note>original: "stridor", meaning a harsh, creaking, or whistling noise</note>. The letter **l** signifies things that are humble, soft, and liquid, whereas **r** signifies things that are harsh, rough, hard, and rugged, as well as vehement and impetuous actions; it is called the <term>dog letter</term> <note>original: "lettre canine"; the letter R was known in Latin as the *littera canina* because its trilled sound resembles a dog growling</note>.

**m** signifies that which is great, like <term>Machines</term> <note>in this period, "machines" often referred to large engines, siege works, or complex stage apparatus</note>, and several other similar things. From this comes the fact that the Romans called it *magnum* <note>original: "magnum", meaning "great"</note>, and that the Poets do not pronounce this letter <note>referring to "elision," where a final 'm' is silenced in Latin verse for the sake of meter</note> because it is rough, as one sees in these words: *monstrum horrendum ingens* <note>original Latin from Virgil's Aeneid: "a monster, horrific, immense"</note>.

**n** has a contrary meaning, for it is suited to express things that are black, hidden, and dark. I leave aside the other letters, of which anyone can easily speak from their own experience, for their pronunciation clearly shows what they are suited for.

As for syllables and words composed of vowels and consonants that follow one another in such a way that they are pronounced softly and easily, they are suited to express things that are sweet, even, and polished; and others, whose pronunciation is harsh and difficult, are suited to signify things that are hard and troublesome. Now, it is enough to have touched upon this difficulty, because the Grammarians and Rhetoricians treat it at greater length, as one can see in Quintilian, <term>Scaliger</term> <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a prominent scholar who wrote extensively on the principles of poetry and grammar</note> in the fourth book of his *Poetics*, Lipsius, Sturmius, Keckermann, Vossius, and many others. > *The hoof shakes the crumbling plain with the sound of four feet galloping.* <note>original Latin: "Quadrupedante putrem sonitu quatit vngula campum."</note>

And when Homer represents a sword that breaks, in the third book of the *Iliad*:

> *And it fell from his hand, broken into three or four pieces.* <note>original Greek: "Τριχθά τε καὶ τετραχθὰ διατρυφὲν ἔκπεσε χειρός."</note>

Scaliger reported the most beautiful verses of Virgil and Homer in the fifth book of his *Poetics*, where he compares them both together, from which one can draw enlightenment for the <term>natural language</term>, if such a thing is possible.

### PROPOSITION LI.

->*Whether those who have no tongue can speak, and whether it is possible to make*<-
->*the mute speak and teach them to read and write when they are deaf.*<-

If <term>trills</term> <note>original: "fredons"; in this context, it refers to vocal modulations or rapid melodic movements</note> can serve to create a language, one can speak even if the tongue has been cut out, since the passages and trills are made with the throat. Certainly, it would be difficult to imagine that one could naturally speak without a tongue, if a child from lower Poitou named Pierre Durand did not demonstrate this experience, of which many in the city of Paris and other places where he has been are eyewitnesses. This invited *Jacques Rolland*, a Surgeon, to write a book titled *Aglossostomography* <note>original: "Aglossostomographie"; from Greek, meaning "description of a mouth without a tongue"</note>, or description of a mouth without a tongue, which he had printed in Saumur. In it, he says that the opening of the larynx of this child is very small and oval-shaped, that the uvula which closes it is thin and long, and that a small fleshy body—which still appears where his tongue used to be—swells in its middle toward the palate. He also notes that the teeth are reversed and elongated inward, and that the <term>buccinator muscles</term> <note>muscles of the cheek used in chewing and blowing</note> are easily involved between the molar teeth, and that all the other parts necessary for the voice have accommodated themselves to the necessity of speaking in the absence of the tongue. For the flattening of the palate, the size of the tonsils, and the recessed position of the muscles he calls *buccinators* so narrow the mouth that it articulates sounds. This is because all these parts, being still tender in children, adapt easily to the necessity of speech, as is experienced in the idioms of different nations and in the different accents of foreigners, who cannot leave behind their ways of pronouncing and accentuating because of the "fold" and long habit they have contracted since their childhood. <header>Book One</header>

the chapters of his book, in which he demonstrates that a tongue that has been cut off cannot be repaired, although one might add the small instrument he describes when it is only truncated at the tip. He also shows how it serves for tasting, moving, and gathering food, and for spitting, and discusses all its other functions.

Now, if the art had been found to attach an artificial tongue to the <term>hyoid bone<note>A U-shaped bone in the neck that supports the tongue.</note></term> upon which the tongue rests, one could supplement the lack of a natural tongue, just as is done for the loss of teeth or a nose; nevertheless, I do not dare to conclude that the movements of the glottis and the epiglottis might not also form some speech.

As for those who are mute, although many believe it is impossible for them to speak otherwise than by the ordinary signs they make with their hands, eyes, and other parts of the body—because they cannot hear any instruction, being deaf—there is no doubt that they can be taught to move the tongue in such a way that they will form words. One can teach them the meaning of these words by presenting the objects before their eyes, or by having them touch the things they signify. From this, one may conclude that one must begin with writing to make the deaf speak, just as one begins with speech to teach others to speak; so that speech and writing are almost the same thing. For one might say that speech is a fleeting writing, consisting of movement, and that writing is a constant speech, which is subject neither to time nor to movement.

This can be confirmed by the example of <note>Pierre de Bellis, known as "le Bène," a famous 16th-century case of a deaf man from Arles who learned to communicate through writing.</note> Monsieur Bene, who responded in writing to letters sent to him, and who consequently could read all kinds of books, as the city of Arles witnesses. His children can still be seen there, of whom only two sons and two daughters did not speak; he wrote the *Genealogy of the Kings* and that of his own house.

Now, the only way to teach the deaf and mute to read and write consists in making them understand that the characters we use represent what is shown to them and what they see. For the pronunciation of letters and vocables—that is to say, speech—does not represent the things signified any more naturally than does writing, whatever form it may take, since both depend equally on the will and the convention of men, without which they signify nothing. This is why the deaf can easily understand that each word signifies what is shown to them; and because they are deprived of hearing, and consequently their imagination is in no way attached to the objects of that sense, they have a mind more capable and stronger for understanding and remembering that the characters shown to them (which are joined to all the things one wishes to teach them) signify this or that thing, more so than those who are not deprived of hearing.

This being established, it is easy to teach the deaf to write all kinds of things, provided they can fall under the sense of sight, or touch, or can be tasted or smelled; but it is more difficult to make them speak, inasmuch as one cannot show them all the movements of the tongue and the other parts that form speech. Those who hear have no need to see these movements, because they move the tongue and try little by little until they have perfectly imitated the words they have heard.

Valesius <note>Francisco Vallés (1524–1592), a Spanish physician who documented the methods used to teach the deaf.</note> says that his friend Ponce <note>Pedro Ponce de León (c. 1520–1584), a Spanish Benedictine monk often credited as the first person to develop a method for teaching the deaf to speak.</note> taught the deaf by means of writing in such a way that he made them speak by first showing them with his finger the things that were signified by the writing, and then by making them move their tongues until they had uttered some word, or made some kind of sound or voice; from which it is easy to conclude that one must begin with writing to teach the deaf, whereas one begins with speech to teach the blind and others who use their hearing.

## PROPOSITION LI.

->*Determining in what manner the ear perceives sound, and what the action of hearing is: whether it is the ear that knows the sound, or if this office belongs to the mind.*<-

One of the greatest difficulties in Natural Philosophy <note>original: "Physique"</note> consists in knowing how the operations of the senses are performed, and in what manner the mind proceeds to know the objects presented to it, along with all their conditions and properties. From this, one has imagined a "representative being," or an image and a <term>species<note>In early modern philosophy, 'species' (often called *species sensibilis*) were thought to be the forms or images of objects that traveled through the air to enter the senses.</note></term> which compensates for the presence of the object, which seems too coarse to be able to enter the senses or the mind. For since knowledge is a representation of what is known, and the faculty that knows must touch the object to which it is united, it must touch it and unite with it by means of its image when it cannot unite with its real presence; and because the image cannot perfectly represent its original if it does not contain it <term>formally<note>To contain something "formally" means it exists in the representation exactly as it does in the real world.</note></term> or <term>eminently<note>To contain something "eminently" means it exists in a higher, more perfect, or more causal form than the object itself.</note></term>—since one must possess what one represents in the same manner that one represents it—the faculty that perfectly knows one of the properties of its object must also contain it as perfectly as it represents it.

From this comes the fact that several theologians maintain that the blessed <note>Those in Heaven who experience the "Beatific Vision."</note> cannot see God clearly by means of any image, representation, or species, for the reason that no image can contain the nature of God formally or eminently; and that God represents and knows all things perfectly because He contains them in eminence. From this I conclude that the ear, or the faculty that apprehends sounds and perfectly knows their properties, must contain them, or must have within itself something more excellent that represents or contains them. But since I speak here only of general knowledge, and of the manner in which hearing perceives sounds, it is not necessary to explain in what perfect knowledge consists.

I say, then, first, that the ear does not know sounds, and that it serves only as an instrument and organ to pass them into the mind, which considers their nature and properties. Consequently, animals do not have knowledge of said sounds, but only the representation of them, without knowing whether what they apprehend is a sound or a color, or something else; so that one can say they do not act so much as they are acted upon. The objects make such an impression on their senses that it is necessary for them to follow it, just as it is necessary for the wheels of a clock to follow the weight or the spring that pulls them. But man, having been touched by sounds, considers their nature and properties, distinguishes them from other objects, and forms very certain knowledge from them; which evidently shows that he has a faculty and a power—

of knowing, which in no way depends on the senses, and by which it <note>The "it" refers to the mind or the intellect.</note> notices and separates what is corruptible and incorruptible, mutable and immutable, and finite and infinite in each thing. For since the nature of things does not enter through the senses—which receive only simple images <note>These "images" refer to the "species" mentioned on the previous page—the sensory data perceived by the body.</note> of which they have no knowledge—and since the mind contemplates the nature of incorruptible things and their properties as easily and perfectly as it does those of corruptible things; and even since we experience that there is more pleasure in knowing and considering what is necessary and immutable than what is merely contingent and changeable, and in contemplating that which exists of itself rather than that which comes from elsewhere and depends on another; it is very certain that the mind has a being distinct from the body and from matter, and which depends only on the one who gave it being—that is to say, from the one who has being of himself <note>A reference to God as the "self-existent being."</note>, whose image it carries, as it testifies through its operations, which share much with the immutable and the infinite.

From this it follows that the mind forms propositions that are eternally true; for example, that if there is some self-existent and independent being, it is necessary that he has always been, and that he can never cease to be, and that he has all kinds of perfections; that this being is most good, and consequently most lovable; that all lines drawn from the center of a circle to its circumference are equal; that the diagonal <note>original: "diametre"</note> of a square is incommensurable to the side of said square; that the whole is greater than its part, and an infinity of other similar propositions that the mind of man knows, or can know perfectly. This cannot happen, however, unless the mind contains them formally or eminently, and unless it has the same incorruptibility <note>In this context, "incorruptibility" refers to the quality of being deathless or unable to decay, a standard argument for the immortality of the soul.</note> that it recognizes in them, since it understands them perfectly—that is to say, by very clear and evident demonstration. Consequently, the mind makes itself equal to them in intellectual and true being, just as one triangle makes itself equal in size to another triangle to which it is perfectly applied: for perfect knowledge is nothing other than a perfect application of the understanding to the thing known, whose incorruptibility it could not comprehend or know if it were not itself incorruptible. But I will explain this reasoning at greater length in another place, where I will show that there is no objection that can weaken it; for it suffices here to suppose that the mind of the Musician who considers sounds is incorruptible and immortal.

Now, to return to the manner in which hearing perceives sounds, I say in the second place that the mind discerns that what has struck the ear is different from what strikes the eye—or at least that the ear is struck differently than the eye—and that it judges that this contact, or this impression which the external agent makes upon the hearing, reveals to it other properties of bodies than the impression made by light or color upon the eye. Although it is very difficult to know how the mind uses the action, or rather the "passion" <note>In the philosophical sense, a "passion" is an effect produced by an external agent; the ear "suffers" the impact of the sound wave.</note> and the emotion of the ear, and how it perceives the movement and the emotion of the auditory nerve. For if one considers the manner in which it acts, one will find that it cannot discern whether the sound is external, or if it is made within ourselves—as we experience with the buzzings and noises that occur inside the ear or the head, which affect us in the same way as if they were made outside.
