First, we must observe that the external air excites the internal air of the ear, and that it impresses an emotion <note>The word "emotion" here refers to a physical agitation or vibration in the nerves.</note> upon the auditory nerve, similar to the one it received. The mind, which is entirely present in every part of the body and consequently in the said nerve, immediately perceives the movement of the organs of the ear and thereby judges the qualities of the sound’s movement and the external objects producing it. Now, one can imagine that the mind is like an indivisible and intellectual point, where all the impressions of the senses meet, like all the lines of a circle at its center, or like all the threads of a spider's web where the spider has spun and woven it. For just as the spider feels and perceives all the movements and impressions that the said threads receive, so the human mind perceives all the impressions of the muscles, the nerves, and their fibers and filaments.

## PROPOSITION LII.

->*To determine whether the ear is deceived more or less often than the eye, or if it surpasses it; and whether one should trust and rely more upon hearing than upon sight: wherein the ways used to deceive the eye and the ear are explained, as well as the methods one may use to prevent or correct the errors of these two senses.*<-

This problem is one of the most useful of all those contained in this book, especially since the sciences depend upon these two senses, whose operations are entirely necessary for making the observations and experiments used to invent, establish, advance, and perfect the arts and sciences. This does not need to be proven, since one cannot see the stars or anything else without the eye, and one cannot learn the observations of others without the eye or the ear. However, it is not easy to judge which of these two senses is the most necessary, or which is the most certain in its operations; for many reasons can be brought forward for both, showing that if one is deprived of a certain prerogative, it has another in compensation that the other lacks. For example, if the eye discovers a greater multitude of present things, the ear discovers a greater multitude of absent things; if the eye enjoys light and...

->**Book One**<-

colors, the ear enjoys the harmony of sounds, and of speech, which surpasses everything that is understood by the eye; for even if the eye carries speech into the mind by means of reading, it must first have been taught by means of the ear, which teaches it the name and the value of letters, and the meaning of words. If the eye is swifter in its actions, the ear, in compensation, hears everything said in front, behind, and to the side, whereas the eye sees only what is before it, and only that which can arrive in a straight line to it. I leave aside several other advantages the eye seems to have over the ear; for example, that it sees light and grandeurs from much further away than the ear hears sounds; that it notices a greater multitude and variety of objects; and that it suffices on its own to discover the arts and sciences without a master or director. Furthermore, a blind person is more inconvenienced than a deaf person, etc. My purpose is to examine the principal of their conditions: namely, which of these two senses has more certainty in its operation. This can best be shown by comparing the errors of the eye with those of the hearing.

Now, the eye is deceived first in the distance of objects, for they always appear smaller the further they are from the eye. From this it follows that among rows of trees, those that are furthest away seem to touch; that the sky seems to touch the horizon of the earth, because we cannot notice any other distance between the eye and the sky except that of the part of the earth visible to us; and that the stars appear further away toward the horizon than at the <term>zenith</term> <note>The highest point in the sky directly above the observer.</note>, because there is nothing remarkable to notice between the eye and the zenith. To this one can relate other causes that make objects appear closer or further than they are, as happens when the object is more or less illuminated.

As for sounds, they are never "distant" in themselves, assuming they are in no way distinct from the movement of the air and that they do not produce any <term>intentional species</term> <note>original: "especes intentionnelles" — a Scholastic philosophical term referring to the "likeness" or "image" of an object that travels through a medium to the sense organ. The author is suggesting sound is a physical motion, not a traveling "image."</note>; so that we must only consider here the location of the bodies that make the sound. Now, it does not seem possible for the ear to discern this distance, because it seems that bodies are closer when the sound is more vehement, and there is only the eye, the report of others, or some experience that can teach us the distance of the place where the sound begins. Consequently, the eye discerns the distance of its objects with more certainty than the ear does. From this one can conclude that the distance of the place where a sound is first made more often deceives the ear than the distance of light and colors deceives the eye. Now, hearing is particularly deceived when it imagines that the one whose speech is heard is absent, and that they do not form it in the ordinary manner—as happens to those who <insert>imitate</insert> spirits, and who often frighten those who do not know the <note>original: "fourbe" — trickery or deceit.</note> fraud. The wind and several qualities of the air are also the reason why we believe those who speak are closer or further from us than they actually are; and generally, whenever a sound is made in an extraordinary way, and we do not use the eye or other senses to alert the ear, it is deceived. For just as the light of a candle, or some other distant luminous body, would seem to approach us if it grew larger in the same place—for example, if a Star became as large as the Sun to our eyes, it would not seem further away, and a candle seen from a league away would seem to approach if it increased its light—likewise, a sound seems to approach us when it increases in volume.

# Of the Voice.

I will provide the remedies that must be used so as not to be deceived by distance, after having explained the other errors of the eye and the ear, or rather of the **imagination**.

The eye is further deceived by dim air, such as it is in the evening, at night, and in the morning; for objects appear further away to it because it does not see them as distinctly as in broad daylight. We find by experience that what is clearer and filled with a greater light appears closer than what has less light, even though it is no further away. From this comes <term>perspective</term> <note>The technique of representing three-dimensional depth on a two-dimensional surface.</note>, in which the most vivid colors are easily made to stand out by shadows.

Hearing is also deceived by weak and faint sounds that we believe to be far off, when we are accustomed to hearing clear and powerful sounds. This shows that the **imagination** is more the cause of these deceptions than the external senses, which always grasp objects in the same manner they are struck and affected by them. For the reason why those who are hard of hearing or partially deaf believe that nearby sounds are further away is the same reason why those who are short-sighted, or who do not see very clearly, believe that what is near them is far off.

It happens similarly that one is mistaken about distance when the sound lasts too briefly and passes almost in a moment; for just as the eye does not have the leisure to direct and steady its <term>visual axis</term> <note>The straight line along which the eye is directed toward an object.</note> upon the light or the colors that pass quickly, so too is the ear not enough affected by the sound that passes too quickly to judge its distance, nor its other qualities, of which we will speak later.

The second way the sight is deceived consists of the size of objects; for when they are viewed under the same angle, and we do not know their distance, we judge them to be of the same size. From this it comes that the ignorant, who believe only their eyes, estimate that the Sun is no larger than the bottom of a <term>bushel</term> <note>A traditional container used for measuring dry goods like grain.</note> or a plate; so that objects always appear to us as large as the angles under which we look at them, even though some may be a thousand times larger, if the other senses or reason do not correct this error.

Something similar happens to the ear, for we think that the sound it hears more clearly and distinctly is stronger, though it may be weaker. For we judge sounds according to how they strike the ear; now, this deception also comes from distance, which weakens the voice; though one might say the ear is not deceived, since it judges the voice to be weaker when it perceives it less; for it is indeed weaker at the moment it strikes the hearing than the one that is heard better.

Furthermore, just as objects always appear smaller to the eye than they are in themselves, sounds also appear weaker to the ear than they are at the place where they are produced. But the reason for these two deceptions is different: the eye sees its objects smaller than they are because the proportion of objects differing in size is greater than that of the angles; but the ear finds the sounds weaker because they have become weakened since the place where they were produced. Those sounds it hears are no longer those that were made at the beginning, just as the first circles made on the water no longer last when the final circles are formed.

The eye is also deceived when it perceives faces as flawless, very clean, and smooth, but then sees great imperfections when it approaches them: <margin>this</margin>

This is something that Composers must note, so as not to worry so much about many small <term>niceties</term> <note>Original: "gentillesses," referring to delicate musical flourishes or clever ornaments.</note> and certain ornaments when making a grand **Concert** of Music for large assemblies, as compared to when one sings in a small room, or before a few people, as we shall say elsewhere. But when reason corrects the eye and the hearing, one easily concludes that objects which appear smaller, or equal, are larger when one knows that the distance is greater, because reason dictates that distance diminishes the form and size of objects. Now, although the other deceptions of the eye do not seem to apply to the ear—because its object consists in the movement of the air, which sight does not need—nevertheless, one may add that the ear often hears sounds more clearly from a more distant place, just as the eye can see its objects more distinctly from a more distant place. This is demonstrated in the same segment of a circle, where the angles being equal make the object appear of the same size to the eye, even though it changes through an infinity of positions and distances that one can imagine within the arc of the segment. This happens similarly to the ear regarding sounds, by reason of the different lines through which it hears the sound. Furthermore, one can place the ear in locations where the same sound will appear more or less weak than it appears from a given place according to a given ratio; just as one can place the eye at points where the same size will appear larger or smaller than it is, in whatever ratio one desires.

The ear is further deceived by the places where the sound is made, for it often judges that they come from one side when they come from the other; and just as the rays by which one sees sizes cause them to appear higher or lower depending on whether the rays are higher or lower, similarly, sounds seem to come from higher or lower by reason of different winds which raise or lower the air in which the sounds are produced. But the ear is more deceived by means of the echo, or the different reflections of sound, than by other ways, as I have said in the discourse on the echo.

I leave aside several other deceptions of the eye, some of which may apply to the ear; for example, that the eye can be so situated that lines which are not parallel will seem parallel to it; that parallel lines seem to approach one another in proportion to their distance; that one can draw two lines whose distance will always appear equal, etc.

The eye is also mistaken in the number of its objects, for faceted glasses <note>An early reference to prisms or cut-glass lenses that create multiple images.</note> make as many objects appear as they have different faces; but the ear cannot be deceived in the number of sounds, unless it be by reflection. as one experiences with glasses of the same size, and with coins made of the same material and of the same weight, and with a thousand other bodies whose difference cannot be noticed by sight; but when one rings the said glasses and the other bodies, the ear distinguishes them all. Indeed, among several hundred glasses and coins, one rarely finds two that have the same sound, even though they appear equal to the eye. Furthermore, the ear is almost never deceived regarding the <term>low and high</term> <note>Original: "graue & à l'aigu." These terms refer to musical pitch; "grave" meaning low or bass, and "aigu" meaning high or treble.</note> of a sound, and if it is occasionally surprised when noises are too high or too low—such as those that do not belong to Music—it can correct itself by comparing the sound in doubt with others that it is more familiar with. From this, it follows that one can prefer hearing over sight; to which one may add that the Patriarch Jacob, who was deceived by touch, was not deceived by hearing <note>A reference to Genesis 27, where Isaac (the Patriarch's father, though the text attributes the encounter to Jacob's experience of the event) recognizes Jacob's voice despite the physical disguise: "The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau."</note>, and consequently that the ear is more certain than any other sense. This is perhaps the reason why God willed that the doctrine of heaven and of faith should enter through hearing rather than through the eye, or through the other senses, so that the reception of a thing so necessary should not be subject to error or deception.

From this comes the fact that speech, which corresponds to hearing, almost never deceives us; for even if it has been so long since one has seen a person that they are no longer recognized by their facial features, nevertheless they are recognized by the voice and the speech. Now, one can confirm the advantage we give to hearing by the choice made by the most sensible men when they are faced with the prospect of deafness or blindness; for all those who are wisest prefer hearing to sight.

As for the manner of deceiving the eye, the discussion of that belongs to <term>Optics</term>; but when the ear is mistaken, the eye can serve as its guide and remedy. For example, when one believes that a sound comes from further away than it does, the eye, which sees the distance of the place where it is made, corrects it; and if the ear were mistaken regarding the pitch, the eye could enlighten it by counting the number of <term>vibrations</term> <note>Original: "retours d'vne chorde." This refers to the physical frequency or cycles of a vibrating string.</note> of a string set to <term>Unison</term>.

There is another remedy which is common to the eye and the ear, which consists in becoming more attentive and repeating the operation; for it often happens that one judges differently of light, colors, figures, and other objects of sight the second time they are looked at than the first. This happens similarly to the ear, which perceives sounds with more certainty when it remains attentive for longer or more often, because the reasoning one does while the ear is fixed upon the sounds is all the more certain because one has more time to judge with the ear and to consider if it is mistaken.

Now, since we have spoken of the tongue and the voice, and since God has particularly given them to us to praise Him, I do not believe I could better finish this book on the voice than by singing His praises through the words of the three children whom He kept from the heat and the flames of the furnace, which **Monsieur Godeau** <note>Antoine Godeau (1605–1672), a French poet and Bishop of Grasse, famous for his elegant paraphrases of sacred texts into French verse.</note>, one of our most excellent poets, has paraphrased very elegantly. For since I am passing from the treatise on speech to that of songs, which are one of the principal ornaments of the voice, those Musicians who desire to merit eternal life by singing and composing will be very glad to find one of the most beautiful subjects one can imagine, such as the **Canticle** <note>Specifically the "Song of the Three Holy Children," a hymn of praise found in the additions to the Book of Daniel.</note> which follows, in order to give it the most beautiful melodies they can find in the whole extent of Music.

# BOOK TWO.

## ON SONGS.

### FIRST PROPOSITION.

->*A Song or an Air is a derivation of the voice, or of other sounds, through certain*<-
->*natural or artificial intervals, which are pleasing to the ear and to the mind,*<-
->*and which signify joy, sadness, or some other passion*<-
->*by their various movements.*<-

There is nothing more difficult than finding the definition of things of which one wishes to speak; this is what happens here: for the nature of song is as difficult to know as it is easy to hear. Now, it must be noted that the word *air*, which is used to signify song, is taken in several ways; for it signifies, first, the third element, which extends from the surface of the earth to the Moon, and which is fifty-one times as thick as the earth—that is to say, fifty-eight thousand four hundred twelve leagues, of which each has three thousand paces, and the pace has five King's feet <note>The "King's foot" (pied de Roy) was a standard French unit of length before the metric system, measuring approximately 32.5 centimeters.</note>: for there are fifteen thousand King's feet in the French league, as I have said elsewhere.

Secondly, *air* signifies the manner in which one speaks, questions, or responds, particularly if one speaks in anger; for we say that someone has responded with "such an air," etc. This signifies almost the same thing as the tone of the voice, or the accent with which one responds. This word can have several other meanings according to the various things to which it can be applied, for example, to faces: for when some painting or some person resembles another, we say that they have "the air" of them. But the third meaning is when it expresses the same thing as the song, or the chant, which we use to sing some fancies, whether we pronounce some words, or whether we sing without words using musical notes, or in some other manner. This being presupposed, I say that the definition I have placed in this proposition comprises all that belongs to the essence of song: first, the *derivation* <term>deduction: in this context, the melodic progression or "leading" of the voice</term>, or conduct of the *voice*, is the genus, for song has this in common with harangues, discourses, and the words we use when speaking to one another.

Book Second

Secondly, I have said, *or of other sounds*, because one can play Airs on musical instruments. Thirdly, I have added, *by certain natural or artificial intervals*, which is what makes songs different from speech. Discourse has no fixed intervals by which we ascend or descend while speaking, even though the voice does rise or fall without us paying attention to the specific intervals it creates.

Nevertheless, some believe that if we raised our voices as required by the discourse we are holding, and if we made all the intervals necessary to persuade others of what we are saying, we would perform wonders—particularly if we added the proper accents for this effect, as I have stated in the treatise on *Accentual Music* <note>Accentual music refers to the study of how the natural pitch and rhythm of spoken language (accents) can be translated into musical notation to better express emotion.</note>.

Fourthly, I said *natural, or artificial*, because we call "natural" those intervals made by everyone—that is to say, as much by the Shepherd in the woods or the countryside as by Musicians. These include the intervals of the Diatonic scale <term>Diatonic: the standard seven-note musical scale (like the white keys on a piano) which was considered the most natural system of music</term>. But the artificial intervals were invented by Musicians to embellish their art and to enrich their songs; these include the minor semitone, the diesis <term>Diesis: an extremely small musical interval, often smaller than a half-step, used in specialized tuning systems to add "color" or precise intonation</term>, and so on, which are not practiced outside of formal Music except by chance.

In the fifth place, I said *which are pleasing to the ear and to the mind*: for even though some airs are sad, they nevertheless often please us as much as, or more than, when they are cheerful. Finally, I said *by their movements*, by which I mean Rhythm, or the metrical feet with which one accompanies airs. These include Dactyls, Spondees, and Choriambs <note>These are rhythmic patterns borrowed from classical Greek and Latin poetry. A Dactyl is one long beat followed by two short ones; a Spondee is two long beats; a Choriamb is a long, two shorts, and a long.</note>, which I discuss in the book on Rhythm. Indeed, a change in movement brings a great difference to airs, even if one does not change their intervals.

It must nevertheless be noted that it is not strictly necessary to change the pitch between low and high sounds to create a kind of air. If we speak of everything that can be called an air or a song in any manner whatsoever, some say that one can play an air on the Drum. Even though all its tones are in unison <note>Unison: when all notes are at the exact same pitch.</note>, the various movements or various measures given to the sounds of the Drum can represent a certain song or a "fantasia." This also applies to the voice, which can represent many things through various measures and all the movements of Rhythm. This occurs in several Psalms which begin, end, and are sung on the same note or the same interval, and in the chant used by many Religious orders. However, others prefer to call this a *simple recitation* rather than a song—such as the chant we use, and several others who imitate us, like the Capuchins and Discalced Carmelites <note>The Capuchins and Discalced Carmelites are Catholic religious orders known for their simple, austere lifestyles; their liturgical chanting was often a monotone recitation focused on the text rather than melody.</note>, because we make no intervals and observe no other measure than that of the syllables.

Nevertheless, strictly speaking, this is not a simple recitation or discourse, nor is it a song or an air as I have defined it; rather, it is something in between that participates in both. Some call it *chant in Ison* <note>original: "chant en Ison"</note> because it is equal and uses only a single interval, for *Ison* <note>From the Greek "isos," meaning equal or same.</note> signifies that which is equal.

Now this Chant in *Ison*, or equal chant, can be distinguished by the different ways in which it is sung or recited; this happens particularly

in two ways: first, when one dwells longer on a certain syllable, pronouncing it more loudly and with more vehemence than the others, giving a certain cadence to the chant. This is observed in the chant of the Capuchins <note>The Capuchins are a reform branch of the Franciscan friars; the author is noting a specific rhythmic quirk in their liturgical chanting</note>, who make the penultimate or the ante-penultimate syllable <note>The second-to-last or third-to-last syllables of a line</note> at the middle and end of each verse of the Psalms much longer, singing it more loudly than the other syllables. These other syllables they make almost equal in length, singing them as if rolling or counting them without dragging, which makes their chant more cheerful and more pleasant.

Secondly, when one exactly observes all the long and short syllables, giving two beats to the long and one to the short, at the end as well as at the beginning and in the middle, without dragging one word longer than another, as happens in the pronunciation of verse. There are several other ways that can vary this chant, by reason of which it is said that such or such Religious orders, or other persons, sing with such or such an "air," even if they do not use melodies in the way I have defined them above.

One could here raise an objection and say that the entire definition of this first Theorem <note>The author uses "Theorem" to refer to the formal principles or propositions of music theory he is establishing</note> fits, or at least can fit and be applied to Harangues, discourses, and the recitations of Tragedies and Comedies. For an Orator, or one who represents a character on stage, can observe all the intervals—whether *Diatonic*, *Chromatic*, or *Enharmonic* <term>Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic: the three "genera" of Greek music, ranging from standard scales to those using half-steps and even smaller quarter-tones</term>—that are found within an *Octave*. Indeed, experience shows us that most Preachers use the *semitone*, the *whole tone*, the *minor third*, the *major third*, the *Fourth*, and the *Fifth*, ascending and descending according to the various accents or movements they employ, now in one place, now in another. From this, some excellent Musicians hold that discourses in which these intervals are found create *Fauxbourdons* <term>Fauxbourdon: a style of harmonized vocal music; here used to describe a "sing-song" or repetitive vocal delivery</term>, and that they can be numbered among the "airs." This is proven by certain Preachers who speak almost as if they were singing, which is why their discourse is less pleasant and less profitable.

Nevertheless, there is no discourse so regulated that it rises or falls by all the specific intervals of melodies—namely by tones, semitones, etc.—for it most often rises by "insensible" <note>Meaning intervals so small or fluid they cannot be easily measured or categorized</note> or unknown intervals, though one could discern them if one paid close attention. However, all the intervals of airs or songs are so well regulated that one never fails to perform them in every place they are marked; from this comes the proverb, *it is as regulated as a sheet of music*. This shows that Airs, and consequently Music, maintain a much better-regulated order than discourses, which have nothing fixed and follow the imagination and intention of the speaker.

This is what Euclid <note>original: "Euclide"</note> recognized and noted at the beginning of his treatise on Music, when he said that discourse makes use of a "continuous voice" <note>original: "voix continuë"; in Greek, *synechēs*</note> which does not cease or rest until the speech is finished, and which keeps no certain rule for intervals when raising or lowering the sound. But the movement or deduction of the voice, or of the sound that makes airs and songs—which Euclid calls *Diastematic* <term>Diastematic: from the Greek *diastēmatikē*, referring to a voice that moves by distinct, measurable intervals or "steps," unlike the sliding scale of speech</term> or *Intervallic*—is not conducted by continuous intervals. Instead, it passes sometimes from a *tone* to a *ditone* <note>A major third</note>, sometimes from a *Third* to a *Fourth*, or to a *Fifth*, etc., and stops sometimes for the space of a ,

Second Book

From which it is easy to conclude if the description of the "air" that I have given is acceptable and legitimate: to which I will add that which follows, so that the other may be better understood.

### PROPOSITION II.

> *An air is a movement, a progression, or a leap of sounds, or of the voice, through the artificial intervals that Musicians have established, namely by Semitones, Tones, Thirds, etc., by which we explain the movements and passions of our soul, or those of the subject and the text.*

There is no need to explain all the parts or terms of this definition, or description, since they can be understood by what we have said previously. I will only add that I have used the word *leap* <note>The original French word is *saillie*, which implies a projection or a sudden movement outward</note> here because speech seems to flow naturally, like a stream that runs gently without any regulated leaps, and without changing intervals, except by chance, which makes it go unremarked or unnoticed. Now we see that sound, in which the voice leaps, jumps, and passes from one interval to another—sometimes high and sometimes low, while strengthening, weakening, or softening—is what some explain by the various bank shots, the bounces, and the diverse reflections and movements made by the ball in games of tennis <note>original: *ieux de paulme*. Real Tennis was a popular metaphor for the movement of sound in the 17th century</note>, or by the different movements and postures of images represented in mirrors according to whether they are closer or further from the objects, and following the different positions or movements of both.

This is why airs can represent the various movements of the sea, the heavens, and the other things of this world, since one can maintain the same ratios in musical intervals that are found in the movements of the soul, the body, the elements, and the heavens. From this, it follows that Music serves the Moral life more, and is more suited to manners than painting, which is as if dead; but Music is living, and transports in some way the life, the soul, the spirit, and the affection of the Cantor, or of the Musician, into the ears and the soul of the listeners.

This is perhaps why the Church of the Jews and of the Christians—under the written Law <note>The Old Testament era</note> and under the Law of Grace <note>The New Testament era</note>—has made use of Music, in order to transport the spirits of the faithful up to heaven, and to make a happy alliance of our hearts and our voices with the celestial Music of the Blessed; for it is reasonable that all creatures should use the same concert to sing the praises and to announce the greatness and the wonders of their Creator.

Secondly, I said, *by artificial intervals*, for although nature seems to give us the intervals of the Diatonic scale—namely the major tone, the minor tone, and the major semitone—nevertheless one could use other intervals, such as the <term>Sesquidecimal</term> <note>original: *Sesquixiesme*; a ratio of 16:15, a type of semitone</note>, <term>Sesquiseptimal</term> <note>original: *Sesquiseptiesme*; a ratio of 17:16</note>, etc., of which I speak elsewhere. This would perhaps succeed very well, particularly when one sings airs for a single voice, or at most two: but Musicians have always used the Diatonic intervals, and particularly those who profess this Art among the Christians, even though they could have chosen other intervals, for example

# Of Songs.
H iij

those of the different species of <term>Tetrachord</term><note>A scale of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth; the building block of ancient Greek musical systems</note>, which I explain elsewhere. And then the sequence of the intervals of the Air and of all Music is artificial: for one cannot use it unless one has learned it through science, or through exercise, and through practice. I have also added the explanation of the movements of the *subject*, insofar as it is not necessary that we express our own movements or passions; it is enough that we imitate the passions of others, or of the proposed subject, as almost always happens to those who sing to give pleasure to listeners. For even though they may be sad, they can sing very gay Airs, or sad Airs even though they are full of joy.

This is why Music is an imitation, or representation, just as much as Poetry, Tragedy, or Painting, as I have said elsewhere. For it does with sounds or the articulated voice what the Poet does with verses, the Actor with gestures, and the Painter with light, shadow, and colors. Let us now see the diversity of Airs and Songs, and particularly those used in France, so that the Musician remains ignorant of nothing belonging to <term>Harmony</term><note>In this period, "Harmony" often referred to the overall pleasing arrangement of sounds and proportions rather than just chord progressions</note>. And afterwards, we shall see what is necessary to make beautiful Airs, and if it is possible to make one that is the most beautiful of all those that can be made on any subject, or without a subject. Nevertheless, before numbering the diverse species of Songs used now, we must propose a difficulty which will perhaps give us a new definition of Song: namely, when, and at what moment, sound or the voice begins to be song. This seems very difficult to determine, for the beginning of natural things is ordinarily imperceptible; nevertheless, song, having something artificial about it, will perhaps have a beginning easier to recognize than if it were simply natural.

### PROPOSITION III.

->*Determining at what moment sound begins to be Song, and when*<-
->*it can be called Air, or Song.*<-

If it is very difficult to notice the beginning of movement and of time, and consequently that of sound (which is nothing other than a movement), it is, it seems, no less difficult to determine when sound begins to be Song. For if all the parts of a Song are homogeneous—that is to say, of the same nature, like those of sound and air—one must conclude that every perceptible part of the sound contains the nature of the Song, and that it can be called an *Air*.

Many hold that every part of Music is a Song, and yet there are parts that always hold steady on the same tone, without rising or falling, as sometimes happens to the <term>Taille</term><note>The "Taille" was the traditional French term for the tenor voice or the middle part in a polyphonic composition</note>. And among the Songs used to sing the <term>Psalms</term><note>The 150 sacred hymns from the Bible, which formed the core of daily liturgical singing</note> in Catholic Churches, one of the <term>intonations</term><note>The opening formula or the melodic recitation tone used in plainchant</note> does not use intervals at all; yet no one would say that one is not singing when using this tone.

And when one uses this intonation, one says just as much that they are beginning to sing as when they use Tones that vary their intervals. The difficulty consists then in two points: namely, whether sound that neither rises nor falls can be called, and is in effect, a song; and whether every part of this sound is Song.

# Book One

...or what duration of time the sound must last to be considered a song.

If we wish to provide some distinctions or divisions between songs, it seems that we can reconcile all the thoughts of Musicians regarding this difficulty: For if we say that a sound—against which one or several parts can be sung to create <term>consonances</term><note>Musical intervals that are pleasing and stable to the ear, such as thirds, fifths, and octaves</note> and harmony—is a song, then one can maintain that a simple sound held steady is one. Consequently, the discourse of Orators and of those who use perceptible intervals, such as the Italians and some Preachers who sing while speaking, can be called songs, provided that one can compose some part of Music against the said sounds or speech. But if we speak of a **perfect song**, it requires changes in pitch and different intervals, as do the <term>Diatonic</term><note>The standard musical scale consisting of seven notes (whole steps and half steps)</note> scales, and certain parts that are not homogeneous and of the same nature, such as the different parts of water and air; because the beginning must be different from the middle, and the end must be different from both.

As for the duration of the song, Musicians have not yet established anything regarding this difficulty: there are long ones, short ones, and mediocre ones. One can say almost the same thing of songs as of verses, for there is no verse that cannot have a song; and if the verse is useless and imperfect, such as those lacking one or several feet, one can call their song *imperfect*.

Nevertheless, one can say that a song must last at least two or three measures to be accomplished and perfect, so that it has its beginning, its middle, and its end; for these three parts are almost always found in all things, particularly in those bound and obliged to movement, as are the songs of which we speak.

But I shall later treat more fully the parts of the song, and say whether it is possible to find rules that serve to create beautiful songs, such that by following them, one cannot fail in judgment or composition. Let us now see how many species of songs are used in France; for as for those of the ancients, both Greeks and Latins, they have left us so little knowledge of them that we cannot speak of them with certainty. And foreign nations have none that we do not imitate quite successfully, and—if I may be permitted to speak to our advantage—that we do not surpass in some regard, particularly in the refinement, the delicacy, and the sweetness with which they are performed; for as for the clarity, the quality, or the strength of the voice, the Italians can dispute these with all other nations, added to which they have many beautiful traits and a quantity of inventions of which our songs are destitute.

### PROPOSITION IV.

*To explain all the divisions and species of Songs and Airs used by Musicians, and to provide examples of Ecclesiastical songs.*

## Second Book

Now, the four melodies that serve the four verses of the Psalms are in use among the Priests of the Oratory <note>The Congregation of the Oratory, founded in France in 1611, known for their musical devotion and the development of the oratorio</note>, who sing them with great devotion; and the last one is commonly used in the prisons of Paris. One could divide all the church chants into Lessons, Verses, Responsories, Antiphons, Psalms, Canticles, Hymns, Sequences, and Masses. Cerone <note>Pedro Cerone (1566–1625), an Italian priest and music theorist who wrote a massive treatise on musical practice</note> reports on a great many of these in his third, fourth, and fifth books; many are also found in the works of Glarean <note>Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563), a Swiss theorist who expanded the system of musical modes</note> and Franchin <note>Franchinus Gaffurius (1451–1522), a leading Italian music theorist of the Renaissance</note>, so there is no need to burden this treatise with them.

This is why I do not include here the ordinary tones of Gregorian chant; furthermore, I have already provided them in the 29th proposition of the second book of *Music*, printed in the year 1627. At the end of that work, I also included twelve melodies in two parts based on the twelve modes; and at the end of the second book, I placed a figured song <note>A composition using complex rhythms and counterpoint, as opposed to simple plainchant</note> in two parts in the first mode, and another in the second, and finally another spiritual air in four parts. One will also find examples of the twelve tones of the church chants at the end of the sixth Latin book, which treats genres and modes. I will only add that the 5th, 6th, and 12th modes seem to me the most beautiful; however, everyone may choose whichever pleases them most for their own personal consolation, and one may even create as many new ones as they wish.

Indeed, it is certain that when one sings various church chants with the required attention and devotion, one will receive great contentment, for there are some that are very beautiful. For example, the Hymns: *Come, Holy Spirit, Creator* <note>original: "Veni creator spiritus"</note>, *At this sacred solemnity* <note>original: "Sacris solemnijs"</note>, *Sing, my tongue, the mystery of the glorious body* <note>original: "Pange lingua gloriosi corporis mysterium"</note>, *Bountiful Creator of the stars* <note>original: "Conditor alme syderum"</note>, *For the merits of the Saints* <note>original: "Sanctorum meritis"</note>, *Hail, star of the sea* <note>original: "Aue maris stella"</note>, and several others. The same will happen when singing the Sequences <note>Hymns or chants used in the Mass after the Alleluia</note> *Praises to the Paschal Victim* <note>original: "Victimæ Paschali laudes"</note>, *Sion, praise the Savior* <note>original: "Lauda Sion Saluatorem"</note>, and the Antiphons *Unviolated* <note>original: "Inuiolata"</note>, *Hail, Queen* <note>original: "Salue regina"</note>, *Queen of Heaven* <note>original: "Regina cæli"</note>, etc., which are used in Catholic churches. But since they are found in the Rituals, it is not appropriate to include them here. Nevertheless, I advise those who love church chants to make use of the *Hours of the Virgin* <note>A private devotional book containing prayers and psalms for various times of the day</note> which was printed by Cavellat in the year 1598, for it contains the chants for everything sung throughout the year in the Church of Paris. Namely, all the Antiphons, all the Hymns, the Psalms, the 8 tones, several Sequences, and entire Masses with the *Glory to God in the highest* <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis"</note>, the *Creed* <note>original: "Credo"</note>, and many other chants that are very beautiful. Thus, I am surprised that these *Hours*, which ought to be in the hands of so many people, are so rare, and that they are not being reprinted.

I shall provide several other sorts of melodies when I speak of Dances, and Ballets, and of all the species of songs used in France. One may also see all those I have given in the 13th article of the 57th question on Genesis. One can also relate all the melodies that Goudimel <note>Claude Goudimel (c. 1514–1572), a French composer famous for his four-part settings of the Genevan Psalter</note>, Claude Le Jeune <note>c. 1528–1600, a master of French Renaissance music known for his 'musique mesurée'</note>, du Caurroy <note>Eustache du Caurroy (1549–1609), a composer for the French royal court</note>, Caignet <note>Denis Caignet (d. 1625), a composer noted for his settings of the psalms</note>, and others have given to the Psalms set in French verse, and all the spiritual songs set to ecclesiastical chants. These serve to lift the spirit toward the contemplation of divine things, and consequently, they follow the goal and purpose of the Church. Finally, one can see the music for all the Motets <note>A complex vocal composition, usually on a sacred text, often featuring multiple independent voices</note> that have been printed since the beginning of singing in several parts.

# On Songs.

### PROPOSITION V.

->*Whether one can find and prescribe infallible rules and maxims according to which one may create good songs for all sorts of lyrics and subjects, and whether musicians possess such rules when they compose airs and songs.*<-

This difficulty is one of the greatest in all of Music. Since no one has yet established certain rules specifically for creating beautiful melodies for every kind of subject, it is a sign that they cannot be established. For it does not seem probable that the musicians who have lived through such a long succession of years and centuries would not have established them—both to use them when needed and to share them with their successors—just as they have done with the other precepts of this Art.

Indeed, the most excellent Masters prove every day by experience that they have no guaranteed rules for creating good songs, as they most often encounter them only by whim <note>The original term is "boutades," referring to sudden, impulsive bursts of creativity or fits of inspiration.</note> and by chance, as they themselves confess. This is why they sometimes spend entire days without being able to create an air or a melody that pleases them or satisfies them; and at other times they create several in a short time, which are born in their minds according to the different dispositions of their imagination and their health.

Now, if they had certain rules, they could create such songs as they wished at any hour or occasion, just as Architects can create the design of a building and Mathematicians can create demonstrations, drawing straight and curved lines of all kinds at any time because they have certain and infallible rules. The manner in which Composers work confirms this truth: they "feel out" several kinds of tones and chords on the Lute, the Spinet, the Viol, or other Instruments to find a melody that pleases them; or else they flip through the pages of Claudin, Guédron <note>Claudin de Sermisy (c. 1490–1562) and Pierre Guédron (c. 1570–1620) were famous French composers; the author suggests that even "masters" often relied on past models or "musical collage" rather than pure theory.</note>, and other Masters to take certain parts of a song from one place and other parts from elsewhere, in order to gather these fragments and make an entire song from them. Now, if they had certain rules, they would use them without taking bits and pieces from here and there, which they sometimes do without much reason or judgment.

But I wish to bring forth more powerful reasons. One is taken from the little knowledge we have of the nature of the Harmonic intervals which must be used to create songs. The other is taken from our ignorance of movements <note>In this context, "movements" refers to rhythm, tempo, and the physical motion of sound.</note>, of which we know neither the theory nor the practice; for we have no Musicians who can establish the sequence of movements necessary to arouse the listeners to whatever passion one desires.

To this, one may add the knowledge of things necessary for the perfect Musician (of which I have spoken elsewhere), such as the temperament of the listeners, and that of the spirits <note>In 17th-century thought, "spirits" (animal spirits) were subtle fluids in the body believed to mediate between the soul and the physical senses.</note>, and the manner which must be used to heat or cool the imagination and the appetite in order to calm or excite the passions. Furthermore, the multitude of Airs extends to infinity, and the quality of songs most often depends on the whim of the Composer and those who make them popular; this prevents us from prescribing infallible rules if

Second Book

...if one does not wish to understand and confine the infinity of human imagination and caprice within the limits of a few maxims that would make a finite thing out of the infinite.

One must nevertheless admit that certain rules can be found so reliably that one will never fail to create good songs on all sorts of subjects, provided that one understands the text; for if a French Musician who understands only his own language wished to set Spanish or Italian to Music, he would not be able to suit the note to the letter <note>original: "accommoder la note à la lettre"; this refers to the practice of prosody, ensuring the musical rhythm and accentuation match the natural flow of the spoken word.</note>. I admit that it is difficult to find and practice the rules of which we speak, especially since they require a perfect knowledge of the nature of sounds, of their intervals, and of the passions and affections <note>In the 17th century, "passions and affections" referred to specific emotional states—such as joy, anger, or mourning—that music was scientifically intended to provoke or soothe in the listener.</note> that one desires to excite or appease. But perhaps this knowledge is not impossible, whether the ancients possessed it—as held by those who believe that Aristotle, Plutarch, and other Authors propose nothing regarding the types and effects of Music that is not true, and who say that the Greeks had knowledge of the temperament of the listeners, of the nature of the passions, and of intervals; or whether the said ancients had no more knowledge than we do, or rather that they knew less about Music than the Masters who compose now, and who teach the practice and theory of Harmony, as many believe, who do not defer as much to the ancients as others do. For since the invention of rules for making good songs depends on reason, judgment, and experience, we would have to be deprived of these faculties and instruments if we could establish nothing except by borrowing from the ancients; I do not wish to speak further of them here, especially since I have written a specific discourse to examine whether they were more learned than we are in Music, and if they made better Songs and better Concerts.

Now, what makes me believe that one can establish rules for songs is that the Masters have already established some, which they use successfully, and that it is no more difficult to invent these rules than those of Medicine and Architecture, which are certain enough for the use of life. And when one has worked as seriously toward the perfection of Music as toward that of the other Arts, and when such a great multitude of learned and judicious men have employed their labor in the search for everything belonging to Music—as have those who taught us Geometry and the other sciences—I believe that one may hope for certain rules for making good songs.

As for the contrary reasons, it is easy to answer them if one assumes what I have said, especially since they are based on the fact that we do not have enough knowledge, or that those who have enough do not wish to employ it in Music; but they do not prove that we cannot have a great enough knowledge to make certain and infallible rules for good songs.

### On Melodies.

...excellent in Music: for as for the composition of two or several parts <note>This refers to polyphony or counterpoint—adding harmony to a base melody.</note>, one finds enough people who succeed at it, but one finds none, or at least very few, who create good melodies on every subject proposed to them. And if one asks why it is more difficult to create a good melody than to add parts to a melody already made, and to compose for two or several parts, I respond that one must be more learned to create good melodies than to compose for several parts, as one can easily conclude from the discourse that follows.

I say, then, firstly, that it is an infallible rule for melodies that one must follow and imitate the movement of the <term>passion</term> <note>In this period, "passions" were seen as physical and emotional states—like joy, sorrow, or anger—that music could scientifically trigger through specific rhythms and intervals.</note> which one wishes to excite in the listeners; for example, if one wishes to excite to war or to anger, one must use <term>Iambic</term> or <term>Anapestic</term> movement <note>These are rhythmic meters borrowed from ancient Greek and Latin poetry. An Iamb is a short beat followed by a long one; an Anapest is two shorts followed by a long.</note>. Here it must be noted that I begin the rules with the movement that must be given to melodies, of which one can say what the Orator said of delivery <note>original: "prononciation"; likely a reference to Demosthenes, who claimed that delivery was the most important part of oratory.</note> (or the reciting of harangues), and another said of humility for the Christian virtues, and Saint Paul of Charity compared to the theological virtues <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:13: "And now abide faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity."</note>—namely, that just as these virtues are the principal ones and the most difficult to acquire, likewise the movement of songs is the principal part of the melody. It is that which has more energy and force upon the listener than all other things that make up and accompany the song; so that he who knows how to give the true movements knows the best part of Music, and the most necessary rule of all those used to make melodies. But this is not the place to speak of these movements, since they belong to the book on Rhythm.

The second rule belongs to the <term>intervals</term> and <term>degrees</term> <note>Intervals are the distances between notes; degrees are the individual steps of a scale.</note> which must be used in songs, which is similarly necessary, for it consists in using the same intervals or degrees used by the passion one wishes to excite. For example, if anger rises by whole tones or semitones, the melody must rise by those same degrees, although this is not so necessary that one cannot use other degrees in singing than those of the passion, particularly when one does not know by which degrees it proceeds. Now, it is certain that melodies were invented to excite the passions; for example, to rejoice the listener, for rejoicing belongs to the passions, of which it is the foundation, the beginning, and the end—for pleasure is nothing other than a perfect and accomplished love, just as love and desire are a pleasure begun and imperfect.

I do not believe that other rules are needed to make good melodies on all sorts of subjects, for the sequence of degrees and intervals of sounds that compose the melody, and the knowledge of the <term>mode</term> <note>Musical modes were traditional scales (like Dorian or Phrygian) thought to possess specific emotional characters.</note> that must be used, are comprised in the second rule; and all sorts of verse and movements are contained in the first. As for the quality of the voice and pronunciation, these do not belong to the rules of melodies, but to the method and manner of singing, and to the Singer, of whom we shall speak elsewhere.

As for the relationship of sounds that compose the melody, such as that of the <term>Tritone</term> and the <term>false fifth</term> <note>Both the Tritone and the false (diminished) fifth were traditionally considered dissonant and "unstable" intervals, often avoided in simple melodies.</note>, which are almost the only bad relationships in both <term>plainchant</term> <note>Traditional, unaccompanied church music (Gregorian chant).</note> and in Music (although these intervals and all others may enter into solo recitals when the subject requires it), these must be discussed in the book on Composition.

## Book Second

It must only be remarked here that melodies are like the nuances of colors, which follow one another in such a way that one does not pass from one extremity to the other without passing through the middle. This is why one can learn to create good melodies by considering these nuances; for just as we have seven intervals, or eight sounds, in the span of the <term>Octave</term> <note>The standard interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</note> which we are accustomed to using, in the same way, we usually take seven or eight colors for each nuance. This is experienced in the nuances of purple, blue, and the green of a tulip or a lemon; so that one can compare each melody to each nuance, unless one wishes to relate all the melodies of one of the genres of Music to a single type of nuance: for example, the melodies used in our <term>Diatonic</term> <note>The standard musical scale consisting of seven notes (the "white keys" on a piano).</note> to the nuance of green, and those of other types of the <term>Diatonic</term> genre to other kinds of nuances.

Now, one could choose the eight principal types of nuances—namely the three kinds of greens, and the nuances of blue, yellow, red, <term>columbine</term> <note>A violet-blue or dove-colored shade, named after the columbine flower.</note>, and purple—to compare them to the eight species of the <term>Diatonic</term>. This is unless one prefers to divide all nuances, like all types of Music, into three genres: namely the nuances of green, yellow, and red, each of which will contain several others, just as each genre of Music contains several species.

To this one may add that if one creates melodies of twelve degrees within the <term>Octave</term> by dividing it by semitones, one similarly has nuances of twelve colors, such as that of red; and that a nuance can have as many colors as the Octave has sounds or intervals, for both can be divided into an infinity of degrees.

Indeed, if it is permitted to learn through the analogy of other things, one can compare simple sounds to simple colors, the intervals of sounds to the mixtures of said colors, and melodies to paintings. For just as Painters, Dyers, and Florists notice that there are simple and primary colors from which others are composed, so too Musicians consider that some sounds are simpler than others. This can be said of the <term>proslambanomene</term> <note>In ancient Greek music theory, this was the "added note," the lowest note of the musical system.</note>, because the beats or movements of air of which it is composed are closer to unity and to rest, from which the <term>nete</term> <note>The highest-pitched note in the ancient Greek musical system.</note> is the most distant. Thus, the middle sounds are composed of these two extremes, because they participate in the slowness and heaviness of the one, and the speed of the other, just as middle colors participate in the two extremes—namely white and black—from which one can imagine that the two primary colors of Painters, that is to say, blue and yellow, are composed, and from which all kinds of green are afterward made.

One can therefore say that the <term>proslambanomene</term> corresponds to yellow, which some believe to be the proper color of the earth, because they say it is always of this color when it is in its purity. They confirm this by the color from which Adam was created, which was a yellow clay, following the etymology of the Hebrew word <note>The Hebrew name "Adam" is related to "Adamah" (earth/ground); while traditionally associated with "red" clay, the author here identifies it as yellow.</note>; by the marrow of all trees which easily takes this color; by the leaves of trees and herbs, and by the flowers of tulips which become yellow after having lost their green; and by other colors which are made of yellow (which always remains, by reason of its salt and its earthiness) and of blue, which evaporates and flies away, as if it were returning toward the heaven which seems to be its origin.

### Of Melodies.

origin, because it depends on its light; this is why they say that this color is similar to the <term>Nete</term> <note>original: "Nete"; the highest note in the ancient Greek musical system, associated with fire and the swiftest celestial spheres.</note>, whose quick and light movement imitates the rapidity of the heavens. For the more one removes movement from the middle sounds, the more one approaches the silence of the <term>proslambanomene</term> <note>original: "proslambanomene"; the lowest note of the ancient Greek scale, literally the "added note," which the author compares to the stillness of the earth.</note>, to which the earth is compared.

From this, one can conclude that the <term>Mese</term> <note>original: "Mese"; the central or "middle" note of the Greek scale, serving as the fundamental reference point for other notes.</note> is the most pleasant sound of all, since it participates equally in heaven and earth, just as fresh green does, which is composed of equal parts of blue and yellow. But if one compares musical intervals to two colors, one can consider whether blue or yellow, when compared with green, produces as good an effect as the <term>proslambanomene</term> or the <term>Nete</term> compared to the <term>Mese</term>, with which they form the <term>Octave</term>. And if one compares melodies to the nuances of colors, one can calculate how many kinds of colors must be used from blue or yellow up to the said green to pass there imperceptibly, or as agreeably as possible; and what proportion exists between these approaching colors, in order to notice if the passages one makes from the <term>proslambanomene</term> or the <term>Nete</term> to the <term>Mese</term> must be filled with as many intervals, and have ratios equal to the said colors, in order to create the most beautiful melody possible and to sing it perfectly.

For it appears that nature always follows the same path in its works, and that the melody which imitates it must be esteemed the most perfect, whether the ear consents to it or not, since reason is the mistress, and consequently she is more believable.

One can therefore examine through how many colors one must shade yellow or blue when one wishes to pass to bright green, or from the said green to yellow and blue, or from one of these to the other, and create as many intervals from the low sound to that of the middle, and from the middle to the high, in order to see if the melody conducted by these nuances will be the best of all.

And because we love the diversity of melodies, like that of paintings (by reason of the state of change in which we live, subjected to its vanity despite ourselves), when we diversify melodies and leave the preceding nuance to pass to distant colors or to separate and disjointed sounds, the sound or the color must have an analogy and a suitability with the others to which we pass. And because we make leaps of the <term>Octave</term>, the <term>Fifth</term>, the <term>Fourth</term>, <term>Thirds</term>, and <term>Sixths</term>, we must look at the transitions of colors that respond to these passages, to know if their pleasing quality is similar, and if what is found beautiful in the sequence of sounds has an equal beauty in the sequence and connection of colors.

One can go even further and see if there is something in Music that responds to light, which contains all colors in eminence and perfection, although it seems to hold more of yellow; from this comes the fact that it is called **golden**, and that the most precious thing is explained to us under the name of a gold that will be transparent like glass in the 21st chapter of the Apocalypse <note>Referencing Revelation 21:18: "and the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass."</note>—that is to say, it will be similar in color to amber, and to crystal in transparency, in order to have the most excellent qualities of all bodies.

Now, there is nothing in Music more similar to light than the high-pitched sound, because it comprises all the others that come from its division or its diminution until it returns to silence; for if it loses a 24th part of its movement, it makes the <term>minor semitone</term>; if it loses a 15th, it makes the <term>major</term>; if a 9th...

For colors lean toward black the more they reflect a smaller quantity of rays to the eye, and they approach brilliance and light the more they reflect a greater multitude of rays. From this it follows that when all the rays from a flat or concave mirror strike the eye, one sees nothing but the luminous body itself—namely the sun or a candle—for light wishes to convert everything into itself. It seems to have no other purpose regarding us than to fill the whole world and to represent itself in all bodies; indeed, these bodies would represent nothing other than the sun if they were perfectly polished. Because light acts naturally, when it cannot perfectly represent the image of the sun due to the inequalities of the bodies receiving it, it represents colors. These colors might be called "disfigured and confused suns," which dull its beauty and vibrancy by breaking and diminishing the strength of its rays.

This will happen when all things are perfectly subject to Him, as it says in the same passage. It should also be noted that there are several colors that can be shaded, just as there are several genres and species of Music; one can compare the degrees of each species of Music with the shading of each color. For example, the shading of green, yellow, and red can be compared with the degrees of the <term>Diatonic</term>, <term>Chromatic</term>, and <term>Enharmonic</term> genres <note>These are the three types of scales used in ancient Greek music, varying in the size of their intervals.</note>. Songs can end with the lowest or the highest voice, just as the shading of each color ends on one side with black—representing shadow, darkness, and silence—and on the other side with white—representing the brilliance of color, light, and the speed of high-pitched sounds.

Furthermore, the middle sound that the Greeks call the <term>Mese</term> <note>original: "Mese"; the central note of the scale.</note> represents the color that is being shaded. Just as one normally uses seven colors in each shading, one likewise uses seven intervals or degrees in each Octave, of which there are 2, 3, or 4 above, and three or four below the said <term>Mese</term>. I say 3 or 4 above or below because there are 4 below when the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Quinte"; an interval of five scale degrees.</note> is below, and 3 when it is above; this is what musicians call <term>Harmonic division</term>. This is why one should see if the shading of a color is more pleasing when there are more degrees of shading below toward black, than above toward white.

But it is impossible, or very difficult, to encounter this perfection. Nature itself, which is guided and governed by the sovereign Author, has perhaps not yet shown the most beautiful face, or the most beautiful body of all possible ones (unless it be that of Adam, our Lord, or the Virgin), no more than the smallest or largest man.

Physicians have not yet encountered the perfect temperament *by weight* <note>The Latin term *ad pondus* refers to an absolute, perfect balance of the four bodily humors.</note>, nor perfect health; and no one can boast of having written the most excellent treatise, or the most excellent book of all those that can be made on the same subject. And if we look at all of nature, and all the artisans, we will find that there is no accomplished perfection in everything they do, there being always something to be desired: which shows us clearly that there is only God alone who is perfect, and who can act, and produce all that pleases Him with all sorts of perfections. This does not prevent us, nonetheless, from seeking whether it is possible to compose or to sing the most beautiful Song, or the most beautiful Air of all those that can be desired, so that we omit nothing from everything that can serve this treatise on Music.

Now one can consider the Song or the Air in two ways: first in its composition, and then after its composition, which can be made in so many ways (as is apparent by the great number of songs encountered in the range of a double, triple, and quadruple Octave, even if one does not speak of the various movements, or the different measures) that it is almost incredible, and it seems to be impossible that a man could compose all the Airs that are found in the number of sounds used ordinarily in songs, even if he composed for the space of a hundred years without ceasing. It would therefore be by chance if he encountered the most beautiful song of all those that can be made, and he could not know if it were the most excellent, since the knowledge of a thing that comes in comparison with others cannot be acquired except by comparing it with those related to it.

Having established that absolute perfection is a divine attribute and that human art often falls short of its own ideals, the author now applies this logic to the specific arts of poetry, rhetoric, and music, arguing that the "perfect" song requires a harmony between the rules of art, the quality of the performer, and the suitability of the subject matter.</meta>

# On Songs

To judge the most perfect and accomplished verse in the books of Homer, Pindar, Anacreon, or Virgil, one must read all their works and compare every verse with one another; for even if one should encounter the most beautiful verse upon first opening the book, it cannot truly be known as such since it has not been compared to all the others. The same can be said of the most excellent of all airs <note>The term 'air' refers to a song, melody, or a specific musical composition for the voice.</note>: even though one might compose a song according to the musical precepts given by the best Masters, and find an air that exactly follows all the rules of Art—judging it the most perfect in its composition—it may not actually be perceived as such after it is composed. This can be explained by an example drawn from eloquence. Suppose one asks if a man can craft a speech or an oration that possesses every part of eloquence to the highest degree of perfection: to this I respond that it is entirely impossible, because one cannot attain all the various types of orations that could be made; therefore, one cannot choose the one that, among all these variations, should be held as the most perfect and accomplished. Nevertheless, regarding the precepts of Rhetoric given by the greatest Orators, a man can observe all the rules of Rhetoric and compose a speech which, according to the rules of Art, should be considered the most perfect, even if it does not seem the most pleasing to the ear, nor the most persuasive.

Likewise, though an air may be the most accomplished of all those that can be made according to the rules of Art, if it is considered outside of its composition—as something sung or heard and received by the sense of the ear—it will not seem as excellent as it truly is unless the voice of the singer and the ear of the listener are perfectly disposed, being the most excellent that can be imagined. For we know by experience that good airs sung by bad voices are not as pleasing as those that are much less excellent when they are sung by good voices.

One must also consider the subject of the song; for if the air is tied to some subject matter, whether prose or verse, it will be more pleasing than if it were separated from any kind of subject. This is because the judgment of hearing takes place in the common sense <term>In traditional philosophy, the 'common sense' (*sensus communis*) is the faculty that processes and integrates information from all five physical senses into a single perception.</term>, and not only within the folds and caverns of the ears. If the air carries nothing with it but sound, it cannot be as well-tasted by the mind as when the sound is joined to a word that has conformity and analogy with the song. This is why it often happens that airs cannot be as well-remembered when they are sung without a subject as when they have lyrics or a theme; the syllables of the words make us remember which sounds must be raised or lowered, and which beats must be long or brief. To this, one may add that the refrains and reprises of the airs are more clearly and agreeably recognized when set to lyrics, which serves greatly to make them esteemed and liked.

Now, just as an air without a subject is less perfect than an air attached to a subject, so too an air joined to a subject whose meaning has only a slight relationship to the song is less pleasing than another air whose subject's meaning is conforming and proportional. For example, if one wished to sing a warlike air to words that were dragging, soft, and faint with love, this air would not be so pleasing as if it were sung to masculine, bold, and warlike words.

# Book Two

for just as one requires a different air <note>The author puns on the word "air," which in French means both the physical breath/atmosphere and a musical melody.</note> to animate and to warm than to restrain and to cool, so too does one require different words.

Furthermore, a subject in verse makes a song more agreeable than prose, since verse strikes the common sense <note>In 17th-century psychology, the "common sense" (*sens commun*) was thought to be an internal power that unified and interpreted the data from the five physical senses.</note> more suddenly, and encloses a more acute and subtle meaning in few words, which gives a particular contentment to the common sense or the mind. For pleasure is produced in the common sense, just as a tickle is to the body, by a sudden and unforeseen movement. Indeed, I believe we must conclude that it is not in the power of a man to find the most perfect air of all, even if it were sung by the most beautiful voices in the world; for as this air must relate perfectly to the meaning of a perfect verse, and as it is not possible to find the most perfect verse of all, one cannot arrive at the perfection of the air of which we speak.

As for singing considered as heard and received by the ears of others, it is no easier to make it perfect than when it is considered in the other way; for individual temperaments, and the humors and inclinations of men being as different as there are people in the world, it is impossible to find an Air that pleases everyone equally, and to provide that sovereign degree of pleasure that one expects from a perfectly agreeable musical song. One person delights in a single voice but cannot taste the perfection of a Concert <note>A "concert" here likely refers to an ensemble of voices or instruments playing together.</note>, and another is quite the opposite: one does not value voices unless they are joined to Instruments, and another approves neither of wind Instruments, nor those that use strings.

Some delight in soft Music, others in that which is plain, strong, and massive. It is as with food, everyone has their own taste—or to put it better, as with Eloquence: one loves it plain and diffuse, the other concise and vigorous. One person delights in lyrical verse who cannot taste the heroic; hardly can two men be found who love and follow the same style. It is the same with Music, for the melancholic <note>Referring to the "four humors" theory of personality; a melancholic person was thought to be somber and analytical.</note> loves a different air than the bilious <note>The "bilious" or choleric temperament was associated with fire, passion, and energy.</note>; and even among the varieties of melancholics, one encounters various inclinations toward different airs and musical songs.

Now, I believe that all the considerations I have reported in this discourse show clearly enough that the best possible song cannot be made by our Musicians, and that they could not even judge if it were the best of all, even if they had encountered it by chance. This is why there is no need to extend ourselves further on this subject, of which we shall speak again elsewhere—such as when we examine whether one can judge which is the better of two or more proposed songs. For although one cannot make the best possible song of all—because if men had made a song in which they could desire nothing more, we could still say that God or the Angels could make it better—this does not prevent one from establishing proper rules for making good songs. Otherwise, one would have to confess that Masters of Music can only make a good song by accident and by chance, and that the ignorant could make them as well as they, which is difficult to believe. And experience does not show us songs composed by peasants that are as good as those of Guédron <note>Pierre Guédron (c. 1570–1620) was a famous French composer at the court of Henry IV and Louis XIII, known for his *airs de cour*.</note> and other Masters, whose principal exercise consists of composing songs and airs.
