<header>On Songs.</header>

## COROLLARY.

Since the beauty of melodies consists particularly in their variety, and since there are those who believe that one can no longer create songs that have not already been made, we must consider this diversity and show that all the men in the world could not have made all the melodies contained within the **Harmonic hand** <note>The "Harmonic hand" refers to the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic device used by medieval and Renaissance singers to visualize the positions of notes in the system of hexachords.</note>, or in the ordinary system and scale of music. This is true even if they had made a thousand different songs every day from the creation of the world until the present, as will be easy to conclude from the propositions that follow. In these, one will learn all the types of **combinations**, **permutations**, and several other things that are very remarkable.

## PROPOSITION VIII.

*The ordinary rule of combinations teaches how many songs can be made from whatever number of notes one wishes, provided that one always retains the same number of notes, and that one never repeats the same note two or more times.*

There is no need to explain the rule of ordinary combinations here, since I have given it in the third book of *The Truth of the Sciences*, chapter 10 <note>Mersenne refers to his own work, *La Vérité des Sciences* (1625), where he explored mathematics and music.</note>. In that book, I explained five theorems that serve to make good songs, and demonstrated how many different songs can be made, whether one uses 1, 2, 3, or 4 notes, or any other number one chooses up to 50 notes, or any other number one wishes. I have similarly written in the same chapter the 120 songs that are found in 5 different notes, namely in *ut, re, mi, fa, sol* <note>These correspond to the modern notes C, D, E, F, and G.</note>. But because most musicians cannot comprehend the number of these songs unless they see them written with the ordinary notes of their practice, I am providing all the different songs that can be made with the six notes of the **major or minor hexachord** <term>hexachord: A six-note musical scale that was the foundation of musical theory before the modern seven-note octave system became standard.</term>, that is to say, with the six notes, *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*, or *re, mi, fa, sol, la, fa*, which constitute all of **Practical Music**. 

Now, it is so easy to find the number of these songs that there is almost no need to explain the method; for one must simply write as many numbers in their natural order as there are notes one wishes to use. For example, if one wants to know how many different songs can be made with the eight sounds, or the 8 notes of the **Octave**, *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, re, mi, fa* <note>Mersenne is using a traditional solfège naming system where some names repeat across the eight-note scale.</note>, one must write 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and multiply these 8 numbers in such a way that the product of two is always multiplied by the next natural number in this manner: one times two makes two; for one must leave out the unit [1], because it does not multiply at all; and say two times three makes six; four times six makes twenty-four; five times 24 makes 120; six times 120 makes 720—namely, the number of all the songs of six notes, of which I will speak in the ninth proposition. Seven times 720 makes 5,040, and eight times 5,040 makes 40,320, which shows the number of songs contained within 8 different sounds, for example in the 8 notes of the first type of Octave. And if one wants to know the songs contained in a larger number of sounds, for example in the 22 notes of the **Twenty-second** <note>In 17th-century theory, the "twenty-second" refers to a range of three full octaves (22 notes total including the starting note).</note>, or in any other number one wishes, one must follow the same method. I will nevertheless place them here, so that they may be found without any trouble.

It is not necessary to explain all the uses of this table, especially since I have presented them in the book *The Truth of the Sciences* <note>original: *la verité des Sciences* (1625), a work where Mersenne defended mathematics and reason against skepticism.</note>. I will only add that when practical musicians do not want to believe there is such a great diversity of songs in 8, 10, or 12 notes, and they desire that one should write them all down in order to convince them by experience (which they follow rather than reason and demonstration), one must offer this challenge to them—provided they supply the paper necessary to record them. This is something one can safely promise them; for if they promise to provide the paper, and one bets against them, it is very certain they will lose. It would take many more <term>reams</term> <note>A ream is a standard bundle of paper, traditionally 500 sheets.</note> of paper to record all the melodies found in 22 notes (even if one never repeats any note twice) than would be needed to stack them one on top of the other from the earth all the way to the <term>firmament</term> <note>In the cosmology of the time, the firmament was the sphere of the fixed stars, the outermost part of the visible universe.</note>. This holds true even if each sheet of paper contained 720 different songs of 22 notes each, and each ream of paper were so pressed and beaten that it was no thicker than an inch—that is, the 12th part of a <term>Royal foot</term> <note>The *pied de Roy* (Royal foot) was a French unit of length roughly equal to 32.48 cm, slightly longer than the modern English foot.</note>. For there are only 28,862,640,000,000 inches from the center of the earth to the stars; yet the number of reams of paper required to record the aforementioned songs is a thousand times greater than this number of inches, as is demonstrated by dividing the number of songs of 22 notes—namely 1,124,000,727,777,607,680,000—by the number of songs that would be in one of these reams, namely 362,880.

### COROLLARY I.

<summary>Mersenne uses a table of factorials to demonstrate that 22 musical notes can produce over a sextillion unique melodies. He illustrates this massive scale by calculating that the paper needed to write them down would form a stack reaching far beyond the stars.</summary>

<header>On the Voice.</header>

### COROLLARY I.

It is not, therefore, the place of the Practitioners <note>Performing musicians who rely on their ears and fingers rather than mathematical theory.</note> to demand experimental or practical proof of what the Theorists and reason teach them, since they do not even have the means to provide for the cost of the paper. For even if the revenue and wealth of all the Masters of Music in the whole world—and even of all the Princes and all the Kings—were employed for this purpose, one would not collect as much money as would be needed to buy the <term>reams</term> <note>A ream is a bundle of paper, usually 500 sheets.</note> of paper required to write down these songs. This remains true even if the poorest among them had twenty thousand <term>crowns</term> <note>Original: *écus*. A high-value gold or silver coin used in 17th-century France.</note> in annual income, as is easy to demonstrate by the number of said reams and the cost, which amounts to more millions in gold than have ever existed in the world. This clearly shows that the mind is far more excellent, and has a much greater capacity, than the senses; and that it is made in the image of God, since it reaches so far that only the infinite itself can bound it. Consequently, Musicians must raise their thoughts higher than their Art, if they wish to show that they are made in the image of God, and that they carry the mark of divinity in their souls and in their minds.

### COROLLARY II.

Since we will require the Combination <note>In this context, "combination" refers to what modern mathematicians call permutations—the different ways a set of items can be ordered.</note> of a number of things greater than 22 in our future discourses, and as it has already been necessary for the difficulties addressed in the book on the Voice, I set it down here from 23 up to 64, so that this book assumes no outside knowledge, and so that it may serve a thousand uses that one may draw from it.

### PROPOSITION IX.

->*Determine how many Songs or different Airs can be made with six sounds, or six notes, by always taking the same notes and keeping the same rhythm; for example, with these six notes: Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la <note>These are the syllables of the hexachord, the precursor to our modern Do-Re-Mi-Fa-Sol-La.</note>, or with Re, mi, fa, sol, la, fa, or with Mi, fa, sol, re, mi, fa, or with Fa, sol, re, mi, fa, sol.*<-

This proposition is one of the most useful and most admirable in Music, insofar as it teaches us to do as much as the Angels, and to know everything that can enter the mind; for it is not possible to create a greater number of songs in all of Music (whether one uses the voice or instruments) than that which I will provide in this proposition and in those that follow. I take here an example to demonstrate what I have just said, in which one sees all the songs that can be made from six notes, where each is of the same value <note>Meaning each note has the same rhythmic duration.</note> and will always hold the same place on the <term>musical hand</term> <note>The "Guidonian Hand," a mnemonic device used by singers to keep track of pitches and hexachords.</note>, and consequently will represent the same string.

He who demonstrates which is the most excellent and the most agreeable of these 720 songs <note>720 is the result of 6 factorial (6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1), the number of ways to arrange six unique items.</note>, and the order each should hold according to their sweetness and goodness, will teach that which is unknown and bring new light to Harmony. And if rules are given to discern the temperament, the natural inclination, or the passions of each person by the song that pleases them most, we shall advance even further; but both are to be desired rather than expected: although I report many things in the 21st proposition of this book which will perhaps serve gifted minds in giving us some light on this subject.

Now these varieties can serve to make 720 <term>Anagrams</term> for every word of 6 different letters, and to change the order of 6 soldiers or 6 other things 720 times: for example, one will find all the varieties or Anagrams of these 3 names of 6 different letters—*Jacques*, *Matieu*, *Iulian*—by placing their 6 letters upon the 6 notes or syllables of the <term>Hexachord</term>; which will happen simi-

| :--- |

| M a t i e u, |
| J u l i a n, |
| 1 2 3 4 5 6, |
</insert> larly to 6 numbers, as one sees here: which can be done without much trouble and without confusion.

As for the method of combining and finding all the varieties of any proposed number of things, I have treated it in the book on the varieties of the Octave, which makes 40,320 entirely different songs, and in the 5th proposition of the 7th Latin book of Songs <note>Mersenne refers to his own *Harmonicorum libri* (1636).</note>; that is why I do not repeat it here. I also leave aside the manner of finding how many songs in this Hexachord have a Sixth, one or two Fifths, one, two, or three Fourths, etc., because it will be found in...

# Of Songs.

...will be found in the volume of the 8 Notes, in which one will likewise see the usefulness of combinations. And because many do not know the name and the value of notes, I first present the 720 variations of the major Hexachord <term>Hexachord: A six-note scale (Ut-Re-Mi-Fa-Sol-La) that was the foundation of musical education and sight-singing in the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</term> *Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la* <note>Ut is the historical name for the note "Do."</note>, for those who know how to read, or who can sing by seeing these 6 syllables, so that nothing more can be desired on this subject: and then I will provide the same variations with the ordinary notes used in Practice <note>Meaning standard musical notation on a staff, rather than just the names of the syllables.</note>, and other types of variations, along with several difficulties that depend on them.

The 7th proposition of the same Latin book <note>Referring to Mersenne's *Harmonicorum libri*.</note> contains all the different songs of the three species of the Fourth <term>Fourth: An interval spanning four notes; also called a Tetrachord.</term>, namely 72: and the 10th chapter of the 3rd book of *The Truth of the Sciences* <note>Referring to Mersenne's 1625 work *La Vérité des sciences contre les septiques ou pyrrhoniens*.</note> gives the 120 songs of the first species of the Fifth <term>Fifth: An interval spanning five notes; Mersenne uses the Greek-derived term "Diapente."</term> *Ut, re, mi, fa, sol.* But the variety of the Hexachord includes both these kinds of variations, just as a greater number always contains the lesser, and as the Hexachord contains the Tetrachord and the Pentachord <note>A five-note scale sequence.</note>; so that it is in no way necessary to put the songs of 4 or 5 notes here, since we have those of the six notes of the first species of the major Sixth, in place of which it is easy to write those of the Sixth that begins with RE, with MI, or with FA.

Now, it is certain that the melodies of this <term>Hexachord</term> <note>A six-note scale (Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La) used as the foundation for musical composition and sight-singing in this period.</note> that contain the interval of the <term>Major Sixth</term>, whether ascending or descending—that is to say, <term>Ut to La</term> or <term>La to Ut</term>—are not good, and that practitioners reject them. This is partly because the interval is too difficult to sing accurately, and partly because it is disagreeable and offends the ear. It is difficult to find the true reason for this, given that the interval of the Octave is permitted and pleasant even though it is larger. Furthermore, the ratio of these two sounds, <term>Ut to La</term>, is easier to comprehend than that of the <term>Minor Sixth</term>, which is very pleasing (particularly when ascending). For the ratio of the minor sixth is 8 to 5, while that of the major is 5 to 3. The latter is the first of the <term>superpartient</term> <note>original: "surpartissantes"; a class of ratios where the larger number contains the smaller number plus two or more parts of it (e.g., 5:3 contains 3 once plus 2/3).</note> ratios, just as the <term>Sesquialtera</term> <note>The ratio 3:2, which produces a perfect fifth.</note> of 3 to 2 is the first of the <term>superparticular</term> <note>original: "surparticulieres"; ratios where the larger number is exactly one unit greater than the smaller (e.g., 3:2, 4:3).</note> ratios. Now, it is easier to understand the <term>superbipartient</term> <note>original: "surbipartissante"; specifically the 5:3 ratio.</note> ratio of 5 to 3 than the <term>supertripartient</term> <note>original: "surtripartissante"; specifically the 8:5 ratio.</note> ratio of 8 to 5.

From this, one may easily conclude that the sweetness, goodness, and pleasantness of <term>consonances</term> <note>Combinations of notes that sound harmonious and stable to the ear.</note> do not depend solely on the mental comprehension or the mathematical primacy of their ratios. Instead, one must seek the cause in the relation and rapport that all intervals have to the Octave, or to its repetitions. In this way, it is similar to the <term>final cause</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "purpose" or "end goal" for which something exists or is done.</note> in Ethics, upon which the goodness of actions depends so much that they are better the closer they approach it, or the better they represent it, or the more noble their relations and habits are. 

However, it is not easy to show that the <term>Minor Sixth</term> represents the Octave better or has a greater connection with it than the Major Sixth, unless one supposes what I noted in the fourth book on Stringed Instruments: namely, that one hears several sounds within every single sound, though many ears do not perceive them—particularly that one hears the Octave above. Thus, when the two sounds of the Major Sixth are heard, the lower sound represents its Octave above (which is 6, for I assume the smaller number in the ratio represents the lower sound of the consonance, as I demonstrated in the book on Consonances and Instruments). Consequently, 3 is the lower sound of the Major Sixth. It follows that this sound produces another at the Octave above, namely 6; thus, one hears these three sounds—3, 5, and 6—without knowing it. In this case, the interval of this Sixth represents a <term>Minor Third</term> (the ratio of 5 to 6) to the mind. In contrast, the Minor Sixth represents a <term>Major Third</term> to the mind: for the 5 produces its octave 10, following which the interval of the <term>Minor Sixth</term> creates these three terms—5, 8, and 10. Since 8 is to 10 as 4 is to 5 (which is the ratio of the <term>Ditone</term> <note>A Major Third.</note>), one can say that the interval of the Minor Sixth is better than the Major Sixth in the same way that the <term>Ditone</term> is sweeter than the <term>Sesquiditone</term> <note>A Minor Third.</note>.

It is certain that one can imagine many objections against this discourse, and that it will not satisfy everyone, but everyone is free to invent better reasons and to consult the most excellent minds both on this subject and on all those in this work. As for the other intervals of the 720 melodies, they are all

# Second Book

good, which is why I do not dwell on it; I only add that there are 240 songs that have the interval of the <term>Major Sixth</term> <note>The distance of nine semitones, such as from C to A.</note>, of which 120 are created by ascending from *Ut* to *La*, and 120 by descending from *La* to *Ut*; from which it follows that there are only 480 songs that are good in the preceding combination. But they would all be good in the 720 songs made from the 6 notes of the minor <term>Hexachord</term> <note>A six-note scale containing a minor third, rather than a major third.</note>, because the interval of the <term>Minor Sixth</term> <note>The distance of eight semitones, such as from E to C.</note> is permitted; this is why I explain the diversity of this Sixth by the notes that follow, which are sung thus: *Re, mi, fa, sol, la, fa*.

One can also begin this Sixth with *Mi*, and if one wishes for the <term>Triton</term> <note>An interval of three whole tones, known as the "augmented fourth." Historically it was considered difficult to sing and was often avoided in strict counterpoint.</note> to be encountered therein, one must begin with *Fa* on the key of *F ut* <note>original: "clef de F ut" — a reference to the F-clef in the Guidonian system of solmization</note>, so that the keys placed at the beginning create 2160 songs with 6 notes; although they are no longer the same, strictly speaking, insofar as the keys change them and make them rise or fall; so that it is better to say that these notes contain three different examples, of which the first begins at the *Ut* of *C sol*, the second at the *D* of *D la re*, and the third at the *Mi* of *E mi la*: and if one begins at the *Fa* of *F ut fa*, one will have the 4th example, and consequently the example that follows contains 2880 entirely different songs. And if one makes these six notes serve other intervals than the ordinary ones of the <term>Diatonic</term> <note>The standard musical scale consisting of seven notes (five whole tones and two semitones).</note>, for example for the semitones of the <term>Lute</term> or the <term>Viol</term>, or for consonances—for example for the two Thirds, the two Sixths, the Fourth and the Fifth—one will have just as many new varieties of 720 songs; to which if one added the diversities of time, that is to say, of the different measures of Music, one would have a number of diversities so great that no one could sing or read them in a thousand years, as I shall show when speaking of that variety which comes from the 7 or 8 types of notes used by <term>Practitioners</term> <note>Professional musicians and composers who focus on the practical application of music rather than just pure theory.</note>.

Now, among several utilities that can be drawn from this variety, one may include that which serves to diversify the same number of notes without fear of becoming confused or troubled, and the advantage that this art gives over the imagination alone; for the Musician who knows this method will be able to wager whatever he wishes against another who does not know it, that he will create more varieties than him from the number of notes proposed; for example, he will make 720 varieties of 6 notes by beginning at the end, in the middle, or at whatever other song he wishes without failing in any way, whereas the other Musician, destitute of this art—however skilled he may be at playing or in any other thing—will not be able to make a hundred of them without becoming troubled and without repeating some of them. The other utility consists in the choice of the best songs, for since one has them all before one's eyes, one cannot fail to choose good ones if one has enough judgment for this subject; and although one may doubt whether one has taken the best, one is at least certain that one has taken those that were most pleasing, and which seemed the best to the ear.

Now, just as these 6 different notes make 720 different songs, if there were two alike they would only make 360 songs; if there were 3 alike, one would have only 120 songs; if 4 were alike, one would have 30 songs; if there were 5 alike, one would have only 6: finally, if they were all alike, they would make only a single song. But 2 and 2 alike give 180 songs; 2, 2, and 2 make 90; 2 and 3 make 60; and 2 and 4 make 15. This can serve for making <term>Anagrams</term> <note>In this context, "anagrams" refers to the combinatorial permutations of elements (like notes or letters) where some elements are repeated.</note>, of which I shall speak more amply hereafter.

As for the triple or quadruple variety of the 6 notes that follow, one shall use whichever <term>Senary</term> <note>A set of six items; here, a six-note sequence.</note> or Hexachord one wishes from the 4 that are signified by the keys that I put before the first variety.

<header>Of Melodies. <note>original: "Des Chants"</note></header>

## PROPOSITION X.

*How many melodies can be made from any given number of notes, when it is permitted to use two, 3, 4, similar notes etc., and while always retaining the same total number of notes from which the melodies are made.*

We have demonstrated in the two preceding propositions how many different melodies can be made by taking notes that are all different, and which always remain the same without being permitted to change anything other than their order; in this one, we must show the number of melodies that can be made from the same number of notes when it is permitted to repeat one or several notes 2, 3, 4 times, etc. And because the number of melodies that repeat the same notes two or more times is not as large as those where no note is repeated, one could say that this proposition is a subset <note>original: "détachement"</note> of the other two.

Now, it is very easy to find this number by dividing the preceding combination <note>In 17th-century mathematics, "combination" often referred to what we now call a "permutation"—the total number of ways to arrange a set of items.</note> that gives the number of melodies (of which I spoke in the two other propositions) by that of the similar or repeated letters. For example, the melody *Ut, re, mi, ut, fa* <note>C, D, E, C, F</note> has five notes, for which the preceding combination is 120; but because there are two similar notes—namely, two *ut*s—one must divide 120 by 2 (that is, by the combination of two notes). The quotient will give 60 for the number of melodies that can be made from the five preceding notes.

<image-desc>Musical notation for five notes on a staff: Ut, re, mi, ut, fa (C, D, E, C, F).</image-desc>

Likewise, if one makes a melody of these 7 notes: *Ut, re, mi, ut, sol, ut, fa*, one must divide the combination of 7 (namely 5040) by that of 3 (namely by 6), since the note *ut* is repeated 3 times. 

<image-desc>Musical notation for seven notes on a staff: Ut, re, mi, ut, sol, ut, fa (C, D, E, C, G, C, F).</image-desc>

And if it happens that the melody has two kinds of similar notes, as in this melody *Ut, re, mi, re, ut*, where there are two *ut*s and two *re*s, one must square the combination of 2 (which makes 4); by which 120 (the number of the combination of 5 notes) being divided, shows that there are only 30 melodies in these 5 notes. 

<image-desc>Musical notation for five notes on a staff: Ut, re, mi, re, ut (C, D, E, D, C).</image-desc>

If there were 3 pairs <note>original: "binaires"</note> of similar notes, one would have to cube 2, etc., following the powers of Algebra <note>original: "dignitez de l'Algebre." This refers to the progression of mathematical powers: squared, cubed, etc.</note>. The same must be said for 2, 3, or 4 triplets <note>original: "ternaires"</note>, quadruplets <note>original: "quaternaires"</note>, etc., unto infinity. For example, *Ut, re, mi, mi, re, mi, fa, re, sol* contains 9 notes, of which there are two that repeat 3 times; that is why one must square the combination of 3 (namely 6), which makes 36; by which the combination of 9 being divided (namely 362,880), the quotient gives 10,080 different melodies.

<image-desc>Musical notation for nine notes on a staff: Ut, re, mi, mi, re, mi, fa, re, sol (C, D, E, E, D, E, F, D, G).</image-desc>

If there were 2 pairs and one triplet, one would have to multiply the combination of the triplet by the square of the combination of two. And if one of the notes repeated four times, and the other 5 times, one would have to multiply the combination of 5 by that of 4 to obtain the divisor.

Finally, if one wishes to know how many different melodies can be made from 22 notes, of which two repeat twice each, one repeats 3 times, and two others repeat four times: one must square the combination of 2 to get four, by which one must multiply the combination of 3 to get 24, which must be multiplied by the square of the combination of 4 (which is 576). The product (namely 13,824) will be the divisor which will divide the combination of 22; the quotient will give 81,307,923,016,320,000 for the number of melodies that can be made with the 22 aforementioned notes.

### PROPOSITION XI.

->*How many different melodies can be made from a certain number of notes taken from*<-
->*another larger number, when the said notes are all different, whether*<-
->*one maintains the order of different positions, or does not, and when*<-
->*it is permitted to take them two by two, or three by three,*<-
->*or four by four, etc.*<-

We have only considered the variety of positions and the order of notes in the three preceding propositions, without being allowed to add new notes; but we show in this one how to find the number of melodies <note>original: "chants"</note> that can be made from notes to which one adds other new ones. Thus, this <term>combination</term><note>In this era, "combination" was a general term for what we now distinguish as permutations and combinations.</note> is larger and more general than the previous one, which it contains, and to which it adds a new consideration.

The following example is so clear that there is no need for other rules. I suppose, then, that one wishes to know all the melodies that can be made of 8 notes taken from 22 notes, such that the melody always has only 8 notes. Now, one must multiply 22 by the number that is less by one unit—namely, by that which follows immediately toward one, which is to say by 21—the product of which is 462; this is the number of <term>variations</term><note>The number of permutations of 2 items chosen from 22.</note> of two notes taken from 22. Then one must multiply 462 by the following number, namely 20, the product of which, 9240, shows the number for 3 notes taken from 22. One must follow this same order up to 22 notes, etc., which will give as many melodies as the ordinary combination of 22. And one will find that the eighth number shows that 8 notes taken from 22 make 12,893,126,400 entirely different melodies, as one sees in this table. The column of Roman numerals contains the number of notes being taken, and the other column, where it says *by*, shows the numbers by which one must multiply each number representing the total melodies across from each number of notes. And if one only wants to know the number of melodies made of 8 notes, it is not necessary to go past the number corresponding to VIII.

As for the utility that can be drawn from this proposition and those that follow, it cannot be fully explained without writing new books on this subject, as is easy to show by the different considerations that can be made in a thousand subjects and a thousand encounters. I shall give some examples notable enough to persuade those who do not see the truth in the tables and in the method of constructing them—as if from very fertile principles, from which one can still draw many others.

I said in proposition 26, whether one keeps the order of different positions—that is to say, the <term>variation of positions<gloss>permutations</gloss></term>, as we have done in all the preceding combinations—or whether one does not, meaning that one does not account for the varieties that proceed from different positions.

Now, to find this particular combination, which is a derivation from the preceding Table, one must divide the given number from that Table by the ordinary combination of the number of things whose combination is sought. For example, to know how many melodies <note>original: "chants"</note> can be made from three different notes taken from the Twenty-second <note>This refers to the "Twenty-second" note of the keyboard, or a range of 22 notes spanning three octaves.</note>—that is to say, within 3 Octaves—one must divide the number 9,240, which is across from 3, by 6, which is the <term>ordinary combination<gloss>factorial</gloss></term> of 3. The quotient will give 1,540 for the number of melodies, in which each will always contain some new note.

From this it follows that this Table serves for two kinds of combinations, insofar as the ordinary combination removes the diversity of positions, and consequently leaves the Table of melodies that all have some different note.

## COROLLARY I.

It should therefore be noted that this table contains two: namely, the ordinary one, of which I spoke in the first proposition; and the one that always has some different note, which can serve to find how many three, four, six, or as many things as one wishes, can be taken differently, so that there is always something new each time in whatever other number one might wish...

one may choose. For example, how many times can 3, 4, 8, or 12 cards taken from a set of 22, 30, 56, or any other number one wishes, be dealt differently to those who play? For if one takes 3 cards from 22, the hand can come differently to each person 1540 times before the same hand returns. And if there is a larger number of cards, as in the game of *Piquet*, or *Ombre* <note>original: "l'homme"; Ombre was a popular 17th-century trick-taking card game for three players.</note>, etc., where there are 36 cards, one will easily find how many different ways a hand of 12 cards can be dealt before the same hand returns. For one must multiply 36 by 35 to get 1260, which gives the number of hands of 2 cards taken from 36 <note>The text says "30" in the OCR, but the math $36 \times 35$ refers to a pool of 36.</note>; then one must multiply 1260 by 34 to get the number of hands of 3 cards, namely 42,840, which must further be multiplied by 33 for hands of 4 cards. This process must be continued until reaching a hand of 12 cards, when one wishes to know the variety of that hand, and of the others that can exist from a hand of a single card (which can only give 36 different hands) up to a hand of 12 cards. And if one wants to have the hands that can exist from 12 up to 36, one must multiply as before up to the hand of 36. But if the deck consists of 56 cards, from which one wishes to take 12, one must multiply 56 by 55, and the product by 54, etc., until one has descended to 44, which will multiply the last product and give the number of hands of 12 cards—provided that one divides this last product (or the one corresponding to the number of cards one takes to play) by the <term>ordinary combination<gloss>the factorial of the number of items chosen</gloss></term> of that same number of cards, as I have already stated.

## COROLLARY II.

One can apply the preceding corollary to the number of notes taken within the range of 36 or 56 notes, and to the number of <term>dictions<gloss>words or units of speech</gloss></term> taken from those same numbers, or any other number one wishes. And if one desires, one need not remove the number resulting from the variation of positions <note>That is, if order matters, you do not divide to remove permutations.</note>. But to know the total number of all dictions, cards, hands, or other things—such as sets of 2, 3, 4, 5, etc., up to 12, or any other number one wishes—one must add together all the preceding numbers, as seen at the end of the preceding table.

## COROLLARY III.

When one is not concerned with finding how many melodies or dictions of 22 notes or letters can be made by taking them one by one, two by two, or three by three, etc., up to 22 (or any other number desired), and is satisfied simply to know all the varieties that can be made by taking them in all these ways—without specifying how many melodies or dictions of two or three letters there are—one need only arrange as many numbers in a <term>doubling geometric progression<gloss>a sequence where each number is twice the one before it: 1, 2, 4, 8...</gloss></term>, starting with unity, as there are units in the total number being used. For example, if one takes 22 things, one must write out as many numbers, each containing twice the one immediately preceding it, in this manner:

### PROPOSITION XII.

*How many different melodies can be made from a certain number of notes chosen from any other number one wishes, whether the notes chosen are all different, all similar, or partly different and partly similar.*

This combination is the most general of all, for it demonstrates how many varieties a certain number of notes (or other things) can undergo when taken from any other number. For example, it shows how 4 notes can be varied, whether one takes them all as different notes, or partly different and partly similar, or all similar, while maintaining the variety of their positions or order. Thus, this rule contains everything one can imagine regarding all the varieties and combinations of notes, or any other things one might wish; for everything said of notes can be applied to numbers, letters, soldiers, flowers, colors, and so on.

This cannot be explained more clearly than by the following example, which includes all the melodies that can be made using 22 notes <note>The number 22 likely refers to the standard range of notes in the musical system of the time, often corresponding to the "Guidonian Hand" or the number of letters in certain alphabets.</note>, whether one uses a single note, or 2, 3, 4, etc., and whether one repeats each note 2, 3, 4, 5 times, or whether each note is different. Now, the construction of the table is quite easy: suppose one wants to know how many melodies of 8 notes can be made from a set of 22. One must take the number 22 as the first number of melodies (which can be made of a single note repeated 22 times) <note>This refers to 22 possible choices for a single-note melody.</note>, then one must square 22 to get the number of melodies of 2 notes, namely 484. This must then be multiplied by 22 until one reaches the melodies of 8 notes, which are expressed by 54,875,873,536, as seen in the following table, which contains all the melodies that can be made from 22 notes.

If one wishes to find the melodies of more than 22 notes, one must multiply the last number (which is across from 16) by 22, and the product again by 22 until one reaches 30, 40, 50, or any other number of notes desired. ### PROPOSITION XIII.

->*A melody being given, to find the rank and the order it holds among all possible melodies within a determined number of notes.*<-

Several things must be noted here before explaining this proposition: first, that the number of different notes from which one wishes to compose the melodies must be determined—for example, 22 different notes. Secondly, that it is permitted to repeat the same note as many times as one wishes—for example, 2, 3, 4, etc., up to 22 times or more. In the third place, one must determine the intervals or degrees one wishes to use. In the fourth place, one must mark the different notes with letters or with other characters.

Now, I shall take only the 22 different notes found in the system of <term>Guido of Arezzo</term> <note>original: "Guy Aretin"; an 11th-century monk regarded as the inventor of modern musical notation.</note>, which begins in <term>Gamma-ut</term> <note>The lowest note of the medieval musical scale.</note> and ends in <term>D-la-sol</term> <note>A high note in the traditional Guidonian "gamut" or scale.</note>, dividing the three <term>B-flat/B-natural</term> <note>original: "b fa ♮ mi"; the two forms of the note B used in the hexachord system.</note> into their two distinct notes; otherwise, there would be only 19 characters. And so that the preceding table may serve for the letters and the words that can be made from 22 letters, I shall place them opposite the letters used for the 22 notes of <term>Music</term>, so that one may know which word corresponds to each melody, or what discourse is explained by all sorts of melodies; and so that, any given number being chosen, one may know the melody and the word that corresponds to it. For just as there can be no melody within the 22 notes that is not contained in the table of numbers, there is similarly no word that is not included therein—be it <term>Latin</term>, <term>French</term>, <term>Greek</term>, <term>Hebrew</term>, or any other that can be imagined—provided it can be written with our 22 letters, or with any other 22 letters one wishes. This must also be noted for the notes and for the intervals, inasmuch as if one wishes to use <term>Chromatic</term> or <term>Enharmonic</term> <note>Refers to the ancient Greek musical genera; chromatic uses half-steps, while enharmonic uses quarter-tones.</note> degrees, or other new degrees, one will always find the number of all the melodies that can be made within the span of 22 notes, which make 21 degrees or intervals. To understand this table, it must be noted that musical notes could be changed to the numbers 1, 2, 3, etc., or to the letters of our alphabet, A, B, C, etc., without it being necessary to use the ordinary names of the <term>Gamut</term> <note>The full range of traditional musical notes (from the lowest G "Gamma" to the highest E).</note>, or of the musical <term>scale</term>: though I have placed them in the third column. Now, there is always the same ratio between the two numbers in the 5th column that follow each other immediately as there is between 1 and 22, so that the first ratio reveals all the others; for all these numbers follow the <term>progression</term> of algebraic degrees <note>In modern terms, this is a geometric progression where each step is 22 raised to a higher power (22^n).</note>, and consequently the ratio of two following numbers is always similar to the ratio of the two preceding ones. From this it follows that one must pass through the 22 notes or through the 22 letters before coming to the songs and "dictions" of two notes or two letters; and consequently one must pass through 22 tens, each of which has two notes, before reaching the first "diction" or the first song of three letters, which holds the place of the <term>hundreds</term>, and which expresses its number 484 times.

One must begin with the last note of the song, namely with <term>Mi</term>, which is the 4th note of the system, and which consequently is worth only its own number; this happens to all the last notes of other songs, or to the last letters of words, which are never worth more than the number marking their rank in the system.

# Second Book

Now, just as one can write letters and discourses using musical notes, one can similarly write melodies and pieces of music using letters and discourses; so that he who receives a letter from his friend will be able to sing while reading. And one could so accommodate the letter with the note that the same letter would serve as both the note and the subject. For example, if the preceding song was good, as can happen with other words, it would serve to pronounce the utterances, for each note would signify each letter. But it would be necessary to establish a different order among the letters of our Alphabet, and to arrange it so that all the vowels were found close to one another, so that one had the freedom to make several utterances within the span of eight or twelve letters, in order that one could make all sorts of songs within the span of an Octave or a Twelfth <note>An interval of twelve scale degrees, spanning an octave and a fifth.</note>.

After having given the method for writing all kinds of songs by means of numbers and letters, it is necessary to explain the method for recognizing the song, and for deciphering it when the number is given; for what I have said in this proposition serves only for writing songs or utterances by numbers, but it does not give the means to read the songs, or the writing that one signifies by the numbers: so that one can write whatever one wishes without being able to read it; and consequently, it is not necessary that Secretaries be able to read what they write.

### PROPOSITION XIV.

->*How to read all kinds of letters and utterances in whatever language they may be,*<-

among the number of all possible songs, I add another method which serves to find the location within the number of songs that have the same quantity of notes, and then I will show how to find the song when the location is given.

Now, the table of the combination of notes teaches how many songs a certain quantity of notes taken from 22 can make; those composed of two notes are 484, just as those of three notes make 10,648, etc. But to find the place that each song holds in the said number, the first note on the right hand must express once the rank it holds in the Harmonic scale <note>The "Harmonic scale" refers to the gamut, the standard range of musical notes used in this period.</note>, and the one in the 2nd place expresses it 22 times, etc. For example, if the first note corresponds to N, it is worth 12: secondly, if it is found in the 2nd, 3rd, or 4th rank, etc., it is worth one less than the rank it holds. For example, if the note corresponding to N holds the 2nd rank on the right hand, one must multiply 11 by 22; if it is in the 3rd, by 484, etc. In such a way that the first note corresponding to A is only a zero, although it can be placed at the beginning of the song, and it is worth one at the end. We will therefore put the 2nd note of *A-re* <note>A technical name for the note A in the traditional hexachord system.</note> for the first, *B-fa* for the second, etc. and *D-la-sol* <note>The note D.</note> will be the 21st, except that at the end of the song each always is worth its own number.

But so that we have no need of notes for the examples, I use the letters of the Alphabet which are opposite them. I suppose then first that one wants to know the location of the word *Eliud* <note>A biblical name from the genealogy of Christ.</note> which has five letters, from which 5,153,632 words can be made, provided they are taken from the 22 letters of the Alphabet. Now the first letter is D, which is the 4th in the Alphabet; the 2nd is V, which is the 19th, but it is only worth 18 here, which I multiply by 22, the product is 396; the 3rd letter is I, which is the 9th, and is worth only 8, which multiplying 484 makes 3,872; L is the 10th, and is worth only 9, which multiplying 10,648 gives 95,832; and then I multiply 234,256 by E which is worth 4, the product is 937,024; so that all these numbers being assembled show that the song of 5 notes responding to *Eliud* is the 1,037,128th among those of 5 notes.

Secondly, this manner can serve to write letters difficult to decipher; for example, if one wanted to write this verse, "If you would but slay the wicked, O God! Away from me, you bloodthirsty men" <note>original: "Si occidis Deus peccatores, viri sanguinum declinate à me"; a quote from Psalm 139:19.</note>, one will find that after an operation similar to the preceding one, one will have the nine numbers that follow for the 9 words of the verse: 361, 1,371,421,453, 34,293, 15,919,222,918,517, 195,875, 879,296,384,835, 174,880,186,11, 225, which one can easily apply to the notes of the song that correspond to these words.

If the given number is divided exactly without any remainder by the number taken from the table, one must put the note signified by the quotient without adding anything to it, and as many *D-sol* <note>The note D.</note> afterward as are required to complete the number of notes of which the song should be composed. For example, 8,712 is divided exactly by 484, for which the quotient is 18, which corresponds to *A-mi-la-re* <note>The note A.</note>, after which one would have to put two *D-la-sol*s. But two things must be noted here: the first is that if one cannot divide by all the numbers in the table smaller than the first divisor, and they are found to be larger than the number to be divided, one must pass them by, putting *G-ut* <note>The note G.</note> as many times as one has passed, just as one does when, in division, the divisor is larger than the number to be divided.

Now, the examples that follow for words [dictions] will make all of this better understood than a longer discourse. The quotient is 9, which gives L, and 11 remains, which cannot be divided by 22; I therefore put A and M for the 11 that remain, so that the word is *Baalam*; and to make *Balaam*, one would need 5,249,475.

The second thing to note is that when writing in this manner of cipher, if words occur that begin with one or several As, one must observe how many letters the word is composed of by putting a period after the number, and then a figure that shows the quantity of letters. For example, in this number 7,536. 5., the 5 which is after the word shows that it is composed of 5 letters; that is why one should divide the said number by 234,256, since it is the 5th in the geometric progression of 22 that starts at unity, and then by 10,648. ## PROPOSITION XVII.

*To determine the number of Songs that can be made from any number of notes one wishes, when they are taken from a larger number (for example, when taking 8 notes as one wishes from the 22 notes of 3 Octaves), and when it is permitted to repeat the same notes 2, 3, or several times in the said songs.*

It is easy to know how many songs can be made from whatever number of notes one wishes, when one is given the freedom to repeat them several times, and when they are taken from a larger number, without being permitted to use variations of order. For this purpose, one must first see how many notes are in the song, without regard to similar notes, which are only counted as one: for example, when in this 1st song which has 7 notes I repeat <term>Ut</term> <note>The first note of the scale, known today as C.</note> four times, one must only take these four <term>Ut</term> notes as one note. Thus, one must only take the 4 different notes of this song, and see how many songs of 4 different notes can be made from the 22 notes of 3 Octaves, where the order is removed; one will find 7,315, which when multiplied by 4 gives 29,260 different songs that can be made from this 1st song.

This table does not need to be extended as far as 22, because there is the same number of songs from 12 to 22 as there is from one to 11; for just as one can only make one song of 22 notes taken from 22 when they are all different, and it is not permitted to change the order, one can also only make one song when they are all similar. And as there are 462 songs when one takes only two similar notes, likewise there are 462 when the song has 21 similar letters <note>The author uses "letters" and "notes" interchangeably here to refer to the individual units in a sequence.</note>; so that the similarity of two corresponds to that of 21, that of 3 to that of 20, and that of 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 to that of 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, and 12.

### PROPOSITION XVIII.

->*To determine the number of songs that can be made from a set number of notes, when there are different notes that are similar to each other—such as when one uses Ut twice, Re twice, and Mi twice, or four times each, and so on.*<-

When the number of similar notes varies—for example, when *Ut* <note>The note C in the early musical naming system.</note> appears twice and *Re* <note>The note D.</note> appears twice—one must look for a song in the preceding table that corresponds to this arrangement. It will be found that it relates to the song of four notes that has two similar notes and two different ones, or to the one with five notes where three are similar (as in the second song). Consequently, these two songs can be varied 4,620 times, because they only consist of 3 different kinds of notes.

<image-desc>Five musical staves labeled 1 through 5, each containing a short sequence of square and diamond-shaped musical notes (neumes).
1: A sequence of four notes.
2: A sequence of five notes.
3: A sequence of six notes.
4: A sequence of six notes.
5: A sequence of nine notes.</image-desc>

Now, the relationship between these two songs lies in the fact that in the first there are 2 notes, and 2, and 1; while in the second there are 1, and 1, and 3 notes. Because 2 and 2 are equal in the first and the third (which is 1) is different, and in the second song 1 and 1 are equal while 3 is a different number, they follow the same mathematical rule.

When a song has 6 notes, and there are 2 of one kind, 2 of another, and 2 of yet another (as in the 3rd song), it is similar to a song of 3 different letters <note>The author uses "letters" and "notes" interchangeably to represent distinct pitches.</note>, because the groupings 2, 2, 2 are similar in the same way as 1, 1, 1. For this reason, only 1,540 similar songs can be created within 22 notes. The same must be said for a song whose notes are in the same ratio as the numbers 2, 2, 2, 2; this relates to songs of 4 different letters even though it has 8 notes total. From this, it follows that there can only be 7,315 variations. This should be understood to apply to those that have four <term>ternaries</term> <note>Groups of three.</note>, <term>quaternaries</term> <note>Groups of four.</note>, etc., of similar notes.

The same thing occurs in songs where the number of similar notes is different: for example, in the fourth song of 6 notes, which has one note of one kind, then 2 of another, and 3 of another; or in the fifth song which has 9 notes, where there are 2 of one kind, 3 of another, and 4 of another. The number of variations for these 2 songs is equal to a song of 3 different notes where the order is accounted for, as seen in the table of the 4th proposition. Consequently, there are 9,240 songs similar to these two within 22 notes.

If in a song of 10 notes there are 1, 2, 3, and 4 similar ones, the number of songs will be 175,560, which is equal to that of 4 different notes with the order preserved. There are just as many varieties when there are 2, 3, 4, and 5 similar notes, because one only needs to see how many *kinds* of notes are present.

### PROPOSITION XIX.

->*To determine the number of melodies that can be made from any number of notes one wishes, by varying the durations or the rhythms of one, several, or all of the notes.*<-

One must first assume that the number of melodies that can be made without considering rhythm is known—whether the number of melodies is taken from the ordinary combination <note>Mersenne uses "combination" to mean permutations: the different ways a set of items can be ordered.</note> or from others, or even if one only takes one, 2, or 3 melodies. Then, one must know how many kinds of durations or rhythms one wishes to use. For example, if one wishes to use 8 durations <note>original: "temps"; in this context, it refers to the rhythmic value or length of a note, such as a whole note, half note, etc.</note>, one must multiply 8 by itself to get 64, which must be multiplied by 8 to give 512, which must again be multiplied by 8 to get 4,096, and continue multiplying in this way up to 7 times <note>Mersenne is calculating $8^8$, or 8 to the power of 8.</note>, from which will come 16,777,216. This is the number of melodies that can be made from a set of notes where it is permitted to use 8 different durations—for example, a sequence of 8 notes that are always arranged in the same order. And if one takes all the variations that 8 notes can undergo because of the different positions and the order they can have—whether they always remain the same or are taken from a larger number of notes—one must multiply the number of melodies <note>The number of possible pitch permutations.</note> by the number of rhythmic variations.

From this, it follows that if one wishes to know the number of melodies in the Great Universal Table <note>This refers to a massive table of permutations Mersenne calculated in Proposition V of this book.</note>, when it is permitted to use as great a variety of durations as there are notes, one must multiply each number of the said table by itself. For example, if one wishes to know the number of all possible melodies when one takes 22 different durations as well as 22 notes, one must multiply the total sum of the table from the 5th proposition by itself to get 1,165,724,954,414,365,496,202,893,614,947,911,393,918,604,879,059,221,018,050,560 different melodies, of which the first group of three is worth 116 seventillions <note>original: "dixſeptilions." Mersenne notes this number contains 60 digits. In modern naming, a number with 60 zeros would be a novemdecillion.</note>, for this number contains 60 characters.

But it is not possible to write out all these melodies with notes, even if the entire earth and the heavens were converted into paper, and if all men wrote perpetually for a million years, as is easy to demonstrate. That is why I will give only the example of one of the melodies of 4 notes, which can be changed 256 times when one has the freedom to use 4 different durations, even if the 4 notes always keep the same order; for 4 multiplied 4 times makes 256—since 4 times 4 is 16, 4 times 16 is 64, and 4 times 64 is 256—as one sees in the example that follows, where the 4 notes of the <term>Fourth</term> <note>The musical interval spanning four scale degrees, such as C to F.</note> make 256 different melodies, though one takes only the first of the 24 permutations that can be made of the 4 notes, as one sees at the beginning of the example.

From this, it follows that one can make 24 times as many melodies with 4 different durations as there are in the example that follows—that is to say, 24 times 256, which makes 6,144. And if one uses the two other types of the Fourth, one will have 18,432 different melodies. But it is enough to put the 24th part of the example here to understand the truth of this proposition.

## PROPOSITION XXIII.

### *To explain several things that can be derived from everything that has been said in this book.*

ALthough it is very easy to conclude many things from what we have said in this third book, I nevertheless wish to give examples to facilitate the method; and for this subject I say first that it is easy to tell the number of guts <term>boyaux: catgut strings made from sheep intestines, the standard material for instrument strings at the time</term> of which each string of a Lute, Viol, or another instrument is made, by the sound it produces: for after having considered the sound of a string that has only one gut, one knows the ratio of its tone with that of other strings of whatever thickness one wishes, whether they have the same or different length and tension, provided that one knows the said tension and length: for example, if a single-gut string one foot long and tensioned by one pound <note>original: "liure," a pre-metric unit of weight</note> produces the unison of C-sol <note>C-sol-ut, roughly C4 in modern notation</note>, and another of two feet long tensioned by seven pounds descends an Octave, it is certain that it is composed of three guts, because if it were tensioned by only four pounds, it would have only one gut—since the tension is in a squared ratio <term>raison doublée: a mathematical relationship where the frequency change is proportional to the square root of the tension</term> of the sounds when the strings are of equal thickness—and because in addition to this double length, the thickness is triple, one must still triple the weight or the tension of the single-gut string to reach the tension of seven pounds.

### COROLLARY.

If one wished to take the trouble to vary a given song according to the variations it can undergo within the same triple meter <note>original: "ternaire"; a musical time signature where the beat is divided into three</note>, and within all the other kinds of measures that rhythmics <note>The mathematical science of proportions and timing in music</note> provides, it would not be possible for all men together to finish the task. Now, one can apply this type of combination <note>The author is referring to combinatorics, the mathematical study of how many ways items can be arranged</note> or variety to every word <note>original: "diction"</note> or letter used in any language—for example, in Latin or French—by adding four types of accents to each word, or by pronouncing it in four different tones. ### PROPOSITION XX.

->*To determine in how many different ways two or more voices can sing a Duet, or another piece of Music.*<-

It is very easy to find in how many ways two or more people can sing together, and at the same time, two or more musical parts: for one must only multiply the number of songs <note>Here, "songs" refers to the total number of possible melodic permutations</note> of one by the number of those of the other; and consequently, when the number of notes and their different values is equal, one must square the number of notes of one of them; if there are 3 parts, it must be cubed; and if there are 4, it must be "square-squared" <note>An early term for raising a number to the fourth power</note>, and so on for the others, following the powers <term>dignities</term> of Algebra unto infinity.

<image-desc>A musical staff with a C-clef showing four numbered musical phrases (1, 2, 3, 4). Each phrase contains seven diamond-shaped notes (semibreves or minims) at varying pitches on the staff. These represent the raw material for the permutations discussed in the text.</image-desc>

For example, the 4 songs seen here all have 7 notes, of which each has two pairs of identical notes; this is why one must divide the ordinary combination <term>permutation</term> of 7—which is 5,040 <note>This is calculated as 7 factorial (7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1)</note>—by the square of the combination of two—which is four—and the quotient will be 1,260.

Now, since the first of these four songs can be sung in 1,260 ways by simply changing the position of the notes, when the first voice sings one of its variations, the second can sing all 1,260 of its own; and just as many again at the same time that the first sings the second of its variations, and so on for the others. This is why one must square 1,260 to obtain 1,587,600, which is the number of songs that can be made with two parts; and this square number, being multiplied by its root, will give the cube 2,000,376,000 for the 3rd part; and if one adds the 4th part, one must multiply the preceding number by the root 1,260 to obtain 2,520,473,760,000.

## PROPOSITION XXI.

->*To know if one can determine which is the best and sweetest melody among several proposed songs—for example, the 24 melodies where each has 4 sounds or 4 notes.*<-

One can judge the goodness of melodies in two ways: namely, by considering the subject for which they were composed, or without regard to the subject, by considering only their sweetness and their good modulation <term>modulation: here referring to the melodic movement and the arrangement of intervals in a sequence</term>. As for the first way, it is a certain thing that the best melody is the one that best expresses the subject for which it was made. But we are not speaking of that matter here, as it involves many other difficulties that must be discussed elsewhere; for example, in what manner each word must be expressed, and how much one should raise or lower each syllable, etc. Instead, we propose no subject here; therefore, we must only speak of the second way, which considers the pleasure one can receive from several different sounds following one another by conjunct <note>notes that move to the very next note in the scale</note> or disjunct <note>notes that skip over scale steps, creating leaps</note> degrees in the Diatonic scale <term>Diatonic: the standard seven-note musical scale (like the white keys on a piano) used in Western music</term> which we use now.

Now, it seems that the sequence of notes that is most natural and easiest to sing must be judged the most agreeable and the best, even if there were only a single man of this opinion and the sentiment of all others were contrary. Thus, one must only determine which is the easiest to sing among several proposed melodies, or which one has a better flow, to know which is the best.

And because one cannot better explain this difficulty than by the example of several melodies, and because a song composed of four notes varies in 24 ways, we will use this example to determine which is the best melody of these 24 that follow:

# On Songs.

...the 8th and the 10th; and finally others believe that the last one is the best: and if one wanted to take the trouble to seek out reasons for all these different sentiments, one would encounter some that would perhaps serve to identify the diversity of temperaments, or of the humors and the spirit of the said *Practitioners* <term>Practitioners: musicians and composers who focus on the practical application of music rather than just theory</term>, the investigation of which I leave to those who wish to pursue it.

Since there is a great likelihood that one of them has encountered the truth, I wish only to examine the 8 songs that have been judged the most beautiful, in order to remark upon the best of all; and because the last one approaches repose and silence, from which the first one moves away, and since the end of each song represents repose, it seems more agreeable than the first: although one might say that it is just as agreeable to work after resting, as one does when singing the first song, as it is to rest after work, as in the last; for when the voice descends it relaxes and unbends, just as it tightens when it rises, since the low and high of sounds comes from the tension or the lowering of the string, as I have demonstrated elsewhere. To which one may add that this *24th* song makes a very good cadence <term>cadence: a melodic or harmonic configuration that creates a sense of resolution or finality</term>, and consequently that the maxim which teaches that the end crowns the work is verified here, and that its first degree begins by the smallest interval, namely by the *semitone* <term>semitone: the smallest interval in traditional Western music, such as the distance between a white key and an adjacent black key on a piano</term>; from which it happens that the movement of this song is easier, since the voice strains itself less than in the first, because it begins by a smaller degree.

The first song also ends with the same *semitone*, which makes it approach repose in some way, because its first degree only increases its tension by a fifteenth part, whereas all the others that end by ascending increase it by an eighth or ninth part, when they end with a *tone* <term>tone: a whole step, consisting of two semitones</term>, or by a third, a fourth, or a fifth part, when they end with a *Fourth*, or with a *Major Third*, or with a *minor [Third]*.

As for the 2nd and the eighth song, they can hold the third and fourth rank, inas-much as they both end with a *semitone*, which is a *Chromatic* <term>Chromatic: related to the scale that moves by semitones, often used to add "color" or emotional depth to music</term> degree, which is sweeter than the *tone* which is the *Diatonic* <term>Diatonic: the standard seven-note scale of natural steps (whole tones and semitones) used in most Western melodies</term> degree: And although it seems difficult to determine which is the best of these songs, nevertheless the second is more natural and easier to sing, because the *minor Third* of the second song is easier to intone than the *Fourth* of the eighth: Furthermore, the order of the beats <note>the author refers to "battemens," likely meaning the physical vibrations or the rhythmic pulse created by the mathematical ratios of the notes</note> made by the first three sounds of the *2nd* is easier to understand than the order of the beats made by the first *3* of the *8th*, for the beats of the *2nd* are explained by the sequence of these terms *9, 10, 12*, whose progression and comparisons are easier to understand; and if one takes the four terms that express their four notes one will have *36, 40, 48, 45* for the *2nd* song, and *40, 36, 48, 45* for the *8th* song.

The *10th* song has nothing recommendable about it except that it ends with a *Fourth*, or that it has the *semitone* in the middle; as for the *13th*, it has the 2 *Thirds*; but the *14th* similarly has the 2 *Thirds* and then the *Fourth*, and consequently it must be better if the goodness of songs is measured by the greatest number of their consonances <term>consonances: intervals or chords that sound stable and pleasant to the ear</term>; which one cannot conclude, for no Practitioner judges the eleventh song to be among the best, although it contains the same consonances, upon which the beauty and goodness of songs does not depend so much as on the sequence of conjunct degrees <term>conjunct degrees: notes that move step-by-step up or down the scale without skipping over any notes</term>; and songs that move by leaps are ordinarily more difficult to sing than those that move by conjunct degrees.

<meta>This page continues the author's analysis of the twenty-four possible permutations of a four-note melodic sequence (a tetrachord). **Book Second**

The 15th [song] has something heroic about it, and is more robust than the others, because of the interval of the Fourth by which it ends; this testifies to the nobility of spirit of the person who judges it the best of all due to the great tension of this ending. Quite the opposite occurs in the 19th and 20th songs, which begin with the Fourth.

Finally, the 18th song has something pleasant about it, because it begins with the <term>chromatic step: a movement of a semitone or half-step</term> which is very sweet, followed by the <term>minor third: a musical interval encompassing three semitones</term> which is also quite sweet, and then it ends with the minor tone <note>original: "ton mineur." In the musical theory of this period, a "minor tone" refers to a specific whole-step interval with a mathematical ratio of 10:9, slightly smaller than a "major tone" of 9:8</note>. From this, one can conclude that the person who is pleased by this more than other songs is of a well-balanced temperament and a gentle disposition. The same may be said of those who prefer songs that end with a semitone. However, it would require an entire book to explain which song is best suited to represent the different temperaments, and for which passion each ought to be employed.

### COROLLARY I.

If I have not demonstrated that the preceding songs are the best, one must consider that this subject is very difficult; one must be content with probable reasons where a formal proof is lacking. For this reason, I in no way wish to prejudice the opinions of those who believe they have better reasons for choosing some other song that pleases them more. Now, I have chosen these 4 notes and their 24 variations rather than another number because the Ancients established all their music upon the Fourth, which they called the <term>tetrachord: from the Greek "tetrachordon," a series of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth</term>, and because it contains no other steps than those of that Fourth. Thus, he who understands the reasons for the steps, the notes, and the sounds of the Fourth understands the music of the Greeks.

### COROLLARY II.

Even though I have taken the first species of the Fourth, which begins with <term>Ut: the syllable for the first note of the scale, now commonly called "C"</term>, the same example can nevertheless serve for the two other species. The second species begins with <term>Re: the second note of the scale, or "D"</term>, and the third with <term>Mi: the third note of the scale, or "E"</term>. To see the 24 variations of the Fourth <term>Re, Mi, Fa, Sol: the notes D, E, F, G</term>, one only needs to raise the clef to the second line. To see the 24 variations of the Fourth <term>Mi, Fa, Sol, La: the notes E, F, G, A</term>, one adds a <term>flat: a musical sign (♭) that lowers a note by a semitone; here called "b mol"</term> under the said clef, as can be seen in this figure. The first clef shows the first species, while the second and third clefs show the second and third species of the Fourth; although it

<image-desc>A musical notation diagram showing a five-line staff divided into three segments, labeled 1, 2, and 3. Segment 1 shows a C-clef on the first line with four ascending notes starting on Ut. Segment 2 shows a C-clef on the second line with four ascending notes starting on Re. Segment 3 shows a C-clef on the second line with a flat symbol (b mol) on the third line, and four ascending notes starting on Mi.</image-desc>

is not at all necessary to add these clefs, since it suffices to begin with **Ut**, **Re**, or **Mi** on the first note in order to continue. Consequently, one can use the notes without the clefs. This example can serve for the 72 different songs of the three species of the Fourth; for although six songs of the first species begin with the first note of the second species, and six others with the **Mi** of the third species, the sequence of the other steps (or at least some of them) is always different from the sequence of the preceding songs. This can be demonstrated by describing the 24 songs of the second and third species of the Fourth, which can then be compared with the 24 songs of the first species to judge which species contains the most beautiful songs, and if one species has a greater number of good ones than the others.

Of Songs. 157

## COROLLARY III.

One can find new charms in Music, whether in simple solo melodies or in compositions for several voices, by mixing the 24 songs of one of the <term>Fourths: an interval of a perfect fourth, which the Greeks called a tetrachord</term> with the 24 of the others. For example, if one follows the 2nd song of the 1st species, namely *Ut, re, fa, mi*, with the 2nd of the 3rd species, namely *Mi, fa, la, sol*; <note>The author is referring to the solfège syllables used in the hexachord system of the time. These specific sequences represent different arrangements of whole tones and semitones.</note> and practitioners will find many very agreeable varieties, which they have not yet considered, if they compare and mix the songs of one species with those of the others. The same must be noted for the 120 songs of each species of the Fifth, and for the 720 of the different species of the Sixth, etc., in order to invent and practice new <term>fugues: a style of composition where different voices "flee" and "chase" each other by imitating the same theme</term> which will perhaps be much more agreeable than ordinary fugues, because the imitation will have more variety and will be more learned and more ingenious.

## COROLLARY IV.

What I have said regarding the songs of the Diatonic Fourth can be applied to those of the Chromatic and Enharmonic Fourths, for which the same notes can serve without changing anything; for it suffices to make the semitone major or minor, or the <term>Diesis: a very small interval used in ancient Greek enharmonic music, smaller than a semitone</term> at the 1st and 2nd degree. This must also be concluded for the degrees of the Fifth and the Octave, as they are not different from those of the Fourth.

## COROLLARY V.

As for the variety and the quality of songs that depend on the different values of the notes, we shall speak of this in the book on Rhythmics, where we will treat the different movements and their properties. For it suffices now to know that these movements bring a very great variety to the songs, as I have demonstrated in the 19th proposition, where it is seen that one can make 6,144 songs, all different, from the four notes of the preceding fourth, and consequently 18,432 songs from the four notes of the three species of the Fourth, when one is permitted to use four different rhythmic durations as well as four notes. From this, it follows that one can sing for a very long time with only the four notes of these Fourths, which can serve to make all sorts of songs without ever repeating the same song.

## COROLLARY VI.

There is a great appearance that the 8th song is the best of all, insofar as the semitone follows after the Fourth, which creates the greatest <term>tension: a term used in early music theory to describe the "stretching" or rising intensity of a melody</term> of this song, and that it diminishes this tension by only a fifteenth part; this leads the ear back quite gently, making it pass almost imperceptibly to <term>remission: the relaxation or lowering of melodic intensity</term>; so as to rest on the *Mi*, which is very sweet and which is the middle voice of the song. For rest is all the more agreeable when the labor that precedes it is greater, because their difference is easier to notice, and strikes the mind and the ear more powerfully; and because labor, when compared to rest, is like sweetness compared to health, and to pleasure.

## COROLLARY VII.

One can also say that each song is all the sweeter and more pleasant as

Now, union is the principle and the source of pleasure and of true beauty, the perfection of which consists in unity: so that one can conclude that songs are better the more <term>conjunct: moving by small steps (like C to D) rather than large leaps (like C to G)</term> and united they are. To this one can add that it is easier to pass through conjunct steps than through those that are distant and disjunct, because the changes in the opening of the throat are smaller.

### PROPOSITION XXII.

->*To know how one must compose songs and create dances to be the most beautiful and excellent of all possible ones: and whether one can arrange Ballets in such a way that one learns all the sciences by dancing and by watching them being danced.*<-

Since the perfection of each thing consists in its essence, its properties, and its accidents, and since its excellence must be measured according to its principles, or following the end for which it is intended, I say that the song which has all that is required for its perfection, and which is best proportioned to its end, will be the most excellent of all. Now, it will have all its parts when it responds perfectly to the text and to the subject one chooses, and it can never be more excellent than when it has the most excellent subject of all, which consists in describing the greatness and the praises of God, and the love and ardor with which we must adore Him eternally.

From this it is easy to conclude that all Court songs which have no other subject than profane ones, and which contain nothing other than the praises of men—which most often exist only in flattery, and which have no other support than vanity and lies—cannot be perfect, since they lack truth, without which there is no perfection, and since they are deprived of the subject that ravishes the Angels and which will serve as eternal conversation for all those who are predestined for heaven.

As for the notation and the melody that must be given to the song, I say first that it should have the range of a <term>Nineteenth: an interval spanning two octaves and a fifth</term>, so that there is no part of the <term>Senary number: the numbers 1 through 6, which Renaissance theorists believed produced all the perfect musical harmonies</term> that is not employed in celebrating the greatness of Him who employed the six days of the world in the creation of the parts of the Universe: or at least that it must contain and have the range of a <term>Twelfth: an interval of an octave plus a fifth</term>, so that everything enclosed by the <term>Ternary: the number three, representing the Holy Trinity</term> serves to explain the treasures of the divinity who exists in three persons, and who has engraved His portrait in every creature, in which one can remark the Ternary of perfections of which I have spoken elsewhere.

Secondly, the song must contain all the most beautiful and ravishing passages that can be found within the preceding range, and all the sweetest and best consonances; for if it lacks any beauty or any rich stroke, one can always say that it is not the most excellent of all possible songs.

In the third place, it must be sung by a very excellent voice, or by several; otherwise, it will not have the sovereign perfection that it has in its composition:
