and several others similar to these.

Now since songs and dances usually go together, and since we must speak of all the types of dances that are in use in France, it is reasonable to consider if they are missing anything, and if one can invent dances that would be more useful and more agreeable than those used here, and in Italy, Germany, Spain, and elsewhere.

Some believe that the ancients practiced certain dances so well-regulated that they preserved men from several illnesses and cured them when they were sick. If one could put this art back into use, one would save large sums of money that are spent on so many medicines. But we do not have a great enough knowledge of the movements necessary to cure or to prevent illnesses; and even if we had it, one would perhaps find very few people who would want to subject themselves to it. However, one can read what Mercurial <note>Girolamo Mercuriale (1530–1606), an Italian physician who wrote extensively on ancient gymnastics and their health benefits.</note> wrote of the different sorts of exercises used by the ancients, and see what remains of these movements in Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>, and in the other Greek and Latin authors, from which one can draw some light to restore what has been stolen from us by time, or to invent a new art and a new method to drive away the indispositions of the body and mind through the regulated exercises and movements of both. Now the foundation of this art must be taken from movement or rest, which are the causes of illnesses, or which are necessary to open or to close the pores of the body, in order to drive out excrement and bad humors, and to retain the spirits and natural heat through oil anointments, from which this aphorism was drawn: *honey within, oil without* <note>original Latin: *melintus, oleum foris*. This refers to the ancient medical belief that health was maintained by consuming sweet things like honey or wine and rubbing the skin with oil.</note>: on which one can read the treatise that Verulam <note>Francis Bacon, also known as Lord Verulam, a philosopher who wrote "History of Life and Death."</note> wrote on life and death.

As for the greatest perfection of dances, it consists in perfecting the mind and the body, and putting them in the best disposition they can have. Now the greatest perfection of the mind consists in knowing and contemplating the most excellent works of nature—for example, the movements of the stars, and the elements, and their sizes, their light, and their perfection—and rising by their means to the Author of the Universe, who is the great master of the Ballet that all creatures dance through steps and movements that are so well-regulated that they ravish the wise and the learned, and serve as contentment for the Angels and all the Blessed.

One has not yet seen ballets so magnificent that they cost a thousand million in gold, and if one were made in some place in the world that cost ten years of the revenue of all that the sea and earth produce, there is no mortal who would not desire to attend at any price; and nonetheless, it would not have as much beauty nor skill as the composition and movement of a gnat <term>gnat: Mersenne uses the "moucheron" (a tiny fly or gnat) to argue that God's smallest natural creations are more complex and beautiful than the most expensive human stage productions.</term>,

### Book Two

...which all on its own contains and encompasses more wonders than anything human art can make or represent; so much so that if one could buy a view of all the internal gears <note>original: "ressorts," referring to the mechanical springs or inner workings of a living body</note> found within this little animal, or indeed learn the art of making automatons and machines with just as many movements, everything the world has ever produced in fruit, gold, and silver would not suffice as a fair price for a simple view of said gears.

Regarding the perfection of the body, it consists of perfect health and a very prompt obedience rendered to the spirit, whose servant it is; this is why the dances that provide these qualities must be considered the most perfect of all possible dances. Now, the walks that serve one’s health form a part of these dances, in such a way that one can compare all the exercises of human life to a Ballet, which consists of all sorts of movements and positions, following the strophes, antistrophes, and epodes <note>These are terms for the structural parts of an ancient Greek choral ode</note> of the songs and dances of the ancients.

But I leave the study of these movements concerning the health of the body to Physicians, so that I may consider those that can serve the mind and the sciences; and I say first that one can create Ballets that will represent and teach Astronomy, particularly if it is permitted to express through singing a part of the science one wishes to represent and teach. For example, one could represent the distance from Saturn to the Sun by a dance of 10 steps, since it is ten times further away than the earth; and that of Jupiter by five steps, since it is five times further from the Sun than the earth. One can represent the distances of other Stars and their movements, both daily and annual, and everything that appears in the Heavens. But it is not necessary to speak further of this matter here, because it suffices to read what I have said in the second book of the *Treatise on Universal Harmony* <note>original: "Traicté de l'Harmonie vniuerselle"</note>, particularly from the 5th Theorem until the end; from which Musicians can draw enough enlightenment to create dances and Ballets that represent and make understood all of Astronomy, Mechanics <term>Mechanics: the study of machines and the forces that act upon them</term> (which I have treated quite extensively from the 10th to the 12th Theorem), Geometry, Architecture, and the other sciences.

Now I have no doubt that the representation of the movement and the size of the Planets and the earth will give great satisfaction to the fine minds who attend these Ballets, and that Chronology, Cosmography <term>Cosmography: the science of mapping the general features of the universe, including both heaven and earth</term>, and all the arts that can be represented by human industry, will bring a hundred times more pleasure to the dancers and the spectators than all the Ballets that have been performed until now.

One can also so effectively represent the happiness of the Saints and the Paradise of the Blessed that upon leaving the Ballet, one will know what pertains to glory and what concerns the faith; and nevertheless, the dances will be no less agreeable than those in ordinary use. To which I add that those through which one represents the sciences and the Liberal Arts will be as well received and understood by the Chinese and all other nations as by the French, and consequently they could serve as a common, natural, and universal language, by means of which commerce, mutual understanding, and reciprocal friendship could be established and preserved throughout the world, so that all may have the same sentiments, and that everyone with the same heart and the same will might recognize and adore the Creator of the Universe, and the God of sciences, that there might not be

# On Songs.

...there may be only one same God, one same faith, and one same law; that diversity ends in unity, and that the creature returns to its creator.
The Ancients represented the daily movement made by the Heavens from East to West by their Strophes, and that from West to East by their Antistrophes, and they signified the stability of the earth, or the movement of libration and trepidation <note>In older astronomy, libration and trepidation referred to the perceived oscillating or "shaking" movements of the celestial spheres.</note> by their Epodes. But we have no evidence from antiquity to testify that they represented the proportion of the magnitude of movements, nor the distance of the Heavens and the Stars, nor that their Ballets served as images to impress Perspective, Catoptrics <note>The branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light, specifically through mirrors.</note>, Mechanics, and other sciences into the minds of the audience. Therefore, one can conclude that it is very easy to create more beautiful dances than theirs, and Ballets that are much more useful and instructive; I leave the invention of these to the Dance Masters and Ballet-makers, as they are so simple that one can invent several in a single day.

### Corollary on the Dances and Ballets of the Ancients.

The Greeks practiced several exercises both for recreation and for the health of the body, of which Mercurialis <note>Girolamo Mercuriale (1530–1606), an Italian physician famous for his work on physical education.</note> wrote a specific treatise titled *On the Art of Gymnastics* <note>original: "De arte Gymnastica"</note>. Now, one of their most frequent exercises consisted of jumping and dancing, although almost nothing remains to us of their dances except the simple names, as can be seen in the books that Lucian <note>A 2nd-century satirist who wrote a famous treatise on dance.</note> and Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius (1579–1639), a Dutch classical scholar.</note> wrote on this subject; the latter merely transcribes what Lucian, Plutarch, Athenaeus, Pollux, and a few others reported about dances—namely, the names alone. Consequently, no one gives us enough light to restore this art; however, the signs and gestures used by the mute to express their thoughts and desires are sufficient to demonstrate that *Chironomy* <note>The art of using hand gestures to communicate or to enhance oratory.</note> can be restored, which consists of signifying and representing all kinds of histories, and everything one can imagine, by the movements of the hands, feet, and other parts of the body.

One may also read the 52nd chapter of the first book that Bulenger <note>Jules César Bulenger (1558–1628), a Jesuit scholar who wrote on the ancient theater.</note> wrote on the Theater, where he speaks at length of the dances used on the stage in both Comedies and Tragedies. For it is enough for me to represent here all the types of songs used for the dances and Ballets practiced in France, after having provided an excellent subject and a very suitable text for the Airs, which Musicians should use if they desire their songs to be pleasing to God. This will happen when Divine Love warms them as strongly as the three Children <note>Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who were thrown into a fiery furnace by King Nebuchadnezzar and miraculously survived.</note> preserved among the flames of the furnace of Babylon, whose Canticle taken from the third chapter of Daniel has been paraphrased by Monsieur Mauduit <note>Jacques Mauduit (1557–1627), an influential French composer of the late Renaissance.</note> in this fashion:

## PROPOSITION XXIII.

### To explain all the types of Airs, Songs, and Dances used by Musicians.

One can reduce all the kinds of songs to three genres: namely, the <term>Song</term> or <term>Vaudeville</term>, <note>In the 17th century, a "vaudeville" was a popular urban folk song with simple, catchy melodies, quite different from the later theatrical genre.</note> the <term>Motet</term> or <term>Fantasy</term>, and all types of dance music; or to twelve kinds of musical compositions: namely, Motets, Songs, <term>Passamezzos</term>, <term>Pavans</term>, <term>Allemandes</term>, <term>Galliards</term>, <term>Voltas</term>, <term>Courantes</term>, <term>Sarabandes</term>, <term>Canaries</term>, <term>Branles</term>, and <term>Ballets</term>. I provide here the definition or description and the origin of each, along with an example of each, so that everyone can understand them very easily. # Book Second

[...in] another place, and as I am reserving Motets and other pieces for two or more parts in counterpoint—both simple and figurative <note>Figurative counterpoint involves more complex, decorative melodic lines compared to "note-against-note" simple counterpoint.</note>—for the book on Composition; I will only provide here examples of Songs or Airs used for dancing and for playing on instruments, the majority of which are suited for Violins.

Now, the song known as the *Vaudeville* is the simplest of all Airs, and is applied to all types of poetry that one sings note against note <note>original: "note contre note"</note> without a strictly regulated meter, but only according to the long and short syllables found in the verses. This is called *Air measure* <term>mesure d'Air: a flexible rhythm dictated by the natural stress of the spoken word rather than a rigid beat</term>; under which are included the plainchant of the Church, *Faux-bourdons* <note>A style of musical arrangement using parallel harmonies, common in late medieval and Renaissance sacred music.</note>, Court Airs, dancing and drinking songs, and *Vaudevilles*. Often, only the top part speaks, which is also called the *subject*, and this is done without chords or harmonies from other parts, because "making a song" simply means setting words to a melody. Now, this great ease of performance is why these songs are called *Vaudevilles*, because even the lowliest artisans are capable of singing them, especially since the author does not usually observe the meticulous complexities of figurative counterpoint, fugues, and syncopations, and is content to give them a movement and a melody pleasing to the ear; this is called an *Air*, taking the name from its principal and almost only part. In contrast, the *Motet* or the *Fantaisie* is a full figurative Music, enriched with all the subtleties of that science. It is called a *Motet* because it uses a very short period, as if there were only one word <note>French "mot"</note> to say; this occurs when one wishes to signify a very brief discourse, which, when set to music, is called a *Motet*. And when the Musician takes the liberty of employing whatever comes to mind without expressing the passion of any specific words, this composition is called a *Fantaisie* (Fantasy) or *Recherche* (Research/Ricercar).

As for dance-tunes <note>original: "danceries"</note>, there are several types that belong to Metric Music, insofar as they are subject to certain measures, or regulated and counted "feet": and one can invent an infinite number of them according to the new ideas that arise every day in the minds of those who involve themselves in it. I will explain in this proposition, and in the two following ones, only those known to us that are specific to France, or native to the other nations from whom we have taken them.

The *Passemeze* <note>The Passamezzo, a popular Italian Renaissance dance.</note> is an Italian melody suitable for dancing: in times past, it served as the entrance for *basses dances* <term>basses dances: "low dances" characterized by graceful, gliding steps without jumping</term>. It is danced by making several turns around the hall with certain steady steps, and then by crossing through the middle, as the name implies <note>The name likely derives from "passo e mezzo," meaning a step and a half, or from "passare per mezzo," meaning to pass through the middle.</note>; or perhaps it has this name from the "step and a half" by which it is measured: its example is of the first mode in its proper tone, and corresponds to the *Choreobachic* foot <note>In ancient prosody, a metric foot usually consisting of two long syllables followed by one short syllable, or vice versa (long-short-short), though here the author uses it to describe a specific rhythmic pattern.</note> <image-desc>Seven metric symbols: three small circles, a character resembling a cursive 'w' or double-loop, another small circle, and two long horizontal dashes.</image-desc> : its measure is binary <note>In duple time, such as 2/4 or 4/4.</note>.

The *Pavane* comes from Spain, and is so named because those who dance it make "wheels" <note>Peacocks spread their tails into a shape called a "wheel" (roue).</note> in front of one another in the manner of Peacocks <note>original: "Paons"</note>, and with such gravity that the cape and sword are no hindrance; indeed, they seem necessary to better mimic the peacock's tail, from which this dance took its name. It moves on the same foot as the preceding dance, and has 16 measures and 14 couplets: its example is of the 4th mode.

The *Allemande* is a dance from Germany, which is measured like the *Pavane*; but it has not been as commonly used in France as the preceding ones: one can call it

<meta>This page continues the classification of dance and song forms begun on the previous page. While the previous page introduced the Vaudeville as a simple vocal form, this page details specific dance types—the Gavotte, Sarabande, Volte, Courante, and Galliard—describing their origins, rhythmic structures, and physical movements.</meta>

<header>of Songs.</header>

The **Vaudeville**, or **Gavotte**, has a binary <note>A duple meter, or two-beat feel.</note> measure. Its example is in the second Mode: today, people are content to play it on instruments without dancing to it, much like the *Passamezzo*, except in Ballets; its example is in the second Mode.

The **Sarabande** was invented by the Saracens, or Moors, from whom it took its name; for it is held that the actress named *Sarabande* was the first to dance it in France. Some believe it comes from the Spanish word *Sarao*, which among other meanings signifies a Ball in Spanish, or from *Banda*, which signifies an assembly, as if many people should gather for this kind of dance; this is perhaps what the Moors observed, even though the French and Spanish only dance it in pairs. Its rhythm is *Hegemeolian* <gloss>short short short long short</gloss> <note>original: "Hegemeolien." This refers to a specific rhythmic foot or meter used in ancient Greek prosody to describe the "feel" of the music.</note>. It is danced to the sound of the Guitar or Castanets, and through countless couplets. Its steps are composed of *tirades* <note>drawn-out movements</note> or glides; its example is in the eleventh Mode transposed one tone lower. Its measure is *Hemiolia* <term>Hemiolia: a rhythmic relationship of 3:2, often sounding like three beats played in the time of two</term>, and follows the beat of the Marshal <note>original: "battement du Mareschal." Likely referring to a steady, processional military rhythm.</note>.

The **Volte** seems to show by its name, which means "to turn," that it comes from Italy, for it is danced while turning; though it has been in France for so long that one might call it naturalized. It perhaps also has this name because, after a few straight steps, the man makes the woman jump, leading her in a turn; and after having led her for a certain time, he takes her by the left arm at the waist <note>original: "par le fort du corps" (by the strength of the body)</note>, and makes her spin for several turns while lifting her very high, as if he wanted to make her fly. Its measure is ternary <note>triple time</note> and follows the rhythm of the small drum. It has two measures and one step, and contains the fourth *Paeon* <gloss>short short short long</gloss>, the *Di-iamb* <gloss>short long short long</gloss>, and the *Minor Ionic* <gloss>short short long long</gloss>; its example is in the tenth Mode transposed.

The **Courante** is the most frequent of all dances practiced in France; it is danced by only two people at a time, making them run to a melody measured by the *Iambic* foot <gloss>short long</gloss>, so that this entire dance is but a hopping run of coming and going from the beginning to the end. It is composed of two steps in one measure, namely one step with each foot. Now, the step has three movements: the *bend* <note>original: "plier"</note>, the *lift* <note>original: "leuer"</note>, and the *placement* <note>original: "poser"</note>. Its rhythm is called *sesquialtera* <note>A Latin term for a 3:2 ratio</note> or triple, and its example is in the fourth Mode in its proper tone. One may nevertheless give it whatever measure one wishes.

The **Galliard** is a dance that took its name from the *gaillardise* <note>merriment or spiritedness</note> used in dancing it, and from the freedom that allows one to move diagonally, crosswise, and lengthwise through all parts of the room—sometimes close to the ground, and sometimes in a *cabriole* <note>a "caper" or jump where the legs strike together in the air</note>, which is done with *entrechats* <note>jumps where the feet cross rapidly</note> and round leaps. Some say it comes from Rome, which is why they call it the *Romanesque*. Its measure is ternary and follows the rhythm of the Italian drum, or the *Pyrrhic-Anapestic* foot <gloss>short short short short short long</gloss>. It ordinarily has three steps and five measures. Its example is in the tenth Mode. But because speech is not enough to provide a perfect understanding of these types of dances without seeing the practice, I am placing examples here; though it should be noted that one can accommodate rhythms other than the preceding ones to the examples that follow.

### PROPOSITION XXIV.

->Explaining all the types of <term>Bransles</term> <note>A group of French dances performed by a line or circle of dancers holding hands, characterized by a side-to-side swaying motion.</note> currently used in France, in Ballets and Balls, as well as in other recreations.<-

AFTER having explained all the types of melodies used in Passamezzos, Pavanes, Sarabandes, Courantes, Galliards, Voltes, and Allemandes, it is reasonable that we explain the various types of Bransles which are characteristic of our nation. Now, there are six types, which are currently danced at the opening of the Ball, one after the other, by as many people as one wishes; for an entire group, holding hands, gives themselves a continuous swaying motion by common accord, sometimes forward and sometimes backward. This is done with various movements, to which several types of steps are adapted according to the difference of the tunes being used. They are danced very solemnly in a circle at the beginning of the Ball, with the same cadence and swaying of the body. The first of these is called the *Simple Bransle*, which formerly had only six measures and eight steps, but is now composed of ten steps, twelve movements, and six duple measures <note>original: "mesures binaires." Measures with two beats.</note>. The example I provide of it is in the transposed seventh mode, a fourth higher, so that it has its <term>B-flat</term> <note>original: "b mol."</note> in <term>B-fa-si-mi</term> <note>A term from the hexachord system of solmization used to identify the position of the note B in different scales.</note>; and its movement is dactylic-spondaic — ◡◡ — — <note>A rhythmic pattern borrowed from classical poetic meter consisting of a long syllable followed by two shorts, then two longs.</note>.

The second Bransle is called the *Gay*, and is danced faster than the first. It is composed of six movements, three steps, and two measures, and follows the beat of the Swiss drum—which is to say it is danced under the minor Ionic meter ◡◡ — —. Its example is also in the transposed seventh mode like the previous one, and its meter is triple <note>original: "ternaire."</note>.

The third is named the *Bransle à mener* <note>The "Leading Bransle."</note>, or the *Bransle of Poitou*. Its meter is <term>sesquialtera</term>, or <term>hemiola</term> <note>original: "sesquialtere, ou hemiolia." Rhythmic terms referring to a 3:2 ratio, where three notes are played in the time normally occupied by two.</note>. It has nine steps, six measures, and eighteen movements; its meter is Paeonic <note>Another rhythmic structure derived from Greek poetic feet.</note>. Now, each person leads the Bransle in their turn; the first one who leads lets go of the left hand and makes a bow to the person they are holding with the right hand; and after having kissed the hand, they take it again and lead the Bransle, which flows very quickly. Having made one or two turns around the hall, they leave the person they were holding by the hand to go find the end of the line <note>original: "la queuë du Branfle," literally the tail of the Bransle.</note> and give their left hand to the person they find at the end. As soon as everyone has led in their turn, they return to a circle to dance the

other Bransles. Some relate the movement of this dance to the blacksmith's beat <note>original: "battement du Mareschal"; likely a reference to the rhythmic, percussive sound of a hammer striking an anvil.</note>: its musical example is also in the <term>seventh Mode</term> <note>Also known as the Mixolydian mode, often characterized by a bright, major-like sound with a flattened seventh.</note>.

The fourth type is called the **Double Bransle of Poitou**: its measure is <term>Hemiola</term> <note>original: "Hemiolia"; a rhythmic ratio of 3:2, creating a feeling of three beats in the time of two.</note>, it has eleven steps, eight measures, and twenty-four movements; and it mimics the rhythm of the blacksmith, or the <term>Iambic</term> <note>A poetic meter consisting of a short syllable followed by a long one: $\cup -$.</note> meter: its musical example is also in the seventh Mode. The fifth is named the **Bransle of Montirandé**; its measure is binary <note>Two beats per measure.</note>, but it is very fast. It has eight measures and sixteen movements, and is divided into three different sets of steps, of which the first has eleven, the second twelve, and the third has ten. Its musical example is in the <term>eleventh Mode</term> <note>In the twelve-mode system, this is the Ionian mode, similar to the modern C-major scale.</note> transposed one tone lower, and can be related to the <term>Anapestic</term> <note>A poetic meter consisting of two short syllables followed by one long one: $\cup \cup -$.</note> movement.

The sixth is called the **Gavotte**, which is to say the "dance to songs": its measure is binary and quite grave, and can be related to the <term>Choreobacchic</term> <note>A poetic meter typically consisting of three short syllables followed by two long ones: $\cup \cup \cup --$.</note> movement; it has eight steps, four measures, and sixteen movements. Its musical example is also in the eleventh Mode transposed one tone lower. It serves as the conclusion to the Bransles, and after having been danced once or twice in a circle, the one who began the Bransle leads the way and performs a <term>reverence</term> <note>A formal bow or curtsy expressing respect.</note> to his Lady. He then dances only eight steps in front of her, and having taken her under the right arm, he has her complete one turn, and then another by the left arm with eight steps each; having made his reverence to her, he returns her to her place and resumes his own. After everyone has done the same thing in their turn, a general reverence is made, and each man leads his woman back to the place where he first took her to dance. Now, it must be noted that one can create an infinite number of Bransles under each of these types, and that one can add as many others as one wishes: for example, the **Passepieds of Brittany**, etc., the examples of which are seen here.

# PROPOSITION XXV.

## To explain the dances and movements of common Ballets; and particularly *the Canary, the Bocanne, the Queen's Courante, the Bohemian, and the Morris dance.* <note>original: "Morefque"; refers to the Moresca or Morris dance, often characterized by exotic costumes and rhythmic footwork.</note>

Ballets are nothing other than a mixture of all sorts of melodies, movements, and steps used at one’s discretion, according to how knowledge guides the spirit of the author of these dances. Their name is general and comes from *baler*, that is to say, to dance. Now, I have intentionally omitted certain dances from the 24th Proposition, namely the *Canary*, which is extremely difficult and is only danced by those who are very well-trained in this exercise and who have very nimble feet. It is composed of several foot-strikes <note>original: "batteries de pied"; percussive steps where the feet strike the floor or each other.</note>, specifically of three, six, and twelve beats, and of half-capers <note>original: "demie cabriolle"; a jump where the legs strike together in the air.</note>, half-pirouettes, and other turns performed in the air, at mid-height, or close to the ground. It has many verses <note>original: "couplets"; sections of the dance or music.</note> without a fixed number. Its musical example is in the transposed <term>tenth Mode</term> <note>The Hypoaeolian mode, often sounding like a natural minor scale. "Transposed" means it has been moved to a different starting pitch.</note>: the measure is of the little <term>hemiola</term> <note>A rhythmic effect where three notes are played in the time usually taken by two, creating a shifting sense of pulse.</note>. It is held that this dance came from the Canary Islands; it moves by the dactylic foot <note>A poetic and rhythmic meter consisting of one long beat followed by two short ones.</note> and is more brisk than the Sarabande.

The *Bocanne* is a choreographed <term>Courante</term> <note>A popular "running" dance of the Baroque era, known for its elegant, flowing movements.</note> which has its own measured steps and particular figures. It has four verses—specifically, the first part of the song is played twice, and the second part twice. It was previously called the *Vignonne*, but the melody that was newly composed for it has given it the name of its author <note>Referencing Jacques de Bocan, a famous dancing master and violinist at the French court.</note>. It uses triple measure, or <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>A musical proportion where three notes are played in the time of two, similar to the hemiola mentioned above.</note>, like other Courantes. Its example is in the eleventh Mode, transposed one tone lower, like that of the Queen's Courante. However, it has nine verses, where the first part is sung twice and the second part once. It is repeated three times and is in the sesquialtera measure like other Courantes. To these, I add two Ballet melodies of different movements; and at the end of the book, I will provide a third, composed of all sorts of movements which can serve for all kinds of melodies and songs.

### PROPOSITION XXVI.

#### *To determine whether the songs called sad and languishing are more pleasant and sweet than those called gay.*

This Proposition is not useless, for if well explained, it will reveal to us the nature of man, or of Music. Now, it seems there should be no doubt that gay songs are more pleasant than sad ones, since all men desire to rejoice and flee sadness, which ruins health and the <term>economy of the body</term> <note>In early modern science, the "economy of the body" refers to the organized system of vital functions and the balance of health within a living being.</note>; from this comes what the Sage <note>A common reference to King Solomon, traditionally credited with the Book of Proverbs.</note> said, that <note>original: "Tristitia exsiccat ossa"</note> sadness dries the bones.

Furthermore, one experiences that the tunes of <term>Ballets</term> and Violins excite more—by reason of their gaiety, which comes from the promptness of their movements or their high-pitched sounds—than the tunes played on the Lute, or on the bass Viols, which are usually more grave and languishing.

And the Trumpets further show us this truth when they use the first Mode <note>In the musical theory of the time, the "first mode" (Dorian) was often characterized as stable, serious, or energetic depending on the context, but here associated with joy and movement.</note>, which is the gayest of all and excites all sorts of men to rejoice: for we experience in ourselves that the movements of the heart and the imagination follow the sounds and the movements of the Trumpet.

To which one can add that the sounds and movements of gay songs approach closer to life than those of sad tunes, since life consists in a perpetual and continuous movement; for the beats of air that make high sounds, and the rhythmic movements that are more frequent, approach closer to continuity than those of grave sounds and the heavy, slow movements of sad tunes, which represent an interrupted and dying life. And one experiences that gay songs are so suited to dancing that even those who have never learned this exercise begin to dance, or show by some movement of the body the contentment they receive from these songs: which does not happen with sad and mournful tunes, which are more suited to making listeners weep and die than making them laugh or live; for these tunes are composed of movements fit to engender sadness, and consequently to cause <term>defluxions</term> <note>In the medical theory of "humors," a defluxion was a discharge of harmful fluids from the head to the limbs or organs, thought to cause illness or paralysis.</note> upon the limbs, which finally render them paralytic and incapable of movement.

Nevertheless, all Musicians are of the contrary opinion, and both listeners and those who sing admit that they receive more pleasure from sad and languishing songs than from gay ones, for which it is not easy to find a reason so powerful that it makes all other contrary reasons vanish. However, I do not doubt that there is some reason for this prodigious effect which seems to combat all the laws of nature, since nature is made and preserved by pleasure.

Now, one may first consider that men have much more <term>melancholy</term> and <term>phlegm</term> than <term>bile</term> <note>These terms refer to the "Four Humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern human temperament and health.</note>, and that they take more after the earth than after the air or the Heavens; and that gay tunes, being of an aerial nature which represents fire, are not as suited to the nature of man as the

sad and languishing songs, which represent the earth, <term>melancholy</term>, and <term>phlegm</term> <note>In the 17th century, health was believed to be governed by four "humors" or bodily fluids; melancholy (black bile) and phlegm were associated with coldness, slowness, and sadness.</note>; and although I have proved in the 31st Proposition of the *Book of Sounds* that high-pitched sounds are more agreeable than low ones, because they participate more in the nature of air and fire; it does not follow, however, that sad tunes must be less agreeable than gay ones, especially since sad tunes are sung by high voices just as well as gay ones. But the reason taken from melancholy is not sufficient, since one encounters <term>bilious</term> men <note>Those with an abundance of "yellow bile," typically thought to be irritable or energetic.</note> who take more pleasure in sad songs than many melancholics do, so that one must rather take the reason from the nature of the sad song itself, than from that of the listeners, since all sorts of listeners take more pleasure in sad tunes than in gay ones—whether because men are more easily moved to compassion than to rejoicing, as is experienced in tragedies and the reading of elegies and sad histories which draw tears from the eyes, or because they dwell longer on the consideration of sad things than on those that are joyful and pleasant.

One must therefore consider the nature of sad tunes, which consists of several things: for the voice in sad tunes represents languor and sadness through its continuation, through its weakness, and through its tremblings; and the <term>semitones</term> and <term>sharps</term> <note>The original French uses "diefes," referring to the diesis or sharps, which were small melodic steps.</note> represent tears and groans by reason of their small intervals, which signify weakness. For the small intervals made when rising or falling are similar to children, the elderly, and those recovering from a long illness, who cannot walk with great strides and who cover little ground in a lot of time; for example, when one makes a <term>major semitone</term> while rising, one makes a movement that rises only by a fifteenth part of the preceding voice, and when one rises by a <term>minor semitone</term>, one only advances one's path by a twenty-fourth part of the sound that precedes it.

And when one is a long time passing through this interval, and staying on the note to which one has passed, this shows an even greater weakness, which imprints itself deep within the mind of the listener, because the dragging voice continues for a long time and gives the leisure to be considered and examined; whereas the movements of gay songs are so prompt that one does not have enough time to notice them, as they do not make a long enough impression on the mind. I do not wish to speak here of the "letter" <note>The lyrics or text of the song.</note>, which increases the sadness when it reminds us of the painful accidents of life by which we have been tormented, especially since sad tunes can exist without lyrics.

But it must be noted that all men are more subject to sadness than to joy; for if everyone wishes to reflect on the actions they perform, or on the thoughts they have when they are all alone, they will find ten sad ones for every one gay one. For sadness fell to us as our <term>inheritance</term> after original sin, and is almost natural to us; whereas joy only comes to us by chance and by accident, as happens in joyful companies where everyone strives to give contentment to their companion—which does not often succeed, and such a person has a laugh on their lips who has sadness in their heart. But it seems that one lets oneself be carried away too easily by the opinion of the common people in agreeing that there are "sad" tunes; one should rather say that they are all "gay" <note>In this context, meaning "pleasant" or "pleasing."</note>, since they bring contentment to the listen—

...listeners; so that it would first be necessary to examine if there can be sad tunes, and if there are, which they are, and for what reasons they are called sad, before asking why they are more pleasing. However, since the Masters of Music suppose that there are lamentable tunes, because they represent the movements of sadness, I do not wish to doubt it now, contenting myself with remarking that they are only called sad because of the relation they have to the voices used by those who express their sadness and their afflictions.

Now one would need to know what pleasure comes from sad things, and how it is engendered in the listeners, to know the reason why sad tunes please more than gay ones; this assumes a discussion of the passions and affections of man, which requires another place. I will only say that one can establish two species of sadness: one of which is moral, because its motives are drawn from the deprivation of a useful, pleasant, or honest good; and the other is natural, which comes from the <term>melancholic humor</term> <note>In traditional medicine, "melancholy" was one of the four humors (black bile). An excess was thought to cause gloominess and sluggishness.</note>, or from <term>phlegm</term> <note>The humor associated with being calm, cool, and sometimes slow or indifferent.</note>, when they "sin" by excess. Now, it seems that sad songs do not engender either type of sadness, but rather they only maintain it; this is why it is held that Music leaves the listener in the same humor in which it finds him. And if we follow reason, it shows that melancholics should receive more pleasure from gay tunes than from sad ones, because the abrupt and fast movements of gay songs are more proper for dissipating the excessive humor of melancholy than the slow and languishing movements of lamentable tunes—for contraries are cured by their contraries, if we follow the sentiments of <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC). His medical philosophy was based on "allopathy," or curing an ailment with its opposite (e.g., treating a cold disease with heat).</note> rather than those of <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>A Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541) who famously argued for "homeopathy," or the idea that "like cures like."</note>, who holds that likes are cured by their likes.

There is still another thing to consider in sadness, namely that the accounts of a sad thing, and of the strange accidents that have happened to men, touch us more than the account of what has happened to their advantage, although we have no interest in their disgraces or their advancement. This is because we are more easily inclined to envy the good of others—as if it were owed to us—than we are to rejoice in the evil that happens to them, because it seems that every kind of evil is contrary to us and destroys our nature. This is why songs that have a sad and tragic lyric move us to compassion, as if we felt a part of the evil; this can also happen because of the imagination we have of being able to fall into a similar accident, or from the memory of past afflictions and pains, which makes us remember the good that consolation brought us—for sad songs are a certain kind of consolation. But this matter requires entire discourses. One can meanwhile consider that the slow movements of sad tunes touch us and flatter us more delicately, and bring the spirit back to itself; the spirit then has more leisure to contemplate the beauty of the voice than when gay songs make it "exit" outside of itself through the <term>rarefaction</term> <note>The thinning or expansion of the blood or spirits, thought to be caused by heat or joy.</note> and boiling of the blood, and by faster and lighter movements. I leave aside several other things, the consideration of which is remarkable—for example, why the fifteenth and the twenty-fourth part of a movement is more proper for sad songs than the eighth, or

### On Songs

...a ninth part, for one only adds a fifteenth part of movement to make the major semitone, and a 24th to make the minor, which are suitable for representing sadness; whereas one adds <note>The OCR shows punctuation where numerical fractions for the major and minor tones—likely 1/8 and 1/9—would usually appear.</note> for the major tone, and for the minor tone which are used for gay songs.

Now it must be noted that a song is all the more sad the more semitones it has in succession, and consequently the Chromatic <note>The Chromatic scale in early modern music theory used successive semitones, often associated with intense emotion.</note> is suitable for singing sad airs, and the Diatonic <note>The standard scale of whole steps and half steps, considered more natural and stable.</note> for singing gay ones; and that it is very difficult to know if the minor semitone is sadder than the major semitone, and by how much it is more suitable for expressing sadness: which can similarly be said of the <term>Enharmonic diesis</term> <note>The smallest interval in ancient Greek music theory, much smaller than a semitone, often linked to the most refined or exotic emotions.</note>.

As for the contrary reasons I reported in favor of gay songs, one can first reply that the sadness conceived from lamentable songs does not destroy the <term>temperament</term> <note>In the medical science of the time, "temperament" was the balance of the four bodily humors. An imbalance led to illness.</note>, and that if it alters it, the spirit would rather deprive the body of some pleasure, and make it lose something of its temperament, than deprive itself of the great contentment it receives from lugubrious songs. But to understand this, it must be noted that music separates the spirit from the body in some manner, and puts it in a state where it is more suited to contemplation than to action, and consequently, when the song ceases, it finds itself quite astonished to see itself deprived of the great contentment it was receiving in the state of abstraction to which Music had transported it.

And because the sounds and movements of sad airs make a stronger impression on the spirit, they ravish it into a deeper speculation; and when it is forced to leave it, it seems to it that it exits a great light to re-enter very thick darkness. This being established, I say that one does not love sadness when one loves lamentable airs, but that one loves the state of separation in which the soul finds itself during the contemplation of these airs.

This demonstrates that the soul does not have bodily pleasure for its goal and end, and that it has no greater pleasure than when it enters back into itself to perform its functions with less dependence on the body, waiting until it can act like pure spirits and Angels in the dwelling of the blessed. And it can be said that the profound melancholy into which the soul enters in the presence of lamentable songs is not sadness properly speaking, but rather a path to reach wisdom, for which melancholy is more suitable than joy, which approaches madness and prevents reasoning and the functions of the spirit all the more as it is greater; from this it comes that some strangers from the New Worlds, having come to Europe, were astonished to see men laughing, and judged them mad according to the word of the Sage: <note>original: "Risum reputaui errorem"</note> *I considered laughter as an error*; and we do not read that our Lord ever laughed, but that he wept.

The other reasons only prove that gay airs excite external joy more, of which animals are capable, than do sad ones: but the internal contentment of the spirit is much greater in sad songs, especially since they lead it to the contempt of all things in the world, and to the esteem it must have for itself and for the author of <term>Archetypal harmony</term> <note>The divine, original "blueprint" of harmony created by God, of which earthly music is a mere reflection.</note>, as we shall say in the treatise on the music of the blessed. The same thing must be said of life, which gay airs approach...

### Second Book

<meta>catchword: eclipse</meta>

more than sad ones, for this life must only be understood as the corporeal, which has need of movement; whereas the life of the spirit is without movement, insofar as it only requires movements to perform its actions. The movements of sad songs, approaching closer to immobility, are more conforming to the spirit than those which partake more of movement. To this one may add that things that are continuous are sometimes not as agreeable as those that are interrupted, for the reason that too much continuity prevents variety, from which pleasure comes: hence it is that the surface of a perfectly polished and continuous steel mirror hurts the sight.

Now one may conclude from this entire discourse that gay airs are more suited to exciting exterior joy, which hinders the functions of the spirit, and particularly that of contemplation; and that sad airs are more suited to producing interior joy, which the understanding receives in its abstraction and in its retreat. For the earthly and gross <term>humors</term> <note>In 17th-century medicine, these were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to govern health and emotion.</note> dissipate and fall away in the presence of lugubrious airs, just as the vapors that obscure the air fall to the earth and vanish in the presence of the Sun: so that the spirit remains free and better tastes the pleasure of the Music; and as if it were beginning to separate itself from the body, it is ravished by a small sample of the beauty of eternal ideas.

And we experience that ecstasy is the most sublime pleasure, and the most spiritual and divine contentment of all those of which men are capable in this world; and nevertheless, those who are transported to this degree have no corporeal joy; on the contrary, their body is deprived of its operations, as if they were dead, while the soul enjoys the most sublime state it can have in this life, by which some explain this passage of Scripture: *Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.* <note>original: "Pretiosa in conspectu Domini mors sanctorum eius." (Psalm 116:15)</note>

Now the airs that are called sad bring the body closer to immobility and death, and the spirit closer to ravishment and ecstasy, as we shall prove in the discourse on the Music of the Hebrews, which they used for Prophecy.

We further experience that one cannot be attentive to vocal or mental prayer when one has run and worked, or when one has become angry, insofar as labor and violent passions agitate the blood and the other humors, which prevent the calm and repose of the spirit by their storms. And those who wish to enter into deep Meditation choose the shadows of the night and secluded places, so as not to be disturbed by external noises and movements, and to have the spirit reunited, and as if dead to corporeal things, to live a spiritual life animated by the contemplation of the eternal being. In this consists the true Philosophy that <term>Plato</term> <note>Specifically referring to Plato's *Phaedo*, where Socrates argues that philosophy is a "preparation for death."</note> calls the Meditation of death, insofar as it teaches us to leave mutable and corruptible things to unite ourselves with the immutable and the immortal, who takes his pleasure in the souls of true Philosophers. One can also find another reason in the greater artifice that the Masters use to compose sad songs, which are ordinarily more learned and have a greater multitude of beautiful touches than gay airs have.

As for gay songs, they trouble the humors and imitate the winter Sun, which raises the mists without being able to dissipate them, and they eclipse

I will only say here that it is difficult to know in what manner pleasure is engendered in the ear, and in the other senses, or in the imagination, and in the spirit, because we cannot perceive the configurations of the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In the 17th century, "animal spirits" were thought to be very fine fluids that acted as messengers, carrying sensory information from the organs to the brain.</note>, which conduct the varieties of sensory delight from the exterior sense to the common sense; and even though we might be able to observe them, we would not know the reason why one configuration or movement gives more pleasure than another.

Now it would be necessary to note everything that pleases each exterior sense most, before determining how pleasure is made, in order to see how all these pleasures differ, and the ways in which the exterior senses perceive their objects, and if there is something common to which they relate: for one cannot make a certain judgment if one considers only the nature of the objects without having regard for the senses, insofar as they must both concur to produce pleasure.

We can nevertheless establish as a foundation that what is well-ordered and arranged pleases more than what is confused and in disorder, for the reason that order is the source of knowledge, and disorder is the origin of confusion, in which no one takes pleasure, unless they have a confused and disordered spirit. This can be observed in many effects of art, some of which are better proportioned than others, and please all the more as they are better ordered and arranged. Now this order is derived from the relationship that the parts have with one another, and with the whole, or that they have with one of the things to which they are compared, for this proportion and the just relationship of the parts facilitates knowledge, and in no way offends the eye or the ear, which together are the two senses susceptible to a more innocent pleasure, and which most closely approach <term>honest pleasure</term> <note>This refers to a refined, virtuous, or intellectual pleasure that elevates the soul, rather than a base or purely physical sensation.</note>.

### PROPOSITION XXVII.

->*To explain all the movements used in French airs, and particularly in Ballets, with an example, and alongside them the Rhythmic arts.*<-

EVEN THOUGH the movements which serve <term>Airs</term> <note>A song or melody, particularly one written for the voice or for dancing.</note> and dances belong to <term>Rhythmics</term> <note>Originally a Greek concept, this refers to the study of musical time, meter, and the duration of notes.</note>, of which we have not yet spoken, it was nevertheless necessary to treat them here, in order to make understood the different kinds of Airs and songs used by the French: but it is so easy to understand everything concerning these movements that it is not necessary to make a separate book for them, since the most excellent <term>metric feet</term> <note>Rhythmical units borrowed from classical poetry, such as the dactyl or iamb, which governed the timing of music.</note>, which gave the name and birth to the Rhythmics of the Greeks, are practiced in the airs of Ballets, in songs for dancing, and in all the others.

# Second Book

Now these feet may be called **movements**, so as to accommodate the manner of speaking used by our practitioners and composers of songs; this is why I shall henceforth use this term, to join Theory to Practice, after having given the example of a <term>ballet</term> <note>A "ballet" in this period was a staged suite of dances and music performed for the court, not just the athletic dance form we know today.</note> which has sixteen different movements. ### of Songs.

I leave aside an infinity of other Examples, in order to add the measured movements, which I explain with the two ordinary characters used to mark short and long syllables in all types of Poetry, just as one does to mark this Trochaic verse, whose long syllables have this
<gloss>- - u - - - u u - u -</gloss>
so that [your servants] may resonate with loose vocal cords <note>original: "ut queant laxis resonare fibris." This is the first line of the *Hymnus in Ioannem*, the hymn used to name the notes of the musical scale (Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La).</note>
little straight line (-) for their sign, and the shorts have this semicircle (u): it must therefore be noted that a brief time is in movement what a point is in Geometry, or unity in numbers; and that the first foot, or movement, is composed of two brief times; the second of one brief and one long, and so on for those that follow, of which the first twelve are simple, and the last eleven are composed; for as for the others which are composed of a simple and a composed, or of two composed ones, I do not wish to speak of them, insofar as they are nothing other than a repetition of the preceding ones, or that they should rather be called verses, or meters, than feet or movements. Now although instead of the brief time one might put two, four, or eight times so short that they do not last longer than the brief time, and though they have a different grace and very different effects, nonetheless they are taken for the same thing regarding the species of time or movement; as happens when for the <term>minim</term> <note>A musical note value; in this period, it served as a standard unit of time, similar to a half-note.</note>, which signifies the first part of the iambic foot, one puts two <term>crotchets</term> <note>Quarter notes.</note>, four <term>quavers</term> <note>Eighth notes.</note>, eight <term>semiquavers</term> <note>Sixteenth notes.</note>, or sixteen <term>demisemiquavers</term> <note>Thirty-second notes.</note>, of which I speak elsewhere.

If our Composers have such delicate ears that they fear these Greek terms might offend them, they may use such names as please them—for example, those they give to their songs, of which they say these have the movement of the Courante, those of the Sarabande, and so on for the others: or those noticed in the different beats of Drums, of blacksmiths <note>original: "mareschaux"; the rhythmic striking of an anvil was a common metaphor for the origins of musical intervals and rhythm.</note>, of flails with which several people together beat the wheat in barns and on threshing floors, and many others observed in various arts. <header>### Second Book of Songs.</header>

It would be easy to provide the method for this, since Terentianus <note>Terentianus Maurus, a 2nd-century Latin grammarian who wrote on poetic meters.</note>, Hephaestion <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century, known for his manual on Greek meters.</note>, Saint Augustine, and many others have left us records of all their types of feet and verses. However, it seems that experience has shown that these do not sit well with this art, and that French music requires a full freedom, without being restricted to any kind of regulated poetry. Nonetheless, if such a project were to succeed, one might expect perfection from Monsieur du Chemin, a Lawyer at Parliament, who has already set many Odes of Pindar <note>An Ancient Greek lyric poet.</note> and Horace <note>A leading Roman lyric poet.</note> to music according to the measure and the proper movement required by the nature of each verse. And if anyone desires to know everything pertaining to metric poetry, I have prepared an entire treatise on it which I will share very freely; I only add here that one will find almost everything that can be said on this subject in the 57th question of our *Commentaries on the first book of Holy Scripture* <note>original: "Commentaires sur le premier liure de la saincte Escriture." This refers to Mersenne's massive 1623 work, *Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim*.</note>. Our musicians will have different types of <term>measured verse</term> <note>A style of poetry (*vers mesurés*) that attempted to replicate the quantitative meters of Greek and Latin in the French language.</note> if they exactly observe the long and short syllables of our rhymed verses; these will perhaps succeed much better for <term>airs</term> <note>A light, melodic song for one or more voices.</note> than the measured verses which I shall speak of in another place.

Regarding this, it is good to advise the Choir Masters who compose <term>motets</term> <note>A sacred vocal composition.</note> and other pieces of music where the text is in Latin, that everything they have sung will have much more grace if they observe the long and short syllables. In doing so, they will encounter almost every type of verse used by Hephaestion and others without even searching for them—though they are not so strictly bound to make every syllable long or short that they cannot dispense with it. For instance, they might lengthen the first short syllable of a word by imitating the pronunciation of prose; for example, one lengthens the first syllable of *Lord* <note>original: "Dominus"</note> and of *God* <note>original: "Deus"</note>, etc.

Now, those who understand Latin will receive a singular pleasure in reading the six books that Saint Augustine wrote on Music, and will see the value he places on rhythmic movements, how he finds and notes them in all things in the world, and how he raises the spirit to God by their means. This is what I similarly desire for those who read these books on Songs, so that there may be no recreation from which one does not draw help to carry the will toward its duty, which consists particularly in worshipping the eternal decrees of the Divine Majesty.

Those who wish to learn the particular rules used to create airs and songs fit for raising the spirit to God will find them in the books on Composition and Art, or on the Method of Singing Well.

# Preface, and Notice to the Reader.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap 'L' featuring floral and foliage patterns begins the first paragraph.</image-desc>

The first thing that I desire from those who will take the trouble to read these books consists in correcting the printing errors, of which I will place some of the most important at the end of this Preface, so that once corrected they do not delay or hinder the reader in any way.

The second thing to which one must pay heed is that I do not repeat here several things that one might desire, because I have already produced specific Treatises on them. For example, I do not include the divisions, definitions, and descriptions of the different types of Music, insofar as I have already given them in the first 17 Theorems of the first book of the <term>Treatise on Universal Harmony<note>Mersenne refers to his earlier work *Traité de l'Harmonie Universelle* (1627), not to be confused with the massive 1636 work this preface introduces.</note></term> printed in the year 1627, where I explain them so amply that it is difficult to add more, whether one looks at the subject and the object—both material and formal—of Music, namely Sound, of which I speak at great length in the 7th, 8th, 9th, and 10th Theorems; or whether one considers Harmony as Speculative, Practical, Divine, Created, Mundane, Human, Instrumental, etc. To this one can add the two Greek Authors whom I have translated into French, namely <term>Bacchius<note>Bacchius Geron, a Greek author who wrote an introduction to music theory.</note></term> and <term>Euclid<note>The famous Greek mathematician, to whom a treatise on music, the *Section of the Canon*, was attributed.</note></term>, whose Music I have provided in its entirety in the 17th Theorem with specific Tables to facilitate its understanding. And then I have given all the principles of Music, both Theoretical and Practical, in the other Theorems that follow up to the 30th, which comprises the best of what <term>Salinas<note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a Spanish music theorist and organist known for his work on intervals and temperament.</note></term> has in his books. As for the second book, it contains all the comparisons that can be made between Sounds and harmony and all the things in the world that are proportional, so that it is not easy to add to the 15 Theorems of the said book.

I have also treated several other difficulties concerning this subject in two specific books, namely in the *Preludes to Harmony* and in the *Harmonic Questions* in the year 1634. For example: what should be the Horoscope of the perfect Musician, where I show by the principles of Astrology that one can predict nothing of the temperament or the life of men through the knowledge one has of the Stars, and where I place three horoscopes of a perfect Musician according to the opinion of three excellent Astrologers of this century. I have also treated the temperament, capacity, and science that a perfect Musician must have; the Judge of concerts—whether it is the ear or the understanding; whether it is expedient to use the <term>Enharmonic genre<note>A style of ancient Greek music using very small intervals, smaller than a semitone.</note></term>; at what point a string, equal in all its parts and pulled equally, would break; why the Greeks regulated all their Music on <term>Fourths<note>The musical interval of a perfect fourth, which was the fundamental building block of ancient Greek scales (tetrachords).</note></term>; why Sounds serve to form the morals of men; what judgment should be made of those who hate Music, and if it deserves the attention of men of great judgment and good spirit; whether it belongs to the learned or the ignorant to judge the quality of concerts; whether Theory is preferable to Practice; whether the Greeks were better Musicians than the French; and from whence it comes that nature and men take pleasure in diversity, of which I speak in the 14th Physical Question. I leave aside what I have said of ratios, proportions, <term>means<note>original: "medietez," referring to mathematical averages such as arithmetic, geometric, or harmonic means used to calculate musical intervals.</note></term>,

It will be difficult to demonstrate to them that the <term>Fifth<note>The musical interval of a fifth.</note></term> is exactly in a <term>sesquialter ratio<note>A 3:2 ratio, the mathematical definition of a perfect fifth in the Pythagorean system.</note></term>, and the tone in a <term>sesquioctave ratio<note>A 9:8 ratio, the mathematical definition of a "major whole tone."</note></term>, or if it misses by a thousandth part, etc.

Now, although one may set whatever order one wishes among these books—which we have been constrained to begin with new page numbers and alphabets—nevertheless those who prefer harmony to Physics can begin to read them with these four books of *Consonances*, which were in effect the first printed; followed by the book of *Dissonances*, of *Genres*, of the *Species* of each Consonance, of *Modes*, and of *Composition*. And then it will be good to read the book on the *Voice and Songs*; and those on stringed, wind, and percussion instruments; and finally that of *Sounds*, and of the movement of all kinds of bodies. By contrast, those who prefer Physics and Mechanics can begin differently, such that they could put the book on the *Movement of all kinds of bodies* first; that of the movement and other properties of strings second; that of *Sounds* third; that of *Songs* fourth; that of the *Art of Singing Well*, etc. fifth; that of *Consonances* seventh <note>Mersenne's numbering in this list skips the sixth book.</note>; that of *Dissonances* eighth; that of *Genres and Modes* ninth; that of *Composition* tenth; and then the four on Stringed Instruments, and the three others on Wind and Percussion Instruments; so that this work will contain 17 or 18 books if it is completed.

The fourth thing of which I notify the Reader is that I have sometimes expanded quite extensively on some Propositions that one may omit if one wishes, though they are very entertaining and contain several things worth noting, such as Propositions 2, 3, and 4 of the book on *Consonances*. # Notice to the Reader.

...those whom they will displease (if indeed one can find anyone who is displeased by the thoughts one has of God while treating the human sciences), but only for those who rejoice in the continual relationship that one makes of all things to God. This is most just, and consequently most honorable, since they belong entirely to Him, and it is never out of place to speak of Him as one should, since He is never absent from any place.

The fifth thing concerns ratios, proportions, and their <term>means<note>In mathematics, a "mean" is a middle value between two extremes. Mersenne is discussing the "harmonic mean," which is essential for calculating musical intervals.</note> or middles, of which I speak in the 34th Proposition of the first book; in which it must be noted that the fifth method, which I said was not general, can be made universal by proceeding in this fashion. One will find the harmonic mean of the **Major Tenth** <note>original: "Dixiesme majeure"</note>—that is to say, of the <term>double sesquialteral ratio<note>A ratio of 5:2. In music theory, "sesquialtera" refers to a 3:2 ratio; "double sesquialtera" indicates a more complex ratio relating to the Major Tenth.</note> of 5 to 2—if one subtracts the smaller term from the larger, and multiplies the difference by the smaller, for the product will be the numerator, and the sum of the two terms of the ratio will be the denominator; but one must always repeat the smaller term before the fraction, and if the numerator is larger than the denominator, one must reduce the numbers into whole numbers. I therefore subtract two from five, leaving three, which is the difference between five and two; and then I multiply three by two to get the numerator six; the denominator comes from the addition of five to two, which makes seven, so that 2 <sup>6</sup>/<sub>7</sub> is the harmonic mean between 5 and 2. One will find all the rest in the same manner.

Now it is easy to find this mean in several other ways: for example, when three fractions have the same numerator, and their denominators are in <term>Arithmetic progression<note>A sequence of numbers where the difference between each consecutive number is constant (e.g., 2, 3, 4).</note>, the middle fraction is the harmonic mean between the two extremes, as one sees in these three fractions <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub>, <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub>, <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub>, for <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub> is the harmonic mean. And if the fractions have different numerators, it is necessary to reduce them to the same numerator, in order to find very promptly the harmonic mean between all the proposed terms: from this it follows that all fractions that have unity for their numerator, and which follow in natural progression, such as <sup>1</sup>/<sub>1</sub>, <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub>, <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub>, <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub>, <sup>1</sup>/<sub>5</sub>, <sup>1</sup>/<sub>6</sub>, etc. to infinity, perpetually have harmonic means; for <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub> is the harmonic mean between <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub> and <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub>; and <sup>1</sup>/<sub>4</sub> is the mean between <sup>1</sup>/<sub>3</sub> and <sup>1</sup>/<sub>5</sub>; and so with the others to infinity.

One also finds this harmonic mean by adding the two terms of the ratio, and multiplying them by half the product <note>Mersenne's mathematical phrasing here describes a specific method of scaling ratios to find whole-number means.</note>, for the sum that comes from the two extremes being multiplied gives the said middle: for example, fifteen is the harmonic mean between 20 and 12, which are in a ratio of five to three; these being added make eight, of which the half (4) multiplying them, one has 20 and 12; and three multiplying five, one has fifteen for the said middle.

I wish to add yet another way, which supposes that three numbers follow in Arithmetic progression, such as 2, 3, 4; this being posed, the first number that can be divided by these three numbers—namely twelve—being divided, gives 6, 4, 3, among which 4 is the harmonic mean. Where it must be noted that these six numbers—that is to say, the divisors and the quotients—are in <term>alternate ratio<note>A term from Euclidean geometry referring to the rearrangement of terms in a proportion.</note>, since 4 is to 6 as 2 is to 3; 3 is to 4 as 3 is to 4; and 2 is to 4 as 3 is to 6; although the three quotients are not continually proportional like the three divisors. But since this mean serves so little in Music, as I have shown in several places, I shall not dwell on it further: those who love the knowledge and practice of ratios, and of...

The sixth thing concerns in general all the difficulties I have touched upon, for which I do not pretend to have given the true solutions such that I would not be very happy to receive better ones from anyone; and I have even included several that do not entirely satisfy me, in order to give the best minds cause to search for such good reasons for everything I have proposed, or everything they might wish to add, so that they satisfy everyone. # BOOK ONE.

## ON CONSONANCES.

### FIRST PROPOSITION.

->*To determine whether there are Consonances and Dissonances in Music, and what they are.*<-

Those who take no pleasure in Music, or who hold all things to be indifferent, deny that there are Consonances or Dissonances, both because they take no pleasure in either, and because they believe nothing in nature is inherently agreeable or disagreeable, since what pleases one person displeases another. Furthermore, what pleasure is there in perceiving that the air is struck two or three times by one string while it is struck four or six times by another? Is the ear and the imagination not more content to remain at rest than to be worked by forty-eight vibrations of air <note>original: "battemens d'air"; the author is describing the physical frequency of sound waves.</note> on one side, and by ninety-six on the other, as happens when one plays an Octave?

Moreover, why are the vibrations that produce the Second or the minor Seventh more disagreeable than those that produce the Fifth or the Third? Certainly, this difficulty is not one of the least in Music; for if true pleasure consists in preserving or increasing what we possess, it is difficult to demonstrate that the air vibrations that create Consonances <term>Consonances<note>Combinations of notes that sound pleasant or "stable" together, such as a perfect fifth.</note></term> aid in our preservation, or increase the perfection of the body or the mind, since we see through experience that those who do not love Music, and who consider it useless or at most indifferent, are no less perfect in body and mind than those who love it with passion.

Nevertheless, it is quite difficult to find men who take as much pleasure in hearing a Dissonance <term>Dissonance<note>A tension-filled or "clashing" musical interval that typically requires resolution to a consonance.</note></term>—for example, the Second or the Triton <term>Triton<note>An interval of three whole tones, famous for its unstable and harsh sound; it was often avoided in early music.</note></term>—as in hearing the Octave and the Fifth. And although some may be found who maintain that there is no pleasure in hearing Consonances, or that there are no Consonances or Dissonances at all, they will be forced to admit that the Triton or the Seconds are more disagreeable than the Twelfth or the Octave, if they give themselves the leisure to consider and hear these intervals; and consequently, even if they will not confess that there are agreeable intervals, they will admit that some are more agreeable than others; or that they imagine—

<header>Book One</header>

...find something slightly less disagreeable in the *Octave* than in the *Triton* <note>The Triton is a harsh musical interval of three whole tones, historically called "the devil in music."</note>; and if they dare not assert anything, for fear of harming their Pyrrhonian liberty <note>A reference to the followers of Pyrrho, ancient Greek skeptics who believed one should suspend judgment on all matters to achieve peace of mind.</note> and losing the *Unison* and equilibrium of their spirit—which they use to suspend their judgment—they still will not dare to deny that dissonant intervals are disagreeable and that *Consonances* are agreeable, since they fear affirmation as much as negation.

But since everyone else confesses and maintains that the intervals we call consonant are agreeable, and that dissonant ones are disagreeable, and because we have sufficiently good reasons to prove this truth, there is no danger in asserting that there are *Consonances* and *Dissonances*. I shall treat these amply in this book, once I have responded to the preceding objections. The first of these opposes all those who find nothing agreeable in nature, which cannot happen: for there is no man, nor even any animal, who does not receive some pleasure, since all men love something, and it is not possible for that which one loves to be unpleasing while one loves it. Now, one finds no man who does not love life and that which is necessary for the preservation of his being; consequently, there is something agreeable, whether the same thing pleases everyone or only some. And if something is found that is loved by all, it will be similarly agreeable to the whole world.

Those who desire to see from where one must derive the judgment of sounds and their agreeableness may read the 6th question of the *Preludes to Harmony* <note>The author is referring to his own earlier work, likely the *Préludes de l'harmonie universelle* (1634).</note>, where I determine whether the sense of hearing should be the judge of the sweetness of Concerts, or whether this office belongs to the understanding. Furthermore, I have reported many things on this subject in the first *Harmonic Question*, in which I examine quite amply whether *Music* is agreeable, whether learned men should take pleasure in it, and what judgment should be made of those who do not enjoy it or who despise it. One will find in the same place an excellent *Skeptic* discourse, whose reasons, when joined to the thirty found in the question, make a fairly ample treatise. There are still other *Harmonic Questions* following that discourse, from which one may draw light for the difficulties of this first proposition.

As for the reasons why the vibrations of air <note>original: "battemens d'air"; the author is describing the physical frequency of sound waves before the modern term "frequency" was standard.</note> that produce *Consonances* are agreeable, and those that produce *Dissonances* are disagreeable, I shall explain them in the particular discourse of each *Consonance*, and in the one I shall provide regarding the Beauty and Proportion that make things agreeable. But so that one may have some slight knowledge of the *Consonances* of which we shall henceforth speak, I shall explain them here briefly in the tables that follow. These show all the simple *Consonances*. The first table explains their terms in such a way that the larger number represents the longest or thickest string, beginning with the *Unison* (marked by unity) and then the others following from the smallest *Consonance*—namely from the *Minor Third*—up to the *Octave*. However, the second table, which begins with the *Octave* and ends with the *Minor Third*, represents the movements or vibrations of the air that create the said *Consonances*. This is why its smaller numbers at the bottom represent the larger strings, whose returns [vibrations] are slower; and the larger numbers at the top signify the greater number of returns and vibrations made by the smaller strings.

### *Consonances.*

Regarding the replicas <note>musical "repliques" refer to octave equivalents, like a tenth being a replica of a third</note> or repetitions of the Consonances, I shall speak of them elsewhere. Nevertheless, I wish to point out all the Consonances that are natural, in order to confirm that there are Consonances in nature, since the Trumpet teaches them to us. For when one plays it, and begins with the lowest sound of all those it can make, one cannot move from this first sound to any closer sound than the Octave; if one wishes to rise higher than that second sound, one must produce a full Fifth; and if one goes further, one cannot make a smaller interval than the Fourth. Thus, these three intervals follow the natural progression of numbers; and if one makes a 4th and a 5th interval, one will produce the Major Third and the Minor Third, the higher note of which is a Twelfth <note>An octave plus a fifth</note> away from the lowest note of the Trumpet.
