# Book Second

### *The Twenty-Second*

The Twenty-second <note>An interval spanning three full octaves (7 + 7 + 7 + 1 = 22 notes)</note>, of which the first column contains 22 notes; the second column contains the numbers that explain the ratios of each degree following the true Theory, which accounts for the inequality of sounds—that is to say, which establishes the major tone and the minor tone, and consequently the just Thirds and Sixths. This theory uses smaller numbers to signify the fewer number of vibrations <note>original: "retours", referring to the oscillations of a string</note> made by the longest or thickest strings, and larger numbers to express the greater number of vibrations made by the smallest strings. This is not the case in the third column, because it contains the Pythagorean numbers, which possess only the major tone and have no other semitone but the Pythagorean one <note>The "limma," which is slightly smaller than a modern semitone</note>, of which we shall speak elsewhere. The fourth column contains the syllables that must be pronounced for each note: where it should be noted that I use the new manner of singing the syllables of the first Octave, in order to show how one can sing without mutations <note>term: muances (mutations). A complex medieval system where singers had to switch between overlapping six-note scales (hexachords). The author is proposing a simpler seven-note system.</note> by using the syllable **BI** instead of **MI**, and by saying *Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, bis vt*, instead of *Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, re, mi, fa*, which follow in ascending order to complete the Trisdiapason <note>term: Trisdiapason. A Greek-derived term for a three-octave range.</note> of this table. However, I shall explain this manner of singing more at length in the treatise on the Method and Art of Singing Well. The fifth column shows all the Consonances that are within three Octaves, that is, within the Twenty-second; and the last contains the Dissonances, which I shall treat more particularly in several propositions: for it is enough for now to consider everything we have just said in the following table.

# Of Consonances.
A iii <note>This is a "signature mark" used by early printers to help binders assemble the book's pages in the correct order.</note>

Now we must begin with the **Unison**, since it is simpler than the **Consonances**, yet less simple than a single sound. For it is not possible to create a Unison unless one uses at least two different sounds; thus, the Unison is as far removed from the simplicity of a single sound as the ratio of equality is removed from unity <note>In period mathematics, "unity" (the number 1) was often considered the source of all numbers rather than a number itself; similarly, the author argues a single sound is the source of music, but a Unison requires two sounds acting as one.</note>. However, one cannot compare sound with unity in all respects, because sound is composed of several <term>air vibrations</term> <note>original: "battemens d'air". The author is describing frequency—the physical pulses of air that create pitch—before the modern term "frequency" was standard.</note>, whereas unity is not composed of anything at all. Furthermore, sound is material, and unity is immaterial; finally, sound depends on the ear and the air, while unity depends only on God or the understanding. But I shall speak more amply on the difference between the Unison and a single sound in the proposition that follows.

### COROLLARY I.

If one understands the last figure of this proposition, and particularly the second column which contains the smallest numbers, one could restore the whole of Music theory, even if it were lost. One would know the Theory better than all those who have preceded us and who have written on it: for the smallest number expresses the number of air vibrations that make the sound of an **8-foot Organ pipe**; and the largest number signifies the smallest of the vibrations of a **one-foot pipe**. From this, one can conclude the number of vibrations made by the other sounds of the **Twenty-second** <note>An interval spanning three octaves.</note>, and even those necessary to produce whatever sound one might desire.

### COROLLARY II.

I could have treated several difficulties in this proposition—for example, whether animals make a distinction between **Consonances** and **Dissonances**, and if some please them more than others; how many Consonances and Dissonances there are, and why there is only a certain number of them, etc. But I shall speak of these in other propositions, for it suffices here to know that Consonances are made of two or more sounds whose conjunction is pleasing to the ear, and of which the first is called the **Unison**, which I treat in the following propositions.

### PROPOSITION XV.

->*To determine the difference between a sound and the Unison, and what the origin and cause of the Unison is.*<-

Many are often astonished by the questions proposed, because they do not know the difficulty encountered therein; but when they have considered the reasons one has for doubting, they admit that the said questions deserve to be proposed. Such is the case here, where the difficulty consists in knowing what difference there is between the Unison and a sound. For if one considers two vibrations of the same sound and compares them together, one will find that they make a Unison, and consequently that the parts of a single sound can make a Unison. And because the two parts of the same sound cannot make a Unison if they are not joined together, and they cannot make a sound if they are not disunited—that is to say, if they do not have their duration in different times—it follows that the Unison is, or seems, simpler than sound, or at least more conjoined and united. For even though the hearing is not subtle enough to discern the discontinuity or the suc—

# Book One

<note>This page continues the sentence from the previous page.</note> succession of the beats of air that create sound; nevertheless, they truly follow one after another and do not strike the ear at the same time, properly speaking.

It does not follow at all, however, that the **Unison** <note>The sounding of the same pitch by two different voices or instruments.</note> is simpler than a single sound, as we have said previously; for one could say that a single sound is twice as simple, since it is never made of more than a single beat of air at any one time. For example, each beat of air that produces the sound of an open four-foot **Organ pipe** lasts 1/48th of a second, so that each individual beat produces a sound.

But a **Unison** cannot be created without two beats of air occurring at the same time: from this, it appears that it is half as simple as a single sound, and consequently that the **Unison** originates from sound as its source. It must nonetheless be noted that the two beats which produce a perfect **Unison** have almost the same effect as a single beat of air, provided that single beat is as strong as the two others combined. For although voices, strings, or the sounds of other instruments almost never possess as great an equality as two beats of air that touch or follow each other immediately within the same sound, nevertheless, the two sounds or beats of two strings on a **Lute** or **Spinet** <note>A small, plucked keyboard instrument related to the harpsichord.</note>—when said strings are made of the same material and have the same length, thickness, and tension, and are struck or plucked from their natural position with equal force—are more equal than two beats that follow one another within a single sound. This is because the first beat is larger and stronger than the second, as I have demonstrated elsewhere. Thus, if those two successive beats could be joined together, they would not create as perfect a **Unison** as the two sounds of the aforementioned strings, whose two uniting beats are as large and strong as each other. From this, it follows that the first type of **Unison** would be similar to that made by two voices where one is stronger or fuller than the other. Now, just as we require several beats of air to create a sound that can be perceived by the sense of hearing (though it is difficult to determine the exact number of these beats), several beats from two strings are also required to make the **Unison** perceptible to the ear.

### COROLLARY I.

One can conclude from this proposition that there are no "low" or "high" <note>original: "graves ou aigus"</note> sounds other than the smaller or larger multitude of air beats occurring at the same time. Consequently, it would be better to say, properly speaking, that one perceives a certain number of air beats rather than saying one hears a low or high sound; though one reflects the other, and one is the cause while the other is the effect.

The same can be said of the beats that produce the **Unison** and the other <term>Consonances</term> <note>Musical intervals that sound pleasing or stable to the ear.</note>: for example, the **Octave** is nothing other than two air beats compared to one air beat. Thus, one could say that two birds flying, where one beats the air twice as fast as the other, produce an **Octave**; for even though we do not hear those beats, they nonetheless create sounds that could be heard by ears more sensitive than our own. The same must be said of all other air beats made by cannonballs and other missiles thrown through the air.

->On Consonances.<-

### COROLLARY II.

It also follows from this discourse that it does not matter if one of the **beats** <note>original: "battemens"; in 17th-century acoustics, this refers to the individual pulses or vibrations of air that constitute a sound wave.</note> that makes up a part of the same sound, or of the **Consonances**, is larger or stronger than the other beat, provided they occur at the same time; for although one has a hundred degrees of strength and the other a hundred degrees of weakness, if they last as long as one another they will produce the same sound if they follow one another. And if they are joined, they will produce the **Unison**; and if one occurs twice as fast as the other, they will produce the **Octave**. But I have spoken of these beats in another place, and I shall say many more things about them in the particular discourse on Consonances, which I begin with the **Unison**, which takes its origin from sound, as has been seen in this proposition. But we must now consider the other difficulties of the Unison—for example, whether it is a Consonance; whether it is more agreeable than the other Consonances; what its nature and definition are, and what its effects are, etc.

## PROPOSITION III.

### *To explain in what manner the Unison takes its origin from sound.*

Excellent minds are not always satisfied with knowing the origin and the beginning of things, and knowing the cause of effects, unless they also know how they were produced, even though the manner is often unknown to us; and as soon as we are taught the cause of an effect, we ask in what manner the cause produced that effect. For example, when **Theology** teaches us that God produced the world, we ask how—whether He produced it necessarily or freely, whether He made it by His power or by His will, etc.

Now, since we wish to penetrate **Music** to the very first root of its proportions, it is reasonable to consider how the **Unison** takes its origin from sound. This is very easy if one imagines sound as a straight line, which is represented by the string of a **Monochord** <term>Monochord: An ancient scientific instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundboard with a movable bridge, used to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</term>, or of another instrument that makes a sound; for if one divides the said string in the middle with a bridge, or with the finger, the two parts of the string being touched at the same time will produce the **Unison**, as is seen in string **A B**, which, being divided in the middle at point **C**, results in strings **A C** and **C B** being perfectly equal, whose sounds produce the Unison. Thus, the division of sound into two equal parts creates the Unison; for **A B** strikes the air only once in the same time that **A C** or **C B** strikes it twice, and consequently one has four beats for one, because each side of the string strikes it twice in the same time the entire string strikes it once.

This is why it must be said that the origin of the Unison comes from the division of time and of the string, or of other bodies, and from the multiplication of movements, and that one can say that resolution and composition concur equally together—

<image-desc>A horizontal line representing a string, with the letter 'A' at the left end, 'B' at the right end, and 'C' at the midpoint.</image-desc>

for each return of **A C** occurs twice as fast as each return of **A B**. From this one can conclude that all Music consists in the relation and the ratio that is made from one sound to another; for if one did not compare the two sounds of **A C** and **C B** together, there would be no Unison, just as there would be no...

Book One

of sound of which one can judge, if one did not consider the speed of the air **beats** <note>original: "battemens"; pulses of air that create frequency.</note> that produce the sound.

One can, however, consider the origin of the **Unison** in another way: for if one takes a **string** <note>original: "chorde"; usually referring to a string on a monochord, a scientific instrument used to measure musical intervals.</note> equal to B A, it will make a Unison with it without using division; so that addition, which is a species of multiplication, suffices to produce the said Unison. Nevertheless, it is easier to find it by division, both because it is easier to have one string than to have two, and because one does not need a new tensioning nor experimentation to know if the two different and separate strings are equally tensioned—for the division one makes of A B at point C gives two equally tensioned strings.

And if the maxim of **Philosophy** is true, which teaches that one must always choose the shortest path in order to avoid superfluous things and multitude when unity suffices, it follows that the origin of the Unison is better taken from the division of the sound, or of the string, than from the comparison of a new sound or a new string equal to B A. Consequently, the Unison comes from the first division, which is the easiest of all divisions, and from which we shall draw the origin of the **Octave** after the discourses on the Unison.

### COROLLARY I.

It seems that when the mind allows itself to be carried away to the consideration of creatures which have their origin from God, it can imagine that they come in some manner from the division He has made of His ideas from Himself, of which they are a rough sketch and an imperfect image, just as the Unison is the portrait and image of the sound. And this is perhaps what **Plato** meant by comparing duality to unity; although these comparisons, and all the others drawn from dependent beings, are too distant and too imperfect to make us conceive of His immense greatness, which has no more relationship with sounds than the immobile has with the mobile, or being with nothingness. This is why it suffices us now to adore Him in spirit and in the truth of faith, while we await the dwelling place where He will reveal to us the splendor of His divinity.

### COROLLARY II.

It must be noted that what I have said of the two beats or the two parts of the sound that make the Unison should similarly be understood of 4, 6, 8, 12, or whatever other number of beats of the same sound one wishes. For example, if one compares the first 48 beats or returns of the string that is at the Unison with an **organ pipe** of 4 feet, open, with the second 48 beats of the same string—that is to say, if one compares the movement of the string or the air that occurs in the first second of an hour with that of the second second—one will have the Unison, which is nothing other than the same sound repeated or multiplied.

### COROLLARY III.

If the speed of the air's movement alone made the high-pitched sound, one could say that all the **Consonances** <note>original: "Consonances"; intervals that sound stable and pleasant together, like the octave or fifth.</note> would come from the same sound, insofar as the first part of the first return of the string is faster than the second part, and as one...

<header>On Consonances.</header>

...that one can find enough different speeds in the **vibrations** <note>original: "retours"; literally "returns," referring to the back-and-forth motion of a vibrating string.</note> that make the same sound to account for all **Consonances** <note>Intervals that sound harmonious or stable.</note> and even **Dissonances** <note>Intervals that sound clashing or unstable.</note>. But since all the vibrations of the **string** <note>original: "chorde."</note> only continue the same sound, and since the two-thousandth vibration of the string is no lower or higher <note>original: "graue ou aigu."</note> than the first or second, it follows that these vibrations, when joined together, can only produce the **Unison**; unless one says that the sound of a string or another body contains within itself all sounds, because of the different **pulses** <note>original: "battemens."</note> of air produced by each point or part of the string moving at a different speed; for the parts move faster as they are closer to the middle; although the equal speed of each vibration of the entire string determines the sound such that it always seems equally low or high. For there is no likelihood in saying that the ear is mistaken, and that it is so influenced and preoccupied by the sound of the previous vibration that it is no longer capable of judging the sound of the other vibrations; since we experience that someone who arrives at the end of the vibrations, and who has not heard the sound of the first ones, finds the same sound as someone who heard the sound of the first vibrations. For if the first person measures the sound of the first tremblings of the string with an **organ pipe**, and the second person also measures the sound of the last tremblings with a pipe, it will be found that the two pipes are in Unison.

### COROLLARY IV.

Since each vibration of the string produces a sound that is equally low or high, it follows that this sound contains several Unisons. For when the string trembles 2,000 times, one can say that it comprises one thousand Unisons, or the Unison one thousand times, insofar as if one adds the two tremblings that immediately follow each other, they will create the Unison. But it must be noted that the Unison of two pulses that follow each other immediately is more perfect than that of two that are distant; and consequently, the first and the last vibration, when compared and added together, make the most imperfect Unison of all those found within the same sound.

### COROLLARY V.

It should also be noted that the Unison can come from the same pulse of air, or the same trembling of a string. For if the pulse has, for example, 2 degrees of force, and one divides this force into two equal parts, one will create the Unison, provided that each part of the sound lasts as long as the other. But because one cannot divide the force without also dividing the sound, and because the sound—insofar as it is sound—can only be divided by becoming higher, it is better to consider the sound produced by a single vibration, or pulse of air, in order to compare the first part of the pulse to that of the middle and the last; because if they were joined together, they would create the Unison. But this consideration is too subtle for practice, for it is not possible for men to separate the parts of a single pulse to join them together.

### COROLLARY VI.

### PROPOSITION IV.

->*Determining whether the Unison is a Consonance, and whether it is sweeter and more pleasing than the Octave.*<-

Those who maintain that the unison is to **Consonances** <note>Harmonious intervals.</note> what unity is to numbers deny that it should be called a consonance, because it has no variety of sounds regarding high and low <note>original: "le graue & l'aigu."</note>. But those who believe that the unison is the "Queen of Consonances" are of the opposite opinion. They argue that it is enough for sounds to be different in number to create a consonance. Since the "union of sounds" is the very definition of these consonances, the unison—which unites them so perfectly that they are heard almost as a single sound—should not be deprived of the name it gives to all the others. This can be confirmed by the names we give to God, when we call Him "Being," "the Good," or "the Beautiful." For although God does not possess being, goodness, or beauty in the same limited way we do, but rather possesses these perfections in an infinitely more perfect degree, it is nevertheless permitted to speak of Him in this manner, as Holy Scripture does for our instruction. Consequently, the unison is the exemplary cause and the end of all consonances, since they all tend toward said unison from which they draw their origin—just as all mathematical ratios of inequality derive from the ratio of equality. It is therefore not without reason that it is held to be the first consonance.

Now, the unison is considered in two ways. First, it can be continued on a single pitch, that is to say, on the same string. This happens when one sings without raising or lowering the voice, as in a choir of monks who do not use **Plainchant** <note>A style of monophonic, unison church music.</note>. This might be called singing in "Isson" <note>From the Greek 'isos,' meaning equal; also referring to the 'Ison' or drone used in Eastern liturgical chant.</note>—meaning equal—where the continuation is the same as the beginning and all parts remain in unison.

The other species of unison is that of plainchant, which uses all sorts of steps to ascend or descend. This has more variety than the first type, which is like a voice holding steady on a single note, having no distinction other than what comes from different syllables or from occasional interruptions, pauses, and rests to take a breath and to ease the voice and the chest.

These two ways of the unison are different in that the first has only a single species of voice or sound, whereas the other has as many species as there are differences between high and low. This is why the first unison is simpler than the second, and both are consonances, since they create the union of two or several sounds that is pleasing to the ear, even though they do not have...

And in the 2nd book of the *Politics*, chapter 5, he says that he who places the Unison among the **Consonances** <note>Harmonious intervals of music.</note> is like one who introduces the community of all things into Republics, and who confuses verse with the foot <note>Aristotle is arguing that too much unity destroys the necessary structure of a system, whether in music, poetry, or politics.</note>. But *Jean des Murs* <note>Johannes de Muris (c. 1290–1351), a prominent mathematician and music theorist.</note> in book 2 of the *Mirror of Music*, chapter 10, maintains that it is a Consonance; a point upon which all those will agree who prefer to follow reason and experience rather than authority. And as for the communal sharing in Republics, which *Aristotle* opposed in order to contradict his Master <note>Referring to Plato's *Republic*.</note>, it is most desirable; but it must not be hoped for as long as people prefer diversity to equality. For all the most excellent things invite us to this equality and communion of goods: since in nature, the earth, the air, and the heavens are made equally for everyone; in the state of grace there is but one same faith, same hope, same commandments, and same law; and in the state of glory, there is but one same God, who shall be **all in all** <note>original: "omnia in omnibus." A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:28.</note>, when all things shall be subject to Him, and when they shall have left behind diversity, which is the source of corruption. So it may be said that *Plato*, whose mind seemed to reach toward the greatest light of nature, contemplated the beauty of eternal ideas when he proposed the happy communion of goods—which his disciple <note>Aristotle</note> is forced to embrace when he admits that the goods of friends ought to be held in common. Now, all men ought to be friends, since they are brothers and children of the same father, and since true religion teaches us that the faithful ought to be one same body and one same spirit, as they all have the love and glory of God for their ultimate end. From this it follows that all Holy Scripture has no other goal than to make us embrace the communion of goods, both of the spirit and of the body, and to unite us to God forever, so that the Unison—which is not held here in the esteem it deserves—may triumph over the diversity from which error proceeds, and may eternally enjoy the prerogatives of which some wish to deprive it within the differences of time and motion used today.

As for the other part of the proposition, namely whether the Unison is sweeter and more pleasing than the **Octave** <note>An interval where the higher note vibrates exactly twice as fast as the lower note.</note>, I say first that there is no doubt it is sweeter, since it unites its sounds more often and more easily. For the Unison being a ratio of one to one, all the vibrations <note>original: "battemens de l'air" (beats of the air).</note> of the air unite at every stroke, whereas the vibrations of the Octave only unite every two strokes. One will always find in the operations of all the senses that that which unites most easily is the sweetest; but it does not follow that it is the most pleasing. For although sugar and honey are very sweet, they are nonetheless not pleasing to those who prefer sour and bitter things; this is why we must see if the Unison is more pleasing than the Octave.

I say then, secondly, that it seems the Unison is more pleasing than the Octave, because it "tickles" the ear more, and it is more easily grasped by the imagination, which is the principal seat of pleasure.

[This equality] provides us with examples in all the sciences, for the great pleasure of **Algebra** <note>In the 17th century, algebra was often viewed as the "science of equations," or the study of hidden equalities.</note> consists in finding all sorts of equations that are met by means of equality. And if we may climb higher, we shall find an eternal **Unison** in the divinity, since the three persons are but one same nature, and have but one same will, same power, and same goodness, even though they are truly distinct. This is perhaps why the **Blessed** <note>The saints and angels in Heaven.</note> will sing perpetually in Unison, so that their song may conform to the equality of the three persons, and to the state of equality which takes its origin from eternal beatitude; this state is susceptible to no alteration, and being most simple, requires most simple songs—which can be no simpler when many sing than when they sing in **Unison**.

One can further confirm the same thing by the beginning and the end of compositions, which are almost always the **Unison**, which is the goal of Music; for we experience that all **Consonances** <note>Harmonious intervals between different notes.</note> tend toward the Unison, as I demonstrate elsewhere. And if one compares the power of the Unison in **Plainchant** <note>Traditional unison church music, such as Gregorian chant.</note> with that of the Consonances of [polyphonic] Music, one will find that it is more powerful, and that it makes a stronger impression on the mind, which is in no way distracted by the variety of Consonances or **Dissonances**; the mind begins to taste the Music of the Blessed when it hears the Unison, which reminds it of its origin, and of the beatitude it hopes for and awaits.

The power of the **Unison** does not only impress its effects upon the mind and the soul, but also upon inanimate bodies; for every time one touches a string of a **Lute**, a **Viol**, or some other instrument, it shakes and makes the other strings tremble that are arranged and tuned to the **Unison** <note>This phenomenon is known today as sympathetic resonance.</note>; and consequently, it can serve to move all sorts of machines, and to fire a **cannon**. But we must reserve this discussion for the treatise on the sounds used in war.

Now, one of the strongest reasons that persuades us that the Unison is more agreeable and more natural than the **Octave** is drawn from experience, which shows that one grows tired much sooner of hearing singing in the Octave than in the Unison, which is heard in churches for the space of several hours with pleasure. And although children naturally sing at the Octave of men, nevertheless their intention is to sing in Unison, toward which all voices tend, being preserved and strengthened by their likenesses; for resemblance is the source of love, and the preservation of the being and nature of each thing, which is better preserved by uniformity than by deformity. Now, the movements that our spirits receive from the Unison are perfectly uniform and equal, while those of the Octave are unequal, since some are twice as fast as others <note>A reference to the 2:1 frequency ratio of the octave.</note>.

And if we compare sounds to objects of touch, we find that the ear receives as much pleasure from hearing the Unison as the sense of touch receives from handling polished, soft, and sweet things, like satin and a thousand other similar things. # First Book

...proportionally greater as it communicates itself more or less; for example, the number one thousand is ten times greater than the number one hundred, because unity communicates itself ten times more to a thousand than to a hundred; but it has an infinite power so much its own that it cannot communicate it, since it cannot make a number infinite, just as God cannot communicate His infinity nor His independence: from which one can conclude that one must look at the Creator in His creatures, as unity in numbers, and as the **Unison** <note>The fundamental state where two notes are the same pitch, representing perfect unity.</note> in **Consonances** <note>Harmonious intervals between different notes.</note>.

Indeed, one experiences that **Consonances** are two, three, or four times better and more excellent, the more the **Unison** communicates itself to them two, three, or four times more, as I will demonstrate in a specific discourse; for when it communicates two degrees of union to them, they are twice as good as when it communicates only one degree, and so on consequently until they are reduced to the **Unison** by the subtraction of the degrees of variety that determine the matter of **Consonances**, just as union determines their form; for if inequality and diversity serve as the body of **Consonances**, equality and union are its soul and spirit, as will be seen in the treatise on *Divisions* <note>Likely referring to the mathematical division of a string to create musical intervals.</note>, and in that of the *Suppositions* of each **Consonance**, where I demonstrate that of all the divisions of each **Consonance**, that one is the sweetest and most pleasant which unites its sounds most perfectly; and that of two or more suppositions of the same consonance, or of several, whether high or low, that one is the best and most natural whose union is greater.

And when we have stripped creatures of their differences and their varieties, and the veil of external and finite appearances is lifted, we will perceive the divine spirit that sets them in motion; and then we shall be one same spirit with God, following the beautiful word of the Apostle: **"He who adheres to God is one spirit with Him"** <note>original: "Qui adhæret Deo, vnus ſpiritus eſt cum eo" (1 Corinthians 6:17).</note>; for as soon as we see that there is no goodness or beauty in creatures except the divine goodness and beauty, our spirit will attach itself so powerfully to this object which ravishes the Blessed, that it will seem to be one same thing with Him, just as the objects understood and the understanding are no longer anything but one same thing in the school of the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who taught that in the act of knowing, the mind becomes one with the thing it understands.</note>.

But just as we patiently suffer, in the imperfection of our current state, to have our ears struck by the variety of **Consonances** while waiting for the dwelling where we shall be ravished by the perfect **Unison**—the beauty of which we cannot perfectly understand while we need diversity for our preservation—likewise we cannot hear the divine beauty and excellence until it has opened our eyes and explained the enigma that hides it from us, and which takes away our sight of it, just as vapors and very thick clouds take away our sight of the Sun. From this comes the fact that broths and jellies do not provide a nourishment so strong, so useful, and so pleasant to those who are healthy as bread, meat, and other foods which are not stripped of their different imperfections, since the body of man has several different parts, each of which requires a different food: so that potable gold or the elixir of which the **Chemists** <note>original: "Chymiſtes," referring to practitioners of alchemy and early chemistry.</note> and **Kabbalists** <note>Followers of a mystical tradition seeking hidden truths in scripture and nature.</note> boast is not suitable for nourishment, because it is too simple and too pure.

# On Consonances.

Furthermore, experience shows that we cannot endure for long here without the variety of different actions and passions, each of which eventually tires us and soon becomes displeasing. For example, when one is tired, one takes pleasure in sitting down; but as soon as one has remained seated for two or three hours, one finds oneself as weary as before, and prefers to return to labor until a new weariness sets in, rather than remain seated any longer. This clearly proves that human pleasure cannot subsist without variety while man is in a changeable state; and consequently, the continuation of the **Unison** <note>The sounding of the same pitch by two or more voices or instruments.</note> cannot be as agreeable to him as when it is interrupted by other chords, or even by **Dissonances** <note>Clashing sounds that create tension requiring resolution.</note>—even though this diversity in no way prevents the **Unison** from being more pleasing than other **Consonances** <note>Harmonious intervals between different notes.</note> when it is used in those places where it is required or permitted according to the rules of art.

Now, this state of variety in which we exist is the reason why we avoid the **Unison** as much as possible, because it is too sweet and too excellent for this life. From this it follows that we prefer to end music with the **Octave**, the **Fifth**, the **Third**, or their **replications** <note>Compound intervals, such as a tenth being a replication of a third.</note> rather than with the **Unison**. And when we do end with it, we accompany it with other chords, because as long as the spirit is subject to matter—which subjects it to **phantasms** <note>Mental images or illusions that obscure pure intellectual truth.</note>, to darkness, and to error—it hardly dares to rise to the perfection of unity, which is entirely stripped of the variety and inequality found in other chords. By this, the spirit bears witness that the **Unison** is almost outside the realm of Music, just as God is beyond its reach; and that when one hears the **Unison**, one must remember that the slightest pleasure of **Divine Harmony** is more excellent than the perfect knowledge of the Harmony we use. As one can infer from this beautiful saying of **Saint Augustine**: *It is of an incomparable happiness more excellent to perceive God from even the smallest particle with a pious mind, than to comprehend all created things* <note>original: "Incomparabili felicitate præstantius est Deum ex quantulacunque particulâ piâ mente sentire, quàm quæ facta sunt vniuersa comprehendere"</note>, in the 5th chapter of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 16. From this one can conclude, by proportion, that the pleasure the spirit (when separated from error and phantasm) receives from the **Unison** surpasses all the contentment that comes from other chords, since it is the image of **Divine Harmony** and the source of said pleasures.

But one might still raise an objection that seems to strip the **Unison** of the prerogative we give it: namely, that the spirit takes more pleasure in conceiving things that increase its knowledge. From this it follows that nature delights in diversity, as I have proved by this same reasoning in a private discourse. Now, one learns nothing by considering the **Unison**, since it contains no interval, and all its sounds are but one and the same thing; whereas in other **Consonances**, one learns the difference between low and high sounds, and the contentment that proceeds from their blending. Consequently, the **Unison** is the poorest and least agreeable of all **Consonances**, since it provides no new knowledge.

And then, if the greater union of sounds is the cause of greater contentment, it would follow that there is more contentment in seeing a room whose walls touch or are very close together, or a small house, than in seeing a grand **Louvre** <note>The royal palace in Paris, used here as a symbol of architectural magnificence.</note>, because the parts of the small house are more united than those of a great Palace. The same can be said of everything that is grand and magnificent, which could be shortened and reduced; because these shortenings...

Finally, the difference between all creatures will be entirely preserved in heaven, where it will please all the Saints more than if they were all one and the same thing, and if they had no difference between them; for it seems that all the pleasure of the knowledge of creatures consists in the relationship and the comparison that one makes of them to God, and of one with another.

But it is easy to answer these objections, since they assume the imperfect state of men, whose knowledge will be much more perfect when they clearly see the great union of all creatures, and when they recognize that the diversity of objects exerts a great tyranny over our spirits, which it diverts from contemplation and from the thoughts that carry us toward unity. This unity can only be reached by stripping creatures of their diversity, in order to find the unity that reigns there absolutely, and to see nothing more than the root of being and the center of sovereign reason—just as one no longer sees anything but the radical terms <note>The simplest whole-number ratios (like 1:1 or 2:1) that form the basis of mathematical and musical systems.</note> of **Harmonic**, **Arithmetic**, and **Geometric** proportions when one has stripped the largest numbers of what they had that was superfluous and useless, and as one perceives only the spirits and the quintessence of mixtures when one has rejected the terrestrial and everything that made them subject to corruption and various alterations.

As for the greater knowledge that comes from the other **Consonances** <note>Musical intervals that sound pleasant together, such as thirds or fifths.</note>, it can be compared to the light of several small candles, or to that of glow-worms; but that of unity and the **Unison** <note>The sounding of the exact same pitch by two or more sources.</note> is similar to the light of the Sun, which obscures all others by its presence, just as the grace and excellence of the **Unison** makes that of the other **Consonances** vanish. For even though we do not enjoy here all the pleasure that can come from the **Unison** because of the distractions given to us by the diversity of **Consonances**, nevertheless the small amount of attention we bring to considering its excellence gives us a much nobler and more elevated knowledge than that of the other **Consonances**; just as the little knowledge we have of the heavens is much more excellent than that of the elements, although the latter is greater and more certain.

It does not follow, however, that a narrow room is more pleasant than a large hall, or that a small house is more beautiful than a large palace, because one does not measure the beauty of buildings by union, but by the relationship and symmetry of their parts—just as one measures that of the **Consonances** by the union of their sounds. And as for the diversity of bodies and spirits in Paradise, it will be so tempered by union that some hold that all the bodies of the Blessed will be encompassed by the humanity of Jesus Christ, as their spirits will be immersed in his divinity, so that God may be all things in all, and that He may reign absolutely in the being of all creatures. These creatures cannot reach a higher degree of perfection than by entering into the perfect **Unison** of created being with the uncreated, which consists in having no more knowledge or love but that of the divinity.

One can also prove that the **Unison** is more excellent than the other **Consonances** through **Astrology**, which finds the **Consonances** in the aspects <note>The angular relationships between planets in the sky, believed to influence events on Earth.</note> of the Stars, since the conjunction <note>The positioning of two celestial bodies at the same degree of the zodiac, the astrological equivalent of a Unison.</note> is the most powerful and the most excellent of all the aspects;

It is only the imperfection of variety that preoccupies us and makes us prefer what is more similar to our fragility and our misery, which cannot exist here below without diversity—which is the mother of corruption—even though we aspire to the **Unison** and to unity. This is represented to us by that excellent word from the Gospel:
> Indeed, one thing is necessary. <note>Original Latin: "Porrò unum est necessarium." (Luke 10:42).</note>

Now, if Music serves any purpose in this world, it should be used particularly to recall the memory of some of these considerations. The ear should only serve as a channel to give free entry to the contemplation of eternal things, and to the pleasure that comes from the thought of the final end, upon which true Philosophers must constantly dwell. But it is time to speak of the other difficulties encountered in the **Unison**, the definition of which is explained in the following proposition, after the five Corollaries that I add to prevent a quantity of difficulties and objections. These are based on the prejudices of Musicians and other persons who imagine many things that are not so; and to shape the minds of those who sing or who love Music to use **Harmony** to lift themselves up to God, and to contemplate the greatness of his goodness, and the sweetness of his blessings and his mercy, enjoyed by all those of whom the Royal Prophet speaks in this first verse of Psalm 72:
> How good God is to Israel, to those who are of a right heart. <note>Original Latin: "Quàm bonus Israël Deus his qui rectò sunt corde." (Psalm 73 in modern numbering).</note>

# Book One

### COROLLARY I.

One can conclude from the discourse I have made regarding the **Unison**, that preoccupation <note>In 17th-century French, *préoccupation* refers to bias, prejudice, or preconceived notions that cloud judgment.</note> prevents practitioners from making a reliable judgment of what is good or bad, worse or better, and agreeable or disagreeable in **Consonances**; and that one must not believe them too easily if they do not provide some reason as proof of what they maintain: and consequently, that one must always follow reason rather than their opinion, since its light surpasses experience and dissipates stubbornness, just as the sun dissipates the clouds that obscure the day.

And if one is astonished that musicians have been mistaken until now in believing that the **Unison** was not the most perfect and most agreeable chord in all of Music, this astonishment will cease if one considers that they are mistaken in several other things: such as when they believe that the **Harmonic** division of the **Octave** is more agreeable than the **Arithmetic** division <note>These terms refer to different mathematical ratios used to divide a string length. A "Harmonic" division results in the major chord, while "Arithmetic" results in the minor chord.</note>; that the **Fifth** is as good or better than the **Twelfth**; that compositions for several parts are better than simple songs; and several other things, the contrary of which I have proven in specific discourses.

But this vice of preoccupation is not unique to musicians alone, for it reigns almost everywhere, as is experienced in the natural movements of heavy bodies descending toward the center of the earth. The heaviest of these do not descend faster from a height of 50 feet than the lightest, as is experienced with a large stone of one hundred pounds and a small one of one pound, and with a ball of iron and one of boxwood of the same size, etc., which reach the ground as soon as one another <note>This is a striking early reference to the law of falling bodies, often associated with Galileo's experiments.</note>. It is similarly experienced that a dead body is no heavier than when it lives, contrary to what has been held until now. I leave aside a thousand other things with which men are so preoccupied and biased that it is almost impossible for them to abandon their old errors, so great is the idolatry with which they cherish them.

This is why one should not be surprised if **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes the Cynic was a Greek philosopher famous for carrying a lamp in daylight, searching for an "honest man" (or a true human being).</note> searched everywhere for a man without being able to find one, even though he was in the midst of populous cities; for one meets so few who use right reason, which gives being and name to man, and which separates and distinguishes him from the beasts. These beasts should make us blush with shame, and from them we should learn our lesson, since they are mistaken less often than we are, even though they have no other light than common sense and natural instinct to conduct their actions.

Musicians can take occasion from this whole discourse—particularly the Masters and those who compose, or who conduct and regulate Concerts—to study reason if they wish to cultivate that part in which God has engraved his image, and if they desire to escape the captivity and the prison of the senses, whose darkness so greatly obscures the judgment that it almost loses its principal function, which consists in judging according to equity and reason. Now, if they have enough affection to wish to climb to the summit of **Parnassus**, or that of **Mount Olympus** <note>In mythology, Parnassus is the home of the Muses (arts/music), and Olympus is the home of the gods; both represent heights of intellectual and spiritual clarity.</note>, where it is said there are no longer any clouds or winds, and where calm, tranquility, and splen—

### COROLLARY III.

Now, if practitioners take the trouble to ask how it is possible that no one has known until now that the **Unison** is better than the **Octave**, it is easy to answer and satisfy them. For the most excellent things are usually perceived only by those who rise above everything material, and who use the body only to carry the spirit and to provide it with the *species* <note>The term "species" (especes) here refers to the sensory images or impressions that the eyes and ears gather, which the mind then processes into abstract thoughts.</note> of objects like very coarse and very imperfect sketches. The spirit immediately strips these of their imperfection and shadow, forming from them most excellent ideas that are no longer subject to place or time, and which possess nothing but the simple ray of an intellectual light. This light surpasses that of the Sun as much as the body surpasses the shadow, and as the spirit surpasses the body.

The light of the Sun is never more pure nor more vivid than when it is reflected by the glass of a parabolic mirror in the place called the *focus*, which is the center of its heat; and nevertheless, it is not possible to perceive this light, though it is very strong and very vivid, unless one opposes to it an opaque body that reflects it back to the eyes, and which makes its vigor appear through its own destruction <note>The author is describing how a magnifying mirror can set an object on fire at its focal point; the light itself is invisible in the air until it hits an object and burns it.</note>. And truth never appears, though it is most excellent and fills the whole world, unless one opposes to it the understanding, which alone can make us see it. This the understanding does without its own destruction, since it draws its perfection from it, which consists particularly in the knowledge of the sovereign truth that God called "all good" when he spoke to Moses in the 33rd chapter of Exodus: *I will show you all good* <note>original: "Ostendam tibi omne bonum"</note>. However, the destruction of the opaque body that receives the point of the burning cone from the parabolic glass happens only because it is corruptible and composed of different parts; consequently, it is not capable of such a great light, which strives to convert the body into itself, or at least to create a **Unison** with it.

### COROLLARY IV.

It is easy to draw such great spiritual profits from this discourse that musicians will have no need for other instructions to lead them toward God, since the Unison of all things in the world conducts them there. For everything the earth produces is created by the Unison of the rays of the Sun and the other stars which unite with each plant when they awaken nature and make it grow. And when the limbs obey the soul, it is by the movement of the **spirits** <note>The "animal spirits" were believed in 17th-century physiology to be subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to communicate the soul's commands to the body.</note> that make it move, just as the Unison makes the strings move; this is easily observed in the heart, whose movement causes the arteries to move at the same time. If one considers the knowledge of truth, one will admit that it is nothing other than the Unison it forms with the understanding; and if one climbs even higher, one will find that it is by the force of the Unison that God makes all creatures act, and that He converts us to Him by **efficacious grace**, <note>A term from 17th-century theology (notably in the debates between Jansenists and Jesuits) referring to divine grace that effectively moves the human will to act rightly without overriding its freedom.</note> which is like a string whose vibrations are so powerful that they always move our wills without them ever resisting.

### COROLLARY V.

I add this fifth corollary to note that I leave it to everyone’s liberty to call the Unison a *Consonance* or the principle of Consonances, as it does not matter which one holds for the establishment of Music; though it seems to me that the reasons I have provided to prove it deserves the name of Consonance are sufficient to make it believable. And if some do not wish to admit that it is more pleasing than the Octave or the Fifth, that will in no way prevent the other propositions from being true, since they do not depend on this one. This is why the conclusion I have followed cannot prejudice what we will say hereafter, although I believe all those who judge the beauty and goodness of objects that strike the senses by their union and sweetness will be of my opinion. They will consider that it does not belong to the ear to so rule the mind that it can only judge in the ear's favor, nor to bind it so tightly that it cannot extend its jurisdiction beyond its reach. For although hearing is seemingly necessary to apprehend sounds before the understanding can judge their goodness, nevertheless it receives only a slight impression of what the ear presents to it, of which it cannot judge in the final resort until it has purified the images it raises up to the nature

## PROPOSITION V.

->*The Unison is the conjunction or the union of two or several sounds, which resemble each other so perfectly that the ear hears them as a single sound; and it is the most powerful of all harmonies.*<-

This definition of the **Unison** <term>Unison: The sounding of the same pitch by two or more voices or instruments simultaneously.</term> has almost no need for explanation if one understands everything that was said in the fourth proposition; that is why I will not dwell on it much. I only remark, in the first place, that I have said *union, or conjunction*, because two sounds cannot make a Unison, even if they are equal, if they do not join and unite together, and consequently if they do not strike the ear at the same time. From this, it follows that the two sounds one uses to ask a question and to give an answer do not make a Unison, even if they are of the same tone—that is to say, even if they are equal in pitch—because they are not heard at the same time, for the question precedes the answer. Similarly, two sounds of which one is made in Paris and the other in Rome at the same time do not make a Unison, because the great distance prevents them from joining together; though one might say that one "responds in Unison" when responding in the same tone, which is to say when those who speak and confer together use a voice that corresponds to the same note or the same **string**. <term>string: In this context, "chorde" refers to both a musical string and the specific pitch it produces.</term>

Secondly, I said *of two, or several sounds*, because the nature of the Unison is always preserved even if the sounds of all the instruments in the world were made at the same time, provided that they have an equal number of vibrations of air in the same amount of time.

In the third place, perfect resemblance or equality of sounds is necessary to make a perfect Unison. From this, it follows that the thickest string of an instrument and the voice of a **Bass** <term>Bass: The lowest range of the human voice or a musical part.</term> cannot make a perfect Unison with the **treble strings** <note>original: "Chanterelles," the highest-pitched strings on instruments like the lute or violin.</note> and the **Treble** <term>Treble: Also called the "Dessus," the highest part in a musical composition.</term> voices, because the sound of the former is fuller and more replenished, and has more "body" than the sound of the latter. Thus, one hears one of the sounds more than the other, or one hears only the strongest, which obscures and hides the weakest, just as a greater light hides a lesser one. And because it is difficult to find strings or voices so equal that one cannot notice some difference, it is likewise difficult to make a perfect Unison.

son, for one of the voices is often more hoarse, clearer, thinner, thicker, or more brilliant, sweeter, firmer, softer, or harsher than the other.

However, the **Unisons** <term>Unison: The sounding of the same pitch by two or more voices or instruments.</term> of instruments and of good voices are usually perfect enough to satisfy the ear, which is not accustomed to hearing more perfect things in this world, and consequently cannot recognize their imperfection. This must be understood similarly for other **Consonances** <term>Consonance: A combination of notes that sound pleasant together due to the mathematical relationship between their frequencies.</term>, so that there is no need to repeat it elsewhere.

Finally, I have said that the Unison is more powerful than the other consonances, because it makes strings vibrate more noticeably and for longer than other chords. This also happens when one drags a finger along the rim of a glass, whether there is water inside or it is empty; for another glass that is in unison vibrates strongly, and if there is water inside, it quivers and bubbles, even if the glasses are quite far from each other, or on different tables, or if one holds them in the air with the hand. This can be tested with a bent pin placed on the rim, which is also used to perceive the movement of strings that are not being touched; but one can use a straw, or any other body one wishes, although the hand is sufficient for this experiment; for if one touches the strings with the fingers, one feels their vibration, which can even be seen without touching them. We will speak of this more fully in another proposition, after having noted several things on this subject in the following corollaries.

### COROLLARY I.

One can conclude from this discourse that a deaf person who is also blind can know if instruments are in tune, since he can find the Unison with his hand; for even though strings vibrate by the force of the **Octave** <term>Octave: An interval where the frequency of one note is double that of another.</term> and the **Twelfth** <term>Twelfth: A compound musical interval consisting of an octave and a perfect fifth.</term>, they nevertheless do not vibrate as strongly as they do by the force of the Unison; so that it is very easy to discern those that are in unison from the others. Now, a deaf person can put all the strings in unison one after another by means of a movable **bridge** <term>Bridge: A piece of wood that supports the strings and transmits their vibration to the instrument's body.</term>, or the finger; and once the Unison of the strings is established and their length is known, he can notice with his hand or with some instrument if a **Lute** <note>Lute: A popular pear-shaped string instrument of the 17th century.</note> is in tune: he can also set it to whatever tuning he wishes. Many people, in the midst of darkness, can know by vibration alone—without using their ears—if a Lute is in tune. The same thing happens with other stringed instruments. But I will explain another way that deaf people can use to set all kinds of instruments to all kinds of tunings in the third book on instruments, without the need to perceive the vibrations through the sense of touch.

### COROLLARY II.

One can invent new problems based on the Unison similar to those of **Archimedes** <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BC): A Greek mathematician and inventor famous for his work on mechanics and levers.</note>, taken from the 40th of his *Devices*, as **Pappus** <note>Pappus of Alexandria (c. 290–350 AD): A significant Greek mathematician whose works preserved much of ancient geometry.</note> remarks, which is stated on this matter: *Given the force, move the given weight* <note>original Greek: "τῇ δοθείσῃ δυνάμει, τὸ δοθὲν βάρος κινῆσαι"</note>. From this, the said Archimedes had the boldness to put forward this proposition: *Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth* <note>original Greek: "δός μοι ποῦ στῶ, καὶ κινῶ τὴν γῆν"</note>, which is to say,

*"Give me a firm place where I may set my foot, and I shall move the earth":* <note>A famous quote attributed to the ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes regarding the power of the lever.</note> This can be done with an endless screw, or with a **Polyspaston** <term>Polyspaston: A system of many pulleys used to lift heavy weights with minimal effort.</term>. On this subject, one may see the calculation of Stevin <note>Simon Stevin (1548–1620), a Flemish mathematician and engineer who pioneered the study of statics.</note> in the third book of his *Statics*, in which he demonstrates that one could move the earth from its place by one foot in the space of 10 years, each of 365 days, by means of the **Pancration**, or the **Charistion** <term>Pancration and Charistion: Names given to powerful mechanical lifting devices or "all-powerful" machines in early modern physics.</term>, assuming that the earth weighs 2,400,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 pounds, and that the person turning the handle of the machine can lift a weight of one hundred pounds three feet high with each turn of the handle, turning it 4,000 times every hour, and working continually day and night. Now, one can state the problem of the **Unison** in this manner: *Given the body that one wishes to make tremble and move, provide the sound:* for if one were to strike another earth that was outside of our own, it could make ours tremble.

Fracastoro <note>Girolamo Fracastoro (c. 1478–1553), a Renaissance physician and philosopher who wrote on "sympathy"—the idea that things can affect one another through hidden resonances.</note> says in the second chapter of his work *On Sympathy* that he saw wax images in a church that trembled at the sound of a bell. And one could make statues of wood, or silver, or another material, which would dance to the sound of bells, or other instruments, or the voice. It is also noted that the sound of some organ pipes causes certain stones in churches to tremble.

### COROLLARY III.

It can similarly happen that a man trembles and falls by the power of another’s word; and the larynxes, along with the other instruments of the voice, being equally tuned, can make one another tremble. But it is difficult to test from what distance sounds can make bodies tremble; for although it is usually only tested across the length of a table or a room, I nevertheless believe they can tremble from as far away as the sound can be heard. Consequently, they could tremble from 10 leagues <note>A league was roughly 3 miles; 10 leagues is about 30 miles.</note> away when the sound is strong enough to be heard at that distance, as happens with the noise of a cannon. But I wish to conclude this discourse by considering the voice of God, which does not only make bodies tremble and fall—as He did when He overthrew the soldiers with the words, *"I am"* <note>original: "Ego sum"; a reference to John 18:6 when the soldiers fall back at Jesus' declaration.</note>—but which makes that which is not appear as if it were. That is to say, He gives being to all things by His word: *"He calls those things which are not as though they were,"* <note>original: "Vocat ea quæ non ſunt, tanquam ea quæ ſunt"</note> as Saint Paul teaches in the fourth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans. He shall also call all the dead to the general judgment He will hold for all men, by the voice of the trumpet, *"In the trumpet of God,"* <note>original: "In tuba Dei"</note> as the same Saint Paul speaks in the first Epistle he wrote to the Thessalonians, chapter four, which he calls the last trumpet in the fourteenth chapter of the first to the Corinthians: *"At the last trumpet; for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible."* <note>original: "In nouiſsima tuba; canet enim tuba, & mortui reſurgent incorrupti"</note>

From this, musicians—who do not stop their thoughts at mere pleasure or profit, and who have eyes penetrating enough to look toward eternity—can find reason to think of the sound of that trumpet which will put an end to the music of this world. It will give a beginning to the music of the Blessed, and likewise to the disorder and the dissonances of the wretched. Among the latter will be all those who used music with evil intent, and who abused their time, their hands, and their minds, if they do not put back into order that which they have perverted by the dissonances and the disorder of their thoughts and their affections.

### COROLLARY IV.

Since sounds are nothing other than a beating of the air, and since the two sounds that create a **Unison** <term>Unison: Two notes of the exact same pitch, occurring when two objects vibrate at the same frequency.</term> are made of two or more equal beats of air, one can express the definition of the Unison in these terms: *The Unison is the comparison made between two or more movements of air, whose beats are equal in number;* this is why two or more bodies never beat the air equally without producing a Unison; and never do equal numbers of air beats strike the ear with enough force without the ear perceiving it. However, one does not give the name of "Unison" to these beats of air unless they are violent enough to be heard so clearly that one can judge by means of the ear that they are equal in number; for when the hearing—or the understanding by means of the hearing—judges the Unison, it is, strictly speaking, judging that the number of different air beats it feels is equal.

## PROPOSITION VI.

### *To explain the true reason and the cause of the vibration of strings that are in Unison.*

Men have introduced "sympathy," "antipathy," and "occult qualities" <note>Early modern scientists often used "occult qualities" to describe natural phenomena (like magnetism or gravity) whose physical causes were not yet understood. Our author here argues for a purely mechanical explanation instead.</note> into the arts and sciences to cover up their defects and to excuse their ignorance, or rather to frankly confess that they know nothing; for it is the same thing to answer that strings in Unison make each other vibrate because of the "sympathy" they have together, as it is to answer that one does not know the cause. The same must be said of the sympathy claimed between the magnet and iron, straw and amber <note>A reference to static electricity; amber (Latin: *electrum*) was known to attract light objects when rubbed.</note>, naphtha and fire, and gold and mercury—and of those attributed to many other things. For when one knows the reasons for these effects, "sympathy" vanishes along with ignorance, as I shall demonstrate regarding the vibration of strings in Unison.

I suppose, then, that two strings A-B and C-D are equally tensioned, and consequently that they are in Unison. I say that the true reason why A-B, when touched and moved, makes C-D vibrate, is taken from the beats of the air made by A-B, of which not one fails to help push and move C-D toward point E. For after string A-B, having been pulled to H, returns toward string C-D, the air it pushes before it strikes the said string at point G and makes it move toward E. Thus, this point E meets exactly at point I when point H sends back the air from its second turn, and consequently, it pushes the string C-D again. I demonstrate it thus: when H has sent the air to C-D against G, it returns from I to F, while G goes as far as E; and while H returns from F toward the place where A-B was first pulled, E returns to G; and finally, while H returns to F, G comes to I. In this way, at the same time that point H wants to go from F to I, it meets string C-D, upon which it impresses a new movement that keeps it vibrating until A-B comes to rest; <image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two parallel horizontal strings, labeled A-B (top) and C-D (bottom). Dotted lines form two intersecting triangles between the strings, illustrating the paths of air movement between specific points labeled F and H on the top string and G, I, and E on or below the bottom string.</image-desc>

as one might experiment with a straw, or another object; for if one prevents the vibration of string CD with the hand, or otherwise, as soon as the obstruction is removed it begins to vibrate again, provided that one does not stop string AB.
   As for other strings that are not at the **Unison**, nor at the **Octave**, or at other **Consonances** <term>Consonances: Musical intervals that sound harmonious and stable together, such as the Unison, Octave, or Fifth.</term> that cause strings to vibrate, they are never found in any disposition that is susceptible to the movement of the air pushed by the string one touches—as I will demonstrate in the discourse on the Octave. Otherwise, all the strings would vibrate noticeably; this does not happen because the first percussion of the air striking the dissonant strings is not aided by the second, nor by the 3rd or 4th, etc., which ruin and prevent the effect of the first movement that the touched string had impressed upon the other, as I will explain elsewhere.
   But I wish to remark on several things regarding this subject in the eight corollaries that follow, so that I do not leave the **Unison**—which is the best part of **Harmony**—without drawing from it the profit that true Christians seek and find in all creatures: to raise themselves to the Creator, who must be the final and sovereign end of our designs.

### COROLLARY I.

One should consider whether other effects attributed to sympathy and to **occult virtues** <note>Occult virtues: Hidden properties of objects that were not yet explained by known physical laws, often used in early modern science to describe phenomena like magnetism or medicine.</note> can be explained by the movement of the air, or by that of spirits and the universal soul of the world (supposing that one exists). For example: whether the spirits of brothers who feel the same pain at the same time imprint some movement and make some impression upon one another; whether the imagination of a mother imprints some particular movement upon the location of the child's body where different figures appear <note>The author refers to the historical belief in "maternal impressions," where a mother's thoughts or fears were thought to physically mark her unborn child.</note>; whether earthquakes and **panic terrors** <note>Sudden, irrational fears that grip large groups, historically associated with the Greek god Pan or astrological alignments.</note> proceed from the movement of some star that creates a Unison or some other Consonance with the bodies affected by these movements; and finally, if there are other effects in nature that can be related to the force of chords.

### COROLLARY II.

Now, one can conclude from this discourse that Consonances are all the more excellent when they cause the bodies tuned to the same accord to vibrate more strongly, since they have a greater power, which follows nature—just as effect and action follow power. And if it is permitted for us to rise from physical things to spiritual ones, one can say that when our wills are in Unison with that of God—that is to say, they are conformed and united to His—they are powerful enough to make bodies and spirits tremble, as is experienced in exorcisms and at the commands of the Saints, who make demons tremble and cast them out from the possessed. Indeed, nothing is difficult for one who is loved by God, and whose will desires nothing but what pleases Him; which led the Apostle to say:
> I can do all things in Him who strengthens me:
<note>original Latin: "Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat" (Philippians 4:13).</note>
and it is most often by the force of this spiritual Unison that the Saints perform miracles, and that the predestined will ascend to heaven to enjoy the harmony of the Blessed.

### COROLLARY III.

It is now very easy to see that the comparisons commonly used to explain the **sympathy** <note>Sympathy: In the 17th century, "sympathy" referred to a mysterious natural attraction or shared feeling between objects, which Mersenne is here trying to explain through physics.</note> of strings that make each other vibrate are no longer necessary. For example, [it is often said] that only liquids of the same nature mix perfectly together, such as two drops of water, oil, or wine; that only stone fruits unite with similar fruits, as experienced in grafts onto wild rootstock; and that liquids that do not mix well, or stone fruits compared to seed fruits, are like **Dissonances** that cannot make strings vibrate—to which occurs the same thing as to men who have a natural aversion to one another. For even though there is some foundation in these relationships—such as those between the magnet and iron, the **sympathetic ointment** <note>Sympathetic ointment: A popular "magical" remedy of the time believed to heal wounds by being applied to the weapon that caused the injury rather than the patient.</note> and the wounds of those absent, the blood shed by a corpse in the presence of the murderer, the person who yawns when they see another yawn, and a thousand other similar things reported to cover for ignorance and to establish "sympathy"—it is nevertheless useless to use comparisons when one has a physical demonstration.

### COROLLARY IV.

If one arranges several strings in such a way that they are held to trigger the mechanisms of a hydraulic or pneumatic machine, or any automaton one wishes, they can be made to move and release by means of the **Unison**. For since force can be applied when the resistance is known, the vibration of the string attached to the machines can make them play; consequently, it could trigger artillery and move all sorts of objects as soon as someone plays the **Lute** or another instrument.

### COROLLARY V.

And if one wishes to have the pleasure of tuning two Lutes, two Viols, or two other instruments to each other without needing to touch them both at once, it is easy to tune the second to the first. For if one tightens all the strings of the second one after another until they make those of the first vibrate, the two instruments will be in tune. Now, one can hear this vibration; for if one plays the Lute, the **Mandora** <term>Mandora: A small, pear-shaped stringed instrument from the lute family, popular in the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</term>, etc., the strings of the other instruments that happen to be at the unison of said strings or voices will respond to them. They will produce a sound so ravishing that if one heard a Concert composed only of this sweet echo and resonance—which occurs without touching the strings—one would never wish to hear any other music until the memory of this extraordinary pleasure faded. This touches the soul so delicately that all other sounds seem harsh, disagreeable, and unworthy of the ear to it—just as the pleasures of the body used in this world are judged unworthy of man by the **Blessed** <note>The Blessed: Those in Heaven who experience the direct presence of God.</note>; for those who possess true goods and true pleasures despise those that are nothing but appearance.

## COROLLARY VI.

Since the **Unison** <term>Unison: The sounding of two notes at the exact same pitch; the most perfect form of agreement in music.</term> has more power over inanimate bodies than over men—given that it causes strings to tremble and ring more loudly than any other consonance, and it makes them tremble all the more strongly as its sounds unite better with one another (that is, twice as strongly as the **Octave**, three times as strongly as the **Twelfth**, and six times as strongly as the **Fifth**)—it follows that inanimate objects should serve as a master and instructor to many. They teach us that some people are as far removed from the solid judgment one must make regarding the goodness of Consonances as inanimate things are removed from the human spirit. This occurs because such people believe that it belongs to the sense of hearing to judge the quality of Music, even though the ear can judge it no better than animals can. Indeed, many animals have hearing more subtle than that of Musicians; however, true judgment cannot be made without reason, which is found neither in the ear of man nor in that of beasts. I have spoken more fully of this subject in the 6th question of the *Preludes to Harmony*, where I examined whether the ear can and should judge the sweetness of sounds and Concerts, or if this judgment belongs to reason.

## COROLLARY VII.

Since the **Unison** represents the virtue and the treasures of divinity, and because it is similar to the primary maxims of morality—which Saint Augustine <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD): A hugely influential theologian and philosopher whose works often linked the mathematical order of music to the divine order of the universe.</note> calls the "rules and light of virtues" in the 2nd book of *On Free Choice*, chapter 10—it follows that music is founded on the principles that one must live justly; that one must prefer good things to bad; that one must give to each what belongs to them; that immortal and incorruptible things are better than those that perish; and on several other general maxims that are acknowledged by everyone. Musicians must take this opportunity to flee vice, embrace virtue, and frequently lift their spirits toward God. They should believe that Music is not worthy of a good mind unless it is used to carry oneself toward eternal things, which maintain an order so perfect that no **Dissonances** <term>Dissonances: Intervals that sound harsh or "unstable" to the ear, often used here as a metaphor for sin or disorder.</term> can be found there. For most sins come from the negligence of men, who almost never think of their final end, as the same Saint remarked in the first book, chapter 3: *To do evil is nothing other than neglecting eternal things—which the mind enjoys through itself and perceives through itself, and which the lover cannot lose—to pursue temporal things... which are sensed through the body, the lowliest part of man, and can never be considered great or wonderful. For in this one category, all wrongdoings (that is, sins) seem to me to be included.* <note>original: "Nihil est aliud malefacere, quam neglectis rebus æternis... mihi videntur includi."</note> From this, one can conclude that he includes both Musicians and their listeners, who praise performances and Concerts so highly when they please them—and when the voices are excellent—that they have no words left to explain themselves other than "ecstasies," "miracles," and "raptures." They must not limit their contentment to sounds and harmony; rather, they must use them only to climb higher and to visit our eternal dwelling, which is none other than God, as Saint Augustine notes in the book *On the Magnitude of the Soul*, chapter one: *I believe that God himself is a certain proper dwelling and homeland of the soul, by whom it was created.* <note>original: "Propriam quandam habitationem animæ ac patriam Deum ipsum credo esse, à quo creata est."</note> This is why one must incessantly aspire to this dwelling, of which it is spoken with such fervor in the Psalm: *How lovely are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the Lord:* <note>original: "Quàm dilecta tabernacula tua Domine virtutum, concupiscit & deficit anima mea in atria Domini:"</note> Where
