The Prophet <note>The "Prophet" refers to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> describes the dwelling that the righteous must make in God; for one must believe that one does not arrive at this torrent of delight, of which he speaks elsewhere in these terms, *You shall make them drink from the torrent of your pleasure* <note>original: "Torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos"; Psalm 36:8</note>; nor to that beatitude which he describes at the end of the preceding Psalm, *Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you forever and ever* <note>original: "Beati qui habitant in domo tua Domine in sæcula sæculorum laudabunt te"; Psalm 84:4</note>, if one does not seek the means to reach it with every kind of diligence and affection. # COROLLARY VIII.

One may say that all Music is almost nothing else than the **Unison**, just as the virtues are nothing other than **love**; and consequently, that love and the Unison are similar. For if **Consonances** <term>Consonances: Intervals or chords that sound pleasant and stable to the ear.</term> have anything good and agreeable in them, they take it from the Unison, just as all virtues hold their goodness and excellence from love. This can be confirmed by the authority of Saint Augustine, who defines Virtue in the book *On the Customs of the Church*, chapter 14: *I would affirm that virtue is nothing at all but the supreme love of God; for that which is called the fourfold virtue is, as I understand it, named from the various dispositions of that same love.* <note>original Latin: "Nihil omnino esse virtutem affirmauerim nisi summum Dei amorem..."</note> And then he defines the four Cardinal Virtues thus: *Temperance is love for God keeping itself whole and incorrupt; Fortitude is love easily enduring all things for the sake of God; Justice is love serving God alone, and for this reason ruling well over all other things subject to man; Prudence is love discerning well between those things that help one toward God and those that might hinder.* <note>original Latin: "Temperantia est amor Dei sese integrum incorruptúmque seruans..."</note>

I wish further to add what he says of Love in the 52nd Epistle written to Macedonius, so that those who love the pleasures of Music are not so unfortunate as to deprive themselves of the pleasure received from the love of God, of which the slightest feeling is worth more than all the favors of Kings, and all the pleasures of the world. *In this life, virtue is nothing but loving what ought to be loved. To choose this is prudence; to be turned away from it by no troubles is fortitude; to be turned away by no allurements is temperance; and to be turned away by no pride is justice. But what should we choose as the chief object of our love, if not that than which we find nothing better? This is God.* <note>original Latin: "In hac vita virtus non est nisi diligere quod diligendum est..."</note>

strong unities in the understanding, since that of the intellect fills the whole world, and penetrates everywhere.
One experiences the same thing in the Geometric point, which can produce no quantity unless it first moves itself, for the line is the movement of the point: but intellectual unity—and consequently equality, which has unity for its foundation—is immobile; and because God is even more immutable and more immobile than unity or equality, it is difficult to understand the manner in which He creates things as different as those we see. Thus, we believe that the creation of the world is the miracle of miracles.
Now, we must examine whether the <term>ratio of equality</term> <note>The ratio 1:1, representing the Unison in music.</note> produces the ratios of inequality, or whether it is merely called the origin and foundation of said ratios because it is the first, or the simplest, and the easiest to conceive, just as unity is easier to understand than the binary <note>The number two.</note> or other numbers.
Those who hold that equality is the principle of inequality say that <term>multiple ratios</term> <note>Ratios like 2:1, 3:1, 4:1, etc.</note> are born from the ratio of equality, and that <term>superparticular ratios</term> <note>Ratios where the larger number contains the smaller number plus one part of it, such as 3:2 or 4:3.</note> come from multiples, and <term>superpartient ratios</term> <note>Ratios where the larger number contains the smaller plus several parts of it, such as 5:3.</note> from superparticulars: which they explain in this manner.
If one compares two unities, they make the ratio of equality (1:1); and if, after having added them, one compares them to unity, one has the <term>double ratio</term> of 2 to 1 <note>The Octave.</note>, which comes from the ratio of equality. Then, if one adds the terms of the double ratio, which make 3, and compares them with 2, one has the first superparticular ratio, namely the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>The 3:2 ratio, which produces the Perfect Fifth.</note>. When its lesser term is compared to its two added terms—that is to say, 3 being compared to 5—it makes the first superpartient ratio, which is called the <term>surbipartient three</term> <note>The 5:3 ratio, producing the Major Sixth.</note>. I leave aside the long discourses that <term>Pappus</term> <note>Pappus of Alexandria (c. 290–350 AD), a Greek mathematician.</note> makes on the generation of ratios in the third book of his *Collections*, where he holds that the ten species of proportions of which <term>Boethius</term> <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was a standard textbook for a millennium.</note>, <term>Salinas</term> <note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a Spanish music theorist and organist.</note>, and others speak after him, are produced by the <term>mediety</term> <note>Proportionality or means (arithmetic, geometric, or harmonic).</note>, or the Geometric analogy that he calls *Divine*. In effect, one finds the aforementioned ratios if one adds unities together in such a way as to make numbers to which unity is compared; but this production comes more from the understanding than from nature; for unity is indifferent to production and engenders nothing of itself, since it remains always unity in whatever way one might take it. So, I do not see how it can engender the ratio of equality, nor how the ratio of equality can engender other ratios: for if one has recourse to the understanding, it can as easily derive the ratio of equality from the multiple ratio as the multiple ratio from equality, since it is as easy to destroy and divide as it is to build and compose. Now, it composes when it derives the multiple ratio from equality, and divides when it derives the ratio of equality from the multiple. As for unity considered in its root and in its sovereign abstraction, it cannot engender the ratio of equality, which always supposes different terms, for it is without any difference in its source. From this comes the fact that it serves to explain the simplicity and identity of the divine nature, which nevertheless comprises two ratios of equality because of the three divine persons who constitute the two aforementioned ratios.
And because these ratios precede all others, and because they are the source and origin of all possible beings, one can say that the ratio of divine equality is the principle of all multiple, superparticular, and superpartient ratios—

...just as omnipotence is the cause of all creatures, since there can be no natural being or <term>being of reason</term> <note>A philosophical term referring to things that exist only in the mind, such as mathematical concepts, as opposed to physical objects.</note> that does not proceed from and depend on sovereign reason.

I know that equations, unity, and the <term>ratio of equality</term> <note>The mathematical relationship of 1:1, representing perfect sameness.</note> serve as the principle of the sciences, because they begin with the simplest and easiest things in order to arrive at the most difficult. But nature does not follow this order, for she so delights in the diversity of her works that she makes almost all of them unequal. Even God himself, who is their author, has maintained a perpetual inequality among the principal creatures of the Universe—whether we consider their qualities or their sizes, as one experiences in the Sun, the Moon, the earth, the water, and the air— and has willed to reserve unity and the ratio of equality for himself, as his own sovereignty and independence.

Nevertheless, the ratio of equality is so sterile that it can engender no other ratio (even if one considers it in God) unless one assumes at the same time a power to act. Thus, it is necessary that the divine power have its object, whether actual or possible, before one can consider the ratios that proceed from those of divine equality—if indeed one can say they proceed from it at all. For even if one were to suppose there were no ratio of equality in God, and one conceived of Him as an immense and omnipotent nature without any Persons <note>Referring to the three Persons of the Holy Trinity.</note>, one would still find the same ratios of equality and inequality in all possible or actual creatures that we encounter now. This is because these ratios are nothing other than the rapports and relations they have to one another, whether one compares the size or the quantity and other properties of some to those of others, or whether they are of such a nature that they can be compared to one another. For it is not necessary to compare them to engender the ratios that are born by a natural emanation accompanying the production of created beings; so much so, that it is not possible for God to create two things without them being immediately equal or unequal.

And if one considers the production of the divine persons (without which there would be no other relation than that of the very simple identity of the divine essence compared to itself), it is necessary that they be equal or unequal—if, however, there can be a ratio of equality between those who are one and the same thing with the principle of the <term>ratio of identity</term>. For if it is necessary that equal things be of different natures, then it is very certain that the divine persons cannot be "equal" in that sense. ...two things, where one is twice as small or twice as large as the other to produce the <term>double ratio</term> <note>The mathematical ratio of 2:1, which in music produces the interval of an octave.</note>; so that, with regard to ratios, we do through multiplication and division what *God* does through creation.

From this it follows that the <term>ratio of equality</term> <note>The 1:1 ratio, where two values are identical.</note> and the <term>Unison</term> <note>The musical interval where two voices or instruments play the exact same pitch.</note> are not, strictly speaking, the principles of inequality and of Consonances. It is merely that the Unison—which comes from the equality of beats, or the movements of air that strike the ear—is simpler and easier to conceive than the other Consonances. Furthermore, it is not possible to consider ratios of inequality unless one first assumes that of equality, because if equality did not exist, inequality would not exist. Conversely, equality can exist without inequality, just as the creator or the power to create can exist without creatures, or without the act of creation.

From this one can draw a powerful reason to prove divinity and the ratio of equality, since it is impossible for there to be ratios of inequality unless one assumes that of equality, or for there to be limited and finite beings unless one assumes an infinite and boundless being. Consequently, there can be no ratio of equality outside of God unless one assumes His action and His goodwill toward limited beings, since there is nothing equal or unequal where there is nothing at all. By this we see that the Unison, along with all the ratios of equality or inequality and all the considerations we may have, should lead us solely or principally to God as to a safe harbor. There, an infinity of ratios meet in their excellence and in their center, just as all the points on a circumference meet at the center of a circle by means of an infinity of lines. These lines should serve us as a mental image or an <term>artificial memory</term> <note>A "memory palace" or mnemonic system used by Renaissance and Baroque scholars to organize complex information.</note> to recall all our thoughts and affections, and to unite and carry them to God. He is, by even greater right, the source and the end of all different beings, just as the ratio of equality or the Unison is the source of the ratios of inequality or Consonances.

->COROLLARY I.<-

One can consider the nature of created beings as the nature of all ratios, and see if there is some creature to which all others relate, or which serves as their measure, just as other ratios relate to the ratio of equality, which is the measure of their perfection. For if one had found some material body or some created thing that was simple, and which created the differences of the beings we see—just as unity creates the difference between numbers through its different repetitions—it would be easy to know the composition and origin of all sensible things. This principle would lead us out of the labyrinth of ignorance and error in which we lose ourselves almost as often as we attempt to reason. Thus, there remains for us no other consolation than to throw ourselves into the arms of the Father of sciences and lights, and to say to Him with <term>Saint Augustine</term>, *"Our heart is restless, O Lord, until it rests in Thee."* <note>original: "Inquietum est cor nostrum Domine, donec quiescat in te." A famous line from Augustine's *Confessions*.</note> For as for the sciences that can be acquired in our current state, they are so imperfect that they cause more affliction and toil than pleasure, as the <term>Wise Man</term> <note>A common reference to King Solomon, traditionally credited as the author of the biblical book of Ecclesiastes.</note> remarked quite judiciously when he said that he who increases his knowledge increases his toil at the same time, and consequently his sorrow: *"He who adds knowledge, adds labor."* <note>original: "Qui addit scientiam, addit & laborem." A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:18.</note>

### COROLLARY II.

The Unison and the <term>ratio of equality</term> <note>The 1:1 ratio where two values are identical.</note> represent the body; for when the weights and the arms of mechanical instruments are equal, no movement occurs, because equal things cannot act upon other equal things. Now, the ratio of equality holds the middle ground between the ratios of minor and major inequality, such that one cannot pass from one to the other of these two ratios without passing through that of equality, which serves as the foundation and the model for the other ratios, just as the Unison does for the other Consonances.

## PROPOSITION VIII.

*To know whether the smaller ratios take their origin from the larger ones, or the larger ones from the smaller; and consequently whether the smallest musical intervals, such as tones and semitones, come from the largest—for example, the Octave—or whether the Octave takes its origin from the said intervals.*

This difficulty is not the least in Music, for there are those who hold that the largest ratios—for example, the <term>multiples</term> <note>Ratios where the larger number is a direct multiple of the smaller, like 2:1 or 3:1.</note>—depend on and take their origin from the smaller ones, that is to say, from the <term>superparticular</term> <note>original: "surparticulieres"; a ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 (a Fifth) or 4:3 (a Fourth).</note> or <term>superpartient</term> <note>original: "surpartientes"; a ratio where the numerator exceeds the denominator by more than one, such as 5:3.</note> ratios. Consequently, they argue that the Octave depends on the Fifth and the Fourth, just as the double ratio depends on the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: "sesquialtere"; the 3:2 ratio.</note> and the <term>sesquitertian</term> <note>original: "sesquitierce"; the 4:3 ratio.</note>, although many others are of the opposite opinion. Now, the former base their view first on the fact that the large ratios and Consonances are similar to large numbers, which are composed of smaller ones and which depend upon unity. From this it follows that the names of the Consonances are taken from the numbers of which they are composed; this is why it seems that unity must serve as their common measure, for Thirds, Fourths, and Fifths are so named by reason of their three, four, or five sounds; and furthermore, small intervals come before the larger ones, just as unity comes before numbers.

Secondly, lines take their origin from points, and figures from lines, and not the reverse. Now, Consonances are similar to figures or lines, and the tones or semitones of which they are composed are similar to lines or points; from which it follows that Consonances depend on the smallest intervals, and consequently that the smallest intervals are simpler than the largest ones.

Thirdly, when one takes two <term>strings</term> <note>original: "chordes"; referring to the strings of a monochord used for mathematical measurement of pitch.</note> at the Unison, where one remains always at the same tone, or on the same note, while one shortens the other, one passes through an infinity of small intervals before arriving at the Minor Third; that is to say, before the second string is shorter than the first by one-fifth part <note>A minor third is produced by a string ratio of 6:5; thus the vibrating string is 5/6 the length of the original, having been "shortened" by 1/6 (the text says 1/5, likely referring to the division of the remaining parts).</note>; for before one shortens it by a fifth part, it must be shortened by a thousandth, a hundredth, and a twentieth part, etc.

Fourthly, we experience that natural things which are perfect, such as man and animals, are composed of their parts upon which they depend; therefore the Octave, being perfect, is composed of tones and semitones as its parts. And one does not find that imperfect things are born

Finally, when one teaches Music to someone, they first make them learn the smaller intervals—that is to say, the tones and semitones—rather than the Consonances, because it is easier to sing *C, D, E, and E, F* <note>original: "Vt, re, mi, & mi, fa"; these are the traditional solfège syllables used in early music education.</note>, which is to say, to sing by conjunct degrees <note>Moving from one note to the very next note in the scale.</note> than by intervals, or separated degrees; just as it is easier to walk step by step than to jump. Now, that which is easier and more natural precedes that which is more difficult, and that which pertains more to art.

But one can respond to all these reasons that musical intervals, whose nature consists of certain proportions, cannot be compared like number to number, because numbers are <term>commensurable</term> <note>Meaning they can be measured against each other using a common unit.</note> with one another, since unity is their common measure; this does not happen to all proportions, but only to some, like the double and the quadruple, which are to each other as one to two. For although the name of the Consonances is taken from the number of their sounds, as I have already said in a specific discourse, nevertheless their nature is not similar to these numbers: for example, the Octave is not composed of eight units, even though it ordinarily contains eight sounds. Moreover, there is no degree, whether consonant or dissonant, that can serve as a common measure for the Octave—whether one takes the <term>major semitone</term> for the smallest interval of the <term>Diatonic Octave</term> <note>The standard seven-note scale used in Western music.</note>, or the <term>minor semitone</term> for the smallest of the <term>Chromatic</term> <note>A scale that uses all twelve semitones.</note>, or the <term>Diesis</term> <note>A very small interval, smaller than a semitone, found in ancient Greek and specialized musical tunings.</note> for the smallest of the <term>Enharmonique</term> <note>A scale system using microtonal intervals smaller than a semitone.</note>. For these intervals, when added together, always either surpass the Octave or are smaller than it: and it is not possible to find an interval or degree, however small it may be, that can serve to measure the Octave or any other Consonance. As for the number of sounds or intervals contained in the Octave, their number is not determined; for since one can say that every ratio is composed of, or can be divided into, an infinity of other ratios, it follows that the Octave or any other Consonance can be divided into an infinity of intervals or degrees, and consequently into an infinity of sounds.

The second reason makes use of the comparison to a point which produces lines, and to unity which begets numbers: but the point is not of the same genus as lines, whereas small intervals of sounds are of the same genus as the interval of the Octave and other Consonances; consequently, this comparison is not strong enough to prove that Consonances come from the degrees they contain. To this one may add that the point can just as well be generated from lines as lines from the point, for one determines points on a plane by the meeting and intersection of lines. Furthermore, no interval can produce any Consonance by its movement, as the point begets the line by its own; for as soon as the interval leaves its proportion, it leaves its nature to pass into another interval. But the nature of the point always remains entirely itself, even if it moves. Moreover, it is not possible for the point to surpass or generate the smallest line of all possibilities unless it moves, even if one multiplies it to infinity: but one can so multiply the smallest interval of all possibilities that it will surpass the Octave and the other Consonances.

The third reason is no better than the others, for if one puts two strings of equal length at the <term>Unison</term>, it is easier to divide one by the hal[f]...

Thus we must consider the whole before its parts, perfection before imperfection, the body before the point, the soul before the body, the understanding before the will, spiritual and intellectual things before material ones, the Creator before his creatures, and the glory of God before all other things.

Now, of all the simple Consonances whose sounds differ in terms of low and high, the Octave is the principal and the most pleasant; consequently, it must be considered as the source and the origin of all other Consonances, which emerge from it like rays from the Sun, like effects from their cause, and like parts of their whole. For if one divides it in two parts, one has the Fifth and the Fourth, the difference of which is the major tone; and if one divides the Fifth, which makes the largest part of the Octave, into two parts, one has the Major Third and the Minor Third, the difference of which is the minor semitone—just as the major semitone is the difference between the Fourth and the Major Third, and the minor tone is the difference between the Fourth and the Minor Third.

As for the smaller degrees, they come from the comparison of tones and semitones: for the Comma is the difference between the major tone and the minor tone, and the <term>Diesis</term> <note>In early modern music theory, the diesis is a very small interval, often the difference between a major and minor semitone.</note> is the difference between the major and minor semitone. This suffices for now to know that the smallest intervals of Music come from the largest, just as the determination of points comes from the division or the intersection of lines, lines from the sectioning of planes, and planes from the sectioning or division of solids. But I will treat more amply the generation of all degrees and intervals of Music in another place.

And although the smallest intervals are found before the largest when, starting with two strings set in Unison, one shortens or lengthens one of them little by little—passing through the comma and through an infinity of other small intervals before meeting the Minor Third, which is the smallest of all Consonances—this does not prove that Consonances or large intervals come from the small ones. One does not necessarily "pass through" the small ones to reach the said Consonances, even though one can encounter them in this manner, and even though one ordinarily sings by <term>conjunct degrees</term> <note>Moving from one note to the very next note in a scale, like a staircase, rather than jumping.</note>. Furthermore, if while leaving one of the strings at the same tone, one begins to place a <term>bridge</term> <note>original: "cheualet"; a movable support used on a monochord to change the vibrating length of a string.</note> under the other, and one always touches the smaller part of the string against the one that remained whole, one will find the larger intervals before the smaller ones. For example, if one first takes an eighth part of the string, it will produce the triple Octave against the whole string; if one takes a sixth part, it will produce the Nineteenth; and if one takes half, it will produce the Octave, as will be seen more fully in the treatise on the Monochord. encounters <note>The text here completes the word "rencontres" from the previous page, referring to the "encounters" or combinations of sounds.</note> that are made of small or large intervals.

The fourth reason supposes that the Octave is composed of tones and semi-tones, which would need to be proven; for those who claim these degrees <term>degrees</term> (the individual steps or notes of a scale) arise from the division of the Octave, or from the difference between consonances, deny this principle. They say that when natural things are engendered, the smallest parts are not produced first, nor the largest last; rather, they all begin together, and the whole exists as soon as its parts, even though it does not appear as large at the beginning as it does in the middle and at the end. But there is no need to consider the production of natural things here to understand that of consonances; it is enough to note that one does not use degrees to produce the Octave or other consonances, but for other reasons—for example, to sing by conjunct degrees <term>conjunct degrees</term> (moving step-by-step between notes rather than leaping); otherwise, one would have to pass through every possible degree contained within the consonances. There is no other reason why we use the ordinary degrees rather than an infinite number of others, except that those we use come from the difference between the Consonances, as I said in the solution to the third reason.

The fifth reason is based on the method used by Masters to teach children, whom they first make sing by degrees rather than by intervals, because the sounds that form the degrees of the tone and the semi-tone are closer to one another and easier to sing than those that form larger intervals. But this experience only proves that it is easier to sing by degrees than by intervals; it does not prevent these degrees from coming from the consonances, from which they had to be derived before their use could be known. For those who invented Music did not begin with degrees, but with consonant intervals, for which it is much easier to understand the reasons <note>original: "raisons"—in this context, it refers to both the logical reasons and the mathematical ratios (Latin: *ratio*).</note> than those of the degrees, as I demonstrate elsewhere.

Now, it matters very little whether one says that the large ratios and consonances come from smaller ratios and dissonances, or that the latter come from the former, depending on the different ways one might speak of them; for Music is made neither better nor worse for it. However, it seems more reasonable to hold that the degrees come from the Consonances—since they exist only to reach them, and they are born from their differences—than to say that the Consonances come from these degrees. But one must leave everyone the freedom to believe what they please, since one can even hold that neither has any origin other than their own terms, or the comparison made between said terms, just as we said in the other proposition that the ratio of inequality <term>ratio of inequality</term> (a mathematical relationship where two numbers are different, creating an interval) does not come from that of equality any sooner than the ratio of equality <term>ratio of equality</term> (the 1:1 ratio, or unison) comes from that of inequality.

had Him make only two creatures, where one surpassed the other by an eighth part <note>A "sesquioctave" ratio of 9:8, which in music corresponds to a whole tone.</note>, the smaller ratio would exist without the larger; and if one contemplates the order of the ratios that are in the divine ideas—that is to say, if one considers how God knows these ratios—one will not find that He considers the double ratio <note>The 2:1 ratio, which creates the Octave.</note> before the sesquioctave, nor that He willed that one should precede the other. For God has nothing in His nature that obliges Him to consider one rather than the other; unless one says that the Father and the Son are in a double ratio to the Holy Spirit, since one can compare the first and second person to the third to find the double ratio in the divinity, and to prove that the Octave is the simplest and sweetest consonance in Music, if one excepts the Unison. The Unison represents in some manner the divine nature, in as much as it is from the Unison that we must draw the reason why the three persons are one and the same thing with the essence of God, without which they would be entirely distinct and would have no unity; just as the intervals of Music would not unite at all, and would always remain distinct, if they did not participate in the influences that the Unison sends to all the Consonances, and even to the Dissonances, just as the Sun sends its own upon all bodies.

But it seems that the ratio of equality must precede that of inequality, both in creatures and in divine thought, because it is impossible to make or to want to make two unequal things if first one does not consider them equal; for if one begins one of the things with a point, when one wants to make another thing unequal, it must begin with that point before being made larger, and consequently it will be equal before being unequal. And if one compares nothingness with the said point in order to find inequality before equality, one will fall back again into equality, in as much as nothingness is before all sorts of points; although nothingness compared to nothingness creates a ratio of identity rather than one of equality, and consequently one could say in some fashion that the ratio of inequality is before that of equality, because the first comparison that one can make is that of nothingness with the point—provided, however, that the point is different from nothingness; which must be reserved for another discourse.

### COROLLARY II.

This second Corollary confirms the preceding one, for if the smaller ratios come from the larger ones, and the smaller intervals of Music from the larger ones, it seems one must conclude that the Octave comes from the Fifteenth, and the latter from the Twenty-second, etc., since the ratio of the Octave is smaller than that of the Fifteenth, etc. <note>In mathematical ratios, the Octave (2:1) is "smaller" than the Fifteenth (4:1) or Twenty-second (8:1), though it sounds like a smaller musical distance.</note> This is nonetheless not true; for the <term>Disdiapason</term> (the double octave) is a doubled Octave, and the <term>Trisdiapason</term> (the triple octave) is a tripled Octave. But all these considerations in no way prevent the smaller intervals from coming from the larger ones, if one limits the size of said intervals to the Octave, whose different divisions produce, or at least make known to us, all the intervals necessary to Music, as I shall demonstrate elsewhere; for as for the large consonant intervals that surpass the Octave, they can be called the shadows, or the effects of the Octave, or of the intervals it contains.

### COROLLARY III.

Since the number two follows immediately from the unity from which it proceeds, and since there is the same relationship between the ratio of equality and the double ratio <note>The "ratio of equality" is 1:1 (Unison), and the "double ratio" is 2:1 (Octave).</note> as there is between identity and equality, or between one and two, it is reasonable to speak of the Octave before speaking of the other consonances. For the Octave has unity as its lower term and the number two as its greater; although this cannot be done without leaving unity and simplicity—which we leave only to consider their power and proportions, just as theologians leave questions of divine essence to speak of His attributes, which are nothing other than the same essence considered in different ways; just as numbers are nothing other than unity considered differently and according to various relationships; and just as the mathematical line is nothing other than the point considered in its movement, and after its movement.

### PROPOSITION IX.

->*To determine whether the chord whose ratio is two to one is correctly called the Octave, or whether it should rather be given another name, such as the Diapason.*<-

It is appropriate to discuss this difficulty, since we are attempting to explain the reasoning behind everything found in music, of which the Diapason is one of the most excellent parts. The Greeks called it *dia pason* <note>original Greek: διὰ πασῶν, literally meaning "through all [the strings]".</note> because it encompasses all the simple consonances and dissonances. But it seems the name "Octave" usually given to it does not suit it very well, given that the double ratio can just as easily be divided into ten or several sounds as into eight; indeed, it is divided into 25 strings or sounds in the Enharmonic genus, and into 16 in the Chromatic, as we shall say later. But perhaps one will answer that it has only eight sounds in the Diatonic genus, which is the natural and first of all the genera. This, however, will not remain without reply, for this genus must have nine sounds to be perfect.

Furthermore, the genus used now in the composition of Motets and Airs has 19 strings, or 18 intervals, as I will show in the book on different notes and all the characters one can use in composing, whether for singing or for playing instruments. We must therefore see what name it can be given, and whether it is more appropriate to call it a Ninth, or a Sixteenth, or by some other name, for the reasons I have just deduced.

For I find it hard to believe that all the ancient Latins and French, and all our neighbors, have given it this name without reason. They may have taken it from the ordinary number of sounds that the Greeks and musicians of other nations placed in the Octave according to our ordinary notes, *Do, re, mi, fa, sol, re, mi, fa* <note>original: "Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, re, mi, fa". ...following the new syllables, *Bo, ce, di, ga, lo, ma, ni, bo* <note>These syllables refer to "Bocedization," a system of musical notation used in the 16th and 17th centuries, similar to modern "Do-Re-Mi."</note>, which we shall discuss in another place. For although the compositions made today require 9 or 12 strings, as is the case for the **Viol**, the **Lute**, and the **Spinet**; or even 16, 19, or 25 strings, as I shall say elsewhere, this nevertheless does not take the name away from the **Octave**. There are other reasons for this name, even if one only considers the effects of the number eight, which has admirable occurrences in Music. This is because there are only eight chords and eight ratios that contain them: namely, the *Unison* which contains the ratio of equality; the *Diapason* <note>The Greek term for an Octave.</note> whose double ratio is the first of the multiples; the *Fifth* which contains the first of the superparticular ratios <note>A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2.</note>, which is called the *Sesquialter*; the *Fourth* which has the *sesquitertian* ratio, which the Greeks call *Epitritos*; the *Major Third* which includes the *Sesquiquartal*; the *Minor Third* which has the *Sesquiquintal*; the *Major Sixth* which contains the *superbipartient-three* <note>The ratio 5:3.</note>; and the *Minor Sixth* which has the *supertripartient-five* <note>The ratio 8:5.</note>. To this one may add that the number eight represents the first cube whose root is two, and the blessedness which is signified by the Octave; for several Psalms have "for the octave" <note>original: "prooctaua"</note> in their inscription, particularly when they speak of blessedness, as Saint Ambrose remarked in the fifth book he wrote on the sixth chapter of Saint Luke.

To tell the truth, the reasons that can be brought forward for either of the two opinions could hold a mind in balance, and cause one to give another name to the Octave, if the length of time had not engraved this word into the minds of Musicians, in whose favor I show that this chord must be called the *Octave*.

The arts can never proceed better than when they imitate nature, whose actions the sciences consider. The names that best express effects are the best given and the best imposed. Now, sounds—which consist only in the movements of the air—cannot be better distinguished by any internal difference or external quality than by low and high pitch <note>In the original: "le graue & l'aigu."</note>. This brings about a great confusion; for assuming one low tone, all other tones unto infinity will be high, and assuming one high tone, all others will be low. This is why Musicians were constrained to call them the second after the low tone, then the third, the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, the seventh, and the eighth. They would have gone further, just as Mathematicians have climbed up to ten; but considering all these sounds, they found that the second note after the low one produced nothing good; they passed over it, and noted it as harmful <note>The author is referring to the dissonance of a "second" interval.</note>. They found that the third mixed easily with the low tone, and that whether held softly or strongly, it always possessed harmony; they called the soft one the *Minor Third*, and the strong one the *Major Third*. They came to consider the fourth high sound after this same low sound and found it good. And then they considered the fifth, which they found even better, because it makes a more perfect mixture than the fourth and is firmer than the third—but it can be neither higher nor lower than it ought to be. They also considered the sixth and found it to be of the same nature as the third, in that it could be stronger or weaker without being disagreeable; that is why they called it the *Minor* and *Major Sixth*.

As for the seventh sound after this low one, they found it to be of the same nature as the second, and placed it in the rank of those from which nothing good should be expected.

But having considered the eighth, they found it so similar to the low note that it is the same rather than another. Now after having considered all the others that follow, they found that they produced the same effect against the 8th as the previous ones did against the low note; thus they stopped at this 8th, and believed it would be in vain to proceed further, since one can sufficiently consider all the effects of sounds within the span of these first eight tones. Holding it for certain that everything that happens to sounds rising above the Octave is similar to what happens to those below, they could not give them names that designated them better than those of their position: *Second*, *Third*, *Fourth*, *Fifth*, *Sixth*, *Seventh*, and *Octave*, which cannot be changed without introducing confusion into the common knowledge of Practical Music.

Some believe that to call it *Diapason* <note>From the Greek *dia pason chor-don*, meaning "through all the strings."</note>, as the Greeks did, is to give a general name to a specific thing, and the name of the genus to the species; and that the makers of Organs and Spinets <note>A smaller, rectangular cousin of the harpsichord.</note> have better named their keyboard, or the measure of their pipes and strings, by the name *Diapason*, which contains forty-nine steps, strings, or pipes to produce as many tones—namely, 29 that proceed by natural degrees to make four Octaves, and twenty others that serve to make *minor Thirds* in certain places (as will be explained in the third book on the Spinet) and major ones in others, and to find the *major* or *minor Sixths*, and the *perfect Fifths* in the places where they must meet when one passes from one Octave to another. For this keyboard contains all the tones by means of which one can make all sorts of melodies, whether simple or in harmony, which can be pleasing to the ear or to the understanding that judges them. As for other divisions of sounds, they are not natural, since no ear takes pleasure in them; and just as nature has set limits to the sea that even the stormiest waves cannot cross, so no human understanding can make a false *Fifth* (that is, smaller than it should be) or a false *Octave* give pleasure, because one cannot cross the boundaries that nature has prescribed for tones without overturning nature itself.

Organists have gone beyond the Octave and have added the *Tenth*, the *Twelfth*, the *Fifteenth*, etc., which they did to designate the keys of their keyboard; for this *Tenth* is only a *Third* higher than the first—that is, repeated; and this *Twelfth* is a *Fifth* at the Octave of the first *Fifth*. This is why one can say that the word *Octave*, used by our Musicians, is more appropriate and more significant than the word *Diapason*, which is more properly used to signify the twenty-nine tones of instruments rather than the eight sounds of the Octave.

Nevertheless, of all the other names that can be given to the *Octave*, the Greek one is one of the most appropriate, and besides, it is already accepted; for it is known that the *Diapason* signifies the Octave, or the harmony <note>original: "accord"</note> that contains all the simple intervals of Music, just as the number ten <note>original: "nombre denaire"</note> contains all numbers. For those added to ten are only repetitions of the other numbers that precede it, just as the sounds added to the Octave are only repetitions of those that precede it.

signifies "through all," <note>original French: *signifie par tous*. The author is explaining the etymology of the Greek term *Diapason*, meaning "through all the strings."</note> seeing as the Octave encompasses all sounds, just as light contains all colors, the circle all planes, and the sphere all bodies; for if light produces all colors by the different divisions or conjunctions of its rays (as one sees in the rainbow) and the sphere all bodies, the Octave also produces all Consonances and Dissonances by its different divisions.

These reasons have prevented the Greeks from calling the Octave "through seven," <note>original Greek: *δι’ ἑπτὰ* (*di' hepta*)</note> even though it had only seven strings in the time of Terpander, <note>An influential Greek poet and musician of the 7th century BCE, credited with increasing the lyre's strings from four to seven.</note> or because it now has only seven natural intervals; and from naming it "through eight," <note>original Greek: *δι’ ὀκτὼ* (*di' okto*)</note> although it contains eight sounds, and they have given names to the Fifth and to the other Consonances which they took from the number of their strings or their sounds. For the ancients placed only seven strings on their instruments—as Aristotle remarks in the 32nd problem of the 19th section <note>A reference to the *Problemata*, a collection of questions often attributed to Aristotle that explores music theory and physics.</note>—so that the seven planets would have their seats upon the strings of the instruments; for the thickest string represented the movement of Saturn, which is the slowest, and the thinnest represented the Moon as the swiftest; and the one in the middle, of which Aristotle speaks so often (as in problems 20, 25, 30, and 45), represented the Sun. The Octave can therefore be named *Diapason*, since we judge all of Music by the Octave, just as we judge an entire building by its foundation, and one can restore Music by its knowledge alone, as one might the entire edifice by that of its foundation. Furthermore, the makers of Organs and <term>Spinets|Small, portable keyboard instruments of the harpsichord family.</term> regulate their entire keyboard based on a single Octave, which they usually take from the middle, as I shall say when speaking of the industry one must use to tune the Organ and the Spinet.

One could also call this chord a *doubled Consonance*, because it is like a redoubling of the Unison, which it repeats and represents to the ear and the imagination, just as an image represents its prototype, and because it is contained and produced by the double ratio, which is two to one (2:1).

The *Diapason* is also known to bell-founders, whose measure is called *Diapason*, or <term>gauge stick|Original French: *brochete*. A physical tool used for calculating the proportions and thickness of a bell to ensure it sounds the correct pitch.</term>, which serves them in making bells of all sorts of sizes, as I shall show in the book on Bells. The same name can also be applied to the measures of other artisans, and to everything that contains and measures several things.

But one must not easily innovate in the sciences, nor change the terms that those who preceded us found appropriate to preserve. Now, the ancients also gave the name of *Eight* to all things, because it has most excellent properties, particularly when one considers its origin and its division, which contains a perfect equality. This is why the Pythagoreans called it *Justice*, seeing as it has its six faces equal, and that it is made of two times two times two; for 2 multiplied twice by 2 makes 8, whose depth is equal to its length and its width. <note>The author is describing a cube (2³ = 8). In Pythagorean numerology, the cube represented stability and justice.</note> It is also the first number that is divided into two other <term>evenly even|Original: *pairement pairs*. Numbers like 4, 8, or 16 that can be repeatedly divided by two until they reach one.</term> numbers, and has so great a relationship with the number 6 that if this number is subtracted from 8, or from any other cube as many times as possible, only the side <note>meaning the cube root</note> of the cube remains; and if this side is not large enough, one need only add 6 to it, or multiple numbers of 6. For example: 6 taken from 8 leaves 2 as the side of the first cube; 27 divided by 6 leaves 3 as the side of the second cube; 64 divided by 6 leaves 4 as the side or the root...

Philolaüs the Pythagorean <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 470–385 BCE) who was the first to document Pythagorean musical theory.</note> called the number 8 **Geometric Harmony**, because it encompasses all the ratios of the simple accords; for the Minor Sixth, being from 5 to 8, has only 8 for its largest term; or rather because it contains the largest system which has three Octaves, especially since the ancients did not include the Minor Sixth among the number of accords. <note>In ancient Greek music theory, only the Unison, Octave, Fifth, and Fourth were considered "consonances" or accords.</note>

But I shall speak further of the Octave when explaining whether its ratio is two to one, or to 4, or to 8, and of the number of tones it contains; I add only that one can derive a new reason for the name of the Octave from the proportion maintained in organ pipes and in bells that produce the Octave: for the weight and the solidity of the largest pipe, or of the largest bell, is eightfold the weight and the solidity of the smallest pipe and the smallest bell. One must therefore retain the name ***Octave*** to signify the best and most agreeable accord in Music, without, however, rejecting the name ***Diapason***.

The ancients called the Octave **Antiphone**, as seen in the 14th and 16th problems of Aristotle, section 19, since the two sounds of the Octave are similar; for this particle "anti" <note>original Greek: ἀντὶ</note> does not signify a contrariety, but rather an identity, as can be seen in the word "god-like" <note>original Greek: ἀντίθεος (*antitheos*)</note> which Homer uses to say that Ulysses is similar to God.

And Salinas <note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a blind Spanish music theorist and organist.</note> remarks in the 7th chapter of his second book that the **Antiphons** sung before the Psalms are so named because they are sung an Octave higher after those same Psalms during solemn Feasts, particularly in the Church of Toledo and of Susa. <note>original French: *Seguse*. This refers to the diocese of Susa in the Piedmont or possibly a Latinized Spanish see.</note> And the Greeks call the two strings *Hypate* and *Nete* <term>Antiphones</term> <note>Hypate was the lowest-sounding string and Nete the highest in the Greek lyre system.</note> because they produce the Octave. Others have called it **Homophony**, or **Equisonance**, by reason of the equality of its two sounds; though this name is better suited to the Unison.

As for the custom of the Church of Toledo, I rely on what Salinas says of it, but this is not practiced in France, where the word **Antiphon** seems rather to have been invented to signify the manner held in choirs that take up and sing the verses or couplets of the Psalms alternately, facing opposite one another.

## PROPOSITION X.

***To determine whether the ratio of the Octave is double, quadruple, or octuple; that is to say, whether it is two to one, four to one, or eight to one.***

All the ancients believed and taught that the accord called the **Diapason**, or **Octave**, is from one to two—that is, that the ratio of the Octave is double—because they found that two strings of the same tension, of which one is double the other in length and equal in thickness, produce the Octave.

But if we consider other phenomena—that is, the experiments observed regarding the different thicknesses and tensions of strings, and the proportion of the bodies that produce the Octave—we will encounter great difficulties; for experience shows that when two strings equal in length and four times as thick are stretched with the same force, they produce the Octave, by

# Book One #

Consequently, one can say that the **Octave** is four to one, and that its ratio is quadruple, since the strings are in a quadruple ratio to one another regarding their thickness and tension. <note>The author is exploring the "law of strings." While we now define the Octave by a 2:1 frequency ratio, early modern scientists observed that to produce an Octave by changing tension alone, you must increase the weight/force by four times.</note> Now, the quadruple <note>A string four times the size or tension.</note> being stretched by four forces, is four times less tense than the sub-quadruple <note>A string one-fourth the size.</note> stretched by four forces; for if one divides the quadruple into four equal parts, one will have four strings, each of which will be equal to the sub-quadruple; to which if one gives 1/4 of the weight of four pounds, each will have only the quarter of four pounds. For it is the same thing to stretch each sub-quadruple by one force as it is to stretch the quadruple by four forces, inasmuch as the quadruple resists the quadruple force just as much as the sub-quadruple resists the sub-quadruple force, since all things here are proportioned.

The second **Phenomenon** is taken from the different tension of strings that are equal in length and thickness; for if of two equal strings, one is stretched by one force and the other by four, they produce the **Octave**; therefore, the ratio of these tensions is four to one.

The third experiment is taken from the vessels that produce the **Octave**, such as bells and pipes; for the largest of two bells that make an **Octave** is eightfold <note>original: "octuple"</note> the size of the smaller one. This also happens with two organ pipes that make an **Octave**, for the diameter and the height of the large pipe are double the diameter and the height of the small one; consequently, the capacity <note>The internal volume.</note> of the largest is eight times that of the smallest. From this, it follows that the ratio of the **Octave** seems to be 8 to 1, if it follows the ratio of the bodies by which it is produced. <note>If you double the height, width, and depth of an object, its volume increases by $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$.</note>

But the surfaces of said bodies are quadruple, for the surface of the largest bell contains four times the surface of the smallest, and the air is only struck by these surfaces; consequently, we again have the ratio of 4 to 1.

As for their diameters, they are in a double ratio <note>2 to 1</note>, for the diameter of the largest bell or the largest pipe is double the diameter of the other.

Similarly, the surface of the quadruple string is double the surface of the sub-quadruple string, which also happens to their diameters. But one does not find this double ratio in strings equal in length and thickness where one is stretched by one force and the other by four; for one cannot say that the more tense string becomes two times thinner than the less tense one to divide the quadruple ratio, since the decrease is almost imperceptible.

As for the **Phenomenon** of the ancients upon which they based their speculations—namely, on strings that make the **Octave** when they are equal in tension and double in length—even though their double ratio seems to demonstrate that the **Octave** is 2 to 1 (as do the double diameters of the quadruple and sub-quadruple string, or of two bells and two pipes that make the **Octave**), nevertheless, if we join everything that creates the **Octave** by means of two strings of which one is half the length <note>original: "soudouble en longueur"</note>, we will find the quadruple ratio. For one must first consider the double ratio of the lengths, and then the double ratio of the movements <note>Vibrations or cycles.</note> and of the two spaces of air that are struck by these two strings; inasmuch as the string that is half the length, being equally stretched, makes its movements—that is to say, its oscillations <note>original: "tours & retours"</note>—two times faster than the double length, which makes only ten oscillations while the half-length makes twenty.

# On Consonances. #

Now, these two double ratios <note>A "double ratio" refers to the 2:1 proportion. Adding two of them (2:1 and 2:1) creates a 4:1 ratio, which the author calls "quadruple."</note> being added together make the quadruple ratio, which is the first ratio doubled, without which the **Octave** is never encountered. For when two strings are equal in length, a double force is not enough to set one at an **Octave** to the other; rather, it requires four forces against one. It seems necessary, then, to conclude that the ratio of the **Octave** is quadruple, or "doubled," rather than simply double, since all **Phenomena** point toward the quadruple ratio. If one then adds the doubled ratio of the two spaces of air, one would have an octuple ratio <note>8:1</note>; for one must consider the volume of the air just as much as the speed of its motion. However, since the motion of the string that is double <note>The longer string.</note> is just as fast as that of the sub-double <note>The shorter string.</note>—inasmuch as they cover an equal path in equal time when the distance of their returns <note>Vibrations or oscillations.</note> is proportioned to their lengths—and since the motion of the sub-double is only "double" that of the double string in a relative sense (that is, in comparison to the number of its returns, which being shorter by half occur twice as fast), it is sufficient to add the double ratio of the length of the strings and the double of the air spaces to create the quadruple ratio of the **Octave**.

Now, one can confirm this opinion by the works of nature, which seem to follow doubled ratios <note>Geometric progressions or squares.</note> rather than the terms of simple ratios, insofar as they are more **Geometric** and more full of reason than **Arithmetic** ones, as is observed in the proportions maintained by qualities as they increase or diminish. And the air, which creates sound through its motion, should not only be considered as a line, but also as a surface according to which it is struck and broken by the surface of the bodies that produce the motion.

Nevertheless, we may retain the double ratio <note>2:1</note> for the **Octave** and prefer it over the aforementioned ratios, insofar as it enters more easily into the imagination; for it is simpler, just as a root is simpler and easier to conceive than its square. The same must be concluded for the ratios used for other **consonances** and musical intervals. And if one wishes to set the **Octave** at eight-to-one because of the octuple bodies that produce it, one can still retain the double ratio for the explanation and the imagination of the **Octave**, since simple ratios are like the roots of doubled and tripled ratios. Thus, by speaking of simple ratios which govern the spaces of air and the size of bodies taken by their diameters, one will have in mind the images of their doubled and tripled ratios which represent their surfaces and their solids. Meanwhile, the **Musician** will have the satisfaction that comes from **Arithmetic**, **Geometry**, and **Harmony**, all of which he will reunite by starting with the simple to arrive at the complex; this will serve to find the causes of the properties and effects of **Harmony**.

Now, after having examined what can be said on this subject, I shall show that it is not only better to choose the double ratio for the **Octave**, but that it is entirely necessary. Since sound is nothing but the motion of the air, and this motion is always found to be double in the **Octave**—and never quadruple nor octuple—it follows that the two sounds of the **Octave** are in the same ratio as these motions. This I demonstrate clearly by the figure that follows, in which A B signifies the string that produces the low sound, and A E represents the string that produces the high sound of the **Octave**, in unison with which one can set A B in...

Furthermore, if it makes the **Octave** below with the string A E, and one pulls A E to D, and A B to F, they will strike an equal part of air, so that one only needs to consider the returns <note>vibrations or oscillations</note> of the strings to know the ratio of the **Octave** and of the other **Consonances**, since they are the immediate cause, or rather the formal cause <note>The "formal cause" refers to the essential nature or mathematical pattern of the sound (its frequency), while the "efficient cause" is the physical object—the string—that produces it.</note> of the sounds which have the [physical] bodies for their efficient cause.

There is no longer any reason to doubt that the two sounds of the **Octave** are in a double ratio <note>original: "raison double"; in this context, it means a 2:1 ratio.</note> to one another, and that this foundation is unshakable, since sounds are nothing other than a multitude of beats of air.

This can be applied to the other **Consonances**, whose ratios must be taken from the returns made by the strings, or from the beats of air made by all other bodies; so that this demonstration is universal for all intervals of sound that one can imagine, without there being a need to repeat it.

### COROLLARY I.

I have omitted several proportions that are found between the solidity of bodies and the highness of sounds, but these will be found in the *Book on the Causes of Sound*: this is why I only add that there are some who have imagined that the ratio of the **Octave** is "double" in such a way that it is not just two to one, 4 to 2, 8 to 4, 16 to 8, etc., but only in the double ratio whose terms encompass all the degrees <note>In early music theory, "degrees" refer to the individual notes or steps within the scale.</note>: that is to say, that the double ratio of the **Octave** is 48 to 24, which are the smallest terms of all those that can comprise the seven intervals, or the eight sounds of the first species of **Octave**, as one sees in the table of the first proposition of this book which contains all the **Consonances** and their degrees with their ratios. From this it would follow that the double ratio of the Pythagorean and Platonic **Octave** would be 972 to 480, which are the smallest whole numbers that can contain the eight sounds of that **Octave**.

If one considers all the species of the three genres <note>The Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic genres of ancient Greek music theory.</note> that I explained in the 8th proposition of the 2nd book on *Wind Instruments*, one would prefer to choose the double ratio of 120 to 60 over any other to signify the **Octave**, especially since these two numbers encompass the seven intervals of all the species of each genre. But if one follows the division of the Monochord of equality <note>A device with a single string used to demonstrate mathematical intervals.</note> divided by means of eleven mean proportional numbers, the explanation of which will be found in the 14th proposition of the first book on *String Instruments*, one would set the double ratio of the **Octave** from 200,000 to 100,000: and if one wants it to encompass the three genres comprised by the 24 intervals that I explain in the 6th proposition of the 2nd book, it will be 57,600 to 28,800. I leave aside the ratio of 72,000 to 144,000, which contains the 32 sounds of the **Octave** that I propose in the *Book of Genres and the Organ*, and an infinity of other terms which all express the double ratio of the **Octave**, because it is certain that the simplest terms 2 and 1 should be

## COROLLARY II.

One could say that the ratio of the **Octave** is like that of the <term>square root</term> of 3 to the square root of 12 <note>Because $\sqrt{3} : \sqrt{12}$ simplifies to $1 : \sqrt{4}$, which is 1:2.</note>, because roots exist in a sub-double ratio of their squares: and the surfaces of bodies that produce the **Octave**—for example, bells—being in a quadruple ratio <note>4:1</note> produce the **Octave**, because their diameters are as 2 to 1. Similarly, one can say it is in the same ratio as the cube roots of one and eight, and likewise for the roots of squared-cubes, cubed-cubes, etc., to infinity: but it is better to retain the simplicity of 2 to 1 of which we have spoken, since the formal ratio of the **Octave** is nothing other than the comparison made of two beats to one other beat of air, or the meeting and union of the said beats within the ear, the imagination, and the mind.

## COROLLARY III.

Even though one cannot perceive whether the **Octave** or the vibrations <note>original: "tremblemens"</note> that produce it are exactly in a double ratio, because the senses are not capable of understanding the very small differences of things—for example, to discern if a thousandth part of a vibration is missing—and since the ear is affected in the same way by two sounds whose ratio is 1000 to 499 as by those whose ratio is 1000 to 500; nevertheless, one must take the double ratio in its exactness for the sake of reasoning. This is because the understanding always follows the precision of ratios and proportions, even though it suffices to approach them to satisfy the senses. This must also be understood regarding the ratio of the **Fifth**, and of other **Consonances** and **Dissonances** of which we shall treat later, so that there is no need to repeat it.

## PROPOSITION XI.

### *To know from where the Octave takes its origin, and whether it comes from sound, or from unison.*

We have demonstrated that the ratio and consequently the nature of the **Octave** is 2 to 1, but we must here explain its origin, just as we explained that of sound and of <term>unison</term>. Now, it seems that it comes immediately

separate the beats of the Unison to make an Octave, and join those of sound
to make a Unison.

### COROLLARY I.

One can conclude from this proposition that the Octave is so similar to the
Unison that one often has difficulty distinguishing them, because they have nearly
the same origin, and they both come from the same division—namely, from
the easiest of all divisions: this is why they strike the ear more
equally and with more uniformity than the other <term>consonances</term><note>Musical intervals that are perceived as stable and harmonious.</note>. However, the Unison
is twice as sweet as the Octave, because it joins its beats twice
as often, and consequently, if that which is less unified comes from that which is
more unified, the Octave comes from the Unison. Indeed, since the two beats
made by the two strings AE and EC—which create the Unison—when joined together
create the Octave against the beat of the string BC, or AC, it follows that the Unison
comes from the Octave, as it does from sound, because two beats of sound being added
together create the said Unison: consequently, the Octave has the same
dependence on the two sounds of the Unison as the Unison does on the two beats of sound.

### COROLLARY II.

If one reflects on the three propositions in which we have spoken of the ratios of identity, of equality, and of the double <note>The "double ratio" refers to the 2:1 ratio of the Octave.</note>, we will find that they serve to conceive of divine reasoning. One may be called the ratio *of identity*, insofar as the Persons are one and the same thing with the divine essence; the other may be named the ratio *of equality*, because the same Persons, when considered apart from the essence, are equal to one another. But the third is the *double ratio*, which can be considered between the Father and the other two Persons. For if the two sounds or the two vibrations of air that create the Octave come from those of the Unison, or from the sound itself, the second and third Persons also come from the first, but in a different manner. This is because one must divide the sound of the Unison into two equal parts to create the Octave, and nothing is divided in God, who is as indivisible as He is invisible. However, if one takes distinction for division, one could say that the second and third Persons are "divided"—that is to say, distinct from the first. For it seems there is no other division in intellectual beings than that of distinction, because reason performs in intellectual beings what force and the knife perform in material bodies. Now, it seems that Saint Augustine intended to speak of these three proportions of the divinity when he said:

> *In the Father is unity, in the Son equality, and in the Holy Spirit the harmony of unity and equality. And these three are all one because of the Father, all equal because of the Son, and all connected because of the Holy Spirit,* <note>original: "In Patre vnitas, in Filio æqualitas, in Spiritu sancto vnitatis æqualitatisque concordia. Et tria hæc vnum omnia propter Patrem, æqualia omnia propter Filium, connexa omnia propter Spiritum sanctum." From De Doctrina Christiana, Book 1, Chapter 5.</note>

as he teaches in the fifth chapter of the first book of *Christian Doctrine*. For sound is the Father of <term>Consonances</term> <note>Consonances are musical intervals that sound harmonious and stable to the ear.</note>, from which comes the Unison like the child of the Father; and the Octave, which comes from both, joins and reunites within itself all the Consonances. Thus, it can serve to explain the passage from the Book of Wisdom used by the Church on the day of Pentecost:

> *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice:* <note>original: "Spiritus Domini repleuit orbem terrarum, & hoc quod continet omnia scientiam habet vocis." Wisdom 1:7.</note>

For just as the Holy Spirit has all the knowledge of the Son, who is called the divine Voice or the Word, so the Octave contains all the voices of music, and consequently all the science of the human voice and of other sounds.

### PROPOSITION XII.

->*The Octave is the sweetest and most powerful of all Consonances after the Unison, even though it is further removed from it than the whole tone, or all the other degrees it contains.*<-

Even though this proposition is true, it nonetheless seems marvelous, given that the two sounds that make the Octave are much further apart from each other—and consequently from the Unison, which is the source and origin of Consonances—than the two sounds that make the whole tone or the semitone. This is seen in the ratio of nine to eight, for eight is less distant from nine than eighteen is, since between nine and eighteen there are eight units, while between eight and nine there is only one.

The strings that create the whole tone and the Octave show the same thing, for the difference between the two that make the Octave is much greater than that of the two that make the tone; and the difference of the two that make the major or minor <term>Comma</term> <note>A comma is a very small musical interval resulting from the difference between two other intervals, nearly imperceptible to the untrained ear.</note>

For we must return to our principal difficulty, namely why the Octave is more pleasing than the tone and the other degrees, which do not move as far from the Unison <note>The Unison is two voices singing the exact same pitch (ratio 1:1).</note> as the Octave does, since one must pass through all the degrees before arriving there. Consequently, the reason usually given—that the Octave is more pleasing than the tone or the Fifth because it is "closer" to the Unison—is false, if one understands by this that the Octave is less distant from the Unison than the other intervals it comprises. This is easy to judge by the preceding table and by reason joined with experience: it shows that the number of air vibrations <note>original: "battemens d'air"—vibrations.</note> that create the Octave is 2 times smaller (or larger) than the number of those that create the Unison. This does not happen with the vibrations that create the tone, the Fifth, or the Thirds. For the number of vibrations making these intervals is not so different from the number of vibrations of the Unison; since the sound making the Major Second above the Unison surpasses it by only one vibration (insofar as it is made by 9 vibrations of air when each sound of the Unison is made by 8 vibrations). But each sound of the Octave above is made by 16 vibrations, so that it surpasses the Unison by 8 entire vibrations, and consequently, it is seven times further from the Unison than the tone, or Major Second <note>The author's logic: if the difference between Unison (8) and Tone (9) is 1, and the difference between Unison (8) and Octave (16) is 8, then the Octave is 7 units "further" away than the tone is (8 - 1 = 7).</note>.

Nevertheless, this greater distance of its vibrations does not prevent it from being softer and more pleasing than the tone, or the Thirds, and the o-

the three intervals it contains, nor even that it is more similar to the Unison than any other interval; as is proven by children who believe they are singing in Unison when they are actually at the Octave <note>In music, singing an octave apart often sounds like the same note to an untrained ear because the vibrations align so perfectly.</note>. And Aristotle, it seems, noted the great difference between the Unison and the Octave when he called it the *Antiphone*, <term>antiphone: from the Greek *antiphōnon*, meaning "sounding against" or "responsive"</term> <note>original: "ἀντίφωνον"</note>, and its great union, when he said in Section 19, Problem 39, that it is the most pleasant of all Consonances. And in the 40th problem, he states that it is the only one that is sung with the "Symphony" <note>original: "μαγαδίζουσι δὲ ἐν τῇ διὰ πασῶν συμφωνίᾳ" — this refers to "magadizing," an ancient Greek practice of singing in octaves</note>. It is also for this reason that Ptolemy and the other Greeks call the Octave *homophonia* <term>homophonia: meaning "same sound"</term> <note>original: "ὁμοφωνία"</note> and *isotonia* <term>isotonia: meaning "equal tension" or "equal pitch"</term> <note>original: "ἰσοτονία"</note>; for the two sounds of the Octave unite so perfectly that they seem almost to be one and the same sound. From this comes Aristotle’s belief that the second strike of the air from the smaller string is the same as that of the larger, <note>original: "δευτέρα τῆς νεάτης πληγὴ τοῦ ἀέρος, ὑπάτη ἐστί" — meaning the second vibration of the high string coincides with the first of the low string</note>. Therefore, I am surprised that he did not give this reason as proof that the Octave is more pleasant than other Consonances, instead of saying it comes from the fact that these terms are "whole," that is to say, the larger is a multiple of the smaller; which does not happen with the terms of the Fifth and other simple Consonances, whose ratios are <term>superparticular: a ratio where the larger number is the smaller number plus one, like 3:2</term> or <term>superpartient: a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part, like 5:3</term>.

For although the ratio of the Octave is the first of the multiples, and consequently is the measure of all other multiple ratios—following the general maxim which teaches that the smallest thing is the measure of the larger things of the same nature—and although Aristotle himself says that the Octave is the measure of melody, <note>original: "μέτρον τῆς μελῳδίας"</note>, nevertheless the true reason why the Octave is more pleasant than the Fifth and other Consonances must be taken from the union of its two sounds. This occurs at every stroke of the lower sound and every second stroke of the higher sound; for pleasure comes from union. This is why it is said that love unites hearts and affections, and that resemblance is the cause of love. Now, one of the strokes made by the high sound of the Octave is similar to, and always unites with, the stroke of the lower sound. Aristotle did not understand this when he said in the 43rd problem that the end of the sound of the string he calls *Netes* <term>Netes: the highest string or note in the ancient Greek musical system</term> changes into the sound of the one he calls *Hypate* <term>Hypate: the lowest string or note in the ancient Greek musical system</term>, by reason of its weakness, and consequently that it makes the same sound. For it never happens that the end of a high sound becomes lower than the beginning of that same sound, as I have proven elsewhere; and the experience of the ear clearly shows that the thousandth vibration of a lute or brass string is in unison with the first vibration and the others—that is to say, it is neither lower nor higher in pitch, but only weaker.

One can therefore conclude from this discourse that the other arguments used in favor of the excellence of the Octave are too weak to convince the mind. The first of these is because the excess of the larger term of the Octave is equal to the smaller, which it surpasses by unity <note>meaning the difference between 2 and 1 is 1</note>. The second is because it contains in excellence and virtue all other Consonances, just as 10 contains all other numbers, and because all the sounds one places above the Octave are nothing other than the repetition of those it contains within itself—just as the numbers added to ten are merely the same ones contained within ten. The third is because the Octave is a perfect whole, from which it took the name *Diapaſon* <term>Diapason: from the Greek *dia pasōn*, meaning "through all [the strings]"</term>, because it contains all sounds, just as the seed and the pit contain the tree and the fruit, or a grain of wheat contains the ears; the light
