The fourth [reason], because the Fifth and the Fourth, which are the most excellent musical consonances, proceed from the Octave, or because they compose it, just as form and matter, or as the soul and body compose man.
The fifth, because if Music were lost it could be restored by means of the Octave, just as one can rebuild a house when one has its foundation, and as one can measure a lion by means of one of its claws <note>This refers to the Latin proverb *ex ungue leonem*, suggesting that a small, perfect part allows one to deduce the whole.</note>. And finally because the Octave is a repetition of the unison; for all these reasons do not have the force of a demonstration, and suffer many objections and replies, as can be concluded from this discourse and several others we will make later. But the reason that I draw from the nature of the Octave—that is to say, from the union of the beats of the air <note>Mersenne uses "beats of the air" to describe what we now call sound waves or vibrations.</note>, which is twice as frequent as that of the unison—is general for all kinds of consonances, and touches upon the true reason for the pleasure one receives from them.

As for the other part of the proposition, namely that the Octave is the most powerful of all consonances, it is easy to prove by experience and by reason, both because it is more pleasant, as I have already said, and because it makes strings vibrate more strongly than other consonances; since the struck string that is at the Octave of another which is not struck, meets and strikes it at every second blow, just as that which is at the unison strikes and pushes the other at every blow—that is to say, at every return. But we must examine whether the Octave makes strings vibrate half as strongly as the unison, as I said in one of the preceding discourses; and how much strings that are struck at the Unison and at the Octave vibrate more strongly than those that are not struck: and consequently by how much the Octave is less pleasant or less sweet than the Unison.

## COROLLARY.

I suppose in this proposition, and in several others, that union is the cause of sweetness and pleasure, for which I will give the reason in the discourse on the force and origin of the pleasure received by the senses and the mind.

## PROPOSITION XIII.

*Explaining why strings that are at the Octave make one another vibrate and sound; how much more strongly those at the Unison make one another vibrate than those at the Octave; how much more strongly struck strings vibrate than those that are not struck; and how much the Unison is sweeter or more pleasant than the Octave.*

This proposition contains four difficulties, the first of which can be explained by the same figure I used in giving the reason why strings at the unison make one another vibrate; for there is no other difference except that those at the Octave do not make one another vibrate as strongly, because they only meet at every second blow, and consequently the struck string does not push the others as often as if they were in unison, which always strikes the others twice at the same time that the one forming the Octave against them strikes them only once.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 52 regarding the physical properties of the Octave. Having established why the Octave is the most "perfect" interval, Mersenne now addresses the "second part of the proposition": why it is the most powerful, focusing on the physics of sympathetic resonance between strings.</meta>

# Of Consonances.

From this it seems one can draw the solution to the second part of this proposition; for if every stroke <note>Mersenne uses the word *coup* (strike or blow) to describe the individual physical pulses or vibrations a string makes against the air.</note> of a string that is at the **Unison** is just as strong as every stroke of the string that is at the **Octave**, and if every stroke of the touched string always has an equal effect on the string that is not touched, then the string making the **Unison** will make the other vibrate twice as strongly as the one at the **Octave**, since the strokes of the former are double those of the latter. <note>In 17th-century acoustics, there was often debate about whether the perceived "force" of a sound came from the frequency of vibrations or the amplitude of the string's movement.</note> Now, one must suppose that the two strings are equally struck, or plucked; for one can strike the string at the **Octave** so strongly, and the one at the **Unison** so weakly, that the latter will not make the other strings vibrate at all, even though the former makes them vibrate very strongly. And if we follow the proportion of strokes and movements, we must conclude that the string at the **Octave** must be struck twice as hard, or pulled twice as far (assuming that this double pull corresponds only to two forces) than the one making the **Unison**, to have the same effect—that is to say, to make the strings vibrate as strongly and for as long—so that the double force of the body of the former compensates for the number of strokes of the latter, which is twice as great. However, there are many other difficulties to consider in the movement of strings of which I have spoken elsewhere; this is why I will not expand any further on the second part of this proposition, so that I may come to the third, which seems to me much more difficult.

For if one says that the string which is touched vibrates two or four times more strongly than the one which is not touched, no one will believe it unless they see the experiment, which cannot be done easily. And then it must be noted that the string which was not touched continues its vibrations for a very long time, even after one stops the one that was touched; so that the vibration and the sound of the former no longer depend on the latter, any more than the vibrations and sound of a struck string depend on the finger that strikes it. <note>This is a foundational observation of "sympathetic resonance," where one string begins to vibrate automatically when a nearby string is plucked at the same pitch.</note>

Now, it seems to me that nothing can be determined regarding this difficulty unless one establishes a certain proportion between the force of the strike with which one hits the string, and the force with which the touched string hits the one that is not touched. Still, some light can be shed on this difficulty by comparing two strings tuned to the **Unison**, or to the **Octave**, one of which can be touched so weakly that it will not vibrate as strongly as the one that was not touched at all. This can be seen in the three lines **A B**; **B C**; **C D**, which I suppose to be so tensioned <note>original: *tenduës*</note> that **A B** and **B C** are at the **Unison**, and that **C D** makes the **Octave**, either higher or lower, with the other two. I say then that if string **A B** is touched in such a way that it only moves as far as point **E**, it will vibrate less strongly than string **B C** when the latter is so strongly shaken by strings **A B** or **C D** (which have been touched) that it moves from **H** to **F**. For, assuming that the space **H F** is double the space **G E**, **B C** will vibrate more strongly and for longer than **A B**; and if string **C D**, having been touched, gives this movement to **B C**, the strings that are not touched can vibrate more strongly by means of those at the **Octave** than they vibrate by means of those at the **Unison**, and can even vibrate more strongly than those that are touched, as I have already said. But it is not possible for the string which is not touched to vibrate as strongly as, or more strongly than, the one by means of which it vibrates. <note>Mersenne is grappling with the law of conservation of energy: a resonating string shouldn't technically have more energy than the source that triggered it, though it might appear to vibrate more widely under certain conditions.</note>

**Book One**

Now I return to the difficulty, regarding which I will only remark upon what experience shows: namely, that when the string which has been touched vibrates a thousand times before coming to rest, the string which has not been touched, and which is at the **Unison**, vibrates as strongly as the touched one by the time the latter has vibrated four or five hundred times—that is to say, when it has nearly completed half of its oscillations. From this one cannot conclude that the touched string vibrates only twice as strongly as the untouched one, because the first half of the vibrations covers a much greater space than the second half, as I have said elsewhere. And if we measure the force of the vibrations by the space covered by the oscillations, we can derive this from the discourse I have given regarding the manner in which the returns or vibrations of strings diminish.

As for the final difficulty, it is quite easy; for since the union of the sounds of the **Unison** is twice as great as that of the **Octave**, it follows that it is twice as sweet. And if the greatest pleasure comes from the greatest union and the greatest sweetness, then the **Octave** is twice less agreeable than the **Unison**. Consequently, there would be twice less pleasure in singing with children at the **Octave** than in singing with equal voices at the **Unison**. However, because we measure the pleasure of **Music** by the passion and the whim of the listeners rather than by reason, one cannot make a conclusion on this subject that is not subject to contradiction—unless one encounters men who defer more to reasoning than to their ears and other senses. <note>Mersenne is touching on a classic debate in music theory: whether music is a mathematical science (Reason) or an emotional experience (the Senses). He suggests that while the Unison is "perfect" mathematically, humans might prefer the variety of the Octave.</note>

### COROLLARY I.

One experiences in the vibrations of two strings, three feet long and tuned to the **Unison**, that the string which is touched does not vibrate more strongly at the 6th or 7th beat of the pulse <note>In the early 17th century, before the widespread use of watches with second hands, scientists like Mersenne used their own steady heartbeat or "pulse" as a standard unit of time, roughly equal to one second.</note>—that is to say, at the 6th or 7th second of an hour—than the string which was not touched. For the first turns and returns made by the untouched string make it appear just as wide upon the **monochord** <term>monochord: a scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to measure musical intervals</term> as the touched string when the latter has vibrated for $\frac{1}{10}$ of a minute. And because the said touched string vibrates for $\frac{1}{3}$ of a minute (since the sound it makes lasts 20 seconds), it follows that the movement of the untouched string lasts 14 seconds, and that the movement of the string making the **Octave** which is not touched lasts only 7 seconds; consequently, it appears as wide on the monochord as the touched one when its movement has lasted 12 seconds.

### COROLLARY II.

If the first turn of string A B and C D <note>Mersenne is likely referring to a diagram on a previous page or imagining two strings of different tensions.</note> suffices to make string B C vibrate, and if one strikes these two strings equally so that they are both stopped after the first return, I say that B C will vibrate more strongly when C D is touched than when A B is touched. This is because C D, being more tightly stretched than A B, follows that it strikes the air more forcefully, and consequently imparts a greater movement to B C. From this, it does not follow that B C must vibrate more strongly by means of the other turns of C D, since every second turn of C D does not help B C at all.

Now, the space that C D covers at each return greatly diminishes its force; from this, it follows that the 3rd, 5th, and 7th turns, with which C D strikes B C, have hardly any force left to strike it...

### PROPOSITION XIV.

> *Even though one multiplies the Octave unto infinity, its lesser term does not change in any way, because unity does not multiply.*

All **consonances** and **dissonances** can be multiplied, as is easy to conclude by the multiplication of ratios—provided, however, that one excepts the **unison**, the multiplication of which can only be conceived in two ways. One is the multiplication of several voices singing at the **unison**, as when 20 sing on one side and 20 or 30 on the other; since two voices suffice to create a **unison**, the multitude of voices simply repeats or multiplies it. The other way occurs when voices rise to sing higher at the **unison**, as when one leaves the low *C sol ut fa* <note>original: "C sol vt fa". This refers to the note Middle C using the Guidonian system of solmization, where a single note could have multiple names depending on the scale or "hexachord" being used.</note> to move higher; for if each voice strikes the air twice in the low register, it strikes it 4 times in the high, so that one must double each term of the **unison**, namely 2:2, to have 4:4. But since the terms of the **unison** never change their ratio of equality, I leave this sort of multiplication aside to explain that of the **octave**, which changes only the larger of its terms, for unity always remains as the lesser. From this, one can infer that it has a great resemblance to the **unison**, since it perpetually contains one of its terms; because of this, all multiplied **octaves** resemble the simple **octave** so perfectly that one often has difficulty discerning them, and one cannot judge how many times it is repeated unless one employs some artifice.

Now, since unity always remains as the smallest term, one must only multiply the largest by itself to have the second **octave** <note>In mathematical ratios of the time, the octave is 1:2. A double octave is 1:4, a triple is 1:8. The "1" (unity) remains constant.</note>; and if one wants the third **octave**, and all others unto infinity, one must always multiply the largest terms by the largest term of the simple **octave**—that is to say, by two. Thus, the multiplication of the **octave** is nothing other than a perpetual doubling of its largest term, which is to say, of the higher sound.

One can similarly multiply it by dividing the low sound by two, for this division will always make it lower by an **octave**; now, this division is done by doubling the length of the string, just as the multiplication of the high sound is done by dividing the string into two equal parts. This is seen in strings A B, or B L and C D, each of which is divided into eight parts; for A B makes an **octave** with C D, of which it is double the length. But if one wishes to double the **octave** by means of the higher sound produced by C D,

And just as the first **bisection** <term>bisection: the act of dividing something into two equal parts</term> or division of a string—or of a number of **vibrations** <term>original: "battemens". In 17th-century science, this refers to the physical pulses or "beats" of air that create sound.</term>—into two equal parts creates the **octave**, so too the second bisection creates the second octave, and the third bisection creates the third, which musicians call the *Twenty-second*. This is seen in string B L: when it is divided in the middle at point H, it creates the Octave below against BH; the second bisection made at point K gives the **Fifteenth** <note>A "Fifteenth" (quinzième) is a double octave—an interval of two octaves.</note>, for BK makes the double Octave against B A; and the third bisection made at point M gives the triple Octave, for B M makes the *Twenty-second* against B A.

One finds the same thing by multiplying the string by 2, that is to say, by doubling it; for the string BK, which is double the length of BM, creates the Octave with it. If one multiplies KB by 2, one gets BH; thus, one achieves the same result by lengthening or multiplying one of the strings as by shortening or dividing the other. And just as the first bisection or division of a string (or a number of vibrations) into two equal parts creates the Octave, likewise the second bisection creates the second Octave, and the third bisection creates the *Twenty-second*—that is, the third Octave. This is seen in string AB: when it is divided in the middle at point H, it creates the Octave below against B, and the second bisection made at point K gives the second Octave, for KB makes the Fifteenth against AB; and the third bisection made at point M gives the third Octave, for BM makes the Twenty-second against AB.

The same thing is found by multiplying the string by two, which is to say, by doubling it; for the string KB, which is double the length of BM, makes the octave with it; and if one multiplies KB by 2, one will have HB, with which it makes the double octave. If one doubles HB, one gets BA, which makes the 3rd octave with BM; and finally, if one multiplies AB by 2, one gets LA, which makes the 4th octave against MB, which is the 16th part of LA.

From this it follows that if, of two strings set to the **Unison**, one divides one by half and always doubles the other at the same time, one creates a double Octave at the first division, a quadruple at the second, and an octuple at the 3rd, and so on. By this, one sees that the **binary** <note>The number 2.</note> is the proper number of the octave, just as unity <note>The number 1.</note> is the number of the unison.

It is easy to pursue this **double ratio** <term>double ratio: the 2:1 ratio that defines the octave.</term> as far as one wishes, and consequently to know how many octaves a string stretched from the center of the earth to the **firmament** <note>In 17th-century cosmology, the "firmament" refers to the sphere of the fixed stars, the outer boundary of the known universe.</note> would be against this smaller string of an inch long: for although many imagine that it would be a very great number, nevertheless it would not be long enough to produce 37 octaves, for it would need to be 707,196,367,360 inches long—that is, the 38th number of the **geometric progression** which gives the 37th octave. And because a string of one inch long (taken from a string of 3 feet which is at the **standard chapel pitch** <term>ton ordinaire de chapelle: the pitch used in French religious music, which varied by region but served as a baseline for Mersenne's calculations.</term>) beats the air 1,728 times in the 60th part of a minute of an hour—that is, in one second—it follows that a string 707,196,367,360 times longer will beat it only once in the space of 16 years and about 3 months.

From which one can infer how far it must be pulled from its straight line to make its first **return** <note>A "return" refers to a single vibration or oscillation of the string back to its starting point.</note> perceptible, and several other things of which one can see a sample in the corollaries that follow.

## COROLLARY I.

It is difficult to know when the movement of a body begins to be so slow and sluggish that one can no longer perceive it; for although all plants move so slowly while growing that one does not know they have moved except by the effect (which shows they are taller and larger, and consequently it is certain that the part by which they grow, compared to the span of time in which they grow, is too small to make the movement perceptible), nevertheless they could grow much more in the same time without their movement being perceptible: and it is very difficult to determine how much they would have to grow in a given time to make their movement perceptible.

The needle or the shadow of the **style** <term>style: the gnomon or pointer of a sundial, or the hand of a clock.</term> of a clock can be so long that their movement will become perceptible, and if one notices the path they take in a certain portion of time, one will know when the movements of bodies begin to be perceptible. From this, one will conclude how far a given string, whose sound or tension is known, must be pulled to make its movement perceptible. This can serve several considerations of nature, where it must be noted that what is perceptible to some is not to others, and it offers a new speculation for considering to what degree the most subtle senses can surpass the coarsest ones.

## COROLLARY II.

Since each return of a string stretched at both ends occurs in the same amount of time—whether one pulls it only by a **line** <term>line: a traditional unit of length equal to 1/12 of an inch.</term> or by the width of a hair—the preceding string will take 16 years just as well to cross this small space to return to its straight line as if it were pulled 9,094 leagues; for since the string of 3 feet long (upon which I took the proportion and number of returns for this one) is easily pulled the space of a line, and consequently the one of an inch can be pulled 1/36 of a line, it follows that the large string can be pulled 9,094 leagues, and that it will go just as fast in returning to its li[ne]...

## PROPOSITION XV.

->*To explain why, of all the doubled or multiplied Consonances, only the Octave remains a Consonance; wherein one sees the manner of multiplying ratios and chords.*<-

It is difficult to provide the true reason for this difficulty. It does not seem to be because the ratio of the Octave is the first of the multiples—that is, that it is **double** <note>original: "double," referring to the 2:1 ratio.</note>—and that the terms of all multiplications made of the Octave are found by 2 (which is the denominator of the double ratio). For one could say the same of the triple ratio of 3 to 1, which makes the **Twelfth** <note>A Twelfth is an octave plus a fifth (3:1 ratio).</note>, and which is the second of the multiple ratios, and consequently has unity as its lesser term just like the Octave. And nevertheless, it is certain that the doubled Twelfth creates a dissonance—namely, the major Twenty-third, which is in the ratio of 9 to 1, or a major tone over three Octaves. **Practitioners** <note>Mersenne often distinguishes between "practitioners" (performing musicians) and "theorists" (mathematicians and philosophers).</note> are mistaken when they believe that the Twelfth is a double Fifth, or doubled, in the same way the Fifteenth is a doubled Octave; they do not know how ratios must be doubled, nor what a doubled ratio actually is.

This is why I shall explain it briefly here: I say that the ratio of two numbers or two other things is "doubled" when one multiplies the two terms of the given ratio by themselves. For example, the ratio of the **Fifth** <term>Fifth: the musical interval produced by a 3:2 string ratio.</term> is 3 to 2; this is doubled by multiplying 3 by itself, which makes 9, and 2 by itself, which makes 4. Thus, the ratio of 9 to 4 is the "doubled" ratio of 3 to 2, and consequently the major Ninth is the double of the Fifth, and can be called a double Fifth, or more properly, a Fifth doubled.

And if one wishes to triple the same ratio, one must again multiply the products of the first multiplication (that is, 9 and 4) by the original terms of the Fifth (namely, by 3 and 2). This will give the terms of the ratio of 27 to 8 for the tripled ratio of the **sesquialtera** <term>sesquialtera: the Latin term for the 3:2 ratio.</term>, which makes the **surtripartient 8** ratio <note>original: "surtripartissante 8." This is a technical term for the ratio 27:8 (or 3 and 3/8), which describes a specific musical interval.</note>. One must use the same method to quadruple, quintuple, and multiply the ratios of other Consonances to infinity.

But to return to the main difficulty of this proposition, I say that the reason why only the Octave is always a Consonance, even when multiplied infinitely, can be drawn from no other source than the great ease with which one can divide a sound, a string, or a line in half. For it is almost as easy to divide it into 4, 8, and 16 parts as it is into 2; and as soon as one has taken half of a whole, it is easy to take half of each half, unto infinity.

<summary>Mersenne explains the mathematical process of "doubling" musical intervals by squaring their ratios, demonstrating why the octave (2:1) uniquely remains harmonious even when stacked, unlike the fifth (3:2).</summary>

### OF CONSONANCES.

Now, the multiplied **Octave** <term>Octave: the interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</term> always maintains this ease in the multiplication or division of its strings and sounds. This does not happen to any other multiplied consonance, as we see with the **Fifth** <term>Fifth: a musical interval encompassing five staff positions, known for its stability.</term>, which is considered the most pleasing of the simple consonances after the Octave; for it is difficult to grasp the ratio of 9 to 4 which represents the two sounds and the two strings of the doubled Fifth.

But I shall speak of this Fifth and the other consonances after the discourse on the Octave, whose triple ratio <note>The author is referring to the 2:1 ratio being multiplied by itself (cubed) to reach the 22nd (8:1).</note> contains almost the entire range of the voice and the greatest beauty of music. Thus, practitioners can content themselves with the **Twenty-second** <term>Twenty-second: an interval of three octaves.</term>, just as geometers are content with the consideration of the Solid. For it is enough that they consider the simple ratio of lines in the Octave, the squared ratio of planes in the **Fifteenth** <term>Fifteenth: an interval of two octaves (4:1 ratio).</term>, and the cubed ratio of solids in the Twenty-second, whose terms are expressed by the ratios of 2 to 1, 4 to 1, and 8 to 1.

->COROLLARY<-

If the lesser consonances could express their dependence, they would admit that they have nothing of themselves, and that they have borrowed their existence from the Octave, to which they return as to their source and center when they compose it. Now, it must be noted that the Octave can only give life to other consonances through its division. This is done in such a way that it gives a more noble and excellent nature to the Fifth than to the **Fourth** <term>Fourth: the musical interval between the first and fourth degrees of a scale.</term>, by giving it a greater ratio. It is similar to God, who gave a more excellent nature to the spirit than to the body, and to the heavens than to the earth; for one can compare the Fifth to the spirit and the heavens, inasmuch as all music borrows its delicacy and beauty from this consonance, which is the eldest daughter of the Octave, and which also produces two consonances in imitation of her mother: namely, the **Major Third** and the **Minor Third**.

But the Fourth is similar to a bastard daughter, or to the body, and to a sterile earth that produces nothing good. It serves no more purpose in music than the zero does in numbers—namely, to complete the Octave, or to create the two **Sixths** <term>Sixths: intervals consisting of six staff positions; Mersenne notes they are formed by combining Thirds and Fourths.</term> when joined with the Thirds. Without these, it is almost as difficult to use the Fourth in music as it is to use **Dissonances**. This will be much better understood through the specific discourses on these two daughters of the Octave, of which the elder always wishes to walk first and hold the most honorable place, because she participates more in the perfection of the Octave. Hence it is that the Fourth displeases when it is found in the place of the Fifth, and the ear has difficulty enduring it, as if judging it unworthy of that place, and that it perverts the order of nature, which gives number, weight, measure, and place <note>original: "le nombre, le poids, la mefure, & le lieu." This is a common 17th-century theological reference to the Book of Wisdom 11:20: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note> to all things. But we shall speak more amply of these two consonances in the propositions that follow.

### PROPOSITION XVI.

*The first and easiest division of the Octave produces the Fifth, the Fourth, the Twelfth, and the Fifteenth.*

One can say that the **Octave** <term>Octave: a musical interval where the frequency of the higher note is exactly double the lower note (2:1 ratio).</term> is like the Sun, which distributes its rays to all other corporeal creatures in such a way that it nevertheless always remains full of the light of which it is the source and origin: for even though one takes the **Fifth** <term>Fifth: a stable interval with a 3:2 ratio.</term> and the **Fourth** <term>Fourth: a musical interval with a 4:3 ratio.</term> within the Octave, the Octave preserves its nature when its endpoints are considered; and everything taken from it serves to reveal its excellence, just as the beauty of created things helps us to understand the power of the Creator. Now, it is very easy to show the truth of this proposition by means of the string A B, which, when compared with A C, makes the Octave; for this Octave, being divided at D, gives the four intervals we are discussing here, insofar as A D makes the Fifth with C B,

->A &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; C &emsp; E &emsp; D &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; B<-

and the **Twelfth** <term>Twelfth: an interval of an octave plus a fifth (3:1 ratio).</term> with C D; A B makes the Fourth with A D, and the **Fifteenth** <term>Fifteenth: an interval of two octaves (4:1 ratio).</term> with D B. But the Fifth and the Twelfth arise more immediately than the other two, which require the subtraction or the residue D B of the string A B for their production, whereas the Fifth and its replicate <note>In period music theory, a "replicate" refers to a compound interval—an interval plus one or more octaves.</note> need only A C and C D for their generation. I leave aside several other matters belonging to the Octave, as they will be easier to understand in the discussion of the other Consonances and their divisions.

### PROPOSITION XVII.

*The Fifth, whose ratio is three to two, or two to three, is the third of the Consonances; but when it is doubled or multiplied, it turns into Dissonance.*

This Consonance, which the Greeks call <term>Diapente</term> <note>original: "Diapente", from the Greek *dia* (through) and *pente* (five).</note>, by reason of the five sounds it contains, is composed of two movements, one of which strikes the air twice while the other strikes it three times: from this it follows that the string which is so divided that it leaves three parts on one side and two on the other makes the Fifth, since the side with three parts strikes the air twice while the other, which has only two parts, strikes it three times, since the number of strikes is reciprocal to the length of the strings, as I have demonstrated elsewhere.

Now one may consider that the three numbers used to explain the mystery of the Trinity also serve to explain these three Consonances: for unity represents the divinity and God the Father; the binary represents the Son; and the ternary represents the Holy Spirit. Similarly, unity represents the **Unison** <term>Unison: two notes of the same pitch (1:1 ratio).</term>, which is one to one; the binary is the proper number of the Octave, or of the unison repeated; so that one can say that the unison is to the Octave as one is to two; and the Fifth is represented by the ternary, which also contains the Twelfth.

We have explained in the preceding proposition how the Fifth is produced by the division of the Octave, or by the second bisection of a string; therefore it is not necessary to repeat it. But when the Fifth is doubled, it is no longer a Consonance, as one sees in these terms 4 and 9, which represent the doubled Fifth, as I explained in the 15th proposition.

<header>Of Consonances.</header>

Now, if one sought only that which is sweetest in Music, one could be content with these three **Consonances** <term>Consonance: a combination of notes that sound pleasant and stable together.</term>, which are so sweet and agreeable that other intervals serve only to provide variety, lest the too-frequent use of their sweetness weary the listeners. We shall see further in the division of the **Monochord** <term>Monochord: an ancient scientific instrument with a single string used to measure musical intervals.</term> how the **Fifth** and other Consonances are generated; for this reason, there is no need to dwell here any longer.

### COROLLARY

It must be noted once and for all that it matters not at all whether one begins with the smaller or the larger term of the **ratios** <note>original: "raisons"</note> to express the Consonances. That is to say, it is just as true to say that the ratio of the **Octave** is **sub-double** <term>Sub-double: a 1:2 ratio.</term> and that of the Fifth is **sub-sesquialter** <term>Sub-sesquialter: a 2:3 ratio.</term>, as it is to say the former is double and the latter is **sesquialter** <term>Sesquialter: a 3:2 ratio, where the larger number is 1 and 1/2 times the smaller.</term>. This second way favors the length or the thickness of the strings, inasmuch as the longest or thickest string serves as the foundation of the harmony and is ordinarily explained by the larger number, because it contains the smaller string, just as the larger term of a ratio encompasses the smaller. But if one considers the vibrations of the strings, the largest string must be signified by the smallest number, since it vibrates less quickly; consequently, the ratio of the Octave will be sub-double when one begins with the thick string. Nevertheless, one may always retain the double ratio for greater ease, and to accommodate common usage and the positions of the ancients.

### PROPOSITION XVIII.

> *All the replicates, or repetitions, of the Fifth are agreeable, the first of which is from 1 to 3, and the second from 1 to 6: and all the others always have unity for their smallest term. It is also determined by how much the Fifth is less sweet than the Octave.*

The replicates of the fifth enjoy the privilege of the Octave—that is to say, they have unity (the number 1) for their smallest term. For it suffices to double the largest term of the fifth without it being necessary to touch the other, as is seen in these numbers: 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, etc., which show the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth replicate of the Fifth, of which unity is always the smallest term. And because the sounds of the Octave unite at every second vibration, and those of the Fifth at every third, one can say that the sweetness of the Octave is to that of the fifth as 3 is to 2. That is to say, the Octave is sweeter by half, and consequently the sesquialter ratio of the fifth serves to express the proportion of its sweetness compared with that of the Octave.

This happens similarly to the **Fourth** compared to the Fifth, and to other intervals compared to one another, when the terms of their ratios follow each other immediately, and the largest term of one is the smallest of the other. For example, the Fourth must be less sweet by one-third than the Fifth, because the vibrations of the Fourth only unite at every 4th stroke, and those of the Fifth unite at every 3rd. From this it appears that the sweetness of the fifth is to that of the fourth as 4 is to 3. We must now speak of the Fourth, since it is the "second stream" or the "second daughter" of the Octave, which always follows the fifth as the shadow follows the body; for as soon as one hears the Fifth, and one understands the Octa-

# Book One

...one necessarily encounters the **Fourth**, which some call a *necessary evil* and a *monster*, though it is among the **Consonances** <term>Consonance: a combination of notes that sounds stable and pleasant when played together.</term>, as I shall show in Proposition 25.

### COROLLARY I.

It is easy to conclude from what I have said in this proposition that Consonances are better and sweeter when the vibrations <note>original: "battemens"</note> of their sounds and the numbers used to explain them are smaller. Consequently, goodness resides on the side of unity, and evil on the side of the multitude, which declines toward nothingness in proportion to its growth—much like the rays of the Sun, whose intensity and strength diminish the further they move from their source. From this, one sees that the smallest musical intervals <note>meaning intervals with very complex ratios</note>, which require larger numbers to express the proportion of their sound-vibrations, are the most disagreeable, even though they approach closer to the **Unison** <term>Unison: two notes produced at the exact same pitch.</term>. No interval can ever truly reach the Unison, because between any two intervals or ratios one might choose, there are always an infinite number of others that can be placed between that ratio and the Unison. This clearly shows that ratios extend to infinity, both as they approach and as they recede from the ratio of equality, or the Unison.

### COROLLARY II.

From this it follows that the second **Fifth** <note>original: "Quinte"</note>, which is the first replicate <note>an octave-displaced version of the interval</note> of the Fifth, is sweeter than the primary Fifth or its other replicates, because its terms, when added together, produce a smaller number, as I demonstrate in Proposition 19. Upon this, one can establish the riddle of the man who enriches himself by losing, and he who impoverishes himself by gaining, since intervals and their ratios become smaller <note>in numerical value</note> in proportion to their larger numbers, and they are larger <note>musically</note> in proportion to how much their numbers decrease.

### COROLLARY III.

It must be noted once and for all that when I say one Consonance is more agreeable than another, this "agreeableness" must be understood as the sweetness and union formed by the two sounds that constitute it, and not the personal judgment of each individual. Otherwise, it would happen that the same thing would be both agreeable and disagreeable, or more or less pleasant, based on the different dispositions of the listeners and the various biases—which one must avoid as much as possible in all types of science and experiments.

## PROPOSITION XIX.

### *To determine whether the Fifth is more excellent than the Twelfth, and which is the sweetest and most agreeable.*

This question is not the least difficult among those belonging to Music, for it seems that the ratio of the **Twelfth** <term>Twelfth: a compound interval consisting of an octave plus a fifth (a 3:1 ratio).</term>, which is 1 to 3, is more excellent, simpler, and easier to understand than that of the **Fifth**, which is 2 to 3. This is because we more easily and readily notice that 3 is the triple of 1, or that 1 is the sub-triple of 3, than we notice that 3 is **sesquialter** <term>Sesquialter: a ratio of 3:2, where the larger value contains the smaller plus its half.</term> to 2, or that 2 is sub-sesquialter to 3.

Furthermore, when the terms of the triple ratio are added together, they only make 4, while those of the sesquialter make 5; and 4 is simpler than 5. However, if one stops...

...with regard to numbers, it seems that the **Fifth** is more excellent, since the number 5 encompasses all types of numbers—namely, the first even number, which is 2, and the first odd number, which is 3—as noted by the author of *The Arithmetic Theology*, who calls the number five **Marriage** <note>original Greek: γάμος (gamos)</note>. This is because it is composed of two and three, which are the first two numbers, one being male and the other female in the philosophy of Pythagoras. This is why the Pythagoreans call it **Mother** <note>original Greek: Εφὸς (Ephos)</note>, according to Plutarch in his book on the procreation of the soul, since this word signifies the mother or the nurse, which presupposes a marriage.

They also say that the quinary [the number five] creates the first tone, or the first sound of all those that can be sung. This, it seems, cannot be understood as the interval of the Fifth; for whether one speaks of the excellence of **Consonances** <term>Consonance: a combination of notes that sound stable and pleasant together.</term> or of the smallest intervals, the Fifth is neither the most excellent nor the smallest interval. The **Octave** is better, and the **Fourth** or the whole tone are smaller than the Fifth. But I do not wish to leave the number 5 without noting what Nicomachus teaches in the second book of his *Arithmetic*: namely, that the ancients called it **Justice**, because it is found in the middle of the first odd square number—that is, in the middle of the number 9, as seen here: 1, 2, 3, 4, **5**, 6, 7, 8, 9. From this comes the fact that if one divides a balance scale into 9 equal parts, the 5th will be found under the pointer; and the further one moves from the 5, the further one moves from Justice. He also notes that 6, 7, 8, and 9, when added together, make 30, which is triple the 10 formed by 1, 2, 3, and 4. When one side of the balance beam is overloaded, it creates an obtuse angle with the frame as it sinks; the branch that rises, because it is lighter, makes an acute angle. The heavier branch that goes down represents the wicked because of the injustices they commit, just as the rising branch represents the good who receive the wrong and rise toward God to implore His assistance; consequently, it is better to receive an injury than to commit one. To this relates the proverb of Pythagoras: **Do not overstep the balance** <note>original Greek: ζυγὸν μὴ ὑπερβαίνει (zygon mē hyperbainei)</note>, by which he meant that one must maintain Justice, and that the pointer of the scales, which serves as the test and demonstration of their accuracy, must always be straight and perpendicular to the beam. 

But I return to the difficulty proposed, which can be resolved by reason or by experience. Now, we experience that the Fifth fills the ear more than does the **Twelfth** <term>Twelfth: an interval spanning an octave plus a fifth (ratio 3:1).</term>, and furthermore, the Fifth is that by which we first divide the Octave, and it is the soul and the beauty of Music. Moreover, the Twelfth has nothing beautiful or pleasing except what it receives from the Fifth; or to put it better, it is no different from the Fifth except in that it is repeated, so that one can call it the "second Fifth," just as the Nineteenth is the "third Fifth." Furthermore, the terms of the Twelfth are more distant from each other than those of the Fifth, for 3 is closer to 2 than it is to 1. Finally, it seems easier to notice that 3 surpasses 2 by one unit than it is to see that 3 surpasses 1 by 2—or at least, one is as easy to notice as the other. Be that as it may, 3 is the greatest term of both the Fifth and the Twelfth, and they differ only in their lower extremes. tio, or the Consonance that exists from CB to BA, is composed of the ratio from DB to BA, and that of DB to CA; that is to say, the Twelfth is composed of the Octave and the Fifth, because the triple ratio is composed of the double ratio and the sesquitertial <note>original: "ſeſquitierce". Note: In musical mathematics, a triple ratio (3:1) creates a Twelfth, which is typically composed of a double ratio (2:1, an Octave) and a sesquialtera ratio (3:2, a Fifth). The author’s use of "sesquitertial" (4:3, a Fourth) here may be a technical slip, as an Octave plus a Fourth equals an Eleventh (8:3).</note>. Nevertheless, it seems one must conclude that the Fifth is more excellent than the Twelfth, which is merely the replica <note>A "replica" refers to a compound interval—one that spans more than an octave but shares the same note names.</note> of the Fifth, which divides the Octave in such a way that it is its principal part: for even though the Twelfth contains the Octave and the Fifth in potential, that which is in potential is not always as agreeable as that which is in action. To this, one may add that the Fifth is the second interval made by the **Trumpet** (for it begins with the Octave, as I have said elsewhere) and consequently that it is the most agreeable of all intervals after that of the Octave, though one might deny this because many **Organ** pipes produce the Twelfth when the wind is pushed stronger than necessary, rather than the Fifth or the Octave; and that the second interval of the Trumpet, being joined to the first, makes the Twelfth. This shows that it is difficult to provide any privilege in favor of the Fifth that does not similarly apply to the Twelfth. However, one can prefer the Fifth because it is encountered first, and because the simple Octave is more pleasant than its replicas; which can also be concluded regarding the **Fourth** and the **Thirds** compared to their replicas.

Nevertheless, one must consider the placement of the Fifth, for it seems more pleasant on high than on low; for example, that which is played on the largest Organ pipes—that is to say, those of the first or lowest Octave—is not as pleasant as that which is played in the second Octave. Experience shows that Consonances are not equally placed in all sorts of locations, for some are better on high and others on low. The Octave must be put in the first place, which is the lowest; the Fifth must follow it immediately; after which one must place the Fourth, then the **Major Third**, and finally the **Minor Third** (which is the smallest and the last of all the Consonances), as shown by the natural order of the numbers containing the ratios of the said Consonances: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. For 1 and 2 make the Octave; 2 and 3 the Fifth; 3 and 4 the Fourth; 4 and 5 the Major Third; and 5 and 6 the Minor Third. This order is taught by the natural degrees made by the Trumpet when one begins with the lowest sound, as I have already said elsewhere; which it has in common with the **Sackbut** <term>Sackbut: a Renaissance and Baroque brass instrument, the direct ancestor of the modern trombone.</term> and several **Flutes**, even though this order of numbers and sounds made by the instruments is not sufficient to prove the order that the excellence of Consonances must maintain. This is because the Fourth is found at the third interval made by the Trumpet, even though the two Thirds, which are found only at the 4th and 5th intervals, are esteemed more pleasant than the Fourth; for they are employed in Duets in simple **counterpoint** <term>Counterpoint: the technique of combining two or more melodic lines so they sound harmonious together.</term>, in which the Fourth cannot enter because it is "worse" than the **Dissonances** used in **Cadences** <term>Cadence: a sequence of notes or chords that brings a piece of music to a point of rest or conclusion.</term>, in which one includes the **Seventh** and its replicas.

# Of Consonances.

It seems one must conclude, therefore, that the **Fifth** is the most excellent of all the **Consonances** <term>Consonance: a combination of notes that sound stable and pleasant together.</term> after the **Octave**; and that the simple Consonances are more excellent than their replicas <term>Replicas: also known as compound intervals, these are intervals expanded by one or more octaves (for example, a Twelfth is a Fifth plus an Octave).</term>, unless one places them in the same rank without making a comparison between them, because of their great similarity or their identity.

But if the excellence of Consonances is measured by the union of their sounds, as is their sweetness, there is no doubt that the **Twelfth** is more agreeable than the Fifth, inasmuch as the two sounds of the Twelfth unite twice as often as those of the Fifth. I demonstrate this by the three strings that follow, which represent the Twelfth divided in this manner: 1, 2, 3. Let there be three strings A, B, and C, where A is to B as 3 is to 1, and A is to C as 3 is to 2. If A employs one moment of time to make each turn or return <note>The author is referring to the frequency of vibration or the cycles of the string.</note>, B will employ 1/3 of that time, and C will employ 2/3.

<image-desc>A small schematic diagram on the right side of the page consisting of three horizontal lines of differing lengths, labeled A, B, and C at their right-hand ends.</image-desc>

Now, I suppose that A and B begin to move together; while A makes one turn, B will make exactly three, and when A begins its second turn, B will begin its fourth; when A begins its third turn, B will be at its seventh, and so on consequently. But if A and C begin to move together, when A has completed its first turn, C will be at the half of its second, and will not be ready to restart with A at the second moment, but only at the third; while A has made two turns, C will have made exactly three. Thus, they only restart together every two moments, whereas the preceding ones <note>Strings A and B, forming the Twelfth.</note> restart at every moment. From this, it follows that the sounds of the Twelfth blend better and produce a sweeter harmony.

And this reasoning is always true in all other sorts of replicas; for if their sounds blend and unite more easily, their sweetness is greater, and consequently they are more agreeable—if indeed the greatest pleasure one receives proceeds from the greatest union, a subject upon which I have written a particular discourse. Now, although it is not necessary to respond to the reasons I have reported in favor of the Fifth—since they are partly founded on certain properties of numbers, to which one may add that the greatest term of the Fifth multiplied by the least gives the greatest term of the **Nineteenth** <term>Nineteenth: a compound interval consisting of two octaves and a fifth (a ratio of 6:1).</term>, namely 6, and that the same least term divided by itself gives the least of the Twelfth, whose greatest term is the same as that of the Fifth—I will nevertheless say that these reasons taken from numbers are sufficient to make one think that the Fifth has something excellent in itself.

However, if one wishes to consider the excellence of other numbers, one will find that the ternary <note>original: "ternaire". The number three.</note>, which is the greatest term of the Twelfth, yields to no other number, as I have shown in the comparison of Trios to Duos; and if one adds these two terms, they make the quaternary number <note>original: "quaternaire". The number four.</note>, upon which **Plato** and the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed that the universe and music were built on mathematical ratios.</note> bestowed great praise. The second reason, taken from the fact that the Fifth fills the ear more, proves only that its sounds unite less quickly and struggle longer than those of the Twelfth. The sixth reason is founded on the equal union of their vibrations, which makes it entirely false, just as it is false that it is as easy to compare 2 to 3 as it is 3 to 1. As for the third and fourth reasons, the Fifth does not bring a greater ornament to Music than the Twelfth, which does not borrow all that it has from the Fifth, since its sounds blend and unite more easily; and although its terms are further apart,

It does not follow at all that it <note>The Twelfth.</note> is less excellent; otherwise the **Octave**, whose terms are further apart than those of all the intervals that can be found within it, would be less excellent than the most disagreeable **Dissonances**, whose terms are closer to one another. And one can say that it is not nature’s intention to produce the **Fifth** at the second interval when one sounds the **Trumpet**, but to produce the **Twelfth** which is found from the first sound to the third. Now, I speak here only of the excellence and the sweetness of the Twelfth, for as to what makes it agreeable, that depends upon custom, preoccupation, the capacity of the ear, and the imagination; this is why it suffices to have demonstrated that the Twelfth is sweeter and more excellent than the Fifth, since its union is greater.

# PROPOSITION XX.

## *To determine whether the Twelfth is more excellent and more powerful than the Octave.*

One will perhaps be astonished that I propose this question, since all Practitioners and Theorists teach that the **Octave** is the Queen of the **Consonances** <term>Consonance: a stable musical interval.</term> that it comprises and produces, as we have said elsewhere. But this universal consent does not prevent some from holding that the **Twelfth** has more force, inasmuch as when one of its strings is struck, it makes the string that was not struck vibrate <note>original: "trembler"</note> more strongly than does the other string of the Octave when its counterpart is struck. They endeavor to prove this in the following manner.

The larger string of the Octave makes one return <note>A full cycle of vibration.</note> while the smaller one makes two; and if one divides the stroke into three parts—namely, the beginning, middle, and end—the middle will strike more strongly than the beginning or the end. Now, the first stroke of the high <note>original: "aigu"</note> sound corresponds to the beginning of the one making the low <note>original: "graue"</note> sound, and the second stroke corresponds to the end, such that no midpoint of the strokes of the high string meets with the midpoint of the stroke of the low string, but only the rest that is betw<unclear>een</unclear> these two strokes; and consequently, the strongest impression of the stroke remains useless.

But because the smaller string of the Twelfth strikes three times while the larger one strikes once, one of the strokes of the high sound always corresponds to the middle of the stroke made by the low sound; this is why the movement of the larger string moves the smaller string more strongly than does the large string of the Octave. And although there occur two rests in the strokes of the high sound of the Twelfth, they are so short that they have no great proportion to the said strokes, and do not last longer than the single rest of the sound of the Octave.

If experience favored this reasoning, it would have some appearance of truth, but I have not observed that a string tuned to the Twelfth makes the others vibrate more strongly than one tuned to the Octave. If this happens sometimes, one must observe whether it is not the force of the larger string of those forming the Twelfth which has so great an impression on the thinner one that the effect is more sensible than that of the string forming the Octave, when two strings are of equal thickness and are only different in length.

As for the rests between the returns, it is difficult to demonstrate whether the string rests

One can therefore say that the **Twelfth** is less sweet and less excellent than the **Octave**, although it may seem more agreeable to many, just as the **fifth** is found more agreeable by some than the **Twelfth**; for there is a difference between the degrees of sweetness and excellence, and those of agreeableness, as I have already remarked, although one could hold the contrary if the division of the movement of the string into three different parts is true, of which we have spoken more amply in the second book on bodies and the movements that produce sounds.

### PROPOSITION XXI.

->*A string being touched makes the one at the Fifth vibrate, but it makes the one at the Twelfth vibrate more strongly.*<-

Many believe that only strings at the **Unison**, or at most those of the **Octave**, cause each other to vibrate <note>original: "trembler," referring to sympathetic resonance where one string moves because another was struck.</note>, but the experiment performed on a **Lute**, on a **Theorbo** <note>A large, long-necked lute used for bass accompaniment.</note>, or on any other instrument one wishes, shows evidently that the **Fifth** and several other **Consonances** have the same property, though they do not possess it to such a perfect degree. But there are few who have noticed these experiments in the fifth, and fewer still who notice it in the **Fourth** and in the **Thirds**, because they do not use instruments that are large enough, proper enough, and well-strung enough for this purpose. For example, one does not perceive it as well on a **Monochord** of three feet, whose soundbox has little depth, as on a Lute, whose <term>concave</term> <note>The hollow body or soundbox of the instrument.</note> is very large; and generally speaking, the experiments succeed all the better as the instruments are larger and better strung.

But the **Twelfth** makes the strings vibrate more strongly than the **Fifth**, the reason for which I explained in the 19th proposition; for that which serves to prove how much the sweetness of one Consonance is greater than that of another also serves to show how much more strongly the strings vibrate by the force of one Consonance than by the force of another. As for the vibrations of the other strings that are moved by the force of the Fourth, the **Major Third**, and their octaves <note>original: "repliques," meaning intervals repeated in higher registers.</note>, we shall be able to speak of them when treating these intervals.

### PROPOSITION XXII.

->*The Fourth or Diatessaron holds the fourth rank among the simple intervals, and consists in the mixture of two sounds, whose ratio is 4 to 3.*<-

I have already said that musical intervals take their name from the number of strings or sounds they ordinarily contain in the **Diatonic** genre; this is why this interval has been called a **Fourth**, because of its four strings which the Greeks call a <term>Tetrachord</term> <note>From the Greek "tetra" (four) and "chorde" (string).</note>. From this comes the name they gave it: **through four** <note>original: "διὰ τεσσάρων" (dia tessaron)</note>, that is to say, "by four"—not that the Fourth must have anything other than the two sounds whose ratio is 4 to 3, but because when one sings by joined degrees that follow each other immediately, one encounters four sounds in the Fourth, as one sees in these four notes: *ut, re, mi, fa*. # Book One

The **Fourth** is a <term>sesquitertial ratio</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus one-third of it, i.e., 4:3.</note> of 4 to 3, because at the same time that the high sound of the fourth strikes the air 4 times, the low sound strikes it 3 times. This is why strings of equal thickness and tension that produce a fourth must be arranged so that one is longer than the other by a third: for example, if one is 4 feet long, the other must be 3 feet. And if one wishes to produce the Fourth with two **flutes** of equal thickness, one must be longer by a third; similarly, the largest **bell** of the Fourth must be taller and wider by a third, as I show in the treatise on **Bells** and other **Musical Instruments**. However, it is sufficient to explain the vibrations of the air produced by the Fourth by means of strings to understand its nature. Let there be two strings, **A B** and **A C**, equal in thickness, material, and tension; I say that **A B** must be 4 feet long to produce the Fourth below the string **A C**, which is 3 feet long,

A_______________________________________B
A___________________________C

so that the string **A B**, which is one-third slacker than **A C** (even though it is stretched by an equal force) because of its greater length, vibrates 3 times—that is, it makes three cycles—in the same time that **A C** makes 4. For the number of their vibrations is proportionally less as they are longer, as I have demonstrated elsewhere.

Now it must be noted that one never hears the fourth unless the longer string has vibrated at least 3 times and the shorter one 4 times; and if **A B** vibrated only 2 times while **A C** vibrated 4 times, one would hear the **Octave** instead of the fourth. From this one must conclude that sounds are nothing other than a vibration, or beating of the string or the air, and that they are higher in pitch as the air receives a greater number of shocks or movements in the same amount of time. Thus, if the air were moved uniformly without any repetition or reiteration of beats, it would produce no sound; or if it did produce one, one could not judge whether it were low or high, for it would be indifferent to both.

### PROPOSITION XXIII.

*The Fourth takes its origin from the division of the Octave, or from the second bisection of a string; and its ratio can just as well be called <term>subsesquitertial</term> <note>The inverse ratio, 3:4.</note> as sesquitertial.*

For when one divides the **Octave** into two parts in this manner—2, 3, 4—(which is the easiest of all divisions that can be made by a middle term, since nothing is easier than putting 3 between 2 and 4), one finds the fourth from 3 to 4, just as one finds the **fifth** from 2 to 3. Thus, these two **Consonances** have the same origin; we also see that one is often taken for the other, as I shall say later, although the production of the **Fifth** must be considered first, and is like the eldest daughter, since one compares 2 to 3 before comparing 3 to 4, which is the remainder of the Octave. From this it follows that the **Fourth** is the third interval produced by the **Trumpet**, as I have noted elsewhere; and that the ancients gave it third place among the **Consonances**, although some modern authors have placed it among the **dissonances**, or believed that it shares qualities of both and consequently must be set apart, as **Papias** <note>Likely referring to a musical theorist or a specific defense of the Fourth, possibly related to the work of Andreas Papius (1542–1581).</note> remarks in the book he wrote in defense of the fourth; but we shall see later what must be held on this subject.

As for the second bisection of the string, from which the **Fourth** arises, I explained it when speaking of the **Octave**. It must only be noted here that the division of the Octave which produces the Fourth is that which comes closest to a division into two equal parts that can be made by means of numbers; for 3 is as close to 2 as it is to 4, even though the larger part is from 2 to 3. For the **Fifth**, which is the most excellent <note>In 17th-century music theory, the Fifth was considered the most perfect consonance after the Octave.</note>, takes the larger place and leaves the smaller to the Fourth, as if to its younger sister.

As for the <term>subsesquitertial ratio</term> <note>original: "raison souzsesquitierce" — a ratio of 3 to 4.</note>, it contains the Fourth when one compares the vibrations of the larger string to those of the smaller, which occurs similarly for all other intervals in music. One cannot rightly say that the proportion of the Fifth or the Fourth is <term>superparticular</term> <note>A ratio where the larger number is the smaller number plus one (e.g., 3:2 or 4:3).</note> rather than <term>subparticular</term> <note>The inverse of superparticular (e.g., 2:3 or 3:4).</note>, unless one sets the lowest sound as the greater term because of its greater slowness; for it is slower by a third than the movement of the high sound, if one takes their beats to be their movements.

## PROPOSITION XXIV.

->*The Fourth is found on a single string when, after having divided it into 7 equal parts,*<-
->*the bridge is placed under the fourth part.*<-

This practice is used for **monochords** <note>A scientific and musical instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to measure mathematical intervals.</note> which have only a single string; these are used to achieve greater equality, even though a single string does not suffice to perform the experiments necessary to establish everything belonging to sounds. Now, it is the same thing to divide a string into 7 parts so that the <term>bridge</term> <note>original: "cheualet" — the piece that supports the strings and limits their vibrating length.</note> leaves 4 on one side and 3 on the other to find the Fourth, as it is to use two strings of equal tension, where one has 4 parts and the other 3. This should be noted for all other musical intervals, which can be found just as well on one string as on two or several. One must simply divide the string into as many equal parts as there are units in the two terms of the interval one wishes to mark on a single string, and place the bridge under the last unit of the larger term. This allows one side to remain to represent the lower sound, and the smaller term—that is, the smaller part of the string—to remain on the other side to produce the higher sound. This is so easy to understand that there would be no need to represent it by a line, were it not useful to provide an example to serve the other propositions. Let the line **A C** then be divided into 7 equal parts to represent the Fourth; I say that if one places the bridge at

point **B**, then **A B**, which contains four parts, will vibrate more slowly than **B C**, which has only 3 parts. **A B** will strike the air only 300 times while **B C** strikes it 400 times, and consequently the beats of **A B** and **B C** will unite at every 4th vibration of **B C**, or every 3rd vibration of **A B**, as I have already said.

## PROPOSITION XXV.
->*To know whether the Fourth is a Consonance.*<-

Some formerly imagined that the Fourth did not deserve the name of **Consonance** <note>A "consonance" is a combination of notes that sounds pleasant and stable to the ear.</note>, for the reason that they did not find it to sound good against the **Bass**, and because they could not use it in **Duets** in simple counterpoint. However, since opinions have now changed and all Musicians place it among the Consonances, it is not necessary for me to dwell on this subject; for it is enough to know that all the ancient Greeks received it among the Consonances, even though they did not recognize the two **Thirds** and the two **Sixths**—which we use—as being Consonances. Now, one of the reasons we have to prove that the Fourth is one of the harmonies of Music is taken from the fact that it is very good when it is joined to the **Fifth**. Furthermore, when the ratio of the Octave is divided **Arithmetically** <note>In music theory, an arithmetic division of the Octave ratio 2:4 results in the sequence 2:3:4, where 2:3 is a Fifth and 3:4 is a Fourth.</note>, as seen in these terms 2, 3, 4, if the middle term is in harmony with the first, the middle term must likewise harmonize with the last, especially since the two extreme terms represent the two sounds of the Octave, which are of the same nature—the Octave being, it seems, nothing other than the repetition or the reply of the Unison.

From this it follows that the intervals added above the Octave produce the same effect as those which divide it and which it contains within itself. For example, the Fifth being joined to the Octave makes the **Twelfth**, which is so similar to the simple Fifth that they are sometimes taken for one another. The other reason is founded on this same resemblance of the two sounds of the Octave; for it is so great that many are mistaken in the judgment of its two sounds, taking the low for the high, or the high for the low. Following this, they judge that the Fifth is the Fourth, and that the Fourth is the Fifth; I have often experienced this, and I wish to explain it so that Musicians may guard against this surprise.

I suppose, then, that the string of an instrument represents the two sounds of the first Octave marked by D. It is quite certain that the string marked by B creates a Fourth below with the note D, and if the ear is not mistaken and takes these two sounds in their proper places, it will hear the Fourth. But if the ear takes the first note marked by A <note>Presumably A is an octave higher than D in this context, or refers to a diagram not pictured here.</note> while hearing the note D, the Musician, though very expert, will believe that the notes D and B are a Fifth, because he is mistaken in taking A for D. From this it is evident that the Fourth is a harmony, since it is often taken for the Fifth; this could not happen if it were a **Dissonance**. But it must be noted that the note B would be the repeated Fourth...

# Of Consonances.

...that is to say the **Eleventh**, if the ear took the note G instead of the note D, so that the **Fourth** <note>In music theory, the "Fourth" is the interval between the first and fourth notes of a major scale, like C to F.</note> gains nothing when one takes the high sound of the **Octave** instead of the low sound, since it always remains within its imperfection—which even increases with the said high sound, as I shall say further below, when I prove that the simple **Fourth** is sweeter than the **Eleventh**, which is its replica <note>An "octave replica" or "compound interval" refers to the same note name shifted an octave higher or lower.</note>: and consequently it is better to be mistaken while descending than while ascending, when it is a question of the **Fourth**, since it turns into a **Fifth** when one descends, and when one takes the low sound of the **Octave** instead of the high. The opposite happens to the **Fifth**, for it degenerates into a **Fourth** when one takes the low sound of the **Octave** for the high, as one sees in the preceding figure, in which F makes a **Fifth** with G, when one takes G in its proper place; but if one takes the low sound of the **Octave** G—that is to say D for G—one will believe that G and F make a **Fourth**, although in fact they make a **Fifth**.

<image-desc>A musical diagram featuring a five-line staff. To the left of the staff, the letters G, F, D, C, and A are positioned next to the lines. Between the lines for D and C is the number 8. Diamond-shaped musical notes are placed on each of these five lines. A series of dashed and solid lines with small circles connect the notes across the staff to illustrate intervals and mathematical relationships between the pitches.</image-desc>

The same thing happens again to the **Fifth** when one takes the high sound of the **Octave** for the low; for example, when one takes D for A, for A B seems to make a **Fourth** instead of a **Fifth**, which loses in every way, and never has a better condition than when it keeps its natural place. This must be carefully noted, because this serves for the understanding of the propositions that will follow later.

The third reason which proves that the **Fourth** is a **Consonance** <note>A harmonious sounding interval.</note> is taken from the proportion of its sounds, which is 3 to 4. This ratio causes these two sounds to always unite at every 3rd **beat of air** <term>vibration or pulse</term> of the low sound, and at every 4th of the high sound: so that the high sound has only two beats that do not unite, and the low sound has only one disjointed, since its first beat meets with the first of the high, and its third with the fourth. Thus, the **Fourth** contains more united beats than disunited, since it unites 4 of its beats and disunites only 3: from which it appears that it holds more of unity and of the **Unison** than of diversity, and that it has more good qualities than bad; and consequently that it deserves to be placed among the number of **Consonances**.

The fourth reason is drawn from the fact that the three sounds A B D, which divide the **Octave** such that A B makes the **Fifth** and B D the **Fourth**, are very pleasant: this would not happen if the **Fourth** were not a **Consonance**, since no **Dissonance** <note>A harsh or unstable sound.</note> can be so "saved" <note>The musical practice of resolving or hiding a harsh sound within pleasant ones.</note> or hidden by other **Consonances** that it does not retain its quality of **Dissonance**, and thus spoil the whole concert <note>original: "concert"; here meaning the overall harmony or ensemble sound.</note>, as one sees with the note C, which always creates a **Dissonance**—which we call a **major second**—whether it is placed above the **Octave** A D in E, or within the **Octave** D A in C, or below the **Octave** G E in D, or in any other manner one might wish.

One can still bring forth other reasons, but they presuppose knowledge of **Thirds** and **Sixths**, of which we have not yet spoken, with which it will be necessary to compare the **Fourth** and determine if it is better than the **Major Third**.

## PROPOSITION XXVI.

### *Namely, how much the Fifth is sweeter than the Fourth, and why the Fourth does not appear as good against the Bass as the Fifth does.*

There are very few men who would not admit that the **Fifth** <note>The Fifth is an interval spanning five notes of a scale, such as C to G. In physics, it has a frequency ratio of 3:2.</note> is sweeter than the **Fourth** <note>The Fourth spans four notes, such as C to F, with a ratio of 4:3.</note>. The reason for this is taken from the greater union of its sounds, which unite at every 3rd beat of the high sound and at every second beat of the low sound, as I have demonstrated in another proposition. Consequently, the 2 beats of the low sound unite with the first and the last of the high sound, such that there is only the second beat of the high sound which does not unite at all; thus, the **Fifth** unites 4 of its beats at the same time that there is only one which is disunited. From this, it follows that the **Fifth** can be estimated as twice as sweet and better than the **Fourth**, whose high sound has two beats that are disunited—or even three times more excellent, because the low sound of that same **Fourth** has one of its beats disunited (namely, the one in the middle). Thus, the **Fourth** has 3 units that do not unite, while the **Fifth** has only one.

But there is yet another way to know how much the sweetness of the **Fifth** surpasses that of the **Fourth**. For when the terms of the **Fifth** are multiplied by one another—that is to say, 3 by 2—they give 6, which shows that its beats unite twice in 6 strikes. And when the terms of the **Fourth** are multiplied, they make 12, which shows that its beats unite 3 times in 12 strikes; that is to say, when the high sound of the **Fourth** has struck the air 12 times, it has united 3 times with the low sound of that same **Fourth**.

And because the high sound of the **Fifth** unites its beats twice with the beat of the low sound, and consequently 4 times in 12 strikes, it follows that the **Fifth** is sweeter than the **Fourth**, and consequently that the ratio of the sweetness of the **Fifth** to the sweetness of the **Fourth** is as 4 to 3. Now, this method is more reasonable than the other, by which we found that the **Fifth** is 2 or 3 times more pleasant than the **Fourth**. This is because the union that occurs at the first strike of each sound should not be considered, since it occurs just as well in **Dissonances** <note>Intervals that sound "clashing" or unstable to the ear.</note> as in **Consonances** <note>Intervals that sound stable and pleasant together.</note>. Rather, one should only consider the union of the final strikes, which causes the sounds to restart together. Thus, **Consonances** are sweeter to the extent that their sounds restart together more often, because they strike the air more uniformly and more equally; now, the closer sounds approach equality, the sweeter they are.

From this I derive the reason why the **Fourth** is not as good as the **Fifth** against the **Bass** <note>The lowest part of a musical composition.</note>, even though the two sounds of the **Octave** <note>The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency, which sounds like the "same" note at a higher register.</note> seem to be the same thing. For when the **Fourth** is played against the **Bass**, it does not unite its sounds except at every 4th beat of the high sound, whereas the **Fifth** unites its sounds at every 3rd beat of the high sound, which makes it sweeter and more pleasant. And when one divides the **Octave** into a **Fourth** and a **Fifth**, the harmony is sweeter when the **Fifth** is at the bottom than when it is at the top with the **Fourth** underneath. This is because the larger intervals should precede the smaller ones, for honor belongs to the things that are most excellent; and that which is placed immediately against the **Bass** must serve as the foundation of the harmony, and consequently must be larger and simpler, in order to imitate the nature of other things, which begin
