by the principles which are the most simple, and which serve as a foundation stone for all the rest.

Now the **Fifth** <note>An interval spanning five notes, like C to G.</note> is simpler than the **Fourth**, insofar as it approaches closer to the **Octave**, to equality, and to unity; for its lesser term is the greater term of the **Octave**—namely 2—just as the lesser term of the **Fourth** is the greater term of the **Fifth**—namely 3. In this way, the **Fourth** begins where the **Fifth** ends, just as the **Fifth** begins where the **Octave** has its end, and the **Octave** begins at the end of the **Unison**.

This can serve us as steps to elevate ourselves to God, and to the manner in which He produced His creatures; for the **Angels** <note>The author uses the hierarchy of musical intervals to mirror the "Great Chain of Being," a historical idea that all life and spirit are ranked in a specific order.</note> cannot begin to be until God exists in all the perfection of His nature, which is represented by unity, or by the **Unison**; and the nature of **Man** begins where that of the **Angels** ends; animals, plants, and other things follow in the same fashion, and all together depend entirely on God, just as the **Consonances** depend on the **Unison**, and numbers depend on unity.

One can also give another reason why the **Fourth** is not as pleasing below the **Fifth** as it is above it <note>In music theory, a Fourth played above a Fifth (e.g., C-G-C) sounds stable, but a Fourth played directly against the bass (e.g., C-F) was often considered unstable or "dissonant" in this period.</note>. This is taken from the fact that we always desire perfection in everything, and particularly in **Harmony**; and because the **Octave** contains in eminence all the perfection of **Music**, one always expects it when hearing other **Consonances**, for it always represents itself to the mind. From this it follows that the **Eleventh** <note>An interval of an Octave plus a Fourth.</note> is represented every time one plays the **Fourth** against the **Bass**; but the **Twelfth** <note>An interval of an Octave plus a Fifth.</note> is represented when one plays the **Fifth** against the same **Bass**. Now, the **Twelfth** is much more agreeable than the **Eleventh**, since it unites its sounds at every 3rd beat of the higher note, whereas the **Eleventh** only unites them at the 8th stroke. Thus, one can say following this reasoning, that the **Fifth** is as much more agreeable against the **Bass** as 8 surpasses 3: and that there is the same ratio for the sweetness of the **Fifth** compared to the **Fourth** as there is between 8 and 3. But because several difficulties, which we will speak of later, depend on this speculation, I will explain it more fully when speaking of **Thirds** and **Sixths**. Nevertheless, it can be understood here by means of the numbers and notes that follow; for when one plays the **Fourth** against the **Bass**, the lower sound strikes the air 3 times, while the higher sound strikes it 4 times. Now, 8 makes the **Octave** against 4—which 4 represents 8, since the part represents its whole—and consequently one perceives the **Eleventh** (which is 8 to 3) when one plays the **Fourth** against the **Bass** whose lower sound is 3, as seen in the notes that follow, which I mark with A, B, C, D, E, F, so that this discourse may be better understood.

This being established, I say that note D makes a **Fourth** against the **Bass** C, and that note D, being touched, represents note F, which is an **Octave** above; and consequently that the **Fourth**, which is from C to D and from 3 to 4, represents the **Eleventh**, which is from C to F, or from 3 to 8. Upon this, one might ask why note C does not just as well represent E (which is an **Octave** higher) just as D represents F? Why does D not represent B (the **Octave** below)? And why does the low sound C not represent A below it, since it makes an **Octave** with the said C? To which I answer that one...

one can say that the sound expressed by an even number of air-vibrations <note>Original: "battemens d'air." This refers to the frequency or pulses of sound waves.</note>, such as the high pitch of the Fourth CD, can represent its Octave above or below, for the reason that it is as easy to divide 4 into 2 equal parts to obtain B, as it is to multiply it by 2 to obtain F; consequently, one can say that 4 represents both Octaves. Now it must be noted that the upper Octave is usually represented when the vibrations of the high sound are an odd number, and the lower Octave when the vibrations of the low sound are an even number. For example, when one sings the Fifth D-E or B-C, the term for the low sound (namely 2 or 4) is an even number; from this it follows that D represents B, and that 2 represents 1. In this way, each thing usually represents another—namely, that which follows or precedes it immediately, and with which it has an alliance that is easier to notice, and a greater friendship and sympathy <note>The author uses "friendship and sympathy" to describe harmonic resonance and mathematical relationships, a common metaphor in Renaissance and Baroque music theory.</note>.

From this have come the "suppositions" of which the practitioners <note>Professional performing musicians and composers.</note> speak when they say that such and such a Consonance supposes another; for example, that the Fourth "supposes" and requires the Fifth below. But I will explain all these suppositions in a specific proposition, which will serve to understand the practice of musicians, by which they "save" <note>In music theory, to "save" a dissonance is to resolve it into a consonance so the ear is satisfied.</note> dissonances or lesser chords by following them with better ones.

I will say many more things about the Fourth in other propositions, where it will be necessary to see if it is more or less "sweet" than the Thirds, and if it is worse or better than they are against the Bass; and then I will show the foundation of these representations in the books on stringed instruments.

### PROPOSITION XXVII.

->*The Fourth is so sterile that it produces nothing good either by its multiplication or by its division.*<-

One should not be surprised if the Fourth, being doubled or tripled, etc., produces nothing good, since the same thing happens to the Fifth, which creates the Major Ninth when doubled, just as the Fourth makes the Minor Seventh of 16 to 9 <note>The ratio 16:9 creates a "small" minor seventh, which was considered dissonant in this period's tuning systems.</note>, which is found from C <term>sol-ut-fa</term> to B <term>fa</term> <note>These are solmization names used to identify specific notes on the musical scale of the time.</note>, and from D <term>la-re-sol</term> to C <term>sol-ut-fa</term>. But the division of the Fourth does not produce two Consonances like that of the Fifth (which produces the Major and Minor Third). For if one divides the Fourth in the same manner as one divides the Fifth—that is to say, by an arithmetic mean, namely by 7 placed between 8 and 6, which make the Fourth—one will have the <term>sesquisixth</term> <note>The ratio 7:6.</note> on the larger side, and the <term>sesquiseventh</term> <note>The ratio 8:7.</note> on the smaller side. This is seen between these three numbers 8, 7, 6, which represent intervals that are not used at all, the larger of which is less than the Minor Third by the ratio of 36 to 35.

I leave aside several other things that could be said of the Fourth—for example, by how much it is less than the Fifth, how many intervals it can be composed of, or into how many it can be divided; how many species it has, that it can be divided Geometrically, Arithmetically, and Harmonically, that it can be increased or decreased on Instruments, and several other things, because these are common to other musical intervals, or they depend on the treatise on ratios <note>Original: "traité des raisons." ## PROPOSITION XXVIII.

->*The two Thirds that are called major and minor come from the 3rd bisection made of a string, or another line—that is to say, from the first division of the Fifth; for the ratio of the Major Third is 4 to 5, and that of the minor is 5 to 6.*<-

It is necessary to double the terms of the Fifth—that is to say, the sesquialter ratio <note>The ratio of 3:2, which defines the musical Fifth.</note>—to divide it into two parts, of which the greater makes the Major Third, and the lesser makes the minor, as one sees in these three numbers: 4, 5, 6. The first and the last <note>4 and 6.</note> represent the Fifth; the 1st and the 2nd <note>4 and 5.</note> represent the Major Third; and the 2nd and the 3rd <note>5 and 6.</note> show the ratio of the minor. One calls the Major Third a *ditone* because it contains 2 tones, and the minor a *sesquiditone* because it contains one tone and a half. Now, to explain how these two Thirds come from the 3rd bisection of a string, one must suppose that the first two bisections of the same string (by which the Unison and the other Octaves, of which we have spoken until now, are produced) have been made, as seen on line A B. When divided at point C, it generates the Unison and the Octave, and when one divides it at point D, it produces the Fifth and the Twelfth.

<image-desc>A diagram representing a line or string divided at specific points. The endpoints are labeled A and B. Between them are points labeled C, E, and D, each marked with a small vertical tick. The points are ordered A, C, E, D, B from left to right.</image-desc>

These two bisections being made, the 3rd which is made at point E generates the two Thirds; for A E (that is to say, five) makes the major against A C, and A D makes the minor against A E. By this, one sees that the Minor Third is only produced by accident, like the Fourth, by reason of the residue of the string E D; and consequently, it has the same proportion with the Fifth as the Fourth has with the Octave, just as the Major Third has the same proportion with the Fifth as the Fifth has with the Octave. And because the Fifth does not bring enough variety to Music, the two Thirds supply this defect, for the greatest variety depends on them, as one experiences in practice; this shows that Music has almost no grace if these Thirds or their compounds are not found therein. But one will better understand the nature of these Thirds by the comparison I make between them and the Fourth, and with their compounds in the propositions that follow.

### PROPOSITION XXIX.

->*To determine whether the two Thirds are Consonances, and how much one is sweeter than the other.*<-

It seems that the Greeks did not at all place these two Thirds, nor the two Sixths, among the Consonances; for everyone from Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who was a pioneer in music theory.</note> to Ptolemy, Aristides, Bryennius, and several others, both Greek and Latin, recognized only the Octave, the Fifth, the Fourth, and their compounds <note>Original: "repliques." In early music theory, a "compound" is an interval expanded by one or more octaves, such as a Tenth being a compound of a Third.</note> as Consonances, as can be seen in the books they have left us. And one still finds philosophers who maintain this opinion, on the grounds that the Fourth is the last interval that has as many good beats as bad ones, as I have already said—that is to say, that the high sound has only two of its vibrations which unite at every fourth stroke, namely the first and the last, and two in the middle which do not unite at all. They believe that those who take Thirds for Consonances are mistaken, and speak more from fancy than from reason. 

But since the Major Third and its compound, which is to say the Major Tenth, make the strings vibrate quite strongly and visibly, it seems that one would have to be devoid of sense to deny that they are Consonances. Furthermore, there is no likelihood that all the ears of the French, Italians, Germans, Spaniards, etc., where Music is received, are mistaken; they testify that this Third, and particularly its compound, is very sweet, and that Harmony would lose almost all its grace if it were deprived of them. It must therefore be concluded that they are both Consonances, although the Major is more agreeable than the Minor in that it unites its movements more often: for the Major unites them at every fifth vibration <note>Original: "battement." This refers to the 5:4 ratio of the Major Third.</note> of the higher sound, and the Minor at every 6th vibration <note>Refers to the 6:5 ratio of the Minor Third.</note>, and consequently the Ditone <term>Ditone: a Major Third consisting of two whole tones</term> is more agreeable by one-fourth than the Semiditone <term>Semiditone: a Minor Third</term>. As for their compounds, I shall speak of them in the proposition that follows.

### PROPOSITION XXX.

->*To determine whether Thirds and their compounds are sweeter than the Fourth,*<-
->*and its repetitions.*<-

This difficulty is one of the greatest in Music: for it seems that experience and reason are at odds here, seeing as most practitioners maintain that Thirds and their compounds, particularly the Major Third and the Tenth, are sweeter and more agreeable than the Fourth. Indeed, the ear seems much more satisfied by Thirds than by Fourths: from this it follows that one may use as many Thirds as one likes in Duos, particularly when the Minor follows the Major. And yet reason is to the contrary, for the ratio of the Fourth is closer to the Octave and the Unison, and its sounds unite a third more often than those of the Major Third; furthermore, the Fourth makes the strings vibrate more strongly than the Major Third, and consequently it ought to be sweeter.

To which André Papias <note>A 16th-century musical theorist known for his work *De Consonantiis*, where he defended the Fourth as a primary consonance.</note> adds in the book he wrote in favor of the Diatessaron <term>Diatessaron: the Greek term for the interval of a Fourth</term>, that if one sings several Fourths in succession, they will be less insupportable

<image-desc>Musical notation containing four examples labeled with Roman numerals. Example I: C, F, A (a Fourth and a Sixth). Example II: C, E, G (a Major triad). Example III: C, A (a Major Sixth). Example IV: C, G (a Perfect Fifth).</image-desc>

Nonetheless, if the ear rightly gives the advantage to the Major Third, one must say that the reason for this marvel must be taken from the fact that every sound represents its higher Octave, which it contains "in eminence" <note>This refers to the phenomenon of overtones, where a single note naturally contains higher frequencies within it.</note>, as can be demonstrated by a string; for a string representing any sound you wish resonates at the higher Octave which it contains, since the whole contains all its parts: for length CB makes the Octave against AB. From this it follows that one often hears the Twelfth above when one plays the thickest strings of a **Theorbo** <term>A large, bass-range lute with extended neck and extra bass strings</term>, for length AB represents its third part CB (or CD), which creates a Twelfth against AD. This is usually heard more distinctly than the Octave, because its greater difference from the sound AB makes us discern it better than the Octave. But I shall speak further of these representations and resonances in the books on Stringed Instruments, and when explaining why **Bells** usually produce three sounds, of which the first is their natural tone, the second is at the Octave, and the third is at the Major Tenth, and sometimes at the Eleventh or the Twelfth.

Now, this resonance of the Octave being established, I say that the Fourth must appear less good than the Major Third. This is because when one plays this Third, which is a ratio of 4 to 5, if the "5" represents its Octave, one imagines "10," which makes a Major Tenth with "4." But when one plays the Fourth of 3 to 4, the Eleventh of 3 to 8 is represented, which is much harsher and less agreeable than the Major Tenth of 2 to 5. For one must not judge the quality of Consonances only by the consideration of the simple intervals, but one must also consider their *compounds* <note>Original: "repliques." Intervals expanded by octaves.</note>. Now, the compounds of the Major Third are more agreeable than those of the Fourth, since they unite their sounds more frequently, as is demonstrated by their lowest numerical terms.

And if we take the representation of the Octave below, we will find that the Third still represents the Tenth, as seen in these numbers 2, 4, 5, and that the Fourth represents the Fifth, as shown by these three terms 2, 3, 4.

### PROPOSITION XXXI.

->*Determining whether the two Sixths, of which the Major is from 3 to 5, and the Minor from 5 to 8, are Consonances.*<-

Since the two preceding Thirds are placed in the rank of Consonances, there is no doubt that the two Sixths must also be placed there, since they complete the Octave. Furthermore, Sixths placed under Thirds, or vice versa, create a good effect and are pleasing; they subsist all alone in Duos of simple counterpoint without being <term>sauuées</term> <note>Original: "sauuées" (saved). In music theory, this refers to "resolving" a dissonance into a consonance.</note> or supported by other Consonances, and they themselves "save" Dissonances, as is experienced with Sevenths, which are used in Cadences between two Sixths. It must nevertheless be confessed that these two Consonances are hardly "good" <note>Meaning "perfect" or "pure" in a mathematical sense.</note>, because the comparison of their sounds is not easy to grasp. This is because the ratio is <term>surpartissante</term> <note>A "superpartient" ratio is one where the larger number contains the smaller number plus more than one part of it (e.g., 5:3 is 1 and 2/3).</note>; the high sound of the Major Sixth contains the low sound once, plus two-thirds of the high sound. From this comes its ratio of "superpartient three," which is the first ratio among the superpartients; and the ratio of the Minor Sixth is <term>surtripartissante</term> <note>Supertripartient: where the larger number contains the smaller plus three parts (e.g., 8:5 is 1 and 3/5).</note> five. Consequently, the sounds of the Major Sixth unite once at every fifth beat of the high sound and every third beat of the low; and the sounds of the Minor Sixth unite at every 8th beat of the high sound and every fifth of the low. From this, I shall conclude in the 32nd proposition by how much one surpasses the other.

Now, since these two Sixths are found between these numbers 3, 5, 8, and because the first and the last make the replica of the Fourth, or the Eleventh <note>An Eleventh is an Octave plus a Fourth (8/4 * 4/3 = 8/3, but here expressed as 8:3).</note>, it follows that the division of the Eleventh gives us the two Sixths, of which the Major is on the bottom and the Minor is on top: although the said Eleventh could be divided by 6 in this fashion: 3, 6, 8. But it seems it is not too easy to know which is the better and more pleasing of these two divisions, unless one gives the advantage to the latter, by reason of the Octave that occurs between 3 and 6.

# PROPOSITION XXXII.

## *Determining by how much Sixths are more or less pleasing than Thirds, or the Fourth.*

It is quite easy to resolve this difficulty if one measures what is pleasing by the union of the beats of the air, as we have done until now; for the Major Sixth unites them at every fifth beat of the high sound, just as the Major Third does; that is why they must be pleasing in that regard. However, the Sixth unites them at every 3rd beat of the low sound, and the Major Third at every 4th beat only; which must undoubtedly make the Sixth more pleasing, if there are no other things to consider in this Third. For example, its greater simplicity and its <term>superparticular ratio</term> <note>A "superparticular" ratio is one where the larger number exceeds the smaller by exactly one, such as 5:4 for a Major Third. These were historically considered more "pure" than "superpartient" ratios like the 5:3 of a Major Sixth.</note>, which is easier to imagine and understand than the <term>superpartient</term> ratio of three <note>original: "raison surpartissante trois"</note> of the Major Sixth; for it is, it seems, easier to discern when, of two proposed lines, one surpasses the other by a quarter than when it surpasses it by two thirds. Furthermore, the Major Third is produced by the third bisection <note>The result of dividing a string into equal parts.</note>, which does not happen for the Major Sixth. From this it follows that the Trumpet produces this Third immediately after the Fourth; which shows that it is the most excellent of all the simple Consonances after the Fourth; although one might say that the Trumpet can produce the Twelfth at the first interval, and the Major Sixth at the second, if one pushes the wind as necessary from the lowest sound of the Trumpet to the Major Seventeenth, which the Trumpet can reach in two leaps.

Nevertheless, this in no way prevents the Major Third from holding the first rank after the Fourth, since the Trumpet can also produce the Seventeenth, the Nineteenth, or the Twentieth from the first leap without passing through the other Consonances, if the wind is blown strongly enough, even though these Consonances are not as sweet as the Octave or the Fifth.

To which one may add that the sounds of the Major Sixth are further apart than those of the Major Third, of which they almost form the repetition, and that the said Third, being produced by the third bisection and by the largest and most excellent part of the Fifth, must be more pleasing; hence it is that some call it the "little fifth," or "fifth of the fifth," of which it is like the eldest daughter.

the Third being to the Fifth what the Fifth is to the Octave. As for the **minor Sixth**, which is in the ratio of 5 to 8, there is no doubt that it is less pleasing than the **Major Third**, since it is merely the residue <note>The "residue" is the interval remaining when one interval is subtracted from another; for example, an Octave (1:2) minus a Major Third (4:5) leaves a minor Sixth (5:8).</note> of the third bisection, just as the Fourth is the residue of the Second. And one usually compares this minor Sixth to the minor Third for sweetness and goodness, for they are of the same nature. The minor Third must, however, be sweeter, since its **beats** <note>The author uses "beats" (battemens) to describe the coincidence of vibrations; the more frequently the vibrations of two notes align, the more consonant the interval sounds.</note> unite at every 6th beat of the high sound, whereas those of the minor Sixth only unite at every 8th beat—unless we consider the beats of the low sound, which unite at every 5th beat in both, for 5 is their lowest term.

Now, it is difficult to determine which is the best of these two Consonances, for each is excellent according to the places where it is well-positioned; and if the minor Sixth is better suited for expressing great sorrows with proportional cries, the minor Third is similarly better for expressing minor displeasures and for flattering. Nevertheless, absolutely speaking, the minor Third is sweeter by a quarter, since its sounds unite 8 times, while the minor Sixth unites its own only 6 times in the same duration.

As for the **Major Sixth** compared to the minor Third, it must be sweeter, inasmuch as it is the larger part of the Octave, of which the minor Third is only the residue; though there are other things to consider in this Third which may compensate for the greater union of the beats of the Major Sixth, which unite 6 times in 30 strokes, while those of the minor Third unite only 5 times; so that the sweetness of this Sixth is greater by a fifth part than that of the said Third. But because it is easier to understand the comparison of the two sounds that make this Third, because its ratio is <term>sesquiquintal</term> <note>original: "sesquiquinte"; a ratio of 6:5, where the larger number contains the smaller once plus one-fifth of its value.</note>, it may seem sweeter and more pleasing. In any case, the sweetness of the minor Third surpasses that of the minor Sixth more than that of the Major Sixth surpasses that of the Major Third: and if one wishes to determine by how much it surpasses it, multiplying their terms by one another will show by how much.

Now, if one compares the two Sixths together, one will find that the sweetness of the Major Sixth is as much greater than that of the minor as 8 is greater than 5, and consequently, these two sweetnesses are in the same ratio as the minor Sixth. And because the two Thirds serve to vary the Fifth, upon which the principal grace of music depends, it happens that they are more pleasing than the Sixths, which desire to be divided by a sound that creates a Fourth on one side and a minor or Major Third on the other; but Thirds cannot be divided. From this, it follows that they are more suitable for **Duos** than Sixths, which can serve in **Trios** by reason of the middle voice that divides them.

But I shall say many more things in the corollaries and in the propositions that follow, which will serve to understand by how much these Consonances exceed one another; and I shall show that one must reason differently about these Sixths if one considers the resonances and representations of high sounds that accompany the low sounds of a single string, than we have done in this proposition—though it is quite easy to conclude all that one can know if one understands what we have said previously.

### COROLLARY I.

->*Demonstrating why the Fourth is not as good against the Bass as the Thirds or the Sixths.*<-

Even though it is quite easy to derive the reason for this experience from the preceding discourses, I nonetheless wish to explain it so that practitioners <note>The author uses "practitioners" to refer to performing musicians and composers, distinguishing them from pure theorists.</note> may understand it. Now, it must first be assumed that the ear always desires to hear a perfect consonance when it hears an imperfect one, and that it always expects or assumes the harmony <note>original: "l'accord"</note> necessary to reach the Octave. For example, when one hears the Fifth, one expects the Fourth; and when one hears the minor Sixth, one expects the Major Third. This being established, I say that whenever the harmony one hears is more imperfect than the one remaining to complete the Octave, it is that much less pleasing, because the harmony one expects and assumes to finish the Octave is more perfect. Consequently, the Fourth against the Bass is the most disagreeable of all the Consonances, because the goodness of the Fifth that remains to make the Octave exceeds the goodness of the Fourth more than the Thirds exceed the Sixths, or the Sixths exceed the Thirds that remain to make the Octave. For when one hears the minor Third against the Bass, the Major Sixth is assumed; this Sixth does not exceed the goodness of the minor Third as much as the Fifth exceeds the goodness of the Fourth. This is why the minor Third is better than the Fourth against the Bass in duos of simple counterpoint.

But there is yet another reason for this practice, which depends on what I have said before: namely, that every sound represents its Octave above. From this, it happens that the Consonances which become better by the addition of the Octave above are more pleasing in duos against the Bass than those which do not become more perfect, or which become more imperfect by the addition of said Octave. Now, it is evident that the Fourth becomes more imperfect when one adds the Octave above, as seen in these numbers 3, 4, 8; for 3 and 8 form the ratio <term>double surbipartissantetrios</term> <note>original: "surbipartissantetrios." This refers to the ratio 8:3, which in music is the "Eleventh" (an octave plus a fourth).</note>, which shows that the sounds of this Eleventh only unite at every 8th beat of air. But when one hears the Major Third, the Octave of the high sound makes it more perfect, because it unites its sounds at every 2nd beat of the low sound, whereas it previously united only at every 4th. For as for the high sound, it always has an equal number of beats, as seen in these numbers 4, 5, 10, which can be reduced to 2, 2 1/2, 5, in order to see the Major Tenth in these fundamental terms. And although the Major Third exceeds the minor Sixth more than the Fifth exceeds the Fourth, nonetheless, the minor Sixth can be placed against the Bass, because the Octave of the high sound of the minor Sixth does not make it so bad compared to the replica <note>A "replica" is a compound interval, such as an octave doubling of a simpler interval.</note> of the Major Third, as it makes the Fourth compared to the replica of the Fifth. And the ratio of 5 to 16 is no more difficult to understand than that of 5 to 8, because the latter is <term>surtripartissantecinq</term> <note>The ratio 8:5, the minor Sixth.</note> and the other is <term>triple sesquiquinte</term> <note>The ratio 16:5, the minor Thirteenth.</note>. Thus, the replica of the minor Sixth is not so bad in comparison to the same Sixth as the replica of the Fourth is in comparison to the same Fourth.

### PROPOSITION XXXIII.

->*Why there are only seven or eight simple Consonances.*<-

This difficulty is one of the greatest in Music; for although we experience that among all sounds, only those that are equal, or are in a double ratio <term>2:1, the Octave</term>, sesquialter <term>3:2, the Fifth</term>, sesquitertial <term>4:3, the Fourth</term>, sesquiquartal <term>5:4, the Major Third</term>, sesquiquintal <term>6:5, the Minor Third</term>, superbipartient-3 <term>5:3, the Major Sixth</term>, and supertripartient-5 <term>8:5, the Minor Sixth</term> are agreeable and deserve the name of perfect or imperfect Consonances, it is nevertheless difficult to give a reason for it.

For why are the two sounds whose ratio is sesquisextal <term>7:6</term>, or sesquiseptimal <term>8:7</term>, not agreeable? And if we consider repeated Consonances, why do sounds whose ratio is 7 to 1, and 9 to 1—that is, sevenfold and ninefold—not please the mind and the ear? Especially since those whose ratio is 8, 10, 12, and 16 to 1 are agreeable, even though those of 7 to 1 or 9 to 1 unite more often, and consequently should be more agreeable, following the reason we have provided elsewhere regarding what is more or less agreeable in Music.

Those who say that the number of Consonances cannot exceed seven, because that number belongs to "rest" <note>A reference to the Biblical Sabbath or the idea of 7 as a number of completion and repose.</note>, assume that the Unison is not a Consonance, though we have proved the contrary. And even if one does not place it among the Consonances, the reason taken from "rest" represented by 7 is quite weak, even if one produces many things in Nature, and in the Sciences, and in the Arts that occur in the number 7; for one finds many things in that same Nature and in the Sciences which surpass the number 7.

We must therefore find some other reason for the number of Consonances which is not taken from the septenary <note>A group of seven.</note> number, since the Unison makes it pass to the octonary <note>A group of eight.</note>; unless one believes that the septenary number is "fatal" <note>Meaning "destined" or "fixed by fate" in this context.</note> to Music, because it comes from the two terms of the Fourth—namely 3 and 4, which make 7—and

# On Consonances.

...that the Fourth <note>The musical interval of a Fourth (e.g., C to F)</note> is so unfortunate that some call it a monster when it is played against the Bass, and that it produces another monster, namely the aforementioned septenary number <term>The number seven (7)</term>, which is the capital enemy of Music.

But this consideration is quite slight; for one can say on the contrary that this number is the most excellent of all, since it contains the ternary <term>the number 3</term> and the quaternary <term>the number 4</term>. Of these, one is assigned to intellectual and divine things, and the other to material and elementary things. However, one might similarly respond that this very reason prevents the septenary from serving the Consonances, because material things (represented by 4) are too far removed from the perfection of intellectual things (represented by 3). They cannot be so united that they create an accord; and because of this distance and disproportion, the body and the senses—both external and internal—cannot coexist in harmony with reason, which they perpetually fight and oppose.

Indeed, one experiences a strange combat between the elementary part of man and the intellectual part, which bears the character of divinity and always tends toward the good. For even if many feel no sting of concupiscence <note>Inordinate desire or lust</note>, and have extinguished the flames and suppressed the movements of the irascible appetite <note>The part of the soul associated with anger, courage, and overcoming obstacles</note>, if they have reached beyond the common state and learned in what the sovereign exercise of the spirit consists, they feel combats much greater than those of the two animal faculties which serve anger and love.

For the combat between phantasms <note>In 17th-century philosophy, "phantasms" were the sensory images or mental pictures that the mind relies on to think about the physical world</note> and the understanding is so great that when the spirit believes itself to be free, and tries to elevate itself above everything created in order to conceive of Him who surpasses all being, all goodness, and all power, it is constrained to fall back into darkness. It is forced to confess that it is a slave to matter while it is bound to the body, so that each man is constrained to cry out with the Apostle, "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?" <note>original: "Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis huius" (Romans 7:24)</note>. For it is a kind of death to be deprived of one’s own function, as happens to the human understanding while it can understand nothing except by means of phantasms, which hinder it as much as darkness hinders the eye. This need not be proven to those who contemplate truths without phantasms—particularly the sovereign truth, which they see almost without a veil and in the open.

There is therefore no solid and perfect contentment except that which one has when considering the naked truth in the source of its essence, to see it everywhere, since truth has no boundaries, and God is everywhere that truth is. Now, those who have reached this degree, and who unite themselves to the source of truth, are no longer subject to afflictions; for they know that he who loves God as he ought can lose nothing, unless God loses it at the same time, as Saint Augustine noted in his book *Of True Religion*, chapter 47: "He is not afflicted by the death of anyone, for whom it is good to cling to God, because he who loves God with all his soul knows that what does not perish for God does not perish for him; for God is the Lord of the living and the dead." <note>original: "Non affligitur morte cuiuſquam, cui hærere Deo bonum eſt, quoniam qui toto animo Deum diligit, nouit nec ſibi perire, quod Deo non perit: Deus autem Dominus eſt viuorum & mortuorum."</note> Although the soul, being in this state, may be seized by a great fear that it is not clean enough to assist in the presence of Him whom it contemplates and loves ardently, as the same Saint noted in the book *On the Quantity of the Soul*, chapter 33: "The more and more the soul feels," <note>original: "Quò magis magiſque ſentit anima,"</note>

# First Book

<note>original Latin: "eo ipso quòd proficit, quantum intersit inter puram & contaminatam, eò magis timet, ne deposito isto corpore, minus eam possit Deus, quam seipsa ferre pollutam."</note> "By the very fact that the soul progresses, and understands the great difference between the pure and the contaminated, it fears all the more that, once this body is laid aside, God might be even less able to bear its pollution than the soul itself can." But I leave behind these phantoms, from which we shall not be entirely freed until after this life, in order to resume the discussion on the number of Consonances <note>Musical intervals that sound stable and pleasant together</note>, and to consider whether Musicians have not been mistaken until now in the determination they have made of this number—just as the Astrologers <note>At this time, "astrology" and "astronomy" were often used interchangeably to describe the study of the stars</note> were mistaken when they believed there were only 7 Planets; for there are six others, namely 2 that accompany Saturn, and 4 that are beside Jupiter; and posterity will perhaps discover an even greater number.

We must then see if a spirit more refined and elevated than that of ordinary Musicians can encounter new Consonances, and if there can be found ears and imaginations of a greater range than those of Practitioners, by means of which new accords might be discovered, just as new Planets were discovered by means of telescopes. For why could there not be found ears which are pleased by sounds whose ratio is a <term>sesquisexte</term> <note>The ratio of 7:6, today called a Septimal Minor Third</note> of 7 to 6, or a <term>septuple</term> <note>The ratio of 7:1</note> of 7 to 1, or a <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>The ratio of 9:8, commonly known as a Major Tone</note> of 9 to 8? This could be said of several other proportions, which perhaps please some animals more than those that constitute our Consonances.

For since ratios cause no pain, and it is not possible to join two or more sounds together without them having some ratio, it seems that if the ear is reasonable—that is, if one judges sounds reasonably—there can be no dissonance. This is because dissonance is defined by the pain or the "beatings" with which it strikes the ear, and there is no union of sounds that can cause offense, since there is no pain without the division of some part of the body, which is called a <term>solution of continuity</term> <note>A philosophical and medical term meaning a physical break or rupture in a continuous substance or tissue</note>, as Saint Augustine teaches in the 3rd book of *Genesis Literally Interpreted*, chapter 6:
> <note>original Latin: "Ipse dolor corporis in quolibet animante magna & mirabilis animæ vis est, quo illam compagem ineffabili permixtione vitaliter continet, & in quandam sui moduli redigit vnitatem, cum eam non indifferenter, sed vt ita dicam indignanter patitur corrumpi atque dissolui."</note> "The pain of the body itself in any living creature is a great and marvelous power of the soul, by which it holds that framework together vitally in an ineffable mixture, and brings it back into a certain unity of its own measure, when it suffers it to be corrupted and dissolved not with indifference, but, so to speak, with indignation."

Furthermore, 8 new <term>aspects</term> <note>The angular positions between planets as seen from Earth</note> have been established in the Heavens; for instead of the 5 ordinary ones—namely the sextile, the square, the trine, the opposition, and the conjunction—13 are now recognized, which I have explained elsewhere, marking all the Consonances produced by these 13 aspects. This is enough to make one doubt whether there are no other Consonances than the 7 ordinary ones. For just as one encounters men whose strength is as admirable when compared to the strength of others as the size of giants compared to the ordinary height of men, there may be ears that will take pleasure in hearing the dissonant intervals of which we have already spoken in this proposition. But there is no need to imagine new kinds of men, or to have recourse to animals to find ears that judge that dissonant intervals should be included among the accords. For Jean des Murs <note>Johannes de Muris, a prominent 14th-century music theorist</note>, Cantor of the Church of Notre Dame in Paris, maintains in the 4th book of his *Mirror of Music*, chapters 44 and 45, that the Ninth, the Sixteenth, and the Twenty-third—which consist of ratios of 9 to 4, 9 to 2, and 9 to 1—are Consonances. He may have believed this if he found them pleasing; as for the reasons he provides, they are too weak to persuade those who know that experience proves otherwise. # On Consonances

...judged them agreeable, since they are composed of two Fifths, or two Fifths and a Fourth, or the Octave, the Fifteenth, the Twenty-second, and the Whole Tone.

Now it must be admitted that it is very difficult to know why the <term>sesquiquinte</term> <note>The ratio of 6:5, which forms the interval of a Minor Third</note> is the last <term>superparticular ratio</term> <note>A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 or 6:5</note> that pleases in the interval of sounds—that is to say, why two sounds joined together, where one is greater than the other by a fifth part, form the final combination beyond which none are agreeable. This is so even though there are an infinite number of ratios below this <term>sesquiquinte</term>, which produces the Minor Third. The ratio of the Minor Third contains two very significant terms: the greater, 6, is a <term>perfect number</term> <note>A number equal to the sum of its divisors, like 1+2+3=6</note>, and both are <term>circular numbers</term> <note>Numbers whose powers always end in the same digit, such as 5×5=25 or 6×6=36</note>.

As for the last Consonance, whose ratio is <term>surtripartissant-five</term> <note>The ratio of 8:5, which forms the Minor Sixth</note>, its terms are 5 and 8. The greater term, 8, is the first <term>cube</term> <note>2 multiplied by itself three times (2x2x2)</note>, and the lesser is the same circular number found in the Minor Third. This ratio creates the Minor Sixth when added to a Fourth. However, when one reaches the <term>Septenary</term> <note>The number seven</note>, nothing good is found anymore, even though it is produced by adding the terms of two Consonances—namely those of the Fourth and the Major Tenth.

Some believe that the intervals of 7 to 1, 9 to 1, and others that do not occur in the third <term>bisection</term> <note>The mathematical division of a musical string into parts</note> of the string are not chords because it would follow that all intervals of the fourth bisection would also be consonant, which contradicts experience. But this reason is not entirely satisfying, for one must first give the reason why only this specific bisection produces chords.

And if one says that the sounds do not unite quickly enough in the proportion of 7 to 1 or 7 to 8 to be agreeable, the sounds of 5 to 8, 16 to 1, and several other consonances unite even less frequently, and yet these proportions remain agreeable.

Others take the reason to be that one cannot divide the aforementioned intervals of 7 to 1 or 9 to 1 into intervals suitable for singing, and that seven cannot form any Harmonic ratio with the numbers that precede it. It forms a <term>Septuple ratio</term> with 1, which is composed of the ratio that makes the Nineteenth (the second octave-repeat of the Fifth) and the <term>sesquisixte</term> <note>The ratio of 7:6</note>, which does not arise from the differences between standard Consonances. It forms the <term>triple sesquialtera</term> <note>A ratio of 7:2</note> with 2, the <term>double sesquitertia</term> <note>A ratio of 7:3</note> with 3, the <term>surtripartissante-four</term> <note>A ratio of 7:4</note> with 4, the <term>surbipartissante-five</term> <note>A ratio of 7:5</note> with 5, and the <term>sesquisexte</term> with 6. This last one is almost equal to two <term>Major Semitones</term> added together (whose ratio is 256 to 226, while the <term>sesquisexte</term> is 256 to 224); consequently, neither the <term>sesquisexte</term> nor any other interval found between the Minor Third and the Major Tone can form a chord.

Kepler believes he found the reason for this difficulty when he says, in his first book on the demonstration of Harmonic figures, that the <term>Heptagon</term> <note>A seven-sided polygon</note> cannot be described geometrically outside of a circle; and even if one inscribes it within the circle, one cannot know the relationship of its sides to the radius or diameter. From this, he believes that God did not make use of this figure for the adornment of the Universe, because He does not recognize the...

But I leave aside now this new difficulty, which requires a particular discourse, to remark that one cannot find the reason for what we seek through the figures of Kepler. This is because the two sounds that make the ratio of 8 to 9 <note>The interval of a Major Second or Whole Tone</note>, or of 7 to 2, or to 1, are not irrational and incommensurable, as are the sides of the Heptagon and several other figures when compared to the radii of the circle. It is also because sounds and Consonances <note>Pleasant-sounding musical intervals</note> must not be compared to planes or to incommensurable lines, since all the beats of air that make Consonances or Dissonances are commensurable; for there is no number of movements or beats of air that are not commensurable to all other numbers of movements.

This is why I marvel that Kepler dared to bring the comparison of figures with Consonances to derive the reason for their number and their quality. This would be tolerable if he had been content to compare the said figures to Consonances and Dissonances by analogy and for recreation, as do those who compare them to the sides or angles of the Hexagon and the Octagon, and to many other things found in nature, as I have done in the second book of the *Universal Harmony*.

Now, what he adds in the 19th proposition of his third book does not prove that the septenary <note>The number seven</note> number cannot produce Consonances. For although one puts two unities in the form of a fraction in this manner 1/1, and the unity compared to these two unities makes the Octave of 2 to 1, the addition of which produces 3, which makes the Twelfth with the unity; and these two terms, which make 4, make the Fifteenth with the unity, with which 5 makes the Major Seventeenth, and 6 the Nineteenth. And finally, even though the preceding numbers make Consonances with one another—as we experience in 2 compared to 3 and to 5, with which it makes the Fifth and the Major Tenth; in 3 compared to 4, 5, and 8, with which it makes the Fourth, the Major Sixth, and the Eleventh; in 4 which makes the Major Third with 5; and in 5 compared with 6 and 8, with which it makes the Minor Third and the Minor Sixth—it does not follow, however, that 7 compared to 6, and to the unity, or to some other number, might not be a Consonance, even though it comes from the addition of 6 and 1, of 3 and 4, and of 2 and 5; just as eleven comes from the addition of 5 and 6, and of 3 and 8; and 9 from the addition of 4 and 5; and 13 from the addition of 5 and 8. For all these considerations cannot prevent these numbers from being fit to make Consonances.

Some imagine, with Plato, that the reasons for Harmony and chords are engraved in the mind of man from the instant of his creation; and that the soul rejoices when it perceives sounds that awaken and recall its ideas, and which respond to its reasons; just as the soul of plants seems to rejoice when it is struck by the sweet influences of the Sun and the other Planets.

The ratio of 8:7</note>, and the others that do not make chords, are not in the soul, or that they do not make as great an impression there as those which serve as the form for Consonances; which is contrary to reason and experience, since we easily understand the rea-

sound of 7 to 6, of 8 to 7, of 9 to 1, and an infinity of other ratios <note>original: "raisons"</note> which cannot make a harmony, such that the definition they give to the soul—namely, that it is a Harmonic number—is not good, since the soul is as capable of understanding the ratios that are enemies of Harmony as those used to explain Consonances.

Those who hold that the temperament <note>The physical balance or healthy state</note> of the ear and the parts of the brain that serve for hearing music is wounded by the intervals we call Dissonant, and that it is preserved or perfected by those called Consonant, would not be able to prove what they say: for the ratio of 7, or of 9 to 1, or to 8, is no more an enemy of temperament than the ratio of 8, 10, or 12 to 1; otherwise, one would have to demonstrate this contrariety to resolve our doubt.

If the spirits called "animal" <note>In 17th-century physiology, these were subtle fluids believed to transmit sensations and commands through the nerves</note>, and which serve the functions of common sense and the external senses, are better preserved or perfected by the proportion of air movements that make Consonances than by those that make Dissonances, and that they receive a greater benefit from the former than the latter, I admit that one could say certain intervals are dissonant and disagreeable because they dissipate and alter the said spirits by the impression of a movement that is troublesome and inconvenient to them. But it would be necessary to demonstrate that the beats of air that make Consonances preserve or perfect the spirits of the brain, and that the beats of Dissonances wound it—which can be proven by experience; for the beats of the ***Minor Third*** and the ***Minor Sixth*** begin to displease and come very close to Dissonances, for they have more air beats that do not unite than those that do, as I have shown in the preceding discourses. In fact, these last two Consonances hardly deserve the name "agreeable," and should only be called Consonances because the displeasure one receives in hearing them is a little less than that received from ***Seconds*** and ***Tritons***, etc.

Now, although we have not encountered reasons strong enough to prove that there are only these 7 Consonances with their Replications <note>Octave equivalents, such as a tenth being a replication of a third</note>, and that the ***Second***, the ***Seventh***, the ***Triton***, the ***False Fifth*** <note>The diminished fifth</note>, and several other Dissonances do not wound the ears of many, and that long custom could introduce the use of the ***sesquisixth*** <note>The ratio 7:6</note> and ***sesquiseventh*** <note>The ratio 8:7</note>, we may nevertheless hold to this number, since practice is in conformity with it, and there are only these 7 Consonances with their Replications that proceed from the triple bisection of a string, as I will show in the discourse on the ***Monochord*** <note>A scientific instrument with a single string used to measure musical intervals</note>; and besides, that concerts are principally composed of the said Consonances; that Trumpets naturally produce these 7 Consonances before making any other interval or degree, as I will say in the discourse on the ***Trumpet***; and finally that the 7 strings which make these 7 consonant intervals make the other strings vibrate more strongly than any others, since their vibrations meet more often, and consequently the said strings being touched strike more often the strings that have not been touched, as I have shown in the discourse on each ***Consonance*** in particular.

Nevertheless, all these reasons do not entirely satisfy me, inasmuch as if the pleasure of music begins with the consideration of the mind <note>original: "l'esprit"</note>, which is capable of contemplating all sorts of ratios, it would be necessary to say why dissonant intervals displease it in sounds, since they do not displease it in bo- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "books" (livres)</note>

### Book One

Now, there is very little likelihood that this pleasure requires the consideration of the mind, which is capable of contemplating all kinds of ratios, since the ignorant receive as much or more pleasure from Music as the learned; this witnesses that this pleasure is natural, and that it has no need of other discourse than the pleasure of sight, smell, taste, and touch, although it is as difficult to find the reason for it as for the pleasure of the ear: for it is not enough to say that these pleasures are created by the <term>tickling of the animal spirits</term> <note>The 17th-century belief that "animal spirits" were a subtle fluid flowing through the nerves to communicate sensations to the brain.</note> and the nerves, if at the same time one does not determine why the stimulations that follow the proportion of Consonances please more than those that do not. But the Corollaries contain many things belonging to this subject.

->COROLLARY I.<-

One infers from this discourse that one can establish more than seven Consonances, if one takes the intervals that are less harsh and less disagreeable than many others as Consonances; for the <term>sesquiexta</term> <note>The ratio 6:5, which produces a minor third.</note> is more agreeable than the whole tone, and the tone is more agreeable than the semitone, and so on consequently following the greater or lesser union of their sounds.

One can similarly say that there are only one or two Consonances, namely the Unison and the Octave, and that the other intervals depart all the more from Consonances as they depart further from union; but I shall speak again of the number of Consonances in the discourse on the radical terms of the first hundred Consonances.

->COROLLARY II.<-

Even though we have not encountered a reason that satisfies perfectly, we have at least a greater knowledge of sounds than of the objects of the other senses; for if one does not know the true reason for Consonances, and why they please, one knows the true proportion that sounds must have to be agreeable; which does not happen with colors and flavors, for one does not know at all how many degrees of light a color must have, nor how many degrees of heat an odor must have to please; and one has not yet reached an agreement on the most agreeable color, flavor, or odor, as one has reached an agreement on the Unison or the Octave. To which one can add that many find distaste in the best meats, and hate the best odors, and that there are no men who do not find the Octave and the Fifth agreeable: which shows that sounds approach closer to the spirit and the intellectual than the object of the other senses.

->COROLLARY III.<-

Since one knows the proportion that makes sounds agreeable or unpleasant, and since it is likely that the other senses require similar proportions in their objects, sounds can bring more light to Philosophy than any other quality; this is why the science of Music must not be neglected, even if songs and concerts were entirely abolished and forbidden; for they are not the principal end of Music, as believed by the <term>Practitioners</term> <note>Professional performers or composers who focused on the "how" of music rather than the mathematical "why."</note>, who despise or ignore the reason. Indeed, if the knowledge of sounds and their proportion can give us entry into the proportions of the objects of the eye, smell, and taste, there is no person of quality <note>original: "honneste homme." Refers to the 17th-century ideal of a cultured, well-rounded gentleman.</note> who would not prefer this knowledge to all the songs and all the concerts that can be made following <note>There is a nasal abbreviation mark over the 'a' in 'ſuiuat'.</note> the rules of art.

### COROLLARY IV.

Since long practice is accustomed to making sweet and easy what previously seemed harsh and troublesome, I have no doubt that the dissonant intervals of which I have spoken in this proposition—namely the <term>ratios</term> <note>original: "raisons." In this context, it refers to the mathematical relationship between the frequencies or string lengths of two notes.</note> of 7 to 6, and 8 to 7, which divide the <term>Fourth</term> <note>An interval encompassing four notes of a standard scale.</note>—could become agreeable, if one grows accustomed to hearing and enduring them, and if one uses them as they ought to be used in recitatives and in concerts, in order to stir the passions, and for many effects of which ordinary Music is deprived.

The same can also be said of the sounds whose ratio is 5 to 7; for since these two sounds always unite together at every 7th stroke of the higher note, and the two sounds of the <term>Minor Sixth</term> <note>An interval such as E to C, represented by the ratio 8:5.</note> only unite at every 8th stroke, it follows that the first two sounds should be more agreeable, or sweeter by one degree, than the second two; although one might say that the two sounds of this Sixth are more agreeable because 8 represents the <term>Octave</term> <note>The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</note>, namely 4, for it supposes and requires the <term>Major Third</term> <note>An interval such as C to E, represented by the ratio 5:4.</note> below it, as I shall demonstrate in the 38th and 39th propositions. But the other two sounds do not suppose any Consonance below, and can only suppose a dissonance above, namely the ratio of 7 to 10, so that ten makes the Octave with 5. Now, these three terms, or sounds—5, 7, and 10—do not unite as quickly together as these other three—4, 5, and 8—which surpass the preceding ones by two degrees of union in the highest sound, by two other degrees in the middle sound, and by one degree in the first. For one must not only judge the pleasantness and nature of each Consonance by its simple sounds, but also by the other intervals it supposes below or above, as I have remarked.

And if one responds that 7 can represent 3 ½ just as well as 8 represents 4, it is easy to show that it is just as difficult to conceive of 3 ½ as it is of 7, since the half-unit forces one to divide the 3 into 6 halves when they are reduced to the same denomination; but one no longer has any use for 8 once one has 4.

### COROLLARY V.

Now, if the two sounds that are related as 7 to 5 do not seem as sweet as those whose ratio is 8 to 5, this happens because 8 and 5 form the repetition of the Major Third; for if one adds 4 to the lesser term of the <term>sesquiquarta</term> <note>The ratio 5:4, which defines the Major Third.</note> ratio, which is 4 to 5—that is to say, if one doubles its lesser term—one gets 8, which can always be divided by half down to <term>unity</term> <note>The number 1, considered the source of all numbers in Renaissance mathematics.</note>. Consequently, it is much easier to understand than 7, which is a prime number just like the lesser term 5; hence it follows that they can only be understood by the reduction one makes of them down to unity.

Furthermore, the ratio of 7 to 5 does not come from any <term>bisection of a string</term> <note>original: "bisection d'une chorde." The process of dividing a musical string into equal parts to find harmonic intervals.</note>, as one can easily conclude from the preceding discourses and from what we shall add in the propositions that follow. Now, the Minor Sixth comes from the third bisection; for the <term>Minor Third</term> <note>An interval such as A to C, represented by the ratio 6:5.</note> being produced by this bisection, its greater term, namely 5, serves as the lesser term for the Minor Sixth, of which the entire string—divided into 8 parts—is the greater term.

### COROLLARY VI.

If we establish the seven Consonances that I have explained in the preceding discourses, we can say there are no more of them than there are primary colors, as Aristotle maintains in the 4th chapter of his book *On Sense and the Sensible* <note>original: "sens & du sensible." This refers to Aristotle's treatise *De Sensu et Sensibilibus*.</note>. He does this so that there are no more species of colors than of flavors: namely, the two opposites, white and black—which he compares to sweet and bitter flavors—and yellow, red, purple, green, and blue, which he places between black and white. To white he relates yellow; while brown, and even blue, can be related to black. Thus he identifies only these seven colors and the two aforementioned flavors, along with salty, pungent, harsh, astringent, and acid. He imagines these to be composed in the same proportions as the Consonances; for example, like the <term>Diapente</term> <note>A Perfect Fifth, with a ratio of 3:2.</note> which is 3 to 2, and the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>A Perfect Fourth, with a ratio of 4:3.</note> which is 4 to 3, as described in the 3rd chapter. To this he adds that colors not composed of a certain number of parts of black and white that follow the <term>ratios</term> <note>original: "raison." The mathematical relationship between parts.</note> of the Consonances are not pleasing, particularly when these parts are <term>incommensurable</term> <note>Having no common numerical measure; irrational proportions.</note>.

Now, if one wished to expand upon Aristotle's comparison, one could compare light to the <term>Unison</term>, insofar as the other harmonic intervals have nothing pleasing except through participation in this root and source of Consonances, as I have shown in my previous discourse. The Octave could be compared to white, the Fifth to green, and so on for the others. This can also be applied to flavors and smells; but I have discussed this matter so extensively in the 2nd Theorem of the 2nd book of the *Treatise on Universal Harmony* <note>original: "Harmonie Vniuerselle." Mersenne’s own monumental work on music theory.</note>, in which one sees a vast multitude of comparisons between sound and all things in the world, that it is not necessary to add anything further.

### PROPOSITION XXXIV.

*To determine in how many ways one can divide each Consonance and each ratio; how to find the* **Arithmetic**, **Harmonic**, *and* **Geometric** *means; and what their differences and properties are.*

One can divide each ratio, and consequently each Consonance, in an infinite number of ways, since every ratio is divisible into an infinite number of other ratios—just as the area of a plane is divisible into an infinite number of other planes, and a line into an infinite number of other lines. 

But because all these divisions contribute nothing to Harmony—which uses only the Arithmetic and Harmonic divisions—it is sufficient to speak of these two divisions. We shall show how to find their <term>means</term> <note>The middle value in a mathematical series.</note>, which are used in the composition of two, three, four, or more parts, and see which is the most excellent mean for musical ensembles.

->### Of Consonances.<-

Now, the <term>Arithmetic mean</term> <note>The "middle" value found by adding two numbers and dividing by two; in music, this divides an interval into two unequal parts that decrease in size as the pitch rises.</note> is the easiest to find; for if one takes half of the sum resulting from the two terms added together, one will have the said mean. For example, the two terms of the <term>Octave</term> <note>The interval between two notes where one has double the frequency of the other, expressed as the ratio 1:2.</note>, namely 1 and 2, when added make 3, of which the half is 1 ½. This is as far from 1 as it is from 2, as there is the same difference from 1 to 1 ½ as from 1 ½ to 2. And if one wishes to avoid the fraction, one must add 2 and 4 (which are terms of the Octave) to get 6, of which 3 is the half, and consequently the Arithmetic mean. Here it should be noted that the discovery of this mean is nothing other than an <term>Arithmetic Progression</term> <note>A sequence of numbers where the difference between consecutive terms is constant.</note>.

As for the <term>Harmonic mean</term> <note>A type of average used in music to divide an interval such that the ratios between the notes remain consonant; it is the "reciprocal" of the arithmetic mean.</note>, it is found by multiplying the terms of the Consonance by each other; for the Arithmetic mean, dividing the sum that results from it, gives the Harmonic mean. For example, the two terms of the Octave, 2 and 4, multiplied together make 8, which, being divided by 3 (the Arithmetic mean), gives 2 ⅔ for the Harmonic mean. And by multiplying these three terms by 3 (the denominator of the fraction) to avoid said fraction, one has 8 for the mean that divides the Octave harmonically by these numbers: 6, 8, 12; or by these, which are the <term>root numbers</term> <note>The simplest whole-number expression of a ratio.</note>: 3, 4, 6.

The second manner used to find the Harmonic mean also supposes that the Consonance is already divided Arithmetically; for the first and last terms, being multiplied by that of the middle—namely by the Arithmetic mean—produce new extremities for the Consonance, and the smallest of the preceding terms multiplied by the largest produces the Harmonic mean. This is seen in this Arithmetic division of the <term>Fifth</term> <note>A musical interval such as C to G, represented by the ratio 2:3 or 4:6.</note>, 4, 5, 6; for 5 multiplying 4 and 6 produces 20 and 30, and 4 multiplying 6 gives 24 for the Harmonic mean: 20, 24, 30. And if one wishes to put the Arithmetic mean back into it, one only needs to square the preceding one, namely 5, to have these four terms: 20, 24, 25, 30.

In the third place, the Arithmetic mean being the lesser term of the Harmonic division, the greater term of the Arithmetic division is the Harmonic mean; so that one only needs to find the last term, which is the largest, by making the Arithmetic mean relate to said term as the lesser term of the Arithmetic division relates to its greatest term. For example, the <term>Twelfth</term> <note>An interval spanning an octave plus a fifth, with a ratio of 1:3.</note>, whose ratio is 1 to 3, is divided Arithmetically by 2, which is to 6 as 1 is to 3; from this it follows that the Twelfth is divided harmonically by these terms: 2, 3, 6.

But because these three manners suppose that one already knows the Arithmetic mean, one can find it by the following method without assuming anything: for if one multiplies the numbers or terms of the proposed Consonance by themselves, and divides the double of that product by the sum of the two terms of the Consonance added together, the quotient gives the Harmonic mean. For example, let 3 and 6 be the terms of the Octave, between which one finds the Harmonic mean of 4 in this manner: 3 times 6 makes 18, the double of which is 36, which, being divided by 9 (resulting from the addition of 3 and 6), gives 4 for the quotient, and likewise for the Harmonic mean.

Let us take another example in the <term>Major Tenth</term> <note>An interval spanning an octave plus a major third, with a ratio of 2:5.</note>, which is 2 to 5. Multiplying these makes 10, the double of which is 20, which, being divided by 7 (produced by adding 2 to 5), gives 2 ⁶/₇ for the Harmonic mean. One will have this without a fraction if all terms are multiplied by 7, in order to have the said Tenth divided Harmonically into these terms: 14, 20, 35; for the difference...

The fifth way, which serves to find the <term>Harmonic mean</term> <note>The harmonic mean is used to find the "middle" pitch that creates a specific set of musical intervals. In a harmonic proportion, the middle term is related to the outer terms by the ratios of their differences.</note>, is even easier than the other, for one does not need to multiply or divide, but only to add the two terms of the given <term>Consonance</term> <note>An interval or chord that sounds stable and harmonious to the ear.</note> to obtain the denominator of the fraction, of which the numerator is the lesser term of the Consonance, for the root Harmonic mean, as seen in the two following examples. The first belongs to the <term>Octave</term>, which being from 1 to 2, has for its Harmonic mean 1 1/3, so that the three <term>root terms</term> <note>The simplest whole numbers that express a mathematical ratio.</note> of this Harmonic division are expressed by these numbers: 1, 1 1/3, 2. These can be had without fractions in root terms if one multiplies the 3 aforementioned terms by the denominator of the fraction—namely by 3—which gives 3, 4, 6. But this 5th way is not as general as the others, for it does not succeed in the division of all kinds of Consonances; otherwise, the Harmonic mean of the <term>Tenth</term> <note>An interval spanning an octave plus a third.</note> would be 2 2/7, when it is actually 2 6/7, as we have demonstrated above. It is only found to be true in Consonances whose terms are expressed by numbers that follow each other immediately, as happens in the <term>Fifth</term> from 2 to 3, in the <term>Fourth</term> from 3 to 4, in the <term>Major Third</term> from 4 to 5, etc. This is why one must use the 4th way, which is the best of all.

### COROLLARY I.

It is easy to conclude from what we have just said that the Harmonic mean is not found between terms that have no <term>Arithmetic mean</term>, since the Harmonic proportion is the inverse of the Arithmetic, and the greatest term of the latter is the middle of the former, just as the Arithmetic mean is the least term of the latter. This is seen in these two following divisions of the Octave, the first of which is Arithmetic and the other Harmonic: 2, 3, 4, 6; for 3, which is the middle of the Arithmetic division 2, 3, 4, is the beginning of the Harmonic division 3, 4, 6.

### COROLLARY II.

Now, it is not enough to do what we have said for the Arithmetic proportion to find the Harmonic mean, unless at the same time one multiplies the terms; this happens whenever the Arithmetic mean has no number greater than itself with which it has the same ratio as the two terms of the Consonance to be divided. This is seen in the Fifth, which is divided Arithmetically by these terms: 4, 5, 6; these must be doubled to find the Harmonic mean in this division: 10, 12, 15. But they must be multiplied for the Fourth, quadrupled for the Major Third, and so on for the others.

We also have the <term>Geometric mean</term> <note>The middle value in a geometric progression (like 1, 2, 4), where the ratio between consecutive terms is constant. In music, this represents dividing an interval into two mathematically equal parts.</note>, which can be found in the divisions of Consonances, or of ratios composed of two Consonances, or equal ratios. An example is the <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>An interval of two octaves, represented by the ratio 1:4.</note>, or the quadruple ratio, which being composed of two Octaves (or two double ratios), has 2 for its Geometric mean in this division: 1, 2, 4. Another is the <term>Major Twenty-third</term> <note>An interval spanning three octaves and a major second, represented here by the ratio 1:9.</note>, or the nonuple ratio, which is divided Geometrically by these numbers: 1, 3, 9; and in all others that are composed of two equal ratios.

<header>On Consonances.</header>

Now these three <term>means</term> <note>Mathematical values used to find a middle point between two numbers.</note> have several differences: for the <term>Arithmetic mean</term> has its differences equal between the first and the last terms, but its <term>ratios</term> <note>The relationship between the numbers.</note> are unequal; the <term>Geometric mean</term>, on the contrary, has its ratios equal, but its differences unequal; and the <term>Harmonic mean</term> has neither one nor the other, but its differences from the lesser and the greater terms have the same ratio as the said terms themselves, as one sees in this example: 10, 16, 20, 25, 40. This sequence divides the <term>fifteenth</term> <note>A double-octave interval, here represented by the ratio 10:40 or 1:4.</note> Arithmetically by 25, Geometrically by 20, and Harmonically by 16.

Secondly, the lesser terms of the Arithmetic division contain the greater ratios, and the greater terms of the Harmonic division have the lesser ratios; but the Geometric division always maintains the same ratio between its greater and its smaller terms.

In the third place, the Arithmetic mean is closer to the greater term, and the Harmonic is closer to the smaller term, but the Geometric is exactly in the middle—both between the two terms of the ratio and between the two other means.

In the 4th place, these two means <note>The Arithmetic and Harmonic</note> when multiplied together produce the same number as the square of the Geometric mean, or as the two <term>extremes</term> <note>The outer numbers of the proportion.</note> multiplied by one another.

Fifthly, the differences between the Arithmetic mean and the extremes are equal to each other; those of the Harmonic mean are equal to the ratio being divided, and those of the Geometric mean are equal to the dividing ratios.

Sixthly, the ratio that divides Geometrically is the <term>sub-double</term> <note>original: "souzdouble"; in this context, it refers to the square root of the ratio.</note> of the ratio being divided, just as the ratio of the Geometric differences is the sub-double of the ratio of the Harmonic differences.

But I will not expand any further on this subject, since it is not necessary for Harmony, and I have treated it quite fully in the 2nd book of *The Truth of the Sciences*, chapter 9; I do this so that I may speak of several other things that serve the composition and the ordinary divisions of Consonances.

Now, the same thing happens to the other divisions of repeated or doubled <term>Consonances</term>, which have two similar intervals, because two or more Consonances of the same kind that follow one another immediately always create <term>Dissonances</term> <note>Clashing or unstable sounds. The Octave excuses several intervals and makes them better, giving them the same privilege as if nothing had preceded them, since the Octave is the repetition or the image of the <term>Unison</term> <note>Two notes of the exact same pitch.</note>.

The Major Tenth has yet another division in these numbers 4, 5, 6, 10, which can only be changed in this manner: 6, 10, 12, 15, because the <term>Major Third</term> cannot follow or precede the <term>Major Sixth</term>, for it would create a <term>superfluous Octave</term> <note>original: "Octaue superfluë"; likely referring to an augmented octave, which is considered a dissonance.</note>.

Now, it is enough to have given examples of the Fifth, the Octave, and the two Tenths to understand the division of the other Consonances, and the variety that can be found in each division by simply changing the placement and order of the intervals. Therefore, I leave the divisions of the other Consonances which are included up to the **Twenty-ninth**, of which the preceding division contains and shows the sweetest and most excellent division of all the Consonances.

### COROLLARY.

All Consonances do not have <term>Arithmetic and Harmonic divisions</term> <note>Methods of dividing a musical string based on mathematical averages. Arithmetic division (equal distances) and Harmonic division (ratios that create musical intervals) were the two primary ways Renaissance theorists calculated scales.</note> that can serve Music; for besides the fact that the two Thirds and the <term>Fourth</term> cannot receive a division where the extremes are consonant with the middle term, the Minor Sixth divided Arithmetically by these terms 10, 13, 16, or Harmonically by these, 65, 80, 104, produces dissonant intervals.

The division made by these terms 5, 6, 8, or by these 15, 20, 24, is better than the preceding ones, even though it is neither Arithmetic nor Harmonic. The same thing happens to the Major Tenth, whose following division 2, 3, 5, or 2, 4, 5, is pleasing, although it is neither Arithmetic nor Harmonic. This clearly shows that the Musician must know other divisions than the two previously mentioned, which are the only ones usually discussed; for he must know all the <term>ratios of strings</term>, sounds, and intervals that can serve Music.
