### PROPOSITION XXXVI.

*To demonstrate that the most agreeable and best division of Consonances is not Harmonic, as has been believed until now, but that it is Arithmetic: and that the Arithmetic division is the cause of the sweetness of the said Consonances.*

When ordinary musicians divide the <term>Octave</term> <note>The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</note> in such a way that the <term>Fifth</term> <note>A musical interval spanning five degrees of a scale (e.g., C to G).</note> is at the bottom and the <term>Fourth</term> <note>A musical interval spanning four degrees of a scale (e.g., G to the C above it).</note> is at the top, they believe that this division is Harmonic and not Arithmetic. I wish to disabuse them of this notion by this proposition; for the 3 sounds of this division are related to each other like these 3 numbers, 2, 3, 4, whose differences are equal. I demonstrate this in the following manner: Let there be 3 strings of the divided Octave, A B, C D, and E F, and let the longest, A B, be divided into 6 equal parts, C D into 4, and E F into 3. I say that these 3 strings will divide the Octave Harmonically, following the <term>Harmonic division</term> <note>In traditional music theory, dividing a string by lengths of 6, 4, and 3 was called "harmonic" because it created a Fifth (6:4) and a Fourth (4:3).</note> of ordinary musicians: for A B creates the Fifth at the bottom against C D, and the Fourth is at the top from C D to E F. Nevertheless, it is a very certain thing that this division of the Octave is Arithmetic; which I demonstrate so clearly that no one can doubt it.

<image-desc>A technical diagram placed to the right of the text. It displays three parallel horizontal lines representing musical strings (chordes). The top line is the shortest and is labeled 'E' and 'F' at its ends. The middle line is slightly longer, labeled 'C' and 'D', and has one vertical tick mark indicating a division. The bottom line is the longest, labeled 'A' and 'B', and has two vertical tick marks indicating divisions.</image-desc>

It is very certain that sound is made by the beats of the air, or by the back-and-forth movements, or the turns and returns of the string, as I demonstrate elsewhere; and that among several strings equal in material, thickness, and tension, the longest make fewer returns and beat the air fewer times than the shortest. The shortest strings have a number of returns that is greater in the same proportion that the longer ones are divided into a greater number of parts: so that the ratio of the multitude of returns made by the strings is the inverse of their lengths, as I have demonstrated elsewhere. For example, a string 100 feet long beats the air only once, while a string one foot long beats it a hundred times.

Now, since the string A B is double the length of string E F, while A B beats the air 3 times, E F beats it 6 times; and while A B beats it 2 times, E F beats it 4 times, and string C D beats it 3 times. Thus, these beats maintain an <term>Arithmetic progression</term> <note>A sequence of numbers where the difference between consecutive terms is constant (e.g., 2, 3, 4), unlike harmonic ratios based on string lengths.</note>, and not the Harmonic progression of numbers, since these beats follow these numbers: 2, 3, 4.

This is why one must mark Consonances according to the number of beats of the air that produce the sounds, and not according to the length of the strings, which is not the formal cause of the sounds, but rather the efficient and external cause.

And furthermore, it often happens that the strings which make the preceding division of the Octave are not different in length at all; it is possible for them to be equal in both length and thickness, as I have demonstrated elsewhere. But it...

This shift in perspective identifies the "beats of the air" as the true cause of musical consonance.</summary>

it cannot be that string A B strikes the air more than twice, while E F
strikes it 4 times, and C D three times; which happens perpetually when the <term>Fifth</term> <note>A musical interval spanning five notes of a scale; in physics, it represents a frequency ratio of 3:2.</note> is
at the bottom, and the <term>Fourth</term> <note>A musical interval spanning four notes; a frequency ratio of 4:3.</note> at the top.

Now when the length of the three strings is in <term>Arithmetic proportion</term> <note>A sequence of numbers where the difference between consecutive terms is constant.</note>, and
the Fourth is found at the bottom, and the Fifth at the top, the proportion of
movements and sounds is Harmonic; which I demonstrate in these three strings,
for at the same time that string A B, which is divided into 4 parts, makes 3 returns,
string E F makes 6, and C D makes 4, as I have demonstrated in the book of
Movements: or while A B makes 2 returns, E F makes 4, and C D makes 2 and 2/3; now 2 2/3
is to 2, as 4 is to 3; and to 4, as 4 is to 6, <image-desc>A small schematic diagram with three horizontal lines of different lengths, aligned to the left. that is to say, the Fifth is at the top, and the Fourth
at the bottom, when the division is Harmonic.

The same thing happens in the division of other <term>Consonances</term> <note>Intervals that sound pleasant or stable to the ear.</note>, for when the
Fifth is so divided that the <term>Major Third</term> <note>An interval of four semitones (e.g., C to E).</note> is at the bottom, and the <term>Minor Third</term> <note>An interval of three semitones (e.g., A to C).</note> at
the top, the division is Arithmetic, as one sees in these numbers 4, 5, 6.
Nevertheless, the Harmonic division is useful, because it serves to arrange
the length of strings in Harmonic progression to find the Arithmetic
progression of sounds and Consonances: as one experiences in the
Arithmetic division of the <term>Octave</term> <note>The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</note>, which is represented by these terms 2, 3,
4, and produced by the Harmonic division of strings, whose lengths are
represented by these numbers: 6, 4, 3.

Similarly, strings whose lengths follow the Harmonic division
of the Fifth, represented by these numbers 10, 12, 15, give the Arithmetic
proportion of the Fifth; that is why the Harmonic division should not
be entirely rejected, and serves at least to know the length of strings
when their different sounds come only from their different lengths.

### COROLLARY I.

It must therefore be concluded that those who imagined Harmonic divisions
have used the largest numbers to signify the longest strings, or
the thickest and the loosest, and have not considered the nature of sound; and that
one must use the smallest numbers to explain the lower sounds, and the
largest to signify the higher ones, since the former are nothing other than a
smaller number of beats of air, and the latter a larger number.

### COROLLARY II.

Secondly, it must be concluded that the Harmonic division of Consonances
is the worst, the harshest, and the most disagreeable, insofar as its terms, or its
sounds, unite with more difficulty: for if one proposes these three sounds 6, 4, 3, they
cannot unite until the string represented by three has made six returns; but when the
division is Arithmetic, as happens in these terms 2, 3, 4, which represent
the returns of the strings, or the beats of the air, the three sounds unite at every
fourth beat of the highest sound, which is represented by 4.

### COROLLARY III.

And because 6 is to 4, just as the harshness of the <term>Harmonic division</term> <note>A way of dividing a string such that the lengths form a harmonic proportion; in Mersenne's time, this often placed the smaller interval at the bottom of the chord.</note> is to the sweetness of the <term>Arithmetic division</term> <note>A way of dividing a string into equal parts; here, it results in the more pleasing arrangement where the larger interval (like a Fifth) is at the bottom of the chord.</note>, it follows that this [Arithmetic] division is half again as sweet and pleasant as the former; since the sweetness and excellence of Consonances is derived from their greater and swifter union; as we have demonstrated in the other discourses;

One must conclude the same thing regarding the Arithmetic and Harmonic division of all other <term>Consonances</term> <note>Musical intervals that sound stable and pleasant together.</note>, both simple and repeated, since the same reasoning applies, and the Arithmetic division represents them to us in smaller terms, which are easier to understand.

### PROPOSITION XXXVII.

->*Given two or several divisions of a Consonance, to determine by how much*<-
->*one is better and sweeter, or more pleasant than the other, and which is the*<-
->*best division of each Consonance, considering all the*<-
->*divisions it can sustain according to the laws*<-
->*of Music.*<-

We have already shown that the Arithmetic division of Consonances is more pleasant than the Harmonic; and consequently that we should call the Arithmetic "Harmonic," if by "Harmonic" one understands the most pleasant; although if practitioners prefer to follow their old routine, I do not wish to prevent them. Now, one can easily conclude from the two preceding propositions that the division of each Consonance is best and sweetest when its sounds are represented by numbers that unite most quickly and easily. But it is necessary here to explain by how much each division is more pleasant than the other, just as we have explained by how much each Consonance is more excellent and sweet than the other.

This is as easy as many believe it to be difficult; for since the excellence of divisions is measured by the ease and speed of their meeting and their union, each division is that much more excellent as its sounds unite more often: and consequently if they unite twice as fast, it is twice as excellent. So that one must only consider the three terms of the divided Consonance, and find by how much the sum of the three terms is larger or smaller than the sum of the three terms of another division; for the division whose terms make a smaller number is that much more excellent, as the number is smaller.

A single example can serve to make this discourse understood; for if one divides the <term>Octave</term> <note>The most fundamental musical interval, where the higher note vibrates at exactly twice the frequency of the lower note.</note> Harmonically in this manner, 6, 4, 3, these three terms being added together equal 13: and the three terms of the Arithmetic division of the Octave, 2, 3, 4, equal only 9; there is therefore the same ratio of the "goodness" of the Harmonic division to the Arithmetic division of the Octave as there is from 13 to 9; that is to say, if the Harmonic division has 9 degrees of goodness, the Arithmetic has 13, because the three strings that make the Harmonic division only unite their three sounds after they have made 13 returns, and have struck the air 13 times; whereas the 3 strings of the Arithmetic division unite theirs at every 9th <term>beat of air</term> <note>A 17th-century term for vibrations or frequency.</note>.

<page-num>100</page-num>
<header>Book One</header>

But it is enough to consider the two largest terms of the division in order to compare them together, to know by how much one division is more pleasant than the other, especially since this comparison almost returns to the other; as one sees in this example, in which the largest term of the <term>Harmonic division</term> <note>A way of dividing a string where the lengths are in harmonic proportion (e.g., 6, 4, 3).</note> is to the largest of the <term>Arithmetic</term> <note>A division where lengths are in arithmetic progression (e.g., 4, 3, 2).</note>, as 6 is to 4—that is to say, in a <term>sesquialteral ratio</term> <note>original: "raison sesquialtere"; a ratio of 3 to 2, meaning one is 1.5 times the other.</note>; 13 being almost in the same ratio to 9, for 12 and 9 are in a sesquialteral ratio; and consequently, the Arithmetic division of the <term>Octave</term> is half again better than the Harmonic.

One can also take the first and last terms of each division and make a comparison of the numbers that come from adding them: for example, the 1st and 2nd terms of the Arithmetic division, namely 2 and 4, make 6; and those of the Harmonic, namely 6 and 3, make 9, which are in a sesquialteral ratio, just like 6 and 4. The same thing happens in the division of other <term>Consonances</term> <note>Musical intervals that sound harmonious and stable.</note>, for example in that of the <term>Fifth</term>, which is divided Arithmetically by these terms 4, 5, 6, and Harmonically by these, 10, 12, 15; for these numbers [10, 12, 15] being added make 37, and the others [4, 5, 6] make only 15: now 37 is to 15 almost as 15 is to 6, or as 25 is to 10, which is to say in a <term>double sesquialteral ratio</term> <note>original: "raison double sesquialtere"; a ratio of 5 to 2, or two and a half times.</note>.

Finally, one can multiply the three terms by one another to see how many times all the terms "recommence" together <note>Referring to the physical synchronization of vibrations.</note> in the time that they strike the air, as many times as the largest term is contained in the number that comes from the multiplication of all three terms: for example, the three terms of the Arithmetic division of the Octave [2, 3, 4] make 24, and the 3 terms of the Harmonic [3, 4, 6] make 72. Now, the largest term of the Arithmetic division, namely 4, goes into 24 six times; and consequently, the 3 sounds (or the returns of the 3 strings) recommence their movements 6 times and unite 6 times together, while the strings strike the air 24 times. And the Harmonic sounds unite only 12 times while there are 72 returns of the 3 strings, so that they only unite 2 times in 12 strikes. Now, since they unite 3 times in 12 strikes in the Arithmetic division, and since three is the sesquialter of two, it follows that the Arithmetic division of the Octave is half again more pleasant than the Harmonic.

It is easy to apply this consideration to the division of the Fifth, and of all the other Consonances. One can further extend this consideration to the comparison of two or several Consonances of different kinds, in order to find by how much the division of some is more pleasant than that of others: for example, one can compare the Arithmetic division of the Octave and that of the Fifth, and determine by how much one is sweeter than the other. That of the Octave unites its sounds three times while the three strings strike the air twelve times; and that of the Fifth unites its own only twice. This is why the Arithmetic division of the Octave must be half again sweeter and more pleasant than that of the <term>Fourth</term> <note>The text says "Quarte" (Fourth) here, though the preceding context compared the Octave to the Fifth; this may be a slip of the pen by the author.</note>; so that there is the same ratio of the goodness of the division of the Octave to that of the Fifth, as there is from the largest radical term of the Fifth to the largest of the Octave, which is to say from 3 to 2; and consequently, when one knows how to make the comparison of Consonances, one can also make the comparison of their divisions.

Having previously argued that Arithmetic divisions are mathematically "better," he now uses corollaries to explain how these mathematical properties relate to the actual auditory experience of a listener.</meta>

<page-num>101</page-num>
<header>On Consonances.</header>

### COROLLARY I.

Since the <term>Harmonic division</term> <note>A mathematical way of dividing an interval where the lengths of the string segments follow a harmonic proportion (e.g., 6:4:3).</note> of the <term>Octave</term> <note>The most fundamental musical interval, where the higher note vibrates exactly twice as fast as the lower note.</note> is half as pleasing as its <term>Arithmetic division</term> <note>A division where string lengths follow an arithmetic progression (e.g., 4:3:2), which Mersenne considers more "natural."</note>, and since the latter is half again more pleasing than the Arithmetic division of the <term>Fifth</term> <note>The interval produced by the ratio 3:2, often considered the most stable consonance after the octave.</note>, it follows that the Harmonic division of the Octave and the Arithmetic division of the Fifth are equal; for they unite their returns <note>Mersenne’s term for the alignment of vibrations: the more often the sound waves "hit" at the same time, the more consonant the sound.</note> an equal number of times. One can similarly compare the Arithmetic division of other <term>Consonances</term> with their Harmonic division in order to see the equalities and inequalities of their "sweetness," and to choose what is best for Composition.

### COROLLARY II.

Nevertheless, I do not maintain that one can make such a certain judgment when comparing the divisions of Consonances of different species to one another as one can with the different divisions of the same Consonance, because they are heterogeneous and of a different nature. From this, it perhaps follows that the Arithmetic division of the Fifth is considered more pleasing by many than the Harmonic division of the Octave. To this it must be added that what is "sweeter" <note>In 17th-century music theory, "sweetness" usually refers to mathematical purity and lack of dissonance.</note> is not always more pleasing, just as we experience with sugar and honey, and many other very sweet things that are hated by many who prefer vinegar and bitter things, as I have stated more fully in a separate discourse.

### COROLLARY III.

One of the divisions may also seem less pleasing than the other, even though its sounds unite just as often or more; this happens when the Consonances are found outside their natural place, as seen in the Harmonic division of the Octave, in which the <term>Fourth</term> <note>The interval between the 3rd and 4th harmonics (4:3 ratio).</note> is at the bottom, whereas it requires the treble <note>original: "l’aigu"; the higher register.</note> following the natural order, of which we have spoken previously.

### COROLLARY IV.

One can also compare the division of simple Consonances with that of their repetitions <note>Also known as "compound intervals," such as a Twelfth (an octave plus a fifth).</note>, in order to consider whether the repetitions, which are sweeter than the simple Consonances, similarly have sweeter divisions. For example, [one might ask] if the division of the <term>Twelfth</term> and the <term>Seventeenth</term>, which are produced by these numbers—1, 2, 3 and 1, 2, 5, or 1, 3, 5—is better than the division of the Fifth (4, 5, 6) or the <term>Major Tenth</term> (2, 3, 5, or 2, 4, 5). But it must be noted that when an interval is divided by the Octave, the Octave brings almost no diversity to the division, and it leaves the repeated Consonance in the same state as the simple one. This is why the division of the Fifth seems more pleasing than that of the Twelfth or <term>Nineteenth</term>, even though it is less "sweet," inasmuch as it has more diversity in its sweetness. Consequently, it more fully occupies the mind of the listener, who seeks two things in <term>Harmony</term>: namely, sweetness and diversity. The listener receives the greatest contentment one can expect from Harmony when he encounters both so well mixed together that they are almost equal, as happens in the Fifth.

<header>Book One</header>

## PROPOSITION XXXVIII.

*To determine what each <term>Consonance</term> <note>A combination of notes that sound pleasant and stable together.</note> presupposes above or below it to produce a good effect, and to be in its perfection; that is to say, to determine what presents itself to the mind or the imagination when one plays a simple Consonance on the Organ, or on some other Instrument, or when one sings it with voices.*

This question is one of the most excellent in Music, and serves greatly for composition, and for knowing wherein the perfection of <term>Harmony</term> <note>The combination of simultaneously sounded musical notes to produce a pleasing effect.</note> consists: for if one knows what each Consonance presupposes, it is very easy to add a third part to Duos, and a fourth to Trios. Now, it is a certain thing that <term>perfect Consonances</term> <note>In Mersenne's time, these were the Unison, Octave, and Fifth, considered the most stable intervals.</note> do not presuppose others at all, because they are very simple and have no need of others for their support and foundation; this is why we shall not speak here of the <term>Octave</term>, nor of its repetitions, nor of the <term>Unison</term>, which is in the composition of Music what unity is in Arithmetic, and the point is in Geometry.

But <term>imperfect Consonances</term> <note>Intervals like Thirds and Sixths, which were considered "sweeter" but less stable than perfect ones.</note> always presuppose the perfect ones, just as numbers presuppose unity, and the roofs of houses presuppose their foundations, inasmuch as all things tend toward their perfection and their end. From this it follows that imperfect Consonances suffer a kind of violence <note>Mersenne uses "violence" in the Aristotelian sense, meaning a state of tension or being "out of place."</note> when one does not add to them the other Consonances they desire, just as a stone suffers violence when it is prevented from going to its center and its rest: for all things love rest, and never labor except to achieve it.

Those who hold that sound is a "sounding number" <note>A reference to the Pythagorean view that music is literally mathematics made audible.</note> can easily conclude what each Consonance presupposes, since all Consonances follow the natural order of numbers; for just as 3 presupposes 2, and 2 presupposes 1, in the same way one Consonance presupposes the other. For example, if the <term>Fifth</term> <note>The interval represented by the ratio 2:3.</note> presupposes any other Consonance, it presuppose the Octave below or above, for its <term>ratio</term> <note>original: "raison"</note> is from 2 to 3; now, there is only 1 before 2, with which it makes the Octave; similarly 4, which follows 3, makes the Octave with 2.

But before passing further, it must be noted that the Consonance which is said to be presupposed is created against the lowest sound of the Consonance that does the presupposing, as seen in the preceding example, in which the lowest sound of the Fifth presupposes the Octave above; and if one takes the highest sound, the Fifth presupposes the <term>Twelfth</term> below, or the <term>Fourth</term> above. The same judgment must be made of all other Consonances, for they always presuppose and demand the Consonances expressed by the numbers that immediately follow or precede the numbers by which the said Consonances are expressed, as I demonstrate in all the Consonances that follow.

The low sound of the Fourth presupposes the <term>Sixth</term> above, or the Fifth below; for its ratio is 3 to 4; and 5, which follows 4, makes the <term>Major Sixth</term> with 3, just as 2, which is before 3, makes the Fifth with 3: and consequently the high sound of the same Fourth presupposes the Octave below, and the <term>Major Third</term> above.

The low sound of the Major Third presupposes the Fourth below, or the Fifth above, for its ratio is 4 to 5; now 4 makes the Fourth with 3, and the Fifth with 6, which follows 5 immediately; and the high sound of the same Third presupposes the Major Sixth below, and the <term>Minor Third</term> above.

# Of Consonances.

The low note of the <term>Minor Third</term> <note>An interval spanning three semitones, such as A to C.</note> presupposes the Major Third below, for its <term>ratio</term> <note>The mathematical relationship between the frequencies of two notes.</note> is 5 to 6; now, 4 immediately precedes 5. However, 7, which follows 6, creates a very poor dissonance with 6; this is why this note can only presuppose the Major Third below, or the Major Sixth above. The high note of this same Third presupposes the Fifth below, or the Fourth above.

The low note of the <term>Major Sixth</term> <note>An interval of nine semitones, such as C to A.</note> presupposes the Octave above, for its ratio is 3 to 5, after which 6 follows immediately. It can also presuppose the Fifth below, since 2 precedes 3. But the high note of this Sixth presupposes the Major Tenth below, or the Minor Third above. Finally, the low note of the <term>Minor Sixth</term> <note>An interval of eight semitones, such as E to C.</note>, which is 5 to 8, presupposes the Major Third below, which is expressed by 4 compared to 5; and the high note presupposes the Octave below.

The same judgment must be made for repeated Consonances—namely the Major and Minor Tenth, the Eleventh, the Major and Minor Thirteenth, the Major and Minor Seventeenth, the Eighteenth, and the Major and Minor Twentieth. These always presuppose some other Consonance, but not always the same as the simple Consonances. For the low note of the <term>Major Tenth</term> <note>A Major Third plus an Octave.</note>, whose ratio is 2 to 5, presupposes the Octave below, and not the Fourth as the Major Third did; for one immediately precedes two, with which it makes the Octave below. However, it presupposes the Twelfth above. The high note of the same Tenth presupposes the Major Seventeenth below, or the Minor Sixth above. Now, the presupposition that the low note makes of the Twelfth, or the high note makes of the Minor Third, is the most agreeable, because it possesses more diversity. This is because the Octave, which is merely the repetition of the <term>Unison</term> <note>Two notes of the same pitch.</note>, is not encountered there as it is in the two other presuppositions. This should be noted in order to understand why the division of Consonances whose sounds unite more often do not always produce the most agreeable effect; for the pleasure we receive from Music, and from other things in this world, requires variety, for which we have provided the reasons in the 46th question of the *<term>Physico-mathematical Questions</term>* <note>The author refers here to his own scientific treatise exploring the intersection of physics and music.</note>.

### PROPOSITION XXXIX.

*To explain by the ordinary notes of Practical Music what has been explained by numbers, and to give the true reasons for all the presuppositions.*

The notes of Music show clearly what we have explained through ratio and numbers, which are again joined here with the notes, so that Theory may be considered within Practice, and that form may be united to matter, and reason to the nature of sounds. Now, the first two examples comprise

# Book One

...as for the <term>minor sixth</term> <note>An interval of eight semitones, such as E to C.</note>, it has only one example, given that 9, which immediately follows 8, creates a dissonance.

Now, the reason for all these presuppositions is derived from the fact that there is no closer <term>consonance</term> <note>A stable, pleasing interval between two notes.</note> that can be assumed, and that nature always moves from one degree to another by the shortest path it can find. Thus, it skips no step, so that the bond of its works may be stronger, and so that what it produces may be continuous and without any interruption.

From this comes the fact that the most perfect bodies in nature are the least open and least porous, as is experienced with gold, silver, diamonds, and crystal, whose parts are better joined than those of many other bodies—for example, those of stones and wood. This is why diamonds and crystal take a very beautiful polish, of which no type of wood is capable; for the polish of ebony, which seems to be the most beautiful of all those wood can receive, is much less than that of steel or crystal.

Indeed, <term>music</term> in which the closest <term>consonances</term> always, or most often, follow one after another is better and more polished than when they do not observe this sequence, because it is more continuous and solid; for it leaves no void, and the ear finds there everything that can reasonably be desired.

Now, the <term>consonances</term> that are presupposed in the preceding examples are the closest ones; for just as there is no number between 3 and 4, nor between 4 and 5, nor between 5 and 6, there is likewise no <term>consonance</term> from 3 to 4 other than the <term>fourth</term>, nor from 4 to 5 other than the <term>major third</term>, nor from 5 to 6 other than the <term>minor third</term>. This is why one cannot presuppose other <term>consonances</term> than those we have mentioned, unless one leaves the closest to take the most distant—just as one cannot go from 4 to 6 without skipping 5, nor from 5 to 8 without skipping 6, etc.

But I do not wish to determine here if it is sometimes appropriate to have distant <term>consonances</term> follow one after another according to the different subjects treated in <term>music</term> and the different effects desired; for it is enough to have shown what is best and most harmonious in compositions, the rest depending on the skill of the <term>composer</term> and the different circumstances that change very often.

It is also necessary to explain why the preceding presuppositions are more pleasing than the sequence of other <term>consonances</term>. The reason is found in the greater ease the imagination has in understanding the sequence of neighboring <term>consonances</term>, since it only needs to add unity to the <term>consonance</term> that follows, or take it away from the <term>consonance</term> that precedes. For example, when the <term>fourth</term> presupposes the <term>sixth</term>, if one adds 1 to the high pitch of the <term>fourth</term> (namely to 4), one gets 5, which creates the <term>sixth</term> with the low pitch of the same <term>fourth</term> (which is represented by 3). Now, there is nothing easier than adding 1 to 3 or to 4; and when one counts 3, one expects 4; and if one counts 4 or 5, one expects 5 or 6; and when one says 6, one presupposes 5, just as 5 presupposes 4, and 4 presupposes 3; and so on.

This reason is founded on the nature of sound and of the other <term>consonances</term>; for the two sounds of the <term>fourth</term>, for example, are nothing other than two movements of air, of which the high one strikes the air 4 times and the low one 3 times. Thus, if one adds one beat of air to the 4 beats of the high sound, one will create the <term>major sixth</term>

-># Of Consonances<-

...with the low sound of the <term>fourth</term> <note>An interval of five semitones, like C to F, represented by the ratio 4:3.</note>; and if one removes one of the vibrations from this low sound, only 2 will remain, which will create a <term>fifth</term> <note>An interval of seven semitones, like C to G, represented by the ratio 3:2.</note> when paired with 3. From this, one can see that nothing is easier, more natural, or better regulated than making the <term>major third</term> <note>An interval of four semitones, like C to E, represented by the ratio 5:4.</note> follow the fourth, or putting the fifth before the fourth.

It is easy to apply this discourse to all the other <term>consonances</term> <note>Pleasing intervals between notes.</note>; and to conclude that it is no different from the discussion we have had regarding their divisions, which are always sweeter when their vibrations or their movements unite more often; although many people do not take as much pleasure in them, due to a preoccupation of the mind, or the difference in imaginations, ears, and capacity, which causes some to desire a greater variety than others, as happens with different tastes and the other external senses. To this one can add that the most excellent and polished things are not always the most pleasant; as we notice in the shapes of bodies, of which the round shape is considered the most perfect, because of its greater capacity and uniformity; yet many do not consider it the most beautiful of all; and they prefer to see a diamond or a crystal with 6 or 8 angles rather than when it is completely round; for too much equality and uniformity takes away or diminishes pleasure: from this it follows that ordinary buildings please more than if they were round: and one would not receive as much pleasure from seeing men and animals all round, as one does looking at the shapes they have now.

## COROLLARY I.

It follows from these two propositions that one can always add a third part to <term>duos</term> <note>Musical compositions for two voices or instruments.</note>, insofar as their consonances, which are quite bare and most often imperfect, always presuppose others; but <term>trios</term> <note>Compositions for three voices.</note> no longer presuppose anything, because one can only add the <term>octave</term>, which is the repetition of the <term>unison</term> <note>Two voices singing the exact same pitch.</note>, to create the fourth part; or the repetition of the other consonances to make 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 musical parts.

## COROLLARY II.

It follows similarly that an <term>arithmetician</term> <note>A mathematician who specializes in the study of numbers.</note> can learn music without a master, and that there is no science so easy, since its best reasons consist only of counting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, etc., and comparing these numbers to one another. It must nevertheless be noted that I speak here of true <term>theory</term>, and not of <term>practice</term>, which requires more time, as the body is heavier than the mind, and one must take almost as much trouble to make it quick and skillful in following the movements of the mind as one does to teach birds to speak and other animals to imitate the actions of man.

## COROLLARY III.

He who knows how to put these last two propositions into practice will be able to add a third part to duos, and a fourth to trios, which will be the sweetest of all those that can be added, because he will add the most natural voice, which will create the best consonance of all those that can be—

### PROPOSITION XL.

->*To demonstrate the radical terms <note>The simplest whole-number ratios, such as 2:1 or 3:2, that define the mathematical relationship between two musical pitches.</note> of the first hundred Consonances and the first fifty Dissonances, along with their use.*<-

This proposition is not necessary for composing, because voices and Instruments never exceed eight <term>Octaves</term> <note>The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</note>; but it is necessary for understanding what I shall say about the <term>Monochord</term> <note>A scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used since antiquity to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note>, because the remaining segments of the string upon which all Consonances and Dissonances are marked can extend up to 14 or 15 Octaves, and to Dissonances of 7 or 8 Octaves; this is why the radical numbers of the hundred Consonances and fifty Dissonances will serve to recognize what each remainder of the string produces against the total string. For example, the last numbers, or the last ratio of the 4th column of the table reported in the 9th proposition of the first book of Instruments—namely from 24 to 1—is across from the Thirty-third [interval] of the table of Consonances which follows, and shows that [the number] 3456 makes this Consonance with the remainder 144. But this remainder being to the total string of 3600 as 25 is to 1, it creates the interval of 25 to 1, which is not marked in the table of Dissonances, since this Dissonance is not in common use; for it is larger by a <term>minor semitone</term> <note>A small musical interval, specifically the ratio 25:24 in the tuning system Mersenne is using.</note> than the fifth over 4 Octaves—that is to say, it is smaller by one <term>diesis</term> <note>A very small musical interval, often representing the difference between a major and minor semitone.</note> than the minor Sixth; this is why I have named it, in the aforementioned table, the "False Thirty-fourth."

Now it is easy to find all these intervals, even though they are not in the table of Dissonances nor in that of Consonances, since they always surpass some consonant or dissonant interval by some ratio, which is easy to find and express, as seen in the preceding example, in which 25 to 1 is larger by one minor semitone than this Thirty-third, which is 24 to 1: so that as soon as one knows the Consonance whose ratio is 24 to 1, one only needs to find the ratio of 24 to 25, since the ratio of 25 to 1 is composed of the ratio of 24 to 1 and that of 24 to 25.

I wish to give another example, so that one understands the use of all the Consonances and Dissonances found on the Monochord in whatever way it may be considered. The sixth column of the general table of the Monochord in the 9th proposition of the 1st book of Instruments shows, across from the number 3200 in the third column and the number 400 in the fifth, that there is the same ratio from 3200 to 400 as from 8 to 1: now these numbers are found in the table of Dissonances, which shows the major Twenty-third—that is, the major second over three Octaves.

# On Consonances.

...without the aid of calculation, whether two proposed numbers form some Consonance or Dissonance used in Music, and for several other things that are very frequently encountered.

But it must be noted that the Roman numerals in capital letters in these two tables signify the number of Octaves to which the Consonances or Dissonances that depend on them belong. For example, this first number **I**, which is in both, signifies that the Consonances and Dissonances following until number **II** belong to the first Octave, and consequently that each Octave contains as many Consonances and Dissonances used in practice as each Roman numeral includes new lines.

Now, each Octave contains 7 Consonances and as many Dissonances; and although the table of Dissonances only contains seven Octaves, and that of Consonances only has fourteen, one can continue both to infinity by always doubling one of the numbers to find the terms of each Consonance and Dissonance of the following Octave.

For example, if one wants to continue the 8th Octave of Dissonances, one must double the largest term of the major Forty-fourth, namely 72, to have 144, and always leave the smaller term: for its ratio of 144 to 1 gives the major Fifty-first, that is to say, the major Third over 8 Octaves. <note>In the mathematical music theory of the 17th century, intervals were calculated by ratios; doubling the larger number in a ratio adds an octave to the interval.</note>

The same method must be used to continue the table of Consonances; for example, if one wants to find the major Hundred-and-first, that is to say, the major Third over 15 Octaves, one must leave the smaller term, namely unity <note>The number 1, representing the fundamental pitch.</note>, and double 10240, which is the largest term, to have the ratio of 20480 to 1, which signifies the major Hundred-and-first.

I did not want to include several other Dissonances in the table of Dissonances that can be found in the Diatonic <term>genre</term> <note>The standard arrangement of whole and half steps in Western music.</note> and in the other genres, because they are not as common as the ordinary ones found there, and because it is easy to add them; for if one knows the radical terms <note>The simplest whole-number ratio for an interval.</note> of the simple Dissonances, one will have all their <term>replications</term> <note>Also called "compounds," these are intervals expanded by one or more octaves.</note> by doubling one of the terms.

For example, if one adds the replications of the minimal Second, that is to say, the minor semitone, which is 25 to 24, one will have 12 to 25 for the first replication, that is to say, for the minimal Ninth; one will have 6 to 25 for the second replication, 3 to 25 for the third; and if one goes further, it will be necessary to double the larger term, since the smaller has no half without a fraction; one must therefore take the ratio of 3 to 50 for the fourth repetition, and 3 to 100 for the fifth, and so on for others to infinity.

As for Consonances, there can be no others in the 14 Octaves than those that are there, for each Octave can only have 7, and things that are good and excellent are accustomed to being in a small, determined number: but bad things go to infinity, as one experiences with Dissonances. <note>The author is applying a common Pythagorean or Scholastic philosophical idea: perfection is limited and orderly, while imperfection/evil is infinite and chaotic.</note> Now, since it is easy to add the simple degrees or dissonances to each Octave of the table of dissonances, and it is not necessary for me to expand further on this subject, the two tables must be placed here, the first of which contains the Consonances, and the second the Dissonances.

### VIII

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 50 | Fifty-first minor, | 5 to 2048 |

---

Now, it is impossible to find sounds low or high enough to descend or to ascend as far as the fifteenth Octave; for the string would need to be more than a league <note>An old unit of distance, usually about 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers.</note> in length to descend to that Octave, unless one compensated for this length with an excessive thickness. For example, if one wanted to create the fifteenth Octave in the low register against the treble string <note>Original: "chanterelle," the highest-tuned string on an instrument like a lute or violin.</note> of one foot in length, using a string of equal length, it would be necessary for that string to be 268,435,456 times thicker than the treble string. This is because the ratio <term>ratio: the mathematical relationship between two values, often expressed here as "raison."</term> of the thickness of strings of equal length must be the square of the ratio of the intervals to which they are made to descend, or the square root of those to which they are made to rise. Now, the ratio of 268,435,456 to one is the square of the ratio of 16,384 to 1, which represents the length of two strings of equal thickness that would produce the fifteenth Octave—that is to say, the Ninety-ninth <note>The author is calculating the total number of individual steps/notes across fifteen octaves.</note>—if they were able to sound.

But since the practice of Music has no sounds so low and so high that they can produce this Ninety-ninth, it is sufficient to consider them through the ratio which infinitely surpasses practice. For there is no string that can produce these sounds, because if it is thick enough or long enough to make the low sound, it will break before it can make any sound at all. And if one uses Organ pipes, one cannot reach as far as the ninth Octave unless they are at least 64 feet long; however, experience teaches us that they can no longer "speak" <note>The technical term for a pipe successfully producing a clear musical tone.</note> when they are 32 feet long. The same thing is encountered with strings, which break rather than sound when they reach that length.

As for the fifteenth Octave in the high register, one must conclude the same thing; for even if the treble string were only one line <note>Original: "ligne," a traditional unit of length equal to 1/12 of an inch.</note> long (that is to say, 1/12 of an inch) and were stretched to the point of breaking, it could not produce that Octave in the high register against a string of 32 feet long, even if it were as thick as a cable. But since nature is more powerful than art, and since we can understand through reason that these Octaves are possible, it is reasonable that the Musician should know all proportions, however great they may be.

For even though those who only know the Practice have their minds limited by the power of art, and believe that the rest is useless and imaginary, it is nevertheless very certain that theory is more excellent and more noble than practice, and that the "beings of reason" <note>Mental constructs or mathematical truths.</note> surpass material beings, as we have proved elsewhere.

<summary>This page concludes the mathematical list of dissonant intervals and discusses the physical limitations of musical instruments. The author argues that while extremely high or low octaves cannot be physically produced by strings or pipes, they are nonetheless mathematically valid and noble subjects for theoretical study.</summary>

<header>On Consonances.</header>

But I leave this proposition after having made some remarks on Consonances & on Dissonances in the Corollaries which follow.

## COROLLARY I.

The larger numbers of the <term>ratio</term> <note>Original: "raison." In this context, it refers to the mathematical relationship between two frequencies or string lengths.</note> of each Consonance that are seen in the table of the hundred Consonances can signify two things: namely, the length of the longest string, or the number of <term>vibrations</term> <note>Original: "battemens & retours," literally "beats and returns," referring to the physical back-and-forth movement of a vibrating string.</note> of the shortest. When they represent the longest string, the number of its vibrations, or the low pitch <note>Original: "grauité," referring to the "gravity" or depth of the sound.</note> of the sound it makes, is signified by the smaller number; and the high pitch <note>Original: "aigu."</note> of the sound of the shortest string, or the number of its vibrations, is represented by the larger number. This is because the ratio of the number of vibrations is inverse to the ratio of the lengths, as I have demonstrated elsewhere.

## COROLLARY II.

When someone asks how many Consonances there are in Music, one can answer in several ways, all of which are true. First, that there are an infinite number of them, since one can continue their ratios to infinity, both ascending and descending.

Secondly, that there are 56, since the range of Instruments encompasses eight Octaves, each of which has seven Consonances; or that there are 57 if one includes the Unison.

Thirdly, that there are only eight, namely the Unison, the two Thirds, the Fourth, the Fifth, the two Sixths, & the Octave, of which the others are but repetitions; these eight Consonances are called "simple." But because the two Thirds, the Fourth, the Fifth, & the two Sixths are diminished or augmented on the Organ, and on other Instruments, one can say, in the fourth place, that there are 14 simple Consonances: namely, the 8 preceding ones which are in their just proportion, and the 6 latter ones which are outside their proportion on Instruments. This is because these 6 Consonances suffer different diminutions and augmentations according to the different <term>temperaments</term> <note>Temperament refers to the systems of tuning where intervals are slightly adjusted (tempered) so that instruments with fixed pitches, like the organ, can play in multiple keys without sounding out of tune.</note> of all sorts of Instruments; this is why one can multiply these 6 Consonances as many times as they undergo different diminutions and augmentations.

In the sixth place <note>The author skips "Fifthly" in the original text, moving directly from the fourth point to the sixth.</note>, that there are only 3 Consonances: namely, the Octave, the Fifth, & the Fourth. This is because the Greeks recognized no more than these, as they had no Thirds nor Sixths, for the reason that they used only the <term>major tone</term> <note>A ratio of 9:8. In the Pythagorean tuning system used by the ancient Greeks, two major tones create a "superfluous" or major third (81:64) that was considered too harsh to be a consonance.</note>, and two major tones make an augmented Third.

In the seventh place, that there are only two Consonances, since the Octave is only the repetition of the Unison, and only the Third and the Fifth bring diversity to Music; for the Sixth is the repetition of the Third, and many hold that the Fourth is a Dissonance.

In the eighth place, that there is only one single perfect Consonance, namely the Unison, and that other intervals, by admitting a contrariety between their sounds, cannot be named Consonances except insofar as they move away from diversity and conflict to approach the Unison, as I have shown very amply in the discourse on the Unison. Finally, one can say that there is only the...

fifth, which is a perfect <term>consonance</term> <note>A combination of notes that sounds stable and pleasant to the ear.</note>, because it alone possesses both the diversity and the union in its movements necessary to be pleasing.

### COROLLARY III.

Consonances that always have unity <note>The number 1.</note> as their smaller term are the sweetest and most excellent. The first of these is the **Unison**, which has only unity for both its terms <note>The ratio 1:1.</note>; this is why it is the sweetest and most excellent of all consonances.

The second is the **Octave**, whose smaller term always remains unity, while the larger term follows a geometric progression in a double ratio <note>Ratios like 1:2, 1:4, 1:8, etc.</note>: such that one only needs to double the larger term of the preceding Octave to find the one that follows. This must also be done to obtain all other Consonances or Dissonances repeated as many times as one wishes: and consequently, anyone can correct the two preceding tables if there is an error.

The third is the **Twelfth** <note>An octave plus a fifth, ratio 1:3.</note>, for the Fifth does not have unity as its smaller term, but rather the number two <note>The "binary" term; the Fifth's ratio is 2:3.</note>: from this, it follows that the Twelfth is sweeter and more excellent than the Fifth, as I have proven in the discourses on the Fifth.

And the fourth is the **Seventeenth**, that is to say the Major Third over two octaves <note>Ratio 1:5.</note>; for the Major Third <note>Ratio 4:5.</note> and the Major Tenth <note>An octave plus a major third, ratio 2:5.</note> do not have unity for their smaller terms, because the former has 4, and the latter has 2. From this, it appears that the Tenth is sweeter than the Major Third, and the Seventeenth is sweeter and more excellent than the Tenth, as I have shown in the discourses on the Third and its repetitions. This is because its multiple ratio is easier to understand, and its terms unite more frequently than those of the <term>superparticular</term> <note>A ratio where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 or 5:4.</note> ratios of the Third and the Major Tenth.

### NOTICE.

Although I have only spoken of the proportions of Consonances expressed by whole and rational numbers, I in no way prevent the use of others that arise from the division of the double ratio <note>The octave.</note> into 12 other equal ratios by means of 11 proportional means <note>This refers to "Equal Temperament," the system used to tune modern pianos, which uses irrational numbers based on the twelfth root of two.</note>. I explain the invention of this in the first and second books on *Stringed Instruments*, and I speak of it in the eleventh proposition of the book on *Dissonances*; for I know that the ear is not capable of perceiving the difference between the Consonances that come from this division and those of which I have spoken. I say the same thing of the double ratio of the Octave, which one could set at 2000 to 999 as well as to 1000 <note>A ratio of 2:1 is 1000:2000; the author suggests the ear cannot distinguish 999:2000 from a perfect octave.</note>, if one follows only the judgment of the ear. But I have preferred to follow the precision and the ease of the ordinary numbers and ratios received by all the ancients, and to prefer the <term>intellect</term> over <term>sensation</term>, which is capable neither of choice nor of judgment. And perhaps those who see the ease of explaining the causes of everything that happens in chords and harmony—by giving them the proportions I have chosen—will take my side, even though the ear is not capable of perceiving their exact precision.

# BOOK TWO
## ON DISSONANCES.

### FIRST PROPOSITION.

->*Determine whether there are Dissonances, and if they are necessary in Music.*<-

<image-desc>A decorative drop-cap "I" containing a small landscape illustration within its rectangular frame.</image-desc>It is, in a certain sense, more certain that there are <term>Dissonances</term> <note>Musical intervals that sound unstable, harsh, or "unfinished" to the ear, traditionally requiring a resolution to a stable sound.</note> than it is that there are <term>Consonances</term> <note>Intervals that sound stable and pleasant.</note>; for it is more certain that one encounters men who are displeased by Concerts—even those full of good chords—than it is certain that there are men who are not displeased by any Dissonances. This may be because Dissonances have more degrees of unpleasantness than Consonances have degrees of sweetness (which we shall discuss in the 10th proposition of this book), or because evil, pain, and displeasure are more keenly felt than their opposites. This is because we imagine that good is our due and that pleasure is natural to us since it preserves our nature, whereas displeasure corrupts and destroys it.

Now, if there should be ears so fortunate, or so easy to please, that Dissonances delight them—as happens with Seconds, <term>Tritones</term> <note>An interval composed of three whole tones; in this era, it was considered highly unstable and difficult to use.</note>, <term>diminished fifths</term> <note>original: "fausses quintes"</note>, and Sevenths, which gladden the spirit rather than wound the ear when they are well-placed and employed with judgment in <term>Counterpoint</term> <note>The art of combining different melodic lines to sound together.</note> of two or more parts, as we shall show in the book on Composition—one might say that they are not Dissonances to such ears. The spirits of such listeners may be so heavy, coarse, and dull that they require the sharpness and harshness of discords to be stirred. We see a similar thing in the tongues of those who have lost their appetite; they cannot truly taste flavors unless they are somewhat salty, acrid, sour, or pungent. Indeed, all the senses share something similar, so that what applies to one can serve to explain what belongs to the others.

As for the second part of this proposition, it is certain that, strictly speaking, Music can exist without discords, since we have very fine pieces for 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 parts in which there is no Dissonance at all, and one avoids them as much as possible in simple Counterpoint. But if one wishes to preserve all the beauties, ornaments, and enrichments of <term>Figured Counterpoint</term> <note>A more complex style of composition involving varied rhythms and decorative notes, as opposed to "note-against-note" simple counterpoint.</note> as it is used today, discords are necessary. Furthermore, one cannot create good melodies without dissonant degrees and intervals, as we shall see in the other books. Thus, it is necessary to treat Dissonances so as not to omit any essential part of Music. For this reason, I shall begin with the smallest intervals and proceed to the largest, though the starting point is of little consequence.

<summary>In this opening to Book Two, the author argues that dissonances are a fundamental part of the musical experience, comparing the need for musical 'discord' to the need for sharp flavors in food to stimulate a dull palate. He concludes that while music can technically exist without them, they are essential for the beauty and complexity of modern composition.</summary>

<header>Book Second</header>

## PROPOSITION II.

->*Explain all the Semitones, and the <term>Diesis</term> <note>A very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone, often resulting from the difference between two other intervals.</note> that are used in Music considered in its greatest perfection.*<-

The Octave was called the <term>Diapason</term> <note>original: "Diapason"; from the Greek *dia pason*, meaning "through all [the strings]".</note> by the Greeks, because it contains all sounds and all the simple Consonances; but it can still be named Diapason because it comprises all the Dissonances. For if one divides it into two Dissonances, one will find the <term>Semidiapente</term> <note>A diminished fifth.</note>, or the false fifth, on one side, and the *Tritone* on the other, since the ratio of 45 to 64 and that of 32 to 45, when added, make the Octave. One can also divide it into a Major Seventh of 5 to 9 <note>Though 5:9 is mathematically a minor seventh in most systems, the author categorizes it here as part of the Octave's division.</note> and a minor tone; or into a Major Seventh and a major semitone. However, I have spoken more amply of the names and divisions of the Octave in the 9th proposition of the preceding book and in others; therefore, it suffices now to remark upon what is necessary for the understanding of Music and of this proposition. Namely, that the **Major Tone** comes from the difference between the Fifth and the Fourth; for the Fifth surpasses the Fourth by a major tone, since the Fourth has only one major tone and one minor tone with the major semitone, and the Fifth has two major tones, one minor, and one major semitone. The Greeks used this major tone to separate their <term>Tetrachords</term> <note>A scale of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth.</note>; and the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who defined musical intervals through strict mathematical ratios based on the number 3.</note> used only this species of tone. The second Dissonance is called the **Major Semitone**, and is the difference between the Major Third and the Fourth.

Now, this semitone is so necessary to Music that it is its soul, its ornament, and its beauty; for it is by its means that one establishes the diverse species of fourth, fifth, and Octave, and the twelve Modes of Music, or the eight tones of the Church, as we shall say elsewhere; its ratio is 16 to 15.

As for the **Minor Tone**, it is composed of two semitones, namely the major and the minor, and helps to compose the Major Third, which contains the major tone and the minor tone.

Now, there are only these two tones and the major semitone which belong to the <term>Diatonic genus</term> <note>The standard arrangement of notes in a scale consisting of tones and semitones.</note>; and because the Fourth is composed of them, it suffices for understanding all Diatonic Music, since it contains nothing other than these two tones and the major semitone, although there are other semitones that serve the Diatonic genus which are used now. The first is the semitone of 25 to 27, which can be called the **Maximal** <note>original: "Maxime"</note>, for it is larger than the major by a major <term>comma</term> <note>A very small interval resulting from the difference between two larger intervals, such as a major and minor tone.</note>.

The second is smaller than the major and larger than the minor, which it surpasses by a major comma, and is from 128 to 135; one can call it the **Mean** <note>original: "Moyen"</note>. Now, the Major Tone is composed of the maximal semitone and the minor, or of the major semitone and the mean, which is smaller than the major semitone by a minor comma.

The third is a little smaller than the mean and comes from the difference of two major tones and the Fourth; its ratio is 243 to 256. The Greeks called it the minor semitone, or the **Pythagorean Limma** <note>original: "Limma de Pytagore"; the small semitone left over when two major tones are subtracted from a perfect fourth.</note>, which was used to complete the fourth after the two major tones; now, it is smaller than the major semitone by a comma.

<header>Of Dissonances.</header>

The fourth is the *Minor Semitone*, which is smaller than the preceding one by a <term>minor comma</term> <note>A tiny musical interval representing a slight difference in pitch, often found when comparing different tuning systems.</note>: its ratio is 25 to 24.

The fifth is composed of the <term>diesis</term> <note>A very small interval, often less than a semitone.</note> and the major comma, whose ratio is 625 to 648; it is the difference between the Maximal Semitone and the Minor one. One can call it the *Minimal Semitone*.

The sixth is called the *Enharmonic Diesis*, insofar as it serves that specific <term>genus</term> <note>original: "genre"; referring to the three types of Greek scales: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note>, for it is the difference between the Major and Minor Semitones: its ratio is 125 to 128. One may also add the *Sub-minimal Semitone*, which I shall explain hereafter.

Now, once all these semitones are presupposed, one can say that the minor tone is not only composed of the major and minor semitones, but also of the <term>Pythagorean limma</term> <note>The smaller semitone in the ancient Pythagorean tuning system, which relies on pure fifths.</note> and the mean semitone; and that the major tone is composed of the Enharmonic Diesis, the minor semitone, and the mean semitone—or of two minor semitones, the Diesis, and the Comma. I have wished to add this so that one might perfectly understand the interval of the Major Tone and the Minor Tone, which all musical genera require.

However, one can establish such an order among these semitones that it will be easy to understand them, for the largest ones most often surpass those that follow them immediately by a Comma (the same amount by which a Major Tone surpasses a Minor Tone). One can name the largest semitone the *Maximal*; the second the *Major*, which is ordinarily from *fa* to *mi*; the third the *Mean*; the fourth the *Pythagorean*; the fifth the *Minor*; the sixth the *Minimal*; and the seventh the *Enharmonic Diesis*, as seen in the following table. In this table, one can add other semitones—for example, the major semitone of Pythagoras, which is called the <term>Apotome</term> <note>The larger semitone in Pythagorean tuning; when added to the Limma, it forms a full Major Tone.</note>, whose ratio is 2048 to 2187, and which completes the major tone when added to the Limma. This *Apotome* is larger than the major semitone by a minor comma. Furthermore, the mean semitone is larger than the limma by the difference between the major and minor comma—that is to say, by the ratio of 10935 to 10936, which appears in the table after the two commas, of which it is the difference. Thus, this table contains twelve degrees, the consideration of which is not useless. But I shall explain several other degrees in the following proposition, which will serve as an explanation for this one.

There is yet another semitone that comes from the difference between the maximal semitone and the minor tone, which is smaller than the minor semitone by a major comma; its ratio is 250 to 243, and it can be called the *sub-minimal semitone*. I leave aside the others that can be found by taking the difference of various intervals or musical degrees, for fear of being too long and too tedious on this matter; for it suffices to know how to subtract, add, and divide ratios to find all possible differences and degrees in Music.

I know that those who prefer the equality of semitones and dieses, and who follow the party of the <term>Aristoxenians</term> <note>Followers of Aristoxenus, who argued that music should be judged by the ear and divided into equal parts rather than being dictated by complex mathematical ratios.</note>, despise or neglect all these small differences and the multitude of these intervals. But their sentiment does not oblige me to abandon them, since my design consists in showing the exactness of intervals and preserving the systems of the <term>Harmonic Canon</term> <note>original: "canon Harmonique"; the traditional mathematical laws of harmony.</note>, though it is permitted for anyone to follow Aristoxenus or any other system they wish. Now, the following table shows what I have explained in this discourse.

As for the use of these semitones, it is easy to explain; for the Maximal [semitone] serves firstly to pass from the <term>minor seventh</term> <note>An interval spanning ten semitones; here defined by the ratio 5 to 9.</note> (which is from 5 to 9) to the major sixth. Secondly, from the <term>tritone</term> <note>An interval of three whole tones, often considered "the devil in music" for its extreme dissonance; here with the ratio 18 to 25.</note> (which is composed of two minor tones and one major tone, and which has its ratio from 18 to 25) to the fifth. Thirdly, from the major third

<column-break/>

(which is composed of two minor tones and is from 81 to 100) to the fourth. Fourthly, from the minor semitone to the major tone. And generally, as many times as one uses the interval composed of the major semitone and the <term>comma</term> <note>A very small musical interval representing a slight difference in pitch.</note> to pass from one place to another, such as when one completes the fourth after two minor tones. There is no need to speak of the use of the major semitone, for it is well enough known to all musicians.

The third semitone, which is called *Mean*, serves firstly to pass from the fourth to the tritone. Secondly, as many times as it is necessary to complete the major tone after one has made the major semitone; for the minor semitone is the smallest semitone of the minor tone, just as the mean semitone is the smallest of the major tone, which is composed of the major and the mean semitone. The <term>Pythagorean semitone</term> <note>Also known as the limma; a semitone derived from ancient Greek tuning based on pure fifths.</note> serves to complete the fourth after the two major tones which sometimes follow one another when singing in several parts, as Jean Benoist demonstrated in his *Epistles*, page 278. The minor semitone serves to pass from the minor third and sixth to the major. I leave aside the other uses of this semitone that I have related elsewhere. The Enharmonic Diesis serves to pass from the minor semitone to the major, which exceeds the <term>Chromatic Diesis</term> <note>In this context, the author uses this to refer to the minor semitone.</note> by the Enharmonic Diesis; for the ratio of 15 to 16 is larger than that of 125 to 128, by the ratio of 24 to 25. We shall explain the other uses of these semitones when speaking of Practice and the manner of composing. But it must also be noted that two or several small harmonic intervals being doubled or tripled are no longer harmonic—that is to say, they can no longer serve for <term>modulation</term> <note>original: "modulation"; here referring to the movement of a melody or the construction of a musical line, rather than the modern sense of changing keys.</note>—just as two <term>consonances</term> <note>Intervals that sound pleasant and stable to the ear.</note> being joined together are no longer consonances. For two fifths make a ninth, two fourths a seventh, two major thirds exceed the fifth by a minor semitone, and two minor thirds exceed the fourth by a major semitone and a comma—that is to say, by a maximal semitone. Similarly, two major tones exceed the major third by a comma, and two minor tones exceed the minor third by the sub-minimal semitone, which remains from the minor semitone when the comma has been removed, or from the minor tone when the maximal semitone has been subtracted. But the Pythagorean limma surpasses the minor semitone by the same ratio that the Enharmonic diesis surpasses our comma, namely by the ratio of 2048 to 2025, which is also the difference between the major and mean semitones; so that the Pythagorean limma surpasses the minor semitone by as much as the major semitone surpasses the mean, and as the Enharmonic diesis surpasses the comma.

One may also notice that six major tones surpass the Octave by one Pythagorean comma, which is from 524288 to 531441; and that six minor tones are less than the Octave by the ratio of 500000 to 531441, that is to say, by a diesis and three commas, which are less than our minor semitone by the ratio of 531441 to 533333 1/3. As for the six tones of the Organ, *Salinas*<note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a blind Spanish music theorist and organist.</note> believes they are less than the Octave by a diesis, although the six tones of the Viol make exactly the Octave; from which it follows that there is a difference between the temperaments of Instruments, as he notes in the 14th chapter of his 3rd book: he adds in chapter 15 that three major Thirds are larger than the Octave by a diesis.

It is also necessary to explain the division that some make of the tone into 5 parts, so that we may consider all the small intervals that can serve Music. *Salinas* says in the 27th chapter of the third book that in his time they used the *Archicymbale*<note>The Archicembalo, a keyboard instrument designed by Nicola Vicentino in the 16th century with many extra keys to play in different ancient Greek scales.</note>, which had its tones divided into 5 parts called dieses, of which the major semitone had three, the minor two, the minor Third 8, the major 10, the Fourth 13, the Fifth 18, and the Octave 31; but he rejects this division as an enemy of Harmony and unbearable to the ear.

*Fabius Colomna*<note>Fabio Colonna (c. 1567–1640), an Italian polymath who invented the *Sambuca Lincea*, a 31-tone-per-octave keyboard instrument.</note> has followed this division; for he says in the book he wrote on the *Sambuque* that the ratio by which the major semitone surpasses the minor is that of the Enharmonic diesis, which makes the fifth part of the tone, and which occurs between 41 1/2 and 42 1/2, or nearly between 75 and 77, inasmuch as 5 is almost 76 times in 384, and precisely 75 times in 375; for the ratio of 384 to 375 is the difference between these two semitones, which, being reduced to its lowest terms, is 125 to 128. But this division cannot be accurate, since two dieses are larger than the minor semitone, as I have demonstrated; and consequently three dieses surpass the major semitone, since we have shown that the major surpasses the minor by only one diesis. From this it is easy to conclude that this division is not well made, and that one should seek no other than that which divides the minor tone into two minor semitones and one diesis, and that which divides the major tone into a major and minor semitone and one comma; for one finds the **Perfect System** through these divisions, which come from the difference of the natural degrees of Music.
